headline: SMART POLICE WORK. / ALIEN EVILDOERS SHIPPED AWAY.
text:
PARASITES DEPORTED:

Possible Trouble

By dint of hard work, the Police have cleared the Colony of an influx of undesirables—recruits for the late Dr. Sun's miscreentary armies, "fed up" with Army life, and deserters from-Canton.

Emphatic denials have failed to keep secret the fact that drafts for Dr. Sun Yat-sen's army have been collected at treaty ports and shipped to Canton via Hongkong.

As many know, the strongest force in Canton at present is the Yunnanese army under General Yang Hsi-man, himself a native of Yunnan. He is said to be co-operating with Tang Chi-yan, Tuehun of that far-off province which is becoming notorious as having produced several adventuring armies to overrun other provinces.

During the last year or two, Yunnanese have been travelling through Hongkong to join the colours. Most of them, as country yokels with little or no military training, are sent overland to the Yangtsze River, down to Shanghai, where they embark for Hongkong and Canton direct. Others have found their way by road and rail to Haiphong and then to Hongkong.

Recently, recruiting had become a trade. Instead of recruiting sergeants, there were canvassers acting with boarding houses in the ports of shipment. Passages were arranged for the men brought together.

Whether in Canton or in the outlying districts, there could always be found a number either dissatisfied with military life or who had committed a crime. To escape they must get out of Canton. To reach home they must travel through Hongkong. It was only natural that the majority of deserters should take boat down here. For preference they choose a vessel on which there might be Northerners who speak their language.

It is the practice of the steamers in question to tie up at West Point. In course of time, a fair-sized non-Cantonese colony grew up in the Western district. Many were bona fide workmen, seafarers, itinerant traders, hawkers, &c. But in the last few months, there came not a few who, without fixed abode or occupation, were nothing more than human parasites. When any of their fellow provincial came ashore with money, they attempted to sponge on them, and very often a fight resulted. Others took to bullying the law-abiding Northern and Yunnan men in the district, and street rows were very common. A few became adepts at cargo pilfering on the water front, while instances of molestation were reported.

Before the nuisance could assume alarming proportions, however, the West Point Police got to work and gradually rounded up every one of the crowd who did not have work or a fixed abode. In almost every case, the men were found to have had some

headline: Canton Parade.
text:
A procession three miles long, writes our Canton correspondent, was the main feature of the May Day celebrations at Canton yesterday. Cries of "Down with foreign religion!" "Down with capitalism!" and "Hurrah for the progressive Soviet!" were heard along the procession. Pamphlets were also distributed.

Some of the Kuomintang troops are also said to have been in the parade but they were unarmed, for fear of being disarmed by the Yunnanese who have provoked a crisis by usurping the power of the Canton civil government. Commander di Pinedo, who left Sesto Celende on April 22 and arrived this week at Bushire, does not anticipate calling at Hongkong until he has circled Australia and jumped from there to the Philippines, Japan and North China. By the time that he gets to Hongkong from Shanghai he will be in a position to look back on by far the most difficult sector accomplished. Commander di Pinedo has been credited with the resolve to break the time record set up by the

Mr. A. H. Crook, of Queen's College, and Mrs. Crook, said for Fiome by the Macedonia this morning. A large number of friends assembled at Blake-Pier to wish them bon voyage. When Mr. Crook returns in November he will succeed Mr. B. Tanner as Headmaster of Queen's College, Mr. Tanner relinquishing the post to retire. Intrepid airmen who have used Hongkong's a temporary haven in the course of their world flight had still before them the greater part of their journey but this will not be so in the case of the Italian aviator when he arrives here.

headline: PRINCE GEORGE.
text:
EMBARKS ON MALWA FOR EAST.

headline: PIRATES SHOT. / KONGMOON RAID
text:
TROUBLOUS TIMES.

PAKKAI, KONGMOON, May 3. Three pirates who took part in the attack on this port on China New Year eve have been captured. They were sent down by train from Kongmoon and shot outside the Pakkai railway station.

This community is once more under ample protection. The Merchants' guards are once more on duty; their support is contributed to by passengers on Hongkong-bound steamers and subscriptions from local residents. Li Yat-ngok, formerly Hokshan magistrate and now a brigadier under General Leung Hung-kai, commands the new garrison here. Although it is premature to consider details of His Excellency's actual departure it is an interesting fact and worthy of note that the final 'touches are being put to Statue Pier,' and upon enquiry, the "China Mail" was informed that it was anticipated that the pier would be ready for use on the occasion of His Excellency's departure. The actual pier is completed and the only work remaining is the polishing up of the stone archway under which cars will be enabled to drive.

In revenge for the shooting of three bandits convicted of attacks on the railway, other outlaws have made several attempts to capture that part of the Sunning Railway at Sanwuf station but were driven off. Every night the railway guards are on the qui vive.

Noting the progress as Shekki following the demolition of the city walls, the magistrate at Sanwul wishes to copy the example set him and pull down the walls at Sanwul city. The merchants and residents have protested on the grounds of the danger of bandit attack, and the prevalence of pirates.

A strike and stoppage has started at Chekhom in protest against the “nationalisation” of private property by Government notification. An appeal has been made to the Civil Governor.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES. / GOVERNMENT SCHOOL SPORTS.
text:
The chief event of the week's end was the third annual sports meeting of the Cheung Chau Government School, which passed off very successfully. The weather was all that could be desired not unpleasantly hot and the rain did not fall till late in the evening. There was a large attendance of visitors, most of the foreign residents were present and some of the visitors as well, members of the local Kai Fong and many of the parents and friends of the schoolboys came to shew their interest in the proceedings.

The entrance to the Ball Ground of the C. C. Residents Association was graced with a floral archway surmounted by the School flag. The Volley ball posts were converted into flag poles for the Union Jack and the Chinese flag with wreaths of flowers and streamers of smaller flags Seats and refreshments were thoughtfully provided for the visitors and on a table were displayed the prizes for which the students were to compete. The starting of the 22 events were in the able hands of Inspector Lane and Mr. Lam Pak-to.

The Judges were Messrs. L M. White, Lo Ip, Lau Wai tai, Lai Nan-sang, Tsang Pak-hong, Lo Mo-to, Lau King chi; these gentlemen had a busy time owing to the very close finishes of many of the events.

All the events (with the possible exception of the lantern race which on account of the breeze, difficulty was experienced in lighting the candles, and some finished with their lanterns in flames) were keenly contested, especially the Hill race, Team race, and the Tug of war. After the last event, the visitors and boys gathered round the

prize laden table, where were displayed silver cups, penholders, choosticks, also in kittens, found in pens, fans and other articles of a useful nature. Mr. E. Ralphs then called upon Mrs. Arnold Jones to distribute the prizes to the various winners, whose names were read out by the Headmaster. The School champion, Fung Wa-hin will have his name inscribed for the second time on the cup, having gained that distinction two years ago. Mr. C. G. Alabaster on behalf of Mrs. Arnold Jones (who was presented with a large bouquet of flowers by the school champion) thanked the students for the privilege of having been asked to carry out the pleasant task. Mr. Alabaster also noted the improvement in the arrangements for carrying out the various events and in the keenness among the students, and hoped the future gatherings would be even more successful. Mr. Ralphs after thanking various gentlemen who had worked hard to make the sports a success, called for three cheers for Mrs. Arnold Jones, Inspector Lane, Mr. Whyte, and the judges, cheers were also given for the members of the Kaifong, to those who had contributed to the prizes, fund the visitors. Mr. Alabaster, and the Headmaster. The proceedings having concluded the gathering dispersed.

The Kung-Yik is supposed to report for duty in about five days' time. Mr. and Mrs. Anderson who have been living in Dr. Heanley's house have returned to Hongkong.

headline: ANOTHER "TIGER.
text:
Angry Growls And Never a Tree To Climb.

Following the stories of the presence in the New Territories of a wholly mythical monster, come reports of a tiger which a party comprising Europeans set out this week to shoot.

The story is being gleefully told in club circles of the all-night vigil of the party. The action of one bold spirit who squatted on a heap of stones armed with a rifle and with two kids as bait has come in for a great deal of amused praise, for there was no tree convenient to clamber up into safety and the tiger is said to have prowled about growling to himself all through the night.

The party were acting on information supplied by the villagers who have from time to time reported animals mailed and tracks found pointing pretty conclusively to the presence of a tiger in the neighbourhood. Although the mid-night sportsmen have nothing to show for the trouble taken in organising the expedition and running the risk, they are firmly convinced that there is a tiger in the neighbourhood to be had for the shooting.

There is nothing improbable in their story of its presence there, for those residents who were in the Colony a few years ago will remember the body of the tiger shot by Mr. D. Burlingham in the New Territories being carried in the streets. A cast of the impression of another tiger's "pugs" was also exhibited in the window of Messrs. Lane, Crawford, Ltd.

There would appear to be a good deal of haziness in the minds of those who remember seeing the tiger which was actually shot in the New Territories as to what happened to it. Several statements were made most definitely to a "China Mail" representative this morning by people who should have known. "It's in the museum here" was one. "It was skinned and made into a rug and was either given to Sir Henry May, who was Governor at the time, or is in the museum," said another. "The skin was taken off badly and had to be thrown away," was a third version.

"From an official source the 'China Mail' learns that what actually happened was that, the skin was sent Home to be stuffed, the object being to have it placed in the museum here. On its way out in stuffed form on a Japanese boat it was torpedoed, and although all the passengers were saved no-one seems to have remembered or cared enough about the tiger to rescue it from a watery grave."

Again, the presence of a tiger on the higher levels of the Peak was reported by a very well-known resident once when he was lying off the foot of Mt. Kellet in his yacht. About the same time "pugs" of a tiger or cheetah were reported in a garden in that locality and the explanation put forward was that the animal had swum across from the mainland at some particularly narrow spot. An explanation of its presence on the mainland is not difficult to give for there is jungle harbouring many such animals between here and Canton.

Responsible people out in the Territories pooh-pooh the rumours of the ferocious animal which is supposed to have eaten a wood-chopper in a glen near Taipo and to resemble a cow, a kangaroo, a bear and a mammoth porcupine.

However. from unofficial sources it is gathered that a tame bear is missing from a travelling show which left Chekiang province when the Shanghai war

headline: MOSCOW'S VOICE? / HUMILIATION DAY TIRADES.
text:
PARKOT CRIES.

LABOURERH AND SOLDIERS DAMONSTRATE

"Down with capitalists, and foreign people" was shouted by hundreds of men and youths taking part in to-dry's procession, the declared object of which is a protest on the university of May 7, against the 21st demands modernity "Imperialistic" Japan.

Pamplets full of tirades were distributed under the names of:—The second national convention of China's laborers, the Kwangtung Agricultural Labourers; the China Young Men's Army, the Kuomintang Military Officers Academy, the publicity bureau of the Huanense army and the association of Cantons citizens.

Students are declared to have taken part in the National Day of

Huniliation procession but I did not see any. They were mostly labourers and soldiers from different provinces. Protests were about, not so much against the demands, but in support of anti-foreign feeling.

headline: BEHANGHAI PARADE
text:
National Humiliation Day is to be marked in Shanghai by a monster parade. The 7th of May this year is the 10th anniversary of President Yuan Shi-kai's acceptance of the Japan Government's Twenty-One Demands.

The demands were forwarded to the Central Government by the Japanese Minister in Peking May 7, 1915, and were accepted on blo: two days later by the second president of the republic, now dead. STRAINED POSITION

A committee selected from officials of various public, labour and student organizations has been appointed to supervise arrangement for the meeting and parade. Both will be held in Chinese territory, unless other arrangements are made and the permission of the Municipal Council is obtained to stage the affair within Settlement limits.

Present-plans provide for several addresses by prominent citizens and distribution of pamphlets donouncing the action of the Japanese and "treachery" of China's officials in 1915.

headline: DOG BITES GIRL
text:
A black Chinese dog, owned by a Chinese living at No. 135, Ki Lung Street, Shamshulpo, was taken to Kennedy Town yesterday for observation.

The animal bit a six-year old child, who was treated at the Kwong Wah Hospital. There is an under-current of feeling that the present strained situation cannot last much longer. It is becoming increasingly apparent that Dr. Sun's followers, in spite of their announcement of a Commission (including the non-Cantonese generals) of Government to carry on in Dr. Sun's place, are merely being tolerated by the autocratic mercenary chieftains who have seized most of the important sources of revenue and are still, extending their influence as witness their action in usurping the control of the Canton Arsenal.

Peking is said to be aware of, and in secret accord with, the recent trend of developments. Yang Hsi-man is believed to be in league with Tuchun Tang Chi-yao of Yunnan although he has issued a denial.

A report that I heard today from a very well-informed source is that Yang is willing, should matters come to a head, to accept Tang's nominal superiority, and to work with Chan. However, it is doubted if Chan will be welcomed back to Cantons although he may regain a footing in a less important part of the territory. I am also told that the aggressors intend to do nothing but by a policy of quiet aggrandisement, attempt ultimately to override the Kuomintang by taking away revenue producing posts from the civil politicians. Meanwhile, they are said to be still discussing with Peking the apportionment of posts when the intrigue results in re-union with the North.

FOREIGN REPORTS. (By Courtesy of Daily Bulletin). Fekinga, May 7.

Recent foreign despatches from Canton report that the situation continues to be tense, with the possibility of an outbreak at any moment. It was rumoured in Canton yesterday that the seige of Nanning was about to be renewed.

headline: PILGRIMS TO THE TOMS OF I
text: Crowds thronging to the unique tomb, in front of the Kremlin in the heart of Moscow, which holds the body of Vladimir Ilich Lenine, upon the recent first anniversary of the Bolshevik pioneer's death. Even as the thousands continue to flock to Moscow from afar, to gaze on the ghost-like features of the Father of Bolsheviks, his successors continue to modify and moderate the extremist measures which he advocated. The Council of Labour and Defence has just decided to invite private capitalists to go into trade in Soviet Russia, and it is known that about four million bushels of rye have been sold to Russia, while three million more, sold to parties in Germany and other Baltic ports are expected eventually to find their way to Russia.

headline: CHILD LABOUR LAWS. / FOLLOWING HONGKONG'S
text:
TREATY PORT

No children under twelve are now allowed to work in factories under the jurisdiction of Hongkong but the absence of such restrictions in other Treaty ports has led to severe stricture being passed by Dame Adelaide Anderson who has recently returned to England from China.

Recalling some of her visits to silk factories, cotton mills and match factories, both in Chinese Towns and in the Treaty ports she states:—

"In silk flatures one saw them stirring cocoons in nearly scalding water, in steam-laden air, for nearly twelve hours at a stretch and mostly standing. In cotton-spinning mills, they are working night and day, 6, 7 and 8 years old, at meal times hastily taking food from the rice bowl, with the dust settling on hair, skin,"

clothes and rice, affecting their general health; digestion and lungs.....Too often one had to leave a sick child, with the illness undiagnosed, standing at work, where there is as yet no organised aid for relief. I asked a Chinese woman what became of the little ones of 6 and 7 who enter silk flatures. When they go to work so early they mostly die young was her reply.

Dame Anderson then explained the progress that has been made since the Child-Labour Commission was appointed in June, 1923, by the Executive Council for the International Settlement of Shanghai. The leading manufacturers in the Settlement have assented on the most difficult point—the age of entry for child workers. Also, the Governments of several provinces have assured the Commission of their assistance. Governor Han of Jiangsu Province issued an Ordinance preparing steps for the appointment of a Provincial Child Labour Commission. After Dame Anderson's address Mr. H. G. Simms, late Chairman of the Municipal Council of Shanghai, emphasised the fact that the report of the Child Labour Commission of Shanghai is the most important forward movement towards improving industrial labour conditions in China. Even if there appears to be no immediate solution of the evil of employing children of 10 years of age and under an night work, there is hope that through gradually educating Chinese public opinion labour conditions affecting child work will gradually improve.

The proposals for the regulation of child labour in Shanghai are similar to those already adopted by Hongkong which the S.C.A. in a report earlier in the year said were being met in a whole-hearted manner by local employers. No children under twelve may be employed in factories here and under fifteen they are not allowed to work more than nine hours a day. Employers here are also compelled to give children one holiday in seven. It is anticipated that similar steps to those already taken by Hongkong and contemplated by Shanghai will be taken at Chefoo and Tientsin. In a report on conditions in factories generally at these and other places in China. Dr. Sherwood Eddy stated: "Unrest is growing in the midst of this awful poverty. The workers in the south and central regions and along the railways are learning effectively to strike for better working conditions. Many employers are attempting to keep them contended with their lot. But God forbid that they should accept it."

headline: WHITEAWAY'S
text:
NEW; FRESH AND UP-TO-DATE

Again quoting the same authority: "Our attitude regarding payment to dependants in the event of death or injury following piratical attacks is that it is certainly not the obligation of the owners to pay a penny towards any such scheme of insurance. It is the duty of the Navy to protect the ships and their officers from such attacks and if they fail the onus of responsibility surely rests on the Government."

“Regarding wireless, it is obvious—and the Hongkong Government recognises this—that it would be impossible to introduce such stringent measures for the carrying of wireless officers as are in operation in respect of boats, trading between other British ports.” There are ships on the run between here and Calcutta, to give only one instance, which are obliged by regulation to carry three wireless officers, who besides being a considerable, and in our opinion an "unjustifiable, expense, find it difficult to occupy their time on the voyage. It would be hopeless to introduce similar measures here and the Hongkong Government have intimated that they are prepared to meet us to a certain extent.

Asked if the School for wireless instruction, instituted under the supervision of the Government wireless officer, was proving a success the "China Mail's" informant replied that it was early yet to express an opinion as to its future usefulness; but a few students had certainly passed the qualifying test, and it might be that in such a scheme lay the solution of the wireless problem aboard ships.

A representative on the local Firacy Committee who was approached, was of the opinion that the report might have served as the basis of very fruitful discussion if the representatives of the ship owners and officers had not withdrawn before opportunity was given to discuss the problem. In his opinion, the Regulations, although imperfect in some respects, needed only to be observed in the spirit in which they were drafted, rather than, as was often the case, in the letter, for the required security to be

obtained. Another matter which could have been discussed to the benefit of all parties concerned was that of insecurity of tenure of office resultant on the 24 hours' notice provision at present existing. "It is not good for discipline — the necessity for the maintenance of which the report stresses — that a man should have the knowledge constantly with him that if he becomes unpopular and sufficient, complaints are made against him he can be so summarily dismissed. In many cases, the complaints, far from having their origin in neglect of duty, are inspired by the very insistence on it."

headline: HONGKONG'S TIGER.
text:
REPORTED ATTACK ON TWO BUFFALOES.

"Further indications of a tiger's ravages in a remote part of the New Territories—believed to be somewhere near Shataukok, at the north-eastern corner—are forthcoming in the report that two water buffaloes have been attacked. They were so mauled that they had to be destroyed, the report says."

After the reference-some-days ago in the "China Mail" to a party of local sportsmen who went out for "big gamb" bunting, there has been talk of other expeditions being organised to kill the man-eater.

Farmers in the locality where the buffaloes were mauled, will certainly render aid, if paid appropriate cumshaw, in the shooting of the tiger. Spoor was found in the vicinity, it is stated.

headline: THE SEAMY SIDE / HONGKONG CRIMINALS SENTENCED.
text:
ARMS EVIL AGAIN

Robberies and possession of arms cases were all that were down for hearing at to-day's Criminal Sessions which give every appearance of finishing this afternoon.

The most interesting case was that in which four men appeared in the dock charged in connection with a robbery from a woman on Victoria Road. A taxi cab driver was mixed up in this, having driven up while the robbery was proceeding. On being intimidated he drove away. The woman made a fight of it but was overpowered, knocked down, and had a bangle taken from her.

The men were sentenced to seven years' imprisonment each.

A gramophone was playing when six men entered the home of a Chinese family near Kowloon City but the strains did not prevent them carrying out their nefarious work. Knocking on the door they obtained admittance, terro�ised everyone in the house and got away with money and vulnuses. Three men were later arrested in connection with the robbery and they appeared at the Sessions this morning. The case against them is still proceeding.

headline: NEW CAPITAL.
text:
THIS MORNING'S MEETING.

At an extraordinary general meeting of the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Company, Ltd., held this morning, the proposals for increasing the capital of the Company were approved.

The meeting was presided over by Mr. D. G. M. Bernard who was supported by Mr. A. H. White, Mr. T. G. Weall, Mr. R. M. Dyer, Chief Manager, Mr. R. F. Mattingley, Company Solicitor, and Mr. E. L. Hosie, Secretary.

The following shareholders representing 5,776 shares, were present: Messrs. Ho Leung, Chau Shui-ki, F. H. Kew, A. A. Guterres, P. M. N. da Silva, A. A. Alves, J. Arnold, T. E. Pearce and A. O. Lang.

After the wording of the resolutions had been given by Mr. Dyer, the Chairman explained them in the following terms:

As shown in the Notice which has just been read by the Company's Chief Manager, this Meeting has been convened for the purpose of increasing the capital of the Company by the issue of 140,000 further shares of the nominal value of $50 each. 60,000 of these shares are to be offered to existing shareholders. In the ratio of one new share for each old share that they hold and at a premium of $10 a share. The Directors are given power to dispose of any of the new shares not taken up, and also of the unissued 80,000 new shares in any manner they think fit.

There will thus be raised additional funds which the Company will employ in the manner indicated in the Chairman's Speech at the Annual General Meeting of the Company held on the 30th of March last. In view of the increase of Capital it has been necessary to alter the Articles of Association, because Article 17 at present provides that no number may hold more than 4,000 shares. We must therefore also that amount by increasing it proportionately to the increased capital. The first of the Resolutions not out in the Notice of this Meeting effects this object by substituting a new Article for Article No. 17. I do not think there is anything

text:
It was due mainly to Mr. Ede's efforts that the Publicity Bureau for South China has come into being.

The Portuguese community of Hongkong will always have a warm corner in their hearts for Mr. Ede. Some years ago he attempted to create a Portuguese Garden City in the Colony to protect the Portuguese clerk from soaring rents. The failure of the scheme did not dishearten him as he turned his attention to Kowloon Tong. He became general manager of the Kowloon Tong and New Territories Development Co. which is building 250 houses and contemplates an expenditure of $3,000,000 to relieve the Colony's pressing house shortage. More recently, the public has read of the latest production of Mr. Ede's brain, a labour cooperative company, the object of which was an end to strikes in Hongkong.

The master of the s.s. Giyo Marn was found $15 at the Marine Court this morning for not carrying the regulation lights whiter lying at anchor. Mr. Ede was always a keen student of politics in China. In Shanghai he was adviser to the Viceroy of Nanking and subsequently to the Tuchun of Szechuan.

headline: BREAKERS AHEAD.
text:
The Kuomintang is the party controlling the little civil power allowed them by their powerful military subordinates. If at any time within the last few years, the Yurianese, merceries have held the trump cards in Canton, they do so even

appear as if their days are numbered, his almost the next, their stars to be again in the descendant. Our Canton correspondent says that those who ought to know are feeling alarmed at the trend of of events which may, indeed, be only be straws in the wind. The Kemiating is an uncertain quantity. Yesterday it may have been at the tender merries of its can't merremaries, but by intrigue and playing off one faction against the object, it may have even gone to the extent of "clipping the Yumpanose wings." On the other hand, General Yang may still, desire to be ruler of Canton in name as well as in fact. In either case, trouble will have to come. It is useless to deny that the trouble will have to come sooner or later as there are too many petty leaders in the province. The quicker the majority of them are expelled, the better it will be for the populace.

Another report has been received purporting to confirm Tang Chi-yao's flight from his own province.

Troops in Canton are on the quivive for emergencies from unexpected quarters. There have been many military movements on both sides of the river and guards have been increased.

headline: PROBATE ACTION. / $189,000 AT STAKE.
text:
A. FOURTH WIFE'S POSITION.

The position of a fourth wife under Chinese law was again the subject of much legal reference and quotation at the Supreme Court this morning when the case was re-heard in which a brother of Chan Yau deceased sues his fourth wife for having, as he claims, wrongfully entered a cavent for letters of administration in respect of estate estimated at the value of $180,000.

It is his claim that as the only next of kin of mature age he is entitled to be regarded as the rightful natural guardian of two infant sons left by the deceased.

The defendant on the other hand holds that as she is the sole surviving wife or concubine of the deceased she is entitled to be consider as the natural guardian of the sons, a claim strengthened, she holds, by the natural mother having expressly nominated her to look after them.

Fubg Sze-lun, a Canton solicitor, was cross-examined at length this morning by Mr. F. C. Jenkins as to Chinese law and custom. It being the defendant's claim that she was entitled to be looked upon as the "compassionate" mother questions as to the legal position in regard to estate of the "compassionate" mother were put to him. It was underflow circumstances, he stated, that the "compassionate" mother's rights were the same as the natural mother.

The plaintiff was represented by the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster K.C. and Mr. Eisley Zetlyn, the defendant by Mr. Eldon Potter K.C., and Mr. F.C. Jonkip (both instructed by Mr. Wu). Twenty miners with large families who were amongst those discharged through bad trade at Aslington, near Blyth, have been restarted on compassionate grounds. more to-day. It is an open secret that General Young Hsi-man, who leads the Yunnan adventurers in Canton, is out to stay as long as he can. With the Kuomintang out of the way, he will be free to pursue any course he chooses. Rumour has associated his name with Tuchan Tang Chi-yao of Yunnan but that worthy seems to be too busy himself to launch his much-vaunted invasion of Canton. According to messages received, says our Canton correspondent, Tang is in hot water. Leaving the security of his domain, he led an expedition into Kwangsi, but his rivals stirred up trouble for him. The latest report now is that he has fled.

Whether he has or has not fled is of secondary importance. His influence on General Yang has been counteracted by vague promises from the Kuomintang Governments. headline: BREAK AT LAST. / CANTON
text:
COMPLICATED SITUATION

Public Safety Bureau Chief Visits Hongkong.

From reports received during the week-end it appears that hostilities have actually broken out between the non-Cantonese mercenaries and the Communistic Kuomintang adherents of Dr. Sun who wield the civil power in Canton.

According to reliable sources, two brigade of Yunnanese have moved forward from the East River sector towards Swatow where they took over outposts in the territory of General Hsu Shung-chi, the Kuomintang commander, who drove out Chan Kwing-ming. Several detachments in the hinterland of Swatow are stated to have surrendered their ms to the Yunnans without offering resistance. In other parts of the province

there have been military movements on both sides. Commander Chu Pui-tak who leads a band loyal to the Kuomintang. Communists is said to be cut off from Canton through other Yunnanese making forced marches by night and occupying Shiukwan to prevent his return by way of the North River and the Canton-Shiukwan Railway.

General Wu Techen, who is head of the Public Safety Bureau (Police Commissioner) in Canton is reported to have come down to Hongkong during the week-end. His name has always been associated with the Communists but although all the Kuomintang offices have been removed to the south side of the river, he remains in Canton city where the allied mercenaries — the Yunnanese and the Kwangsi-ites—are in power.

Canton merchants, reports the "China Mail" correspondent, have been discussing means to protect themselves should the worst come to pass.

It is the concensus of opinion that one side must make a move within a week or so at the most as the present impossible situation cannot last indefinitely. There is still another Yunnanese warlord come into the picture. This is General Fan Shek-sang, Canton's erstwhile strong man, who led an expedition into Kwangsi, to make for his native province where he wished to avenge the putting to death of his father by Tuchun Tang Chi-yao. Should General Fan take it into his head to return to the Kuomintang banner and fight his fellow provincials, there is a chance of Dr. Sun's followers holding out. To become the soldier of the hour, he would have to fight his way through hostile territory. Meanwhile the question is—Can the Kuomintang hold out in Honam with dwindling revenue and, on paper, inferior forces, while their subordinates are beyond the North and East Rivers and their ally is in Kwangsi? From what has been seen so far, it seems as if the Communists will endeavour to fight for a stand, such stand to be maintained by intrigue rather than military domination.

Happily, this time neither side has the sympathies of the civil population, who have had their lesson and prefer peace without persecution.

headline: EVERY DEPARTMENT IS FULL OF NEW, FRESH AND UP-TO-DATE
text:
The hour was not that at which a group of suffering humanity daily gathers at the benches inside the main entrance to have what are generally minor ailments attended, but immediately on the left of these benches a glimpse could be caught through an open door of several neatly attired and very capable looking Chinese girls, or rather young ladies, seated round a table obviously intent on study. These, the newspaper man was informed, were undergoing the course of training to which prospective nurses had to submit themselves, a system which was responsible for the turning out of many valuable helpers.

Passing through and up a flight of stairs leading to the compound of the London Missionary Society, in connection with which the hospitals here are run, the newspaper, man was given a choice of which to visit—the Nethersole (erected in 1893); the Alice Memorial "Maternity opened in 1924) or the Ho Miu Ling (opened in 1906).

At the Ho Miu 'Ling he was surprised at the outset by the lady missionary in charge.. Referring to the manner in which the fame of the hospital spread through the reports of patients returning in whom cures had been effected, this lady remarked that in the near future there would probably be an influx of "patients blind or with eye trouble of varying degree, as there were several patients in the Hospital at the present moment who had entered blind and by means of the removal of cataracts or other operations were now well on the road to recovery of their vision. Cases such as these were by new means unusual, she assured the astonished newspaper man, who was wondering how he ever could have been numbered among those who passed with indifference an institution where blind men made to see were looked upon as "by no means nothing unusual."

That her heart and soul were in the work it was perfectly obvious when the lady talked of her patients with most of whom she could converse, although she admitted that the dialect of one old man was too much for her. "The funny part of it," she remarked, "is that the patient in the next bed can talk both this dialect and Cantonese but when we talk to him in Cantonese and tell him to pass on a question to the other patient he appears to do it all right but his mind simply won't work back into "reverse" to allow of his telling us the answer in Cantonese."

"These two dear old men (indicating two happy old bodies gazing contentedly at everything in general from their beds) were so quaintly humorous when they underwent eyesight tests after having had cataracts removed. When they came to the Hospital asking that they might be made to see they were holding each other's hands for all the world like two little kiddies. Successful operations over, they were tested by means of fingers and other things held before them. One, who is 70, could not see quite as well as the one who is 60 and it was very amusing to watch him going over the actions after was by himself with the means of his own fingers and other objects nearest to him also to hear the two comparing notes."

headline: MARTIAL LAW. / CRITICAL CANTON POSITION.
text:
GENERAL STRIKE?

CHAN KWING-MING COMING BACK?

Once more General Chan Kwingming's name is mentioned in connection with Kwangtung politics. This time he is only making a mild attempt to regain a footing in the province instead of striking for complete conquest.

Martial law was declared this morning by the Yunnanese mercenaries in the East Suburb, where soldiers are on guard in public streets with fixed bayonets.

General Hsu Shung-chi, the Kuomintang general, is reported to be coming back to Canton to make a grand effort to stem the tide of anti-Communistic aggression and to expel the non-

Cantonese knight-errants who now hold the city. He is stated to have declared that he will fight to the bitter end.

While General Hsu is making for Canton, so the account goes, Chan Kwing-ming will stage a come-back by leading about 10,000 riflemen to harrass Hsu's rear and thus assist the Yunnanose.

Meanwhile, General Fan Shek sang, the Yunnan soldier of the hour who nominally acts in unison with the "Reds," is reported to be also returning to Canton. Rumour has it that his vanguards will soon be contesting their way down the Canton-Samshul Railway.

In addition to the threatened political upheaval, Canton may face a general strike. The Yunnanese have declared that they will protect the electricity and water works from unruly strikers.

Gradually the process of converting Canton into a mercenary capital is being carried out. I am told that even the Cement Works at Honam, formerly Dr. Sun's headquarters, are now guarded by the Yunnanese.

headline: RAID ON TOWN.
text:
(From Our Own Correspondent

Pakkai, Kongmoon, May 29. Once again the folly of leaving an inland township unprotected has been amply demonstrated. Just as the Romans withdrew when their Empire was tottering to its ruins and left the ancient Britons to the tender mercies of invaders, so did the “Fook” garrison at Kamchuk (where Mr. Rasmussen was captured) depart for Canton to increase the strength of the hemmed-in Communistic Government, leaving Kamchuk to be ravaged by “To

On May 22, the garrison embarked for Canton whither they had been ordered by General Li Fook-lam who is holding out in Honam. Since the Saikwan coup, the Kamchuk Volunteers have been disbanded. Accordingly, the place could offer little or no resistance to the marauders.

Like vultures' eager for their prey, a band from two to three hundred strong entered Kamchuk openly on the morning of May 23, the day after the regulars' departure, and secreted themselves in the opium divans, etc. Not thinking that the bandits had come to start trouble but, rather, to exact further "squeeze" from the gambling saloons, business houses opened their doors as usual.

About ten in the morning, the reign of terror started. In Kamchuk is a rice and wine shop, the master of which, as a Volunteer officer who had shot down several pirates, was singled out for first attention. He fled only in the nick of time and his shop was ransacked and then burned down.

Spreading out from this point, the bandits entered each building—tenement or shop—and pillaged methodically. No resistance was offered and organised opposition was impossible now that the outlaws had got the upper hand. Practically every house was cleaned out and then the pirates set fire to the township. Fortunately a heavy rain began to fall and by nightfall, the fire had burned itself out but not before 70 per cent. of the buildings had been destroyed or partially damaged.

Next day, the bandits remained collecting their huge loot. Rice, cattle and even doors were packed away.

In the afternoon, Mr. and Mrs. Rasmussen arrived in an A.P.C. motor-boat to inspect one of the up-country sub-agencies, and stepped on a hornet's nest. Mr. Rasmussen was hailed when on the river and captured, but was released the next day as has already been reported.

Having served his apprenticeship, as he openly brags, by shooting down Captain Willox and instigating the "Tai Lee" piracy, Pang Cheong, former Boatswain of the Hongkong-Kongmoon boat, directed the gang's operations in most businesslike manner.

There were no casualties but over ten persons were forced away into captivity, for ransom.

Subsequently regular soldiers from Lak Lau (about three miles away) arrived and took charge.

Before the bandits left Kamchuk, they indulged in target practice at vessels passing on the rapids, taking pot-shots and firing volleys. However, all the craft successfully ran the gauntlet and escaped. At present all the Canton and Fatshan junkes for this part of the delta go via Yungki instead of making the rapids. Other encounters with pirates are reported. I learn that Sheung Shul Hau in the Sanwui

headline: FIGHT IN STREET.
text:
Coincidently with the arrival of Prince George who is going to Weihaiwei to-morrow, the anti-Japanese rioting was resumed this morning.

As a result the Municipal Council declared a state of emergency. An excited meeting of 1,500 students and workers at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce yesterday evening forced, the Chairman of the Chamber to sign a notice calling a general strike to-day.

They also passed a resolution in favour of boycotting foreign banks and bank notes, placing the control of the municipal police in Chinese hands, withdrawal of the foreign warships from the Huangpu River, release of the arrested rioters, punishment of the "murderers" of the students and workmen, compensation for the sufferers in the riots, and suspension of municipal taxes.

An hysterical workman orator collapsed and died during a meeting.

The students this morning massed in the street and attacked the police, but they were met with a deluge from a fire hose. The rioters tore up paving stones and hurled them at the police. A number of police and onlookers were injured. The police fired on the rioters seriously wounding five, after which the crowd dispersed.

The students are endeavouring to enlist the co-operation of the workers for stressful services, but the Municipal Council is taking measures accordingly. A student attacked a Sikh constable in the street but was himself seriously wounded.

The city is calm at present but the situation depends to some extent on the backing which the Reds intend to give the rioters.

headline: General Strike Threat.
text: The situation is tenser to-day, following a meeting attended by fifteen hundred, mostly students, at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce last evening, whereat many wild resolutions were passed. A student named Ling Ku-yung presided. Members of the Chamber vainly attempted to keep down the excitement and moved that a special meeting, consisting of two delegates from each society represented, be appointed to deal with the business under discussion. The extremists demanded a motion in favour of a general strike also that the acting Chairman of the chamber, who was not present be called on to explain his attitude. The extremists motion was carried a large unproviding action obviously being terrorised.

M. Merlin, and in order to demand indemnities for the victims of the criminal attempt.

Hongkong and the whole world was startled by his outrage on the occasion of M. Berlin's visit to Shameen, after calling here on his return to Indo-China from Japan. M. headline: CANTON'S
text:
Situation Explained.

Such is the rapidity with which the situation can change in Canton politics that the Communist adherents of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen, only a week or two ago struggling for a slender foothold in the province, are now morally masters of the position.

In an interview with a Chinese gentleman whose business takes him to Canton about three times a week, a "China Mail" reporter who met him as he was stepping off the s.s. Kinshan yesterday afternoon, was told that fighting was not expected. On his recent trips he had noticed a gradually increasing exodus of families of non-Cantonese officials and military officers. His opinion was that although numerically, financially and strategically the stronger, the Yunnanese and Kwangsi allies are being frightened out. Even now, the non-Cantonese mercenaries are much superior in men and munitions. To counteract the inferiority, the Kuomintang (the party name of Dr. Sun's government with Soviet leanings) point to the manner in which they crushed Chan Kwingming. As has been pointed out

in the “China Mail” on dozens of occasions, no campaign in Kwangtung has been won entirely on the battlefield. Prestige, morale and the goodwill of the civil population have always proved important factors.

From what was gathered, it appears that the mercenaries dread the so-called "Students Army" or Whampoa Cadets, in reality ordinary regulars commanded by Red Russian officers. These detachments are equipped with shrapnel pieces which won the day against Chan. Shock tactics were employed then. After a spasmodic bombardment far behind anything seen in the Great War, the "Students" would be moved forward to administer coup de grace. Where other divisions were employed, "the "Students" would be used to keep behind the advance guard and now then down should they deter from their objective. It is such do-or-die methods that have driven fear into the hearts of the Yunnanese and Kwangsi men, rich and powerful as they are. At present, the couple of thousand or so Red "Students" are drilling hourly at Whampoa.

To prevent any surprise attack from that quarter, the mercenary warlords are stationing their out posts to the east of Canton. However, it is the desire to save Canton from devastation, the city being such a rich source of "squeeze," that will stave off the clash.

Another important factor in favour of the Communists is the unqualified goodwill of the labourers. Propaganda has been so intensive that it is expected the labourers will strike, should hostilities break out, whichever the non-Cantonese are in power. For the benefit of those who may not be acquainted with the events leading up to the present strained relations it should be mentioned that the opposing sides are, nominally, obedient to the cause of Dr. Sun. The mercenaries came into the province and reinstated Dr. Sun. At one time they allowed his civil satellites to rule on sufferance. Now the Communist politicians want the mercenaries either to be subservient to their cause which means, principally, sacrificing the main sources of revenue in their hands, and doing the Reds' bid-dance. Since they have lived on the fat of the land, it is not to be expected that the soldiers will tolerate an attempt to strip them of their power. It was the Communists who first made threatening gestures, but when the Yunnanese and Kwangsi concentrated their forces in the city, the politicians found the place too hot for them and retired to Honam (across the river) or to Whampoa. In a few weeks, their intrigue and bombast has given their hopes a decided fillip and according to the gentleman interviewed, they may yet win the day.

headline: STUDENT PARADE.
text:
To demonstrate their sympathy with the Shanghai rioters, hundreds of students held a mass parade yesterday afternoon, shouting "Down with Imperialism and "forgivers," when they marched past Shameen.

It has been stated that the Maritime Customs non-Chinese staff were called back to Shameen for safety about 2 p.m. until the parade was over.

Shannon's gates were closed but crowds of residents watched the proceedings from inside. The Police were armed and a picket of bluejackets was landed on the island.

When the parade was passing the French Bridge, the French commission police treated it non-relatively, taking little or no notice.

So-called cadets are again active with anti-foreign propaganda.

headline: FIGHTING STARTED?
text:
Reports have reached Canton of rival outposts having opened fire at one another in the East River district. The troops concerned are said to be those of General Yang. Hsi-man, commander-in-chief of the non-Cantonese mercenaries, and General Hsu Shungchi, commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang forces.

Troops are also on the move in the North River region.

The Yunnanese have been given a taste of the civil opposition the Soviets are stirring up against them. On the advice of "Red" Kuomintang Labourites, locomotive drivers have deserted the train services.

Yunnanese detachments are camping at the Railway Station. Anti-Communist staff officers have been trying to round up the skilled labour of the Canton-Samshui and Fatshan railways to run the trains on the Canton-Kowloon line (Chinese section). Heavy field-guns, weapons of all kinds, munitions and war waggons were transferred, this morning from Shekwaiting to the Canton-Kowloon Station (to the east of Canton) as the Communists may come from that direction).

The Communists are rallying at and around Honam where they have been mobilising, ostensibly, as a jumping-off point for an attack on the mercenary non-Cantonese headquarters in Canton. Their press announces that General Hsu will soon be back in Canton when their party will immediately "nationalise" the electric light and waterworks plant.

Refugees are crowding the Hongkong-bound boats and much property and valuables are, as usual, finding their way into Shameen. The eastern outskirts of the city are full of Yunnanese patrols and martial law is still in force.

People coming into Hongkong from the East River district report considerable alarm over the recent trend of events. Two EMPRESS DELAYED. The “Empress of Australia” has been delayed by 6am and will now arrive in Hongkong at 8:00 a.m. to microw Friday morning.

The students, this afternoon, proceeded to the Waichaopu: "where Minister Shen, Jnai-lip saw their representatives. He pointed out that the Government had already lodged a protest with the Powers and had sent Commissioners to Shanghai.

headline: "Explicit Protests."

text:
A. Note, dated June 1., though hunded to the Italian Minister this afternoon, says:—

“I have the honour to draw the most serious attention of your Excellency to the unhappy facts following, which occurred on May 30, in the International Concession, Shanghai. Following the arrest of students and acts of violence towards Chinese workers, several of whom were wounded, a certain number of students from the different universities at Shanghai proceeded on the afternoon of May 30, to the Police Station of the International Concession as a protest and made speeches. The armed intervention of the police led to more than 40 students being arrested, four being killed outright, six seriously wounded, of whom two succumbed a little while afterwards, and 17 were slightly wounded, three of whom, however, died after. On learning with emotion of the above facts, I beg to remark that whatever might have been the character of the demonstration by the students, who are young men of good families and full of patriotism and unarmed, they should not have been treated as ordinary malefactors, but instead of calming them by appropriate means, the police had recourse to extreme mis翅，which are essentially condemned by humanity and justice. “Consequently, I find it absolutely necessary to address to your Excellency the most explicit protests, while reserving the right, when further reports giving complete details are received, to formulate all claims which may result from this deplorable incident for which the authorities of the Concession are entirely responsible.” “Further beg your Excellence to bring what has exceeded to the knowledge of the Minister on the

text:
This morning's papers in their leading articles comment upon the Shanghai situation, the general opinion being that the situation has been caused by the (ommunistic influence working on the anti-foreign sentiment bred by the unilateral treaties between China and the Powers.

Whilst sympathising with China's position, the papers emphasise that the present action frustrates rather than helps the cancelling of extraterritoriality.

The Diplomatic Body are meeting tomorrow, when it is understood they will discuss the Shanghai affair, and probably despatch a reply to the Walchiaopu Note immediately afterwards.

headline: CHINA'S FATE.
text:
CIVIL WAR PLAN.

Much attention has been attracted to a statement by the Washington correspondence of the Associated Press declaring that he possesses information pointing to direct Soviet participation, in the impending armed struggle for the control of the whole of China. text:
To-day, the outward position was one of stalemate. The mercenaries have given the impression that they will not start fighting unless attacked and, meanwhile, will keep their hold on the city.

On the other hand, the Communistic element of the Kuomintang is resorting to a general economic strike in Canton city, to starve out the non-Cantonese troops by cutting off all communication.

I have already reported the stoppage on the three railways entering Canton. Since then, the cross-river ferries, both native craft and motor-boats have been "got at" by Communist labourites. To day a cargo-coolie strike is threatened and it may not be long if even the essential services are suspended. If Canton was economically isolated, the mercenaries could still carry on by commanding supplies. Such a stoppage would seriously inconvenience everybody, including the foreign communities. There are some who predict that the economic strike has as its object not so much the staying out of the anti-Communists but rather the holding-up of the city's commerce so that the merchants will be according to the cedent when the Corporate war lords had to be bought out to prevent bloodshed and destruction. It is felt that fighting may even be averted at this moment if the merchants and bourgeois will come forward to negotiate, by payment, of course, for the Yunnanese and Kwangsi-ites to vacate the city. With trade as it is, money will not be so easily found as in previous instances.

Inquiries in Hongkong this morning tended to show that the report of the cargo stoppage is substantiated by the river-boats not accepting cargo for Canton during the week-end. Yesterday's and last night's steamers were full of people from Canton.

headline: Foreigners Warncd
text:
(Frôm Our Own Corréspondent.)

Canton Sunday 2:45 p.m. Yesterday's action of the gunboats has brought on a real state of war. All Saturday night till the small hours of this morning and to day, there has been intermittent sniping from both sides.

Shameen is in little or no danger as the shots are not falling in that direction. But there is no telling what may happen to Europeans in or outside the city. "Consuls have warned their subjects to find shelter in Shameen or leave" Canton, and some of the girls at St. Hilda's School (near the East Parade ground) sailed for Hongkong "to-day. Other residents in Tungshan have left for Shameen.

After the gunboats and armed launches had passed out into the Back Reach, the Yunanese began to take up positions behind sandbag barricades on the Western and Central Bund. Snipers were busy on both sides of the river and several proved their marksmanship. One Yunnanese post was close by the Tung On S. S. Co.'s wharf. When the s.s. Sai On went alongside this morning, the position was obscured by the vessel. The mercenaries accordingly left that post but returned when the steamer sailed shortly after 3 o'clock and re-opened fire at the opposite bank. On the other side, the Communists had their points of vantage from which they replied to the rifles on the city side. At most only two or three rounds could have been fired from artillery and both sides used rifles and measers.

headline: Forlorn Hopes
text:
In the small hours of this morning (about 2 a.m.) the Communists sent out a forlorn hope to land in Canton. They embarked in the night in several fast launches from Honam and crossed the river under cover of Dutch Folly Island in the middle of the river. Before they had reached the Bund, they were sighted by the Yunnanese sentinels. Guards were called out from the vicinity. The launches used machine guns and the mercenaries on the Bund replied with mausers. Eventually the launches were driven off. This morning bodies were seen in the "river and it is believed that some of the attacking party were killed. The Yunnanese immediately withdrew their dead and wounded.

About 410 a.m. the attack was repeated but further down the river. This was also unsuccessful and the Communists retreated very quickly.

headline: Housetop Ambush.
text:
Carrying the fight into enemy territory, the Yunnanese sallied across the river at 5:35 a.m. There were only about forty of them and they ventured out into the river in small commandeered rowing boats. It was light then but I could not follow their movements as they were hidden behind shipping, having zig-zagged as soon as they started. When they returned about an hour later, the commander told me that they had reached some Honam steps but had not landed as they had spotted. Communists in ambush on housetops! This is given for what it is worth.

During the day, both sides spotted away at one another. The Bund was deserted and the Honam front was lined with sandbags and nothing else. The firing resembled the letting off of firecrackers, by lads in Hongkong streets after the first flush of China New Year. I saw at least two Yunnanese dead carried away and seven wounded. I cannot say what casualties there were on the Honam side as cross-river traffic has ceased on account of the general strike. Inside the city and in the western suburb people were walking about quite calmly.

Several determined efforts were made during the day to take and re-take Dutch Folly. This island, almost within a stone's throw of the Bund, was in the hands of the Communists. Trenches

had been dug and from these, Commu ist marines opened fire at Yunnanese outposts and pickets on the Bund. After several mercenaries had been picked off, the Yunnanese burst open the doors of the Tai Sam Yuen restaurant as its roof is the highest in the vicinity. Previous to this, the staff had locked and barricaded the doors and fled. Finding a vantage point on the restaurant roof which had battlements of a kid, the mercenaries took cover and sent over volley after volley with their mausers. Finding their position untenable, the marines withdrew. Some fled in waiting while others jumped into the river, with full equipment in sheer fright.

I was privileged to watch the return action from a roof forty feet away. The Communists re-conustered and stole back on to the Island from the far side. They opened fire once more and caught mercenaries unaware. The latter returned to their unfailing roof, almost out of the range of the fire from the marines and banged away till the marines retreated once more. SOUTH FOLLOWING EVENTS: CLOSELY

When I left, the Island was, apparently, vacant, neither side venturing to take possession as it has no means of retreat. The marines were by no means accurate in their shooting although they did smash a considerable part of the restaurant's front. Some of their shots went wider than where I was a spectator.

When the river streamers arrived this morning, the Paul Beau was leading and it dropped anchor in the stream. The Sai On went ahead to her wharf and the Kinshan followed suit. The Honam was already anchored in the river. As far as I could see, none of the shot were directed at the boats and the mercenaries on the Bund were particularly anxious to avoid hitting the steamers.

At the moment of writing, firing seems to have slackened.

headline: $250,000 Bribe?
text: Canton, Saturday 4:30 p.m. Fighting broke out a short while ago through the River defence Flotilla steaming up the Canton River in line and opening an aimless bombardment. There were about twelve of these craft in all, ranging from obsolete wooden gunboats to armed launches. Most of them were equipped with small quick-firers, probably 3-pounders. For what their shots were intended nobody knows. In connection with their actually firing the first shots brought on the war, some conflicting, but neverheles important, rumours are current. From a source friendly to the Yunnanese, learn that the Flotilla was bought over by the mercenaries for a quarter of a million dollars. Presuming that this is true, the Wingfung (flagship of the Communists) became suspicious and they fled up the River to pass out through Pak Ngo Tam (the passage by Sha. (Continued on page 9.)

headline: THE SHANGHAI RIOTS
text:
"INTERFERING POWERS."

London: June 7.

A special meeting of the Union of Chinese Associations held in London, has passed in resolution protesting against "the rise of armed forces by interfering flowers to suppress the strike who shot down defenceless workers and students" and recording full support of the strikers.

Moscow telegrams show that the Soviets are closely and sympathetically watching events in China. "The newspapers are publishing detailed accounts.

headline: Wednesday Developments.
text:
Through walkouts of almost all workers in cotton-mills and in many other factories and industrial establishments, the ranks of Chinese out in the general strike were yesterday swelled to an estimated 100,000.

wounded in clashes in the North-ern section. None was between mobs and police.

Many reports of assaults on foreigners, particularly seriously injured, were received.

An American Volunteer was arrested by Chapel authorities when he stepped over the border, but was released after being detained some hours.

Hundreds of foreign men and women volunteered for emergency duty in response to the Council's appeal.

Two British cruisers arrived in port. Landing parties will be brought ashore to-day.

Shooting Affray.

Yangtzepoo district was the scene of Wednesday's shooting affray, which resulted in the death of two rioters and the wounding of several more. The disturbance occurred at a Japanese ice factory on Lay Road, within a few minutes walk of the Yangtzepoo Police Station. A crowd of about 3,000 assembled at the gates of the factory, forced their way in-side and for the next few minutes set about smashing up everything breakable. Matters became very serious and the Sikh constable on duty nearby summoned assistance which came from a squad of foreign and Chinese Police. The mob turned its attention to the Police who were forced to fire. One of the rioters was killed instantly while several suffered minor wounds. Later a hand to hand struggle took place between the police and the crowd and one of the most troublesome rioters received a blow on the head from a police baton which killed him.

They all turned back, waiting until daylight when they negotiated the spot with no further untoward occurring.

Although the steamboat companies have received no notification, it is thought that the Cantonese object to boats proceeding to the City at night time because they have no means then of ascertaining if recruits for the Yunnanese are on board. The Companies have, of course, legal right to go to Canton at night but it is thought if they are wise that they will wait until daybreak in future.

Samples and particulars on application.

Towards yesterday evening, cross-river firing decreased and last night was somewhat quieter. This development is considered to be the usual lull before the storm. Hourly, the campaign is becoming more intricate and an initial success would do much to bring in the waverers in on the victors' side. Particulars have been obtained

of the casualties caused by the bombardment on Saturday afternoon and in the city during the sniping from Honam. Altogether there have been a dozen or so Chinese non-combatants killed in the various parts of the city and on the Bund. The round that fell in the Public Park has left a big cavity there.

The Red Navy is still more or less inactive although their guns are trained on Canton and all the vessels have steam up.

There have been no more struggles for Dutch Folly which is now vacant and untenable by either side.

A fair amount of damage has been done to buildings on and near the Bund.

Shameen's Safety.

To-day the river steamers are not going alongside their wharves as these have been declared to be in the war zone. They are at anchor in the stream off Shameen.

All the foreign gunboats—three British, two American, two French and one Japanese—are standing by.

Allies of the Cantonese Communists are coming down the West River. Their artillery has been finding its mark and shots have passed over Shameen which is still immune from immediate danger.

headline: Firing Increases.
text:
After the lull of last night, the Yunnanese have been renewing and increasing their sniping at Honam and the Cantonese on that side have replied hotly. I am informed that the Yunnanese will try to keep up a barrage till they can effect a landing in the Red St-onghold, but without artillery it will be very difficult for them to do so. Although the firing has increased, the effect has decreased as both sides are taking good cover behind their sandbags and barricades.

(Continued on page 9.)

headline: Shanghai; June 9.
text:
Three hundred Chinese seamen on six Butterfield & Swire coastal and river steamers at Shanghai went on strike yesterday evening. Ocean-going steamers are not affected.

Japanese lines are also meeting difficulties and are considering replacing the Chinese crews with Japanese.

Jardine, Matheson & Co. report unrest but no actual crew strike. A Jerdine coaster sailed yesterday night.

The strike of the dockers has interrupted dock work. Very little cargo is moving because the Chinese banks and shipping hongs which finance and handle cargo are closed down.

headline: A Bishop's Views.
text:
The Bishop of St. Albans, speaking at the Diocesan conference, said they must not lay all the blame for the disturbances in China on Bolshevism. They are largely due to the appalling conditions prevailing in industries in China and the fact that many Europeans have sought to make money from China without considering the native.

The conference passed a resolution declaring that greater sacrifices must be made by the Church at Home in order to further foreign missionary effort.

The question of the Shanghai shooting incidents was raised at a meeting of the workers' delegates of the International Labour Conference in a statement signed by Mr. Joshi (India); Mr. Lawson (Australia) and Mr. Suzuki (Japan) submitted to the Chairman.

The latter declared the question could not be raised in conference under standing orders, whereupon the meeting resolved to despatch through the Amsterdam International a message of sympathy to the workers of China.

headline: Strikers' Demands.
text:
Various Chinese Commercial and Student Unions met in the Chinese Chamber of Commerce last evening. They passed seventeen resolutions, which were handed to the Chinese delegates. They include four demands, which the strikers consider essential as preliminaries to official negotiations.

They are:—(1) The cancellation of a state of emergency; (2) the withdrawal of the marines; (3) the release of the arrested rioters; and (4) the restoration of closed schools.

Apologies Sought. Other resolutions reveal wide aspirations, including, the early cancellation of extraterritoriality; that the British and Japanese Ministers meanwhile should apologise to the Chinese Government and guarantee no further similar action; the abolition of the Mixed Court; the appointment of high Chinese officers to the Municipal Police; Chinese representation on the Shanghai Municipal Council in accordance with the amounts paid in taxes; payment of damages to the dependants of those killed or injured in the strike; payment of business losses

Approached this morning and asked how the system was working, Dr. Addison said that it was proving of the greatest possible use. At present nothing but the report of the nature of the disease and the number of deaths (or the recording of a clean bill of health is the case might be) was sent, but it was hoped that when the system was more firmly established, ed reports would be made of the nature of the steps taken to combat the disease and the measure of success which had attended them.

The number of ports making use of the Bureau was continually growing and his weekly cable from Singapore now included statistics from ports in Australia, said Dr. Addison. He himself sent off a cable to Singapore once a week telling them what was happening, and this was despatched by Singapore to all the ports who were partier to the scheme.

The advantages of the Bureau were that steps could be taken to deal with ships from infected ports arriving in Hongkong very much more quickly and with consequently more favourable results than when the news merely "filtered through" as Dr. Addison put it. He was confident that the result of the new system would be that the movement of infectious disease would be much more effectively restricted and when the system expanded and it was made possible to follow the result of the putting into practice of latest scientific discoveries he was confident that this would constitute an even greater step forward.

The Bureau was being made use of, said the P.C.M.O., by ports in Japan, Shanghai, French Indo-China, Siam, the Philippines, Dutch East Indies, Borneo, Australia, Singapore, Penang and British India, in fact practically over India.

It is interesting to recall that this matter of the incidence of epidemic diseases formed the subject of debate at the Medical Conference recently held at Hongkong and Dr. Lim, one of the first students to graduate from the Hongkong University, who has since interested himself in matters of health primarily in relation to Shanghai, had some interesting comments to make.

Dr. Lim pointed out that in these days of rapid communication and means of communication the control of infectious diseases, instead of being a matter of purely local significance, had become a subject of international concern. Improved means of communication had resulted in bringing cities and nations into closer touch, but this had not been without its attendant evils, as it had introduced diseases into territories where they had been non-existent. The fight would have to be waged on a worldwide basis if there was to be success, said Dr. Lim.

headline: Marines Landed.
text:
Two hundred marines from H.I.J.M.S. Tatsuta landed this morning.

Two Japanese gun-boats from the Yangtze have left for Shanghai. Four Japanese destroyers have arrived, two of which have gone up river to protect foreigners at Yangtze ports.

The student demonstration at Foochow was a fiasco, owing to the Tupan's precautionary measures.

Chinkiang, Tsingtao, Kiukiang and Hankow are now quiet. While there have been no disturbances at Shanghai, the strike situation is unchanged. Defence measures are continuing. Further arrivals of naval men have enabled the authorities to lighten the duties of the volunteers.

Diplomatic Investigation.

Reports from Nanking indicate that the situation there is becoming more serious.

A telegram from Taiyuanfustates that rioter's wrecked the local agency of the Asiatic Petroleum Company, smashing windows and tearing down the sign. It is understood that Chang Tso-lin contemplates issuing a circular telegram advising the students to refrain from acts of violence pending diplomatic investigation.

Members of the diplomatic delegation left for Shanghai this morning by the "blue express." It is stated that they will not sit as a commission nor take formal evidence, but make independent investigations returning within a few days with their report.

The directors of the local Chinese Bankers' Association this morning decided: Firstly, to telegraph to the Chinese banks at Shanghai urging them to support the students; secondly, to telegraph to public bodies urging them to pursue the present agitation to the end; thirdly, to furnish $10,000 strike relief funds; fourthly, to advise native banks to refrain from co-operating financially with the foreign banks concerned.

The students here have gone out on a sympathetic strike. There is growing intensity against foreigners and the situation is most serious.

headline: MORE TROUBLE.
text:
KIUKIANG COOLIES STRIKE.

A telegram from Klukiang says that all the coolies struck work to-day.

The agent of the Indo-China Steam Navigation Company does not recommend passengers to proceed to Kuling.

A Chinese received injuries to his head in a motor accident at Queen's Road Central yesterday, the motor car did not stop and so far has not been traced.

headline: HOME POLICY.
text:
Support for the British officials on the spot is the keynote of the Home Government's policy as regards the trouble in Shanghai.

Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co.'s crews struck at nine o'clock yesterday evening and their steamers are laid up at the wharves.

Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co. propose concerted action by the big shipping companies.

The Nippon Kisen Kaisha boats have up to the present adhered to schedule.

The Fengyang Maru left Shanghai for Hankow this morning carrying passengers but no cargo, the former including representatives of the Chinese Associations known to be going to Nanking and Chinkiang with the object of disaffecting the crews of foreign steamers at those ports. Further: Nippon Kisen Kaisha

Further Nippon Kisen Kaisha sailings are unlikely.

A student demonstration and general strike took place to-day. The situation is quiet, but it is strained.

Trooper Attacked. (Shanghai Mercury) SHANGHAI. Jure 5 Tough no. Very serious, a number of incidents took place to-day to remind the authorities of

the acute situation with which they are faced and served to keep alive the fact that hostility has by no means abated.

The most serious incident today was an ambush attack in the early part of the forenoon upon Trooper Beale of the Bubbling Well Police Station. Trooper Beale was patrolling the Jessfield Brennan Road district and was about to cross the junction of these two roads when reports of guns rang out and three or four bullets whizzed past the mounted police man who sprang from his pony, unslinging his rifle at the panic time.

Crouching behind the bank at the side of the road, the officer waited for further firing, and he re-mounted after a glance around and returned to report to the Bubbling Well Station. About half a dozen shots are believed to have been fired in all. This district is approximate to that patrolled by the Chinese Volunteers, who have been protesting against Municipal Police patrols of late.

In the House of Commons, reply-ing to questions by Mr. F. W.

Pethiek Lawrence (Labour) and the Rt. Hon. C. T. Trevelyan (Labour), with regard to the troubles in China, Mr. Ronald McNeill, Under Secretary of Foreign Affairs, emphasized that the international authorities on the spot were faced with a situation of imminent danger to life and property and could not wait to obtain instructions from their governments before taking the necessary steps to restore law and order. Mr. McNeill deeply regretted that the attack of the forces of disorder had been conducted behind a screen of misguided students, but said the British Consul General at Shanghai, with whom he understood the American, French, Italian and Japanese representatives were fully agreed, had reported that the police were very patient and could not have acted otherwise than they did. The British Government was confident the Chinese Government was anxious to co-operate with the other governments concerned in reaching an equitable and satisfactory solution of this deplorable affair.
