It was not intended, however, that they should purge their offences in jail where accommodation and food was superior to that being received by those strikers seeking the hospitality of Canton. They would be given the opportunity of proving their value to the community by undertaking useful—though somewhat unattractive—duties in connection with the sanitation of the Colony.

His Excellency asked the public to realise that it did not follow that the Government was doing nothing because it did not talk about it and said that there were occasions when it was wiser to say nothing in order that measures about to be taken might be the more successful. He asked the public to help by not believing rumours until the Government had confirmed them and not to pass them on whether or not they believed them in the first place. His Excellency referred to the rumours which had been spread of men, being stabbed for staying at their work and quoted two cases where they had originated from bodies of people who had died from natural causes being placed in the street. The police, he said, picked up on an average something like eight bodies a day in this manner. The public could also help by attempting to instil into servants remaining loyal that the best way of dealing with an intimidator was to intimidate him. If the intimidator injured him the "cat" could redress the balance, whereas if his injured the intimidator it was not only the intimidator's fault, but the loyal servant if he handed the man over to the police would receive a handsome reward.

If these measures were adopted His Excellency was confident that intimidation would quickly cease and business could be gone about in peace.

headline: CHEUNG CHAU. / FERRY MEN GOING ON STRIKE.
text:
SERVANTS LEAVE.

The strike of workers on craft in the harbour received a further extension this morning when all the men on the Cheung Chau ferry boats stopped work on orders received from the Seamen's Union in Canton. The ferry service was at a standstill this morning, but arrangements had been made in advance for such a contingency, and the ser-the men on the Cheung Chau mediately. The inconvenience caused to residents on the island will be therefore only temporary.

The decision of the employees on the ferry boats has apparently influenced the servants at European residences at Cheung Chau. During the past two days the workers started to leave the houses, but on finding out that they were liable to be arrested as idlers, they started to come back. According to a telephone message received at police headquarters this morning, all the servants have left.

Other craft affected are the small ferries running to Tai O, Aberdeen, Shaukiwan and Kowloon City. These all stopped running this morning. No arrangements have so far been made for the resumption of these services.

headline: SHAMEEN SERVICE.
text:
STEAMER TAKEN OVER.

GOVERNMENT'S ACTION

In order that communication with Shameen may be maintained regularly and that there may be additional means of food transport to the naval tugs which have been running from Hongkong the s.s. Tung On, brought down last night by European and Japanese passengers, left this morning manned by a crew from the naval boats in the harbour.

The Government have issued tickets (which are at an increased rate) and in spite of the fact that the number of Chinese leaving was not so large as usual a goodly sum was collected.

Revenue officers are acting as ticket collectors and they left with the boat this morning. It is understood that a regular service will be maintained.

headline: LOCAL & GENERAL.
text:
Mr. M. H. Turner to be Adjutant of Special Police Reserve.

Mr. W. J. Lockhart-Smith has been appointed a Police Magistrate.

The total amount of bank-notes in circulation on June 30, 1925, was $54,823,072.

His Honour the Chief Justice has ordered that no Criminal Session be held during the month of July, 1925.

H.E. the Governor has appointed Mr. Edward Boys Reed to be a Second Lieutenant in the Hongkong—Volunteer Defence Corps, with effect from July 6, 1925.

It is notified in the "Gazette" that the Christian Chinese Cemetery, Kowloon City, will be closed from July 2, 1925. New Kowloon Cemetery No. 1 is announced.

H.M. the King has approved the appointment of Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster as Unofficial Member of the Legislative Council while the Hon. Sir Henry Pollock acts as Attorney-General.

His Excellency the Governor has approved the following appointment:

Mr. D. A. Goodwin, Mr. A. F. B. Silva-Netto, Mr. A. C. Botelho and Mr. F. C. Mow Fung to be Chief Inspectors.

Four men armed with a revolver and daggers gained admittance to the first floor of No. 164 Queen's Road East, shortly before noon yesterday. After binding and gagging the inmates the robbers escaped with a haul of over $3,500 in money, jewellery and clothing.

It is learned that with the permission of the Secretary of Chinese Affairs, a Hongkong Labour Maintenance Association has been formed with its temporary headquarters at the Wuh Keu (Overseas Chinese) Hotel, Connaught Road Central. The object of the Association is to help workmen who have gone on strike or who are forced to strike by intimidation to obtain work or to remain at their present posts.

headline: SHANGHAI STRIK LEADERS SQUABBLING.
text:
"PINCH" AND "PINCHINO."

There is believed to be a shortage of strike funds. The Union has approached the Chamber of Commerce and Banks for funds to carry on. It is understood to be ordering men to resume work for other British Japanese with a view to cutting down expenditure. Growing tension is reported among the strike leaders owing to alleged mis-

The day passed very quietly, hough intomulation and kidnapping ontinue. The tram situation has improved.

The Fengtien commander of the Shanghai and Woosung Defence Force and the Chief of the Shanghai Woosung constabulary jointly issued a proclamation exhorting the strikers to resume peaceful auctions and a warning that lofers disturbing the peace under the good name of patriotism will be severely punished.

headline: ELCHO SHIELD.
text:
ENGLAND'S SUCCESS AT BISLEY.

At Bisley, the Elcho Shield was won by England with a score of 1,706.

London, July 10.—According to the newspapers, Rakovsky has brought back from Moscow trade orders for British firms amounting to £15,000,000, including £10,000,000 for factory equipment and agricultural machinery. —Reuter
Count Aisuke Kabayama has been elected to the Upper House, and Count Michimasa Soveshima has been-unseated-owing-to his outspokenness on the Far Eastern situation, against the Soviet.

headline: RIVER PORTS.
text:
SKELETON* SERVICE MAINTAINED.

CANTON FARES.

It was rumoured on the wharf that the Sal On, the sister ship to the Tung On, was also to be taken over by the Government upon its arrival in Hongkong on Saturday, but this proved untrue, the Government apparently considering the Tung: On sufficient for their needs in maintaining a food supply service to Shameen. The Sal On therefore went to anchorage at Stonecutters where are many others of the crewless river boats. She was the last boat to run on the service without naval help and had to be 'worked down from Canton by her European officers with assistance from Indian guards.

The Tung On, the boat which the "China Mail" announced on Saturday had been taken over by the Hongkong Government, now flies the White Ensign and is under the command of Lieut. Hemsley, of Submarine L.4, with a crew drawn from H.M.S. Titania and the Submarine Flotilla. The crew has nothing but praise for the culinary exploits of a bluejacket cook whose duty during the trip was to look after the inner man.

The Tung On is coaling at the Kowloon depot, Naval Yard, and will undertake the next trip tomorrow morning when bread and other stores will be put aboard.

The fares for Canton by the s.s. Tung On (tickets for which have been prepared by the Hongkong Government) are: First Class, $10, Second Class, $7.50, Third Class, $5.

During the week-end the river steamers plying between Hongkong and Kongmoon ceased 'their run for the time being'. Among the boats which had lost their crews earlier were the Tai Lee, On Lee and others...

On Friday the San Nam Hoi and the motor vessel Fook On went up to Fakkai as usual but the Fook On lost her crew there and the vessel had to tie up. The San Nam Hoi was more fortunate, a skeleton crew being left behind in all departments. She proceeded up to Kow Kong, discharged the balance of her passengers and returned direct to Hongkong, picking up the European master and officers of the Fook On who boarded the San Nam Hoi in a Customs launch.

It is gathered that another Hongkong-Kongmoon vessel, the Leung Kwong, is tied up at Pakkai but the Europeans are expected back this week. The San Nam Hoi returned to Hongkong and is now lying idle.

Last week it had been reported that the s.s. Chuen Chow which is a regular Hongkong-Macao ship and the Wing On had both lost their crews and tied up. However, communication between Hongkong and Macao has been maintained. On Saturday and yesterday the former West River steamer Anjou made the trips to Macao and back and this morning the Ko Chow had her Blue Peter up with a notice in Chinese "bound for Macao."

headline: FERRY SERVICES.
text:
DAILY TRIP TO CHEUNG

The strike of workmen on the Cheung Chau and Aberdeen ferry services on Saturday did not affect transport to any appreciable extent as volunteers were soon found to maintain them. The Cheung Chau service was resumed yesterday with Captain Lossius in charge of the Tung Yik-assessed by Mr Edwards as engineer. For the present, however, there will be one trip each way daily, the Tung Yick leaving Cheung Chau in the morning for Hongkong and returning to the island in the evening.

The report made on Saturday that the Shaukiwan and Kowloon City ferry services had ceased to operate owing to the crews having gone on strike was found to be incorrect. Owing to a misunderstanding these two services were included amongst the others which were really affected on Saturday. The Shaukiwan and Kowloon City ferries are running to-day as usual, the crews of these boats having no intention to go on strike.

The Yaumati, Shamshuipo and Mongkok ferry services have not been affected in any way.

headline: AT THE HOTEL. / COMING BACK TO NORMAL CONDITIONS.
text:
Signs of a nearer approach to normal times, although in each case it may be attributed rather to the energies of Europeans and Chinese who refuse to be intimidated, rather than a return to work of strikers, are the new arrangements at the Hongkong Hotel and the re-opening of an old established Chinese restaurant in the centre of the City.

For the first time for three weeks, the public bar, soda fountain and the tea lounge of the Hongkong Hotel were open today, loyal Chinese clerks remaining with the hotel, Filipinos and foreigners being responsible for the maintenance of these. Needless to say, the return almost to normal service was welcomed, and the hotel received more patronage than ever.

All these establishments will be open until 12.30 a.m.

To-day dinner is to be served from 7 p.m. instead of 7.30 p.m.

headline: ELECTRIC LIGHTING / POSITION AT HUNGHOM.
text:
A part of the workers at the China Light and Power Company's station at Hunghom, who remained at their posts on Saturday, were reported to have left this morning. Without exception all the regular workers have joined the strike body. As stated in the "China Mail" of Saturday, the Company had made arrangements in advance for substitutes to take the places of whose who intended leaving. These were drafted in during the week-end, and the lighting service was maintained without any interruption.

An assurance has been received from the Company that the departure of the workmen will in no way affect the supply of electric current.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
According to the Chinese papers a number of Chinese Taikoo employees who are tenants of houses erected by the firms, have been arrested as idlers on their refusing to work. They were, it is said, found in houses, which they had rented from the companies.

The Police are still busy interrogating Chinese in the streets and rounding up suspicious looking persons. In different parts of the town last night, a "China Mail" reporter came across several police pickets. This morning some more were noticed to have been taken up to Central.

Among the Chinese it was reported that business concerns which had put up shutters were told to open again by July 15. Whether the supposed warning had any effect or not, the teahouses and restaurants are making feverish preparations to start work again. Where their staffs are springing from is a matter of curiosity.

At the Central Magistracy this morning, three persons arrested and released on bail for cutting pine trees at Stanley Village failed to appear. The Magistrate estreated their bail money. In another case from the Shankiwan district, a woman was fined $10, or in the alternative two weeks hard labour.

In addition to the forming of special guards by Maine Road residents, other district guards are announced. One section is for Wellington Street and On Hing Terrace, says the "Wah Taz Yat Po" with headquarters at the servants' quarters of the Hongkong Hotel (in Wellington Street). The native bankers' guild has also circularised members with regard to nominating two employees from each firm for two hours duty at night.

headline: Who. They Are.
parent_headline: SWATOW UNREST. / SITUATION BECOMING MORE CRITICAL
text:
Since the rout of Chan Kwingming, Swatow has been actually and nominally under the rule of General Hsu Shung-chi, commander of Canton's Kuomintang armies, who led the offensive on that port.

When it became necessary to place the campaign against the Yunnanese mercenaries above the safety of Swatow, General Hsu withdrew his troops and began a trek back to the capital. Before his departure he made overtures to Commander Hung Leuk, who is, or has been, one of Chan Kwing-ming's lieutenants. Hung and Hsu had been colleagues under Dr. Sun Yat-sen in 1922. It is stated that General Hsu preferred to bury the hatchet. Accordingly, Hung Leuk came out of his hiding and took up a position near Swatow, professing harmony with Hsu Shung-chi. However, one or two of Hsu's own subordinate commanders stayed behind in Swatow. By "rival commanders" is probably meant Hung Leuk and Hsu Shung-chi's man—rivals in the sense that they both desire control of the place.

headline: BACK TO NORMAL
text:
MORE SIGNS OF THE TIMES.

CAUSES FOR OPTIMISM.

No further defections on the part of workers are to be reported this morning and although no general body or workers has returned to work, attempts to be reinstated, have been made by "boys" and amahs in many districts.

The more moderate estimates which are now being given regarding the beginning of the inevitable return of workers are supported by the reports of distress among Hongkong strikers in Canton. There are known to be 80,000 of these in Canton and the purse of the Government there has been so severely taxed that few of them are receiving the 40 cents a day. Meanwhile the food situation (with the restriction placed on exports from Hongkong) is on the way to becoming grave.

That trouble is anticipated at Canton by the Hongkong authorities is evident from the fact that no European lady is allowed to travel to Canton.

Meanwhile, Hongkong is still carrying on and the action of the Café Wiseman management in inaugurating from this morning a breakfast service from 8 o'clock and the anticipation of a return to service of the soda fountain marks yet another step forward in the return to normal functioning of benefits which, although they may hardly be considered vital, are things which make an enormous difference: in these times of stress.

Even more important still as a sign of the times is the statement made by Mr. N. L. Smith, Food Controller, to a “China Mail” representative this morning that the services of the army “killers” had now been dispensed with, owing to a return to more normal conditions. Beef was now available in large quantities in the more central markets, also pork, the difficulties in connection with the retailing of which had now been overcome. It was hoped to extend the market services to more outlying districts now that the situation was so well in hand.

headline: SHAMEEN ECHO.
text:
QUERY IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.

NUMBER OF CASUALTIES.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. Will Thorne (Lab.), Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said the number of Chinese casualties in the recent firing at Canton was not accurately known. They had been reported to be about 30 killed and 70 wounded but may have been more. The foreign casualties so far known were one Frenchman killed, four British and one French wounded.

headline: "CARRY ON." / SHAMEEN POSTAL SERVICE.
text:
MORN TILL NIGHT.

Great credit and the thanks of all foreigners both in Canton and Hongkong is due to the Postal Commissioner, his deputy and two assistants, who have worked from early morning till night under adverse circumstances to clear both incoming and outgoing mail in the Shameen branch and have laboured cheerfully and smilingly to "carry on" with this service. Without their efforts the Shameenites would have missed much of the cheer that has come with their epistles and newspapers from Hongkong.

headline: STRIKERS RESTIVE.
text:
ALLEGED PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT.

DISSATISFIEDSEAMEN.

Employed at one time as an “excise officer” when the Opium Monopoly was farmed out years ago, a Chinese who was one of the last to reach Hongkong before the steamers ceased running to Canton, told a “China Mail” reporter that unrest was growing among the strikers on account of alleged preferential treatment.

This man came down with the express intent of warning his family not to leave Hongkong. He is now awaiting resumption of steamer traffic to return. In Canton, he said, funds had reached a very low ebb. The nominal strike chairman is said to have been a Hongkong Seamen's Union official at one time and he is accused of sympathy toward the idle seamen. Those dissatisfied state that seamen each get two meals a day and some of the favoured ones receive an additional twenty cents. Among those who have found fault are the cargo coolies, who belong to a guild strong in numbers. Somehow or other plans went wrong. The guild in Hongkong is believed to be very wealthy, but no money was forthcoming. Accordingly, the coolies had to draw rations from the strike executive, and they are complaining.

An attempt, the informant concluded, was now being made to float a loan or issue bonds. Meanwhile the strikers' pickets were trying to exercise strict discipline. Correspondence to individuals in strike quarters from up-country or Hongkong is held back and passes must be obtained to leave the dormitories for fear of the rank and file running away.

headline: “WE WANT TO WORK”
text:
SHANGHAI'S UNPAID, ANGRY STRIKERS.

POLICEMAN CHEERED.

A thousand strikers this afternoon assembled outside the General Labour Union in Chinese territory and angrily demanded strike pay which, it was alleged was three days overdue.

The money was not forthcoming. The crowd grew very hostile to the Union officials who, on seeing themselves endangered, called the assistance of Chapel Volunteers. The latter dispersed the crowd with difficulty, levelling their rifles.

The crowd rushed into the Settlement followed by Volunteers. A Municipal policeman ordered the latter to leave the Settlement borders and they obeyed. The policeman was cheered by the strikers who were shouting "We want to work."

Five hundred Fengtienites are now keeping order on the Settlement borders.

headline: BLOWN OVER. / RED V. ANTI-RED TROUBLE IN CANTON.
text:
YUNNANESSE QUIET.

Evidently better.counsels have prevailed in Canton and the so-called Red v. anti-Red trouble appears to have blown over if only for the time being.

Business correspondence received by Hongkong Chinese firms yesterday indicated that the dispute seems to have been patched up, and that a political disturbance is not expected just yet: One letter says that but for the cessation of communications there might have been just a little trade before the mid-autumn season.

Anti-foreign feeling, writes the “China Mall” correspondent, is not so pronounced and non-Chinese have been able to go about in various parts of the city. Honam Island, on the south bank of the river, is very quiet. Agitators are still active on the Bund and on the River, “welcome home” deputations meeting strikers from Hongkong who have gone up overland, and pickets preventing the rank and file from getting out of Canton.

The Yunnanese invasion from Kwangsi has receded into the background, but an outbreak between competing militarists at Swatow will not occasion surprise.

headline: STRIKERS FINED.
text:
TWO COURT. CASES IN KOWLOON

At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, a former amah in the employment of Mr. H. E. Scriven was charged with leaving without notice on July 6. She was subsequently found to be working at Armand Buildings and arrested.

The amah said that she was employed as a temporary servant on a wage of $12 a month and left as she had too much to do. She claimed that the regular amah was paid $20, and since the latter went on strike she (accused) had to do double duty.

His Worship observed that, although the legal aspect was quite clear, he could not think of a more tactless case, as the amah had only served six weeks and was required to do more than her legitimate share of work. The accused was ordered to pay $14 to the complainant as compensation, or in default three weeks' hard labour.

Another case tried by Mr. E. W. Hamilton was that in which Mr. J. H. Oxberry charged a bar boy at the Palace Hotel with leaving without notice: It was stated that the accused was engaged in April on a monthly wage of $11 and left with the other servants on June 23.

The accused pleaded guilty and was fined $25, or one month's hard labour, in addition to payment of $11 to the complainant as compensation.

headline: PARTNERS' DISPUTE. / ALLEGED INTIMIDATION TO STRIKE.
text:
A partner in the Mow Ling Restaurant, Kowloon, appeared before the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton), yesterday as a result of the complaint of a fellow-partner that he had threatened the latter- and attempted by intimidation to get him to close the shop.

No evidence other than the complainant's statement was forthcoming, although it was stated that a pantry boy had made a statement through the complainant. At the Magistracy, however, this lad stated that he had never heard the complainant being threatened, nor was he told to cease work himself.

The complainant's story was that his fellow-partner told him that the shop would be destroyed unless it was shut. On the complainant pointing out that the firm would lose money, and probably its licence, the defendant had said that by destroying the building they would be able to get $5,000 insurance.

A few days later his fellow-partner told witness that unless he struck he would have to buy a coffin.

In spite of cross-examination, the pantry boy adhered to his statement that he had never heard any of the conversation mentioned by the complainant. His Worship commented that it was obvious from his terrified demeanour that the boy had been intimidated himself and adjourned the case until tomorrow.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS
text:
The “Wah Tsz Yat Po,” in an extra mentions the fact that a large number of members of the South China Athletic Association and the Chinese Swimming Club have volunteered for public service, and have registered with Dr. S. W. Tso, Assistant Labour Controller.

Considerable importance is placed by the Chinese masses.on the manner in which business houses, restaurants, and teahouses on both sides of the harbour have responded by re-opening their doors and catering for public wants as best they can.

Several Chinese-owned restaurants, supplying foreign-style food, in Yaumati have started business again, and others are following suit. It is expected that nearly all establishments of this class will be open as usual in a day or two.

Quite a number of nightsoil coolies of both sexes have returned to their employers and asked for work. As these are not Government servants but work in collaboration with contractors, no record can be kept.

A good many small barber shops have re-opened to-day, the staffs emerging as if from "nowhere."

headline: COMING BACK.
text:
STRIKERS REALISING FOOLISHNESS OF ACTION.

A LONG WALK.

Daily there are to be observed fresh signs of a more general realisation on the part of those who left work of the foolishness of their action and their desire to make amends by attempting to return to their former occupations. In the case of those who are near enough at hand to put their desire into practice they are finding, however, that their reinstatement at former wages is by no means an accepted thing; in fact, that in many cases they will have to begin all over again and that their action has discounted many years' service.

Those at Canton find it even more difficult to return to the service which they so unthinkingly left, but such is their plight and their desire to obtain work that many have chosen a walk which in this weather must be far from pleasurable. The "Chim Mail" bus it from an authentic source that 2,000 ex-strikers from Hongkong, endeavoured to return to the Colony yesterday by turn and were turned back on the borders. Not to be defeated in their object and under the pretext of returning, large numbers of them went back to "intermediate stations" and by a circuitous route eventually crossed the border.

It was probably one of these who made his way to the office of Dr. S. W. T'so, Assistant Controller of Labour, yesterday. Dr. T'so passed no opinion on the matter himself, but he certainly told a "China Mail" representative this morning that of the many coming forward and asking for work had been one man who was in great need of food and who had to pawn his trousers to get across the harbour. However, he must have had another pair, for Dr. T'so assured the reporter that he was respectably injured when he made his application.

Dr. T'so' felt convinced that the tide had well turned as regarded the return of general labour, and said that it had been noticeable ever since the issue of the proclamation dealing with idlers. Deck hands were among those now coming forward and asking for work.

Taken in conjunction with the fact that the police have seamen enough to man ships at present in the hubour, this might be taken to mean that there is nothing to prevent the ships here from leaving at once and for a complete return to be made to economic normality.

This, unfortunately, is far from being the case. The strikers in Canton may be anxious to return to employment; strikers who remained may have been frightened even more of being deported than of being intimidated, thus expressing a willingness to return to work; but the fact must be faced that trade here has been dislocated considerably.

Even crews to man the ships won't be much good unless there is the cargo to take" said a shipping man to a "China Mail" representative this morning. He added that as regards mercantile business there is "simply nothing doing" and boevcotting at Amoy, Foochow and other ports would still further affect the position. Earlier activity had, he said, been connected almost entirely with transhipped cargo.

headline: NO INTIMIDATION. / PARTNERS MERELY FALL OUT.
text:
At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, a partner of the Mow Ling restaurant, of 450 Shanghai Street, was charged with alleged intimidation of a fellow-partner. At the previous hearing of the case it was stated by the complainant that the accused threatened to destroy the shop if he (complainant) refused to join the strike.

The defence put forward by Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by Messrs. d'Almada and Nephew) was that there had been a dispute between the two partners in connection with the purchase of stores. The accused had no desire to close the shop, as he was afraid of losing his money. His Worship held that there had been a partnership disputed and discharged the accused.

headline: CANTON RUMOURS
text:
PRISONERS FOR WHAMPOA.

PLACED IN FOREFRONT IN NEXT RATTLE.

As the only intermediary between the city and Shameen is an American attache, it is naturally almost impossible authentically to detail events there but a rumour of even greater insistence than usual and in which credence is being placed in many circles is that the occupants of the Canton prisons have been sent to Whampoa, there to be trained in connection with the much talked of "attack on Shameen" when, so another rumour goes, they will be placed in the forefront.

headline: THE "TUNG ON. NOW LEAVING FOR KONGMOON.
text: Shameen being fully stocked with food supplies for the time being, the s.s. Tung. On, which the Government of Hongkong has temporarily taken over, is to leave to-morrow morning on the Kongmoon run with mail and a certain amount of provisions, also for passengers, the fares for whom will be much above the usual. The Tung On. will have the monopoly of this run also. The s.s. Tung On put in at the Douglas wharf when it returned from Canton this afternoon. The Government have temporarily assumed control of the wharf.

headline: INDIAN HELP.
text:
The Indian detachment of the St. John's Ambulance Brigade are working in co-operation with the Fire Brigade and have had many cases to contend with. In some of these they have been required to give assistance not only in getting "cases" to the hospital but also, owing to defections of hospital workers, to get them to bed. They have not only responded well but have been fully equal to the work and have received commendation. These volunteers are manning the new (Austin) motor ambulance and their hours are long, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. They are displaying as much eagerness and promptitude as are the firemen in answering calls, a "China

especially for us in the Straits the centre of interest in China has now shifted from Shanghai, the Yangtze ports and Peking to our own Colony of Hongkong, where the strike-evidently fostered by the Kuomintang authorities in Canton, is spreading rapidly and business has been disorganised to such an extent that the Stock Exchange has been closed and the June settlement indefinitely postponed. The situation cannot fail to be a trying and uncomfortable one for the local residents; but, with the ready co-operation and a certain amount of self-sacrifice on the part of the European population, the willing assistance of such bodies as the Boy Scouts and the Girl Guides, and the priceless help of the handy men of the Navy, the Colonial administration will doubtless be able to keep the essential public services going and we need entertain no fears as to the ultimate outcome. A number of emergency measures have already been proclaimed and we may rest assured that the whole of the law-abiding community of Hongkong will stand firm behind the Governor, Sir Reginald Stubbs, who has postponed his departure for England and expressed his determination to see the trouble through, with a significant hint to the lawless elements that his remaining on the spot does not betoken a settlement to their liking. The Government, in a crisis like the present one, can draw upon very extensive powers, usually held in reserve, and it is satisfactory to know that it will not hesitate to use them, if necessary; for, however true it may be to assert that the unrest in the first place had an industrial origin—and even of that, we have our doubts—it has long passed from that stage. The movement throughout China today is openly political and anti-foreign, more particularly anti-British, and in Shanghai and Hongkong the issue has been definitely joined between the forces of anarchy and those of law and order. In Hongkong, especially, there can be no shadow of an excuse for the outbreak, for as regards labour conditions and the social welfare of the working classes generally, that Colony has always been a model for China and only a day or two ago we were able to record the latest successful advance in legislation designed to protect the labourer's interests. In such circumstances there can be no thought of compromise. Whatever the inconveniences and discomfort—and they may be very unpleasant—or the temporary financial loss—and it may be very heavy—that individuals or corporations have to suffer, the community of Hongkong cannot afford to temporise with the leaders of disorder, for the slightest sign of weakness will be seized upon at once as a pretext for still more extravagant demands. The worker, who downs tools because he has a grievance, genuine or imaginary, in connection with his work may be ill-advised, but, provided he breaks no contract, he is well within his natural rights. The strike is recognised as a legitimate weapon against excessive hours of labour, unhealthy or oppressive conditions, and harsh employers. But when it is organised, not on industrial grounds, but from political motives and in order to terrorise the community and embarrass the Government, it falls in a different category altogether. And, accompanied, as it is in Hongkong, by a boycott, it becomes a direct challenge to constituted authority which must be accepted and fought as such, unless the whole basis of society is to be destroyed. Meantime, we have the satisfaction of feeling that the situation in Hongkong at any rate is in sound, firm hands, and we have no doubt also, that the authorities in British Malaya are fully alive to the possibility of some slight percussion in this part of the world and quite prepared to meet

headline: CHINA'S STATUS. / U.S. PRESIDENT MAKES STATEMENT.
text:
WASHINGTON SIGNATORIES.

President Coolidge has expressed the hope that conditions will permit the holding of a conference in the near future to discuss extra-territoriality in China as well as the Customs

He asserted that America's efforts in this connection were confined to the attempt to secure the participation of the nine Washington signatories. The President added that the United States had not entered into any agreement with Britain or Japan regarding China.

It is explained that Mr. Coolidge contemplates that the conference will consider all problems covered by the Washington Agreement.

The State Department is now communicating with the Washington signatories with the object arranging a conference in taking shortly.

Hitherto, those implying at the Police Station for work (where it is seen that it found employment they are paid in accordance with the work done) have been restricted to the coolie class. Included in their ranks lately, however, have been qualified men and enough seamen have now come forward, it is said, to man several vessels. Enquiries for their services should be made to the office of the Chief Detectiveist Inspector at Police Headquarters.

headline: DOSSER CASE.
text:
DENIAL OF SOVIET BRANCH IN SHANGHAI.

The American Assessor and Magistrate Loh heard the Fortuna toff case.

The British Assessor and Magistrate Shud are trying Dossier who denied a branch of the Soviet Communist Party existed in Shanghai, also all knowledge of the Agitation Department in Shanghai, adding he first saw the certificate when the Police produced it. He said "It is a rough forgery, made by a man not familiar with Party documents."

headline: EARLIER CABLE
text:
Eugene Fortunatoff, the Soviet Consulate Doctor appeared in the Mixed Court this morning, charged under Articles 142 and 143 of the Chinese Provisional Criminal Code with offering to bribe a public official.

Evidence of arrest was given, and the accused remanded on bail. $10,000 was offered, but has not yet been produced, but the Police expect to receive it this afternoon from the Soviet Consul.

The Police assert that the accused offered $10,000 to Municipal Constable Kedrolivansky (a witness for the prosecution in the Dosser trial) if he would sign a document stating that he forged the Dosser certificate on instructions from his British superiors, after which Kedrolivansky was to leave Shanghai.

headline: PLEA FOR UNITY. / FRENCH AMBASSADOR'S SPEECH.
text:
DANGER TO FOREIGNERS.

Ambassador Fleuriau, receiving the French Colony in London on the occasion of the National Fete, referring to the situation in China, said the existing system of treaties could not be touched without exposing foreigners in China to the greatest dangers. Agitators who excited good Chinese against foreigners would not engage in deadly work unless they were encouraged from outside.

He hoped all Governments concerned would unite to defend their nationals, not merely now by concerted measures for immediate protection, but in future by retaining the guarantee of old treaties until China was able herself completely to assure the safety of lives and property of all residents in China.

M. Fleuriau concluded by saying that world peace depended on the Franco-British Entente.

headline: BIG RAID.
text:
TRÓOPS AND POLICE CO-OPERATE.

IDLERS DEPORTED.

That the deportation order is not a mere bluff has been proved by the large numbers of idlers who have come under its provisions and have been despatched to Canton and other ports. That the object of the order is not merely vindictive but solely to give opportunity to those who are not working to do so and justify their subsistence on the Colony is also proved by a police report of a raid on Belchers Street, West Point, in the course of which one of the ringleaders of the striking butchers was found. He returned to work immediately on being threatened with deportation to Canton.

This raid was on a large scale and was made at 7 a.m. on Tuesday. A cordon was drawn around the area by troops, whilst the searches were carried out by the police. No arms were found, but 41 persons were arrested and taken to the Central Police Station. Of these, 34 were subsequently released and the remaining seven were sent to Canton. Those released had all got employment and were not strikers. In addition several butchers were provisionally detained, being released at the request of Sanitary Inspector Knight, who explained that there was no work for them at the moment.

Among those present at the raid were the C.S.P. (Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E.), the D. C. I. (Mr. T. H. King), the D.S.P. (Mr. D. Burlingham), and the A.D.C.I. (Mr. L. H. V. Booth).

Police raids of a similar nature are to be carried out so long as the present situation continues.

The s.s. Tung On, temporarily being run by the Government, on its last run to Canton took up 168 deportees. The run to Kongmoon will not start until to-morrow morning, when it will leave its temporary quarters at the Douglas wharf.

headline: EGG SUPPLIES.
text:
There has been no great scarcity of eggs since the strike began, but it was noticeable in the markets yesterday and this morning that the demand was likely to exceed the supply. The result was that no eggs of any description were to be obtained under 60 cents a dozen.

It is said that dealers have plenty of stocks in cold storage, but are unable to get the labour to take delivery.

With the expressed intention of "discussing means whereby a settlement of the present trouble may be arrived at" a combined meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and representatives of guilds, commercial societies and labour organisations, has been arranged at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce on Saturday 6th 2:00 p.m.

TO-DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, demand, to-day was 2s. 15/16d.

headline: CANTON REDS.
text:
REPORTED TO BE GAINING GROUND

Politically, there is no telling what may happen in Canton within the next few weeks, writes the "China Mail" correspondent.

As previously, reported differences appear to have been smoothed over on the surface. Now indications have become apparent that the section of the Kuomintang described by one Home paper as the Leftists of the Young China Nationalists, a term which may serve for the time being — the section which has displayed pronounced Communistic leanings, is gaining the upper hand and gradually asserting its power behind the scenes if not actually laying down the law on the surface.

In these abnormal times the Government must needs find revenue, especially as the ruling body has declared its intention of shunning the gambling and opium revenues. As was the case a year or two ago, attention has again been diverted to private property. So-called nationalisation is one of the main planks in the Leftist platform, and it is very difficult to ascertain if the programme once threatened will be carried out now.

Rumours are, of course, attached to these movements in the background. One to which considerable credence has been given by the merchants is known as the four-four-two plan. Given for what it is worth, the story goes that its sponsors have in mind the pooling of private-owned property—forty per cent. of the proceeds to go into Government workers, forty per cent. to the Labour movement, and the remaining twenty per cent. to the original owners.

The situation is neither tense nor normal. People seem to be of the opinion that neither side, i. e., the Left and those who do not approve of their teachings, feels strong enough to risk testing its strength, but that unforeseen circumstances may precipitate a crisis.

A Hongkong vernacular paper reports that strike pickets comprising men in uniform are now on duty on the Canton Bund, collecting $25 from every Chinese who wishes to leave for Hongkong. There may be truth in this, but it is doubtful if the money thus taken finds its way back to the Strike Executive.

headline: MOCK TRIAL.
text:
MANY CANTON STRIKERS INJURED.

BUILDING COLLAPSES.

Between forty and fifty Hong- kong strikers have been injured, some seriously, at a mock trial of an alleged spy and "traitor" at Tung Yuen, near the second bund, Canton, writes the "China Mail" correspondent.

A few days ago a Chinese who bore the appearance of the average workman was surrounded by a strike picket and accused of being a spy. It is believed that the unfortunate man is a striker himself but he had, apparently, incurred the enmity of a strike official. At any rate, he was roughly handled and subsequently marched off to the Strike Executive headquarters. A trial was ordered and was held, subsequently, close to a partly completed building which was propped up by beams.

Before the trial started, a large crowd of idlers had assembled to watch the fun. To obtain vantage points some of them entered the building in course of erection. Their weight was such that a collapse ensued, throwing the “court” into confusion.

Of those injured the majority were seamen. The "prisoner's trial has yet to come off.

headline: MORE RETURNS.
text:
EAMEN AMONG APPLICANTS FOR WORK.

A sign of the more hopeful outlook in the strike situation was the presence of a more varied class of workers at the Police Station this morning.

The Chief Detectiveive Inspector (Mr. Grant) supplied 1,000 cosies this morning against orders in hand from the various concerns requiring labour. All the orders were filled, and Mr. Grant was in a position to supply 500 more if necessary from the cooiles waiting on the compound for work.

A large number of seamen also applied for work. These included 60 sailors, a number of engineers, and coxswains. The engineers secured ready employment, as also some of the sailors and coxswains. Six coxswains, all holding certificates for steam launch work, attended this morning for work. They were being detained at the office pending the decision of the "Star" Ferry Company who had been communicated with as regards employment for these men.

headline: OFFICER'S INJURIES.
text:
Mr. Patrick, Chief Officer of the Hop Sang, which vessel was at the time at Kowloon Dockes, sustained injuries to his buck and wrist as a result of a fall into the hold yester-day.

Some of the staff of the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock were near at the time, and with their assistance Mr. Patrick was conveyed from the hold, and after temporary first aid had been rendered, the injured officer was taken by launch to the French Hospital at Causeway Bay.

The rainfall for the month of June at the Botanical Gardens was 24ins. 74 on 21 days, at the Matilda Hospital, Mount Kellett, was 21ins. 11 on 21 days, and at the Police Station, Taipo, it was 21ins. 17 on 18 days. The lowest barometer reading at sea level was 29ins. 582 at 18h on the 6th.

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
LABOUR TRIPLE ALLIANCE

PROPOSED MUTUAL AID:

. (Reuter's Service.)

The Conference of Trade Unions in London has approved the constitution of the proposed alliance between the miners, railwaymen, engineers and transport men, representing over five million workers, for “mutual aid” and more particularly to support the miners in the present dispute. The matter has been referred

The matter has been referred to the various Unions to consult constituents and to report to a further conference.

The word "Earthquake," is printed in large letters in Oxford Street. It only calls attention to the announcement, underneath it, that to show sympathy with the sufferers in the earthquake in Tokyo one should buy Japanese pearls in a shop next door.

Moscow, July 16.—General Hsu has arrived here and is to stay ten days.—Reuter.

headline: RASH LETTER.
text:
A PARIS EDITOR'S SENTENCE.

"KILL HIM LIKE A DOG."

Charles Maurras, editor of the "Action Francaise," has been sentenced to two years' imprisonment or, in default, to be fined 1,000 francs, on a charge of publicating an open letter declaring if the Minister of the Interior Schrameck attempted to disarm members of the League Action Francaise without disarming the Communists, he will kill him "like a dog."

headline: STRIKE NEWS. / FEW STRIKERS RETURN VIA
text:
POSITION LITTLE CHANGED.

The local strike position remains in a position of more or less deadlock in so far as strikers in Canton are concerned, although workers continue to dribble back who have never left the Colony but merely awaited developments. Still more have applied for their old positions at the Naval Yard, but they have, as warned before they left, to start again in their respective jobs. Many of them have lost their chance of reemployment as they are now called upon to pass a medical examination before they can reenter the service, and in the cases of the older men particularly this has meant rejection.

On enquiry at the Naval Yard concerning a rumour that the Naval Yard contemplated discharging all employees and closing down for a few weeks, the "China Mail" was informed that it was without foundation.

Although it is difficult to say whether strikers are walking in large numbers from intermediate stations on the Kowloon-Canton railway in order to avoid being turned back at Sumchun, it is known that more have re-entered the Colony in this way. Still more are taking ship from Canton to Macao, where they are allowed to land providing it is for the purpose only of transhipping. By this means many have returned to Hongkong, as three boats still maintain communication between Hongkong and Macao.

headline: Police Raid.
parent_headline: STRIKE NEWS. / FEW STRIKERS RETURN VIA
text: Another raid for the purpose of ridding the Colony of idlers was carried out by the Police at Hunghom this morning. Troops also assisted and a cordon was drawn round an area embracing Bulkeley Street and Wuhn Street. Houses were entered by the Police and as a result 62 persons were taken to the Police Station, where they are detained pending enquiries.

headline: RICE FOR STRIKERS. / CANTON OUTLOOK NOW WORST.
text: In spite of boasts that North China rice would be imported into Canton by way of direct shipment from Shanghai, prices of the staple food are shooting up, writes the "China Mail" correspondent. That there is a pronuncement of the event from the proposal of the Strike Executive to place an embargo on wine (Shamshu) brewing. Although a fairly large quantity of rice is used in this manner, the quality is poor and the percentage very small. If even the Samshu rice is needed to prevent a famine things must be fairly serious. Unrest is growing in the strikers' camp now numbering about 40,000. Within the last few days a very large number has departed by tow-boat for up-country points, so it is stated, to escape being enrolled in the Labourers' Corps. Had it not been for the pickets and the lack of direct transport to Canton, the number would have been reduced even further, concludes the correspondent.

headline: LEFT IN THE COLD. / CANTON STRIKERS DEBACLE.
text:
MISCHIEVOUS POLITICIANS.

Guild Professionals Lay

Throwing considerable light on the present outlook in Canton is a communication by an occasional correspondent to the "China Mail," which arrived via Macao and is given for what it is worth.

In effect the correspondent writes:— Down

It is now an open secret that both the Conservative and the "Leftist" parties in the Kuomintang are regretting having espoused the "professional" strike leaders' cause.

Shortly after the Yunnanese were expelled the "Leftists" began to assert their newly-found strength. The Left party, by the way, is that which is said to have Communistic tendencies. As was the case in the campaign with the mercenaries, labour assistance was very helpful. Accordingly, the Conservatives made it their policy to be friendly with the guild officials as well. In this way the labour "professionals" were given certain powers to organise the strike. Monetary help had also to be forthcoming and in this the politicians had to play a large, but now unwilling part.

After three or four weeks the politicians have found the policy unremunerative both practically and theoretically. The Conservatives are too busy looking after their own affairs and the Leftists are hard put to in finding means to provide 50,000 idle men with food. While the opposing cliques have been thus engaged, the strike leaders have more or less taken the law into their own hands by sending out their own police in uniform, collecting levies and even administering the civil power in their own weal. Neither side wishes to antagonise the strikers but to a greater extent, nobody wishes to shoulder the burden of providing for them. To get rid of so many hungry mouths it will first be necessary to clip the wings of the leaders who are preventing the rank and file getting away so that present conditions will continue and their sources of revenue will be maintained which is also for their own benefit.

During the last day or two, strikers have left Canton on a "pretence of wanting to go up country on some urgent private business. As they do not "declare" for Hongkong as their destination no poll-tax of $25 is collectable; to disencourage deserters a new rule has been put into effect, namely, that of obtaining a guarantee, by a well-established firm, of return within a certain period.

Even with pickets, levies and other impositions, strikers are running away from the fold, the majority being from the batches, which have been put through their paces in physical drill and military training on two scanty meals a day!

Were it not for the strict lookout in Hongkong and the rumours circulated in Canton of numerous deportations a debacle would have started already in Canton no matter what regulations had been imposed. If a free return to

Malicious rumours as to what is happening in Hongkong are not now believed so readily as Hongkong Chinese papers have reached Canton by roundabout routes and even purchased by strikers at fancy prices.

Even in the Seamen's Union itself there is discord. One official orders one line to cease running and another cancels it immediately. It is impossible to prove "squeeze." But I (writes the correspondent) have known people pay "tea money" for the privilege of shipping away vegetables even though the strike leaders have placed their own embargo on export.

Requests it is stated, have been addressed by Canton to the boats now on the Macao-Hongkong run asking the men on the ships to make sure that strikers are not taken back to Hongkong. This request, needless to say, carries not the least weight.

Since Saturday there has been a persistent rumour that shipping communication between Canton and Hongkong will be re-established. Once this is a fact, it will be safe to assume that the rank and file will leave Canton in ship-loads.

[By a curious coincidence the vernacular papers—of—Hongkong this morning all refer to the possibility of the steamers being back on the run.—Ed. "China Mail."]

headline: REGISTRATION OF SERVANTS. / A PRIVATE BUREAU.
text:
—In view—of the increasing demand for a system of registration or control of servants, it may be of interest to residents to note that a private concern — the Domestic Servants' Employment and Registration, Bureau—has been opened at 15-17, Queen's Road Central.

This Bureau was established just prior to the strike, and naturally, with the servants flying to Canton, its activities were stopped. At the termination of the strike, however, it hopes to supply servants of all kinds for a nominal fee. The Bureau supplies a registration card for a dollar, giving name, photograph, and finger print of the servant.

In the absence of any official scheme of registration of servants—upon which a pronouncement is most desirable, by the way—there ought to be room for a private Bureau, which deserves every possible support from the many who have reason to be impatient with. "the vexed servant problem." If some of the larger employers of domestic servants, such as the Hongkong Hotels, were to support the Bureau, it would give the rest of the community a much desired lead.

The matter of registration of servants is also to be dealt with at a meeting this evening of the newly formed Mid-Levels Residents' Association.

Beyond expressing it as the opinion of the meeting that such a scheme is desirable, it is unlikely that any further action will be taken for the present (nearly all of the members are said to be in favour of such a scheme, however).

Co-operation with other associations will be sought and the desire has been expressed that the registration should be through official channels. Falling this it is probable that members will endeavour to formulate a scheme on their own account. TO DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar on demand to day was 2/3.15/16

headline: Căn tải
text:
An indication of the stringency of money in Cautions is forthcoming from the proposed issue of bonds to the value of $180,000 for the Municipality. The issue is to be at $90, making the proceeds, if fully subscribed, $162,000: The odd $2,000 will be used, it is stated, for printing, and the remainder will provide the exact sum required to carry on.

From the "San Kwok Wa Po," one of the organs of the Kuomintang Party and the self-appointed mouthpiece of the strikers, I see that the compradore department of a ship which was to have brought back a cargo of rice for the hungry strikers, is accused of assaulting strike officials who went on board! Negotiations are pending. Meanwhile, the crew of the ship has struck, and the steamer has not sailed.

The Strike Executive has also run foul of the Police Department. Commissioner Techen Wu, chief of police, has, apparently, refused to hand over a number of men "arrested" by strike pickets as spies and the Executive is not in good humour. Then, again, the Police have issued an order forbidding strike pickets from searching business establishments for Hongkong notes, the Police maintaining that it is a duty for the law.

headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
AMPLE SUPPLIES FROM HONGKONG RESIDENT ENTERVIEWED.

That the Hongkong Government is Keeping Swatow well supplied with food now, that Chinese shops in Swatow are no longer supplying Europeans, was the statement of a well-known Swatow resident who arrived in Hongkong yesterday and with whom a "China Mail" representative chatted shortly after his

The food is being taken up by Japanese (chiefly those of the O.S.K.) and has to be unloaded by the foreigners themselves. Because of this, plenty of supplies were in hand, said the China-Mail-informant, and so long as this source continued, the situation would give no cause for anxiety.

Following are interesting facts, also emanating from the same source:—

Anti-foreign feeling is limited to a small section of the Chinese community, and the proclamations of the Chinese military general's calling for moderation are believed in official circles to be genuine expressions of opinion and in fact, to represent the wishes of the greater number of Chinese residents.

The Swatow Chamber of Commerce is actively opposed to the boycott in operation against British and Japanese goods, and is doing its best to defeat it.

The restriction against foreigners is not supposed to apply in the case of Americans, but as Chinese find difficulty in differentiating between degrees of nationality, they are in many cases suffering the inconveniences of others, particularly in regard to street conveyance, richest pullers, refusing to take any foreigners for fear of incurring the displeasure of those who have engineered the present state of affairs.

Mission doctors are allowed to retain the services of one boy and a cook each, they and the Americans being the only ones so "privileged." That no great alarm is felt as to the situation is shown by the fact that no residents have left other than one or two of the ladies and a few children. "Unless there is trouble in Canton, we shall be all right," was how the "China Mail" informant put it.

headline: OUR FLOGGING LAW. / THE QUESTION : RAISED AT HOME.
text:
HONGKONG'S NECESSITY.

As presumably it must, Hunkong has been, in the English gain at Home, and the measures taken by Sir R. E. Stoke have been endorsed.

In England."

Both Chinese and Europeans approved of the Ordinance to deal with terrorism which was being organised from outside for purely political motives. Mr. Morrison suggested the promulgation of the Ordinance would very seriously affect anti-British feeling in China. Mr. Ormsby-Gore replied that the Governor of Hongkong's first duty was to protect the lives of innocent people threatened by terrorism and bomb-throwing and if emergency threatened they must have emergency measures to prevent outrages on innocent people. He was sure the Governor had considered the matter from the viewpoint of its effect in China and he was supported by the Chinese members of the Legislative Council.

Mr. Will Thorne (Lab.) asked were there not other forms of penalty than flogging. The Hon. Mr. Ormsby-Gore pointed out that we did the same thing in England in cases of personal violence and he did not think it would be proper for the Colonial Secretary or the House of Commons to interfere with the discretion of a Colonial Governor and Colonial Legislature in the face of such an emergency.

headline: INTIMIDATION. / NO FLOGGING FOR A WATCHMAN.
text: A Chinese watchman employed at the Kowloon Docks, who was found guilty at the Kowloon Magistracy last week on a charge of intimidating a servant in the employment of Mr. "Kid" Marriott, was sentenced this morning by Mr. E. W. Hamilton to six months' hard labour. In passing sentence, His Worship said that he would not impose flogging in addition, as he considered that the accused had been in the Colony for some time and was one of those people who came from Canton to make trouble.

headline: Boys Charged.
parent_headline: INTIMIDATION. / NO FLOGGING FOR A WATCHMAN.
text:
Two Chinese houseboys in the employment of Mr. A. P. Glover, of the Tramway Company, and Mr. A. Kirk, of the P.W.D., were charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with intimidating a 'bus inspector at Shamshuo.

The evidence of the inspector was to the effect that he was stopped at Shamshuipo and told by the first accused that he would be killed if he continued in his work.

Mr. Glover stated in evidence that the second accused applied at the tramway depôt for work as an emergency conductor; but there being no vacancy he was offered work as a houseboy, which he accepted. Later the first accused visited his house to see his servant, and was suspected of being an intimidator but on finding that he was also looking for work he was passed on to Mr. Kirk. The man's visit was skid to have upset Mr. Glover's amah almost to the point of leaving.

headline: LESS WAGES.
text:
ISE FOR RETURNING STRIKERS.

KOWLOON DOCK POSITION.

With the exception of that aspect of it which involves the trade of the Colony, also the general body of seamen, the strike in Hongkong may almost be said to be at an end. Cases were reported yesterday of the tables having been turned on the strikers and their jobs having been filled by workers obtained from other sources. Yet another example of the determination of employers, wherever possible, to do without strikers is furnished by the action of the Kowloon Dock Company, the management of which has informed many launch men and others who have returned and applied for their old jobs that they can return again in a few months' time. In other cases the option has been given Kowloon Dock employees of returning to work but at greatly reduced wages and has been accepted by many. The strikers have learned, probably much to their surprise, that they are by no means indispensable, all departments of the Dock having carried on right from the beginning of the trouble:

headline: Seamen's Position.
text:
The general situation on the water front shows little sign of change, although the rumours of a likely start being made very shortly with some of the Canton boats are even stronger. It is said that the fear of consequences if they work the Canton boats is becoming less with many of the volunteer seamen than the fear of being deported if they refuse to work. They would certainly have the benefit of police protection and not be forcibly ejected at Canton in the event of them deciding to do the former.

That there is still intimidation even on the water front there can be little doubt, for the volunteer crews which were to have manned the s.s. Charles Hardouin and the s.s. Paul Beau failed to put in an appearance and consequently these ships were unable to leave for Macao to day, according to schedule. From inquiries made it appears that double, and in some cases treble, wages are being asked by these volunteers but, needless to say, it is extremely doubtful whether concessions of any kind will be made; and it is probable that, when faced with the alternative of working or of being deported, they will be glad to sign on at the ordinary rates of pay.

It is thought that sufficient seamen will be available to man both boats, and the arrangements at present are that the Charles Hardouin leaves at 8 a.m. tomorrow and the Paul Beau at 2 p.m. A service each way will be maintained.

headline: SWATOWS POSITION
text:
MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS EXPECTED.

DISPUTED AUTHORITY.

Reports were current in the Colony this morning that important, military developments were pending at Swatow with possible reaction on the Canton Government.

From inquiries in the most reliable sources it appears that General Chan Kwing-ming's subordinates are now asserting their authority, and that this has been resented by the commanders left behind by the Kuomintang. Another report is that General Chan himself is returning to Swatow to take charge of affairs but, in view of his recent complete defeat, and taking into consideration the fact that his lieutenants are not in unison, this is-improbable.

headline: ALLEGED THREAT.
text:
CHARGE AGAINST HOUSE COOLIES

INTIM昌ATION DENIED.

The hearing of charges of intimidation against two house coolies in the employment of Mr. A. P. Glover and Mr. A. Kirk respectively, we contended before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning.

The two accused were alleged to have threatened to kill a "bus inspector if he did not cease work. Two witnesses were produced by the accused house coolies, and both of them stated that they did not know the accused.

The second accused Mr. Kirk's servant said that he had had a quarrel with the bus inspector over a debt and was merely asking him for the money. He denied the charge of intimidation.

His Worship adjourned the case for one week, saving that he had a sound reason for doing so.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
Another sign of an early return to normal times is the prosecution of a number of unlicensed hawkers who persisted in selling food within market limits.

Another instance of the resolution to deal with strikers is that of an old lift “boy” who left his employers with about twenty years' service to his credit. He has been refused employment.

The small steamers Tack Hing and Sui. Yick are announced as due to resume sailings between Hongkong, Shanmei and Au Tau, a run which should appreciably augment the egg supplies of the Colony.

Thanks to efforts of Mr. Ho Kwong, chairman of the Trade Association, says a vernacular paper, a local Chinese merchant has obtained permission to ship away 10,000 sacks of flour to a “neutral” port so that stocks need not be unnecessarily tied up.

An occasional correspondent informs the “China Mail” that among the rather unusual means devised by the Strike Executive at Canton for raising the wind are the giving of theatrical performances by actors who are now taking their annual holiday, a sale of so-called donated art treasures, and the opening of a subscription fund among the tea-house singing girls.

headline: SEAMEN TIRED.
text:
WANT RIVER STEAMERS TO RUN.

CHANGE OF FRONT.

I have been informed on very good authority that some branches of the seamen have sent their own delegates to Hongkong to negotiate with Chinese owners of river shipping so that the Canton-Hongkong steamers will be in service once more. It is also stated that other guilds are more than sympathetic, as their members now openly desire direct communication with Hongkong to facilitate their getting back to work.

From another source I learn that strike pay and food are still being doled out, although distribution is irregular. In their campaign to raise funds the Strike Executive has now found that the Government coffers are not unlimited; and the leaders are turning their attention elsewhere. Property owners have had pointed out to them the boom in Canton as a result of the strike and influx into the city—hence an invitation to them to make advances to the cause. Native bankers are also said to have been approached, as some of them made fortunes in the rise of Canton subsidiary silver when the outcry against Hongkong banknotes started.

The split between the pro-strike and anti-strike factions is widening. Those who have made money are in favour, likewise some of the politicians who find in the men a useful weapon behind the scenes. At least one or two officials are beginning to realise what a nuisance 50,000 hungry men can be, but they are not powerful enough to lay down the law, and they are busy strengthening their respective positions.

During the last two days the exodus of strikers has increased, some going direct to Macao, and others by up-country routes. A few have preferred the land route or even a tedious junk journey.

headline: RETURNING BY MACAO.
text:
Each of the four steamers plying between Hongkong and Macao has brought several hundred passengers per trip on an average during the last two days. That there is plenty of “offering” on this line is revealed by the fact that other vessels are taking up the run, as reported elsewhere in this issue.

One man who came from Macao says that instead of holding the men, strikers leaving Canton are now told merely not to bring any vegetables with them.

headline: PATIENCE TRIED. / WHY CHINESE COME TO HONGKONG.
text:
Says the Singapore “Free Press”

"The patience of the Hongkong Government is sadly tried. It is a Crown Colony, and there is no question of retrocession or extraterritoriality. The Chinese go to the Island of Fragrant Waters because there is safety of life and property and good profits to be made. They voluntarily go under British rule, and therefore must be amenable to the just and firm hand which the Governor spoke about. A man has a right to strike, if he does it properly, but he has no right to break the laws at the instigation of a foreigner. Much more patience will be needed before calm succeeds to turmoil. Time is a great healer, however, and the object of the prime movers, the creation of a state of things favourable to Bolshevism or communism, has failed. But Governments have to be on continual guard lest the danger recurs."

During the 24 hours ended on July 24, one Chinese case of enteric fever was reported.

Paris, July 21. The final statistics of the elections of Consells Generaux show that the Left bloc has won 91 seats. In spite of the violent propaganda in regard to Morocco the Communists have suffered a complete defeat, obtaining but two seats.

headline: CANTON'S WAIL.
text:
“NATIONALIST” GOVERNMENT COMPLAINS.

HOME LABOUR HOAXED.

The Labour Party Press Bureau has issued a copy of a long cablegram from the Canton Nationalist Government complaining that the people had been misled in regard to the issue in China which, it asserts, is really agitation against "unequal treaties" imposed on China, alleging "inhuman exploitation" of Chinese in foreign Concessions, asserting that Chinese militarists are tools of Foreign Powers seeking to maintain their position in the economic and political domination of China, and demands the equality of other nations.

headline: RUHR FREE.
text:
CROWD'S MINDNIGHT REJOOLING

END OF OCCUPATION

The ringing of church bells, blowing of trumpets from spires of churches, sounding of syrens in factories and general rejoicing in the streets of the Ruhr at midnight greeted the end of the Franco-Belgaian occupation.

Euthusiastic crowds at Bochum and Gelsenkirchen sang patriotic songs, especially "Deutschland Uber Alles," but the hoisting of a black, white and red flag at a hotel in Bochum led to conflict between the Republicans and Nationalists, the former demanding removal of the flag. The police were called in to arrests were made, and peace was restored; after the hotel proprietor's request the police removed the flag.

headline: FLOCKING BACK.
text:
SHANGHAI MEN DEFY INTIMIDATORS.

BOYCOTT CAMPAIGN.

Numbers of strikers are still flocking back to work in spite of violent intimidation of which there has been a recrudescence in the last two days.

The Chinese Chamber of Commerce has decided in favour of the confiscation of British and Japanese goods in the possession of Chinese, and fining merchants who are not participating in the Brito-Japanese boycott.

The boycott campaign will commence on July 30 and be carried on for a year. A friendly gesture from the British Chamber was discussed, dubbed as insincere, and left over.

headline: "STAGNANT TRADE"
text:
MANCHESTER'S STOPPAGE FOR A WEEK.

LOW YARN PRICES.

(Reuter's Service:

The Short Time Committee at Manchester has recommended a weak's stoppage, in addition to the annual holidays, on the ground of stagnant trade. The decision is mainly due to
