text:
ion with the maintenance of military communication with Stonecutters and the landing of stores, applied for re-instatement to the military authorities. Knowing that, in accordance with the warning issued before they left, they would lose all benefits and even if they were taken back again would have to start all over again, they presented themselves yesterday and put in a list of impossible demands as conditions for re-employment.

The ridiculous demands made included the dismissal of a European officer who had been over them, the payment of the highest grade-pay in respect of each man, strike wages and guarantee of no victimisation. Needless to say, their demands were treated with contempt, and the water police were communicated with. The names of the men were given and if they are caught they will doubtless be deported.

The military authorities have managed quite well in the absence of these strikers and a regular service has been maintained along

correspondent has already reported an incident in which strikers pickets set sail in long row boats and took off a large number of passengers from a departing steamer, the passengers being mostly workers returning to Hongkong.

It now appears that the strike bosses at that port have not been allowed to do as they please nor to dominate men and women who do not wish to remain any longer.

A report has reached Hongkong and has been confirmed that a military officer at Kongmoor, with pronounced anti-Bolshevik lean-

headline: STRIKE OVER. / AUSTRALIAN SEAMEN TO RESUME.
text:
The shipping strike is regarded as definitely settled. The Federal Executive of the Seamen's Union has telegraphed all branches urging acceptance of the agreement reached by the sub-committee of the conference of owners and seamen. It must have been in a spirit of pure bravado that over 20 coxswains, engineers and lighter men previously employed in connect

the more conservative element of the Kuomintang Government is evident from a dispute which is being violently contested between the strikers and the authorities. To day the Strike Executive announced that they would petition the Government for permission to set up their own courts of justice to try their own cases. The strikers have been keenly disappointed because men they have arrested as “enemies” and “spies” have been liberated by responsible police officials to whom they were sent for custody. It is hinted that the Executive desires to usurp the ordinary power of local law officers to achieve their own ends. Over thirty men have been captured by strike pickets, and many of them have not been dealt with as the strikers would have wished. There has been friction already between the Police and the Executive, and an article in a Canton vernacular paper speaks in no uncertain terms as to what is wanted. Canton's Strike Executive has sent a telegram to the Shanghai headquarters pointing out that the military in berangling are helping stickers and the regarding them like the Pongeng and the

ings, has taken it on himself to snub the strikers by escorting passengers to ships departing for Macao, from whence a change may be made for Hongkong.

headline: DAYLIGHT ROBBERY.
text:
Five men who are alleged to have carried out an armed robbery in Kowloon at the residence of Mrs. Pabla Rojos were committed for trial at the Criminal Sessions yesterday after a hearing at the Kowloon Magistracy. Witnesses alleged against them that they were the men who knocked at the door of the house in question, in Tung Hing Road, and on being admitted by the amah, gagged and bound the inmates, relieving them of their valuables which amounted to about $180.

The robbery occurred during the hiffin hour and one of the victims was Mr. J. A. G. de Bernedo who was on a visit and participating in the meal of the time. He was bound and gasped by cold the court, and rocked of his money watch, the most重大. To-day being the first of the month was looked to by many to bring forth new developments in connection with the strike in Hongkong in connection with which there have been so many signs lately as the so-called strikers realizing the foolishness of their action, there was ever any danger of returned workers leaving again en bloc the fear of deportation to Canton has evidently been too strong for them and no further developments are to be reported this morning.

headline: STRIKE BOSSES. / KONGMOON'S SOUND COMMONSENSE / ORDER TO DEPART.
text: About three hundred strikers returning to Hongkong have to thank Chinese military officer who, by his action, condemned the Communistic policy of espousing the cause of Canton's labour china tains.

headline: STRIKERS' COURTS?
text:
RESULT OF FRICTION IN. CANTON.

COMPLAINT AGAINST MILITARY. It is stated that twenty picked soldiers were told off to protect about three hundred people embarking by the s.s. Foo Cheong from Pakkai for Macao. Those departing were put on board small boats at Kongmoon and conveyed to the steamer where the military soon let it be known that they would brook no interference. As it was the strikers pickets could do nothing but stare and the workers sailed in peace. They will have reached Macao in due course from whence they are expected to make for Hongkong.

That Canton's Strike Executive is becoming more and more estranged from the sympathy of the more conservative element of the Kuomintang Government is evident from a dispute which is being violently contested between the strikers and the authorities.

headline: LOADED PISTOL.
text:
Two Magistrates sat together, under powers invested in them by a recent “Gazette” announcement, to try an arms case at the Police Court this morning.

Divisional Inspector Blackman prosecuted two Chinese for the possession of a revolver, loaded in four chambers.

Accused pleaded “not guilty.” It is alleged that Sergeant Gough led a picket along the Shaukiwan main road. When near No. 4 bridge, which is about 150 yards from the tram terminus, he saw accused acting suspiciously and challenged them. As the sergeant and a Chinese constable went up, accused are stated to have discarded the revolver which was subsequently recovered by Sergeant Gough.

After evidence had been given and accused had denied possession, Mr. S. B. B. McElderry and Mr. R. A. D. Forrest adjourned the case till 10 a.m. on Wednesday.

Bail of $7,500 was allowed to a Chinese prosecuted at the Central Magistracy this morning by Revenue Officer Beattle for attempting to export saltfish. The case was remanded for a week when important developments are anticipated.

headline: AGREEMENT COMPLETE
text: The “Daily Telegraph’s” diplomatic correspondent states that the agreement between London, Washington and Tokyo is now complete regarding their and other Treaty Powers' reply to the demands contained in the Peking Government's Note of June 24. All remaining to be settled is, firstly, whether the reply shall take the form of a diplomatic note or an open declaration to the Chinese people; secondly, the dates when the fiscal conference and the extraterritorial commission will start work.

headline: ESPITE THE STRIKE.
text:
Hongkong has been without its noisy Chinese theatres for some time. Before the strike began, the "stars" of the professional troupes which were playing in the Colony, took panic and bolted. Since then there has been no show.

On Friday night the armateurs of the Chung Shing Benevolent Society opened a short season at the Ko Shing Theatre; below the Government Civil Hospital. It was just like old times with an enthusiastic house appleading; the fents of arms performed and the songs rendered.

The Chung Sling Society promotes entertainments on the lines of the plays given by the professional companies, the proceeds being mainly devoted to running a number of free schools and other objects of charity.

headline: RUSSIAN BONDS.
text:
The "Petit Poursien" says that since Krassin's return from Moscow the negotiations over the settlement of Russia's debts have become more active and it is hoped to reach a settlement shortly which will partially satisfy the holders of Russian bonds and will also be acceptable, both politically and financially, to the Soviet.

The Times correspondent in Paris says the Soviet offers to recognise in paper francs forty per cent. of the pre-war Russian debts amounting up four milliard paper francs or ten per cent. of the pre-war Russian debts calculated in gold, interest since 1918 to be added to this sum. The Soviet will issue new bonds representing the total obligation, which will take the place of the pre-war bonds, and after conclusion of the agreement a sum, covering interest payable on these bonds, will be included annually in the Soviet budget.

headline: HATE THE STRIKE.
text:
CHINESE' BUSINESS MEN'S DILEMMA

A Chinese of the merchant class was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with possession of a seditious pamphlet.

Mr. C. A. S. Russ, defending, said that he thought the document forming the subject of the charge was violently anti-British, but said that although business men hated the strike like poison these saitious pamphlets were forced on them. The accused, Mr. Russ said, came from Kogn moon where the pamphlet was handed to him and served the purposes of a passport. His Worship imposed a fine of $25 and issued a warning to the accused.

headline: LOCAL & GENERAL
text:
The return of notifiable diseases for the 24 hours ended Friday, shows a clean bill of health.

Passengers for the north per s.s. President Taft included Mr. J. Pasquier, Mr. T. H. King, and Mr. E. Rouilon, Peruvian Consultant Hongkong.

St. John's Cathedral notes for August is notable by reason of an interesting article on "The Art of Suggestion" by the Rev. R. J. Northcott

The engagement is announced between Lieutenant-Commander General Jackson, Royal Navy, of H.M.S. Defiance and Beryl, second daughter of Dr. and Mrs. G. Montagu Harston, of Hong-Kong.

The rainfall for July, at the Botanic Gardens, was 23.11 inches. On July 16 there were 10.88 inches following 3.04 inches on July 14 and 3.10 inches on July 15. On sixteen days during the month there was no rain at all.

Foreign residents at Pakhol were roused at midnight and ordered to the French gunboat, which eventually took them to Hongkong. Dr. Watson and the Rev. E. T. Loader, of the Church Missionary staff remain, the former in charge of the extensive medical and leper work controlled by the Society Messrs. Bell, father and son, long resident in Pakhol, absolutely refused to leave and are carrying on as well as such a thing can be done in the anti-foreign crisis.

An unfortunate occurrence attended a Chinese funeral which had gathered near the Victoria British School. The mourners had gathered at the foot of the hill, and there was much noise from a number of instruments blown by a number of young Chinese. A large motor lorry rounded the bend, making its approach known in the usual manner. One of the mourners misjudged distances and was knocked down. He was placed in the lorry and taken to hospital.

The preface to the sermon by the Rev. W. T. Featherstone published in Friday's issue was unfortunately omitted in the copies sent to the Press, due to the fact that in the manuscript it was in brackets. The preface was—“This sermon is based upon, and large extracts have been taken from, a chapter in a book called “China—An Interpretation” by J. W. Bashford, a Bishop of the Methodist Episcopal Church in China.” The figures “350,000” in column three should be “250,000 to 300,000.”

headline: SOVIET MODEL. / SUN YAT-SEN'S HOME TO START?
text:
Strikers

There have been persistent rumours that Canton intends to embrace Communism. It is now reported that a start is to be made with a "model district."

headline: TRAINED OFFICIALS.
text:
News has reached Macao that Canton intends to use the Heungshan districts—just across the border—as a model of Soviet government. By beginning on a small scale, the advocates hope gradually to extend the movement all over the province. Specially trained officials have arrived at Shekki, the district capital, to make a start. It remains to be seen how the idea will be received. [Heungshan is the birthplace of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen.] Java sugar intended for up-country ports has been seized in large quantities by strikers' pickets at Chinshan — opposite Macao, where the Shekki tow-boat calls. The strikers confiscated the sugar on the ground that it is British produce and, trading in such a commodity is violating the boycott order.

Some Japanese torch batteries were also seized. Instead of dumping the batteries in the river, the pickets distributed them among themselves for use to carry out other duties, when they are supposed to be the champions of the boycott movement. A strict watch is still being kept on boats leaving for Macao but foodstuffs and passengers are still arriving, the latter generally re-shipping for Hongkong.

headline: EDUCATION BOYCOTT.
text: Making all the money under a pretence of having to feed strikers, labour leaders now suggest appropriating flood relief funds. About $200,000 was left over from the previous flood relief campaign, contributions to which had been made by Hongkong and other ports.

headline: CANTON UNMASKS.
text:
OPIUM BOILING AND GAMBLING LICENSED.

Having started off with what it probably hoped would be looked upon as a gesture signifying its having at heart the true welfare of those at Canton, the Canton Government has been obliged to discard even the pretention of observance of its pious aspirations in regard to the suppression of opium and other evils. It has now granted permission for the resumption of opium boiling and the fees obtained from this source are to be paid into strike funds.

Gambling houses, also, are to be re-opened, and the money obtained from these sources is to be used for the purpose of making the new road from the East Bund to Whampoa, which is "to commemorate the strike."

The hold which the strikers have even in the administration of so-called justice, is apparent from the following incident.—Two launches used for the purpose of towing at Shek Ki have been seized by strikers and used for the purpose of visiting junk and boats. When the owners protested to the Magistrate at Heungshan the latter made an order for the return to them of the launches. The strikers retaliated by sending a telegram to Liu Chung-hoi, whereupon the Magistrate was deprived of his post.

headline: SWATGW RESTRICTION
text: Seamen controlling affairs at Swatow have announced that all persons wishing to return to Hongkong must first obtain a permit from strike headquarters, for which they will be charged $20. Delegates have been sent to Kongmoon to demand the balance deposited with merchants there. Liu Chung-oi, the Labour Finance Minister, is reported to have proposed drastic financial reforms.

headline: China / LOYAL CHINESE. / IMPORTANT RESOLUTIONS CARRIED. / BOLSHEVISM OPPOSED.
text:
"That the Chinese merchants resident in the Colony are desirous of expressing their thanks and gratitude to the Governor of Hongkong for his promptness in enforcing the emergency measures for the preservation of peace in the Colony, to which they owe their safety."

That regarding the present strike, we merchants are dead against it, and that in our opinion, the striking labourers themselves are not in

favour; but they have been forced to declare a strike by pressure from outside, and terrorised to leave their employment by intimidation.

That, with regard to the enforcement of Bolshevik measures by the de facto Government in Canton, which are aimed at the disastrous destruction of commerce and serious entanglement of finance as well as cutting off the supply of foodstuff from Canton to Hongkong, as preliminary steps to Sovietise the place under their rule, we merchants are desirous of expressing our strong opposition thereto."

The resolutions were put to the meeting, and passed unanimously. Mr. Ho Kwong, in thanking those present for their attendance said that he would communicate the result of the meeting to the two Chinese Unofficial Members of the Legislative Council, and request them to convey same to the Government, so that the above resolutions may be forwarded to the Home Government by cable.

It has been stated that the students of Canton are to boycott British and French educational institutions such as the Holy Trinity, St. Hilda's, Sacred Heart and other schools.

Some of the malicious propaganda served out here includes a report of a strike at Singapore whence several thousands of strikers have returned to Canton by way of Hongkong!

headline: RESOLUTIONS APPROVED BY AMOY. / PROMPT ACTION URGED.
text:
Strong approval and endorsement of the resolutions passed at the public meeting of residents in Hongkong are signified by the residents of Amoy in a cablegram received this morning by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak. A combined meeting of the committee of the Trade Protection Bureau and those of the Co-operative Society of the 24 Commercial Guilds was held at noon to day on the first floor of the City Hall. Mr. Ho Kwong presided. The object of the meeting was to consider; and if thought fit, to pass the following three resolutions:

The cablegram adds that the anti-British boycott, which is causing incalculable loss to British interests, is not supported by the Chinese merchants generally; and the threatened strike is being forced on unwilling employees by direct threats of violence.

The state of terrorism existing in the Chinese city is distinctly traceable to Canton Bolshevik agencies, the message goes on to state, and the residents consider that strong and prompt action is necessary to prevent the situation in the coast ports from becoming hopelessly out of hand.

The residents of Amoy request Mr. Holyoak, as one of the conveners of the meeting in Hongkong, to wire the endorsement and statement of facts to the same quarters in London at their expense.

The cablegram signed by Mr. Hinton, Secretary of the Chamber of Commerce.

Mr. Holyoak informs the "China Mail" that he has passed on the contents of the cablegram to the Government at Home.

headline: BHANGHAI POSITION.
text:
The time elapsed since the meeting was held in Hongkong is not sufficient for comment, yet to have appeared in Shanghai papers, but the actual resolutions have been favourable commented on.

As regards the general situation in Shanghai, there is a slight improvement in clearances, but the attitude taken up by the Chinese Seamen's Union is delaying a settlement. Even when the boycott is lifted, it is felt among business circles that it will be a long time before conditions are established favourable to free movement of goods inland.

headline: EXPERIMENTAL RUN. / HAI NING LEAVES TO BRING BACK TEA.
text:
POSITION OF DOUGLAS BOATS

The s.s. Hai Ning (Douglas Steamship Company) leaves this afternoon for Foochow, the intention of the owners being that a cargo of tea should be brought back. Foochow will be the only port of call.

It will be recalled that a similar trip was accomplished a short time ago, but on that occasion Swatow and Amoy were called at and owing to difficulties experienced not all the cargo could be discharged although passengers were landed.

Probably on this occasion, as on the last, loading of tea at Foochow, or rather Pagoda anchorage, will have to be carried out by the crew of the Hai Ning owing to the strike of labour, but in any event there should be guarantee of conveyance of the goods as far as the anchorage as the launches of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire and Jardine's are being manned by Europeans and loyal cews. Seen this morning by a “China Mail” representative, Mr. H. P. White, principal, Douglas Lapraik & Co., said that the impression that had unaccountably gone abroad that the last run of the Hai Ning was disastrous financially was quite wrong. As regarded future movements of Douglas boats they were only waiting for the cargo; there was no difficulty as regarded crew. To-day's departure was more or less an experimental run, said Mr. White, but the tea season was now in full swing.

A riosha coolie was knocked down at Connaught Road Central yesterday by a motor car driven by Dr. Li Sung. The man sustained injuries to his body and had to be taken to hospital.

At the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday, the mistress of a junk was fined $48,000 and $12,000 on charges of unlawful possession of 100 tails of prepared opium and 600 tails of raw opium respectively, or on the alternative twelve months hard labour in respect of each charge. the exception of 3s. a gallon on wine and 11s. a gallon on spirits. You can rent a nice house and garden for about £2 a month, and a regular country mansion with big grounds for a modest "fiver" a month.

headline: China / MR. SUN FO. / SUDDEN MISSION TO PEKING.
text:
WHAT HAS HE GONE FOR?

Sun Fo arrived at Peking this afternoon accompanied by the Canton Foreign Commissioner, Mr. Fu Ping-chang. Governmental departments sent representatives to meet him. Mr. Sun Fo is reported to have come here to make arrangements for his father's funeral, but it is stated that he will also probably discuss the Shameen affair with the Government.

headline: POLITICAL SIGNIFICANCE?
text:
Mr. Sun Fo, as most people will know, is the son of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen. He was at his father's bedside when the latter died in Peking but returned to Canton subsequently.

Prior to Dr. Sun's departure for the North, Mr. Sun Fo had been Mayor of Canton for some time, being the first to hold that post when municipal administration was mooted.

In the subsequent re-organisation of the Kuomintang Government at Canton, after the Yunnanese and Kwangsi mercenaries had been expelled, Mr. Sun Fo was given the post of Minister of Communications.

According to rumours current at the time of Mr. Sun Fo's departure from Caxton, he was going either to Shanghai, Peking or to interview Marshal Chang Tso-lin. Mr. Sun Fo is not considered to be one of the Canton radicals. When party strife was being waged in Canton, Mr. Sun's name was connected with the "Prince" party which did not see eye to eye with the allegedly Communistic party. His present mission to Peking may have even more significance than hinted in Reuter's cable, perhaps discussion with either Feng Yu-hsiang (the Christian general), Tuan Chi-jul (the Chief Executive) or Chang Tso-lin (the Mukden warlord).

[As reported in the “China Mail,” Mr. Fu Ping-chang (or Fu Ping-sheung, in Cantonese) is the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs in Canton. He is fairly young and belongs to Mr. Sun Fo's clique. Educated at St. Stephen's College, he graduated from the Hongkong University. Last year he took part in the negotiations regarding the Sha-meen strike.]

headline: LIGHTNING TOLL. / FATE OF TWO VILLAGE CHILDREN.
text:
A sad accident befell two children from the village of Lok-machau, in the New Territories, when they were returning to their home early on Monday morning after completing an errand

The children were forced to seek refuge under a tree from the rain, which later developed into a violent thunderstorm. NATIVE REPORTER AS COMPLAINANT.

A clap of thunder which shook the village caused uneasiness in the minds of the relatives, and as soon as the storm had abated they set out in search of the children. They found only the charred remains of the unfortunate children, as the lightning had struck both the trees and those who sought shelter at the foot. A reporter of a vernacular newspaper was the complainant in a case at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese shopkeeper was charged with intimidation.

headline: ALLEGED INTIMIDATION.
text:
An application made by Mr. J. A. Gordon Leask for bail was refused by the Magistrate (Mr. E. W. Hamilton) who characterised the offence as a serious one and running on a par with those perpetrated in Peking.

According to information given by the complainant, Lau Mancho, when applying for a warrant of apprehension, he had been threatened by the accused for reporting a case concerning a night soil coolie heard before the Secretary for Chinese Affairs and had been asked to publish a different statement and an apology. The case was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: STRIKER'S PAY.
text:
WHAT ARE THE NAVAL YARD DOING?

A PECULIAR REPORT.

Reports still continue to be received of strikers returning on the one hand and others being employed to take the place of strikers on the other.

The Dairy Farm has had a number of workers return and about 40 per cent. of old Naval Dockyard employees are now at work. The Government Civil Hospital has taken on a large number of men to replace strikers.

The China man learns from a reliable source that the attitude that the Naval Yard authorities are taking to returning strikers is that they should be placed on the lowest grade payment of their particular class of work only for a week or two after rejoining, the opinion being that this is sufficient to bring home to them the unlawfulness of their action in leaving. Many strikers are now reported to be earning pre-strike pay.

The Naval authorities refused to confirm or deny this, however, a “China Mail” representative being told that they had nothing to impart to the Press as to the attitude they were adopting.

headline: NO NOTICE.
text:
AMAH WARNED BY MAGISTRATE.

A Chinese amish until recently in the employment of Mrs. Gibbieson, of No. 3, Torres Buildings, was charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning for leaving without notice.

It was stated by the complainant that the accused first left the house on June 3. She came back on July 1, worked five days and left again.

Questionsed by the Magistrate as to the date on which the accused was stated to have first left, which was long before the strike commenced, the complainant stated that there had been no mistake. She said that she did not desire to press the charge, but only wished that the accused would not molest a new family since engaged by her. His Worship discharged the accused with a warning.

headline: MACAO PICKET. / STRIKERS' BRANCH AT CHINSHAN.
text:
LEVIES FROM TRAVELLERS.

Because workers from Hong Kong have managed to get here by the Shekki tow boat, a striker's branch depot has been started at Chinshan, which is in Chinese territory, just outside the Macao boundary. Instead of coming direct to Macao, the Shekki tow boat now calls at Chinshan where passengers landed. All those who want to pass the Chinese border are interrogated by a picket. It is stated that workers are not allowed to go and that others are mulcted in “fines” of $20 or $25 for the privilege of going through.

headline: ANTI-STRIKE ORATOR / ALLEGED THROWING OF STONES. / TWO CHINESE CHARGED.
text:
A case of much interest to the Chinese community was again adjourned by Mr. R. A. D. Forrest when informed this morning that the proceedings would last several hours owing to there being a number of witnesses on each side.

Sam Choi, an accountant of the Kwong Sang Hong Company, defended by Mr. C. A. S. Russ, and Wong Chuen, defended by Mr. C. H. Lyson, were the accused persons in the prosecution which is being conducted by Mr. T. H. King, Director of Criminal Intelligence.

The two accused were taken into custody for alleged stone throwing at a street lecturer, who is stated to have been delivering an oration against the strike under the auspices of the Labour Maintenance Association, and in addition to disorderly conduct they are charged with intimidation.

Bail for the second accused was fixed at $500. Mr. Lyson's application for a reduction was unsuccessful.

The case was fixed for hearing at 12 noon, to-morrow, and during the afternoon.

headline: LOCAL TRADE.
text:
MERCHANTS AND FUTURE PROSPECTS.

Seen this morning in connection with the departure yesterday of the Wosang for Tientsin and the Hangsang for Bangkok, Mr. Ho Leung, compradore of Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., in reply to the question whether such movements could be taken as representing a return to anything like normal trade conditions, said that the merchants were doing their best and would continue to do so. It was hoped for instance, to get another boat away for Tientsin on Thursday or Friday, but it was impossible to forecast regarding prospects of future general movements of goods, so much hinged on Canton. The Wosang, with a cargo of rice and sugar, was the second boat that the Indo-China Steam Navigation Company had got away to Tientsin since the strike, and in all eleven had been cleared.

headline: ARMS CASE. / LENIENCY FOR PANTRY BOY.
text:
At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, before Mr. E. W. Hamilton, an Annamite pantry boy of the French steamer Angers, was charged with the unlawful possession of an automatic pistol and ten rounds of ammunition. The accused was given a good character by an officer of the vessel, and His Worship took a lenient view of the offence by imposing a fine of $500, or in the alternative, six months hard labour. Lloyd George goes on making his phrases. "Mr. Baldwin has ceased to be a Premier," he said the other week. "He is now

other passengers eventually, his story to the pickets being that he was going on his business to Mucao. There could be no question of Club boys leaving Canton en bloc, the "China Mail" was informed, as the homes of some only were at Canton, and those of others at Heungshan and many other districts. It had been understood from two cook boys who returned that a few other cook boys in Canton wished to return, but so far they had not put in an appearance. The two, who had actually got through had done so by junk.

headline: CAPT. NEVILLE. / LEAVES FOR HOME TO-MOUROW. / AN UNFUNDED RUMOUR.
text:
Rumours that have circulated as to the departure from the Colony this week of His Excellency the Governor must have had as their origin the imminent departure of his A.D.C., Capt. R.A.R. Neville, R.M.T.I., who has booked passage Home by the Empress of Australia and leaves tomorrow. He was last seen alive by the assistant superintendent of the Home at 10 o'clock on Monday night, and he then appeared to be his usual self.

Both by reason of his important post and his keenness and proficiency at polo (the was Secretary of the Polo Club) Capt. Neville was a well-known figure in the Colony and none is in a better position to testify to the never-failing courtesy shown by him to all who had occasion to call at Government: House than the local Press representatives. His presence here will be missed and the "China Mail" echoes the sentiments of all residents in wishing Capt. Neville a holiday at Homemone the less pleasant by reason of it being delayed through the strike of recent origin and a successful future in whatever sphere of activity to which he may be called. His departure was not in the nature of an indication of His Excellency's imminent departure, he informed a "China Mail" representative this morning. His Excellency's intention was to remain at Hongkong for at least another month. No news had been received as to future appointments here or as regarded the future post to be held by His Excellency. The deceased was Captain W. K. Richardson, late of the s.s. Confucius, which is at present operated by a Chinese firm at Bonham Strand.

The police officers found the deceased lying on the floor in a pool of blood with two broken lemonade bottles beside him. The upper part of one of the bottles, which had broken with a sharp point, was found embedded in the right foot, and this had severed an artery. A sponge rag wound round the foot indicated that the deceased had made an unsuccessful attempt to stop the flow of blood by bandaging the wound. One of the heads of the lemonade bottles was found outside the window. It was clear that the deceased had attempted to open the lemonade bottles by striking the heads against the window sill and in doing so dropped a fragment on to his bare foot just above the slipper.

None of the inmates appears to have heard any cries for help from the deceased, and his accidental death was only discovered in the morning.

The body was removed to the public mortuary, and the arrangements for the funeral were made by the superintendent of the Sailors' Home.

The deceased is said to have been about 50 years old.

passengers were put ashore and the vessel taken to Canton by the delegates who were backed up by armed pickets. It is believed that the “confiscation” was because of alleged carrying of foreign cargo, a contravention of the strike leaders' orders. A shipper of Chinese preserved delicacies and sweetmeats told me that he has been informed that his property was not “confiscated” because it is Chinese produce; but because of its “having been contaminated by being put on board a vessel which had foreign goods” it is not to be returned and has already been eaten by the labour representative who took charge of the boat on its arrival at Canton.

In spite of all that has been lone, native foodstuffs are still moving about, although dealers in Chinese territory have to act like mugglers to get past the pickets.

headline: NOVA SCOTIA STRIKE
text:
PROTRACTED STRUGGLE ENDS AT LAST.

AN INTERIM CONTRACT

Halifax (Nova Scotia), Aug. 6. The protracted coal strike has been settled. Both miners and directors accepted the Nova Scotia Government's proposal for an interim contract for six months, pending a thorough investigation of the industry.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
Halifax (Nova Scotia), June 12. Five hundred local militia and permanent forces entrained last night for duty at the Cape Breton coalfields where clashes took place yesterday between striking coal miners and the police and officials of the British Empire Steel Company, which resulted in one miner being killed and thirty-strikers and police injured.

The strikers number 12,000 and have been out for three months. The miners controlled the power house from where they were ousted by the company's officials and police after a pitched battle. The company is endeavouring to keep maintenance men in the mines to prevent further flooding.

Glaes, Bay (Nova Scotia), June 12. Further acts of violence on the part of the Cape Breton strikers were reported early this morning, the men looting four companies' stores and damaging the fixtures. The, strikers forced an entry into the power station and destroyed switch boards and other essential plant, completely cutting off the supply of power from the mine pumps. The provincial police have arrived and are restoring order.

(Place Bay (Nova Scotia), June 13, During an attack on the Power Station, fifteen mounted police charged the mob but fell into the hands of the strikers who beat them severely. The injured police were removed to jail where an infuriated crowd gathered. Only the intervention of two clergy-men prevented the lynching of the police.

Sydney, Nova Scotia, June 14. While the attention of the Police and Fire Brigade was distracted by a fire alarm in another quarter of the town, strikers raided the premises of the Steel Corporation, Sydney. The mines were looted for food and clothing which were carried off in the Company's wagons.

The Company's stores at Hali-fax and "Glace Bay" were also raided. It is estimated that during the past three days the Company's property has been damaged and looted to the extent of $250,000.

Military reinforcements are on the way to the scene of the disturbances.

The committee of the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce will meet at 2 p.m. tomorrow to discuss business matters of importance.

headline: FOOD SHIPMENTS.
text:
STRIKERS "CONFISCATE" TOW-BOAT.

DELICACIES APPRECIATED.

It has now transpired that the tow-boat which plies between Macao and Shekki has been “confiscated” and taken to Canton.

When steamer communication between Canton and Macao was suspended, the tow-boats carried full loads of passengers and cargo, thus maintaining connection between Hongkong and up-country ports. Evidently the Strike Executive at Canton took exception to the tow-boats continuing the run and sent down delegates to the spot.

On her last trip, the tow-boat eferred to was ordered to stop in Chinese waters. The crew and

headline: NAVAL YARD WORKERS.
text: The Commodore informs the "China Mail" that the report published as to the re-instatement of returned strikers at the Naval Yard at pro-strike scale of wages is incorrect. The question of pre-strike wages is still under consideration.

headline: FRENCH BANK
text:
STRIKE SPREAIDS TO THE PROVINCES.

READ POVERTY ALLEGED

The strike of bank employees is spending, especially in the Provinces where the South Western Bunk Employees' Federation has joined in.

The clerks of the Banque de France decided to send a delegation to the management demanding an increase in the salaries of clerks. Delegates of the Paris strikers waited upon the Labour Minister, who promised to exert his influence with the bulk managements to give a prompt answer to the men's demands.

The inter-banking business has not suffered, though business with customers has been considerably affected and the Bourse inconvenienced.

Whilst the management's declare that bank dividends have not changed since 1913, although salaries have increased three and four fold, the men assert that real poverty exists, a man of 40 receiving only 800 francs monthly.

headline: PEKING STRIKE. / BRITISH LEGATION SERVANTS LEAVE.
text: Some servants belonging to the British Legation staff and the Legation Guard have walked out; presumably, owing to Student Unions' intimidation. It is understood that the Waichiaopu Is-taking steps with a view to arranging a settlement. NO WATER FOR CUSTOMS OFFICERS?

headline: FRENCH LOSSES.
text:
THE HEAVY COST OF REBELLION.

It is learned that the French casualties in the recent engagement against Druse rebels, amounted to 200 killed and 600 wounded. Civilian traffic between Damascus and Sermakh is suspended. TO DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar on demand to the market was not as high as the price of the货币. The coolies and sailors, however, showed fight and a brawl ensued between them and the anti-foreign pickets.

headline: Sleeping In Safety
text:
There is no change to report in the “strike” situation at Pakkai. With the exception of crews and domestic servants, all employees of foreigners are at work. The foreigners are now sleeping in the Customs compound to ensure safety at night.

The s.s. Foo Cheong is maintaining communication with Macao. Only passengers are carried. The strike pickets are preventing people leaving for Macao even by tow-boat.

Over a hundred Kung Tuen ("Labour Corps") soldiers have arrived here from Canton. Irresponsible people say that a few appear to have been enlisted from pardoned outlaws.

headline: CANTON RULERS.
text:
GENERAL LEUNG HUNG-KAI DETAINED?

DISPUTE OVER REVENUE

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Aug. 2. (Arrived by post yesterday.) Persistent rumours have been circulated here that General Leung Hung-kai has been detained by the Kuomintang Government at Canton.

General Leung commands an army under General Hsu Shungchi, commander-in-chief of the Cantonese Army and he proved his loyalty to the cause by sending his troops to attack Canton from the West when the Yunnan and Kwangsi mercenaries were routed about two months ago. Since then there has been reorganisation with the result that gambling and the sale of opium have been pro-

headline: COAL CRISIS.
text:
PARLIAMENT OR SOVIET— WHICH?

A VITAL QUESTION.

On behalf of the Mining Association, Mr. Philip has made public that the public is in the same form next May, unless the situation is resolutely faced in the interval. He declares that the small body of extremists controlling the Miners Federation never intended to arrive at a settlement, of the dispute and did not want industrial peace, but the overthrow of private enterprise and the existing structure of society.

A lasting settlement is impossible until the constitutional issue is faced: viz., are we to be governed by Parliament or a Soviet acting in the name of the Labour movement?

Mr. Saklatvala's View. London. August 7.

The House of Commons agreed to the report stage of the coal subvention; after a few speeches by Labourites.

Mr. Saklatvala contended that if profits in the British coal industry could be restricted in order to preserve wages, the same thing ought to be applied to British mine-owners in South Africa, China and India. Wages in those areas could not be reduced to the minimum and react on British wages.

Mr. Purcell declared that conditions in the coal industry in China and India were shameful.

Mr. Bromley and Mr. Purcell both denounced what they described as the threats made yesterday in regard to what would happen if the Trade Unions supported the miners again. They declared that no threats would prevent them from again supporting their comrades, if it was necessary to secure fair conditions.

headline: STRIKE REVIEWS.
text:
PROTECTION TO WORKERS ON RETURN

REASSURING STATEMENTS.

Important statements which should undoubtedly reassure the Chinese were made by Mr. T. H. King, D.S.P. and Director of Criminal Intelligence, yesterday afternoon, when interviewed at Police Headquarters by a reporter representing the vernacular Press.

The reporter pointed out that rumours had been circulated giving the impression that strikers returning to Hongkong were harshly dealt with by the Police, such rumours causing workers to refrain from coming back for fear of getting into trouble. An assurance was sought and given. Mr. King said that during the last fortnight several hundreds had returned to the Colony, this number including skilled labour. After the usual interrogation and bona fides were proved, the returning men were not only given liberty but protection was also extended to them, said Mr. King.

In the interests of peace great care had to be exercised in examining people who came here, such examination being to prevent agitators getting in to create trouble or an unsettled feeling. Inquiries had to be made, but men detained from incoming ships were not managed when they were taken up to the detective offices to be questioned. Should satisfaction be given by putting out an employer, or a shop, or by giving a guarantee, those detained were released.

The reporter also asked about the procedure adopted in sending idlers from the Colony in view of rumours having been heard that deportees were put ashore at Chek Wan (which is just beyond Deep Bay, in Chinese territory and a good distance from Canton) because whole batches had been refused admittance into Canton by the authorities up there.

Mr. King replied that no such thing had ever occurred. Owing to the vessels on which deportees were sent away not going alongside wharves at Canton, idlers had to be put ashore in rowing boats; hence arose the Chik Wan rumour—as a matter of fact, no batch had been sent back by Canton, added Mr. King, as quoted by the vernacular papers.

Mr. King also said that the Police had heard of wild stories about agitators who were bent on getting into Hongkong and creating trouble. Accordingly the Police had exercised the greatest care in supervising the arrival of people from other places. The strike had now lasted about two months and the reporter himself, as a pressman, would know that order had been maintained, continued Mr. King. Latterly there had been one or two cases of fuses being let off, but there was no panic over the incidents.

headline: MACAO STEAMERS.
text:
TWO DEPARTURES THIS MOBNING

INTIMIDATION AGAIN?

This morning the Steamboat Co.'s S.S. Sui Tai left as usual for Macao, but the other steamers which fly the British flag are not keeping up the services. If is stated that intimidation by the Seamen's Union at Canton has had an effect on the crews on arrival at Macao. The Paul Beauleth Hongkong this morning, but the Charles Hardouin did not go. The Sai On is stated to be ready to leave tomorrow morning. The Chuen Chow is tied up at Macao and the Ko Chow at Hongkong.

headline: FATAL CLASH. / EXCITING SCENES IN TIENTSIN.
text:
A riot took place shortly after the withdrawal of the main police guard from the cotton mills last night. A crowd of rioters attacked the mills and destroyed the machinery. The strikers were reinforced by farmers and peasants from neighbouring villages. Before this an angry crowd made the small police guard absolutely helpless.

All machines were damaged and the loss is estimated at $1,000,000 in one mill alone.

When the news reached the Chinese Yamen, a strong force o police and military was sent to ound up the rioters.

Early this morning 800 police and soldiers were around the mills and a crowd estimated at 10,000, who greeted the guards with showers of stones and mud. The troops then attempted to arrest a number of the most prominent agitators, but were strongly resisted. The position of the guards then became serious, many being roughly handled, and rifle butts being used freely, but the rioters appeared to the determined not to give any quarter, and the guards were compelled to fire low at first and then to kill.

headline: Police Too Strong.
parent_headline: FATAL CLASH. / EXCITING SCENES IN TIENTSIN.
text:
Riot's then ensued amid an indescribable scene of panic. Unable to get away from the rifles of the police, the leading ranks of rioters turned to fight those behind, while the unlucky ones dropped dead or were wounded. Many jumped in the Hailo River to avoid bullers and a number are believed to have been drowned: The total casualties are believed to be in the neighbourhood of 60, of which eight were killed. No police were killed, but several were badly injured.

Later 376 rioters were arrested and taken under a strong guard to the Yamen on the ex-Austrian Concession.

The police have now closed all Labour Union Offices in the Chinese city and arrested many Union officials. No gatherings of students and strikers are being allowed.

The Chinese authorities are now giving full protection to crews of steamers. The police escorted a number of men to Tongku, where they are embarking on vessels. This action is necessary owing to the kidnapping of several Chinese members of British crews.

headline: FRENCH STRIKE.
text:
BANK CLERKS ACTIVE IN THE PROVINCES.

GOVERNMENT'S DECISION.

The strike of employees of some of the smaller banks, especially in the provinces, demanding increase in salaries is beginning to assume importance owing to its effect on the subscriptions to the Consolidation Loan in regard to which it is now reported that lists close on September 19 instead of September 5, owing to the strike.

The matter was discussed at a Cabinet meeting after which the Minister for Labour announced that he would introduce a Bill aiming at a compulsory conciliation of labour disputes.

Work For Glaziers.

A number of striking bank clerks demonstrated at the Place Trocaderq. They broke the windows in several bank buildings. They were dispersed by the police, but reassembled in another square. They were again dispersed and went to the Bolevards. Two were arrested.—Reuter.

Captain Arrachart has returned to Le Bourget.

An earlier message reads: Captain Arrachart, accompanied by the engineer, M. Carol, left Villa Coublay at 4.50 a.m. on Monday to attempt to circum- navigate Europe in three days. He reached Belgrade at 12.45 in the afternoon, Constantinople at 6 p.m., Moscow at 9 p.m. on Tuesday, and telegraphed to the Under-Secretary for Air that they were warmly received in Moscow.

headline: TIENTSIN RIOTS.
text:
CHANG TSO-LIN SENDS TROOPS.

FALSE REPORTS CIRCULATED.

The Yuta mill, which was wrecked, is owned by Japanese. The Paocheng mill, where the strike started, is partly wrecked and is Chinese owned and American managed. No further disturbances have taken place today. A number of workmen presented themselves at the mills, but it will probably be months before the Yuta mill is working.

A detachment of special gender-darmerie, sent from Mukden by Chang Tso-lin, has arrived. It is stated that a number of students and strike leaders have found refuge in the Foreign Concessions.

Twenty rioters and nine police who were wounded, have been admitted to hospital in the native city. Five of the former are reported to have very little chance of recovery, whilst some of the police are not expected to live. It appears that many of the wounded were carried to the country, fearing arrest.

Many false reports have been circulated among Chinese, in which foreigners are blamed for the trouble.

headline: SEARCHER CHARGED.
text:
THEFT DURING RAID

STORY OF A WATCH

It was alleged this morning against a searcher employed by the police that he had taken a watch and chain from the occupants of one of the houses searched in the course of a raid in the Western district two days ago.

Mr. D. McCallum, who represented the searcher when the case was heard at the Central Magistracy, stated that his client's case was that the watch and chain were given him by the wife of the complainant in order that he might not search a certain box.

Det. Insp. T. Murphy said that the defendant was to all intents and purposes a policeman having been duly sworn in for duties, in connection with the strike. Upon a complaint being received, the defendant was searched and the witch and chain found in his breast pocket. The value of the property was about $3.

headline: BORDER SHOTS.
text:
FIRING INTO BRITISH TERRITORY.

VUIT OOMANDERRIID.

Incidents on the border have already being reported in which Chinese Labour pickets have fired on anyone attempting to cross from Chinese into British territory but in affluor occurring yesterday morning is more serious in that the shooting was into British territory. About 11 a.m. yesterday some Chinese men and women were carrying baskets of fruit from their own villages in British territory to Sheang Shan railway station when five rounds were fired into them by a Labour picket. This was near the To Fung Customs station where the Chinese and British frontier road are only a few yards apart. No-one was injured although shots struck the ground near to the prospective fruit vendors who promptly dropped the baskets and took to flight. The Labour picket then crossed the frontier and took away the baskets.

headline: Canton: August 12.
text:
From what can be seen and heard the strike leaders in Canton are going to mark time in definitely, and they seem to have the backing with which to support their huge crowd for some time to come.

It is difficult to realise that there are a few hundred "parasites" who can only earn big money when trouble is created. It is they who can approach the so-called Labour politicians, and the Soviet agents invariably deal with them. In this way they are in a position to demand a daily contribution from revenue to support all the different guides now idle in Canton; but when it comes to asking for funds for "special" objects they make their own terms and, incidentally, their own profit. As their orders are obeyed by armed pickets, their word is law. Accordingly, no matter how anxious an ordinary striker may be to get back to Hongkong, he is prevented from doing so. And as long as the leaders retain the temporary dormitories and provide the two meals a day, they have no excuse for breaking away; rather, they are not sufficiently united to act, or even think, for themselves. This band of labour "professionals" has been increased during the strike, branch executive offices having been established at all places where there is a likelihood

This band of labour "professionals" has been increased during the strike, branch executive offices having been established at all places where there is a likelihood of men departing, via roundabout routes, for work.

To-day the rank and file are maintained as when they first came up. But there is no pocket money or money for the folks at home or in Canton. Some of the first batches who came up, and thought that they would enjoy a short holiday had a good time in the flower-boats and the Honam fantan saloons. When funds ran short they disposed of what spare cash they had with them. Then went clothing, until now some of them are virtually in rags with footwear that defends description.

The Tung Tak coolies' guild of Hongkong has been "making hay while the sun shines." Being more adept at cargo handling and claiming priority as patriots, they have displaced regular Canton workers in competition for work with the result that the Canton men are dissatisfied.

headline: Drill Not Appreciated.
text: Other strikers with relatives or influence have obtained small capital or stock and set out for themselves, in the streets, as hawkers. A much greater number has been enrolled in the semiliary "Labourers Corps" where the drill and training are not at all appreciated. It seems that the project of building an army out of Hongkong's prodigals is still far from being realised. Although no strikers have come up from Hongkong, the fold is still being increased. Batches of seamen from trans-Pacific lingers and steamers, who atruck at Japan ports, have come here without calling at Hongkong. I am told that subscriptions were raised among Chinese merchants and other residents in Japan and that the men paid their passages to Shanghai, whence they transhipped for Canton direct. headline: TIENTSIN QUIET.
text:
POLICE AND UNRULY STUDENTS.

FIRM ACTION TAKEN

The Chinese police have decided to release all the workers arrested recently provided they obtain shop guarantees to return to work and do not have anything to do with further strikes and disturbances.

All the students have not yet been released, the police demanding that those who have gone out of town return to their homes. Those having homes here are being held until they obtain guarantee that they will not again interfere with the workers and will remain in their homes until the schools recommend. Also they must agree to resign from the Students' Union.

The situation is now very quiet.

headline: END IN SIGHT?
text:
FOREIGNERS IN CANTON AGAIN.

AMEEN'S GATES.

News reached Hongkong on Saturday that Shameen's gates had been re-opened and that intercourse between the French and British Concessions and Canton city had been resumed.

Shameen is, of course, connected to the mainland by two bridges. The “east” bridge is that leading into the French Concession and the “west” bridge links up the British Concession with Shakee.

It was stated that the decision had been arrived at to allow Chinese who had, at the time of the Yunnanese siege, deposited valuables and other property in Shameen for safe keeping, to withdraw whatever they wished. Another part of the report to hand was that domestic and other Chinese employees, formerly of Shameen, had indirectly signified their intention to return as opportunity occurred.

On inquiry from the best informed source in the Colony, it was learned by the “China Mail” this, morning that Shameen's gates are still closed. Their reopening had not even been discussed, nor would such a step be contemplated until adequate protection was given by the Chinese authorities on the spot. Shameen was still, virtually, in a state of siege. Nothing had been done to change conditions.

However, Canton's "gates," meaning the right of entry into the city, were opened on Saturday. It is surmised that the report referred to mistook Shameen for Canton. Foreigners, with the exception of British, are now allowed in Canton for purposes of ordinary intercourse. The supposition is that a beginning has been made to restore trade.

Trustworthy Chinese business circles express the opinion that the trouble, as far as Canton was concerned, would "blow over" in less than three weeks from to-day. A Chinese merchant with large interests in Canton predicted to a "China Mail" reporter yesterday that most of the Chinese-owned river steamers, if no others, would be running between Canton and Hongkong again, by the 15th of the 7th moon if not earlier, the equivalent of "that date" being September 2. He had reason to think that the huge army of unemployed in Canton were getting restless, that the "professional labour bosses" were becoming alarmed as to the outcome, and that negotiations had been made by those indirectly interested but not directly concerned, for river shipping to move again, with the object of facilitating a gradual return to normalcy.

Macao Steamer Back.

This afternoon, the s.s. Chuen Chow (Captain Jones) put in at Hongkong again after having tied up at Macao for the second or third time since the strike began. For a reason which has not been given, the crew have not made the voyage, lying up and then making a fresh start again.

Poultry and Livestock. Housewives were pleasantly surprised yesterday morning when hawke s offered fowls in the street at 65 cents per catty, which is about equal to 50 cents per pound, for live chickens, and capons at a slightly lower figure. Later in the day the price went down to 58 cents per catty which is about the figure in ordinary times. This sudden drop is attributed to a very large shipment having arrived. The source has not been divulged, but the Chinese are particularly grateful for this bit of enterprise. Arrivals of cattle, pigs and other livestock have also been reported, but the market prices for meat are still prohibitive.

The engagement is announced between Vivian Geoffrey, second son of the late Mr. F. Smyth, of Hongkong, and Mrs. Smyth, of The Red House, Oxshott, Surrey, and Joyce, only child of Captain F. Cresghan Osborne, C.B., R.N., and the late Mrs. A. R. Cresghan Osborne, of Dillon Park, Langley, Bucks

headline: Macao).
text:
Canton is despatching a strong expedition to quell Waichow. The force which is to carry out the offensive consists partly of Whampoa Cadets and partly of General Hsu Shung-chi's divisions. This punitive army might have been greater had not the necessity arisen of keeping an eye on recalcitrant generals nearer to Canton.

Waichow city, far up the East River, is in the hands of Commander Yeung Kwan-yu who has several thousand bayonets in his command. Owing to the complexity of Cantonese politics he has, within the last year, been a subordinate of Chan Kwing-ming, the Yunnanese and Hsu Shung-chi, three factions which are opposed to one another. Latterly he has held Waichow, nominally under the Kuomintang. But when Canton sent a delegate to control his actions he rebelled. It is with the object, either of bringing Yeung to reason, or disarming his following, that the punitive force has been sent. This force, it is stated, has reached Sheklung.

En route, the Canton army may encounter the guerilla troops of Yuen Ha-kau ("Coffin Sampan"). Yuen now roaming the hills near Tsang Shing and a fugitive from the Whampoa Cadets.

Should Canton take Waichow, as they did in the last campaign when they bought over a Lieut.-General and Commander Yeung fled, then the other leaders of Chan Kwing-ming's army, in and around Swatow, may also be embroiled but it is safe to assume that they will not take to the field unless they are threatened.

headline: TROUBLE AT SHEKKI.
text:
News has reached Canton that disorder has broken out at three important villages near Shekki,

Whampoa Cadets who were sent there, so it is stated, as the nucleus of the “nationalisation of property” (Soviet) experiment have fallen foul of the local “Man Tuen,” which are really civil guards.

The Cadets were fired at first, when they lost over thirty men in casualties through trying to overrun some padi-fields.—They took instant revenge on the civil guards and the situation is now tense.

headline: NO BOYCOTT. / HOIHOW SHIPPING UNFETTERED.
text:
RESIDENT'S REPORT.

The reports as to a trade boycott of British and Japanese goods being prosecuted with vigour at Hoihow would appear to be without foundation for a resident of Hoihow who arrived in Hongkong by the Talkwa Maru (leaving Hoihow on Friday morning), reports that a full cargo was brought to Hongkong, this consisting of 230 head of cows, over 200 hogs and large numbers of chickens.

This resident reports that there is absolutely no attempt on the part of the students to prevent shipment of freight either to Hongkong or Hoihow and states that when the boat left shipments were arriving regularly from Haiphong, Hongkong and Bangkok.

There had been a boy in the town of Hali-man Island, according to our informant, is determined that none shall occur. He has arrested and executed four or five students who were known to be Reds from Canton and were attempting to stir up trouble. There is absolutely no anti-foreign-feeling at Holhow, according to this same source, and the women and children who left for Holhow were all now returned. The women and children of question set a banana cell on their own in Canton and no one could have brought them to the home.

headline: TRAMWAY COMPANY. / SOCIAL GATHERING AT THE DEPOT.
text:
VOLUNTEERS THANKED.

A volunteer worker of the Tramway Company during the strike writes as follows:—

Eleven o'clock yesterday morning saw the disbandment of the volunteer car drivers and conductors when a group photograph was taken, including the tramway officials.

In a short speech, just after the photograph was taken, Mr. L. C. F. Bellamy, the General Manager, on behalf of the Tramway Company, said that they were very sorry to lose such a fine body of men whose loyal co-operation helped them to see the strike through thick and thin, besides contributing in no small measure towards organising and training new men to undertake permanent work. It was, he said, with mixed feelings that he parted with the volunteers, and he thought—although he hoped nothing untoward will happen to have recourse to their services again—it would be much more appropriate to say "Au revoir" than "Goodbye." He also paid a tribute to the very efficient manner in which the volunteers carried out their duties. Mr. Bellamy's speech was received with much applause and hand clapping, after which the gathering dispersed.

I understand that the Tramway Company intends to present the volunteers with autographed copies of the group photo, and I think I voice the sentiments of all the volunteers when I say that we shall cherish the same as a memento of an unusual and extraordinary incident in our lives. In closing, I beg, on behalf of my co-workers, to tender the tramway officials our very hearty thanks for the gentlemanly and gallant treatment, accorded to us during our term of service.

headline: NO FIGHTING.
text:
OPINION ON CANTON OFFENSIVE.

THE WAICHOW SITUATION.

A Mr. Lau, who formerly held a high command under General Chan Kwing-ming, has informed the “China Mail” that little concern has been felt by the general’s subordinates in the hinterland of Swatow, over the punitive expedition despatched by Canton against Waichow.

According to Mr. Wong, some of the senior generals now holding territory under General Chan's banner are now in Hongkong to attend the funeral of the father of General Ip Kue (Chan's right-hand man and Chief Director of Military Operations), the old man having died at his house in Kowloon City (near the Sung Emperor's Pavilion). Other generals have just returned to their commands after interviewing Chan in Shanghai. It is unlikely, therefore, that Chan's men will march to Waichow to aid its holder Yeung Kwan-yu in his opposition to Canton. It is known that Kuomintang troops have arrived at Sheklung but the feeling is that Canton will have its hands full with recalcitrant (anti-Bolshevik) leaders nearer the capital.

headline: IN OTHER PLACES.
text: From inquiries made in another direction it appears that the trouble near Shekki—reported in yesterday's issue — has been quelled, the local civil guards not being able to resist the detachment of Whampoa Cadets. Considerable attention has also been diverted to General Tang Pun-yan, who holds Hainan (the "eight districts") as people are looking to him to unite General Leung Hung-kai (Kuomintang, reputedly anti-Bolshevik) who holds the territory between Tang and the districts near Canton.

headline: ANOTHER STRIKE.
text:
SHANGHAI POST OFFICE TROUBLE.

CHINESE DETECTIVE MAULD.

Nearly a thousand postal employees, comprising clerks, sorters, postmen, and coolies, struck this morning demanding a substantial

Employees Union, shorter hours payment for overtime, gratuity of a year's pay for every 10 years; immunity of strike leaders, right to demand abolition and rejection of unequal treatment and a guarantee that foreigners would not be employed after 1925

The strikers this morning attacked a Chinese detective and battered him with stools and chairs.

Tie detective finally used his revolver and wounded a coolie in the leg.

The police rushed to the scene and restored order.

A detachment of marines from His Majesty's Concord is now guarding the Post Office.

The strikers have issued a pro- elaboration complaining of being badly paid and compelled to work I'k• cattle, while foreigners occupy superior positions and draw en- emours salaries.

A meeting of strikers decided to withdraw the demand that only China should be employed in the Post Office after 1926.

headline: NOT DETAINED.
text:
S. S. FOO CH.E O N G "STRANDED" AT PAKKAI.

Definite news is now available regarding the 8.8, 100 Chsong which was, some days ago, suspected of having been detained by Chinese at Pukkai, the part of Kongmoon.

The steamer was on the Macao. Kongmoon ran and did not return after leaving Macao one evening. It has been stated that the Macao authorities had taken steps as the vessel was under the Portuguese flag, her port of registry being Macao.

It has now transpired that some bare-faced intimidation at Pakkai caused the crew to desert. Hence the ship is now tied up there awaiting a new crew to bring her back. The officials at Pakkai are reported to have denied interference.

There is still no direct communication between Macao and Canton, the last batch of delegates from the Strike Executive at Canton being very definite about the matter. However, the tow-boat is now running again between Macao and Shekki, where passages can be obtained, under 'passports' from the strike office there, for Canton. Passenger fares on the tow-boat are high owing, it is stated, to'squeeze' having to be paid for the privilege of keeping up the service.

Two modern Portuguese warships are reported to have reached Macao.

headline: AN ACT OF WAR? / REPORTED CANTON SHIPPING RULES.
text:
TREATIES VIOLATED?

British

Boycott

Shipping regulations which may amount to a declaration of war are reported to have been imposed by Canton, but whether they have official backing remains to be seen.

Japanese?

headline: HITTING HONGKONG.
text:
The Chinese authorities have drawn "up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

headline: LOCAL COMMENT.
text:
Opinions in Hongkong vary as to the outcome of the telegram. A gentleman who controls a fairly large number of ships vitally interested in trade with Canton pointed out to a “China” Mail” reporter that such a state of affairs had existed practically from the beginning of the “strike.”

"With the exception of ships under the Chinese flag," he said, "all vessels calling at Canton have been interfered with, even Chinese-owned shipping under foreign registry. Latterly Chinese steamers have discharged and loaded at Canton, but," so he believed, "only under payment of'squeeze' to strike officials who work hand in hand with administrative politicians. More recently some foreign tonnage had reached Canton, such as tramp and chartered ships with cargoes of rice from Bangkok, etc. Even food boats had to be'squared' before they could be cleared."

Continuing, the speaker said he took the message to mean that the so-called Canton Government had now actually come out in the open to sponsor the activities of the Strike Executive which was probably the “Anti-Imperialist Union” referred to in the cable. Certain shipping would continue to call at Canton, without coming to Hongkong but trade would suffer to an untold extent if British and Japanese hulls were prohibited.

headline: CANTON MOVES.
text:
TREACHERY TO CRUSH ENEMY.

HONAM BOUGHT OVER?

The “China Mail” learns from a reliable source that the Kuomintang Government is attempting to buy over General Li Fook-lam's troops before crushing him, so as to extend their power and remove opposition.

General Li has several thousand Cantonese troops who have been in Honam (the island opposite Canton) for some time. He is accused of refusing to obey the Bolshevik order to prohibit gambling and opium—from which are derived substantial revenues.

Recently General Li has moved his troops into surrounding villages for fear of being disarmed by the Reds and news has reached Hongkong that the Red leaders are aiming at "buying over" some of his detachments before challenging him to battle. At any rate, without support, Li would have been an easy prey for the Reds. with river shipping, noted the fact that Hongkong would still be in communication with Canton if the order ever took effect, because there was nothing to prevent steamers running between Canton and Macao, and between Macao and Hongkong. This speaker expressed some very pronounced views. He said that the Kuomintang were imposing their will on the merchants regardless of whether foreign trade was crippled or not. In his opinion if the drafting of the rules could be legally brought to the door of the Kuomintang Government in Canton—and such could be done by obtaining the officially approved notices in all parts of the city—declaration of war was the only alternative. He was positive that by fouting trade treaties Canton rendered herself liable to war.

SHANGHAI POST OFFICE WORKERS RETURN

Foster smokers returned to work last night, agreeing to refer matters to Peking and or the promise that officials will recommend consideration of demands. General Sir W. headline: DRIVERS CONVICTED.
text:
A narrow escape was that of Mr. J. H. Simmons, Inspector of the Hongkong Tramway Company, according to the evidence given yesterday at the Central Magistracy against a taxi driver who was charged with negligent driving. As a result of the taxi running into his ricsha Mr. Simmons was thrown and the ricsha completely turned over. Ricsha puller and occupant both sustained minor injuries. In decision on the part of the taxi driver as to what direction to take was said to be the cause of the accident which occurred near the Tramway Shelter at Causeway Bay. Defendant was fined $10 and ordered to pay the ricsha coolie $10 compensation. Peckless driving also formed one of the items in the list of breaches of Traffic Regulations brought against Chinese motor driver who was yesterday charged at the Kowloon Magistracy. The evidence showed that he drove round a band at Kwai

ences in the North, which in any case can never settle the Southern situation, or the report to the British Government of possibly some special Commissioner sent out from home, who, it may be, has not even been selected yet, to advise them of conditions out here, and meanwhile this Colony and British trade throughout Southern China drift daily nearer to utter ruin. Telegram upon telegram of the gravest possible nature has poured home from all sources, Government, public and private, stating the plain unvarnished truth: — manifestly they are either misunderstood or not believed—or else what is still more incredible nothing can be done.

The Theatre Royal has been booked for 5.15 next Tuesday, the 25th, and arrangements are in progress for a meeting at which the Colony will no doubt express its views in a telegram to the Prime Minister in no uncertain manner.

I trust the promoters may count on the united support of the "entire Press" here and all who are convinced of the vital necessity for prompt action in making the meeting as widely known and as successful as the extreme gravity of the situation demands. It cannot be too clearly stated again that it is apparently still not realised at home that this is no question of a "Strike" but of an organised and inspired attack upon British trade and interests in all our Treaty Ports and Concessions and upon this Colony in particular.

Yours, etc., P. H. HOLYOAK. Hongkong, August 19, 1925.

headline: SHANGHAI CONDITIONS.
text:
DEFALCATION OF STRIKE

POSTAL OFFICIALS WAGES.

A secret meeting of a number of unions affiliated to the general union of labour, education and commerce, have passed a resolution seceding from the latter. The action is due to the alleged defalcation of strike funds on the part of general union officials.

The situation on the waterfront is improving gradually: Wharf coolies mostly have resumed.

The Ministry of Communications at Peking has authorised the local post office officials to offer strikers an increase of wages, but the strikers have rejected it. Junior clerks starting at $20 a month were offered $35, but demand $52.50. The officials have requested the public not to use pillar boxes and to call at the post office for their mails.

headline: KILLED.
text:
CANTON RED LEADER'S FATE.

REPORTED ASSASSINATION

According to a rumour which has yet to be confirmed, Mr. Liu Chung-oi (also spelt "Liao Chung-kai") the present "Canton Finance Minister, was assassinated in Canton this morning.

Liu has been head of the Labour Unions in Clinton and was one of the first of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen's party to encourage intercourse with Russia. He is very much opposed to foreigners and to the Chinese merchants as a class. Long before even the Shameen strike of last year he had been secretly working for Communistic ideals.

When the reorganisation in the Canton Government was put in effect about two months ago, he was appointed Finance Minister and is now one of the chief executives of the Kuomintang. The rumour current is that Liu

The rumour current is that Liu was fired at by an assassin and that he died almost instantly.

headline: CHINESE SEIZE SHIP.
text:
MACAO VESSEL TAKEN TO CANION

gi NboAT'S EFPORT BALLS.

The Portuguese Naval ship Coloure arrived here from Málano on August 9, and tried to tow away the s.s. Foo Cheong, a vessel flying the Portuguese flag which has been tied up here since her crew deserted through intimidation.

The Colours did not succeed through, it is stated, the Labourers Corps preventing any help being given and the warship returned alone to Macao.

On August 14, the Foo Cheong was commandedered by strikers. Manned by her original crew who, according to one report, were made to work, the steamer was taken out of the port, it is believed, for Canton.

MERCHANDISE SEIZED. To-day a junk fully had so with groundnut oil, salt fish and other cargo, arriving from Macao, was seized by the Labourers Corps at Pakkai.

headline: China the Jilil / BRITISH ADMIRAL'S MISSION. THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF SAILS FOR CANTON. CANTON SHIPPING EMBARGO SEQUEL.
text:
Vice-Admiral Sinclair has gone to Canton aboard H.M.S. "Petersfield."

It is learned in London that his visit is undoubtedly due to the Canton Government's embargo on British shipping.

Vice-Admiral Sinclair has not been specifically instructed to make representations to the Chinese authorities but as Commander-in-Chief of the China Station he will take such immediate steps to protect British shipping as he thinks fit without first-consulting the Government.

The storm centre of the South-Canton under the Reds

manding the Troons in China, Major General C. C. Luard, had accompanied the Admiral on his visit. The opinion that the Naval authorities held was that the Admiral would return to Hongkong to-night.

The Chinese authorities have drawn up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong.

All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-Imperialist Union.

The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed.

It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official.

parent_headline: China the Jilil / BRITISH ADMIRAL'S MISSION. THE COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF SAILS FOR CANTON. CANTON SHIPPING EMBARGO SEQUEL.

To the incident at Shataukok where troops crossed from Chinese territory and carried off junks is to be added another which might be termed deliberately provocative. A British armed launch has been fired on from Canton "by Bolsheviks" according to report, and temporarily, at any rate, withheld from replying.

Upon enquiry at the Naval authorities this morning this report was not definitely confirmed. A report of firing had been received but this was “by no means uncommon” and in the particular case in question might have been, like so many others, from irresponsible pirate gangs.
