headline: RUSSIAN ARRESTED IN HONGKONG
text:
“UNDESIRABLE” PROSECUTED.

That he was found in the Colony without a valid passport wins the charge-framed against Joseph L. Teplitchi, an Ukrainian, before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning.

The accused was arrested by the Police on information received that he was a violent "Red" and had been seen taking an active part in directing the labour pickets during the strike at Sha-meen last year. His presence in Hongkong was therefore deemed undesirable, apart from the fact that he had no proper passport.

Mr. P. P. J. Wodehouse, C.I.E. (Captain Superintendent of Police) said that the accused was in Macao when the strike commenced. From there he answered an advertisement in a local paper calling for volunteers, secured a billet as fireman on the Empress of Asia, and was discharged after a trip to Vancouver and back.

The accused had in his possession a document which was stated to be a “certificate” in Rumanian, on which appeared the chop of the French Consul in Canton. His Worship said that he had an idea that the passport regulations were relaxed, and he was under the impression that a document with a vise by a French Consul was sufficient for landing in the Colony. After making enquiries, Mr. Wodehouse pointed out that there was an arrangement between the British and Japanese Governments and the British and French Governments under which a passport issued in favour of one of its nationals andvised by its own Consul was sufficient to entitle the holder to enter a country belonging to the other Government.

On being asked what he had to say to being found in the Colony without a proper passport or document authorised by the C.S.P., the accused stated that his passport was stolen while serving on the Empress of Asia. He made a report of the loss to the second engineer of the vessel, but not to the Police.

Addressing the accused, His Worship said that he was guilty of the charge, but before passing judgment he would remand him for two days in Police custody to enable him to produce any friends he may have to testify to his character. The accused said that he had many friends and could call them.

headline: BORDER FIRING.
text:
NIFERS USE PASSENGERS AS SCREENS.

THIS MORNING'S OUTRAGE.

Reports of two more shooting outrages at different points on the border were issued by Police Headquarters this morning.

A gang of Government coolies working on the road between Sheungshui and Ta Ku Ling were scared away from the scene by a shot fired at them from Chinese territory yesterday afternoon. This being apparently the object desired, a man crossed over into British territory and removed a bicycle belonging to the foreman of the coolie gang.

The other incident took place at 9 o'clock this morning at Lokma-chau. Below the Police Station here is a ferry, and. Sergeant Swan heard two shots being fired from that part of the river. Getting out of the station to investigate, he saw a man jump overboard from the ferry and swim to the other side.

The Sergeant sent a strong party of Police to the river, and on their way down they had several shots fired at them. They saw the pickets taking the passengers off from the ferry, and also observed two men in uniform, who did the firing. One of the men placed himself in the middle of a group of passengers, and, using the latter as a screen, fired at the British Police. The other man took cover behind a bank and sniped occasionally. After firing nearly a dozen shots, all of which, fortunately, missed their mark, the man behind the bank rejoined his comrade and all the people disappeared.

The Police did not return the fire for fear of hitting the passengers who were being used as a screen.

The shots heard by the European Sergeant in the first instance are believed to have been fired by the labour pickets to stop the attempts of some fruit sellers to cross the border.

headline: UP-COUNTRY NEWS.
text:
ENCOUNTER WITH PIRATES.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, August 17. The Hongkong steamers are still lying idle, without crews, at their respective berths.

One company (about a hundred strong) of Labourers' Corps-wearing blue shirts and khaki shorts—have arrived here. Their very first act was most unexpected; they drove away the strike pickets which had been keeping the domestic employees of Europeans out of employment. These new troops have orders to prevent strikers getting away, the export of foodstuffs, and the import of foreign goods. They are stationed at Kongmoon, Pakkai and Sanwui city.

Considerable damage has been done by gales to the sugar cane and orange crops. At this time in other years the river is flooded but now it is as dry as in winter. The price of rice has gone up again.

The Kongmoon-Fatshan towboat has had another encounter with pirates when off the Kamchuk lighthouse. The towboat escaped.

Fatshan and Kongmoon have been placed under municipal administration with mayors independent of the district magistrates.

The Chinese gunboats Kwong Ching and Kong Hon have arrived to drive away pirates who have assembled at Hoi Chau with the supposed intention of attacking Ngoi Hoi.

Foreigners resident here at present comprise six on the staff of the Customs, Dr. McBain of the Marion Barclay Hospital and the local manager of the A.P.C. One of H.M.s armed launches is always on duty here.

headline: China / HOW HE DIED.
source: (Photo by courtesy of the "Tsun Wan Yat Po.")
text:
ANTON RED MINISTER'S MURDER.

LATEST DETAILS.

The assassination of Liu Chung-oi, the notorious Canton Bolshevik —exclusively reported in yesterday's “China Mail”—has now been established beyond doubt.

.Nearly all the local vernacular papers came out with. "specials" yesterday afternoon but details were not available till this morning.

Some time before noon yesterday Liu left his private residence in Tungshan (the suburb to the East of Canton, in which are many foreign residents) to attend a meeting of the Kwangtung (Kuomintang) Government Commission which is established at the Waichow Association building, also in the east of Canton.

When about to enter the gate Liu was fired at by an unknown Chinese wearing the customary short jacket and trousers of black pongee silk, the fabric so much used by the lower and working class Chinese. The assassin drew a revolver and opened fire from almost point-blank range. One round entered the upper part of Liu's body and he expired almost immediately. In the subsequent confusion the assassin is believed to have escaped in the crowd nearby.

ONE OR TWO SHOTS? The "Tai Kwong Po" states that the fatal shot entered Liu's abdomen and that suspicions exist that the culprit was connected with a labour union opposed to the Communistic party.

The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" learns that one of Liu's relatives received a cable yesterday stating that the bullet entered Liu's chest and that he died shortly afterwards.

Another report, says the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," is that Liu had already been suffering from lung disease and was about to enter hospital for treatment in a few days when the murderer ended his life. Liu's relatives in Hongkong are leaving for Canton to-morrow. Yet another version reported in the same vernacular paper is that two shots were fired, one entering Liu's right side and that the assassin escaped before the police arrived.

Other rumours current were that Liu was shot by colleagues while actually attending a meeting of the Government Commission, that the murderer was one of Liu's personal bodyguards and that the assailant had been captured.

Several Chinese papers published in Hongkong say that a telegram has been received by the father of Liu's wife, definitely confirming the report but giving no detail.

A Reuter telegram from Canton reads:—Liu Chung-oi, one of the leading Bolshevik members of the Canton Government, was assassinated last night.

NOTABLE CAREER. As stated in yesterday's "China Mail," Liu is one of three executive members of the Kuomintang Government Commission which succeeded the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen as chief of the Bolsheviks party in Canton and which comprises about twenty members.

About forty-six years of age—although he appears to be not more than forty—Liu is a native of Waichow, the home of General Chan Kwing-ming, the Cantonese leader who so strenuously opposed Canton. Liu was born in America and returned to China when about ten years of age. He studied at Queen's College, says the "Toun Wan Yat Po" and subsequently entered a Japanese University.

After graduating in law and economics he entered the Government service under the Manchu regime. Since the Revolution of 1911 he has steadfastly followed Dr. Sun. He has been Finance Minister and Chief of the Finance Bureau at Canton and Civil Governor on one or two occasions. Several years ago there was a notorious Tse Ying-pat who missed so-called Labour backing. Life mined in the movement and Tse recaded into the background. Later he has been

advocates of dividing up private property in the province:

There is little doubt that a greater part of the recent trouble can be attributed to Liu Chung-oi (spelt Liao Chung-kai according to Mandarin pronunciation). Not over scrupulous, Liu has made many enemies since his recent rise to power. Those very bitter against him include some of Cantou's leading merchants, some bona fide workers who have not bent to his sweet will and rivals in the political camp.

headline: SHAMEEN AFFAIR. / CANTON AND PEKING DISAGREE.
text:
SUN FO RETURNS?

According to news reaching Chinese circles in this Colony, progress in the “Shameen incident” negotiations will be difficult owing to differences between Peking and Canton.

The "Wah Kiu lat Po" publishes a cable to the effect that Mr. Sun Fo, son of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen and recently Mayor of Canton, was to have left Peking yesterday.

It will be recalled that Mr. Sun Fo, accompanied by Mr. Fu Ping-sheung (Canton Commissioner for Foreign Affairs) went to Peking to discuss the Shameen incident.

The “Tsun Wan Yat Po” says that Peking has asked Canton for full details but Canton has failed to comply. Therefore, it is felt that as Peking has decided to negotiate itself, little will be accomplished.

headline: STRAWS IN THE WIND.
text:
That nine provinces of China are to unite in an armed movement against the Canton Bolsheviks is the purport of a report in this morning's vernacular papers.

General Hung Shui-lun of Chan Kwing-ming's army is stated to have come to Hongkong to embark for Shanghai where he will join his chief in a council embracing some of the most important leaders in the country.

Because of a feeling that the Bolshevik movement may spread from Canton, Wu Pei-fu (the former strong man of China) and several provincial rulers are, says the report, uniting to bring Canton under Ghana's central government.

headline: FURTHER DETAILS
text:
This morning's "Wah Tsz Yat Po" publishes a message from its special correspondent in Canton to the effect, that when Liu Chung-oi, the notorious Red leader was shot on Friday, Chan Chowlam, formerly editor of the "China News"—a Hongkong vernacular paper which was raided and closed by the Police—was seriously wounded.

The effect of this action of the Canton authorities has been to cause a complete stoppage of the export of silk from the Canton Delta through Hongkong and of the import of British piecegoods into Canton and interior; thereby causing disastrous losses both to British and Chinese merchants in this Colony and to the export trade of Lancashire and Yorkshire, which must result in further very considerable and increasing permanent unemployment in Great Britain and the closing of many of their mills.

headline: SEAMEN CAUGHT.

headline: RIFFS ACTIVE. / DELAY FATAL
text:
The Canton-Hongkong problem is entirely separate and distinct from that in any other part of China owing to the fact that Canton does not recognise and is in rebellion against the Central Government at Peking and that no conference held at Peking on tariff or extra-territoriality or any other questions can possibly assist this Colony in the remotest degree, in its present most serious and urgent need; and any delay in dealing direct with Canton and on the South China situation can only result in daily losses to this Colony, of increasing and ruinous magnitude; moreover the British Government, if it delays decisive action now will most certainly have a far larger problem to face at Canton in the future than that confronting it at present. By prompt action now, the Naval and Military Forces, in this Colony could easily place alternative and friendly Chinese authorities in power at Canton.

The Acting President of the Directory announces that Colonel Monasterio, commander at Alhucemas, is gravely wounded. The Riff attack on the island which opened last night was resumed this morning.

The Spaniards vigorously replied. It is noteworthy that Alhucemas is reported to be the spot from whence the coming Spanish offensive, in co-operation with the French is being launched.

There is no question whatever of making war on China but simply of ousting the present violent anti-British Bolshevik faction which has recently succeeded in seizing the reins of power at Canton.

headline: FIGHTING SOON?
text:
CANTON SPLIT BECOMING INTENSE.

LOCAL INTEREST

Those who were in the Colony during the last seamen's strike may re-call Chan Ping-sang, who achieved notoriety as one of the men's leaders and who was alleged to have murdered his wife, for infidelity, at Canton, but was pardoned by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen.

Chan, it is stated by a reliable source, is now at Namtau, a town just beyond Deep Bay and not far from the New Territory frontier. From this port Hongkong receives fish and other foods, and a ferry runs regularly to and fro. Recently there has been violent intimidation at Namtau and anti-British propaganda; and Chan is said to be the local head of the military-cum-labour self-established pickets.

headline: WHERE IS HSU?
text:
That General Hsu Shung-chi, who is considered the only man in the Kuomintang capable of offering armed resistance to the Reds, is moving away from Canton for fear of being enveloped, is the belief of those who are well-posted.

General Hsu is supposed to be leading a punitive expedition against one or two of Chan Kwingming's satellites on the upper reaches of the East River. Such was the gist of one of my former reports. I am now told that Hsu is really taking his army away from the capital as he believes that a Bolshevik v. Moderate crisis is imminent.

General Li Fook-lam, Governor of Honam, is gradually bending to the orders of General Cheung Kai-shek, commander of the Whampoa Cadets. He has abolished the opium monopoly in his territory, but he is still defying the Reds in that, so it is reported, he has declared he will continue the gambling monopoly until Canton pays him arrays of pay. The Red chieftain, Chaming, is mentioned as having retorted by thirstening to land his Gadgets in Honam if Li is adamant. Li, on the other hand, has driven out all strikers from his domain. The trouble at Shekki, the capital of Heungshan (Dr. Sun's birthplace and the proposed model), Communistic district), has not been settled. A body of Cadats are trying to ret in but the old garrison and local civil guards are strenuously opposing them. SQUARBLE OVER SQUEEZE

headline: SCARED.
text:
VOLUNTARY SURRENDER.

The periodical raids on idlers' dens carried out by the Police on different areas almost every time have brought back to work a large number of those who would otherwise be numbered amongst the strikers.

That the effect of such action had, the desired result may be gauged from the fact that the idle hands in an area which was very much in the Police eye, and over which a raid was impending, voluntarily came out expressing a desire to work, according to a report furnished this morning. The returning workers included a large number of house servants and amahs.

headline: BLOCKADE MACAO?
text:
CANTON THREATENS NAVAL ISOLATION.

ABOYREMB ASK FOR HELP.

Reading very much like an inspired message is a report in a Canton vernacular paper, the "Kwok Wu Po," in which it is suggested that Macao be blockaded because "there are five steamers playing between that port and the Imperialistic Colony of Hongkong." Briefly, the article says that several butches of strike pickets and delegates have returned to Canton after making investigations in Macao and adjacent Chinese territory. The Executive of the National strike is satisfied that nothing can be done to cut off steamship communication between Macao and Hongkong. But Macao is only acting as a clearing house for its hinterland. Accordingly the Executive must take steps to prevail on the Kuomintang Government, says the "Kwok Wu Po," to send Canton's warships to the waters outside Macao. Those armed vessels could then blockade Macao and cut it off completely, as regards river traffic, with China. It is also suggested that the Canton Navy act in conjunction with the Strike Executive in maintaining the proposed blockade on Macao as the strikers are better able to carry out an embargo on passengers, foodstuffs, and any other merchandise. What will be the terms to be

What will eventuate remains to be seen.

headline: Shekki Cut Off.
text:
The tow-boat which runs to Macao daily from Shekki has been prevented from coming. Accordingly there are fewer passengers from that port who arrive here and re-embark for Hongkong. Most of these are real workers returning to their posts.

Recently the local commander at Shekki has gone out of his way to extend protection to people who want to sail from his port for Macao and to merchants importing cargo from Macao or exporting produce thereto. Unfortunately, he has been overcome by a batch of Whampoa Cadets sent there to obtain a footing for the first model of district government by Communism.

At first the commander forbade the Cadets to land in Shekki. Eventually he wavered and was soon overpowered. With the Cadets getting in, the local strike delegates—who had been in hiding from the former commander—came out into the open and held up the towboat. Previously the strike pickets had been kept away by threats of imprisonment for intimidation.

headline: LOCAL SCHOOLS.
text:
ALL TO RE OPENED AS USUAL.

AWATING A LEAD.

Enquiries made as to the position of local schools in relation to returning students show that without exception they will be re-opened as usual in September, although nothing is known as to the numbers

of those returning. The same applies to the University where, of course, there is a large number already in the Colony at the various Halls.

Some of the students who are due to take examinations, and whose parents are not willing for them to return, are making arrangements to take those examinations as external students.

Much surprise is expressed in local educational circles that the Government has given no lead in the matter of policy to be adopted toward students who are known to have been responsible for much of the trouble which resulted in the Easter term being prematurely ended.

headline: NEW LEADERS.
text:
MANY POLITICAL CHANGES IN CANTON. “The excessive charges made in respect of coal coolie hire is making thousands of dollars difference to us” was how he explained matters. “Whereas before the strike the average daily wage of a coal coolie was 80 or 90 cents, the coal coolie contractors inform us that their labour cannot now be obtained under $8.40 a day. The reason given is that, whereas

there were 7,000 coal coolies in the Colony before the strike, there are now only a few hundred; but this is ridiculous," said our informant. He gave as the reason for misbelieving these figures facts regarding coal coolie boarding houses in the Colony.

It would appear that coal coolie labour, as being one in connection with which there is always in normal times a very strong demand, is very highly organised in Hongkong. Shipping firms have to deal through contractors who in their turn pass on orders for labour to the No. 1 coolies in charge of large numbers of coal coolie boarding houses scattered throughout the Colony. He had made enquiries at these houses and was satisfied that the percentage of coal coolies who had left the Colony was nothing like so great as had been represented said the "China Mail" informant. "It is nothing but a ring to send up charges beyond all reason" was his comment.

Asked if ordinary coolie labour was not now plentiful and whether arrangements could not be made direct for the supply of such labour, our informant said that the work called for great stamina and a certain amount of skill. Orders had to be performed quickly in a stated time and the contractors and "No. 1 coolies" certainly seemed to be able to get work accomplished in half the time that ordinary street coolies were able to. There was not the slightest reason why they should be making such exorbitant charges, however, as the decrease in the number of coal steamers to be attended to was in proportion to the decreased number of coolies. The only shortage there might be was purely artificial in that a coolie who, before to day's exorbitant charges earned $7 a week by working all the week, was content to work for two days only for the same money. The matter was one calling for intervention, was the opinion of the shipping representative in question, who thought very strongly on the matter.

headline: RECOMMENDED BY REDS.
text:
(From Our Own Correspondent.

Recommended by M. Borodin, the Soviet emissary in Canton, Koo Ying-fan is mentioned as the most likely successor to Liu Chung-oi (the murdered Kuomin-tang Minister of Finance). Other names have been put forward for the post of chief of the labour unions.

Hu Han-min (Wu Hon-man) is stated as about to be despatched to Peking owing to the alleged failure of Sun Fo and Fu Ping-sheung to come to an understanding with Peking in connection with the Shakkee shooting incident.

Dr. C. C. Wu is rumoured as contemplating retirement, for the time being at least. The reason can only be guessed and the report has yet to be confirmed. Tuchun Wu, the chief of Police, is publicly stated to have aendered his resignation as the suspects arrested after the assassination of Liu Chung-oi are said to be connected with one of his departments.

Chan Chow-lam, the editor of the Hongkong "China News"—a vernacular paper which was closed by the Police—has died in the Kung Yee Hospital. After his release by the Hongkong authorities about two months ago, he came up to Canton when he was given an appointment. He was with Liu Chung-oi last Friday and mortally wounded.

headline: Canton Troops Disarmed.
text:
Before this edition went to Press the "Wah Tsz Yat "Po" issued an extra to the effect that General Yeung Kwan-yu, a pro-Chan Kwing-ming, commander on the East River sector, had disarmed some Kuomintang troops this morning.

Those defeated were under Lam She-ngai, who, it is stated, is not in favour at Canton.

Macchi-guns were brought up into action when Lam's men refused to surrender and there were several casualties.

It is not supposed that the action has more than local significance.

headline: Foodstuffs Seized.
text:
On Saturday morning a sampan proceeding from Macao to the Revenue Cruising Launch, Paktan at Chinsan with fresh beef, tinned foods and ice was stopped by troops who seized these goods. Later in the day, the beef was returned, but putrefaction had set in.

For weeks these troops have been impeding the importation of

fresh vegetables and eggs into Macao, but this is believed to be the first occasion locally in which they have opposed the supply of food to the men on board the Chinese Maritime Customs launches. Significant of the dire consequences which the strike is having on local Chinese is the fact that as many as twenty destraints (the selling up of the personal property of tenants who cannot pay their rent) are being enforced daily on behalf of lenders and in respect of arrenging.

headline: NOT TRUSTED?
text:
CANTON STRIKE LEADERS DISARMED.

ASSASSINATION SEQUEL

(From Our Own Correspondent.) 20 PESTRAINTS DAILY.

Because of suspicion spreading to labour guilds after the assassination of Liu Chung-oi, strikers are not allowed to carry weapons indiscriminately as heretofore: The defaults relate to shops, business houses and ordinary household tenants and an official with whom a "China Mail" representative conversed this morning said that such numbers had never been known before. In the ordinary course of events there might be one or perhaps two in the course of the day but very seldom any more.

Ever since the strike began everybody who bore a badge of the Strike Executive could carry arms. Now orders have been issued by the Kuomintang that only pickets, actually on duty and in uniform, can carry short or long firearms. It is understood that a few of the principal leaders still retain their revolvers. There is an under-current of

headline: MONEY BEST.
text:
CHINESE MILITARY DEFY STRIKERS

FOODSTUFFS FOR MACAO.

Although it has been reported that Centon's Strike Executive has asked for the Chinese warships to cut Macao off-from communication—by water; with its hinterland, vessels are still reaching this port.

Now that the Shekki tow-boat has ceased running, armed launches bearing the standards of local military commanders are arriving at the vicinity of Macao. Such boats carry both passengers, and fruit and foodstuffs, and take merchandise back.

Apparently it is a case of the military making hay while the sun shines, irrespective of the labour professionals' desires.

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
GOVERNMENT'S FIRM ATTITUDE. SENIORS EXPELLED

The lead which was promised over a month ago on behalf of the Government with regard to striking students will probably be made public at the next meeting of the Board of Education, for the main lines of the Government's attitude have now been decided.

These, the “China Mail” learns officially, are that “strikers” will not be taken back to Government schools, the definition being applied in respect of students who were absent on certain days. As a notice has already appeared in the Chinese Press notifying, on behalf of the Queen's College authorities, that students who were absent on June 17, 18, 19 and 20 need not present themselves for admission it may be deduced that these are the dates considered crucial in respect of other Government Schools.

The Government will "only enforce this expulsion in the case of students of 16 years of age and over, as it is considered that younger students may have absent themselves through intimidation; whereas senior students, after having the position fully explained to them, had no reason to act from motives of fear.

The co-operation among head masters which members of the Board of Education urged as necessary at the last meeting for any measures decided upon to prove effective is, in fact, in being, for a conference of head masters of all local schools was held yesterday at which, the “China Mail” understands, it was agreed that non-Government schools would co-operate in excluding any expelled striking students who might apply for admission. The action taken by such non-Government schools in regard to any of their own students who associated themselves with the strike must of course rest with the head masters of those schools.

The fees in respect of Government Schools are to be increased as from the next school year, although the "China Mail" was assured officially that this was not a direct outcome of the strike but merely revision which would be considered necessary in any case.

"Caution" money will also, it is understood, be required from parents and guardians in the future (also as from the commencement of the next school year). This will be to guarantee the Government against any loss from unwarranted interference with the normal course of study and will be returned after the course of study is complete, providing the conduct of the student in question has been satisfactory.

headline: BORDER INCIDENT.
text:
SHUMCHUN STILL HELD BY REDS

As far as can be ascertained from, reliable sources; yesterday morning's fighting at Shumchun was, as already stated, not to have had more than local significance.

Police Headquarters are awaiting the receipt of further details from Lokimachau Station, where the firing was distinctly heard, but the latest news indicates that Shumchun is still in the hands of the Canton Government, and is not controlled by a rival faction as is generally supposed.

The "Red" Government at Canton suspected signs of disloyalty on the part of the troops at Shumchun, and accordingly ordered a commander on the East River to proceed there, with a force and drive them out. This was accomplished yesterday morning when the local troops book to flight after a small engagement with the East River force.

The Whampoa Cadets, numbering about 100, who were near at hand, are reported to have taken no part in the fighting.

The commander who made

the successful coup is believed to be a former adherent of General Chan Kwing-ming, but who later joined the ranks of the Canton "Reds" and has remained faithful to them.

headline: DISHONESTY
text:
CHINESE VOLUNTEER SENT TO JAIL

In the early days of the strike a self-defence corps was formed at Tai Han village for the protection of the inhabitants, who, in addition to offering their services as volunteers, contributed to the cost of clothing and equipment. A Chinese member of the corps, who had been entrusted with the work of collecting subscriptions and placing orders for clothing, was brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning to answer a charge of misappropriation. It was stated that he collected a sum of $200, and bought a certain amount of clothing, leaving a balance in hand of $88. This sum, it was alleged the accused failed to return to the treasurer. The accused pleaded guilty and was sentenced to two months. As a sequel to the assassination of Liu Chung-oi, the Whumpou Cadets sent a detachment on Tuesday to surround the Foreign Ministry. Hu is stated to have been detained. His brother, Hu Sui-ching, is believed to have been forewarned and to have escaped. "Another detachment failed to arrest Ngai Bong-ping but a Mr. Lum, a former Superintendent of the Canton-Kowloon Railway (Chinese section) is believed to have been detained.

headline: REDS FALL OUT?
text:
An extra by the Wah Tsz Yat Po issued this afternoon, broadly translated, reads:

PO $ ^{th} $ Issued this afternoon, broadly translated, reads: News has been received from Canton that M. Karakhan has sent a secret telegram to M. Borodin in which it is alleged that the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen's testament was signed by Wong Tsing-wai. It is also alleged that both Weng Tsing-wai and Hu Han-min (former Governor and present Foreign Minister in Canton) have joined the finti-Bolshevik party.

headline: COURT MARTIAL.
text:
ARMY DOCTOR'S EXPLANATION.

"Is gastritis the same as what is popularly known as 'pains in the stomach'?" asked Captain C.J. F. Bensley, R.A., when cross-examining Captain R.F. Walker, M.C., R.A.M.C., at a District Court Martial at Whitfield Barracks, Kowloon, this morning. Captain Walker was giving medical evidence as to the results of alcoholic poisoning. He explained that gastritis was in the stomach. People often spoke of stains in the stomach, he continued, when they actually referred to the abdomen and in this was the distinction.

Major W. P. A. Hattersley-Smith, D.S.O., R.A., was President, The other members of the Court were Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman, Surrey Regiment and Lieut. B. R. Wright-Neville, 2nd Punjabis.

Sergeant Samuel Robson, 38th Heavy Battery, R.A., pleaded “not guilty” to a charge of being drunk on August 8 at 10.45 p.m., and a second charge of being unfit for duty for nine days through indulgence in liquor.

Captain Bensley was the prosecutor and Lieut. H.L. C. Hall, R.A., acted as prisoner's counsel.

Battery Sergeant-Major Brice gave evidence that he saw accused helplessly drunk in the sergeants' mess. When accused complained of being ill, Battery Quarter-Master-Sergeant Moore and Lce/Bdr. Dunne helped to remove him to hospital.

B.Q.M.S. Moore gave cor- roborative evidence.

Major Pollard, R.A.M.C., of the Kowloon. Military Hospital said that accused was rather excited when he got to hospital, smelt of alcohol and had acute pains in the stomach.

The next day, accused was bent over to the Military Hospital at Bowen Road. There he was treated by Captain Walker who said that the pains complained of were due to alcoholic poisoning. When accused started to cross-examine Captain Walker's discussion, in which Major Hetersley-Smith participated, ensued as to what effect brandy would have on pains in the stomach and as to which specific part of the body was meant when the word "stomach" was used. The query by the prosecutor led to the answer which has already been mentioned.

On oath, accused told the Court that he suffered from chronic indigestion, that his depression was due to trouble at Home, that he had a severe attack of gastritis when coming out on the boat and that his health had been further impaired by the increased consumption of tinned foods since the strike began. On the day in question he felt ill and sent for some brandy. He had reason to believe that the brandy was of very inferior quality, thus causing his condition as he took very little. In reply to the President, accused mentioned the brand. Accused also emphasised his good conduct.

si mercenaries were ejected about three months ago. These Northern mercenaries are now over running Canton and turning on their masters. A conservative estimate places their strength in the field, at 50,000 bayonets. All the other factions combined, in the province of Kwangtung, can hardly be a match for them with their superior munitions and strategic position.

As this edition went to press the "China Mail" received a message to the effect that the Whampoa Cadets are concentrating their main strength in the city of Canton. Practically all opposition to them has subaided and they are the undisputed masters at the moment of the situation. General LL. Fook-lam is reported to have fled from Honan, the island opposite Canton, for the village of Pal. Tode, where he is in hiding. The Cadets are momentarily expected to cross the River and take possession of Honan. The most serious of the several border incidents that have happened since the strike began took place yesterday when a decided scrap occurred between Chinese soldiers and the Taituling Police.

headline: REDS
text:
rb Where Foreigners Live Involved.

That fighting has actually started in Canton has been learned from two different sources but it remains to be seen whether the struggle will have any effect on the political position in that city.

This morning, on inquiry at the office of the Naval authorities, the "China Mail" was informed that there had been shooting in Canton. It was not possible to say whether anything more serious than rifle fire had taken place. Besides Canton city, the suburb of Tungshan—in which a good many foreign business men and missionaries have residences—is also believed to have been involved.

A strike picket commander from"Canton, who arrived here from Shekki late last night, has informed me that the Whampoa Cadets at their Canton headquarters have been firing indiscriminately in the city.

He believes that a campaign has been launched to disarm anybody who is not an out and out Bolshevik. This is a sequel to the assassination of Liu Chung-oi. There is no distinction maxix. The Cadets are attacking all who can't arms. Those who surrender are allowed to disperse.

However, resistance has been offered by military and gender-merie detachments who are suspected of favouring the anti-Bolshevik cause. One determined scrap witnessed by my informant was close to the City Police Headquarters. Everywhere in Canton, the Reds are guining the upper hand and they are making no attempt to hide their bid for power.

DETAILS OF THE COUP. Intelligence received in Hongkong has since borne out the report in yesterday's "China Mail" of a coup by the Red party in Canton. Several versions have come down as to what actually occurred and there are material divergences. The one given most credence is that Hu Han-min (formerly acting Generalissimo in the absence of Sun Yat-sen, Governor, and now Foreign Minister) has been denounced by the Bolsheviks; also that General Cheung Kai-shek, commander-in-chief of the Cadets, General Hsu Shung-chi, commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang's Cantonese troops and Wong Ching-wai (who made a sensational plot to assassinate the Prince Regent before the Manchus fell) are creating a triumph in the return of the war with which to rule Canton and to give full play to Communistic ideas.

The “Industrial and Commercial Daily Press” (“Kung Seung Yat Po”), a new Chinese paper published in Hongkong, hints that Hu's capture by the Reds may be attributable to alleged appropriations of funds from the sale of Soviet oil, such as oil having been imported to meet Canton's needs. A representative of this paper proceeded to Conduit Road last night to interview Hu Ching-sui, a brother of the arrested politician: Hu Han-min, it may be stated, has a house at Excelsior Terrace, which is between Conduit and Robinson Roads. The brother is supposed to have come down to Hongkong by train after an anxious time in custody.

Hu Han-min is said to have escaped, to be detained at the Whampoa Academy, and to have left for Shanghai by a vessel which did not put in at Hong-kong.

A very well-informed quarter in the Colony told a “China Mail” reporter, this morning that although it was assumed that the interests of Hu Han-min, Ngai Bong-ping (a former Canton general and chief of police), General Li Fook-lum of Honam and General Leung Hung-kai of Kong-moon, would unite against the Reds, their combined strength was small as contrasted with the armies of Generals Cheung and Hsu.

Hu Han-min's Capture. According to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," Hu Han-min escaped from the Foreign Ministry when the Reds surrounded him and proceeded to the house of Wong Ching-wai. Wong was out but Mrs. Wong assured him that a mistake must have been made and accompanied Hu to interview General Hsu. Once in the presence of Hsu, Hu Han-min was placed under arrest for removal to Whampoa. A military council comprising General Cheung, Techen Wu (chief of police) and Chu Pui-teh (a pro-Kuomintang yunnanese commander) and two others examined Hu Han-min's brother. Lam Chik-mien (formerly superintendent of the K.C. Railway, Chinese section) was bound in ropes until released on assurance

that he had nothing to do with the murder of Liu Chung-oi.

Ngai Bong-ping has fled either to Kongmoon or the West River. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that Ngai's family escaped through the good graces of a German medical doctor and another paper states that Ngai's house was burned down by the Reds.

General Leung. Hung-kai's whereabouts are unknown. Some time before the present crisis came to a head, it had already been reported that he had disagreed with the Canton Reds although he was, nominally, a subordinate. On good authority, the "China Mail" is informed that he is still at his Kongmoon headquarters, and out of danger. Vernacular reports say that he has either been shot in fighting at his Canton quarters, or that he has been captured together with two of his leading subordinates who were among the first to dispute the authority of the Canton Commission of Government.

This morning's "Wab Tsz Yat Po" publishes a report from a correspondent to the effect that Sun Fo has been reconciled to Chan Kwing-ming and that these two have promised to co-operate in an offensive against the Canton Reds. It will be recalled that Sun Fo went to Peking where he, apparently, got no satisfaction. The supposition now is that he is dissatisfied with the present Canton rulers. The address (in Chinese) of the house in Shanghai, where Chan and Sun Fo are said to have sat down at dinner is actually given.

History Repeated. In the time at its disposal it is difficult for the "China Mail" to review the situation at any length. History is repeating itself. The Kuomintang politicians have always relied on troops to subdue those with whom they did not agree. The so-called Whampoa Cadets served their purpose when the Yunnanese and Kwang.

headline: CHINESE WOUNDED
text: At 2.45 p.m. yesterday three Chinese soldiers fired a few shots from positions which they had taken up near the Customs house across the border at a picket of Indians from the Punjabi Regiment, who were on a hill on the opposite side in British territory. The Punjab's retaliated by firing four rounds, and one of the Chinese soldiers was seen to drop. The man was apparently wounded rather badly, as he was unable to get away and remained where he fell for nearly three hours. A party carrying a stretcher was

headline: CANTON QUIET
text:
RED ATTACK NOT, YET BEGUN.

"SPASMOLIC FIRING ONLY"

More definite news to hand from Canton gives the indication that the so-called grand offensive of the Bolsheviks has yet to materialise. There have been reports of a cross-river attack on Honam but from eyewitnesses on the spot it is gathered that the “expedition” which was sent must have been of little consequence as it attracted hardly any notice. On inquiry at the office of the Naval authorities, the “China Mail” was informed this morning that. Canton is quiet. It was understood that the party in power were taking steps to remove all opposition and had met with a little resistance. There is no organised fighting to speak of.

headline: Honam Position.
text:
Contradictory reports have reached Hongkong since yesterday afternoon. Some say that an offensive against Honam (the island on the south bank of the river) was launched yesterday and that General Li Fook-lam's troops were routed. Over a week ago it was announced in the "China Mail" that General Li had withdrawn his forces from the busier parts of Honam into the surrounding villages, instancing some ancestral halls being used as barracks for the first time since their erection in the city of the Sung Dynasty—several centuries ago. It may be that some Red detachments have landed in Honam to disarm the skeleton corps left behind by General Li but in that event there would hardly be any fighting.

One of the best informed gentlemen in the Colony said to the "China Mail":—People do not seem to have realised that the trouble this time—although the political aspect may be much wider—has, so far, been nothing like the last scrap with the Yunnanese when there were a few determined "actions." Spasmodic firing has been heard; and that is all, but the Whampoa Cadets seemed to have achieved their purpose.

headline: Strikers Disarmed.
text:
A presumption that, during the present upheaval, the “strike” movement in Canton has occupied little attention, seems to have been borne out. As is generally known, an exodus of the civil population usually follows a crisis in Canton city. At present there is no direct communication by steamer with either Macao or Hongkong. Nevertheless, in spite of strikers' pickets, quite a number of people have left for minor ports in the river delta and others have departed by the Canton-Kowloon Railway.

In their campaign of disarming everybody the Red, soldiers in Canton have also extended their activities to the strikers. Many of those doing picket duty and individuals carrying weapons have had such forcibly taken from them. In fact, some of the strikers seem to have incurred the suspicions of the Bolshevik leaders in connection with the death of Liu Chung-oi. A rumour is current, says a correspondent, that the Canton authorities suspect a member of the Hongkong-Wuchow (Steamer) Guild, a body previously in Hongkong but closed by the Police.

headline: Leung in Custody.
text:
Most of the vernacular papers agree that General Leung Hung-kai, who has about 10,000 anti-Red troops in and around Kong-moon, is in custody, having attended a meeting at Canton when he was overpowered by the guards of the General of the Cadets.

Of the fighting that has taken place, reports the "Kung Seung Yat Po," there was a real action on that part of the second bund in the east of the city where several hundred men, attached to the divisional headquarters of a Kongmoon commander, were disarmed after being surrounded. At Taishatau, a brigade headquarters was disposed of in the same way. Ngal Bong-ping's flight to Kongmoon has been confirmed and Hu Han-min is still stated to be in detention at the Whampoa Academy.

headline: STUDENT KILLED
text:
NEW KOWLOON CYCLING ACCIDENT.

As a result of losing control of the push bike on which he was riding, a Chinese student of Kwan Mun Ho village was killed yesterday.

The scene of the accident was the step by bill at Kan Pa-Kang lying between Tsun Wan and Shamsupo. Another student was astride of the machine at the time and he was injured, but not seriously.

The “China Mail” is informed by the Chung Shing Benevolent Society that Captain Chan Kum (Chan Kwoon-hing), who is one of the members, has been released by the pirates which pirated the S.S. Kwong Hung on the West River. Captain Chan has been in command of the steamer for some years.

Pakkai, Kongmbon, Aug. 26. News has reached this port that the compradore of the

strikers claimed special privilege as... they were performing "patriotic service." The pirates stripped them of even their singlets and all they had and turned them loose.

A batch of Hongkong amahs who, after much pleading, obtained permits to travel to Macao, were turned back by strike pickets at Chinshan, which is just across the border here. Very few people, if any, are getting through by that route. Armed pickets are on duty at the large pavilion on the Shekki road, thus preventing people leaving. Meidourne, August 28. After a vigorous debate lasting two hours, the House of Representatives by 85 to 22 votes permitted the Prime Minister, Mr. Stanley Bruce, to introduce the bill mentioned earlier in which the specials are described as "peace officers" and the Attorney General is empowered to appoint as many as he considers necessary for the preservation of peace throughout Australia.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
SOUTH AFRICA BEING INVOLVED.

AUSTRALIA'S PREPAREDNESS.

The position as regards the seamen's strike is more serious. Meetings of British seamen are being held in favour of a strike unless the grievances are remedied. There seems to be a prospect that all South African ports will be rapidly affected. The steamship Ballarat and the mail boat Arundel Castle have been held up.

headline: . CAPE DIEMMA.
text:
The day has been one of abortive conferences to settle the strike. Both the authorities and the shipping companies are in a dilemma as there does not appear any local way of dealing with the situation. The strike leaders admit that they signed the agreement in England, but say that they did so in order to get away from the Dominion ports where they have the whiphand to enforce a case-and-the-only way out was to pay the old rate until they reached England. The release without stain upon the character of two men sentenced at Durban is the only development of the situation. Stewards of the steamer Ballarat, persuaded the steward of the Arundel Castle to join the strike. The Premier, Mr. Hertszog, has cabled Mr. Havelock Wilson stating that British seamen are taking action on their own volition and are not incited by anyone in South Africa. EARLIER, EARLES Durban, August 28 The shipping strike has assumed serious proportions. The Continued at foot of next Column

crew of the Balmoral Castle have refused to work, and sailing has been postponed indefinitely.

The strike has occurred at a critical period because the ports are congested with steamers waiting to remove an unprecedented maize crop.

Two strikers of the Sandgate Castle who were sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment, have had their sentences suspended for a fortnight to enable them to reconsider their position and assist in getting the vessel away.

SITUATION IN AUSTRALIA. Melbourne August 09

There are further indications of the Seamen's strike ending. The Trades Council of Melbourne announces that it was in nowise in charge of the strike which is now in the hands of the British seamen themselves. The liner Chital has arrived and is being loaded with stevedores who intend to work all the British manned vessels.

There was an uproar in the House of Representatives when Mr. Bruce asked leave to introduce a bill to appoint special police in connection with the seamen's strike. Mr. Charlton, a labour leader, vigorously protested against "springing" such a bill in the House. The Senate after a vigorous debate, had adopted by a vote of 20 to 9 the ministerial motion that the Senate meet to borrow to consider special legislation and posting special police owing to the New South Wales Government's refusal to assist the Commonwealth to carry out the law in regard to possible deportations.

headline: CARGO OF BEER. / SCHOONER SEIZED BY DRY AGENTS.
text:
Key West, Florida, Aug. 28. The schooner "Fannie Prescott," bound from Havana to Nassau, with 750 cases of beer on board has been seized three miles from here. The crew of ten have been arrested and detained.

Philadelphia, August 28.—The Miners' Union has ordered a strike in the anthracite coalfields on September 1.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: BAD MAN.
text:
"Pardoned" by Dr. Sun Yat-sen for the alleged murder of his wife, subsequently deported from Hongkong as an undesirable, accused of having misappropriated public funds in this Colony, Canton and Shanghai, a notorious "labour boss" is now active once more in the strike against Hongkong.

Reported exclusively in the "China Mail" about a fortnight ago was the fact that Chinese coming to Hongkong from Nam-tau were being "squeezed" of various amounts. It was then stated that Chan Ping-sang, the notorious man whose career has been briefly given, was mainly responsible.

Namtau is a small port, in Chinese territory, just beyond Deep Bay. At least one big steam launch makes the journey to and fro each day. Fish and other foodstuffs, and passengers come to Hongkong from Namtau. With other routes temporarily closed up it was only natural that Hongkong strikers should make their way, overland or by native river craft, to Namtau to return to work. As soon as Canton heard of the port they opened up a strikers' branch office there. Pickets were sent out and soon Chan Ping-sang was the No. 1 man.

headline: $100 Per Head.
text:
For a time very few people got through and little or no fish was shipped here. Then the restrictions seem to relax. According to the vernacular papers Namtau's strike office is now letting cargo and trayellers through, on a consideration. Each person leaving Namtau for Hongkong, so the report goes, must pay a cash deposit of $100 which will be forfeited on failure to return the same day. In other words, those wishing to return to their old positions must pay $100 for the privilege. As many know, there are a good many domestic servants, coolies and seafaring Chinese from the hinterland of Namtau and the majority of market fish stall holders are also natives of that place.

It seems to be the same old story. Chan sprang into the limelight when the seamen's strike negotiations began. Then he was found guilty of murdering his wife at Canton but was released by Sun Yat-sen. He came back to Hongkong to be deported and returned to Canton where he fell into disgrace through alleged embezzlement of union funds. For a time he was in Shanghai till he got into trouble there. Since then he was not heard of until at Namtau, he cropped up again. It has also been rumoured that he has incurred the displeasure, by his actions, of the native garrison.

Troops Disarmed. In-coming passengers from Namtau have been able to throw some light on the recent Canton "war." Several hundred of General Hsu Shung-chi's Kuomin-tang (Cantonese) troops were seen to march on Namtau which was held by another band of Canton men who evidently did not satisfy the Bolsheviks.

The new-comers were far superior in numbers to the garrison and in a short while the defenders were disarmed.

It now means that the whole of the Chinese territory adjoining the British border is in the hands of Canton's trusted troops, including both the non-Cantonese "Cadets," and Cantonese regulars.

headline: Uhtarsja si / NATURALLY
text:
CANTON OFFICIALS DISOWN EMBARGO

THE USUAL DODGE.

" Canton, August 30. The Government has replied to the British Consul General disclaiming the report that it published and approved the coastal shipping regulations.

The wording of the Canton Government's reply to Sir James Jamieson, the "China" Mail's understand, was that the proclamation regarding the embargo on shipping had not been authorised by the "Government Department" but had been issued by the Strikers' Union.

The opinion expressed to a "China Mail" representative by local business men approached on

the matter was that the denial was only what had been considered inevitable, but that in view of the fact that the Strikers' Union was an administrative arm of the Government, particularly as regarded orders in respect of shipping, the denial carried no weight at all.

It was pointed out to the reporter that agents of neutral and even Chinese firms had received official intimation from Canton that if their boats touched at Hongkong they would not be allowed to land cargo in Canton. How then, it was contended, could the official denial be treated at all seriously or as justifying an attitude that it removed the casus belli. TELEPHONE LINE CUT

A Reuter cable dated August 18 stated: The Canton Chinese authorities have drawn up rules with regard to coastal navigation providing that steamers of any nationality except British and Japanese shall be allowed to run to and from any ports, provided they omit Hongkong. All steamers entering the port must be inspected by a picket of the anti-imperialist Union. The export of foodstuffs or any other raw material from inland is not allowed. It is understood the British Consul General has written to the Chinese Government asking if the regulations are official. A London cable dated August 19 read as follows: — Authoritative circles in London are concerned at the action of the Canton Government in banning the free movement of British ships to and from Chinese ports, as it constitutes a flagrant violation of the treaty rights of foreign governments. The British Government will give the fullest and most careful consideration to the whole position before coming to a definition decision. headline: REDS ON TOP. / AUTOCRAT EXTENDS HIS SPHERE
text:
TRIUMVIRATE IN NAME?

Startling events took place in Canton during the week-end as a result of which the Bolshvik faction now holds undisputed sway in the city and in several important districts which were not hitherto so are now directly under Red influence.

There has been no fighting to speak of. As pointed out in the "China Mail" there was no offensive against Honam. In fact it now seems that General Li Fooklam—of whom little was expected—has surrendered to the Reds but has been allowed to retain his command.

Latest messages to hand confirm the first details of the campaign of expansion by the Bolsheviks. This morning it was

stated that the victors have not been resting on their laurels but rapidly following up their successes.

Reinforcements are believed to have arrived at Kongmopn which fell, during the week-end, into Red hands. The army of General Leung Hung-kai, who is still reported to be in custody at Whampoa, is fleeing into the interior. A prediction has been made that it will shortly be in the territory of General Tang Punyan, who is a subordinate of Chan Kwing-ming. Canton war vessels are mentioned as having reached Kongmoon and the Red vanguard is penetrating inland to take over districts vacated by Leung's men.

Nowhere is there any possibility of offering resistance. General Cheung Kai-shek, c.i.c. of the Cadets, is now the autocrat of Canton. A triumvirate is supposed to exist but the other two—General Hsu Shung-chi and

headline: Wong Ching-wai—are very much in the background.
text:
West River Movement. Along the West River Red contingents are moving to attack a flank of the Cantonese garrison. Brigades of Cadets were thrown out in short time, occupying, without fighting, nearly all important points on the river, and railway. These troops, according to latest intelligence, are moving towards the Sze Yan. The Cadet/chief in is said to have refused the nomination of commander-in-chief of the Kuomintang Army, stating that he was satisfied to be President of the Whampoa Academy and garrison commander of Canton. He has appointed five army commanders, each with two divisions. In doing so he has named Hsu Shung-chi, hitherto the standby of the Cantonese Bolsheviks, as his subordinate. Li Fook-lam is also one of the chosen as are a Yunnanese and a Hunanese general, and Li Chai-sum whose sway extends along to Wuchow and parts of the West River.

In the excitement following the death of Lin Chung-oi, some of the strikers came in for rough treatment at the hands of Cadet patrols in Canton.

The position is that once having taken the guild leaders into confidence it will be necessary to provide for the rank and file. Liu Chung-oi's immediate subordinates are still officiating at the Finance Bureau and these are paying out the daily quota to maintain the strikers. Nominally, the Canton strike position has not changed. Actually, the possibility of a debacle is further removed and the outlook is not at all bright. With the pronounced Reds in the ascendant, it is only natural to presume that the politicians will maintain their policy.

headline: MAILS HELD UP.
text:
QUEENSLAND AND BOYCOTT PROTEST.

STRONG MEASURES NEEDED.

Following the action of the Queensland railway strikers in boycotting the malls, the Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce, has telegraphed the Premier of Queensland regarding the holding up of 26 mailbags at Rockhampton in consequence of the railway strikers' boycott of malls. Mr. Bruce points out the seriousness of such illegal action and requests an assurance of prompt measures to deal with the offenders. The Senate passed the third reading of the polled bill.

headline: CAUTION QUIET. / RESISTANCE TO REDS FADNS OUT.
text:
CADET COMMANDER RULES.

Having wiped out any possibility of resistance for the time being, the Bolsnevik party in Canton is now consolidating its position.

Not taking into consideration the Chan Kwin-ming forces now between the upper sources of the East River and the Fukien boundary, there is hardly any integrate force able to challenge the Reds. General Cheung Kai-shek, c.i.c. of the Whampoa Cadets, is the man of the hour. He only sprang into prominence earlier in the year in the campaign against Swatow but he is now the asocrat of Canton, ruling the city and other parts of the province with the aid of Bolshevik counsellors.

News from merchants indicates a feeling of unrest in apprehension of coming radical changes. Honam, like Canton, is also quiet but Li Foxk-lam's troops are still in the "provinces."

Strict vigilance is being maintained in the city and the comb out with which the coup began has no quite ended.

Otherwise there is little to report. Riserring to houses in Hongkong

headline: STRIKE CHANGES.
text:
THE BEGINNING OF THE END?

GENERAL LI TAKES "OATH."

Said to be commanded by Russian officers, Chinese naval vessels are patrolling the river and approaches at Canton. At night there is marked activity. It is not known if the precautions are a sequel to the recent Bolshevik coup.

While the “Canton Gazette” writes about the severance of steamer communication to and from Macao, in support of the boycott of Hongkong, a Canton vernacular paper, at a subsequent date, reports as follows:—As conditions in Canton are abnormal the Strike Executive has decided to give permission to all or any persons to leave for Macao or Hongkong, provided they give a written undertaking to return within a week.

This is in direct variance to the

policy professed all along by the agitators. Some think that it may be the beginning of the end. Having been so busy in the last week the Canton Government may be finding the strikers too heavy a burden to bear.

There is still little traffic from Chinese ports to Macao but military leaders in the vicinity are making fortunes by escorting trading junk, passengers, foodstuffs, cargo, etc., to Macao.

No change has been reported at Canton. General Li Fook-lam is stated to have taken the oath of allegiance to the Kuomintang, or rather the Red party. Hu Han-min is believed to have been removed from Whampoa to Bocca Tigris. Further inland than Kongmoon, the anti-Bolshevik troops of General Leung Hung-kai are moving southwards from the Cadets and it is predicted that they will eventually co-operate with Chan Kwing-ming's army in the outskirts of the province. Rockefeller Jr., has been very active in philantrophic work.

headline: NO GERMAN EXODUS.
text:
FACTS CONCERNING TUNG ON PASSENGERS.

RETURNING BUSINESS MEN.

The return from Canton to Hongkong aboard H.M.S. Tung On of passengers of German nationality who were not taken up by that vessel has led to the assumption that there has been an exodus of German business men from Shameen.

A “China Mail” representative who made enquiries this morning was informed that the numbers of Germans returning to Hongkong from Canton was but few, and that in nearly every case they had previously gone up from Hongkong, by train or other means as in view of the responsibility that the naval authorities had to assume for passengers on the Tung On, it was difficult to get a permit to go up unless one had exceptionally pressing business. It was less difficult to get a permit for return at Canton.

A German business man who returned to the Colony from Canton yesterday assured a "China Mail" representative that German residents' safety and their businesses were affected in the same degree as British, but there was no talk of an exodus.

As regards the general position in Canton, the “China Mail” informant could say little “apart from confirming the news that Li Fuk-lam's forces had submitted to the Red regime which appeared to be established as firmly as anything could be said to be in Canton. There was still no communication between Shameen and Canton, he stated.

headline: “HONAM” LEAVES.
text:
300 PASSENGERS AND 15 TONS OF CARGO.

TO ANCHOR OFF SHAMEEN.

Crowds of Chinese this morning gathered on spots along the Praya adjacent to the Steamboat Company's Canton wharf long before the hour for departure of the A.S. Honam on its trip to Canton. They were still there, gazing, incredulously, when prompt to the minute and after the last bells had rung, the paddes revolved and the steamer left the wharf. This was at 8 a.m.

Total passengers aboard numbered a little over 300, of whom 15 were Europeans. General cargo, consisting chiefly of foodstuffs, amounted to about 15 tons. The ship is to anchor among the men-of-war off Shameen and will not discharge at the Canton wharf which, of course, is in Chinese territory and where there might be trouble with pickets. Passengers who wish to board or leave must make their own arrangements and Shameen is also to make its own arrangements for taking off the cargo if no coolies are available. The Honam leaves Capton at 8 a.m. to tomorrow morning, arriving back at Hongkong at 3 p.m. It is probable that she will then run regularly, the “China Mail” understands.

headline: PIOUS HOPES.
text:
WHEN WILL TRADE START AGAIN?

BUSINESS MEN'S VIEWS.

Chinese business men are evincing great interest in the trip of the s.s. "Homen" to Canton. They think it a happy inspiration to have despatched the vessel and wondered why the matter was not broached before.

Several seen to-day by a "China Mail" reporter, the majority with extensive Canton business interested predicted that to-day would mark a definite stop forward to bring conditions to normal.

General Cheung Kai-shek is not a native of Kwongtung. He is not a politician but only a militant and it will be advantageous to him to see trade restored. His word will be law. To-day he may be too busy to attend to strikers and labour unions and the "Honum" may be ignored. But if the stand he has taken is any criterion he will soon reduce the power of the guild. Meanwhile, everybody is so impoverished that the strike pickets will be glad to squeeze cargo and passengers. For a time this will continue till the Hongkong workers have had sufficient opportunity to return. Then there will be no more power behind the so-called labour politicians and that is the end.

Another was not so optimistic. He thought that intercourse would be winked at but only under substantial payment of bribes so that trade with Hongkong would be under a serious handicap.

headline: “HONAM” RETURNS.
text:
PASSENGERS LEAVE BUT FEW EMBARK.

CARGO BROUGHT BACK.

The s.s. "Honam" returned to Hongkong from Canton shortly after 4.30 p.m. yesterday.

Crowds of Chinese assembled on the Praya from the early afternoon at first in groups and then in crowds. Eventually, traffic being hindered somewhat, the crowd had to be cleared back to the pavement, the sight of a revenue officer with a broom proving quite sufficient enough for the purpose! The talk among these Chinese on the Praya, a "China Mail" representative was informed by one who spoke the language well was that the "Honam" had sunk with all hands aboard! On the wharf itself were a few Europeans who were expecting friends to arrive from Shameen, Mr. T. H. King, D.C.I., with police officers, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, the Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer, Mr. J. Arnold, Mr. J. D. Lloyd, Superintendent, Imports and Exports Department, and revenue officers.

When the ship approached near enough for figures to be observed, it was noticed that there were not many aboard apart from officers and Indian guards. Actually, it transpired that there were about thirty Chinese, nearly all women and children and the rest were mostly "white" Russians who had helped to take up the "Sui An" and the "Sui Tai" and had remained in Canton looking for work.

The cargo which was taken up was brought back again, as there were no lighters available. The passengers who went up, however, managed to get off by sampan. The reason for so few boarding the ship was undoubtedly that pickets were busy intimidating the sampan people who had evidently been instructed that they might take anyone away from the ship, but none to it.

The skipper of the vessel told a "China Mail" representative that he did not see vessels which he could say with definite assurance contained pickets but other officers told the reporter that they had been assured by the Customs officials who came aboard that certain boats and launches were those of strike pickets. The only way in which the few passengers had managed to get aboard was that when these craft were on the other side of the ship the sampans in which were those desirous of boarding came nearer the ship and then occupants were hauled in, much to their triumph and satisfaction.

The following incident shows how keen the Chinese in Hongkong are to know more intimate details of events in Canton and the prospects of their friends there being able to get away. A Chinese woman who came off the "Honam" was questioned outside the wharf by representatives of the Trade Maintenance Association whose intentions were entirely friendly and who merely wished to obtain information as to how she had boarded the "Honam."

The woman, however, took fright, thinking that they were seeking to intimidate her. She took to her heels, being pursued by the Chinese seekers after information. She finally rid herself of them by jumping into a ricsha. The only hitch, and it hardly deserves to come under that head since those who were responsible for it acted on their own account, was the disappearance of two Press representatives who went up as passengers—Mr. F. Oliver, of the "South China Morning Post," and Mr. J. S. Cox, of the "Hongkong Daily Press." They went ashore in the Customs launch shortly after the boat arrived on Thursday afternoon and were seen to land on the Customs steps on the Bund. Their nonappearance was not reported to the Captain of the "Honam" until the ship was under way about 10 a.m. yesterday. He immediately caused a wireless message to be despatched to the Senior "naval officer" informing him that Mr. Oliver and Mr. Cox were saboreous. headline: BACK TO HONGKONG / HOW A STRIKER DODGED THE PICKETS.
text:
How a striker found his work on a long from Canton this week, in risk of his life, was related to a "China Mail" reporter this morning. After a stay of about two months in Canton he began to get tired of the inactivity. Some of his colleagues were earning money there by working at 20 cents a day — in addition to food provided by the Executive— on the road to Whampoa. This road was now as long as “the eye could see” but people whose property adjoined the highway were up in protest as their paddi fields had been ruthlessly cut up without compensation. Others, who had a few dollars, pitched stalls in the streets. They snipped off electric wires, took whatever current they wanted—also without payment— and made money by hawking. This man's batch was quartered in a block of new buildings but they got their meals in a disused Tantan house. Mosquito nets or even beds were absent. They slept on the hard floor. A trip to Shekki had proved abortive as the tow-boat carried about ten batches of new pickets for Chinshan. Taking the train at Qaishatau, the striker reached Samchan, the fare for a third-class ticket being $8. At Samchan Market, he passed the night in an improvised boarding house where he slept on the floor for 20 cents. Several "mushroom hotels" had spring up there to cope with the people always passing through. On being turned back at the point of the hayonet at the Chinese ridgehead on the Samchun River he striker paid $1.60 as a bribe and walked ten miles to a space where the river could be forged. When in knee-deep water some body opened fire at him and he ran for over three hours till he cached. Sheungahul station (in British territory) where a train took him to Yaumati for 35 cents. headline: ANTI-RED COUP?
text:
CADETS DISARMED AT KONGMOON.

LAND AND SEA ATTACK.

A GENERAL TORTURED TO

A coup, resulting in an appreciable check to the Whampoa Cadets, has been reported from Kongmoon, where several hundred of Canton's crack regiment are stated to have given up their weapons to preserve their lives. "To-day's "Kang Seung Ynt Po" ("Industrial and Commercial Daily Press")" says that the expedition of Cadets sent from Canton has met with disaster. After last week's crisis in the capital, the Reds attacked General Leung Hung-kai's "Troops in Kongmoon and its hinterland. The Canton force landed without opposition. Of the 2,000 men, the majority were sent inland to round up the wavering anti-Reds and several hundred stayed behind to maintain communications.

Taking advantage of the situation, General "Li Chai-sum of the West River," launched an offensive against Kongmoon. The vernacular report goes on to say that his fleet of armed vessels moved down river with the tide and a combined land-and-sea attack succeeded. Not only was the garrison of Cadets disarmed, but the line of the up-country force has been threatened.

[Note: Li Chai-sum has already been appointed one of General Cheung Kai-shek's army commanders but the Chinese papers hint that he is aiming at the overthrow of the Cadets to ensure his own safety.]

headline: Generals Shot.
text:
Other vernacular papers report the shooting, under orders from Canton's military directorate, of Lam Chik-mien (former Superintendent, Kowloon-Canton Railway, Chinese section), Commander Lam Shu-ngai and Commander Yeung Kam-loong, who fell into Red hands when the Cadet chieftain effected his coup.

Little is also known of Hu Hanmin. A Chinese paper says that it has now transpired 'that his arrest was not due to suspicions of his loyalty to the Kuomintang—or the Bolshevik party as it is designated—but that the trouble is only an outcome of the periodic scramble for power, events which happen in Canton regularly when several aspire to rule Kwangtung as a despot.

Chan Ping-sang, the former notorious seamen leader who was pardoned by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen for the murder of his wife, is once more in the public eye.

Recently his actions as chief of the strike pickets at Nam Tau were reported. It now transpires that for the space of 36 hours he occupied the post of district magistrate at Nam Tau, which is just beyond Deep Bay and, of course, in Chinese territory.

Shortly before the arrival of the proper magistrate the embargo on cargo and passengers for Hongkong was withdrawn with the result that in two days several hundred people returned to the Colony.

The restrictions have been re-imposed but Chan Ping sang is a mandarin no longer.

The closing rate of the dollar demand, to-day was 2/5 5/10

This, the "China Mail" learns from another and reliable source is due in part to the relaxing of efforts of the pickets on the borders or the devising of more effective means of circumventing them. It is certainly a fact that considerably more produce is coming in from outlying districts. The attitude that has been taken by the hands of Government schools, a "China Mail" representative learned on anquiry this morning, is that all boys who were absent without leave before the term was closed and whose parents had not written explaining, extinguishing circumstances at the time or shortly after their absence have been expelled. headline: China / "TELL THE KING."
text:
"I can tell the King", were words alleged by the prosecution at this morning's District Court Martial as having been used by the accused when the spoke to a military police men.

Private Henry Barber, East Surrey Regiment, was charged with striking a non-commissioned officer. Major E. S. Halford, R.A., presided and the other members of the Court were Captain Montamaro (Surrey, Regiment) and Lieut. Wright-Neville (Punjabi Regiment). Liout. A. E. Cottum prosecuted. Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman acted as prisoner's counsel.

Fra必Corporal Doubtfire, regimental police corporal, deposited that on the night of August 22, after roll-call he questioned accused at EVASIONOR COMPLICITY OF PICKETS?

Wellington Barracks and accused replied that he was going for a walk. Witness played accused under open arrest for attempting to break out of barracks. On the way back, accused—as alleged by witness—remarked that "it seems a pastime in the battalion, placing 'blokes' under arrest." Witness pointed out that this should be told to the company commander next morning whereupon accused rejoined "I can tell the King."

After another remark witness placed accused under close arrest. It was then that accused was supposed to have struck witness a blow in the face.

Private W. Moore, who was with the Lance-Corporal, gave similar evidence. He added that accused said something about looking for his dog.

Accused said that he was taking his dog for a final run before "lights out" when his pet chased another dog round the R. E. tennis courts. It was while following the dog that he was questioned by Lee. Cpl. Doubtfire. After being placed under open arrest and returning; as ordered, to his room, he said something to a friend. Lee.-Opl Doubtfire stood over him in a threatening manner, one hand on his hip and the other wagging a cane. He accused, was provoked and lost his temper. He made to strike with his fist; he nearly did so but realised his mistake and withdrew his hand in time.

Captain Drake-Brockman, who had taken great pains in cross-examining the witnesses for the prosecution, addressed the Court on behalf of accused. He submitted that the offence had provoking circumstances and suggested that the military police corporal had acted hastily. Subsequently Captain Drake-Brockman made a statement as company commander of accused. The speaker took over command on May 1, 1925, and had always found accused to be an efficient and clean soldier. On his recommendation accused was employed as an officer's servant. He had never had trouble with accused who was short-tempered and needed tactful handling. Lienk Colam then read out accused's record. In service of three years 71 days he had been charged once with neglect of duty and once with absence.

headline: BARON HAYASHI. COLONY'S DISTINGUISHEI VISITOR.
text:
Baron Hayashi, who is returning to Japan on the conclusion of his term of office as Japanese Ambassador in London, arrived in Hongkong yesterday by the s. "Fushimi Maru." He was met by the Japanese Consul (Mr. Takahashi) and other well-known Japanese members of the community. He launched at Government House and in the evening was present at a dinner given by the Japanese community in his honour at the Consul's residence.
