"Hobnam" to and from Hongkong, says the "Canton Gazette" of September 16, the General Department of the Pickets of the Strike Committee, has ordered an additional force of 200 pickets to patrol the Pearl River: Passengers intending to travel by this steamer will be detained together with any sampan attempting to carry them or to

headline: STRIKERS CAUGHT.
text:
STREET BRAWL TLEADS TO ARNEST

Throughing squabbling over an old enmity, two members of the Sam-clown strike pickets are believed to have fallen into Police hands at Nathan Road, Yaumuti.

According to one report the men are alleged to have been banished from Hongkong after several terms of imprisonment. They are also said to be have been suspected of implication with a notorious Hongkong secret society.

Indications are forthcoming that they both did duty with the strike pickets at Shumchun. They were arrested by Chinese detectives through a brawl in the street.

headline: SELF-PROTECTION.
text:
CHINESE WHO DEFED THE STRIKERS..

A Chinese watchmuron a steamer was charged before Mr. E. W. Hamilton at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with unlawful possession of a revolver and eight rounds of ammunition.

Mr. J. M. d'Almada Remedios appeared for the defence and tendered a plen of guilty. It was stated on behalf of the accused that he was one of those who refused to throw in his lot with the strikers and remained at his post. There had been no unlawful intent in the man carrying a revolver on his person, and it was only done as a measure of self-protection against any attack by intimidators:

Sub-Inspector K, W, Andrew, who had charge of the case, expressed himself as satisfied with this explanation.

His Worship said that he could not acquit the accused of the offence altogether, and imposed a fine of $25, or in the alternative three weeks' hard labour.

headline: FOOD SHIP.
text:
MORE LIVESTOCK REACHES HONGKONG.

The U.S. Phranang (formerly of British registry but now under the Chinese flag) has arrived here from Pukhot and Hojhow.

There was an board a quantity of poultry and livestock comprising pigs, cattle, etc.

Hoihow is the port of Hainan Island which, with part of the opposite mainland, forms the domains of General Tang Pun-yan, a subordinate of General Chan Kwing-ming. General Tang has held out for the pro-Chin cause for years in the south of Kwangtung province and has prevented agitation from anti-foreign outbursts.

One reason, given for there being no trains for the public on the Chinese section of the Kowloon-Canton Railway is that all traffic is now monopolised for transporting Whampoa Cadets to the East River to disarm Hsu Shung-chi's Cantonese men in that area.

One thousand five hundred tails of prepared opium vined at over $10,000 are stated so have been found by Police on board the

headline: MANY PASSENGERS / PEOPLE COMING FROM MACAO.
text:
Boats coming over from Macao yesterday afternoon brought more than the usual number of passengers. The Steamboat Co.'s S.S. "Kinshan" was very well patronised.

As explained in yesterday's "China Mail," small river steamers are now playing between Macao and Kwong Hoi city in the Sze Yap district. Some have also travelled down to Macao from Hongmoon on junks used for transporting (Chinese) military coal.

Should the Macao-Kwong Hol service continue, more strikers are expected to return in addition to the 2,000 or so who came back yesterday.

headline: S.S. "CHANGTE." / THIS AFTERNOON'S RECEPTION.
text:
A SPLENDID SHIP.

An "At" Home" is being held this afternoon on board the s.s. "Changte" by Captain Gambrill and the owners prior to the sailing of the vessel on her maiden voyage next week.

A frequent launch service was maintained between Murray Pier and the steamer for the convenience of the guests, many of whom took advantage of the kind invitation from an early hour.

As has already been reported, the s.s. "Changte" made a successful trial run last Saturday and demonstrated her seaworthiness to a large company on board. Aspeed of 14.77 knots was attained at the trials against 13 knots according to the contract.

The vessel was built by the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Co., Ltd., for the Australian-Oriental Line, Ltd. (Messrs. G. S. Yuill and Co., Ltd., Sydney) and the local agents will be Messrs. Butterfield and Swire. The "Change" with her sister ship will replace the two old vessels now on the Hongkong-Australia run.

All the features of a modern ship and everything conducting to the comfort and safety of passengers are seen in the new vessel, which has already received favourable comment from visitors.

headline: STRIKE THREAT.
text:
HOME COAL TRUCE HITCH DEADLOCK.

CONFERENCE - ABORTIVE.

The miners conference at Downing Street broke down after Mr. Baldwin had explained that the settlement of July does nothing beyond continuing the agreement of the owners and miners of 1924 and variations in district rates thereunder do not concern the Government further.

Later.

Mr. A. J. Cook made a statement controlling Mr. Baldwin's statement declaring that pending a settlement of the dispute the miners would not participate in the proceedings of the Coal Commission, but would appeal to the Labour movement to support him as it did in July.

headline: Ready For Trouble.
text: An influential organisation has been formed presided over by Viscount Hardinge, the members of the council including Lord Jellicoe, Searborough, and Falkland and Sir Rennell Rodd with the object of establishing over the country a system of volunteers to maintain supplies vital to the services in the event of a general strike. The scheme is already partly developed in London. Sir Rennell Rodd, interviewed, declared the organisation was non-party, non-political, and unpaid, and not formed for the purpose of opposing legitimate Trade Union activities, but to prevent the severe privation of the mass of the people who did not have a direct part in the actual dispute. He added that the Government had been informed of what they were trying to do and in the event of an emergency the whole organisation would be placed at the disposal of the authorities.

headline: CARGO MOVING.
text:
BUT NOT THROUGH. HONGKONG.

DOLLAR LINE VENTURE

For some months now the only effective method of moving cargo from Hongkong to Canton and of getting cargo from Canton has been by way of Shanghai and in the run between these ports Japanese and Russian vessels have been engaged. The Dollar line has now entered the field and the "Grace Dollar" which proceeded to Canton from the Philippines loaded up there yesterday with Pacific and Atlantic coast cargo. The s.s., "Hanover," of the same service, is due there on October 7 and will load for Honolulu and the Atlantic coast. The Dollar line has established an office in Canton City for the purpose of assisting shippers. This will also be used in connection with the service the Dollar line is to maintain between Whampoa and Shanghai with the "Lake Farrar," one of the recently purchased boats from the Shipping Board. This will handle local or transhipping cargo for U.S. ports.

The “China Mail” understands that no difficulty has been or will be c-erienced by the Dollar Line with regard to loading up British Canadian cargo at Canton but no such incoming cargo will be taken delivery of sp long as the present regime lasts.

headline: SWATOW OUTLOOK.
text:
MERCHANTS SAY "CLEAR OUT COMMUNISTS."

CHAN'S ARMY ADVANCES.

“Clear out the Communists” is the translation of banners exhibited by merchants of Kit Yang, the capital of an important district near Swatow, when General Chan Kwing-ming's forces advanced on the town.

Kit Yang had previously been held by Hsu Shung-chi's men but they fled on the approach of the Chan army. New officials, civil and military, have been appointed.

The "Wah. Tsz Yat Po's" Swatow correspondent says that the Swatow telegraph office has handled over 300 messages a day, this abnormal number being due almost entirely to trade inquiries; indications are apparent that trade between Hongkong and Swatow will take on definite shape almost immediately.

headline: STRIKE TO END?
text:
CANTON GOVERNMENT'S INITIATIVE.

ABORTIVE CONFERENCE.

On Wednesday the Canton (Kuomintang) Commission of Government had a conference with the Strike Executive Committee to discuss whether the present strike should be called off.

No decision was arrived at, some of the strike leaders advocating a “settlement” and others continuation. However, the sponsors of the meeting have hopes that negotiations in certain directions may have the desired effect.

headline: STUDENTS CAUGHT
text:
ESTERDAY'S ARRESTS.

Alleged to have been student agitators at Swatow, five Chinese (Chiu Chow) youths were arrested yesterday and they are said to have had with them portraits of Lenin and Sun Yat-sen, pernicious literature in their scrapbooks and a circular from the Hoi Fung Labour Guild.

Found strolling about on the Praya, the five youths told the Police that they had arrived at Shaukiwan by a junk from Shamei and were looking for a boat for Canton as they wanted to go to the Sacred Heart School there. When a search was made the writing; etc., was found.

Suspicions exist that the band of students left Swatow on the approach of General Chan Kwingming's forces, that they trekked to Shanmei whence they came on to Hongkong to pass through to Canton. One of them is said to have had a receipt for propaganda funds of over $100.

They will be brought before a Magistrate after inquiries have been made.

headline: CHAN'S ADVANCE.
text:
WAICHOW AND OTHER POINTS THREATENED.

LATEST SWATOW NEWS.

During the week-end news reached Hongkong that General Chan Kwing-ming's' forces were moving forward from their base, Swatow, and retaking territory which they formerly held. It is gathered from a very reliable source that the present objective is not Canton. Rather, it is proposed to advance where there is little chance of resistance, taking advantage of the possible disagreement between the Cantonese element of the Kuomintang and the Whampoa Cadets.

Some of Chan's armies are now moving on Waichow city, Tam Shui and Ping Shan, all points of strategic importance on the West River. All through, there has been little or no fighting. A small detachment of Whimpon Cadets has been cut off.

Waichow city is controlled by General Yeung Kwan-yu, for years one of Chan's most ardent supporters but now nominally, a subordinate "of Hsu Shung-chi who has fled to Shanghai. A commander by name of Yu has practically surrendered to Commander Yeung. Yu states that he was holding a garrison with the Whampoa Cadets referred to but he separated from them when he learned of the Canton coups. Yeung has about 7,000 bayonets and the amalgamation with Yu will bring his strength up to 10,000. His declaration for Chan—a not altogether unexpected event—would mean the automatic return of Waichow city to Chan's cause. So far, commander Yeung does not seem to have prepared any resistance to Chan's vanguard. Summed up, the position to-day means that Chan's troops have retrieved a large part of Ka Ying Chow prefecture and a part of Waichow prefecture. The taking of Waichow city, Tam Shui and Ping Shan will mean the holding of points within two days' march on the Kowloon-Canton Railway (Chinese section) but it is thought that the next offensive will be made with Poklo as the final objective. Hop Pa, the scene of stubborn fighting several months back, is also in Chan hands. Canton can offer battle by using the decontrolled troops on the East River, formerly under Hsu Shung-chi or by sending Cadets

headline: STUDENTS CAUGHT.
text:
PROPAGANDA LITERATURE IN COURT.

Five Chinese youths were charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning for having in their possession pocket books and documents used for propaganda purposes.

Sub-Inspector R. Shannon said that they were arrested on the Hongkong wharf on Friday morning as they were leaving a ferry from Shaukiwan. The men informed him that they had gone from Swatow to Shanmei and later to Shaukiwan by junk, and they were looking for a boat to go to Canton.

The documents, which included photographs and receipts for propaganda funds, point to the men being student agitators, and they were apparently forced to get away from Swatow on the approach of General Chan Kwingming's forces.

The accused were remanded for one week for the documents to be more fully looked into.

The Dollar Stemship Line's office in Canton, recently set up in connection with special arrangements for the loading up of their ships at Canton, is at 508 Ka Nam Tong building, West Bund. Notifications issued from that office, refer to the sailing of the a.g. "Grace Dollar" and to the loading of another steamer there on Oct. 5 and another in the first half of November providing sufficient cargo is forthcoming.

TODAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar on demand, 10-day was 2/61/10

headline: NEAR THE END? / STRIKE NOW REPORTED DOOMEO.
text:
IMPORTANT DEVELOPMENTS:

From the Chinese point of view important developments have taken place during the week-end in regard to a settlement of the present strike.

On September 11, the Canton Strike Executive sent a letter to the Combined Association of (Hongkong) District Commercial Guilds welcoming delegates to Canton. This letter did not arrive till last Thursday. Yesterday afternoon a meeting was held, delegates were selected and the delegation was to have proceeded to Canton by the early train this morning.

Last Thursday, in response to an invitation from the Canton (Kuomintang) Commission of Government, the Strike Executive sent representatives to attend a meeting, a move having been made to express the view that the time had come to "settle the strike." The strikers are stated to have suggested several demands regarding labour unions in Hongkong, presentation on the Legislative Council, the reinstatement of strikers and the payment of wages during the strike period. However, so the report goes, Canton's decision is likely to be regulated by the word of the men now in power and there is a belief that they wish to end the present position.

headline: CANTON'S RULER.
text:
GEN. CHI JNG KAI-SHE'S

Another indication that General Cheung Kai-Shek (the Whampoa Cadet commandant) is monopolising the control of Caution is forthcoming from the report on Saturday, in a Canton vernacular paper, that Tam Yin-hoi (commanding the Hunanese army) has resigned the appointment as Chairman of the Military Commission (in succession to the departed Hsu Shung-chi). Tam pleads being busy and ill-health.

headline: BOMBS FOR CHINA.
text:
The arrest at Pogranelhna of a Bolshevik alleged to be a diplomatic courier, who was found in possession of bombs en tout to China, is confirmed in several reliable sources, all of which agree that his luggage also contained $50,000 in American gold. The Bolshevik Tasse Agency, however, denies that it was a Soviet diplomatic courier who was arrested, maintaining that this is "a pure fabrication of interested circles."

Because he had had trouble with the chief officer and dared not return was the excuse advanced by Almat. Din Kitchell (Malay), a quartermaster of the 8.8. "Taiyuan" who was charged at the Marine Court this morning with absence from the ship without leave. He was given permission to go sailors at Mandla on July 17, but did not turn up when the ship sailed on July 28. He was detained there and handed back on the ship's return on September 23. He was sentenced to a health's hard labour, and days may be deducted and his prison maintenance was to be paid for out of pay due to him.

headline: TROOPSHIP SEIZED.
text:
ARMED MEN IN LOCAL WATERS.

COXSWAIN'S ALLEGED. RUSE.

Beyond the fact that the so-called Chinese soldiers on board the s.s. "Sui Yik" might be placed across the border no decision was given out by official quarters when inquiries were made this morning concerning the vessel seized on Saturday evening.

As has been reported the "Sui Yik" was proceeding to Au. Tau (a Chinese port) and is believed to have sailed from Canton with reinforcements for the Bolshevik troops. The ship formerly plied between Hongkong and Shanmei until she fell into Red hands since when she is believed to have been used as a transport. One story current is that the old coxswain took the opportunity of entering Hongkong waters so that the vessel could be seized, his wish being to get the boat out of the control of the Canton military.

Sighted near Cheung Chau (Dumbell) Island, the "Sui Yik" was escorted into harbour by H. M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" and a police launch. The Chinese force on board made a show of resistance when ordered to hand over their arms. The soldiers were about 150 in number; they had about 71 rifles and 75 bandoliers, of native make. About 300,000 rounds of ammunition were found in the hold.

Berthed at No. 6 Admiralty buoy, the "Sui Yik" was guarded by the searchlight on H.M.S. "Hermes." This morning a police launch was going round the vessel to prevent disembarkation.

headline: STREET MISHAPS.
text:
BOY CYCLIST'S COLLIDE WITH MOTORS.

A Chinese youth riding a push bicycle sustained injuries to his head when he collided with a motor 'bus at Nathan Road' on Saturday. The force of the impact rendered him unconscious. He was treated at the Kowloon Dispensary and later sent to the Kwong Wah Hospital. The machine was badly damaged.

Another accident occurred at Praya East yesterday near the Police Station when a small boy lost control of his machine and ran into a motor car driven by Mr. B. E. Maughan, of the Government Audit Department. The boy ran away leaving his wrecked machine behind.

Melbourne, September 26.—Most of the Federal Ministers have returned to their constituencies and the election campaign is in full swing.—Reuter Moscow, September 28.—M. Litvinoff will be acting Foreign不可靠的 during the absence of M. Chcherim, who will take the eure abroad owing to ill health. Reuter. Tokyo, September 28.—A message from Seoul says that in a ty- phon yesterday morning a north- pouring village was damaged. Merch than 300 houses were damaged. 17 being destroyed. There were several casualties and one death. Reuter

headline: SWATOW BOYCOTT.
text:
BRITAIN AND JAPAN NOT EXEMPT.

ANTI-RED MEASURES.

DECLINE OF FEELING AGAINST FOREIGNERS.

According to latest advices from Swatow the anti-Reids are taking measures to ensure non-interference with foreigners there and to encourage a certain amount of trade but the Seamen's and Firemen's Unions are still a power in the land and it is still impossible to land British or Japanese cargo in Swatow. This, a skipper who returned from Swatow yesterday was able to confirm

Our informant stated that there is no lack of evidence in Swatow of opposition to the Canton faction. Ships which put in with rice for Canton are allowed to discharge at Swatow but no clearance is granted. Threats were even held out to a Soviet ship from Canton on its way to Shanghai with cargo and vegetables that soldiers would be placed aboard her and the ship seized. Clearance was refused.

The boycott on British and Japanese goods is still enforced, said our informant, and the proclamation which has been made calling upon the people to encourage trade does not apparently apply to these. Another proclamation states that foreigners must not be interfered with and the anti-foreign feeling would certainly appear to be on the decrease. Chinese servants have not, however, returned in large numbers and the consul, for instance, is still servantless.

The landing of passengers which was such a difficult task during the Red régime is now comparatively simple and sampans are allowed to go alongside ships and tout for passengers. Some ricshas will carry a foreigner in the street; others will not, but it is only in the course of the last few days that even a few ricshas have been available for foreigners.

Our informant, brought up in a nautical school in which discipline is considered the first essential for efficiency, was most unfavourably impressed by the untidiness and lack of system on board the Soviet ships he had the opportunity of observing whilst he was in port.

headline: "RED" OFFICIAL SHOT.
text:
An incident, our informant actually witnessed during a brief period ashore, was the procession of armed soldiers with Chinese in the middle with his hands tied and a large mob following. Rifle shots were heard shortly afterwards and the information was the executed man was one of the principal officials in the late Red régime at Swatow. The charge on which he was convicted was that of “squeezing” money for the Chinese and using it for his own purposes. Although the subject is hardly one to trifle with, it was stated naively to our informant that the late leader's heavy expenditure was due to the fact that he had eight wives!

The procession which, as already reported, was nipped in the bud, was to have been for the purpose of protesting against the proclamation in favour of resumption of trade and allowing passengers ashore. The leaders were informed that the procession would be fired upon if it took place.

The general opinion in Swatow appears to be that the "Reds" have to many domestic problems on hand at present to concentrate at present on the recapture of Swatow. LOCAL INCIDENTS. An enlargement, which can be only described as a fake, of a photo of the Shameen shooting, was found on a passenger arriving this morning on the O.S.K. steamer "Kaijo Maru" from Swatow and ports. The owner of the picture was a Chinese. The print depicted for sign troops, under cover, and lined up for action, firing as a crowd of Chinese women with many dead bodies lying on Shakea but no Chinese soldier in. The vengeance! The owner was dealt with by the Police searchers. Continued of foot of West Colum.

headline: PEACE NEWS.
text:
TELEGRAM EXPECTED SHORTLY.

LAST NIGHT'S MEETING.

A telegram has been eagerly awaited from Canton by the sponsors of the peace delegation which went up on Monday morning. Last night the Hongkong delegates met the Canton strike authorities with a view to bringing about a settlement and it was rumoured in town that a report by telegram had been sent down.

On inquiry from Mr. Wong Tong this afternoon, a “China Mail” reporter was informed that no message had arrived. However, Mr. Wong had cabled up for news as to the outcome of the conference. Mr. Wong is the chief manager of the On Lok Yuen Co. (Hongkong and Canton) and came down from Canton when local Chinese merchants first mooted the idea of a peace talk. He has been mainly instrumental in paving the way to a conference.

headline: ABSENT PICKETS. / CHINSHAN STRIKERS NOT ON DUTY
text:
NEWS FROM MACAO.

Alleged to have been “seen off” by a detachment of Whampoa Cadets, the strike pickets are not now on duty at Chinshan, the Chinese point just outside “the Macao border and” on the main road from the Portuguese Colony into the interior.

Accordingly, people in the vicinity who wish to get away are taking advantage of the opportunity.

From small, up-country ports in the Sze Yap, batches of people are also reaching Macao, having chartered junks for the purpose. The fare is $5 a head, this high price being necessary as the junky have to pay heavily for "safe duct" through a pirate-infested area which is not on the usual route. Pickets are stationed along the usual routes, hence the necessity to trust pirates.

The small steamers from Kwong Hoi city to Macao are still reported to be sailing.

headline: LOCAL FOOTBALL / POLICE TO PLAY AT KOWLOON.
text:
SATURDAY'S MATCH

Proceeds from a football match will be devoted to a deserving object and the game will be played at the Kowloon Football Club's ground on Saturday, kick-off at 4.30 p.m.

The opposing sides will be the home team and the Police eleven. Payment is to be made at the gate.

The Harbour Office notifies mariners that the Engineer Co., Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps will hold searchlight runs at Belchers Fort on-Thursday, October 1, commencing 5.30 p.m.

Japanese and Chinese were the majority of the hundred or so passengers who went up to Canton this morning by the Steamboat Co.'s s.s. "Honam." The departure was without incident. A proposal is being considered to run the China Navigation Co.'s s.s. "Fatshan" next week in conjunction with the Steamboat Co. as hitherto.

Over 200 passengers came in from Swatow on the Kalo Mart.

After many conflicting reports the "Hydranges" at last sailed for Swatow, leaving yesterday afternoon. This is presumed by Chinese business men to mean a return to normal conditions at that port. The "Hydranges" took up a full ship of cargo but few passengers. About 20 Chinese, alleged to be Whampoa Cedate who fled from Swatow when the coup was carried out against them arrived by the Douglas Co's as "Haining" and were sent back by the Hydranges. It is expected that there will be regular communication to the two Hongkong and Swan.

headline: BORDER LOOT
text:
POLICE INTERCEPT RAIDERS.

CHINENE OPEN FIRE.

Details of another border outrage were received from the New Territories this morning, the scene being in the Shattankok district, where the strikers made a raid last Wednesday and carried off a number of pigs valued at $2,000 and also kidnapped two grocery-skip employees.

Emboldened by their success on this occasion, a large body of strikers and coolies paid a visit to the same shop, the Yuan Tai Tsan, on Sunday, and removed practically everything in the shop, including some more pigs.

They were proceeding with their loot across the frontier near Shataukok when they were intercepted by a party of Police, who fired a shot at one of the strikers. The whole crowd then turned back, and shortly after the Police party, which included some Punjabi soldiers, were greeted with a fusilade of rifle fire from Chinese soldiers who had concealed themselves in some bushes in British territory.

It is estimated that about fifty shots were fired at the Police, who were fortunately not hit, and they were forced to take cover without returning the fire as the ambushed party of Chinese could not be located.

Advantage was taken by the men carrying the loot to get away while the Police were covered by the rifle fire of their confederates.

headline: “MORE SERIOUS.” / CANTON REPORT ON THE STRIKE.
text:
NOT "ANTI-FOREIGN."

Highly lauded by the "Canton Gazette" is a long survey on the recent situation in Canton by the correspondent of "an important news agency in North China."

The strike, strange to say, is becoming more serious owing to the strengthening of the strike organisation. It is hoped, however, that with the departure of the delegation, new developments in the strike situation may be expected. Very much depends on the nature attitude of Hongkong. Unfortunately she still demands intervention in Canton instead of pursuing a policy of reconciliation and mutual understanding. There is not the slightest trace of anti-foreignism in Canton. I learn from reliable sources that the Whampoa incident in which a Japanese launch was shot at with casualties already reported, has been settled in an amicable manner by both parties. Evidently neither side cared to give prominence to the incident. The blockade seems to have affected Canton very little. The import-export business is deeply affected, while the silk of this season has found a way out directly to Shanghai, it cannot be said that the problem of the export of silk from Kwangtung has been completely solved.

headline: BRITISH CARGO.
text:
UNAFFECTED BY WHAMPOA SERVICE.

HUROPE TARIFF RATES.

Enquiries made regarding the movement of cargo between Whampoa and Shanghai, to which reference has already been made, go to show that there has been no relaxing of the boycott against the import or export of British goods even where direct loading or unloading is done at Whampoa. So long as the present state of affairs continues at Canton the institution of indirect communication between Whampoa and Hongkong by way of Shanghai can therefore help but little, if at all, in the clearance of British cargo at present in godown in Hongkong. In so far as direct trade between Whampoa and Europe is concerned the purely British boycott is as rigid in its application, and two German boats are thought to have been the only ones to have loaded there for Europe since the present trouble. As, however, there was no direct loading by ocean steamers at Whampoa prior to the strike and boycott, some tariff rate was considered necessary by the shipping companies concerned in the event of there being any considerable movement of cargo between Europe and Whampoa direct.

headline: SNUB TO REDS
text:
LABOUR CONFERENCE DEFEAT.

COMMUNISTS NOT WANTED.

The Labour Conference adopted the Executive's recommendations against affiliation with the Communists by 2,600,000 against 480,000 votes rejecting the third Communist attempt to refer the matter back.

Complaints of the Communists that the Standing Orders were invoked to burke discussion, evoked an emphatic denial from Mr. Arthur Henderson, the Secretary who said the Executive considered it was not desirable to waste further time on a question which the Labour movement had already decided.

Mr. Harry Pollitt, Communist, declared that whatever the Conference did it could not keep the Communists out, adding that the Labour Party should be wide enough to include not merely those who dined at Balmoral, like Mr. Ramsay MacDonald or stayed on a yacht at Cowes with Lord Inchcape, like Mr. J. H. Thomas.

Mr. T. Bromley, of the locomotive Union, said the decision of the conference meant the beginning of a heresy hunt in the ranks of Trade Unions.

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald was ringingly cheered when he told the Communists to come out of the Trade Unions and propagate their opinions honestly outside.

headline: SEIZED SHIP.
text:
PORTUGUESE BOAT AT CANTON.

NOW IN STRIKERS' HANDS.

In the early days of the strike the s.s. "Foo Chebng" was "abandoned" at Pakkai, the port of Kongmoon, through the native crew deserting.

Subsequently a report went round that the ship had been seized by the strikers. A Portuguese naval vessel from Macao was stated to have failed to bring the boat back and the "Foo Cheong" was last heard of in Kongmoon.

Saturday's "Canton Gazette" says:—Owing to the transportation of "undesirable" goods the s.s. "Foo Cheong" was detained recently by the pickets at Canton and for various reasons, the case has not been settled.

The same report says that the Ning Hoi Co. wishes to charter the steamer from the strikers, for the Canton-Wuchow run, promising $1,200 a month as charter hire, and stipulating the services of 20 pickets on board "for protection." The “Foo Cheong” was well-known on the Canton-Macao run prior to being superseded by the s.s. “Hang Cheong!” It is under Portuguese registry and when the strike started, was put on the Kongmoon-Macao run till it was forced to tie up through the crew going ashore on being intimidated at Pakkai.

"Wah Shan" Sequel.

Negotiations are continuing for the release of the Chinese s.s. "Wah Shan" which was seized by Canton while conveying livestock from Kwong Chow Wan to Hongkong. According to one report the owners may be willing to pay a few thousand dollars as a "fine" and it is likely that an amount may be named by the strikers holding the ship.

NEWS WANTED OF MISSING SHIP. "YUE YING WA" MYSTERY. "Upright and honourable men are requested to take note of an advertisement in the vernacular papers, asking for news of the missing son. "Yue Ying Wa" which has been posted missing for over a month. The vessel was on a voyage from Hohhot to Houtong and has not been heard of after Contacting from the same port early in November. The vessel said to have perished by the sea in the same hand.

headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
ASSURING NEWS FROM CANTON.

From the tone of a letter received yesterday by Mr. Wong Tong, it appears that some of the "points" raised at Tuesday night's conference in Canton will be modified. Mr. Wong of the On Lok Yuen Co., was mainly responsible for sending the Chinese delegates from Hongkong to negotiate, with Canton, an end to the strike. The letter to Mr. Wong stated that the military, civil and labour authorities of Canton were very friendly to the Hongkong representatives. Certain demands at first raised would be changed for submission to a second conference which was to have sat last night. Mr. Wong, attributed the delay in news getting through to the temporary dislocation of the cable services. He was confident that excellent results would be forthcoming. His opinion was based on the warm welcome extended to the delegates, and the elaborate precautions regarding a private train with poured cars for prevention conveying troops. Mr. Wong felt that a much better tone would have prevailed at last night.

headline: SEIZED VESSEL.
text:
DISARMED TROOPS SENT TO CANTON.

BOAT TO BE RESTORED.

The disposal of the locally-owned steamer "Sui Yik" and also of the Cantonese troops and arms found on board the vessel, which has been, moored in the Admiralty anchorage since her capture in British waters last Saturday, has now been decided by the authorities.

The 150. disarmed Chinese soldiers were taken off the boat and conveyed to the Kowloon Railway station, where they entrained for Shumchun at noon to-day. They will be escorted until they are over the British border.

Prior to handing over the vessel to her local owners, the Fuk Hoi Company, a further search of the holds will be made. The vessel will be taken alongside the Police Pier at Kowloon for this purpose.

The arms and ammunition found on the vessel will be confiscated.

headline: SAI YINGPUN SCHOOL
text: In reply to the question asked by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak at the Legislative Council meeting to-day, the Colonial Secretary stated that if no unforeseen circumstances arise, it is hoped to complete and open Saiyingpun School by the 30th June, 1926. The work was delayed for about two months mainly owing to the Strike.

headline: SWATOW IMPROVES.
text:
CARGO LANDED BY S.S. "HYDRANGEA."

BOX COTT BELIEVED OVER.

This morning the s.s. "Hydrangea" returned to Hongkong from Swatow.

There was no incident in the voyage. All the cargo shipped from Hongkong was landed and fresh cargo was brought back. About a hundred passengers also travelled from Swatow on the ship.

The agritators are now believed to have put a good distance between themselves and the port of Swatow and the anti-foreign boycott has been described as all over.

headline: "UNIVERSITY" MEN / CANTON STUDENTS FINED
text:
SEDITIONS LITERATURE CHAPGE.

Possession of a seditious pamphlet and two Chinese newspapers containing pernicious references to the boycott position led to two Chinese students being brought before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday. The students came from Swatow by the s.s. "Haining" and the documents were found in their luggage when searched on the wharf.

One of the accused was fined $25, and the other was remanded until this morning as he wished to call a witness.

A shopkeeper from Shamshuipo informed His Worship that he was acquainted with the accused, who was a student from the Kwangtung University, and he had never heard of the man getting into trouble during the time he was in Hongkong.

His Worship was satisfied that the accused had no intention of passing the documents round and imposed a fine of $25.

headline: MOONCAKE FEAST
text:
FENNY'S GREAT CHINESE FENTIVAL

ENIERRES CONCUBINE.

Moin-eoke festival, or, Mid-Autumn Festival, or Chung-chin which to give its chiscal rendering, falls this year on Friday (to tomorrow the 15th day of the 8th moon.

Tradition places its origin about 2,150 B.C., when Wiedith famous which emperor Hao I (Hao Ngai in Cantonese). He shot nine of the ten suns illuminating the heavens when the sun-goet besought him not to make a butt's eye of the tenth. For this been he was given a motion which would make him immortal with a home in the sun. Before he could take the potion which had to be prepared in an turn at night with devout prayers meanwhile, a naughty concubine by name of Sheung Ngo-drinad, the last drop while her spouse slept through, the wake night service. Light as a fairy the woman fled to the moon to escape the archer's wrath. Every year she returns to mother earth and moon-cakes are eaten in her honour.

This episode has been commercialised into a favourite stage-play being one of the star numbers of Mei Lan-fung's repertoire. Mei will be remembered as the famous Northern actor who was down here in 1922. The legend has been slightly lengthened and ends up with Hao I being thrown out of the moon after a hot pursuit of his concubine.

It is a harvest festival in that the tea-houses reap their annual harvest. Moon-shaped cakes with wonderful ingredients are made months ahead of the festival and shipped to all parts of the world where Chinese are to be found. Chinese delight in the delicacies. All other aspect is the making and sale of beautiful lanterns with which Chimatown will be decorated with a night. Actually the men-folk take little note of the religious side of the festival except to organise a feast at West Point. Schools and various working guilds make a holiday of it and it is also one of the four settlement days in Chinese business circles. The women, of course, must "chin-chin joss."

This business settlement, of course, will not be like that of other years, owing to financial stringency. With the announcement of the £3,000,000 loan, there is practically no possibility of a panic. A special week of celebration is announced for the Lee Gardens, East Point.

headline: SWATOW QUIET?
text:
NO OUTPORT REPORTS TO HAND.

CANTON MOVING TROOPS.

As no further intelligence has come in from Swatow or the out-ports it is presumed that there is no change to report.

Transportation of Canton (Red) troops—mainly Whampoa Cadets—on the Kowloon-Canton Railway is continuing. The Kuomintang is rushing forces out to points (in their zone) in the East River region.

headline: HONGKONG, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 3, 1925. / CANTON WARSHIP.
text:
VISIT TO HONGKONG EXPLAINED.

MUTINY STORY DENIED.

Lying in Shamshuipo Bay is the Canton Navy sloop "Kwong Ching"—little larger than a launch but with a six-inch gun mounted on board. She has been allotted a berth there just like any other foreign man-of-war visiting Hongkong.

In the vernacular papers of the last few days has been an entirely erroneous report of the "Kwong Ching" having been "seized" for "trespassing in British water." The report went that the crew had deserted the Reds, resenting the appointment of a Russian commander on board; during the absence of the Chinese commander—so the report states—the crew took the ship out with the intention of joining the Chan Kwongming faction at Swatow. While on her way she came into Hongkong.

The “China Mail” is informed on the highest authority that there is no truth in the local vernacular report. The actual facts are as stated. The “Kwong Ching” may stay here as long as she likes and can be seen best on the Yaumati ferry.

headline: GAP IN THE LAW.
text:
HOW TO GET ROUND THE ORDINANCE.

HAPPY VALLEY PESTS:

Leighton Hill Road residents who have complained about the hawker nuisance in their part of Happy Valley will be interested to hear that a licensed seller cannot cry his wares but a man who illegally hawks with permission can shout as much as he likes!

As Mr. S. B. B. McElderry (Magistrate) remarked in the Police Court this morning, there is evidently a gap in the law.

Divisional Inspector Ogg added that the gap had been widened by the strike when unlicensed hawkers were immune from prosecution. The anomalous position then was that a licensed man had to keep silent while those who did not have to pay for licences could make all the noise they wanted.

A man was up charged with hawking Chinese newspapers without a licence. The offence he had actually committed was “crying his wares” in a prohibited area. But as he was unlicensed he could not commit a breach of the licence and he therefore had to be prosecuted for a misdemeanour. However, he satisfied His Worship that he was only a distributor and was, accordingly, discharged.

headline: TRADE TREATY.
text:
RUSSIA AND GERMANY FRIENDS.

IMPORTANT MILESTONE.

The Russo-German understanding is now much more advanced than described in an earlier cable. Germany is ready in principle to sign a commercial agreement with Russia as soon as the German Foreign Office Commission returns from Moscow, where the final text of the treaty will be drawn up. It is officially announced that the impending agreement is regarded as a milestone on the road to further consolidation of Russo-German friendly economic relations.

headline: CANAL MISHAP:
text:
SLAVIC PRINCE STRIKES BANK.

SUGAR CARGO DAMAGED.

. The British steamer "Slavic Prince" from Hongkong and Batavia. to New York, struck a bank of the Suez Canal and is leaking in. No. 1 hold, containing sugar, some of which is wet as a result.

A survey has been recommended. The lives holes have been plugged and the vessel will proceed to Alexandria.

[The "Slavic Prince" left Hongkong on August 5. Very little cargo, if any, was placed on board here. When the "China Mail" inquired, the local office had not received any news from London.]

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / SENSATIONAL FREMANTLE INCIDENT.
text:
STEAMER BOARDED

Fremantle; October 3. Hundreds of strikers last night raided the steamer “Demodocus,” drew the fires and dropped the firebars, and threatened the cap tain and officers with violence if they resisted.

It is noteworthy that Mr. Bruce recently telegraphed the Westralian Premier condemning the failure to afford police protection to the "Demodocus" which the strikers boarded and persuaded the crew to join the strike.

The Marine Workers' Union has received a cable from the strikers in South Africa, asking: 'Is it advisable for strikers in South Africa to accept the following terms:—No prosecution of men; no victimisation and no pay until men resume work. Cape and South African Governments to urge Imperial Government to hold an impartial inquiry. Forty-eight hours given us to reply. Men at Durban solid if Marine Workers' Union considers strike should continue. Reply giving us your absolute confidence.'

A special meeting of the Union is to be called to decide whether these terms are satisfactory. A cable has been sent to the strikers in South Africa that the matter is being considered. A further cable will be sent immediately a decision is reached.

headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
EXPORT EMBARGO ON FOOD.

LATEST NEWS FROM PORT.

At present Swatow has an embargo on the export of food-stuffs from that port. It is not known if the embargo is being enforced as a result of the temporary regulations issued by the new authorities, or as part of the anti-foreign movement.

Chinese merchants who returned yesterday on the "Hydrangea" state that business conditions are returning to normal, and the situation is quiet. When the ship sailed, a number of men boarded the ship to search for foodstuffs but the speaker did not know if they were from labour unions or were empowered by the Government.

The "Hydrangea" brought back general cargo and a good many passengers.

headline: CADETS PAY $3,000.
text:
COMPENSATION FOR KILLE JAPANESE.

WHAMPOA RIVER SEQUEL

Compensation is reported to have been paid by the Canton Government in respect of the Japanese sailor who was killed by the Whampoa Cadets firing at a Japanese vessel, from the shore, on July 30.

For the dead man, $3,000 was offered and $500 each for the two men wounded, so it is stated, on a protest being made by the Japanese Consul at Canton, and following representations.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
CHINESE HOSTILITY TO PICKETS.

FARMER USES HIS POLE.

Reports of 'open hostility, and the loss of life in at least one instance, between Chinese strike pickets and the civil population, have reached Hongkong during the week-end.

headline: THREE STRIKERS KILLED?
text:
Mácao, October 4.

It is reported from Chinshan that strike pickets had the worse of a brawl with farmers in Chinese territory, resulting in the death of three strikers.

Early yesterday morning, a farmer was stated to be coming into Macao with vegetables. On nearing the border he was challenged by pickets. He threw down his two baskets and moved away. On three men of the picket coming up, he belaboured them with his bamboo pole until all three were badly bruised and unable to stand. Even with the pickets down, the farmer is alleged to have continued the assault until, so it is stated, life was extinct in each case. None of the pickets was armed.

headline: Shots: Fired.
text:
In the district of Po On (which adjoins the New Territory) trouble is believed to have broken out between armed tickets and the farmers' volunteers. Feeling has been running him for some time owing to the prompt of export of products to trongkong and consequent consscation.

Firing is said to have broken out between the rival factibns.

headline: Canton Incident.
text:
A passenger who returned on Saturday by the "Honam" relates an incident which he witnessed on the West Bund.

He says that among the food-stuffs sent up to Shameen from Hongkong was beef, in quarters, the dripping of which was cut off and often thrown into the river. Some of the very poor Chinese are said to have dived in the river for the dripping. On going ashore the divers were caught by strike pickets who set upon the divers for picking up cast-off food. One man was tied up on the Bund and beaten for half an hour.

headline: SOVIET CITIZENS.
text:
CONDITIONS OF RECENT AMNESITY.

The council of Commissaries has issued a decree that former prisons of war and interned persons of the old Imperial and Red armies, also participants in risings of White armies who come under conditions of the, amnesty shall lose their citizenship if they neglect to apply for restoration of citizenship within the period laid down by the decree.

This did not apply to persons who have not renewed their citizenship owing to lack of Soviet representatives in the country of their residence.

headline: PEACE DELEGATES:
text:
MERCHANTS RETURNING TO HONGKONG.

NO CONCRETE PROPOSAL.

No proposal that can be described as concrete has been put forward as the result of Hongkong delegation of Chinese merchants to Canton.

Some of the delegates returned yesterday and others are due back this week. They are to prepare a document reporting their activities in Canton, such as reporting the District Commercial Associations — the general guild having sponsored the peace delegation—to be held at 7 p.m. tomorrow.

Summed up briefly the position is that the delegates desired to confine themselves to asking for communication to be resumed whereas the Canton Strike Executive wished to include in the discussion a number of points that can hardly be called relevant.

Unless an improvement results from the conference (in Canton) of last night, it is difficult to see where a. settlement is going to start.

The strikers are reported to have put forward terms, in addition to those published last week, such as the free use of Chinese subsidiary coin in Hongkong, the liberty of deported strikers to return. etc.

…

headline: MALARIA SCOURGE
text:
INTERNATIONAL CONGRESS OPENS.

The inaugural meeting of the International Congress on malaria has opened at the Capitol.

The Premier, M. Mussolini, and a large number of international experts, on malaria were present, including representatives from Burma, India and the Malay States.

Signor Mussolini paid a high tribute to Britain and her dominions for their striking example and collaboration in fighting the scourge of malaria.

The Argentine delegate proposed the establishment of an international anti-malaria institute at Rome to collect worldwide information and to undertake research work for the redemption of infected regions and to organise practical teaching for the training of malaria specialists.

The Italian delegate promised that Italy would support the proposal and was ready to provide building and supply funds towards "be organisation of an institute.

The Congress approved the proposal and entrusted its council to draw up a scheme.

The Board of Education is to sit at a p.m. this Wednesday. Shanghai, October 4—The talopsh strike has been settled. Enter. Enjoy the Offers of the Day at the January Board meeting at 15 p.m. to enter a series of interesting items relative to the return for Embargoes and this year.

headline: China the Jail
text:
No. 19,616

was ordered to attend the headquarters of the Kuomintang Government to answer a charge of moving his troops without orders. There he was ordered to be detained by General Cheung, says the report. Simultaneously, his army headquarters in Canton city was surrounded by a detachment of Cadets who immediately disarmed the bodyguards. Military pickets were also sent out to search the residence of Hung's higher officers.

A later message to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" suggests that an armed force is being sent to the North River to bring about the capitulation of General Hung's main force.

Yesterday there was a rumour in town concerning a Red coup in Canton but it could not be confirmed.

headline: HONGKONG, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1925. / THIRD COUP.
text:
CANTON RED'S LATEST MOVE.

GENERAL DETAINED?

Yet another coup—the third of the present régime—has been brought off by General Cheung Kai-shek, the commander of the Canton Cadets. This coup has resulted in the disarming of several hundreds of non-Cantonese mercenaries in Canton, the rounding-up of about sixty officials and the reported detention of General Hung Hak-mu of Szechuan.

The net result is the further strengthening of the hands of the Cadet commandant. General Hung has a strength estimated at 10,000 bayonets on the North River, and the morale of his rank and file is bound to be badly shaken.

It was only a few weeks ago that General Hung, together with another non-Cantonese adventurer, brought his following into Canton province. Inspired reports from Canton hinted that he was welcomed by General Cheung who had a view to a non-Cantonese alliance to overcome the Cantonese armies should they ever become united.

General Hung once held a command in his native province. In the earlier days of the Republic he was an ardent admirer of Choy Ngok (Chai Yo) who died after inflicting the first check on Yuan Shi-kai's monarchical plans. Hung is said to be allied to Tuchun Tang Chi-yao of Yunnan.

headline: “SUI YIK” SCENES.
text:
DISARMED TROOPS SENT TO CANTON.

MORE ARMS SEIZED.

The large number of Cantonese troops from the s.s. "Sui Yik" were safely placed over the border on Thursday. The Chinese authorities at Shumchun later conveyed the soldiers to Canton by train.

Prior to the men being placed on the train at Kowloon, they were again searched and several loaded revolvers were found on them. The weapons had apparently been secreted on the vessel and the attempt to take them away proved unsuccessful.

The vessel was handed back to her local owners, the Fuk Hoi Company, but not before a thorough search had again been made when 30,000 rounds of ammunition in addition to the seizures already made were found concealed in unlikely places on the boat.

headline: JUDICIAL INQUIRY.
text:
BOYCOTT BY SHANGHAI CHINESE.

CHAMBER OF COMMERCE FIẾT.

The Shanghai Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, in a full page advertisement in the foreign newspapers, declares that all Chinese citizens will under no circumstances be identified or associated with the judicial inquiry.

The Waichiaopu in a Note to the Senior Minister given out this evening and dated October 2, states that the Chinese Government informed the British Charge d'Affaires on September 1, that judicial enquiry into the Shanghai incident would only further complicate the issue and involve a waste of time, and the Chinese Government does not waver from this attitude.

The Note reiterates the view that the lapse of time has changed the circumstances. Most the requisite evidence has become un-obtainable or, has disappeared.

The Note states that after the Shanghai incident and the Chinese Government's protest the Powers sent diplomatic representatives to Shanghai and these representatives i.e. vestigated the case.

headline: WAR OF REVENGE.
text:
YUNNAN PROVINCE IN DANGER.

CANTON'S EX-STRONG MAN.

General Fan Shek-sang (the strong man of Canton last year who left on a long trek, to his native province before his colleagues—the Yunnanese generals — were expelled by the Kuomintang) was reported yesterday to be on the move again. This time he seems to be in real earnest to secure revenge on Tuchun Tang Chi-yao who is alleged to have put Fan's father to death. Fan has 15,000 men, new equipment and both large and small guns. It is said that he will be satisfied with nothing less than Tang's head.

On a previous occasion Fan was thought to have been repulsed. It now appears that he only withdrew to renew provisions, his vanguard having made this necessary by denuding the country in which he was to operate.

Fan is also mentioned as having telegraphed many of the leading merchants asking them not to let Tang leave before he (Fan) arrives, which will be in a few days, he says.

In this connection, Fan's ally from Kweichow is advancing from that direction with Yunnanfu as his objective; also Yang Sen is marching on Yunnanfu from Szechuan. If these reports are correct—and there is no reason to disbelieve them—Tang will find it difficult to repel the invadera.

Brigands have been creating trouble at Chaotung up north and the city gates were closed for a fortnight. When the soldiers did arrive to drive them off, the trouble was intensified.

Missionaries living outside the city were requested to move inside. Subsequently they were given permission to fetch their property with the stipulation that they return by a certain hour. They failed to comply and found the gates closed. Nothing could induce those inside to let them in. Failing at another gate, the foreigners had to leave their horses and climb the city wall by ropes. Firing had been going on all the time and was thought to be directed at the brigands. It transpired that the fire was directed by the soldiers at their own men retiring before the outlaws. Several men were killed. About 3,000 soldiers have been sent to Chaotung and district to

Inside the capital there does not seem to be much excitement but there is an under-current of feeling which is difficult to probe.

headline: THE VITAL FACT. / WHY PEACE MUST BE KEPT.
text:
LOCARNO COMMONSENSE.

Herr Stresemann had an hour's conversation with M. Briand this morning.

The latter subsequently expressed himself as well satisfied and said all the statesmen at the Conference were obviously determined to see the whole problem confronting the Conference from the European standpoint, and anyone at present wishing to unfurl the banners of war in Europe would scatter the seeds of civil war. All parties at the Conference must make concessions in view of this fact.

headline: STRIKE DOOMED.
text:
COLLAPSE EXPECTED SHORTLY.

FREMANTLE TRUCULENCE.

The National Sailors' and Firemen's Union headquarters report that the strike is expected to collapse in the near future. A definite decision is to be taken at a meeting in London on Sunday.

A similar meeting will be held at Bristol and a ballot will be taken at Southampton while it is believed the strike has collapsed at Liverpool.

In consequence of the violent form, assumed by the seamen's strike at Fremantle, the Australian Steamship lines have decided to discontinue the call there until the restoration of normal conditions.

headline: "SUI YTK" OFFICERS
text:
THE LAST OF THEM.

CHOICE OF DESTINATION

A decision has been arrived at by the Police in conjunction with other officials which will finally dispose of the complement of the s.s. "Sui Yick," the ship seized by the strikers at Shannai, transferred to the Canton Government. The ship was not allowed to troops and returned now to the owners owing to the coxswain having brought it into British waters.

Most of the men were put across the border last Monday but a few officers and others were detained for further enquiries. It has now been decided to send these away from the Colony to places of their own choosing and the last will be seen of them in the course of the last few days.

headline: ANTI-RED SUCCESS.
text:
RIGHT WING TAKES PRISONERS.

ADVANCE TOWARDS RAILWAY.

Further successes have been gained by Chan Kwing-ming's party, according to reports which have arrived during the week-end.

The anti-Red right, wing has taken Ho Yuen, in the East River region and advanced to Lung Mun. Commander Lin Yin-hung, who has been described as the Cantonese "Black Douglas" for his border exploits, has taken several hundred prisoners.

Lung Mun is considered the key to an important, fertile district close to the Canton-Kowloon Railway. The latest news is that the advance is being pushed forward to Tsang Shing, the district next to Tung Kun.

By reason of the geographical position, the right wing is in closest proximity to the Red lines and the nearest, as the crow flies, to Canton. As the main strength of the Reds is at Sheklung and Shektan it means it at real fighting is expected shortly.

headline: Wutichow Falls
text:
Another success for the anti-Reds is the declaration of Commander Yeung Kwan-yu of General Chan's 6th army. Yeung has been holding Waichow city, nominally, under the Reds but he has always been a stunach pro-Chan officer. After the last debacle he surrendered to Hsu Shung-chi but has now come out again for his old master. He has been strengthened by the addition of about 3,000 Cantonese Reds who turned over to him when the Caiets began disarming their colleagues. In his declaration, Yeung is alleged to have described Cheung Kai-shok (the Cadet commandant) as a thief.

From Canton, the "Wah Tsz at Po" has been informed by a special correspondent that fighting is expected to break out at to Yuen.

headline: China
text:
WAR IN THE AIR.

↑

Friday's "Canton Gazette" confirms the detention of General Hsiung Keh-wu (Hung Hakmo), the commander of the Szcehuan mercenaries in Canton, by the Kuomintang.

Hung, is reported to have jotted against the Reds by pre-ending to join them, but at the same time to have been conferring with the anti-Reds.

It is also admitted that General Tan Yen-kai (the Hunanese mercenary) has been ordered to take over Hung's troops on the North River.

That Canton does consider of importance the advance of the anti-Reds on the East River is evident from much trumpeting by the “Canton Gazette” of the despatch of Red troops for the front and the departure for the war zone on October 6, of General Chang Kai-shek who now takes the official time of commander-in-chief of the Expeditionary Force. Formerly he was content to be principal of the Whampoa Military Academy. Then he was only garrison commander of Canton and now he is the official chief.

明月松间照清泉石上流

headline: REQUEST REFUSED.
text:
CANTON MERCHANTS WANT STEAMERS.

SHIPS FROM LONGKONG.

Canton's (Chinese) General Chamber of Commerce has requested the Strike Committee for permission for the s.s. "Paul Beon" and "Charles Hardwin" to ply between Hongkong and Canton, says the "Canton Gizzelle."

Five regulations for the operation of these two ships were put forward by the Chamber. The Strike Committee considered the request to be contrary to the strike rules and the request was refused.

[Note: 'The "Paul Beau" and "Charles Hardouin'" belong to the Caution Navigation Co., Ltd. and were flying between the two ports till the strike had lasted several weeks. They were the last boats called off. Most of the capital is Chinese but the vessels fly the British flag.]

headline: CHINA'S TROUBLES.
text:
HONGKONG UNIVERSITY'S GOODWILL.

VICE-CHANCELLOR'S MESSAGE.

A “double-ten” (tenth day of the tenth month) concert at the conclusion of which they were briefly addressed by the Vice-Chancellor, and a dance which the Vice-Chancellor allowed to continue until 2 a.m., was the manner of celebration by the undergraduates of the Hongkong University of the fourteenth anniversary of the institution of the Republic of China.

At the conclusion of the concert, Mr. W. W. Hornell, C.I.E., Vice-Chancellor, speaking on behalf of the many present, said that they were glad to see that in spite of the troubles of the last few months the undergraduates were celebrating the national festival as usual. Speaking twelve months ago he had wished for the Republic of China a happy issue out of all her afflictions and he would repeat that there was no institution in the world which longed more for a peaceful and contented China than the Hongkong University.

The University of Hongkong continued the Vice-Chancellor, had no solution to offer for the present difficulties of China but he did believe that by their life at the University in friendly relations with the members as a whole students were able to leave better equipped to face the grave complications of the world of to-day. That evening's celebration was an example of the friendliness and good will which existed between all members of the University, and in the name of all the guests present, he desired to thank the undergraduates for inviting them and all those who had been responsible for the ar-ranging of, such an excellent entertainment.

headline: THE CONCERT
text:
The most popular of the items on the programme was that which occupied the entire second half—a skit on University life in nine stages entitled "The Great Unveiling". Mr. C. K. Ong, the author, is to be congratulated on its good taste and humour and Mr. W. H. Sling on the adaptation of the tunes parodied.

Particularly good was the Chinese music which is always such an enjoyable part of University concerts. In the Cantonese Phantasy the following took part: Messrs. C. W. Chan, K. Y. Chan, S. C. Chan, S. C. Lam, S. W. Lam, Y.S.O.W.S. Chung. Mr. Lo Lo gave a Cantonese song which also was very well received. He was accompanied by Messrs. H. C. Chu, T. K. Chung and others.

An item among the others deserving of special mention was the recitation by Miss P. Ruttonjee, "The English Schoolmaster." Miss Ruttonjee has the making of a very good reciter.

Other well rendered items were as follows:—Piano Duet, Norwegian Dance, Edward Grjeg, Spanish Dance, M. Moszkowski, by Miss A. Remedios, and Miss E. Bell; Violin and Piano, Two Fragments from the 18th Century, Sonata No. XII in D. Minor, A. Corelli, Chanson Louis XIII et Pavane, L. Couperin—Krieser, by Mr. V. F. Vicajee, and Dr. J. Fenton; String Quartette, Quartette in G. Major, K. von Dittersdorf, Bourree from "Water Music," G. F. Handel, by Messrs. V. Vicajee, J. M. Alves, J. M.S. Rosario, and N. U. Botelho.

The Chairman of the University Union which arranged the concert is Mr. C.Z. M. Ma and the Secretary, Mr. C. K. Ong. The three Committees were as follows:

Concert Committee: — Messrs. W. H. Sling, V. B. R. Vicajee, R. Sung, S. C. H. H. N. Balhat, chef, A. T. Tofin Miss Ruttonjee and Miss A. dos Comedion Decoration Committee: — Messrs. C. W. Lam, W. Young-asy, T. P. Wu, B. R. Ng, T. F. Lo, S. W. Tso, Miss F. Thom and Miss T. Ho Tang. Reception Committee: — Messrs. K. S. Chung, J. C. Chan, M. B. Cyre, E. B. Horn, T. Z. Rait, M. H. C. B. Sam, J. headline: FRENCH STRIKE.
text:
ANOTHER COMMUNIST FIASCO..

POLICE ON THE ALERT.

“Humanité,” the Communist organ, published an order for a general strike all over France on October 11 to protest against the wars in Morocco and Syria and the new taxes.

The opinion is generally expressed that the strike will fail like the transport strike in which the Parisian taxi drivers alone decided to participate.

The Government has taken all measures to suppress attempts to prevent freedom of work.

The Communists' long-expected 24-hour strike principally to protest against the war in Morocco is due on October 12, according to an order issued by the headquarters late last night.

A second order calls on Communist members of the Paris transport services to strike today and remain out till their wage demands are granted.

The transport strike called by the Communists proved a fiasco. The number of strikers was in-significant and the public was in-nowise inconvenienced.

In the afternoon the police searched the offices of the Communist organ "Humanité" and seized several thousand letters inciting the workers to participate in the projected general strike.

headline: China be Jitail / HONGKONG, TUESDAY / BARE ARMS.
text:
CANTON'S AMAZON DETACHMENT.

BORBED HAIR FIGHTERS.

With their hair bobbed and their arms bared, about twenty women bodyguards have arrived at Canton. The complete description of them in the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" is that they are also barefooted, they carry rifles, appear to be ferocious, and roll their eyes about when looking ahead!

This body of Amazons marched into Canton with the commandant of a detachment of Farmers' Volunteers, the last-named having been defeated and disbanded by General Chan Kwing-ming's troops.

The Volunteers once held sway in the Hoi Luk Fung area, reports the special correspondent of the "Wah Tsz Yac Po."

It is presumed that when the Farmers found that the anti-Reds had expelled the Reds from that territory, the leader mustered his awe-inspiring Amazons and made his way to Canton to offer his services to the Reds.

Reds move to Base. Trainloads of Red troops have been leaving Canton by rail for Shektan, the railway station on the Canton side and next to Shekhang (40 miles or so from the southern metropolis).

The 1st division of the Red Army has arrived at Shektan and encropped. General Cheung Kai-shek has made Shektan his army headquarters and his main strength is massed there.

Having gone to Whampoa and there obtained an issue of a large lot of arms. Wong Kam-guen, commander of the Strike Pickets, is reported to be equipping the pickets with a view to their volunteering for active military service against the anti-Rede on the East River.

headline: CONFUCIUS DAY.
text:
TO-MORROWS CELEBRATION IN TOWN.

This year has seen a marked tendency towards observing Confucius Day, which falls on the 27th day of the 8th moon (tomorrow) according to the Chinese Calendar) as a general holiday. It seems as if the time is not far distant when the anniversary of the birth of China's most famous sage—although not ranking as one of the four big festivals—will take second place to New Year in the round of Chinese festivities in Hongkong.

It is estimated that more than half the shops in the Colony will be closed to-morrow whereas in previous years only a small percentage observed the day. At the Tai Ping Theatre, the local Confucius Society will hold a mass meeting with speeches from the society's officials, followed by a dramatic show. Nearly all the schools attended by Chinese students will have a day off and some of the schools have arranged their own celebration. The amisture of the Ching Shing Harvest Society are assisting the Confucius Society by presenting old-style Chinese items on the stage.

headline: BOYCOTT OVER?
text:
SWATOW FREE TO TRADING VESSELS.

ALL NATIONS WANTED.

Merchant vessels of all nations can now proceed freely to Swatow, says the Foreign Commissioner of the port. Mr. Wong Keung. In a letter to the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Wong explains that since the troops of his party retook Swatow, steps have been taken to restore commerce. Accordingly all mercantile marine ships may put in there for commercial purposes, he concludes.

headline: MAGISTRATE'S ORDER.
text:
Before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning, a young American seaman named David Boyd was charged with being a vagrant.

Defendant said that he arrived from Shanghai and worked with the Green Island Cement Company at Hok Un for one year. He was out of work shortly before the strike and his efforts to secure a billet on any of the vessels suiling to Canada or America failed. He then spent all his money and fell sick with malaria, which confined him to hospital for four weeks. He had just left hospital, and was without money or his discharge papers, which he said were lost in Kowloon before his illness. The American Consul had assisted him several times, and he could desired to get back to Shanghai.

His Worship made order for the refunds to be kept in the House of Mission and Covered that the mission has roughen the notice of the American Council.

headline: Britain's Lead.
text:
Referring to the Bifference of opinion existing as to whether Great Britain should have acted on her own, to protect her trade in the Far East in preference to the painfully long process of consulting other Powers, the "Telegraph" states:

Three months have passed by since the fatal riot in the international settlement at Shanghai provoked the Chinese boycott of British residents which has done untold harm. It is now announced that the Treaty Powers, some eighteen in all, have agreed upon the text of the Notes in which they will reply to the Chinese Government's demands in respect of the Shanghai affair, and in respect also of the revision of the foreign treaties with China. Delays are doubtless inevitable in diplomacy, especially when so many Powers have to be consulted and brought into line. But for Great Britain, whose commercial interests in China are older and still more important, relatively, than those of any other Power, this long postponement of action of any kind has been peculiarly unfortunate. If the settlement had been under British control, the Shanghai affair could have been promptly investigated and amicably arranged. As it is, though the representatives of the British ratepayers predominate in the Municipal Council administering the settlement, the Council itself is responsible to the whole diplomatic corps at Peking. Whether the Foreign Office could have done more by independent diplomacy without violating the principle that the Powers should deal in concert with Chinese questions is a matter on which our Government and the British firms interested in the trade of the Far East seem to differ. But it remains true that British interests have suffered severely and are still suffering, while the Power have been slowly exchanging Notes. We can only hope that events will now move more rapidly, and that the British Government will take the lead in the important negotiations this autumn at Peking.

that "American would abandon such rights for her own citizens if China could show that Americans would enjoy full protection for their lives and property under Chinese law and administration." So far as we know, our own policy is identical with that of Mr. Kellogg. The British community in Shanghai, which has built up a thriving city on what was a marshy waste, has not organised the municipal services out of any wish to colonise and dominate, but merely for the sake of comfort and protection, which the Chinese Government could not and would not give. If China were an orderly and law-abiding country, instead of a mere chaos of military despotisms, the extra-territorial rights and the conventional tariffs would present no serious difficulty. But, as Mr. Kellogg cautiously observed, "conditions in China have not been such as to further her aspirations." The Peking Government's efforts to restrain the anti-foreign demonstrations "have not been completely successful," which is a very mild way of limiting that the Government is virtually unrecognised outside the capital. At the moment, there America is no more ready to surrender her rights in China than we are. But America and Great Britain are agreed in wishing to discuss the question thoroughly, and to deal with China in a most generous fashion as soon as order is restored and foreigners can count on enjoying such privileges as are recorded to Chinese nationals abroad. The attitude of Japan is less clearly defined but her vast trading interests in China must incline her to take much the same view as Great Britain and America. If the three Powers can act together, energetically and firmly, the Treaty Conference and the Extra-territoriality Commission ought to lead to some tangible results, and at any rate should assunge the bitterness of the anti-foreign feeling among the more responsible leaders of Chinese opinion.

headline: SWATOW POSITION.
text:
The action of the Chinese contractors in conveying food stuffs to H.M.S. "Magnolia," British cruiser which replaced the "Fox-glove," is significant of the general improvement at Swatow.

This is the first time the contractors have done this since the institution of the boycott.

headline: China" the Atail / FEWER TOURISTS.
text:
LOCAL SILK STORE LOSE TRADE

EFFECTS OF THE STRIKE

SHAMEEN STOCKS BROUGHT TO HONGKONG

Looking at their glittering windows and splendid wares, most people think that the local Indian stores are among the Colony's few thriving concerns.

Yet the local Indian merchants were also badly hit by the strike and the position which it created. However a gradual improvement is now taking place.

The silk stores have suffered heavy losses owing to the Canton market—the source of their supplies—being closed, and the coast ports discontinuing purchases of Indian goods.

The branches at Shameen are all closed, and to prevent deterioration stocks of valuable material have been removed to Hongkong.

Orders from foreign places for Chinese silks, shawls and other goods are for the major part held up. In the earlier months of the strike Canton goods were unobtainable, but the position has improved by small supplies coming via Shanghai, which involves delay and higher cost.

The trade with local customers also suffered for economic reasons. In normal times tourists visiting at odd intervals other than the excursion season increased the turnover of the silk shops, but the number visiting the Colony during the strike has been small and business has naturally suffered.

With an improvement taking place gradually, the silk stores are making reduced profits and are on the whole not so badly affected as other trades.

The imports consist largely of shellac, gunny bags and Indian produce. The business is done on an indent basis, and with the tightness of money and the closing of the Canton market, which received a large share of the purchases of the local Chinese customers; trade came to a standstill during July and August. A little business, however, is now being done in gunny bags, the larger part of which is re-shipped to Shanghai.

Cassia, which forms an important article of export to India, comes from Canton, and since June not a single bag has been shipped, although the merchants have large orders on hand. The trade in Chinese produce is also at a standstill.

headline: EAST RIVER
text:
CHAN'S ARMY REFUSES BATTLE.

STRIKE AGAINST STRIKERS.

("W'ah Tsz Yat Po.")

As the Chan Kwing-ming army is retiring on its own account in preference to giving battle, General Cheung Kai-shek (the Cadet chieftain) has ordered Li Chai-sum (on the West River) to enter the East River war zone to establish himself at Tamshui. [Note: The telegram hints that the Reds fear being enticed into enemy territory and there being enveloped. General Cheung will take command in person.] Ex-Admiral Chan Chak (of Kongmoon and "Wing Fung" fame) has been appointed Director of Operations, under Chan Ming-shu, in the projected offensive against the Chan troops in the south of Kwangtung province. A general strike has been declared against the Reds by the merchants at Fu Mun (Bocca Tigris) and Tai Ping (on the opposite bank of the Canton River). Over 10 strikers' pickets were killed in a squabble over an embargo on saltfish and this has caused the strike. The Red civil authorities on the spot have cabled Canton.

headline: TO-DAY'S FESTIVAL.
text:
Fishing to the losses they have suffered through the strike, the local London stores are not celebrating day. Biscuit Festival this year with the customary festivities.

The rainfall for the month of September at Botinical Gardens was 10ms.94 on 15 days, at the Matilda Hospital, Mount Kellatt, it was 5ins.25 on 14 days, and at the Police Station. Taipo, it was 5ins.50 on 7 days. The lowest barometer reading, at sea level, was 20ins.622 at 17h. on the 5th. The maximum squall velocity, as recorded by the Dines-Baxendell anemograph, was at the rate of 54 miles per hour at 0h. 58m. on the 1st.
