headline: EXPORTING MONEY.
text:
TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE.

NOT CROSSING THE BORDEER

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who abandoned with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumuti was tendered at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempling to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force. Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

TO-DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, on demand, to day was $5.5/18.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERUTORY GAINED BY THE REDS:

RAILWAY REPORTED CLEAR.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwing-ming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Simechon, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by丙ontic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the fall of Wuchow the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
RESUMEES, EXCEPT ERITISH.

LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

From Our Own Correspondent.)

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Caneolian) and schools are still closed.

The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good.

H.M.S. "Mourhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of the strike.

There is a shortage of kerosine and' liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junks have seldom got through the strike pickets' cordons.. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed.
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates and established "themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaw and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hung-kai's remnants. Pirates have again been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "Mai Tain") have authority to pay for the before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-layn is brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa is at Chekhom and Yamping with his troops. General Li Chai-sum, the Red nominee, holds Sunning. Kungyick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Saiwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only import permitted from Macao but boats are low running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 20 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the "Kwok Ning" piracy (report) previously in the "China Mail").

headline: CANTON ITEMS. / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST PASSENGERS.
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the s.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hongkong. The prices charged by the junk and samparas operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing.

The "Honam" left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The "Fatshan" will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the "special tugs" which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high-handed actions. These clerks had spiked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Cantor.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Whichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: CHANGE OF FRONT.
text:
BETTER CANTON LANDING FACILITIES

MILITARY CONTROL

The “China Mail” reported a few days ago that facilities rather than difficulties were being placed in the way of passengers wishing to land in Canton from the “Honam.” From later reliable reports it would appear that this change of front is due to the action of the military authorities who in this and other directions are evincing their determination to curb the activities of the strikers, as the exercise of power of the latter since the absence of certain troops has incurred disfavour and is looked upon with suspicion.

The supervision of the craft which are now actually placed at the disposal of passengers wishing to land is now in the hands of the military—Whampoa cadets—and although nothing definite can be ascertained as to what transpires when passengers from the "Honam" and "Fatshan" are once ashore it is certainly a fact that no actual charge for transportation is being made. Prior to the handling of disembarkation by the military, a visit to strike headquarters was necessary for the purpose of payment of money for the privilege of landing. It is thought that a small sum has now to be paid at military headquarters instead.

The military have also taken control of outward bound passengers from Canton and greater facilities are thus "available, although a charge in excess of that paid by incoming passengers is said to be levied on them. As the strikers' pickets and the military are still at loggerheads over the matter, most of the sampans bearing outward bound passengers go alongside at night, but the greater freedom which is being exercised in the matter of the issue of passes is evidenced by the number of passengers brought from Canton by the "Honam" yesterday afternoon—150, a record number since the run was re-established between the two ports after the outbreak of the strike.

headline: STRIKERS KILLED.
text:
TAIPING INCIDENT CLOSED?

With an armed escort and supported by soldiers, new strike pickets have entered the port of Ta' Bing (near Bocca Tigris, at the entrance to the Pearl River delta) and assumed duty.

As previously reported, a squabble broke out over trade in saltfish and the local merchants are alleged to have killed four of the pickets and wounded thirty-seven in a pitched fight.

Since then the trouble is stated to have been patched up, hence the despatch of new pickets. Trade between Tai Ping and Canton has resumed.

The bodies of the four dead strikers were conveyed with ritual to Canton and the wounded were sent to the Canton Labourers' Hospital for treatment.

headline: BITER BIT
text:
How strikers' armed launches carrying pickets were defeated in a running duel with a Chinese passenger vessel is related by a passenger who admits that he hid in galley of the merchant steamer and lay flat while the shooting was going on.

Having left Macao for Kwong Hoi city, in the Sze Yap districts, the s.s. "Ng Tai Chow" (meaning "Five Great Continents") was challenged in Chinese waters by armed launches. Pickets from Canton had already forbidden the ship to run as it was alleged that passengers had travelled by roundabout routes to get to Macao.

As the “Ng Tai Chay” ignored the strikers she, so the passenger states, was fired-upon. But the strikers reckoned without the arsenal carried by the merchant-man. The fire was returned and the pickets retired, defeated. Subsequently the quarrel was patched up and the “Ng Tai Chow” returned to Macao.

headline: SWATOW WAR.
text:
NO NEW DEVELOPMENT REPORTED:

ANTI-REDS SHORTEN LINE.

Conditions at Swatow have, presumably, not changed, there being no direct report to the Colony of any development.

From a semi-official Chinese source it is gathered that the Reds have not made any material advance since the capture of Wai-chow but they may be making fresh dispositions to start another offensive. Although the anti-Red troops have suffered a reverse they are still an integrate fighting force and the initial defeat has been counter-balanced by their shortening the line and joining together.

“Heavy losses” are admitted by the “Canton Gazette” of Monday, in its description of the assault on Waichow, a part of which reads:—

"The defenders of the fortress, certain of ultimate victory, displayed considerable bravery. No sooner would the artillery fire cease than the defenders would creep out from their hiding places and keep up a deadly machine-gun and rifle fire against our attacking troops. Twice were the 21-foot walls being scaled by our Kuomintang troops and twice they were repulsed with heavy losses. Thus a commander of a Kuomintang regiment was killed, several battalion commanders were wounded or killed, a warning not to distinguish between officer and soldier in battle insofar as uniform is concerned. The means employed by the defenders of the fortress were those of the middle ages, mixed with modern weapons. Cotton soaked in inflammable liquids and thrown at the invader. Blankets soaked in the same liquid used to light up the approaches to the fortress at night." Stones, boiling tar, a sort of Greek fire, machine-guns and rifles, even artillery."

headline: “UNSOUND DEALINGS.”
text:
Legislative Control

Legislation to deal with the situation is not recommended by the Stocks and Shares Commission, the report of which was laid upon the table at to-day's meeting of the Legislative Council.

In view of difficulties involved in amalgamation, the Commission does not recommend the limitation of Exchanges to one. The obvious remedy is considered to be the reorganisation of Exchanges by their members by amending and adding to rules and strictly enforcing them. It had been given in evidence, stated the report, that there had been no recent case of a member of any Exchange being expelled, suspended, or even censured for failing to meet his obligations.

The members of the Commission have reason to believe that the share market has been carrying on its business for some time past on a thoroughly unsound basis and, even if the financial crisis had not taken place on the 22nd June, the time was bound to come in any case when a general slump in the market would have had very serious consequences.

After reviewing the growth of the three Exchanges and their rules, the causes for the large increase in speculative operations are referred to, this being attributed to the influx of Chinese money owing to interior disturbances, and the consequent cheapness of money. The balance sheets of many local companies reflected a certain amount of real prosperity leading to higher value of shares but in many cases prices of shares had risen beyond a figure justified. The causes of the collapse of the market in June were the following:

Dealing by unsound brokers with unsound clients.

Dealing by unsound brokers with sound clients.

Over-financing by native banks who, we are informed, were in the habit of advancing up to 80 per cent. or 90 per cent of the market value of the shares. Even 100 per cent. has been mentioned.

The general apprehension felt by the Chinese community as to the probable effect of the threatened strike and a boycott on the prosperity of Hongkong. At the last moment occurred the moratorium granted to the native banks, the closing of the Stock Exchange, the postponement of the Settlement and the sudden withdrawal of the extensive credit facilities—which had hitherto existed.

At the same time we are of opinion that if the first two factors, (a) and (b), had not been present the results would not have been nearly so serious and would not have affected so large a number of persons.

headline: CANTON NOTES. / REGULARS ROUTED BY MERCHANTS.
text:
STRIKERS' PERMITS.

Canton soldiers under General Li Fook-lam of Honam are stated to have been defeated by Merchants' Volunteers ("Man Tuen") at Kaukong when attempting to enter the district.

Permits from the strikers to leave Canton for Hongkong, and Maeso will be issued as usual as from October 20, states the "Wah Tsz, Yat Po."

Hu Han-min, the former Canton Foreign Commissioner, has reached Moscow where he spoke at the "Sun Wen" (Sun Yat-sen) University.—Wah Tsz Yat Po.

There is little appreciable change to-day in the quotation list issued by the Share & Real Estate Brokers Society of Hongkong, as compared with yesterday.

A cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" states that foreign warships are proceeding along the Yangtze River to Hankow to protect nationals in the event of trouble breaking out. Parents and friends of students at St. Joseph's College are reminded of the opening ceremony of the new reception hall and science laboratory, generally by H. E. the Children at Tzackie tomorrow. This is what he recalled was to have taken place in Yuhua but was not the first to be seen at the time.

headline: MR. HOLYOAK'S SPEECH.
text:
After the Colonial Secretary had moved the second reading of the budget Bill, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak said: Your Excellency.—It will perhaps be useful in discussing the draft estimates of revenue and expenditure for 1926, if in the first place I deal with your Excellency's speech introducing the budget before discussing in detail such points as appear to us to call for further explanation or special reference.

To commence with, we should like to congratulate you, sir, on the extremely able and comprehensive survey of the past year and the present situation, as well as upon the statesmanlike budget, taking which we have learned from successive budgets, to expect from you. Whilst sympathising with the difficulties of attempting any accurate forecast for the coming has naturally been a response that "for the present, the right course is to increase income and that there before you do not think it necessary to provide for additional direct taxation for the present." We were glad to hear from your Excellency that the Colony's revenue is already showing signs of improvement.

We most fully endorse your Excellency's statement that "you cannot believe that the intelligent people of Kwangtung—a race which has been famous for centuries for commercial ability and practical sense—can be content much longer to put up with the oppression of a régime imposed from outside and supported by mercenaries from other provinces," and we, too, believe that the traditional sound common sense of the people of Kwangtung, as well as the old-time deeply sincere friendship between the Cantonese officials and people and the British Government and its citizens residing in Hongkong and China must before long re-assort themselves, and conditions become once more normal for them—and us.

It is perhaps fitting at this stage to express the fervent hope that the conferences about to commence in Peking will materially assist in reinstating normal relations with China.

Turning now to the details of the Budget, we note for the first time that all junior clerks now come under the definite heading of Junior Clerical Service. Whilst appreciating the explanation that this has been done for the sake of economy in time and labour, we are not fully satisfied that it is not preferable to debit these salaries to the various departments concerned, that we may arrive at definite knowledge of the cost of running each department.

headline: China the Initial / ROBBERS BUSY.
text:
PROGRESS MAKES THIEVES!

HoiHow (Hainan Is.), Oct. 20. National Day (October 10) and Confucius Day (October 14) passed off without any trouble or demonstration. The Government schools have opened with about one-third of their usual enrol ment. The students seem very friendly.

The country is still very unsettled and robber bands are working in every district. In Vun Sang district the robbers are so bad that people are fleeing to the district city for protection or locking up their homes and sleeping hidden under bushes or trees in the open country at night.

It is reported that at Nam I recently, fifty miles south of Hoihow, a band of robbers burned about a hundred houses and killed over a hundred people. About fifty robbers were among those killed. It is an opinion among some of the Chinese that the rapid development of motor cars and roads in the island have driven chair coolies and burden bearers out of business and turned them into thieves!

A regiment in Dam Tsiu district rebelled against the Government and all the motor cars in the vicinity of Holhow were used to rush troops to that district. It is reported that the rebellion has been put down, fifty rebel soldiers captured, and the remainder forced to retire to the mountains. The local Government has a cartridge factory supplying all ammunition necessary and guns of an inferior quality are also made in Hainan. These facts are the recently constructed roads and the phones enable the quick despatch of troops and give the present Government great advantage in case of uprisings.

On October 3, Dr. Henry M. McCandliss suffered a slight stroke of paralysis from which he is making a good measure of recovery. He completed, last July, forty years of active medical work in Hainan under the American Presbyterian Mission. He founded the Hoihow hospital and has been at the head of it up to the present time building it up to one of the large hospitals of China. As soon as he is able to travel, Dr. and Mrs. McCandliss, who also leaves behind her a large record of work accomplished among the Chinese, will leave for Hongkong and probably for América, although their plans are not yet formulated. Dr. Clarence G. Salsbury is now in charge of the hospital.

headline: Customers' Appreciation.
text:
Appreciation of the milk supplied by the Company was shown by the increased number of customers and greater quantity sold up to the time of the strike, which unfortunately interrupted the progress made. I am glad to state, however, that a steady recovery is now being effected. The health of the herd is good. During the year 49 head were imported to cope with the demand, and the total now stands at 1,043 head. Early this year the Company's secretary was asked to visit Australia and New Zealand and I am glad to say the result of his visit proved as usual very gratifying and profitable to the Company. Whilst there Mr Manuk entered into agreements for the sole agencies in Hongkong and China of the "Daisy" brand butter of Messrs Presc�ts Ltd. and the "Anchor" brand butter of the New Zealand Co-operative Dairy Company. Both these butters are the particular brands exported from Australia and New Zealand respectively. Shanghai Science

arrangements just mentioned, your directors decided to open a branch of the company at Shanghai. This was done in June and is in charge of Mr. Letton, formerly a director of Messrs. Prescotts, Ltd. Mr. Letton was engaged for this purpose by Mr. Manuk during his visit to Australia. Mr. Letton has had 20 years' experience in dairy produce business, and under his management the Shanghai Branch has so far done very well and we expect greater results in the near future. I should like to say that your directors have found Mr. Manuk's annual visits to Australia to be of great importance and benefit to the Company and are well satisfied with the results attained. These visits enable us to keep in close and intimate touch with our suppliers and the market in general. Australia Visit.

The political unrest and boycott in June again taxed the resources of your Company to its utmost, but as you are aware we were able to cope with all demands and keep the colony supplied, thanks to our practice of carrying Heavy stocks of meat and butter, and also to the presence of your Secretary in Australia, who was able to secure extra supplies and freight space for our requirements. The European staff, and some of our Chinese staff, who remained loyal, worked most willingly throughout the trying period, and their services, have been suitably recognised by your Directors.

The Company's property and machinery are shown at a very conservative valuation in the balance sheet. You will be pleased to learn that the leases of our Pokfulam properties have all been renewed on a uniform basis and will continue in force for the next 31 years. We gave up certain building sites to the Government for which we received other sites adjoining our present property.

The Company's investments as shown in the balance sheet are well under their present market values, but as there are no official quotations we have refrained from giving the market valuation as formerly.

I need hardly reiterate the fact that everything possible is done to supply the Colony with pure food of the highest quality and the thanks of the directors and shareholders are due to the manager, secretary, and their efficient staff, for maintaining the standard of excellence which is always associated with this Company's supplies. With these remarks I beg to propose the adoption of the report and accounts. Seconded by Mr. P. Tester and carried unanimously.

Mr. Bridger proposed and Mr. Chan Tong seconded the re-election of Fr. Robert and Mr. R. M. Austin, the retiring directors. Mr. Makeham proposed and Mr. Abraham seconded the re-election of Mesars. Percy Smith, Seth and Fleming, as auditors, at a fee of $1,000.

headline: MACAO COUP.
text:
WARSHIP CAPTURES LAUNCHES

STRIKE PICKETS VANISH

A small Chinese gunboat, the "Ching Hoi," sailed round Macao harbour yesterday afternoon and collected eleven launches which flew the flag of the Canton Government. These launches were brought together and moored close to one of the Northern cruisers which were in Hongkong a few days ago. The launches now fly the red-white-red flag of General Chan Kwing-ming.

While the rounding-up process was being carried out, the strike pickets at Lappa Island disappeared from view.

It is rumoured here that Shekki is in the hands of General Chan's allies and that the Canton garrison has fled from the neighbourhood

headline: WEST RIVER GAIN
text:
In yet another part of the province of Kwangtung has occurred a rising against the Canton Kuomintang.

A report which is given considerable credence is that San Hing, not far from Shihing, has been taken by an anti-Red commander who rais ed about 3,000 troops for his coup: The local Red nominee, who had about a hundred bodyguards, is stated to have fled without offering resistance.

headline: LINER'S MISHAP
text:
STRIKES TANKER DURING

BEACHED THEN DOCKED.

The “Marella” from Australia, approaching Singapore yesterday afternoon, ran into a squall and came into collision with a tanker. The “Marella” was damaged amidships and the engine room became flooded; the holds remained intact.

The "Marella" was beached but eventually docked.

An Italian cruiser landed the passengers.

headline: SAFETY FIRST.
text:
RE-OPENING OF SHAMEEN

DUE PRECAUTIONS TAKEN.

The small Shameen gate, part of the larger one, was to be opened to day, Sir James Jamieson having communicated this intention to the usual meeting of residents at the Club.

When the smaller French gate was opened, zig-zag barricades leading to the bridge were placed leading from the open gate, and have remained there since, the object being to render impossible the success of any rush, however remote such a contingency may be. Similar precautions, it is thought, will be taken to-day at the British gate.

Discussion has centred round the possible opening of the gate and the removing of the barricades for some considerable time, many holding that the continuance of such measures are unnecessary and leading to the creation of bitterness. On the other hand it is held that there should be some measure of reciprocity by the Canton Government.

Acceptation of the responsibility for the safeguarding of Shameen against further attacks, the removal of pickets and restriction of movements of British residents in Canton are looked upon by them as the first essentials for the removing of the barricades. Again, there is the possibility that should an attack eventuate from the anti-Red forces in the north and the Red troops be defeated chaos may reign in Canton and measures of defence for Shameen will be vitally necessary.

The pickets outside the French gate have again resumed their activities and the importation of all food into Shameen is forbidden. The pickets claim the right, and exercise it, of searching all belongings of people entering. Americans also being subject to search. The American Vice-Consul was stopped as he was returning to Shameen with rice birds and these were taken from him.

The move which the Canton merchants have made in the direction of peace is the inevitable outcome not only of their direct losses in trade but of the taxation which has been particularly heavy because of the expenditure for the campaign on the East River.

There is in Canton money hardly sufficient for the feeding of the strikers for any considerable period and certainly none for clothing them for the winter.

headline: PEACE MOVES. / CANTON'S DELEGATION ARRIVES.
text:
TRADE RESTORATION WANTED.

Delegates from Canton's four leading commercial institutions arrived in Hongkong or Saturday, states the vernacular papers, to discuss with local Chinese merchants steps to restore communications between the two ports and to end the "strike.

It is stated that the delegates desire to ascertain in what way the Hongkong district commercial associations can assist in the matter. The Canton representatives are also mentioned as having expressed themselves as keen to take the matter up with their Government on their return as they particularly desire a resumption of trade.

According to the vernacular report the delegates sought an intellect view with Mr. Ho Kwong and Saturday and were to have preached the two Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council this morning.

headline: CABINET CRISIS.
text:
NATIONALIST MINISTERS. RESIGN

GERMAN AND LOCARNI

Berlin October 26.

The members of the German National Party in the Reichstug have approved a decision that their representatives in the Cabinet, Herr Schiele and Dr. Neuhaus and Dr. Von Schliaben, respectively. Ministers of the "Interior," National Economy, and Finance shall enter their resignations in consequence of the Party's dissatisfaction with the Locarno decisions.

headline: EARLIER CABLES. Berlin. October 24.
text:
It is anticipated that the ministers belonging to the German National Party in the Cabinet will retire, in consequence of a resolution by the Governing Board of the Party that the results of the Locarno negotiations are unacceptable. A Government majority for the ratification of the treaties is expected notwithstanding the defection. Although the decision of the Nationalist Party has caused considerable excitement, it is premature to speak of a Government crisis, as the final word is resting with to-morrow's decision of the German National Reichstag Party. Meanwhile President Hindenburg, Dr. Luther and Dr. Stresemann have cancelled their engagements and are remaining in the capital to negotiate with the Party leaders, with an aim to reaching a settlement.

Dr. Stresemann speaking at an election meeting at Karlsruhe vigorously repudiated the suggestion that the Powers represented at Locarhe intended to form an anti-Russian bloc, and declared that Germany would have nothing to do with such a policy, since she said the greatest value on her old relations with Russia.

headline: ANTI-RED WAR.
text:
FAMILIES NOW LEAVING SWATOW.

VICTORIES CLAIMED:

Naval intelligence to hand this morning states that some of the anti-Red families are leaving Swatow. This, on the face of it, refers to the families of the anti-Red party now in possession, of officers in General Chau Kwing-ming's fold.

It has been customary in Kwangtung politics for an exodus of the camps of leaders to precede a crisis. However, in this instance there may be other reasons as during the last week-end some of the highest officers in the Chan party returned to Swatow, leaving almost immediately for the front, these including General Hung Luek.

To-morrow the s.s. "Hydrangea" is due to leave for Swatow and the company reports that it has not been advised to postpone departure. The Douglas Co.'s s.s. "Hairing" is also leaving on Friday.

Coincident with reports published elsewhere on this page is the unconfirmed statement that the Whampoa Caders and other Red detachments are advancing towards Swatow, having completely taken the Hoifung district and threatened the Chiu-Mui area. On the other hand, the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" gives full particulars of the capture of Hoifung city by the anti-Reds, the officers in charge being specifically mentioned. One fact seems to have been definitely established—that Waichow is still in the hands of the Cadets and that the anti-Reds are very far off.

With practically every source of communication in Red hands and most outlets of information dominated by them it is difficult to expect any report of a substantial reverse for the present Canton regime. The position must be judged, to a certain extent, by the trend of news from Canton. In the absence of any report from the Red capital claiming any major success it may be presumed that neither side has moved any distance in the Swatow war but that the anti-Reds do not feel their position secure.

headline: STRIKE NEWS.
text:
QUEER CANTON “OFFICIAL REPORT.

MERCHANT DELEGATION.

That a steamer from Bangkok had been detained by strikers at Canton is the gist of a report to hand. Neither the steamer's name nor any other particulars have been divulged. The "Wah Tsz Yat Po" is in receipt of a cable to the following effect from Canton: All grades of officials in the Kuomintang Government favour the settlement of terms to end the strike. In connection with the report that a delegation of Canton merchants has come to Hongkong to pay the way to ending the strike, it is now learned, states the "Kung Sheung Yat Po" that the news is premature. A Hongkong Chinese merchant has been asked to inquire as to the prospect of such a mission. TO DATE DOLLAR The following is the dollar and dollar terms used in this list.

headline: China" the Jilil / CHAN'S ALLIES.
text:
CONFLICTING REPORTS.

Tang Pun-yan, (the pro-Chan general now holding the southern peninsula of Kwangtung) is advancing by two routes to attack Kongmoon. Fighting has broken out at Yanping (in the Sze Yap districts). The Kuomintang Government is sending the 5th, 7th and 8th brigades of the Hunanese Army to cope with the movement. (Special cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po.")

[Yesterday a report was published from the "China Mail's" Pakkai correspondent that Sunning had fallen into anti-Red hands. The "anti-Reds" referred to in this respect are probably those formerly under General Leung Hung-kai, alleged to be in detention at Whampoa, those troops retiring into the interior on the approach of the Reds from Canton.]

headline: Shekki Position
text:
Passengers arriving from Macao yesterday are quoted as having stunted that there is little truth in

the report that anti-Reds have captured Shekki, the capital of the Heungshan district which, incidentally, is the birthplace of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The travelers are said to have added that all the fighting that took place there was between about 200 semi-bandit irregulars under Yuen Tai, who was once a notorious outlaw, and the armed strikers pickets near Chinshan, resulting in the strikers being disarmed.

Another special telegram to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" states that Canton has ordered General Li Fook-lam and Chu Pei-tah to recapture Heungshan.

Yet another report is that the Reds, being in great apprehension as to the outcome of the fall of Shekki-on account of its proximity to Canton and other important centres—have fitted out a naval and military force to retake the place. The report goes on to say that fighting is expected in a day or two.

In response to urgent representations from the magistrate of San On (the district just across

Yesterday a fishing junk arrived in Hongkong. Forty-seven Red soldiers had gone aboard at Shanmei, ordering the crew of five to set sail immediately in spite of their being no provisions. Until the soldiers disembarked at a spot described as "the Chinese hill behind Cheung Chau," both crew and military had to subsist on one bowl of congee a day. When the crew tried to make for a Chinese Customs station they met with rough treatment. The Reds had aight machine-guns and ammunition with them when they left.

Among the seaplanites from H.M.S. “Hermes” exercising this morning were five machines flying in different formations to the bewilderment and evident enjoyment of the Chinese crowds in the streets.

A European who was discharged from, jail yesterday after serving a period of imprisonment for a traffic offence, was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, with attempting to smuggle a letter out of the prison on behalf of a French fellow prisoner. The Magistrate imposed a fine of $25.

headline: SWATOW FIGHTING.
text:
CHAN VICTORY CLAIMED OUTSIDE

From an authentic source it was learned this morning that fighting has been in progress for a day or two outside Swatqv.

Possibly the trend of operations may have had an influence on the reported departure of officials' wives and families, reported elsewhere in this issue.

However, those who received the news claim that "the Chan Kwing-ming forces got the better of the scrap. One point is that if a battle is taking place anywhere near Swatow, it means that "the Reds must have gained some ground after the last halt. The words "near" and "outside," on the other hand, may mean any part of the large area forming the hinterland of the port.

On October 24 there was a Red debacle at Shanmei, a smaller port nearer to the Red line of advance than Swatow. People from Shanmei state that 3,000 Whampon Cadets and other Red soldiers

headline: WORLD COAL
text:
STHILH HOILIDING OUR OWN

EXPERI S. OPINIONS.

Giving evidence to the Coal Commission, Sir Richard Redmayne said he could see no striking change on the world basis, detrimental to British coal interests.

Britain's could exports in 1024 were 51.2 per cent. of the world exports, compared with 49.8 in 1913.

He opined that in a quarter of a century there would be no oil in the United States, and the world supply of oil would suffice more than 80 to 100 years.

headline: POLITICS TABOO.
text:
MOSCOW'S SUN YAT-SEN UNIVERSITY.

The Chinese University named after the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen will be 'opened at Moscow at the beginning of December.

It will accommodate 250 Chinese students.

M. Radek, who has been elected Rector, said the work of the University would be strictly scientific, principally social and would be entirely free from propaganda.

headline: UNMOLESTED.
text:
SHAMEEN RESIDENTS AND ANTON

CANTON

ANITARY ARRANGEMENTS

No untoward incidents have taken place since the opening of the postern of the Western (British) gate on Shameen and residents walk generally unmolested and almost unnoticed in the City. Their presence there occasions no comment on the part of passers by and unless they bring parcels back to Shameen they are unmolested. Strike pickets claim the right to examine parcels and to prohibit the carrying into Shameen of foodstuffs.

It was inevitable that in the absence of Chinese workers the sanitary arrangements of the City have had to be left to individuals themselves and conditions as regards the streets and other public places have been of necessity not of the best. Since the arrival of non-Cantonese Chinese scavengers arranged for through the Sanitary authorities at Hongkong, things in this respect have improved considerably.

headline: BLOCKING THE WEST RIVERS
text:
GREATER ACTIVITY.

Whatever the chances of an attack may be, the Reds at Canton are undoubtedly "nervy" with regard to the presence of northern cruisers in the vicinity. The presence of one of them at Hainan taken in conjunction with the fact that Hainan, itself favourable to a resumption of trade and antagonistic to the present Canton administration, have two small gunboats, has led the Reds to greater activity in the matter of laying mines and the patrol of armed launches in the West River. headline: SWATOW FALLS?
text:
DEBACLE AT FRONT?

LACK OF ORGANISATION LEADS

That the entry of the Canton "Red" troops into Swatow was imminent was the first of a message received by the Naval authorities this morning.

Beyond this no subsequent advice has arrived stating that Swatow had actually fallen but on the face of the intelligence, and in view of events during the weekend, it is more than a presumption that only a miracle can save the last—and the most important—base for the anti-Reds, under General Chan Kwing-ming.

Information from other sources has been very meagre. From one reliable quarter it was gathered that the anti-Red centre which had inflicted a defeat in the field, not far from Swatow, had become disintegrated, letting in the Reds through the salient in the line.

General Li Tik-piu's army is stated to have failed to join the counter-offensive at the height of that last anti-Red victory. When the Reds came back all the territory gained was sacrificed, the anti-Red morale being badly shaken.

A simultaneous advance of the Red right wing, along the coast (from near Bias Bay and Shanmei) in the Hoifung prefecture left the anti-Red centre open to vital flank attack and a debacle's surmised to have ensued. It was even stated that the anti-Red resistance has been completely broken and that the Red vanguard is only waiting for gains to be consolidated before actually SWatown. That bad news was expected to be reflected in there being no stem

That bad news was expect. I reflected in there being no stem er clearances for Swatow during the week-end.

This material defeat will also decrease the anti-Red prestige on the southern front. The “Canton Gazette,” although claiming victory, admits the presence of anti-Reds at Taan Shui How, very close to Kongmoon. With the pressure on the East River relieved the Reds will carry the offensive to the south.

A rumour current is that Shekki has also been vacated by the so-called Chan allies who effected a coup there. At any rate, their position is very insecure especially as Red warships have moved up to that part of the delta.

headline: DRUNKEN BRAWL.
text:
R.G.A. MEN GET INTO TROUBLE.

ASSAULT ON POLICE.

Before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning, Driver A. E. Blackman, of 38th Heavy Battery, and Gunner Kamm, of Victoria Barracks, were charged on four counts of damaging public ricshas, drunk and disorderly behaviour, and breaking the. cells of the charge room. Kamm was charged in addition with assaulting an Indian constable in the charge room.

The evidence disclosed that after 11 p.m. on Friday the defendants while in a drunken state damaged two ricshas left at the junction of Peel Street and Queen's Road Central. They were arrested by two Indian constables and brought to the charge room where the second defendant pinched one of the constables with his clenched fist.

Sub-Inspector C. McNab Wilson stated in evidence that he was in the charge room when the defendants were brought in at 12.30 a.m. They were both badly under the influence of liquor, and the second defendant was very violent in his behaviour, refusing to submit to a search or answer questions, and later knocking down an Indian constable in his presence. The first defendant walked quietly to the cell, but four European officers had to assist in placing the second defendant in the cell. The prisoners then proceeded to smash up the cells and tore off the flooring boards, keeping up a disturbance until 3:30 a.m. A military escort arrived later and took them away.

Both defendants accepted the evidence; Kamm stating that he did not remember any of the incidents of that night.

His Worship fined the first defendant $5 on each of the four charges, and a total of $5 compensation for damage to a ricsha and the cell.

Addressing the second defendant, His Worship said that he had aggravated his offence by striking down a constable in front of the Inspector, and he was not prepared to overlook this offence. He imposed a fine of $5 for damage to the ricsha and $4 compensation. On the charge of being drunk he was fried $5, and for damaging the cell he was ordered to pay $10 compensation. On the charge of assaulting the constable, defendant was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

headline: Umu'a / SWATOW FALLS.
text:
RED ARMY ENTERING THE PORT.

"ANTIS" TOO PROUD TO FIGHT?

-

According to the fast wireless report to the Naval authorities the Reds are already entering the port of Swatow.

Since yesterday's report it has been ascertained that the Red victory was due more to internal discord in the anti-Red camp than to a grand finale.

At present the bulk of the anti-Red army is retreating towards the Fukien and Kiangsi borders (to the North). It also seems that the bulk of the Canton Reds are still in the field, the presumption being that only a comparatively small detachment has been sent to occupy Swatow.

One anti-Red detachment is surrounded as a result of the sudden debacle. It was fighting in the thick between the anti-Red centre and left, and Reds have now poured to their rear. Another force sent to extricate them stayed to deal with a rising of Farmers' Volunteers—friendly to the Reds—and was itself hemmed in before reaching the objective.

A feint by the Reds—the withdrawal of the Whampoa Cadets from the centre and their replacement by Cantonese—led to that last victory for Chan Kwing-ming but when the Cadets counter-attacked, the rout began.

The panic seems to have started in the rear rather than in the front.

Hopoh, the key to Kityeung, was vacated and then the Red right wing moved up in no great hurry, consolidating their gains.

Russian gunners are said once more to have been the deciding factor in the struggle. Knowing that the anti-Reds were running short of ammunition and that the absence of a central authority had led to the alignment not being preserved, the Reds brought their artillery up in the salient they had made. This assault ended the resistance by the anti-Reds who were fighting and they fell back in precipitate retreat. Up till Saturday Swatow, had been "quiet". Once 'disquieting' news came through from the front, the officials, in charge began to leave. There has been no exodus of any size to Hongkong. A Japanese steamer arrived here yesterday from Swatow and the s.s. "Sunning" also came in from Shanghai via Swatow.

One or two Northern Chinese warships are stated to have been at or near Swatow. The anti-Reds, before leaving, are said to have requested the Navy, to blockade Swatow so as to cut off its communication, by sea, with Canton.

Southern Front.

Disquieting news continues to arrive from the “southern front.” There is more than a possibility that the anti-Reds have lost the grip on Shekki, the capital of Heungshan district.

In the Sze Yap, the Reds are regaining control at the more exposed positions but the up-country is still full of anti-Red semi-irregulars.

Merchants Volunteers are patroing to keep order and to protect their own interests, if possible.

text: A thousand strikers rushed the steamer "Argyllshire." The police intervened and a two hours' fight ensued. A number of policemen were among the injured sent to hospital. A hundred arrests were made

headline: Utt / HEAVY FINE.
text:
JAPANESE SHIP MASTER'S APPEAT

HARBOUR MASTER'S DECISION.

Whether by coming into the waters of the Colony the master of the steamship, "Kia Lee" had made himself liable for prosecution in respect of the passengers he carried was the point before a Full Court of appeal at the Supreme Court which opened this morning.

The master, a Japanese, had already been fined twice on this charge at the Harbour Office by Lieut. Commander Hole, R.N., Harbour Master. The second fine of $5,200 was the one in respect of which the appeal was made.

The ship, which is Chinese owned, was on a voyage from Shanghai to Whampoa and came into the waters of the Colony to pick up a pilot in order that the Canton river might be navigated. Whilst under way after anchoring outside the western limits of the

PORT OF HONGKONG an officer from the harbour office boarded her and stated that by reason of her 97 passengers carried and the fact that the master carried no licence the ship would have to put into the port of Hongkong. The Harbour Master having inflicted a fine of $1,000 and ordered the passengers to be removed from the ship, the latter proceeded on her way and on her return, again passing through the waters of the Colony, she was boarded and 52 of the passengers were found never to have left at all but to have concealed themselves in different parts of the ship. It was then that the $5,200 fine was imposed. Lieut. Commander: Hole had taken the attitude, said Mr. F. C. Jenkin, representing the master this morning, that any ship passing through the waters of the Colony was liable under the section of the Ordinance calling for the possession by the master of a passenger ship of a licence. The actual wording of the Ordinance was that it was required by masters of passenger vessels to or from, or to or between place within the waters of the Colony said Mr. Jenkin, and he claimed that this could only measure the either the place of setting out or the place of destination must be within the waters of the Colony. text: ANTI-BRITISH BOYCOTT RESUMED! CARGO STILE HANDLED! Although communication with Hongkong will be maintained as yet, a boycott against foreign goods—and primarily British manufactures—is stated to have been resumed at Swallow. Other cargo was handled both for import and export after the latest Red regime had been set up. Prospects will depend on whether the Red occupiers will have their hands full with other matters.

text:
CHAN'S TROOFS LEFEATEI

Newly brought back yesterday by a Japanese team from Swatow is that the strike pickets are very active preventing any cargo from being worked. General Chan Kwing-ming's team have added a further defeat while retiring on the Polien border.

No anti-Reine are now in Shekki but the Reds have not moved up to re-occupy the town.

headline: MERCHANTS MOVE.
text:
CANTON'S STEPS TO END STRIKE.

LATEST CABLE NEWS

Further news has reached Hong- ong with regard to the move- rents by Chinese merchants in anton to end the strike.

As reported in the "China Mail," the four leading commercial chambers held an informal meeting. The "Wah Taz Mat. Po" has now been informed by cable that a delegate has been appointed to interview. Wong Ching-wai, chairman of the Kuomintang Commission of Government, on the subject.

headline: REDS ADVANCE:
text:
ENTERING SOUTHERN KWANGTUNG.

HEUNGSHAN RECAPTURED

Heungshan is now completely in Red hands again, the anti-Red adventurers having fled without being actually threatened by military force, on account of dissent among themselves as to sweets of office.

The Red expedition against Tang Pun-yan (Chan Kwing-ming's subordinate in the south) has actually penetrated enemy territory and taken Yeungehun, a town near the southern peninsula.

headline: China the Initial / HONGKONG, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1925. / PRAYA COLLISION.
text:
FIRE ENGINE AND MAIL VAN

PEDESTRIAN SEVERELY INJURED.

A collision occurred yesterday morning between a Post Office mail van and a fire engine which resulted in injuries to five persons, one of whom is now at the Government Civil Hospital in a critical condition.

The van was standing on the side of Connaught Road near the lane separating the Post Office building from the P. and O. offices. The fire engine with the usual crew on board turned from Pedder Street near the statue; and through some circumstance which is now being investigated struck the mail van in the rear. The force of the impact was so strong that the van destroyed an electric lamp post and ran a distance of about 30 feet before it was brought to a halt by striking the pillar on the pavement at the entrance to the P. and O. building.

The van being empty, and with

the brakes out of action, broke one of its front wheels in colliding with the pillar. The fire engine was completely disabled and very badly damaged. Special emergency equipment had to be brought to the scene, and the engine was taken across the harbour to the railway workshops for repair.

In addition to the Chinese pedestrian who was severely injured by the mail van in the course of its run, a Chinese officer on the engine, a fireman, and two others sustained minor injuries. The driver of the van who was on his seat at the time was not injured.

headline: SOVIET CIVIL CODE. / PROPERTY RIGHTS RESTORED:
text:
The presidium of the Executive has considerably amended the Civil Code with a view to annulling restrictions as regards the right of inheritance, particularly the clause limiting the sum of inheritance to 10,000 roubles.

Property will only pass to the possession of the State in the event of the absence of a will and lawful heirs.

The efficient traffic arrangements made to cope with yesterday's holiday attraction averted any special accidents, two incidentals, attended with minor injuries, apart from the big collision on the Praya, being accidents of every day occurrence. Yesterday afternoon a tram car knocked down a Chinese at Praya East, near Bowrington Canal, and he had to be taken to hospital with internal injuries. The vehicle failed to get out of the tram lines owing to the excavation work on the roadside. The passengers, however, escaped injury. A motor lorry driver has reported to the police that he collided with a motor cycle the driver of the latter a European, being thrown off his machine. headline: REDS EXECUTED.
text:
NAVAL OFFICERS SHOT AT KONGMOON.

CANTON FLAGSHIP STIR

Obscurity shrouds the motive behind the execution of three Red naval officers at Kongmoon. It is believed that the three officers were attached to the "Chang Shan," (formerly, the "Wing, Fung" and renamed in honour of Dr. Sun Yat-sen), flagship of the Canton Navy.

When the Soviet influence reached its zenith a Russian commander, was appointed to the "Chang Shai." Since then several vague reports—not all substantiated—have been given in connection with her. One was a supposed mutiny in which the Russian chief was supposed to have walked the plank. A subsequent story was that the cruiser had disappeared!

Capt. Au-Yeung is the Chinese commander and it is thought that the executions were under his authority. "The officers are stated to be suspected of disloyalty but there is also a hint that a scramble for power behind the scenes may have some connection with the matter. Captain Au-Yeung is at Pickland, the port of Kongmoon, write the "China Mail" correspondence, is command of the Center River Defence Field.

headline: RED SCHOOL ROW. / AGITATOR STUDENTS AID POLITICIANS
text:
BIG SUMS COVETED.

By stirring up agitation among the younger students attending colleges and universities Canton politicians are alleged to be making a determined move to secure control of the very large sums tied up in endowment funds.

Several months ago the Kung Yee Hospital control was transferred to the Cukton University of which Chew Loo is the principal Dr. S. F. Lee of Hongkong was said to have given up his post at the Kung Yee because he did not concur with the decision.

Now organisations of junior students are said to be actively working on Red political initiative to get the properties standing to the name of the educational institutions out of the present holders' hands.

A telegram to the "Wah Tsa Yat Po" says that educationalists have been refused payment of 40 per cent expenses which they asked for. A general meeting is to be held which may decide to hold a strike in all schools, etc., in Canton on Monday if the request is not accepted to.

ANT-NORTH OFFERSIVE? Canton is also reported by the same paper to be forming bases on Kwanglung's northern friendlies for an offensive against the provinces of Fukken and Kiangsi.

headline: CHRISTMAS MAIL.
text:
PARCELS COUNTER SCENES

The parents' counter at the General Post Office was literally besieged from morning by those anxious to deliver their packages before the last minute rush for the Christmas and New Year mail closing for Home at 5 p.m. to day. This mail is due in London on December 17.

Over 1,450 parcels had been received for despatch by the s.s. "Mantua" up till yesterday afternoon, and it is expected that last year's total of 3,050 parcels will be exceeded.

Although faced with an impossible task owing to shortage of hands and the calls on the parcels' staff to attend to inward deliveries, they are determined to get away all the parcels offering to-day even by working well into the night.

The Christmas letter will close on November 24.

Mrs. B. Thompson is in the French Hospital with malaria. Her friends will be pleased to hear she is making good progress.

Moscow, November 12. M. Karakhan goes to Peking at the end of the month to resume his post of Soviet Ambassador.

headline: TIT FOR TAT?
text:
ANTON SCHOOLS THREATEN STRIKE.

SEIZED STEAMER SEQUEL

Canton is not finding educational institutions and direct steamship communication such as easy matters as it had at first supposed. Last week the agitation by a section of junior students was reported to be culminating in a threatened strike of schools, colleges, etc., throughout the whole city. The latest news now is that if the Government does not pay certain arrears to the schools by tomorrow the strike will come into effect.

Then boycott of Canton is alleged to have been threatened by Cantonese merchants in Shanghai. The "Wah Kiu Yat Po" says that on November 2, the s.s. "Hsien Wah" was "seized" by the military in Canton who claimed $20,000 damage from the China Merchants Co. for damage to a telegraph cable. The report continues that Shanghai has hinted that the company's steamers will not make the Canton call until the steamer is released. The Cantonese guild in Shanghai, therefore, has cabled the Kuomintang Government to release the ship pending discussion.

On inquiry from the local office of the China Merchants Co., the "China Mail" was informed that no report of any of the alleged occurrences had been sent to Hongkong.

headline: PEACE MOVES.
text:
16 CANTONESE DUE TO-DAY?

LATEST STRIKE RUMOURS.

It was rumoured this morning that the Canton peace delegation is expected to arrive by the s.s. "Hônam" this afternoon, and that the committee of the Tung Wah Hospital and representatives of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce and the Twenty-four Guilds will hold a reception.

The discussion will probably take place at the Tung Wah Hospital.

The delegation is to number 16 and is said to be representative of Canton's commercial interests, including also two representatives from the strike executive.

A cable received by the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" last night states that the Canton delegation's departure has been postponed till Friday.

Another message is that the Canton chambers of commerce have drafted a list of "terms" on which to base negotiations.

headline: RED INVASION.
text:
TERRITORY AND ARMS CAPTURED.

ANTI-RED WAR COUNCIL

Having successfully launched their final offensive the Canton Reds are rapidly taking over territory in the South of, Kwangtung vacated by General Tang Pun-yan and his allies.

Last night the following, Reuter cable arrived from Peking:—

Official messages from South China indicate the Reds to be steadily gaining the upper hand in Kwangtung. The Reds have driven out the anti-Reds from Kwangtung and are preparing to enter Fukien. General Tang Punyan, (the pro-Chan) Tupan of Hainan Island, has telegraphed Peking asking for the despatch of a cruiser to prevent the Reds from landing in Hainan. With communication severed news from that front is unreliable. According to the best informed sources the Reds are actually in—or they control the keys to—the Ko Lui peninsula from which Hainan is separated by the Hainan Straits. Several important towns have been taken without fighting. A commander is stated to have gone over to the Reds who claim the capture of men and over 1,000 rifles. headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
SEDITIOUS CONSPIRACY CHARGES.

ORDERS FROM MOSCOW

The trial of the 12 Communists recently arrested on a charge of seditious conspiracy, was opened at the Old Bailey this morning, with two women as jurors.

All the defendants pleaded not guilty.

The Attorney-General, in opening the case, said the nature of the conspiracy which the prosecution undertook to prove was that the defendants were heads in Britain of an illegal organisation calling itself the Communist Party of Great Britain, the supreme control of which was in Moscow, with the object of forcibly overthrowing by arms the existing state of society and as a means thereto, seducing the armed forces of the Crown from their allegiance.

headline: "THE TRIAL IS A FARCE."
text:
A man who shouted "the trial is a farce" was ejected from the court.

The Attorney-General stated the Communists spent at least £12,000 annually on salaries and newspaper propaganda, and undoubtedly the money, or a greater part of it came from Moscow.

The Communists were therefore bound by orders from Moscow, which were illegal and criminal in England.

The Attorney-General's speech lasted over four hours. The trial was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: TIME RIPE?
text:
SIGNS OF DESIRE TO END STRIKE.

LOVES BEHIND THE SCENES.

Although they are no more than straws in the wind, there are several indications that an all-round feeling exists in favour of ending the strike and boycott. Friday is, now stated to have been definitely fixed as the day of departure from Canton of a peace delegation to Hongkong. Over twenty merchants will be included, it is reported.

Yesterday the Hongkong Chinese General Chamber of Commerce held a committee meeting which discussed the details of a reception for the Canton traders. Meanwhile representatives of Canton's four leading commercial associations—all designated as "chambers"—have interviewed Mr. Wong Ching-wai, one of the principals of the Kuomintang Commission of Government—and he is said to have lent a favourable ear. There is, however, a qualification Mr. Wong is quoted as having approved a mission to Hongkong, more for the purpose of ascertaining what can be done, than declaring an end to the present conditions.

Yesterday afternoon the Steamboat Co.'s s.s. "Honam" came down with about 400 native passengers—a "record number—who state that they made their way to the ship, when in Canton harbour unmolested by pickets.

Another sign of the times is a report from Canton that the present mercantile movement was engendered by the Hongkong Association of District Commercial Guilds, also that the sponsors of the Canton peace delegation, have put out feelers to the Strike Executive. The strike leaders, on the other hand, seem to be divided. One section is adamant and strongly disfavours any mission to Hongkong. Another party is reported to have declared itself as willing to abide by what the "majority of the people" say. In other words they will be guided by the Canton Government but they will not turn an entirely deaf ear to the merchants and middle class.

headline: BLIND HOME. / TO-DAY'S SALE OF WORK
text: A sale of work in aid of the Industrial Institution for the Blind, Kowloon, opened at the Y.W.C.A. rooms, Caine Road, this morning and will be continued till 5 p.m. Useful and舒適的 work in aid of the Industrial Institution for the Blind, Kowloon, opened at the Y.W.C.A. rooms, Caine Road, this morning and will be continued till 5 p.m. Useful and skillfully made articles of knitted woollens, embroideries and other goods adorned the tableau, and the blind girls made a striking appeal for sympathy by singing at intervals. headline: DANGEROUS
text:
The master of a fishing junk was brought before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning on two charges of unlawful possession of an old rifle and a quantity of detonators and dynamite. Evidence of seizure was given by Sergeant Carevel.

Pleading gully to the charge of possession of the explosives, Mr. C. A. S. Russ submitted that the junk occasionally visited the outskirts of British waters, but that the fishing was done in Chinese waters where there was no law against the use of dynamite.

A plea of not guilty was tendered on the charge of possession of the rifle. Mr. Russ explained that the weapon was kept on board as an assurance of security against possible molestation from strike pickets. The junk, he said, had at one time been used for the transport of vegetables to Hongkong from an outlying district and the owner had in fact held a permit to carry firearms while engaged on this mission.

His Worship convicted on both charges, among a fine of $150 for carrying explosives, which he considered was the more serious of the two, and $50 on the other charge.

Bangkok has been declared an infected port on account of cholera.

headline: NOT AGAINST MOSCOW.
text:
Mr. Ramsay MacDonald severely criticised the recent speech of Mr. Ormsby. Gore, on which he said evil suggestions had been based that Germany had been brought into the new alliance against Moscow.

He asked was it the Government's view that Locarno was engineered for the purpose of uniting Western civilisation against Russia.

Mr. Chamberlain replied: "No," and "I constantly repudiated any idea of pursuing such a policy. (Ministerial cheers): Mr. MacDonald said he was very delighted to hear it and congratulated Mr. Chamberlain on his successful efforts to create the peace spirit, but said unless the opportunity was taken swiftly to seize the chance thus opened up, the harvest would never ripen. He added that as regards the Dominions and India, he was unable to conceive a more calamitous system of conducting an Imperial foreign policy, than the method enshrined by the Locarno Fact.

headline: PERTINENT QUESTION.
text:
Mr. Chamberlain warmly denied the Government's policy as being hostile to Russia. He declared that it was only perverted ingenuity to devise an argument that Locarno was establishing a new balance of power, namely, between Europe and Asia, and pointed out that Eastern nations were members of the League like the Western nations.

Japan, with whom we were happily on terms of intimate friendship and co-operation, was a member of the League.

He asked whether Mr. Ponsonby meant that Britain must not attempt to put relations with Germany on a better footing unless we received the sanction of the Soviet Government.

headline: DESTINY!
text:
THE NEW COMET AND THE STRIKE.

SIMPLE CHINESE BELIEF. Connection between the new comet and the local strike has been pointed to by some of the

simple Chinese in the Colony. Yesterday Reuter cabled the report of the discovery of a new comet in the constellation of the "Hunting Dog" by Yerkis Observatory, U.S.A. This comet is brightly visible through a small telescope.

A week or so ago local star-gazers were watching a “destiny” star from streets and housetops, shortly after sunset. The “discoverers” claim that they were even quicker, with the unaided eye, than the powerful apparatus worked by qualified astronomers. One even went so far as to maintain that the presence of this “broom” star (the Chinese colloquial for comet) would have a great influence over the settlement of the strike!

headline: MR. AMERY SPEAKS.
text:
HONGKONG'S WONDERFUL

CONFIDENCE IN FUTURE.

Mr. L. C. S. Amery is a speech at the annual dinner of the China Association declared the situation in China was the subject of anxious concern on the part of the British Government.

He mentioned "the wonderful history of Hongkong" and said he was glad to think they were able to give Hongkong the help for which she appealed. They found it not from the Imperial exchequer but in the patriotic and willing co-operation of the West Africa, Malay States and Hongkong, and Shanghai banks.

Mr. Amery was firmly convinced that Hongkong's difficulties were transient. He believed though the period of waiting might be anxious, the Chinese people's commonsense would never allow the present state of affairs to continue for ever, nor would the patience of the British Government witness for ever the impoverishment and retrogression of a great British Colony.

headline: DR. WU'S HELP. / HOPES OF ENDING THE BOYCOTT.
text:
MONEY EXPORT EMBARGO?

Dr. C. C. Wu (Wu Chao-chu) is now reported to be strenuously exerting his influence towards ending the present Canton boy-cott.

Among the. Kuomintang officials Dr. Wu is probably the "best. know and most respected diplomat. In the discussions between delegates of the merchants and the Canton Commission of Government Dr. Wu is reported to have used his good offices.

Another favourable report is that General Cheung Kai-shek's officers at Swatow are quietly supervising the strike pickets there and restriating them from any possible excesses.

Meanwhile the next step is eagerly awaited by Chinese merchants in Hongkong—the promised arrival of the Canton delegation to-morrow afternoon.

Passengers coming into Hongkong by train from Samchin state that the pickets just across the border have been exercising strict vigilance during the last two days in the matter of money and valuables. Those who take with them anything over $20 or excess jewellery have been sent back along the Chinese section of the Railway, or asked to deposit the surplus pending their return from Hongkong. No official notice has been given of any order by the Strike Executive regarding the export of money or valuables.

headline: REDS MARCH ON / PENETRATING SOUTHERN PENINSULA
text:
'EX-REBELS' SURRENDER.

Tien Pak, a flourishing town in the southern peninsula, has fallen to the Canton forces without a fight.

Brigadier-General Chan Ming-shu, commanding the Reds on that front, has reported to Canton that General Tang Pun-yan's anti-Reds are not offering battle. There is now no possibility of a counter-offensive on the mainland and it seems that Tang will withdraw his following into Hainan Island in the hopes of lasting out a blockade by the Reds. Some "ex-rabels," who took part in the recent demonstrations in the Sze Yap districts (interlor of Kongkiou) have been embodied by the Reds on the former surrendering. Two commanders have been given by the Canton Military Council, the rank of division generals

From the East River sector a large number of Cadde have been sent back to Whampoa. The impression is that General Chang Kai-shek may postpone its projected invasion of Pakistan provided it is more favourable opportunity.

headline: MURDER TRIAL
text:
BUILDING

X YOUTH ARRAIGNED

The disappearance of it building implement is alleged to be the cause of a dispute between two employees, one an old man and the other little more than a youth. After high words had passed it is alleged that the young man who suspected the other of taking the tool, struck the old man with a knife in the abdomen. As a result of his injuries the man in question died at the Government Civil Hospital and the other is arraigned at the Criminal Sessions on a charge of murder.

He was represented this morning by Mr. H.S. Fitzroy and the Attorney General, Sir Henry Pollock, K.C., prosecuted.

The only alleged eye-witness is the man to whom belonged the tool which was the source of the trouble and on whose behalf the prisoner had taken up the cudgels. This man said that he saw prisoner strike the old man, with a knife and he (witness) then ran away. Later at a house at East Point he saw the prisoner who admitted that he had stabbed the man.

This witness was cross-examined, minutes by Mr. Fitzroy. Asked to account for the fact that it was he (witness) and not the prisoner who stayed away from work for two days and seemed to have most apprehensions, whereas prisoner went on with his work the witness replied that he ran away and hid because he thought if the police could not get the prisoner they would come for him. Witness maintained that he had heard the prisoner make the statement as to having stabbed the old man. This despite the fact that Mr. Fitzroy pointed out that another man who had heard the alleged confession stated in the witness box that he was the only person there at the time the confession was made. Medical evidence of the terrible nature of the wounds from which the old man died was given and cross-examined by Mr. Fitzroy witnesses said that they did not think that the wound could have been self-inflicted through the old man falling on the weapon clenched in his own hand.

The case is proceeding.

headline: PEACE DOINGS.
text:
INTERESTED PARTIES WORK HARD.

DELEGATION DUE TO-DAY.

Until the delegation arrives from Canton to-day it is not known what the nature of their discussion will be.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngnam, who at one time owned considerable property in the Colony, is the latest to have interested himself in a settlement.

Another good sign is the order by the Canton Government to their Police to disarm all pickets engaged in “protecting” transport (both of passengers and cargo at feels).

Then again Canton is desirous that another delegation go up frbn Hongkong.

A gentleman has received a letter, however, stating that even though the Canton delegates have the goodwill of the people in power, they may be placed in such a position that terms will have to be submitted again and that, consequently, the solution lies in a middle party finding a compromise.

headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
FREEDOM OF OPINION INVOLVED?

SEDITIONS OF THE MIGHTY.

... Sir Henry Slesser, counsel for defence, concluding a six hours speech in the trial of the Communists, said this was one of the most important cases submitted to a British jury in many years.

On the decision depended the liberties and opportunities of men to write and express opinions for many years to come.

Sir H. Slesser called only one witness who testified to purchasing at His Majesty's Stationery Office, copies of the Government report on Russia.

The defendant, Harry Pollitt, addressed the jury and was refused permission by the Judge to quote speeches by Lord Birkenhead, Lord Carson and Sir W. Joynson Hicks, the Judge remarking: "We cannot have their editions mixed up with yours."
