headline: STRIKE
text:
The strike threatened by the staffs of Canton educational institutions has been called off, it is stated.

Rehabilitation work progresses in the East River region. The dismantling of Waichow's city walls is almost completed and it is proposed to convert the historic Sai Wu Lake into a public park.

The capture of Lo Ting, by the Canton armies, in the southern sector, has been reported to Canton.

Chang Waiz, who governs that part of Kiangsi province adjacent to Kwangtung is said, according to a "Wah Tsz Yat Po" cable, to have ordered the army of the anti-Red (Gantonese) General Hung Shui-luo, to leave Kiangsi. General Hung-li-Sak, a�ulatory there after being defeated but Chang deems his presence a menace as he apprehends an invasion by General Cheting Kai-shek, the Cadet chief.

headline: STUDENT STRIKERS.
text:
CHANGE IN OFFICIAL ATTITUDE?

"OFFENCES. EXPIATED."

It is significant that coincident with the moves that are being made in the direction of closer cooperation between Hongkong and Canton certain proposals have been mooted for a modification of the edict barring from admission to Government and Government aided schools students who were absent from study on certain dates.

The period of this suspension, or expulsion as it was then generally regarded, was not mentioned when the attitude of Sir R. E. Stubbs was outlined by the Chairman of the Education board and it is understood that the penalty paid during the period that has elapsed since their having been de-arred from entrance has been advanced to the Government as sufficient for the students to have expiated their offence. The end of the school year has been suggested as the date when such stringent measures might no longer apply.

The Government attitude is expected to be announced shortly.

It may be recalled that at the Education meeting at which Sir R. E. Stubbs' attitude was endorsed, nearly all the members who spoke were in accord with that attitude but a few thought it was too severe. Father Valtorta thought that temporary suspension and postponement of examinations would meet the case. Mr. J. M. Alves suggested the formation of a "humiliation" class of strikers in each school would be sufficient punishment and Dr. Wan spoke at length or "the need for taking a more liberal and considerate view."

Dr. Pearce thought that the balance had been struck between justice and generous consideration. Now, if ever, was the time for emphasising the importance of discipline. The matter should be left to the heads of schools. No one else could do anything in the matter.

The Chairman's final remark was that he thought that the matter could be safely left with the headmasters who, he was sure, would be sympathetic in their consideration.

headline: School Fees.
text: The “China Mail” also understands that the Government has under consideration the proposed raising of fees which was not the outcome of the strike but revision which was considered necessary in any event. Representations have been made that the present is hardly opportune for an extra financial burden to be imposed on parents and it is likely that the Government may postpone or mitigate the increases.

headline: MISSING LETTERS.
text:
VIA SIBERIA ROUTE CHARGES.

ALLEGED TAMPERING.

Serious allegations were made at a meeting of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce of heavy delay and miscarriage of mails from Britain to the Far East via Siberia.

Delegates asserted that many mails are missing and letters are tampered with apparently when passing through Soviet territory. The matter was referred to the Postmaster-General.

headline: Railway Deadlock.
text: A semi-official message says: "In view of the refusal of the Chinese Government to sign an agreement regarding the through passenger communication between the Soviet railways and the Soviet and Japanese Chinese railway, the conference concerning the matter has been temporarily suspended on the suggestion of the Soviet delegates. The Russian and Japanese commission on goods traffic will begin work in a few days' time."

headline: MEANING OF THE DAY
text:
No official function marked the observance among Americans locally of Thanksgiving Day but several business houses were closed, also the American Consulate.

Americans commemorate to-day, has no fixed date and commemorates no particular event—it is rather the expression of a sentiment and hence has not always been observed on the same date or even in the same season.

The harvest home idea—the appropriateness of rendering thanks after the crops are garnered, has made the autumn season, however, the preferred one. The last of November having been chosen by President Johnson, this selection became the precedent for all subsequent years.

Thanksgiving Day is a universally observed national holiday, the head of the Government issues a proclamation and business closes down entirely. As it has to do with the safe reaping of harvests it is observed more in the country districts than in the cities. In a Thanksgiving address at Nanking, Judge Lobinger gave a historical sketch of the national occasion and said in conclusion: "Our Thanksgiving Day as we have seen, sprang from various faiths. It is no longer sectarian. It is a product of ideas originating in different lands and has outgrown sectionalism. It needs only to pass the bounds of narrow nationalism to become a day of humanity. And it is one of the most gratifying features of this happy occasion that its participants are of various nationalities."

headline: BANISHEE CHARGED.
text:
DEFENDANT'S EXPLANATION IN COURT

STOPPED BY PICKETS.

A. Chinese was charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning for returning from banishment.

According to the evidence of a Chinese detective, the man was escorted to Shumchun on September 30. It was stated that defendant had five previous convictions three for returning from banishment.

headline: BORDER INCIDENTS.
text:
RICE CARGOES STOLEN BY STRIKERS.

The peace of the border War disturbed by two incidents which took place on Monday morning. In the first, a party of strikers on mischief bent fired a couple of rounds in the direction of two European officers doing patrol duty on the banks of the Shumchun River. The fire was returned and the strikers took to their heels. This was followed by a theft of rice from coolies on the British side.

At another point near Lqkma-chau, armed men crossed the border and compelled some cookies carrying rice to take the cargo into Chinese territory.

headline: JAIL FOR REDS. / SEMITTOUS CONSPIRACY PROVED
text: The trial of the 12 Communist leaders at the Old Bailey has resulted in all the accused being found guilty. Five namely: Inkpin, Rus, Politt, Gallacher and Hannington have been sentenced to 12 months in the second division. The others refused to be taking over and were sentenced to six months in the second division.

headline: OBITUARY
text:
CHINESE DEATH AT 86TH BIRTHDAY

WELL-KNOWN METALS DEALER

Fifty-seven years a resident in Hongkong, Mr. Chin E-tin, the well-known metals merchant passed away at his residence, No. 23, Wing Woo Street yesterday at the ripe age of 86.

By a strange coincidence yesterday was the late M. Chin's birthday and it was after receiving congratulations from his many friends and relatives that he expired peacefully.

When Mr. Chin first arrived in the Colony he founded the firm of E. Hing & Co., now one of the oldest and most respected hardware firms. Many of the older members of the mercantile community will recall Mr. Chin, who from a very humble origin, rose to great wealth by integrity and shrewd handling of his business.

The funeral takes place tomorrow afternoon, and the remains will be deposited at the Tung Wah Hospital repository. The cortege passes the Yat Pit Ting, Kennedy Town, about 1.15 p.m.

News from Canton to-morrow is that alleged strike pickets have forcibly exercised a censorship of mails, particularly on letters and/or packages to Hongkong. It is stated that a number of men called at the office declaring themselves to represent the Strike Executive and conducted themselves in such a manner that the Canton Post Office has had to make representations. A message to the Wah Tez Yat Po" says that Mr. Yeung Sai-ngaam has been appointed, by the Canton Government, "special investigator to Hongkong and Macao."

headline: Governing Cabinet Suggested.
text:
Tuan Chi-jui summoned another special meeting at his residence last night, which was attended by most of the members of the Cabinet. He again advocated resigning and suggested the formation of a governing Cabinet under Huang Fu, as after the coup d'état of last year. Most of those present opposed, and urged Tuan Chi-jui to remain for the sake of the conference. No decision was reached.

The students are arranging a big demonstration to-morrow, at which in addition to the demand for unconditional tariff autonomy, they will urge the abolition of Tupanships, placing provincial control in the hands of Civil Governors, and disbandment of superfluous troops. It is not expected that the police will prevent the demonstration.

Feng Yu-hsiang's third division arrived at Nanyuan from Kalgan last night. Half are remaining at Nanyuan and half proceeding to Changsintien.

Tuan Chi-jui has sent his aide-de-camp to see Lu Chung-lin. He said he would take personal responsibility for political suspects and requested the immediate release of Tseng Yu-chun. The latter was accordingly released on bail this morning.

headline: SECOND MISSION
text:
WAIT FOR HONGKONG."

LATEST ADVICE FROM RELIABLE

That a second "peace quission" from Canton-comprising two delegates—was coming down by river steamer today, was the gist of the latest message received regarding the "strike settlement." Mr. Yeung Sai-nguam and Mr. Kan Kum-shek are the two gentlemen expected. Mr. Yeung has been reported, according to Canton vernacular cables, as having been appointed special investigator by the Provincial Government. He was formerly a well-known merchant and at one time owned extensive property in Hongkong. Mr. Kan is one of the principals of the Canton Nanyang Brothers Tobacco Co. He was one of the last delegation and is quoted as having said that the present trouble is due to a class war the world over.

It is also gathered that Mr. Young and Mr. Kan have no

special duties to perform in connection with their visit.

The "China Mail" informant said: — Canton is probably waiting for Hongkong to make the next move. Meanwhile Messrs. Young and Kan. will sustain and add to the good feelings already express

headline: DESTITUTE TROOPS.
text:
200 ANTI-REDS PUT OVER BORDER.

Yesterday morning the Police completed arrangements for repatriating the detachment—over 200 strong—of anti-Red soldiers who arrived here from Amoy after being “on their last legs” through the fortunes of war.

As reported yesterday they were in General Chan Kwing-ming's army. A long trek into Fukien province followed defeat by the Whampor Cadets. In supposedly friendly territory they were stripped of their fighting implements. Going without food for three days, they reached Amoy and came on here.

...They were taken in hand on arrival and were put across the frontier at Samehun.

headline: WIRELESS STRIKE
text:
ACTION BY BOARD OF TRADE.

REGULATIONS RELAXED.

The strike of wireless operators does not involved the land stations, but the Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists, which called the strike, claims as members 98 per cent. of the wireless operators aboard British merchantmen.

Wireless operators have been instructed to report to the union as ships come into port and not to sign on for fresh voyages, but ships already at sea are not endangered as existing contracts will not be broken.

The opinion is expressed that if the Board of Trade insists on the full observance of the regulations with regard to the carrying of wireless operators, many ships must be held up.

headline: CREATING RIDICULE?
text:
The Association of Wireless and Cable Telegraphists says that approximately 200 operators up to the present have refused to renew their signatures on ships articles and asserts that one Liverpool, one Glasgow and two Hull boats have been held up.

The Association criticises the Board of Trade relaxation cabled earlier as a move in favour of shipowners which will create suspicion and ridicule of Government regulations.

The two ships held up at Hull later sailed with Board of Trade clearances.

It is reported from Liverpool that operators on the White Star boat "Celtic" are among those who refused to sign but the Cunard, Alfred Holt and Brocklebank lines are not affected as they employ their own operators and have not given notice of any reduction in wages.

An earlier cable stated: The Telegraphists Association has issued strike notices in the case of all wireless operators aboard British ships, land have instructed the men not to sign for further voyages pending a settlement of the dispute regarding conditions of service, including the proposed reduction of wages of 22s.6d. monthly.

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
CANTON TO APPOINT DELEGATES? THE NEXT SOBE!

THE FROSPECTS ARE ROSY

To day the "salient point in the movements towards a settlement of the "strike" is that everything now hinges on the appointment by Canton of a delegation to negotiate with Hongkong's representatives.

This morning the "Chinn Mail" was authoritatively informed that the departure of the Colony's mission, namely, the Hon. Sir Paul Chater, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shouson, the Hon. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. D. G. M. Bernard, will be fixed when, Canton, he announced the constitution of their body. In the best informed circles it is considered that the report published of actual appointments is premature. Interviewed by a vernacular paper representative at a private Cainese club last night, the spokesman of the second merchant mission "emphasised that he had come down to Hongkong on private business and in a purely personal capacity.

In reply to a query he indicated that the prospects were rosy and that favourable intelligence would be available shortly.

It is believed that the sailing of Messrs. Yeung Sai-ngaam and Kan Kim-shek from Canton was delayed from "Saturday" to yesterday owing to their being called to an important conference almost on the moment of embarking, though the discussions were stated to be of an informal nature.

Since the return of the first Canton, “unofficial”, delegation many steps have been taken behind the scenes.

The Hongkong Union of District Commercial Associations has written to Mr. Wong Ching-wai (chairman), Nationalist Provincial Government) outlining the recreation accorded the merchants here and laying stress on Hongkong's cordiality and friendliness.

The merchant delegates also got in touch with the Kwangtung authorities and Mr. Wong is reported as having consulted Dr. C. C. Wu on the matter.

Another noteworthy incident is the return to the Colony on Saturday of Dr. S. W. Ts'o who maintains that his trip to Canton was entirely in connection with private affairs. On Sunday he was one of those who met Messrs. Yeung and Kan at the Steamboat Co.'s wharf.

This morning the "Wan Kiu Yato" published a cable from Canton, dated yesterday, to the effect that in connection with the ending of the strike, the labourers would select a delegate and the merchants one. The merchant nominee, however, would act strictly as a third party, using food offices as mediator and not participating in the actual deliberations.

This afternoon the China Mail was informed that a meeting of the delegates will be held at 4 p.m. at the Chinese Merchants' Club, when interesting developments were expected. Confirmation has been obtained that the report of 'Canton's approvalments' was premature. It is admitted that Messrs. Yeung and Kan are down here in connection with the negotiations. They were acting strictly as individuals—not even could their visit be described as "semi-official," it was stated—but in their personal capacities they were assisting in bringing matters to a head. Chinese gentlemen who have received correspondence from members of the last delegation declare that most of the pioneering work is accomplished. Accordingly more definite information is anticipated.

TO-DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, on demand, to-day was 2/47/18

headline: FAKLIEK CABLES
text:
Peking, Nov. 20. A mandate issued accepts the resignation of Yen Kung-cho and approvals Kung Hsin-chan as acting Minister of Communications. To-day's demonstration had a decidedly Communistic tendency, the students assembling being not only Kuomintangites but also a large number of workers, ricsha and other coolies. No national flags were observed; the students carrying the Canton flag and the workers had left. The workers were all armed with stout sticks and accompanied by motor cars with doctor's and nurses. The demonstrators are now parading the streets and distributing pamphlets, demanding itter also the overthrow of Tuan Chi-juli, to kill Chu Shen and shoot all traitors; to dissolve the Tariff Conference and arm all the people for a popular revolution and a real national conference. So far there is no violence.

This afternoon's student demonstration for the purpose of receiving Lu Chung-lin's reply to demands made was not so largely attended as yesterday's gathering, probably because yesterday's display of violence aroused misgivings among the more timorous as to the likely consequences. "The immediate dissolution of the Tariff Conference" was one slogan prominently displayed this afternoon and the list of Tuan Chi-jui's alleged crimes against the people was posted up.

Pleading indisposition Lu Chung-lin refrained from attending the gathering and the students proceeded to discuss plans for the next move which threatens to include an attack on the “Chen Pao” on account of its anti-communistic tendencies.

The Manchurian situation is clarifying, Kuo Sung-ling's van-guard in twelve trains arrived at Chin Wang Tao yesterday, he claims to have occupied Shan Hai Kuan and his headquarters will be at Chin Wang Tao. The Chang-Tso-limits have a division and a half and Chung Tsien-so two divisions at Chinchow. The Jehol army is going to Chinchow to assist Chang Tso-lin and the first clash is expected at Wanchatun near Shan Hai Kuan. The twelve aeroplanes which Kuo Sung-ling seized have now flown to Mukden and are being used to drop propaganda pamphlets over Kuo's troops.

The advance of the Hongenroops into Shantung continues. Chang Tsung-chang is concentrating at Weihsien and Chinchowfu, and is apparently preparing to leave Shantung with the remnants of his army and go by gunboat to Manchuria. Shanghai, Nov. 29. Kuo Sung-ling has issued a manifesto against Chang Tsung-lin, which he declares that it is possible any longer to see his brethren working suffering and

fighting for nothing but the glory and selfish ends of a few persons. Therefore, in compliance with the will of the people he is directing a military movement toward Mukdan, as it is proper that he should overthrow the ruling caste of the Mukdan "minds whose brutal militarists, such as Chang Tao-lin especially, have been poisoned by the cruel doctrine of militarism." He is determined to bring forth upon Manchuria a new government in which the governed will govern themselves and he must strive to achieve per mantra's people not only in Manchuria but in China. headline: THE WEATHER:
text:
This morning's weather report states that the anticyclone has weakened further and is now central over the Eastern Sea. Moderate monsoon may be expected along the S.E. coast of China and over the China Sea.

Until noon to-morrow, the forecast is N.E. winds, moderate; fair.

Moscow, November 29.—In connection with the complaint of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce alleging that mail to the Fur East via Siberia is delayed and sometimes lost, the Commissariat posts declared that they have not yet received any complaints of delay or lose. The average time in transit is a fortnight. There have been two cases of railway wrecks but the mail was delayed only a few hours. Reuter.

headline: ROBERTSON ASBESTOS PROTECTED. METAL ROOFIN
text:

concerts, bridge parties, "horse races," etc. The horse races are exceedingly popular.

headline: OPEN INVITATION
text:
TO ENCOURAGE FRIENDLY RELATIONS.

An open invitation to as many Chinese in Hongkong as would wish—the more the better—has been extended for a “bright tour” of Canton.

Mr. Kan Kum-shek in his address at the Chinese Merchants' Club indicated that much benefit would be derived it oversea Chinese went up to Canton to see things for themselves.

It is now stated that a project is on foot to get together not less than 200 persons to travel together on this tour. The name implies "see the brightness" and the sponsors' ideas to convince the sightseers that the Canton Government is not "Red." It is also suggested that the tourists use their personal influence with the Labour leaders to hasten a settlement of the strike.

headline: BOYCOTT MODIFIED. / CANTON'S NEW IMPORT SYSTEM.
text:
FOREIGN TRADE RULES

As quoted by the “Canton Gazette,” the Strike Executive has agreed that “the regulations restricting the importation of foreign goods formerly, were too strict for the merchants.”

The Executive says: "So as to express our friendly feelings between the labourers and merchants, we draw up a modified system of imports." The modifications published are:—

(1) Cargo of non-British manufacture that come directly from Shanghai, although they are marked with the word "Hongkong," are allowed to be imported.

(2) Goods of non-British manufacture which have been stored in Hongkong and transhipped to Shanghai for shipment to Canton by another steamer, are allowed to be imported, if they are proved to be in accordance with our regulations, by any bill of lading and customs permit.

(3) Goods of all countries, even of non-British manufacture, if inscribed with the word “Hongkong,” when transhipped to Canton from the coastal ports of Kwangtung, namely, Swatow, Hainan, Kwang Chow Wan, etc., are considered infringements of our rules.

headline: College Benefactor.
text: The Rev. W. H. Hewitt, in a short address, dwelt on the services as benefactor to St. Stephen's College of the late Mr. Chau Su-ki and referred to the manner in which he had freely spent himself in the service of the community. Referring to the willingness with which the late Mr. Chau Su-ki had advised and helped the Council and the school, Mr. Hewitt mentioned that in June he, together with the Chinese members of the Council, took the trouble to go to the college and talk to the students and masters to put before them the situation as it appeared to the older members of the Chinese community. It was largely owing to the efficiency of such advice that the students and staff at that time were able to take a sane outlook on the situation and prevent the work of the College from being interrupted.

headline: ANTON REPORTER
text:
After mentioning that Hong-kong's delegates were to have gone up during the last week-end, the "Canton Gazette" quotes a letter to the Strike Executive by Wong Ching-wa (chairman of the Police Council); as follows:—

The question in regard to the despatch of delegates to negotiate with the Hongkong representatives for settling the strike was discussed at our meeting held on November 27. It was decided afterwards that three representatives should be elected by the Strike Committee and one by the Four Chambers of Commerce.

Although Mr. Yeung Sai-ngsaam has been reported as having emphasised that his visit to Hong-kong is purely personal and in a strictly private capacity, it is interesting to note that the "Canton Gazette" of Tuesday, says:—

During the period of the present strike which is being carried on, so vigorously, the intercourse with Hongkong and Macao has been absolutely cut off. Recently our Government, in order to investigate the latest conditions in Macao and Hongkong, specially appointed Yeung Sai-nguam as special delegate for the purpose. After the appointment, Mr. Yeung proceeded to Hongkong on November 29 on the 8.3. "Honam."

headline: PEACE MISSION.
text:
EX-CANTON OFFICIAL DUE 10DAY

THE HONGKONG "TOURISTS."

A series of reports continue to reach Hongkong from Canton, in the absence of official intelligence regarding the preliminary moves towards negotiation for strike settlement.

Mr. Yeung Sai-nganm (the former Finance Minister) is due back here to day but it is insisted that he is not vested with any office.

Registration of names for inclusion in HongKong's party to visit Canion is almost complete and the unofficial mission may leave shortly. Vernacular news is that the projected tour is viewed with much satisfaction by both the Political Council and the labour executive.

In view of the contradictory nature of the news it seems likely that the next moye will be decided when General Cheung Kaishek returns to Canton. He is still stated to be in the East River area directing reorganisation. Last week he reviewed the troops at Chinghsi.

Meanwhile the merchant and labour bodies are still discussing the basis of representation at the proposed negotiations.

headline: FROM FAR EAST
text:
THROUGH ROUTE ACROSS SIBERIA.

The international railway conference has opened to discuss the problem of through traffic from the Far East to Western Europe via Soviet Russia.

The conference is attended by representatives of the Soviet Government, France, Germany, Japan, Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania and Poland.

The proposed through route will cover about 8,750 miles and will be the longest in the world. The journey from Tokio to Paris will take a fortnight.

headline: WIRELESS STRIKE / SHIPS SAIL WITHOUT OPERATORS
text:
In the House of Commons, Sir Phillip Cunliff Lister stated that reports from the principal ports showed that up to the evening of December 4, 25 passenger and 124 cargo ships had left without wireless apparatus.

The number of passengers affected was unavailable.

headline: UNIONS CLOSED / TURBULENT SEAMEN AT SWATOW.
text:
CANTON PARTY ACTS.

That the Seamen's Union at Swatow has gone too far and has accordingly been stripped of its power to use weapons and uniforms is the gist of part of a special message to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po."

Various charges were laid against the pickets controlled by the Union, including the levying of "squeeze" in sums of $25 each on passengers for Hongkong and $2,500 each for permission for ships to discharge cargo, usurping the power of the civil authorities as to arrest, etc.

After a protracted hearing at the Mayor's yamen a decision was given against the Union, states the report.

Hongkong Unions' Distress. Rumours have been current among the Chinese as to the reason for the closing of a number of local labour unions in Hongkong. It has transpired that landlords of premises occupied by 27 Labour guilds have taken "out distress warrants for arrears of rent.

When the strike began the majority of guilds were left in the hands of a "boy" or coolie. After several months the rent began to accumulate and the respective owners had to resort to action.

In most of the guilds affected the furniture, and fixtures have been auctioned under authority: One result is that "Paddy's Market" is now plentifully stocked with union signboards, photographs of guild presidents and other paraphernalia.

Among the best known unions thus affected are the Chinese Sena men's Union, the two Federations of local unions and nearly all the guilds for domestic and/or office servants of European employers.

headline: PARTY SPLIT. / REPORTED KUOMINTANG DIFFERENCES.
text:
SUN FO AND WU TE-CHEN.

Activities by Kuomintang members in Shanghai, alleged to be directed against the Canton authorities, are reported by cable to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po."

It is hinted that Sun Fo and General Wu Te-chen (former Police Commissioner) are co-operating closely in Shanghai where the Right Party of the Kuomintang is not working in harmony.

The message states that General Wu's departure from Canton was due to pressure by General Cheung Kai-shek (commander-in-chief) and that proposals are a foot to drive out the "Communistic" (or Left) Party of the Kuomintang from Canton.

A telegram from Canton to the same paper says that the Investigation Bureau has accused Wu Te-chen of incompetence in his duties as Police Commissioner and with regard to the assassination of Liu Chung-ol. Liu Long-u is the new Police Commissioner.

headline: CANTON BOYCOTT. / BRITISH OFFICIALS EFFORTS.
text:
FURTHER ATTEMPT

STATEMENT IN HOUSE OF

COMMONS.

In the House of Commons, questioned as to the extent of the Government's efforts to end the boycott at Canton, and Hongkong, Mr. Locker Lampson said that the conditions prevailing at Canton necessitated the leaving to the local British officials large discretion.

Their efforts had been unremitting, and although hitherto unsuccessful, he understood a further attempt was now being made to reach a settlement.

Local Notes.

Until Monday it is not expected that any definite step will be made in the steps toward actual mediation.

An published yesterday Mr. Young Sui-ngaam has been quoted as having communicated a request, from the Canton Government, to H.E. the Governor that an official delegate be appointed in addition to the four already nominated. This request, it is understood, is under consideration.

The date of departure of Hong Kong's delegation has yet to be fixed. No litch has been reported in the preparations of Hongkong's "fraternity visit of Chinese merchants to Canton.

headline: THE P. & O. LINE
text:
REVIEW AT ANNUAL MEETING

ECONOMIC QUESTIONS.

Lord Inchcape, presiding at the meeting of the Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co., Ltd., touched on a number of economic questions affecting the Company's interests. He said the replenishment of ships suspended in consequence of the high shipbuilding costs reduced the dividend distribution, which was only made possible by the help of investments and drawing on reserves.

He condemned the Protection- ist policy in the application of the Safeguarding of Industries Act.

Referring to the question of the Dominions tariffs, he drew attention to their disposition to shut out manufactures by tariffs or subsidies, and mentioned in this connection the latest proposal of India to put an Import Duty on British coal, while in the case of Australia, it was concluded from statistics that immigrants were increasingly entering urban industries as against settling on the land, and the former were being more and more protected against imports.

Lord Inchcape said it appeared to be the aim of India and the Dominions to manufacture all their requirements and to import nothing. Therefore Britain could not rely on Empire trade. He declared we could not escape the dependence of foreign markets.

He was convinced that the restoration of the gold standard was proper.

He considered that Trade Unionists would never succumb to the seditious doctrine which had its headquarters at Moscow. He was of the opinion that not ten per cent. of the seamen had at heart the recent strike in Australia and South Africa, which was led by avowed Communists. The significant fact was that only British vessels were involved.

These extremists in Australia were defeated by Mr. S. M. Bruce, "a statesman with both courage and determination."

headline: CHINA'S FUTURE.
text:
PAYING OF FOREIGN CREDITORS.

TRADE TO BE DOUBLED.

given by the Chinese Students' Christian Union in Britain to Mr. Chao Hsin Chu. Charged 'Affaires, who lengthily reviewed the political and financial conditions in China and emphasised China's intention to pay her foreign creditors to the last farthing when it had tariff autonomy.

Mr. Chao expressed the opinion that when China had a stable government as result of financial reforms, foreign trade could easily be assessed a 100 per cent. more than at present.

headline: EARLY CABLE.
text:
The report of General Laidoner, the Commissioner appointed by the Council of the League of Nations to investigate the Mosul deportations, presented to the League Council, says that statements of refugees show that Turkish soldiers, commanded by officers, occupied villages and obtained arms, pillaged houses and subjected the inhabitants to atrocious violence, even massacre. General Laidoner's personal observations confirmed the pitiable condition of the refugees, who lost everything. The report emphasises the importance of the deportation of Christians in the region of the Brussel line and adds that the deportations are proceeding.

After reading the report, General Laidoner announced the receipt of a telegram from Mosul stating that all was quiet on the frontier.

The presentation of the report coincided with the receipt of a letter to the Council from the Turkish delegation announcing withdrawal in consequence of the Council's decision on the Mosul dispute.

headline: MEETING A
text:
KOWLOON UNION CHURCH PROGRESS.

ANNUAL MEETING ITEMS:

At the annual meeting of the Kowloon Union Church last night, the Rev. J. Kirk Maconachie (Hongkong pastor) said that today nobody would say they had been ahead of time as it had become more evident that the church was greatly needed.

The Rev. J. Horace Johnston, B.A., presided over a large attendance of the congregation. Mr. C. Wallace, the hon. treasurer, reported an increased balance, viz., $731.74.

Items in the report of the hon secretary, Mr. D. J. Purves were:—

Great advance on attendance at services since 1924.

Many improvements and additions to Church and grounds.

Mr. Andrews replaced Mrs. Craig as organist, & presentation

having been made to the latter. Mr. Fleming took the place of Captain Davies as choirmaster.

In the New Year the minister gave a party to children on his own outlay. A social sub-committee was appointed in January; a gathering was held in March and another in November. Weekly bathing picnics were held till the strike intervene. $85.80 was realised for a crockery account. The committee recommends a monthly social event.

Collections have been most liberal; special thankofferings at the anniversary making up for lean strike months.

Thanks are expressed to Sunday school workers, attendance having increased from 25 to 45.

Five marriages and eight baptisms had been performed and 100 names were on the communion role.

The Rev. Mr. Maconachie presented to the Church a bible purchased at Home.

Officers elected were:—

Ladies—Mrs. J. A. Craig, Mrs. D. Davies, Mrs. Dick, Mrs. D. F. Warren, Mrs. D. M. Nelson, Miss Farrell.

Gentlemen—Messrs. Arnott, D. Gow, J. Cameron, W. McFarlane, D. F. Warren, E. C. Tregilles, J. Smith, D. J. Purves.

headline: WAR IN SOUTH.
text:
PAKHOI NOW IN "RED" "HANDS."

HOIHOW TO FALL NEXT?

Quoting a passenger from that port, the local vernacular papers state that Hoihow is now in the hands of the Canton (Kuomin-tang) army.

An anti-Hongkong boycott has been started and conditions are similar to those prevalent at Swatow. Order has been maintained. Hoihow has not yet been brought into line but the speaker at its position will be the same as that of Pakhol in a few days' time. It is notified that the name of the Dapusta York and Company Limited and The Cooperhouse Trading Association, Trusted have been struck off the Register.

headline: MATTER OF PRIDE.
text:
TRIBUTE TO VOLUNTEER WORKERS

ST. JOHN AMBULANCE BRIGADE

Having proved their usefulness to the community more than ever this year in attendance on street resident cases, strike work and more particularly at Po Hing Fong where they were the first on the scene and rendered valuable aid the St. John Ambulance Brigade of Hongkong assembled at Government House this morning for the presentation of awards.

His Excellency the Governor, Mr. Cecil Clementi, stood at a table above the steps of Government House and the ambulance divisions, mostly in their khaki uniforms and the railway employee ambulance men in blue, were lined up immediately in front.

With the Governor were:—The Hon Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Colonial Secretary, the Hon Mr. H. T. Creasy, the Hon Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Mrs. and Miss Holyoak, the Hon Mr. C. G. Alabaster, the Hon Mr. Chow Shou-son, the Hon Mr. J. H. Kemp, the Hon Mr. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. Ho Kom-tony, Dr. W. V. M. Koch, Dr. E. Stuart Taylor, Dr. E. P. Minnett, Dr. B. C. Wong, Mr. A. R. Sutherland, Mr. L. G. F. Nightingale, the Rev. G. T. Waldegrave and Commissioner E. Ralphs. In charge of the ambulance brigade were Corps Superintendent, Mr. A. Morris, Division Superintendents, Messrs. J. Ralston (Kowloon division) and A. eleArculli (Indian division).

headline: WAGES CLAIM.
text:
EUROPEAN LADY SUED AT KOWLOON.

WITHOUT NOTICE.

DISMISSA1

A Chinese coolie and an amah summoned Mrs. McKim, of Humphrey's Flat, for a month's wages at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. The evidence was that the defendants were dismissed on November 27 without notice. They were asked to call for their wages later, but on calling the defendant refused to pay.

Defendant claimed to have paid $30 between the two servants whom she engaged during the strike. She informed the servants on November 22 through Mr. Mackintosh's boy that their services would not be required after November 26, and the money was paid the day after the conversation.

The case was adjourned for the boy to be called.

headline: PEACE MOVE.
text:
CANTON MERCHANTS OFFER?

LOAN TO END STRIKE:

"Extras" have been issued by a Canton vernacular paper, says a merchant who arrived here yesterday and was interviewed by a Hongkong Chinese reporter, stating that a large sum of money will be advanced by a Canton merchant—to be ultimately repaid by the Canton Government—to bring about a settlement of the strike and boycott.

After reviewing the steps already taken and the appointment of delegates, the publisher of the "extra" says that he understands that a certain wealthy merchant in Canton is willing to advance this large sum, which will be repaid in due course, after the strike is ended, by the Provincial Government.

Mr. Kan Kum-shek also arrived here yesterday, and stated that he came to ascertain when the Hong-kong "fraternal" party would leave.

Mr. Yeung Sai-ngzaam is expected to return to Canton early this week.

The list of names for inclusion in the party closed yesterday. According to present expectations the party may leave on Thursday or Friday.

Mr. Kan had nothing new to report in connection with the appointment of delegates by Canton.

headline: "ANTI-FOREIGN."
text:
STRANGE REPORT FROM CANTON

DEMONSTRATION TO-MORROW?

Moves to organise an anti-Christian and anti-foreign demonstration in Canton to-morrow are said to be disfavoured by the Provinciall Government.

The demonstration, or procession—about which word has reached the Canton authorities—may be the predecessor of something promised for Christmas for which a certain section had planned things on a fairly extensive scale.

It may also be that the preparations for to-morrow—and there certainly have been signs that the organisation is ready—may be more anti-Christian, essentially, than anti-foreign.

At any rate the Canton Government is rumoured to be striving to restrict the demonstrators to the city which is taken to mean giving the Shakee and adjacent parts of the Bund a wide berth.

Some of the more conservative of the Kuomintang politicians are even said to be opposed to the idea of a procession along the waterfront, this report emanating from a statement that steps have been taken to be ready for emergencies.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE. / BIG CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.
text:
FORTHCOMING LEGAL BATTLE

Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen have applied for writs claiming £20,000 each from the Government alleging wrongful arrest and imprisonment.

Mrs. Walsh and Mrs. Johannsen are also claiming £5,000 for loss of their husbands' services.

It may be recalled that Mrs Walsh was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, the militant. suf-fragette.

This is an echo of the recent seamen's strike in Australia when the Government felt compelled to use drastic measures of arrest, imprisonment and deportation. Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen were arrested, but subsequently released on an order of the Supreme Court of Australia, and are now claiming against the Government.

Mrs. Walsh, was formerly Miss Adela Pankhurst, of the Pankhurst trio who led the suffragette movement some years ago. When the movement succeeded, the Pankhurst family withdrew from it. The other sister is engaged in religious work.

headline: FRENCH FINANCE AN OMINOUS SYMPTOM
text:
Páris, Dec. 14.

An ominous symptom in the politic and financial situation is revealed by the Finance Committee of the Chamber referring back the Finance Bills dealing with further taxation and the establishing of a Sinking Fund.

[An earlier message states:—

M. Loucheur's financial proposals is taking active form in various parts of the country, business groups regiotering protests. A Carcassonne a solemn pledge was taken by all local tradespeople to refuse to pay taxes if the pro

posals were adopted, while the Nimes Commercial Union has decided on a two hours strike as a protest.

The fall of the franc is causing a steady rise in the prices of commodities. Figures published by the General Statistics Service show a rise of nine per cent. in wholesale prices in France in October and November compared to a fall in Britain, Germany, Sweden, Czech, Slovakia, Switzerland.

headline: £3,000,000 LOAN. / HONGKONG AND THE BOYCOTT.
text:
FURTHER ASSISTANCE POSSIBLE

In the House of Commons, Mr. A. Spoor asked for information of the purposes of the loan of £3,000,000 to the Hongkong Government; and whether the Government had taken steps to terminate the boycott of British trade in Hongkong.

Mr. Ormsby Gore replied that the Governor had applied in September for a loan of the amount mentioned for the purpose of restoring confidence and financing trade.

· The loan had saved the Colony at a serious moment.

It is possible that if the boycott continues and trade worsens, further assistance may have to be considered next year.

headline: COAL AND OIL.
text: Agreements for a concession of 45 years for coal and oil fields in North Saghalien to Japanese firms recommended by the Japanese Government, were signed to-day under the Japan, Soviet and Peking Treaty.

headline: THE BOYCOTT.
text:
EDWARD

WHAMYOA AND HONGKONG.

Sir Edward Stubs, ex-Gover- er of Hongkong, was the guest of the Colonial Institute at a City luncheon at which no em- phasised that the troubles of Hongkong were started by Rass- in a legislators at Canton who made no self-retest of their intention to rain Hongkong.

Sir E. Stubbs contended that his counter-strike methods were not unpopular amongst those they were meant to protect. He did not think the trouble would last much longer.

He had great faith in the commonsense of the Kwangtung Chinese, who, before long, would purify Canton of the "Red" element.

When the situation was normal, Hongkong would have a future far exceeding the past. There was no possibility of Hongkong being cut out by any other part. The Cantonese were talking wildly of developing Whampoa, which, however, would require much dredging, whilst there were other drawings.

Tho really important question was the completion of the will way from Canton to Hanking. He feared that the late Dr. Sun Yat Sen. misunderstood him during the recent abortive negotiations on finance in connection with the Canton line from Hongkong.

As a result of Dr. Sun Yat Sien's death, power had passed into the hands of certain persons who had neither his interest, tolerance or British grip, which was the beginning of the Botswana movement in South China.

headline: THAT NEW PORT. / LOWER THAN WHAMPOA FAVOURED? RIVER HEAL SCHEME
text:
“A certain gentleman who comes from Canton” is quoted by the vernacular papers of this morning, as having expounded a project by the Provincial Government to organise a big port at the mouth of the Canton River, further down than Whampoa.

At first, so the speaker is reported, the Kwangtung Government considered the Bak Ngo Taam (that part of the Canton Harbour by Shameen and leading to the "back reach") the widest anchorage. It was the intention to accommodate bigger ships at Whampoa but the water there has been found to be too shallow. Accordingly, a project is being mooted to develop the port of Tai Ping (at the head of the estuary and close to Bocca Tigris) and its suburb of Sha Kok (sometimes known as the Sha Kok Fort).

headline: STRIKE EXAMINATION
text: The Canton Admiralty has despatched the "Kong Hon" to patrol the Bocca Tigris Passage to examine incoming foreign vessels. It having been reported to the Strike Executive that merchandise is being shipped to Canton from Shanghai under changed labels special examination pickets have been added.

headline: LOCARNO PACT. / THE SOVIET'S OPINION.
text:
RUSSIA AND HER DEBTS.

Bombarded with "questions in the course of an interview at the Russian Embassy, by Pressmen from all over the world M. Tchitcherin reiterated the opinion that the Locarno Treaties were part of a "British policy against the Soviet crusade.

The Soviet desired an immediate conference on disarmament but maintained against the League of Nations' attitude, though it was the Soviet's duty to attend conferences on humanitarian objects "whether summoned by the League or the devil himself."

He explained that the Soviet aimed at separate treaties of friendship.

headline: Geneva, Dev. 15.
text:
at Mosul are contained in additions to M. Laidou's report. The Commissioners place the responsibility on the shoulders of the 62nd regiment of the Turkish infantry, and depict the horrors of forced and hurried deportations and massacres, and relate incidents of women violated and buried alive under stones.

They state that at Baijo alone 40 men were taken from their families and assassinated in a remote building by Turkish soldiers who were anxious not to be disturbed during their orgies.

Columns marched six to ten days foodless; several falling out were immediately massacred. The Commissioners draw attention to the fact that Christians were not ill-treated by Kurds who protested to the Turks and freuse Turkish orders to massacre deportees, upon which Turks shot several Kurdish chiefs.

A number of Kurdish Moslem chiefs on the frontier expressed a desire to be placed within the Iraq frontiers in order to procure their safety.

headline: MOSUL QUESTION.
text:
Unoffitala news is that under the League sub-committee's arbitral award, Iraq retains Mosul under certain conditions, the chief of which is the extension period of the mandate, while the Brussels line is maintained. There is to be provision for free economic intercourse between Mosul and Turkish. Turk distan; also a guarantee for the use of the Kurdish language and the ratification of the 25 years' Anglo-Turkish treaty.

Commenting on the Mosul, discussions: "Le Oeuvre" says the decision of the League will be

a rude shock to Mustapha Kemal and hopes the latter will reflect carefully on the consequences on an eventual attack on the forces at Iraq of Great Britain. “Le Gaulois” says the whole danger of the situation lies in the possibility of Turkey being supported by Soviet Russia, making a desperate gesture. “Le Gaulois” opines that the League Council’s verdict is prompted by the hope that the dispute will be subject to direct Anglo-Turkish negotiations. “Le Petit Parisien” foresees a vigorous Turkish opposition to the decision, and adds that if the Turks indulge in a war-like adventure, Great Britain could invoke “the covenant of the League to claim sanctions.” “Le Echo de Paris” says the Turks will only bow to strength and the only way for the British Empire to safeguard the peace is to exercise its strength resolutely.

The League Council, in public session, has announced the unanimous decision to award Mosul to Iraq, making the sub-called provisional Brussels line the definite Turco-Iraq frontier provided British Government submits a new Anglo-Iraq treaty ensuring the continuation of the mandate of 25 years. The latter is to be subject to the reservation that Iraq may be admitted to membership of the League before the expiration thereof or as soon as possible within three years hence, and the execution of the stipulation with regard to the mandate is to be brought to the Council's knowledge. The present decision is pronounced definitive, and the Council will indicate measures required to ensure the definition of the frontier line. The Turkish delegates did not accept the President of the Council's invitation to attend but a letter from Tewfik Ruhdi Bay the chief Turkish delegate was received reiterating the Turkish view of part and declaring that Turkey maintained a sovereign right over Mosul. headline: うん / HIS WIFE'S MONEY.
text:
The European wife of a Chinese named China's level figured as the principle "witness in a case in which the return of $800, money lent was epimid." The woman was question who has a boarding routine in Waterloo Road. Yaumat said that he advanced the money to her husband to his cousin whom she had known in Liverpool prior to her coming to Hongkong with her husband. She was reluctant to do so as it constituted her passage money back to England but the cousin told her that he would lose his job if he did not get the money.

The defendant had been the No. 1 saloon boy on the "Empress of Canada" and had told her that he had to pay the boys for what they required to take with them of board the ship, this being advanced on their future earnings. As he had no money at the time he was afraid of losing his job. The case for the defence was that only $100 had been lent to the defendant and the rest of the money claimed for had been lent direct to the "boys" of the "Empress of Canada." Defendant denied liability for their debts. Plaintiff, in evidence, said that he had been engaged by the Government during the strike to get coolies for ships. He still did work of this sort for the C.P.R. and engaged and put on board their "boys." He denied that the money had been lent to them direct and said that his cousin was responsible.

A book, was produced by Mr. M. W. Lo (for the defendant) in support of the claim that the plaintiff went on board the "Empress of Canada" collecting the individual debts from the boys and jotting down their names and the amounts.

In view of this Mr. Justice Wood said that he did not think it much good proceeding with the case. Mr. L. D. Turner (for the plaintiff) concurred. He had evidently been misinformed by his client and had no option but to drop the case.

Judgment was entered for the defendant with costs.

headline: HARBOUR COLLISION. / FISHING JUNK DAMAGED.

headline: JAPAN'S INTERESTS
text:
INTERVENTION IN MANCHURIA.

CHINESE THREATEN STRIKE.

headline: HILSIDE MURDER.
text:
PRISONER WHO FLED TO SUMICHUN.

UREID HY A WOMAN.

DBTERMINED STRUGGLE WITH

Having been entitled from across the border in Chinese territory to British territory at Sumchun by a women, Shing Wai-tat found the police waiting to arrest him in British territory on a charge of murder. He put up a determined struggle but was eventually taken into custody.

Fleiss said to be identified by several witnesses and the police allege that he is the man who, being left in charge of an Indian constable at Nguu Shi Wan for the latter to take him to the Kowloon City police station on a charge of wood-stealing shot the latter and escaped.

The Hon. Mr. A. H. Kempl Atterney-General, reconstructed in supposition at the Criminal Sessions this morning the events which led to the constable's death. He said that the facts pointed to the prisoner having pushed the constable off the path into a nullah, for here were found the constable's turban and the log of wood which the prisoner was being made to carry to the police station as evidence against him.

Dropping his burden it would rather appear that the prisoner rain up the hill with the Indian constable after him. "The latter, finding himself outstripped fires a shot," continued the Attorney-General. "The accused stops and waits for the constable to come up and then struggle with him. I do not say he set out with the intention of murdering the constable but merely to disable him sufficiently for escape. Tempers rise in the course of a struggle and after the one in question the Indian constable was left wounded on the hillside."

The law throws a peculiar attraction about a public servant performing his duty in execution of the law, continued the Attorney-General. If he is killed in the execution of this, the law will imply malice and the offender will be found guilty of murder, no matter whether the circumstances, if applying to a private individual, would justify only a charge of manslaughter.

Prisoner's Disappearance

The disappearance of the prisoner about the time that the struggle on the hillside took place was referred to by the Attorney-General. Prisoner was eventually found to have gone over the border and the wife of one of his acquaintances enticed him to British territory with a story about having disposed of a house he owned in Kowloon City.

In a statement, made after his arrest, the prisoner accused this woman's husband of having offered him a bribe of $100 to kill the constable and a further $50 for going away. The Attorney-General suggested that "filled with rage at the trick played him he might have said to himself, 'I'm in for it now but I will try and get this woman's husband into trouble.'

III Treatment Alleged.

In another statement made later the prisoner denied everything and said that he was falsely charged. He had been roughly treated when first taken to the station, he alleged. He had become silly; he did not know where, heaven was, or earth was. He was thrown into a cell.

There was no direct evidence of the shooting, stated the Attorney-General. A hawker who lived lower down, not far from the scene, heard a shot about the time and a police whistle being blown. He also saw two figures struggling, the one a constable in khaki and the other a Chinese. By the time he had reached the spot with some Europeans who lived not far away the constable was lying wounded in the face and side.

Two constables who had been with the murdered constable when the arrest of the man cutting down wood was made, identified the prisoner as the man who was arrested. They had left their comrade to take the prisoner back to the police station as they

saw other forest pillifers at work. Mr. Elsley Zeitlyn (instructed by G. K. Hall Brutton) represented the prisoner at to-day's Criminal Sessions proceedings where the case is still being heard.

headline: China / KOWLOON SHOOTING
text:
CRIMINAL SESSIONS PROCEEDINGS.

The prisoner who is alleged to have tired at Sergt. Clark "in Chatham Road on November 13 appeared at the Criminal Sessions this morning charged with shooting at the Sergeant " with intent to main, disfigure or disable him and to resist lawful apprehension."

Prisoner is a domestic servant employed by Capt. L. D. Joll, M.C., and the revolver alleged to have been used is the property of his master. It was left in an unlocked drawer and it is the case for the Crown that prisoner took the weapon and returned it afterwards.

Sergt. Clark detailed the incident this morning. He became suspicious of three men and followed them down Chatham Road in the direction of Holt's wharf. Seeing one of the men turn round and becoming of the opinion that they suspected he was following them, he turned into "Observatory Road for a time but retraced his steps.

Where "Cameron Road" joins Chatham Road there is a lamp and it was here that he finally called on them to stop. He commenced to search one of the men and this man threw a revolver in the direction of one of his companions. This, the sergeant alleges, is the prisoner. The man in question picked it up and made off. The sergeant fired a shot into the air and alleged that prisoner turned and fired back. Sergt. Clark fired another shot without effect and for the time being the man escaped.

Prisoner was arrested at 2, Chatham Road, Capt. Joll's residence, one of his companions who had been arrested by the police taking them there. Prisoner was found hiding under a bed. The watchman outside had seen the two servants of Capt. Joll running back to the house shortly after the time of the alleged shooting.

In a statement made shortly after arrest the accused said he fired a shot by mistake.

At the Criminal Sessions, this morning the prisoner said "I picked it up; I had it in my hand; I did not intend to shoot him."

The jury found prisoner not guilty of shooting with intent and guilty of possession. The man who was searched first and arrested by the police on the spot pleaded guilty to being in possession of ammunition (five rounds were found on him).

Sentence will be passed on him and the other prisoner to-morrow morning.

REVOLT LARGELY OVER.

(Reuiter's Strategy)

A distinct change in the situation in Syria was announced by M. Briand in a statement in the Chamber of Deputies on the subject.

He said the Druse revolt had largely subsided. The local inhabitants were at present defending themselves against bands of marauders.

M. Painleve, reviewing. the situation, argued that General Sarrail was forced by the facts of the situation to fire a few shells into Damascus "to avoid very serious events."

M. Briand again spoke, being ontinually interrupted by the Communists.

The Premier pointed out that France had become exhausted, financially and militarily, after the Great War, and had no taste for fresh and warlike adventures but had been attacked.

France could not evade the execution of the mandate.

The speech was loudly cheered, except by the Communists.

headline: PEACE HOPES.
text:
A NEW TURN IN THE NEGOTIATIONS.

ISSUES SIMPLIFIED

Friendly discussions have taken place in the last few days with the result that the terms of settlement of the Hongkong-Canton situation have been greatly simplified. A delegation of Hongkong Chinese merchants will shortly join with the Canton Chinese merchants in negotiations with the Strike Committee for the cessation of the boycott.

headline: RED UNIONS.
text:
WORLD CONGRESS TO BE CONVENED

NATIONAL LABOUR DECISIONS.

The Congress of the National Labour Secretariat presided over by the Dutch Communist, Mr. Sneevliet, and attended by representatives of the British Minority Party, also by the Soviet, adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 4, instructing the Executive to give effect to the resolution adopted by the referendum of 1923 to join the Red Trade Union International. It also adopted a resolution by 118 votes to 3, in favour of the Red Trade Union International issuing invitations to the World Congress of Red Trade Union International, and to the International Federation of Trade Unions and organisations not belonging to both internationalis.

headline: “GUILTY.”
text:
VERDICT AGAINST SIR BASIL THOMSON

AN APPEAL NOTIFIED:

On the resumption of the case against Sir Basil Thomson, who yesterday pleaded not guilty, Sir Henry Curtis-Bennett, cross-examining the Police witnesses suggested that accused gave his own name "Hume". Thomson, which the Sergeant mistook for "Hugh" Thomson. The Magistrate (Mr. H. L. Cancellor) remarked that that was a mistake which might easily be made.

Mr. Curtis-Bennett, in his speech, said that a man with the knowledge of accused must have been insane or drunk to go to such a place for such an offence. The evidence showed that he was absolutely sober. Counsel was glad that the Magistrate had last night personally inspected the spot and asked the Magistrate to say that it was impossible to see what people were doing from the place where the Police said they saw them. He submitted that the story of the two constables in this connection was untrue.

Mr. Reginald McKenna, and Sir Reginald Ball, M.P., testified to accused's high character, after which accused entered the witness box. He said that since his retirement he had devoted himself to literary and journalistic work, particularly criminal and police matters. He had recently contemplated investigating and writing about Hyde Park and West End solicitation. He had discussed the matter with Mr. Douglas Straight, ex-Inspector-General of Police in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and with Mr. Barry Higgins, the well-known solicitor. He was also very keenly interested in the Communist movement. He went to Hyde Park to investigate the conditions there. A woman spoke to him and told him that she was hard up. He gave her two or three shillings and asked her about the people who were sitting round. Immediately afterward the Police appeared. Accused emphatically denied that the woman was acting improperly toward him.

Incident In Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said after his arrest "How can I keep this from my friends?" He said that what he did say was that such a charge would ruin anybody.

Counsel for the defence called attention to Laurie (the policeman who arrested Sir Basil Thomson) standing close to the witness box and grimacing whilst the questions were being put.

The Magistrate ordered Laurie to leave the Court.

Sir Basil Thomson denied that he said to Laurie that if he overlooked this he could leave the police to-morrow. He swore that there was not the shadow of foundation for the charge.

The second summons was dismissed.

Sir Basil Thomson was found guilty on the first charge and fined £5 and £5 costs.

An appeal was notined. [It was reported in yesterday's cables that a huge crowd besieged Marlborough Street Police Court, London, on the appearance of Sir Basil Thomson, Assistant Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police from 1918-1919, in answer to two summonses, one accusing him of Indecency with a woman in Hyde Park, and the other requiring him to show cause why his recognisances of £5 should not be forfeited for his non-appearance in Court on the day named in the original summons.]

headline: INTIMIDATION.
text:
HOTEL PANTRY BOY'S STORY.

TWO CHINESE CHARGED.

A pantry boy employed at the Hongkong Hotel and who remained at his post throughout the strike was the complainant in a case at the Central Magistracy this morning in which two Chinese were charged with alleged intimidation.

headline: HARBOUR MISHAPS.
text:
STAR" FERRY BUMPS LAUNCH

CARCO JUNK CAPSIZES.

Shortly before 11 last night, the “Morning Star” bumped a Taikoo Dock launch, striking the latter on her port quarter.

This took place near the Hong- kong wharf of the "Star" Ferry. Co. In his report to the Harbour Office, the ferry coxswain makes certain claims as to his steering, being on the quivive, etc.

Two women and four men were thrown into the harbour on Tuesday afternoon and were rescued by a passing Police launch. They were the crew of a cargo junk which was making for a P. & O. steamer at the Kowloon Godowns. A strong blow and the wash from a passing steamer is believed to have caused the capsize.

headline: COAL STRIKE?
text:
STRONG REVULSION OF FEELING.

MOVE BY PUBLISHERS.

The strong revulsion feeling against a coal strike is indicated in a telegram from the publishers of the leading newspapers in the anthracite region to the mine owners' and miners' representatives, who have reached a deadlock at the conference here.

The telegram calls attention to the colossal financial loss, paralysis of business, loss of market for hard coal; and heart-breaking distress that would be caused among the miners.

It adds that the parties' differences regarding arbitration do not justify further division, and the public shall hold the leaders on both sides responsible for the misfortunes of everybody concerned.

headline: U. S. STRIKE.
text:
The conference between the employers and the representatives of the strikers in the anthracite coal mines was adjourned without a settlement and without a date for the renewal of the negotiations being determined.

The mine owners insisted upon complete arbitration, whilst the miners maintained that arbitration was only acceptable on the basis of increased wages without any reductions.

It is announced from Wilkes-barre (Pennsylvania) that the Grievance Committee of the Pennsylvania Coal Company today decided to launch a movement to call out all anthracite mine maintenance men for the purpose of forcing the issue and it is generally believed there that the strikers will make a determined effort to tie up the mines completely.

headline: DISARMAMENT.
text:
SOVIET ACCEPTS LEAGUE'S INVITATION.

AN IMPORTANT CONDITION.

The official Tass Agency learns authoritatively that the Soviet has decided to accept the invitation of the League of Nations to participate in the preliminary Disarmament Conference, and will not object to the participation of Soviet experts in the preliminary Commission on Economic Subjects, provided that these Commissions do not meet, on Swiss territory.

headline: TOWN SHELLED.
text:
MERCHANTS FIGHT STRIKE PICKETS.

GUNBOAT $ \underline{\text{OPENS}} $ FIRE.

Pakkai (Kongmoon), Jan. 8. Shells were dropped on Muk Chow on January 3 and a few shops were burned following a brush between merchants and strike pickets.

The pickets reached Muk Chow on the gunboat "Kung Hon" and started to examine goods imported. At first the natives raised opposition. Troubles soon broke out and the civilians fled when the warship opened fire.

About three hundred pickets arrived here from Canton on January 8. Sixty remained and the rest moved on to Kongmoon, Kwonghoi, etc.

News has come down that an anti-Christian demonstration has taken place at Sanwui city where posters have been freely distributed and posted conspicuously on walls.

On January 4 a fire broke out on the Hongkong-Kongmoon steamer "Kung On". At the beginning of the strike the vessel was tied up. In August she was removed to her owner's village, Kongmei. Subsequently she was taken to Taiping town. The stamer suffered considerable damage from fire. A few junks carrying firewood were also involved and a good many shops on shore also caught fire.

headline: GROWING GRAVITY.
text:
DISPUTE BETWEEN CHINA AND SOVIET.

HOSTILITIES NOT LIKELY.

The Diet re-opened this morning, after the New Year recess. Speeches were made by Viscount Kato, the Premier, and Baron Shidehara, K.E.E., the Foreign Minister.

Following their speeches this morning in the Upper House, Baron Sakatani grew attention to the growing gravity of the Sino-Russian situation and enquired about the "government's attitude." In reply, Baron Shideharstated that the matter was regarded purely as a Sino-Russian problem and unlikely to culminate in hostilities, though the Government was watching possible developments vigilantly test future action might be required.

Most of the morning papers offer no comment on the Sino-Russian friction, though the "Hochi" voices the opinion that the trouble is due to Chan Tsolin's desire to re-establish, his damaged prestige by stirring up Chinese national settlement in his favour.

The "Fleochii" forecasts in Chinese success, as the Soviet action is fettered by fear of damaging relation with Japan.

According to an “Asahi” despatch from Duiren, Chang Tso-lin ordered the arrest of M. Ivanov. President of the Chinese Eastern Railway, and the Mukden authorities to resume the railway service by force if necessary. A despatch to the “Asahi” from Harbin reports that the gravity is increasing and the Chinese troops are preparing to concentrate in Harbin in greater numbers.

According to Press reports, M. Kopp, the Soviet Ambassador to Japan, when interviewed, declared that "the Russian Government is prepared to back up its demands by force; if necessary meeting troops with troops."

In spite of all this, the vernacular papers generally indicate that the Japanese Government and people are maintaining a calm attitude.

headline: RAILWAY WAGES
text:
DELEGATES: REJECT BOARD'S AWARD.

CRITICAL CONFERENCE

Trouble has again arisen in the railway world.

At to-day's conference of the branch delegates of the National Union of Railwaymen rejected the award of the National Wages Board which, after considering the Companies' claims for a reduction in wages and the men's counterclaims for increases, issued a report on December 9 practically maintaining the status quo. It is noteworthy that the men's leaders, Mr. J. H. Thomas (former

Though to-day's conference is generally regarded as the most critical since the last big strike, it is gathered that the decision merely reflects the movement for the re-opening of the negotiations, the delegates being not anxious to commit the Union to strike action.

The decision creates a delicate situation as the award is due to come into operation on February 1. The conference will again meet to-morrow to consider the next move.

Though it is believed that no decision for strike action will be taken until the Unions' Executive have met, the Companies have endeavoured to re-open the negotiations or secure a postponement of the application of the award.

headline: CRISIS OVER?
text:
RAILWAY DELEGATES VOTE FOR AWARD.

A NARROW MAJORITY

...Rugby, Jan: 25.

At the meeting between representatives of the railway companies and of the National Union of Railwaymen, which was held this morning, there was a full discussion of the objections raised by the men to the award of the National Wages Board. As explained in previous messages the men object to the finding of the National Wages Board that men hereafter joining the railway service and not promoted shall receive only the basic wage of those grades to which they are appointed without cost of living bonus, and they ask for an assurance that the railway companies will accept the basic rates as an irreducible minimum. The exact tenor of the railway companies' reply has not been announced.

At a conference of railway-men's delegates this afternoon two resolutions were moved. One resolution was for refusing to accept the award and declaring a strike next Friday. The other was for acceptance of the award. By a very narrow majority the resolution accepting the award was adopted. It would appear therefore that the railway crisis is over.

headline: THE CRITICAL STAGE
text: London, Jan. 25. Critical negotiations between representatives of the railway companies and the N.U.R. were opened at Euston this morning in regard to the Union's demands. Several Branches of the Union have already adopted a resolution in favour of a national strike if the Union's demands are refused. At the conclusion of the negotiations the companies submitted a memorandum which the delegates' conference of railwaymen will consider.

headline: PASSIONATE SPEECHS. London lat
text:
