headline: SMALL INVESTORS / SAVING GRACE IN GREAT BRITAIN
text:
Rugby: March 18.

Some remarkable figures regarding small investors in Britain were given in an address by Mr. Walter Runciman, who said that they showed that there was to-day a wider distribution of wealth in Britain than ever before.

There were now about 16,000,000 capitalists in this country; he said, and the total amount of their savings was not far short of £2,000,000,000.

Of this immense sum, £285,000,000 was deposited in the Post Office Savings Banks, £223,000,000 in National Savings Certificates, £198,000,000 in small Government holdings, £470,000,000 in ordinary and industrial Life Assurance Funds, £140,000,000 in Building Societies, and £300,000,000 in other approved Societies.

headline: PEKING INCIDENT.
text:
COMMUNISTS ARRESTED

A manidabe has been issued ordering the arrest of five alleged @ommunist leaders.

In asserts that they led the student demonstrators yesterday, and otherwise made use of the Communist doctrine to disturb the peace, and engaged him widespread intrigues calculated to unbalance the masses.

With reference to the shootings in Peking delayed telegrams from Peking state that a group of students visited the Chinese Foreign Office on Wednesday evening for the purpose of presenting an uncompromising reply to the Powers ultimatum on the Taku incident which they wanted the Government to adopt.

Yesterday morning nearly 1,000 students paraded the streets and finally reached the Cabinet headquarters in the afternoon, where they intended to demand the dismissal of those responsible for the official reply, a forecast of which the vernacular morning papers published.

Prevented in the attempt to enter the students attempted to force their way when the guard used bayonets and finally fired point blank.

Eye-witnesses state that three or four volleys were fired, after which the crowd scattered in all directions the soldiers continuing to shoot as the students fled.

It appears that there had been a certain amount of bad blood between the students and the body-guard. owing to a clash on Wednesdays evening.

High integration prevails among the students, against whom the Government is said to contemplate further drastic measures including the arrest of a well-known quartette who are regarded as the ring leaders of a Communist agitation. It is thought that this will be the prelude to wholesale arrests of suspected Communist agitators.

Measures Against Communists.

The total casualties are now estimated at 120, including two girls and a woman.

headline: LOCAL INDUSTRY:
text:
GOVERNMENT HELP?

The "China Mail" has been courteously supplied with an advance proof of the annual report for 1925, of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, which is to be issued to members on Monday. A chapter on "Ginger cultivation in the Colony" reads:

The members of the Shun Shau Tong, the Preserved Ginger Association, addressed a circular to the Chamber and all Export. Firms on August 20 stating that the new season preserved ginger of the current year—both wet and dry, and both packed in casks and in cases—contracted for with foreign firms, could not be delivered during the months of August and September, as, unfortunately, owing to the Strike in Hongkong, many workers had stopped work and left the Colony. "Moreover," the writers added, "the Canton Authorities have prohibited the Exportation of goods to Hongkong and have also stopped all steamer traffic between Canton and Hongkong. As you are aware, though preserved in Hongkong, all ginger is imported from Canton. Though conditions in this Colony are gradually becoming normal, the importation of raw ginger from Canton is still impossible. Under these circumstances we are unable to deliver the goods at the above mentioned times and hope you will inform buyers and consumers abroad to this effect. As soon as conditions improve, every effort will be made to make deliveries under contracts as early as possible."

In this connection the Export Sub-Committee discussed the practicableability of promoting the growing of ginger in the New Territories, and as a result a letter was addressed to the Government, on September 22, stating that the Chamber had recently had under consideration, information from the Chinese Preserved Ginger Dealers, stating that no raw ginger, was available for this market owing to the non-arrival of supplies, due to the strike, boycott and generally disturbed conditions in South China, and it was a matter of common knowledge that large stocks were lying rotting in the Interior for the same reasons. The Trade Return, for 1924, showed that the value of the exports of ginger from Hongkong in that year amounted to £314,023, of which £139,570 went to the United Kingdom: £53,107 to Australia: £10,130 to New Zealand: £30,002, to the United States of America: £43,959, to Holland, and £10,378, to Germany. It was understood that increasing quantities of ginger were grown in the New Territories, where the soil had proved suitable. The Chamber, therefore, ventured to suggest to the Government that enquiries should be made as to the possibility of developing this valuable industry in the New Territories, where cultivators would be working under very favourable condition as compared with the Interior of China, as they would have a considerable market at their doors and enjoy freedom from the continual interference with their operations which so unhappily persisted in China. At the same time, the ginger preserving industry in Hongkong and Kowloon would gain the advantage of more regular supplies, and the export trade in the commodity would not suffer the damage which must ensue, when the demand of Oversens Markets was entirely disappointed at a period when supplies were expected. It is hoped that, at a convenient opportunity, the Government will thoroughly investigate this question.

headline: 80 CASES OF BOMBS
text:
Stirring events are believed to have occurred in Canton on Saturday, the most important of which was the surrounding of the Strike Headquarters and the disarming of a large number of boycott pickets.

No official confirmation of the reports had come to hand when the "China Mail" went to press. However, the best informed sources were of the opinion that there was substance for most of the conflicting drop of rumours. It has been definitely established that troops—said to be Cadets of General Chang Kai-shek's army landed at the East Bund on Saturday morning and proceeded to Tung Yuen (strikeheadquarters). A subsequent message says that the military have been withdrawn.

The strike (of boycott) pickets there were mostly disarmed, it is stated, when the troops arrived on the scene. The number of weapons taken is variously given, but it is believed that the majority of pickets had their arms taken from them.

Meanwhile troops were moving about in other parts of the city. The state of suspense lasted till the afternoon. During the period telephone communication was suspended. In parts of the city, military cordons held up traffic and then retired. Railway stations were also the scene of animation. For short while a rumour went around that Canton banknotes were being accepted but the scars said to have passed over quickly.

A vernacular report says that 100 soldiers were sent to Tung Zhen but a statement alleged to

Yuen but a statement, alleged to have emanated from the chairman of the strike committee, indicates that the troops were sent to a building adjoining Tung Yuen.

In the afternoon, Tung Yuen issued two notices emphasising that the movements referred to were only connected with military developments and that their normal course was thereby interrupted but the "position of labour" was not affected.

The coup—if it was one—also involved the Canton naval forces. Detachments were sent to the "Chung-Shan" (flagship) and other boats, and the vessels steamed up river. Naval headquarters, it is also rumoured were surrounded.

The guards posted at the Canton shell factory have been disarmed, according to several vernacular reports. One paper hints that the authorities allege that secret manual-factures have been detached, including 80 cases of bombs and some machine-guns.

Although official intelligence hits yet to arrive, the above re-forts are gaining strength in Hongkong.

One rumour which is not likely to mean much is that the family of a leading official has left Canton.

A Chinese was found in an unconscious condition at Queen Street yesterday. He was taken to the Government Civil Hospital and died after admittance.

During blasting operations at the Government quarry at North Point on Saturday, a Chinese worker was killed by a flying fragment of rock striking him on the head. The Chinese who was charged with the attempted theft of six tons of crude oil from the A.P.O. installation at North Point was sentenced to three months' hard labour at the Magistracy on Friday. As the result of an accident in which a Chinese was injured near the Bowrington Canal on Saturday, a motor kerry driver and learner were formally charged at the Central Magistracy this morning and remained. It was stated that the injured man was in hospital and a charge of mania aughter might result if he were to life.

headline: HELD IN CHAINS. / CRUEL TREATMENT BY CANTON STRIKERS
text:
The following are facts concerning the capture, by Chinese Strike pickets in Canton harbour of two Indian watchmen employed by the Asiatic Petroleuns Co. They show the efforts made to effect the release of these men, their imprisonment in chains for many days, and the cruel treatment meted out to them. They also prove the existence of a Strikers' Court and prison in Canton which was denied by Mr. C. C. Wu, Mayor of the city, and a member of the Executive and further clearly indicate the impotence of the Government to deal with the strikers in that they were unable to afford protection to subjects off a foreign nation who were left incarcerated in a strikers' prison for 18 days.

At about 5:30 p.m. on December 18, 1925, Mr. Cadman, Resident Engineer of the A.P. Co., together with two Indian watchmen, whilst on their way to Fati Installation were fired on and held up by an armed launch manned by strike pickets. They were taken to Headquarters in the city and Mr. Cadman, after a form of trial by a Strikers' Court, was handed over to the Police Bureau the same night and subsequently released and the request of the British Consul-General. The Indians were retained in custody by the strikers. The following morning, the British Vice-Consul, accompanied by the Manager of the A.P. Co., proceeded to the Foreign Office and recorded the strongest possible protest from the Consul-General in regard to the incident and demanded the immediate release of the Indians, the Vice-Consul informing the Foreign Secretary that his orders were to return without them. Mr. Fu Ping-sheung, Secretary for Foreign Affairs, pleaded ignorance of the matter and, after discussion, despatched his Assistant, Mr. Luk, to accompany the Vice-Consul and the A.P.C. Manager to the Police Bureau. On arrival, the Vice-Consul informed the Acting Police Commissioner, Mr. Poon, that he had come to take away the two Indians whom the strikers had captured the previous day and that he could not return without them.

After some discussion between Mr. Luk and the Police authorities a letter was written to the Strike Hendouarters and delivered personally by Mr. Luk. He returned within an hour stating that the Indions would be detained until they could, be questioned, and that they would be released that afternoon.

The Vice-Consul thereupon informed the authorities that he was very dissatisfied with what had been done and stated his determination to go direct to the strike headquarters and request the release of the Indians.

The officials strongly advised against approaching the strikers whom they stated were ignorant men, who would probably insult foreigners and begged that matters be left in their hands.

The Vice-Consult, accompanied by the A.P. Co. representative, then proceeded to the Strike headquarters but was refused admittance. They were, however, informed by an English-speaking gentleman that the Indians had just been released.

On December 21, two days later, Mr. Luk, of the Foreign Office, was on the British Concession and stated that the Indians had been released from Strike Headquarters at 4 o'clock on the previous Saturday afternoon. Two days later, on December 23, the British Consul-General informed the A.P.C. that a strong protest had been despatched to the Government that day in regard to the incident. No further news of the Indians was received until December 27 when the A.P.C. heard from an Indian watchman employed by a Chinese firm that he had seen the two men in chains in the Strikers' Headquarters' prison on December 24.

This information was immediately passed to the Consultant General, who sent his Vice-Consult, accompanied by an A.P.C. representative, to the Foreign Office to endeavour to test this information and make a further attempt to effect the release of the captives.

On arrival the Foreign Office informed them that they were under the impression that the Indians had been released some days before and pointed out the possibility of their not wishing to return to the A.P.C.

However, in view of the new information they promised to make immediate enquiries. On December 31 further information was received to the effect that the Indians had been seen in chains in the strikers' prison on December 25, and the British Vice-Consult and an A.P.C. representative again proceeded to the Foreign Office, who suggested in view of the information that the Police might send inspectors with them to the strikers' prison.

They proceeded to the Police Bureau and were informed by the officials that nothing could be done against the strikers. They then returned to the Foreign Office and explained what had happened, "whereupon" Mr. Fu Ping-sheung, Foreign Minister, issued a written order to the Police to obtain the release of the Indian and informed the Vice-Consult that they would probably be set free next day.

Nothing, however, was heard for some days and on January 4 the British Vice-Consul again proceeded to the Foreign Office and was informed that the Strike Committee had promised to release the Indians, but had subsequently stated that they (the Indians) preferred to remain in Canton rather than return to the A.P.C. The Vice-Consul pointed out that he would like to see the Indians and get them to state their wishes before him and the Foreign Office promised to endeavour to arrange a meeting at the Police Bureau in the near future. Nothing further having trans-pired, the Consul-General on January 6, despatched the following communication to the local

headline: 3000 / CANTON'S BLAME.
text:
STATEMENT IN THE COMMONS

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. S. P. Vlant (Labour, West Willesdon), Mr. L. S. M. Amery, Secretary of State for the Colonies, said that the Canton Government's offer to mediate between the strikers and the Hongkong Government was based on a claim that it was not a party to the strike and boycott, but in the Hongkong Government's view that claim was vitiated by the fact that the Canton Government had taken no steps to put an end to the intimidation of workers or other illegal activities of the Strike Committee, by which alone the strike and boycott in Canton was maintained in flagrant violation of Treaty obligations. Therefore, the Hongkong Government was unable to regard the Canton Government as other than a principal on whom the responsibility for the continued boycott lay.

His Majesty's Government fully supported the attitude of the Hongkong Government, and it now remained for the Canton Government to give proof of its sincerity and translate from words into deeds its professed desire to see the present situation brought to an end.

Mr. H. W. Looker, (Conservative, South-East Essex) suggested that the Canton Government could end the strike in a moment if it wanted to, but it was influenced by its Russian advisers. Mr. Amery was of opinion that that was so.

[Mr. Looker was formerly a partner in the local legal firm of Deacon, Looker and Harston, now styled Deacon's.]

headline: ONE OF A SERIES. / POLITICAL INTRIGUE IN
text:
SITUATION NOW NORMAL.

Latest reports from Canton indicate that there has been nothing of importance since Saturday afternoon.

Canton Government banknotes are now circulating as usual and the feeling of suspense has blown over.

The only difficulty is to say whether the Reds or anti-Reds, or Left Party as against the Rightists, strengthened their position in this last of a series of political coups since May last year.

What was reported in yesterday's "China Mail" as having occurred at the strike headquarters—the disarming of pickets—seems to have had an internal, political bearing, rather than any relation with foreign intercourse.

From the maze of conflicting reports it is assumed that General Chang Kai-shek or his army of Cadets, has removed possibility of opposition in Canton. Which individuals have been eclipsed as a result of the coup is not known.

headline: CANTONS BOYCOTT.
text:
Incorporated with the annual report of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce is a review of the principal events preceding and subsequent to the strike and the and the other events on the Common

It is explained that the review is mainly intended for the eye of overseas readers, and therefore there is much that can be passed over by the local Press as with much of the ground we are all familiar.

Thus, the Shanghai riots of May 30 are dealt with also the Shameen incident of June 23—the latter creating the necessary atmosphere in Canton for conducting the newly-established "National" Government on Bolshevik Lines.

It is carefully explained that the strike in Hongkong—as a demonstration of sympathy with those who had been killed in Shanghai—was not actually a "strike" though that word was mistakenly and carelessly used and was responsible for much misunderstanding in Labour circles at Home. It was an organised withdrawal of workers for political purposes, a form of non-co-operation—a Labour boycott. From June 19th onward Chinese employees of foreigners left their work, with many expressions of regret and distress, and without making any demands for higher wages or improved conditions of labour—or indeed, any demands whatsoever. They went out in response to methods commonly practised by agitators in China where secret societies, employing subterranean and unscrupulous methods, are common.

Reasons Unfathomable: Unjust and unreasonable though it was, the reasons why Hongkong was included in this attack are not difficult to fathom. For many Chinese Hongkong and Canton are alternative places of residence; the two cities have always been closely associated commercially, and in recent years, during the frequent recurrence of civil strife in South China, Hongkong has often been crowded to its last Chinese cubicle with refugees. A daily ebb and flow of 50,000 people between the two places is not uncommon at such a time.

An anti-British agitation having begun—however, unreasonably—Hongkong, as the familiar local exemplification of the British Empire, was from the Canton point of view an obvious target. Hongkong school boys, emulating the example of students elsewhere, were the first to make a demonstration by ceasing to attend school, but the first serious manifestation of Hongkong's inclusion in the hostile policy took the form of a withdrawal of ships' crews on June 19. On June 20 the usual British river steamer from Hongkong failed to out in an appearance in Canton, der crew having left some hours previously. On June 21, all Chinese employed by foreigners on Shameen, Canton ceased, work, leaving the foreign community practically isolated. Meanwhile, in spite of reassuring announcements (one of these was dated as early as June 12) issued by the Hongkong Government, promising full protection against intimidators, there was a general exodus of workers from the Colony. In the course of the next two months, however, disillusioned "demonstrators" began to find their way back to Hongkong by devious routes, in order to avoid the attentions of pickets at Canton who dealt unmercifully with anyone whom they caught attempting to board steamers or trains for Hongkong. A form of punishment frequently adopted was to tie up the victim naked in the sun all Payment of a bribe to the pickets usually enabled the worker to reach Hongkong without interference, though later permits to visit Hongkong were only issued if shops guaranteed the worker's return within seven days. After the Shameen incident the anti-foreign boycott was increased in severity, the Russian Bolsheviks utilising the Shanghai and Shameen shopping episodes to initiate their campaign against Great Britain, which having failed in Europe, was transferred to the East. But it was quickly realised in Canton that it was impossible to conduct a boycott of all nationalities at the same time. It was therefore decided to withdraw the boycott against all except British and Japanese.

CANTON SITUATION. EACH SIDE BIDING TIME FOR A COUP CITY "OUTWARDLY QUIET." Reports from Canton indicates that the situation is quieter and that conditions are reaching normality. There is no darring time for Kuomintang Party continues. Each side seems to be waiting for an opportunity to bring off a coup. Although General Chang Kaishek's partisans scored the major material successes last Saturday, a number of leaders (believed to be loyal to him) have met with rebuffs.

headline: Chairman's Speech
parent_headline: Uinn / DOCK MEETING. / CHAIRMAN REPLIES TO CRITICISM
text:
The Shipbuilding Industry all over the world has, as you are all aware, been passing through a very depressed period and only a minimum of orders for new ships have been placed. Here we have had to contend with this world-wide situation and also with the strike of labour last year which lasted for several months and the boycott which is still, with us. The effects of these last two circumstances have hit this. Company harder perhaps than any other entirely local Company.

- We started the year fairly well and had three new vessels under construction. With a small profit for the first six months working we were looking forward to a moderately successful year when the troubles to which I have referred began.

A working nucleus of our Chinese Artisans to whom we are very grateful stayed with us and I venture to think that it was in a measure due to the loyalty of these men in sticking to their work in spite of intimidation that the labour troubles of this Colony both industrial and domestic were overcome. Unfortunately, however, a great number of our essential men absented themselves. The result of these labour troubles was to drive repair work away from this port, and to delay and thus very considerably increase the cost of any new construction we had in hand. This new work though it has not been profitable we were fortunate in having as it kept the nucleus I have referred to employed during the months in which there was little else for them to do, and let the outside world know that we were still alive and a going concern.

headline: CURSING MOB.
text:
WUCHOW MISSIONARIES

Passage to Shore Cut

An organised attempt by the Strike pickets and others in Wuchow to obtain possession of the very fine hospital and school buildings there, run by the American Baptist Mission, was described to be "China Mall" representative this morning by Mr. Rex Ray who has been in charge in Wuchow and who arrived in Hongkong yesterday by the s.s. "Lungsham."

Life at Wuchow had become so impossible under the conditions precipitated by the strike pickets and the lack of protection by the police and military that the schools and hospitals have had to be closed down. Mr. Ray thinks, however, that the mission has defeated the ends of the pickets which he is convinced were that the hospital fixtures and staff should be taken over and run under Chinese administration.

Demands had, in fact, been presented to the hospital and school staff on March 23 that they should sign an agreement handling over all the property to a representative Chinese committee and on being met with refusal one of the leaders amongst the Chinese entered the hospital and stated that from that time, all the funds of the hospital were to be turned over to him. The comprudore was told that if he failed to comply he would be put to death. The intruder was removed but it was apparent that the movement was well organised and fairly widespread and that the mission would get no support from the police or military who stated openly that all they would afford was a safe transport from Wuchow to the mission staff.

An attempt was made to seize the girls' school but this also was defeated and it became apparent that there was nothing to do but to leave. Determined that the hospital and schools should not fall into the hands of the pickets and others who had set themselves out to make of it an entirely Chinese concern, arrangements were made by which the whole of the buildings were locked and sealed with the American seal.

The escape of the mission staff was made under difficulties. "All day long as we worked," stated Mr. Ray, a howling, cursing mob did all they could to interfere and annoy. In spite of assurances of police and military facilities for our departure, no labour for removal of the baggage was forthcoming. What is more, the mob were allowed to tear down the elevated train way that leads from the shore to the Sai Hing Company's floating pier where we were taking the baggage and from where the boat to Canton puts in. As I was on the pier at the time, together with Mr. Lang, we had to jump into the water, which was waist high, and wade ashore. I used a pole to vault over the deeper part."

"During the last day, whilst the staff was moving the baggage out, some of the mob were throwing brick bats and knocking out the front windows of the dispensary of the hospital," continued Mr. Ray. "As this and the jeering was going on, one of the pickets said to them 'Don't keep on destroying the property as it will all be ours in a few days.'". Mr. Ray is convinced, however, that the action of sealing up the locks with the American seal will effectively check any such action. The U.S.S. "Pampanga" is standing by.

The trouble between the mission and the strike pickets dates back to the latter part of 1924 when it was discovered that a former teacher was making use of the Mission's book store to spread Bolshevik doctrines also to August, 1925 when the bookstore was found to be filled with hideous cartoons on the Shameen affair of June 23. These were torn down and the store closed and this was the beginning of the trouble. headline: SOVIET COMMERCE.
text:
DEPRECIATION ON THE CHORVONETZ.

"MRELY TEMPORARY."

The depreciation of the chervonetz is causing alarm in Soviet commercial circles.

The Soviet Press has now published statements made by M. Kalinin, President of the Central Executive Committee in February, when the depreciation was only ten per cent., and M. Briukhanoff, Commissar of the State who is endeavouring to quell the alarm, pointing out that the depreciation is merely temporary.

Nevertheless the authorities are contemplating further restrictions on imports and increased duties on postal phreels and luggage from abroad.

M. Cheka has initiated a campaign against rising prices and many private traders have been arrested in Moscow.

[The chevronetz is worth 10 doubles gold or $1 2/3 sterling.]

headline: Juli / TURFING TALK
text:
LOCAL EXPERTS "DO'S AND DON'T'S."

LITTLE KNOWN INDUSTRY.

Weather vagaries in Hongkong have a great bearing on the turf required for various purposes, necessitating a good deal of attention.

That the turfing industry is fairly extensive is evident from the fact that there are experts who have been constantly engaged in it.

Many think that the Chinese gardener is the only person who does turfing jobs. This is not the case. Mr. Yeung Wing-hong, principal of Messrs. Yeung Fat (Fat Lee), of No. 69, Wanehal Road, who has kindly supplied the information to the "China Mail," has been a student at the Hongkong University. His firm have been contractors to the Botanical and Forestry Department for many years.

Nearly all the "material" used in the Colony comes from the New Territories, from places like Sal Kong and Un Long where there are unlimited supplies.

The workmen have been brought up in the trade—like every other Chinese artisan—by experience and are specialists.

First of all, the ground—whether it is a tennis court or garden lawn—must be “loosened” and well raked. If the soil is not suitable, then black soil must be used; this being obtainable (on the surface) from the Peak and other places. Black soil has nutritive effects on grass. It is used, the turfing may last for several years; if not, the “life” is appreciably shortened, but it all depends on the nature of the soil. The ground may be “too salty,” or the siting may be shaded by trees (or buildings) which prevent the grass, making sufficient sunlight. In such cases, “repairs” may be needed after a year, or longer.

How It Is Done.

Turf is taken about in sods of from 10 to 14 inches square. Mixed up with earth, each piece is about 1½ to 2 inches thick. It has to be well beaten down with a wooden hammer, in case the ground is not uniformly loose. Each sod overlaps its neighbours to ensure a good "fit." Otherwise, in dry weather there is contraction and cracks appear.

Spring is the best season to pu in turfing and autumn the mos unfavourable.

Workmen who dig up the turf are also employed in laying it down where wanted. They dig to a certain depth with spades and shovel up each sod in a stereotyped way.

For a plot of about 400 or 500 square yards (which would be the area of the average tennis court), the price would be from 40 to 45 cents per square yard on the upper levels, and from 80 to 40 cents a square yard for Kowloon and the lower levels. Such rates do not include the expense of raking or black soil, as these items must be dealt with according to requirements.

Mr. Young advises: Do not roll immediately after turf is laid. Give it a chance to sink in and for the roots of the grass to grow. For tennis courts, one should wait till the grass has grown and is rolled three or more times, before there should be any cutting. How long turf takes to be firmly embedded depends on the weather and the soil.

headline: PEACE TALK.
text:
SETTLEMENT RUMOURS.

How even "in the ten-houses and restaurants" everybody in Canton is daily discussing the settlement of the boycott is related by Japanese correspondent who came down to Hongkong on the "Lung-shan" yesterday.

Speaking to the representative of a vernacular paper, the correspondent said that he had no private capacity) interviewed Mr. So Snuching (chairman of the Boycott and Strike Committee). Mr. So is quoted as having replied to the effect that the Political Commission of Government has already held one meeting when instructions were given to the workmen to bring about a quick settlement. Further than that, and as to what had been done, Mr. So would not say, added the correspondent, but Mr. So said that something would be known before long. The correspondent also said that the Canton public was hopeful and that there were persistent rumours of an early resumption of communication between Hongkong and Canton.

A local business man who came down on the same steamer is reported to have seen Mr. Lul King to (who took a large part in the settlement of the 1922 seamen's strike), but had nothing to say beyond the lack of reference in the Canton press to negotiations.

Another report says that the re- fectories in Canton for the use of the strikers will be shortly removed to Whampou.

As is well known, buildings were requisitioned at the beginning of the strike for the use of strikers. The report indicates that people have falsely represented themselves to be strikers. To prevent malfides, a large matshed will built at Whampon where strikers will be able to get their meals. The cost has been approved at about $40,000 and the building will be ready shortly.

headline: "WILD STORIES."
text:
BOLSHEVIST PLANS IN SHANGHAI.

PHANTOM OF THE BRAIN.

(From Our Own Correspondent):

Whilst the recent threats of disturbance in Shanghai, arising out of the shooting of students in Peking, came to nothing, save one or two orderly demonstrations, there is still evidence that Shanghai must be prepared for some trouble in the next few months. Whilst the reverse of Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang in the North, and the coup d'etat of General Chang Kaishek in Canton may be taken to constitute serious reverses for the Bolshevik policy in China, it has yet to be shown that the local representatives of the Soviets are relaxing in their endeavours to create disorder. There has been a number of strikes in the industrial districts, called on the filmsiest of pretexts. Particularly is that the case in connection with the cotton milds, where, fortunately for the owners, surplus stocks would enable them to shut down for a few weeks in the present state of trade depression, did they desire. This undoubtedly proved a strong weapon in their hands, for they would have been able to face a lock out with no little equanimity. Possibly this was recognised by the agitators behind the strikes for it is a significant fact that none of them lasted any appreciable length of time.

It has been suggested that these were more or less in the nature of ballons d'essai to discover the strength of the labour leaders in Shanghai; but this is probably incorrect. If it is not, then the labour leaders have nothing at the present moment of which to be proud.

In the meantime no little anxiety and a great deal of what is nothing about of the man's has been created by the wild stories of what the Bolsheviks intend to do in Shanghai Curing the next three years. That the Communists have some plans for Shanghai goes without saying. They regard Shanghai as the centre of British influence in China, and a place where a very shrewd blow could be struck which, if successful, would go a long way toward damaging British prestige and business. Indeed in a recent Communist speech Shanghai was spoken of as an important place from the Communist point of view. Whilst the authorities doubtless have a very fair idea of what the local Bolsheviks is planning—for the intelligence service in Shanghai is of a high order of efficiency—all manner of alarmist reports gain currency to the disquiet of the ordinary person in the street, until the "North China Daily News" rightly thought it necessary to do something to allay anxiety by a judiciously worded editorial.

The wildest story which gained currency was that on a night to be selected the Bolsheviks would rise and seize the city. They would detail men to the houses of all the Volunteers, Police, and members of the various defence forces, and overpower them during the night; seize the women and children and place them in the buildings along the Bund to prevent the warships firing into the Settlement; and then hand the place over to sack. Quite a pretty little scheme, if it could be worked

But there seem to be many objections to such a plan even from the Bolshevik point of view, which is the most important, for the foreign opinion on the subject can so well be imagined that it needs no description here. The other foreigners strongly disapprove of the idea, and possibly if any such attempt were made would forcibly express their opinions on the matter. When we come to consider the large number of Bolsheviks that would be needed to pick off every individual member of the defence forces, it becomes apparent that they would need a force of some thousands of men, and the maintenance of secrecy amongst such a body would be impossible. It is obvious that if the authorities obtained the slightest inkling of the plan, their precautions would be made accordingly. Then, again, there is little to be got out of it, except loot, and whilst Shanghai would be an attractive place to pursue so engrossing a pastime, it is more than likely that the Chinese merchants themselves, with large interests at stake, would be the first to disapprove. Nor is it possible to

overlook the contention that the Bolsheviks would gain little else from it, for doubtless the despatch of adequate foreign forces would soon rescue the city from their hands, leaving them with no permanent political gain.

Arrayed against the Bolsheviks there are at present the Copstitutional Defence League, and a Chinese anti-Bolshevik League, both organisations capable of doing useful work, with, however, this limitation, that a propaganda of discontent is easier to preach than one to the contrary. Possibly, therefore, they may both find their work more difficult than does the Communist, but provided with sufficient money they may find means, not perhaps of averting trouble, but of minimising it when it does come.

Meanwhile we in Shanghai are watching the way the wind blows as the fated month of May draws near. There may, of course, be trouble, but believing it to be true that a watched pot never boils, your correspondent is not disinlined to believe that the month will pass off much more quietly than many at present anticipate. If it does not, possibly the opportunity of giving the Bolsheviks comrade as shrewd a crack as he has received in the North and South would not come amiss, though the failure of his plans in those localities may cause him to walk a little more circumspectly up here.

headline: TEST TRIP. / BOYCOTT ENDING IN AMOY?
text:
B. AND S. CARGO LANDED.

News from Amoy during the holidays is that the first British steamer to arrive there with cargo, since the boycott pickets began activities, has been discharged.

The matter has been the main topic of conversation for some days and, in the opinion of the Chinese merchants, normal conditions are returning at that point.

It was the China Navigation S.S. "Ichang" which put in with a cargo of beancake. Hitherto cargo in British bottoms had not been discharged nor loaded. Passengers, however, had been land-ed or permitted to embark, the majority being in connection with the coolie transport for southern ports.

On the first day, nothing was done. Then the merchants are believed to have pointed out that the cargo was a Chinese product, from a Chinese port, and for Chinese consumption. Friendly influences prevailed and the cargo was landed.

[Amoy is further North along the coast (from Hongkong)] than Swatow. It is in the province of Fukien and not a part of Kwangtung. The present rulers of Fukien province cannot be described as antagonistic to, nor actually in sympathy with, the Kuomintang of Canton.]

headline: EASY MONEY. / PRIVATE CAR DRIVER'S TEMPTATION.
text:
The practice of using private cars for public hire was described as a proper nulsance when Divisional Inspector Peter Grant charged a Chinese driver with the offence before Mr. R. B. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning. According to facts stated in Court, a vigilant European Sergeant had observed the car, which belongs to one Law Cho, of No. 98, Bonham Strand East running backwards and forwards with passengers at 3:30 this morning. Defendant was arrested in the act of striking a bargain with two passengers to take them to Stanley Street for $1. Defendant was given the option

" Defendant was given the option of a fine of $50, or four weeks.

headline: MILL STRIKE.
text:
ALLEGED ASSAULT AND ITS SEQUEL.

GRAVE SITUATION

A very grave situation is reported from Gouripore, 25 miles from Calcutta, where thousands of mill workers have struck as the sequel to a European's alleged assault on a coolie, who died.

The situation became worse in the evening, Europeans being assaulted and four injured: Armed police have been summoned.

The arrival of armed police from Barrackpore has quieted the rioters at Gourippre, though the coolies have not returned to work.

The European mentioned enlier denies the allegations of assaulting a coolie.

Religious ferment in Calcutta itself has not yet subsided, being nurtured by false rumours of assaults, desecarations of temples and mosques, and Mohammedans being killed in the streets.

To-day a British lady was injured.

A number of Hindus and Moslems are in hospital suffering from lathi blows and stabs.

headline: MARCH 18.
text:
CABINET AND NON-COMMUNIST VICTIMS

COMPENSATION ANNOUNCED

The Cabinet has resolved to compensate the non-Communist students who were wounded and the families of those who were killed in the demonstration against the Cabinet on March 18.

headline: HONGKONG, / NOFFICIAL MISSION.
text:
CHINESE

CANTON'S DELEGATES.

Although details are not given, considerable significance is attached in the vernacular papers to the visit to Canton of three Hongkong Chinese merchants, whose mission is stated to be in connection with the settlement of the boycott.

These three merchants have been prominent in the movements by the Association of District Commercial Guilds of Hongkong. They were previously in Canton with the unofficial delegations. One report says that they were taken by Mr. Kan Kum-shek to interview an official of the Canton Government.

It should also be noted that when Chinese merchant delegates last visited Canton as unofficial peace mediators, their movements were made public. There has been no announcement this time, nor has there been any communication—even strictly unofficial—as to the purport of their trip or their status.

In. Canton the consensus of opinion, is supposed to be an favour of an early peace. A quarter identified with labour is quoted as having indicated that the matter had best be left to the Canton Government. From this it is presumed, says the same report, that the Canton Government is of the opinion that the best interests would be served by its active participation in the pour-parlers.

A Canton vernacular paper attributes to a labour representative the statement that the boy-cott committee will not seek a part in the proposed conference.

The names of Dr. C. C. Wu, Mr. T. V. Soong and Mr. Chan Kung-pok are freely mentioned as the delegates to act for Canton. A private communication from Canton, dated Sunday, attributes to the mercantile leaders a desire to get all three, or any one or two of

tations; but the writer qualifies his information by adding that he did not know whether the proposal had been put forward. A Chinese firm of sugar merchants in Hongkong yesterday received instructions (from its Canton branch) that shipments via Shanghai be suspended, also that unless the Shanghai market was especially favourable, purchases should not be made there for ultimate disposal in Canton. This is merely given as a hint as to the direction in which the wind is veering, and not to designate that there is any substantial ground for assuming a definite trend in developments.

headline: "Through": Truins: Again?
text:
As from to-morrow, there will be an improved train service between Hongkong and Canton—an improvement which will be much appreciated by Chinese travellers. Hitherto, the trains of the Chinese section (of the Canton-Kowloon Railway) have come down as far as Samchun, whence passengers must get off to walk across the bridge and, it is alleged, sometimes have to "arrange" with the boycott pickets to pass through to Lowu, where the British section trains stop.

The new arrangement is that the Chinese train will run over the bridge (into British territory) to Lowu. It is understood that the Chinese management would run their train straight down to the Kowloon terminus were it not for their shortage of rolling stock. Each day the Canton train is expected to arrive at Lowu about 12.15 p.m. An express (1st, 2nd and 3rd class) will leave Kowloon at 11.42 a.m. to meet this train for the double object of bringing on the Canton traffic, and sending on the passengers for Canton. (via the Chinese train). The Kowloon express should arrive at Lowu at 12.22 p.m., which is ample time as the Canton up-train does not leave Lowu till 1.15 p.m. Canton passengers should be in Kowloon by about 2.30 p.m. The up-traffic should arrive at Tai-shata before sunset.

Two cases of enteric fever were notified yesterday. One patient was a Chinese and the other a Japanese.

headline: CANTON'S BOYCOTT.
text:
CONFERENCE TO FOLLOW?

The Hongkong Government Attitude.

Although there is nothing, very definite as to the outcome of such conversations which are referred to below, in an official communication received today for publication—one presumption is that in "pence conference" to end the Canton boycott will be held. The statement reads:—

The Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp, K.C., C.B.E., Attorney-General, held informal conservations at Canton on April 8 and 9 with Mr. C.C. Wu as a preliminary to the formal conference which is in view for the ending of the boycott. The conversations were friendly and exhaustive, and Mr. Kemp took the opportunity of making it quite clear that the Hongkong Government would not pay strike pay or compensation for non-reinstatement of strikers, nor would it countenance any such payment.

The conversations were adjourned sine die but it was agreed that they should be resumed before the meeting of the formal conference.

Preceding Events

It will be recalled that the Canton Government signified its willingness to appoint three officials delegates to meet representatives of Hongkong in a conference.

Mr. C. C. Wu (Dr. Wu Chao-chu) is the present Mayor of Canton: Previously he has been Foreign Minister. His name has been mentioned as one of Canton's delegates.

headline: POSTMEN STRIKE / MAIL VAN DRIVER TWICE ARRESTED. / GUILD INTERVENES.
text:
A strike of postmen in Canton, on Saturday, which lasted only a day, throws light on the present position.

On April 4, the driver of a motor maffan was detained by the city police after a soldier had been injured in an accident, in which it was alleged that the soldier had been knocked down.

Subsequently the driver was released on ball. Then a letter was sent demanding $500 compensation for the injuries which the soldier had sustained. The driver was detained a second time when in charge of the van.

The postal employees' guild organised a procession. A delegation interviewed Mr. Techen Wu, Commissioner of Police, and the driver was released. In the meanwhile, work had ceased on the Saturday. The guild issued a statement, a part of which indicated that the Post Office would be responsible for settling the matter of injuries. Work was then resumed on Sunday, there having been no disorderliness in the interval. Pickets are alleged to have been on duty to notify all men, during the period, to stay away from work.

[Note: — As is probably well known, the Chinese Post Office is run on lines similar to the Maritime Customs.]

Mr. So Shiu-ching, chairman of the Boycott and Strike Executive, has signified to the Canaverin government that in matters relating to the settlement, Government guidance will be accepted without implications.

During the last few days, there have been persistent rumours that the strike will be settled shortly, and that the Canton delegates (for the conference) will leave for Hongkong.

headline: Small-pox Campaign
text:
In order to guard against small-pox, special attention was devoted to a campaign for vaccination.

In the crowded parts of the city, 54 centres were selected for carrying out a vaccination campaign. On March 3, a joint conference was convened at the Municipal Hospital, at which the staff and students of the Hackett Medical School, the Kwong Wah Medical College, the Sino-Franco Medical College, the Medical Division of the National University, the Tau-keung, the Women and Children's Hospital, etc. attended. The vaccinators started work in the various sections from March 4 to March 11 for one week, with the result that 31,018 persons were vaccinated.

This campaign aroused widespread public interest and showed that the citizens of Canton readily appreciated the value of this prophylactic measure. The report closes by stating that the training of the Sanitary Police will be continued.

The Coast Inspector for Shanghai has issued a notice that on or about May 4, 1926, the "Tungsha" light-vessel, moored in the South Channel entrance to the Yangtze River, will be withdrawn from her station and replaced by the new light-vessel "Tungsha". The new light-vessel has a red hull with "Tungsha" on her side, a foremast with spherical daymark, an iron column surmounted by a lantern and a mainmast with spherical daymark. [Other particuars are also given in the notice]

headline: CHINESE HUMOUR.
text:
AN ARTICLE IN A LOCAL NEWSPAPER.

PUBLISHER SUMMONED

was summoned to appear before Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning for publishing matter in the Chinese language without the permission of the Secretary for Chinese Affairs. Sub Inspector Shukla said that the article which appeared in the issue of April 2 had not been submitted to the S.C.A. although a warning had been issued last month not to publish matter without submitting for censorship. He thought the present article was of an anti-foreign nature and bore a hidden meaning which was that the Chinese are willing to kow-tow to Europeans and not help their own people.

At the outset, Mr. E. S. C. Brooks defending, tendered a plea of guilty and asked for leniency by pointing out that the censorship was instituted during the commencement of the strike and that the regulations were not strictly carried out now, as they were no longer necessary. He termed the article in question as a mild satire in regard to a gentle man who gave $10,000 for a charitable cause and refused to allow time to a tenant to pay his rent of $30.

The translation of the article stated that a fat, rich gentleman sitting in a rocking chair with spring, wind all over his face (meaning an affable countenance) was chatting with a long-nosed gentleman, the result being that the latter secured a cheque for $10,000 which was later ascertained to have gone to the authorities at "X port" for a building fund. The next day a thin man dressed in rags (a peasant) appeared before the gentleman in the rocking chair to ask for an extension of time to pay his rent of $30 owing to the failure of his crops, but the gentleman's countenance turning to one of anger, the peasant was refused hearing and driven by a servant. An in-depth of the S.G.A department was questioned. Her His Worship as to the impression gained by a reader of the article. He said that the "long-nosed gentleman" was an allusion to a European and that "X port" stood for Hongkong. His Worship remarked that he gathered the Chinese were open-handed with foreigners but close-fisted in dealing with their own people.

The case concluded with a fine of $100.

headline: STRIKE PICKETS.
text:
WARRANT FOR ARREST OF NO. 2 CHIEF.

ALLEGED DISAPPEARANCE.

According to Canton vernacular papers, a warrant has been issued (not by the Government but by the Strike Executive) for the arrest of the deputy chief of the "Communications Department." The "Communications Department" is in charge of pickets. Whilst the chief was away from Canton, on duty, the No. 2 is alleged to have acted for him, and then to have absent himself on the No. 1's return.

Canton papers also refer to the detention, in Chinese territory, just across the Macao border (in Chinshan) of the second principal Chinese police detective of Macao, by the boycott pickets. It is stated that a death penalty has been applied for on the grounds of alleged lack of sympathy when the anti-Canton risking (by so-called pro-Chan adherents) in the Heungshan district last year, caused some of the pickets to seek sanctuary in, or near Macao.

For being found asleep while in charge of the Praya East Police Station, a Chinese constable was fined $50 at the Magistracy this morning. During six months of the man's total service of one year, the record showed that he had ten reports all of a serious nature.

TO DAYS DOLLAR The closing rate of the dollar, on demand, to day was 2/2.15/16.

headline: UNPRECEDENTED?
text:
ALLEGED EXCESSES OF STRIKE PICKETS.

HOPS REOPTED "SEIZED"

Great prominence is given in Chinese business circles to a report that labour pickets in Canton have foribly seized two piecegoods shops in the city.

One message refers to the region as "unprecedented". On the afternoon of April 12 (Monday) a batch of pickets alleged to have been sent by the piecegoods employees" guild, armed with weapons, moved to a shop in the business centre and turned out the master and men. Not even private effects were allowed to be taken, it being stated that the pickets occupied everything.

The same procedure is said to have been repeated at another shop. Both names and addresses of the shops are given in the vernacular papers.

Representations have been made to various "merceantile and official bodies.

headline: CHINA POSITION.
text:
NO DANGER TO BRITISH LIVES.

REFERENCE IN COMMONS

The House of Commons invited Captain J. G. Fairfax (Conservative, Norwich) to make a statement in regard to the situation in China.

Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, said that this was impossible usefully at the present juncture since it was not yet possible to foresee the result of the present contest for Peking. There was no reason at present to anticipate danger to British lives or property. Legitimate undertakings could be carried on except in the province of Kwangtung where there was an anti-British boycott. The Diplomatic Corps had made representations in regard to Peking on April 6 in consequence of the fighting there.

headline: CARGO COOLIES STORM RIVAL GUILD:
text:
FREIE RIDE DISPUTE:

Pukkai: Kongmoon April 6.

Representatives of two coolio guilds, which originated in Hong Kong have been engaged here in a determined campaign against each other.

The Tung Tak is the shore-coolies' guide, whilst the Chap Yin embraces the employees of steved-dores and other harbour workers. A dispute as to the right of landing coal from lighters for the Sunning Railway Co. led to a pitched battle being fought at the Pakkad station. The Tung Tak men stormed the Chap Yin guild headquarters, and completely wrecked the place.

[Note: — Both the Tung Tak and the Chap Yin guilds were prominent in Hongkong during the 1922'seamen's strike'.]

Truin Fired, At.

Pukkai, Kongmoon, April 10. Four village guards of Sunning city were arrested by the railway guards for refusing to pay their fares. On the village guard headquarters sending a despatch, the four men were released.

On April 7, a train from Tau-shan approached the east quite. About 300 of the village guard-sure alleged to have posted themselves in position and to have fired at the train. A native lady passenger was killed, and a ticket collector was wounded.

The train continued on its way till it reached the west gate, where a report was made to the Railway Co.'s head office. As there has been no settlement, the trains have stopped running, the last one on April 7 arriving here at 9 p.m. (five hours late).

headline: PARIS RIOT. / DEMONSTRATION BY CIVIL SERVANTS.
text:
(Router's Service.

Rioting occurred here in consequence of attempted demonstrations by Civil Servants, who are claiming salaries on a sliding Scale.

A crowd of several hundreds, mostly Communists, defied the prefectoral prohibition to demonstrate, and tried to force the police barrier in order to raid the premises of an electrical undertaking. Fighting then ensued, one policeman being seriously injured and two slightly injured.

Three hundred arrests were made but only two were detained.

headline: PICKETS DOINGS
text:
TWO JAPANESE SEAMEN DETAINED

Two of the crew "(Japanese) of a Japanese steamer in Canton harbour are reported to have been detained on Wednesday, only to be subsequently released on the representations of the captain.

These men are stated to have landed at Chow Tau Tsui (on Honam, opposite the city) to buy provisions. They were taken by pickets to their branch headquarters and closely questioned, says the report.

The captain confirmed their statement that they were merely obtaining ship's provisions, and they were released after a few hours.

On Tuesday, an "inspector" of the pickets, who was stationed at Samchun (the market town just beyond the British border, New Territories), was arrested by the military.

The report is that he was taken into custody by the colonel of the third regiment (stationed at Samchin) acting under orders from the officer commanding the second division. An allegation is that the inspector has been concerned with the smuggling of arms. He was taken to the second division headquarters in Canton. Representations by the Boycott Executive have been of no avail, says the report.

headline: WINES BUSINESS.
text:
RESULTS OF MESSRS. GANDE PRICE & CO., LTD.

A SATISFACTORY YEAR

A tribute to the able manner in which the staff had looked after the students of the shareholders in spite of adverse circumstances and keen competition was paid by Mr. S. C. Pank, presiding at the nineteenth ordinary general meeting of Messrs. Gande, Price and Co., Ltd. held at noon to-day at No. 2, Ice House Street.

The chairman was supported by Messrs. Kenneth Chan and Leung Yan-po (directors), Mr. C. Bond (secretary), shareholders present being Messrs. Chow Tung-sang, Pang Kok-sui, Pang Kwok-fatt and D. Rumjahn.

Chairman's Speech

The notice convening the meeting having been read by the secretary, the chairman said:—

Gentlemen,—Before commencing the business before the meeting, I wish to express, on behalf of the directors, staff and shareholders, our deepest regret at the untimely death of our late chairman of directors Mr. C. H. Lyson. His valuable services to the company during his term of office, not only as a director but as a legal adviser, were of great assistance to his co-directors.

The report and statement of accounts for the year ending 1925 having been in your hands for the prescribed period, I propose with your permission to take them as read.

The net profit for the year under review is $5,050.42, to which must be added the balance at Profit and Loss account brought forward from 1924 of $218.96, making a total at credit of Profit and Loss account of $5,269.38. This sum your directors' recommend should be appropriated as follows: To pay a dividend of $25 cents per share on 18,105 shares, which will absorb $4,526.25 and to carry forward the balance of $743.13 to this year's account.

I regret to state, "gentlemen, that our profits show a decrease on the previous year, but with the abnormal condition of things in China together with the "very keen competition prevailing, what other results can we expect? I think you will agree with me that in spite of these adverse circumstances we have had a satisfactory year," and I am sure I am only voicing the sentiment of the shareholders when I say that the staff have in an able manner looked after our interests, especially in such strenuous times, and I hope with their continued cooperation and the early solution of the present situation, we shall have better results to place before you at the next annual meeting.

With these few remarks I have much pleasure in proposing the adoption of the report and accounts as presented and after this have been seconded I shall be pleased to answer to the best of my ability any questions the shareholders may wish to ask.

There being no questions, Mr. Pang Kok-sui seconded the adoption of the report and accounts which was carried.

headline: LEE KEE Agent for HENRY RICHARD TILE CO'S
text:

then over control. The Kuomineham forces outside the city streamed in, demoralising the gaurison, and the evacuation allowed him trains, cars, carts and n.

The Nationalist commander gave the control to General Wang Shih-hien, who telegraphed to the llied leaders that there was no need to besiege the capital.

Present indications are that the Kuominchun will not halt before reaching Nankow pass, north of Peking, which is now threatened by a Manchusian column.

The Kuominchun troops fought fiercely at Fengtai until the afternoon, when they retreated. (General Wang fears the Manchurians will insist on entering the capital to morrow.

The foreign quarter is examined with "Chinese treasures. The hotels and foreign buildings are crowded with panic stricken refugees.

"Puan Chi-jui has returned to the Legotion quarter"

Nankow Pass Reached.

"Fle Kuominchun Nationalist Armies, after evacuating "Peking, have reached Nankow Pass, leaving only a few stragglers but no gains or supplies."

Their retreat was followed by heavy fighting. Rain increased the difficulties of their withdrawal, which marked the second stage of the allied Chinese General's campaign.

Tuan's Mandate.

Tuan Chi jui will issue no mandate "to-morrow saying that he is impelled to resume the responsibility of Chief Executive pending the reconstruction of the Administration, with which he will not interfere, and stating his readiness to retire immediately a responsible head of the Government is elected.

The Allied Generals are expected in Peking tomorrow to confer regarding the general situation. Marshal Chang Tso-lin has not yet entered Peking, which is now quiet.

headline: An Earlier Message.
text:
The conference at Headquarters last evening decided to treat with the Kuominchun under no other conditions than absolute unconditional surrender.

A telegram was subsequently received by Marshal Wu Pei-fu from Marshal Chang Tso-lin stating that General Lu Chunglin's invitation was an endeavour by the Kuominchun to create bad blood between himself (Chang)

and - Wu Pei-fu, and further stating that the capture of Peking and the destruction of Bolshevism were absolutely assured.

Marshal Wu Pei-fu replied that he had already on several occasions made it perfectly clear that he had no intention whatever of treating with the Kuominchun, neither had he vouchsafed an answer to Lu Chung-lin's telegram.

Orders have been issued to the troops to move on and capture Peking.

headline: MR. C. C. WU.
text:
EXPECTED IN HONGKONG NEXT WEEK

CURRENT PEACE RUMOUR.

According to a well-informed source, Mr. C. C. Wu (Dr. Wu Chao-chu) is expected to arrive in Hongkong, from Canton, on Monday or Tuesday.

Dr. Wu is now the Mayor of Canton and the head of Judicial Reform investigation committee. His name has been mentioned as one of the Canton delegates to the conference to end the present boycott. The latest rumour is that Dr. Wu is coming to Hongkong to continue the unofficial conversations, which were the subject of a communique by the Hongkong Government on Tuesday.

The Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp, K.C., C.B.E., Attorney-General, held informal conservation's at Canton on April 8 and 9 with Mr. C. C. Wu as a preliminary to the formal conference which is in view for the ending of the boycott.

The conversations were friendly and exhaustive, and Mr. Kemp took the opportunity of making it quite clear that the Hongkong Government would not pay strike pay or compensation for non-reinstatement of strikers, nor would it countenance any such payment.

The conversations were adjourned, since die; but it was agreed that they should be resumed before the meeting of the formal conference.

headline: SOLIDARITY WITH MINERS.
text:
Brussels, April 16. The International Miners Federation unanimously adopted a resolution declaring that the only way of emerging from an international coal crisis was to examine the International system of production and distribution.

It affirmed its complete solidarity with the British miners in the present dispute, and expressed its readiness, in the event of trouble, to take measures to prevent the exportation of coal to Great Britain.

In the event of an international strike, it would recommend that it be not discontinued before the National Associations are satisfied that there sufficient grounds for resuming work found in all countries involved in the conflict. The Federation would act as a Strike Committee for all countries.

headline: RENT RESTRICTION. / WHAT CHINESE TENANTS MAY ASK FOR. / SUGGESTED PETITION.
text:
As reported in Thursday's "China Mail," the Hongkong Tenants' Protective Association proposes to present a public petition to the Government, with regard to the notice to discontinue the present Rents Restriction Ordinance as from June 30, 1926. Interviewed by a reporter yesterday, Mr. Wong Kam-ying (chairman of the Association) is quoted as having indicated that certain suggestions will be put forward before tomorrow's meeting.

In view of the bad trade conditions prevailing, one argument is that both residents and shopkeepers will find it very difficult to pay any additional rent during the boycott.

The main proposals are, that subject to the boycott continuing at any rate, the Ordinance be retained; or that landlords of houses at present under restriction be only allowed to raise rentals in accordance with a scale (to be fixed).

headline: CANTON PASSPORTS.
text:
A passenger from Canton, says the vernacular papers, can now obtain a pass (from the Boycott Executive) to leave that port for $13.20. This sum, it is stated, will cover permission to any destination and does not stipulate any time limit for return.

(Hitherto passes were issued on guarantees and, it is alleged, on payment, for persons to visit Hongkong, but to return to Canton within a week)

His Excellency the Governor has appointed the following officers to be Honorary Extra Aldes-de-Camp with effect from December 11, 1925: Captain George Edward Swinton, M.O., 1st Battalion, the East Surrey Regiment, and Lieutenant Allen James Levinge. Whyle Royal Engineers.

headline: TOWBOAT STRIKE.
text:
THREE THOUSAND MEN OUT IN NEW YORK.

INERS' DELAYS.FEARED.

Three thousand towboat men, representing half the 800 tow-boats operating in New York, were ordered to strike last night for higher wages and a ten-hour day.

Fears are expressed that some of the big liners may be delayed in starting, as nearly all the to-boats commonly used to assist them in and out of their berths are tied up.

headline: CANTON FIRING.
text:
PICKENS ATTACK FISH COOLIES.

CARGOES FOR HONGKONG.

Either by ingenuity, or by force, coolies in change of fresh water fish for Hongkong," succeeded in evading the Canton boycott pickets on Saturday night when a number of volleys were fired from the shore.

Witherto the pickets had either rounded "up small craft or maintained a cordon from the shore. Only last week they prevented fish getting through for a few days. In the latter part of last week, supplies have again reached the Hongkong stemmers.

During the dark hours of Saturday night, prior to the "Lungshan's" departure at 8 a.m. yesterday (for Hongkong), a number of junks are believed to have put off for the boat. Before they had reached the "Lungshan" shots rang out and became more intense.

One who claims to have been near enough to have seen what was going on is of the opinion that the crowds of the junked took cover under the guagwhale and bulkhead and that they even returned the fire. The speaker remarked that there were too many of them to be rammed by the pickets' motor-boats, and the coolies eventually got out of range to complete their job. It is even said that they were armed for their own protection.

headline: In Nick of Time.
text:
Captain Estevez is progressing, and desires to continue his flight.

He said that he was forced to land for lack of petrol after in-effectual endeavours to strike the Bagdad track.

Eight British machines engaged in the search. Before leaving here the Spaniards were warned by the Royal Air Force to take three days' supplies of food and water. It was thanks to this advice that Captain Estevez was alive after six days in a barren country. As it was, he and his mechanic were only rescued in the nick of time. Their trials were aggravated by a sand storm that lasted for two days.

King Alfonso has cabled to the Royal Air Force his appreciation of their admirable work and de-ploring the loss of two British airmen.

Comrades at Calcutta.

The other two Spanish aviators have arrived here from Agra.

headline: Closer Ties
text:
The steady increase in the volume of trade during the last quarter of a century between this Colony and Indo-China was created and nourished closer commercial ties, from which have sprung that spirit of mutual confidence, so necessary to beneficial trade, and I feel sure that it is this same spirit of confidence which has prompted those who guide the affairs of this Institution, to decide upon the wise step of acquiring even at heavy cost their own permanent premises in this important commercial centre of the British Empire in which one and all can meet in friendly commercial rivalry.

"This decision was arrived at shortly after the War and when Mr. Lecot's predecessor received instructions from his Head Office to study the question, the desirability of acquiring this site, which at the time was possible, naturally presented itself, with the result that after some very delicate negotiations on the part of our friend, the Bank became the happy owner of this valuable property."

The building was started just two years ago and in spite of all labour troubles brought on by the strike and boycott, the contractor, imbued with the spirit of energy and courage, imparted and sustained by our friend the manager, succeeded in overcoming every obstacle that arose in his path and we find ourselves to-day in this palatial building, finished to time. The work throughout, which, I am told, has been satisfactorily done, speaks highly for Hang On, the contractors, and Messrs. Clark & Iu, the architects.

headline: DR. C.C. WU. / NOT YET ARRIVED IN THE COLONY.
text:
NO OFFICIAL NEWS?

Dr. C. C. Wu, the Mayor of Canton, who is reported to be likely to visit the Colony this week, did not arrive yesterday.

Up till tiffin time to-day there had been, as far as is known, no official intimation that he was coming down by the Steamboat Co.'s steamer this afternoon.

Vernacular papers indicate that if Dr. Wu does come down, his visit may only be in the nature of a complimentary return call to the Hon. Mr. J. H. Kemp (Attorney-General) who went up to Canton some days ago and entered into unofficial conversations with Dr. Wu, relative to the projected conference to end the boycott.

headline: CAPTAIN FINED:
text:
CAUSING OBSTRUCTION IN HARBOUR.

RESULT OF "STRIKE:"

A fine of $40 (or, in default, one month's hard labour) was imposed on the captain of a local steamer, at the Marine Court this morning.

Defendant was Captain J. N. Catela, master of the m.s. "Wong Shek Kurig" who pleaded not guilty before Lentus Com. G. E. Hole, R.N. (Marine Magistrate), to a charge of anchoring in the harbour so as to obstruct the fairways at 3.30 p.m. on April 14.

Mr. W. R. Hillyer, boarding officer of the Harbour Office, testified that the steamer was three ships' lengths west of buoy No. B47, and that there was not enough room.

Replying to the bench, witness said that the ship was actually causing an obstruction to the s.s. "New Mathilde," whose captain he was going to call as a witness for the prosecution.

Captain E. G. Rapley, master of the s.s. "New Mathilde," said that he was taking his vessel from the mooring to Stonecutters Island and had to alter his course, thereby cutting through the line of buoys, because of the other steamer being in the way. Defendant stated that he left Canton, owing to the strike, and had only a crew of two. He was short of gasoline and his company had promised to have gasoline ready near Green Island. The fine was paid.

headline: Mr. Alabaster's Point
text:
Before the charges were read out at this morning's proceedings, Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K.C., made an application before the second prisoner (Lam Fuk-chiu) was called upon to plead.

Mr. Alabaster pointed out that the two prisoners had been charged on the same indictment where as from the particulars as set out by the prosecution it was clear that the second prisoner was not charged with perjury. He moved that either the indictment be quashed or with the alternatives that the two last counts referring to the alleged perjury be struck out or that the prosecution be called on to elect which counts they would proceed with. Mr. Alabaster pointed out the anomalies of prisoner being called upon to plead on a count on which he was not charged.

Mr. Jenkin pointed out that the same facts in the conspiracy charge stood for the perjury charge and after cases had been quoted and some legal argument, His Lordship held that he did not see any ground for alleging that the second prisoner would be aeriously embarrassed by the inclusion in the indictment of those two counts. He did not, at any rate, propose at that moment to exercise his discretion in favour of striking out the counts or hearing the case separately, although if, as the case proceeded, he should see reason, he might exercise his discretion. Mr. F. C. Jenkin (together with Mr. Sheldon) was for the prosecution; Mr. C. G. Alabaster, K. C. for one prisoner and Mr. Elaley Zettlyn for the other. The case is proceeding

headline: CANTON LABOUR.
text:
MERCHANTS FLOUTED.

Canton merchants are now reported to be in communication with the Provincial Government in regard to the suggested removal of all "strikers" to Whampoa.

Last week specific instances were mentioned in which so-called armed labour pickets marched into business premises and took possession whilst the Police remained inactive.

This interference, alleged to have originated in disputes between masters and their employees' guilds, is regarded very seriously. To-day the vernacular papers record another case of workmen taking the law into their own hands, ignoring the representatives of law and order. The proposal that all strikers be accommodated at Whampoa in matsheds is mentioned as having been disfavoured by the labour leaders. On the other hand, the Canton merchants are said to have put forward statements that the labourers should not be allowed in the city, their presence being looked upon in the same light as the unruly military elements of the past.

headline: “FOR VALOUR.”
text:
MEDALS' PRIZIES, ETC.

As announced in Tuesday's "China Mail," the annual inspection of the Hongkong Police by E. E. the Governor, has been postponed till next Wednesday.

This change is of course, due to the weather. As a matter of fact, the refreshments for the subsequent entertainment were being laid out and arrangements completed, when one of the "Mail" reporters was informed of the postponement.

text:
