headline: KARAKHAN TO GO.
text:
CHANG TSO-LINS GRAVE WARNING.

DRAMATIC EXPOSURE

A Mukden (correspondent publishes a report that Chang Tso-lin has requested the Soviet Consul-General here to warn the Moscow Government of the necessity of replacing M. Karakhan, the Soviet Ambassador, Peking, on the ground that "since his arrival in China he has employed bribery to cause student riots and assisted Feng Yu-hsiang with arms in order to create internal strife in China, which actions constituted a misuse of his Ambassadorial position and a violation of international usages."

The Consul-General was further informed that when Peking was occupied by the allied troops M. Karakhan no longer would be considered entitled to the protection of international law.

headline: CHINA'S WARS.
text:
PROTECTION OF FOREIGNERS IN PEKING.

ELIMINATING BOLSHEVISM.

The Superintendent of Police visited the Senior Minister to-day and gave an assurance that, although Tuan Chijul's Government had suddenly been dissolved, the Police authorities would take all necessary measures to protect foreign life and property. It is reported from Hankow that Wu Pei-fu at a conference of his lieutenants, expressed the opinion that Bolshevist influence in China should be eliminated and that the Tariff Conference should proceed in compliance with the people's will.

headline: PROTEST "STRIKE."
text:
HOIHOW MERCHANTS AGAINST PICKETS

BOYCOTT BOYCOTTED

A boycott has been declared by the merchants of Hoihow against the pickets, who are maintaining the anti-foreign boycott at that port.

As a matter of fact, the commercial interests have suspended operations against what they consider to be the high-handed action of the local boycott committee.

This Monday, a foreign steamer (said to be the "Mingsang") was in port. A junk, loaded with poultry for export, was making for the ship when pickets—vigil

ance having been increased on the steamer's arrival—gave chase. Rather than let the goods fall into the hands of the pickets, the shippers' fokis threw most of it overboard. As the birds were in baskets in crates, some of the

abandoned poultry was retrieved. At any rate, one foki was arrested. He was sentenced by a "committee of cargo, investigation-tion" to be marched, in shame, around the town, as a lesson to others.

The mercantile bodies considered the punishment too harsh. Business organisations decided that doors should be closed in protest.

Several hundred men are also reported to have marched to local government offices to petition redress.

A subsequent incident was the capture of one of several lecturers (or street speakers) sent out by semi-official authorities. He fell into the hands of a crowd but was rescued by the action of boycott pickets, who took into custody a bad character.

headline: PEACE MISSION?
text:
That he is believed to have acted under orders by the Canton Government in coming to Hongkong, in connection with the negotiations to end the present boycott, is stated by the local vernacular papers regarding the visit of Dr. Giri Tzafling.

Dr. Lam is described in the Chinese report as the Deputy Superintendent of Customs (Canton). Mr. Fu Ping-sheung is Superintendent of Customs and Commissioner for Foreign Affairs; and for a number of years the same official has held these two posts jointly. The conclusion is that Dr. Lam holds the position of Deputy Superintendent of Customs but he also is acting for Mr. Fu Ping-sheung in other matters.

Broadly translated, the report reads:—

"Dr. Lam arrived here from Canton on Tuesday. He conversed with the Hon. Mr. R. H. Kotowall who, of course, is one of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council and also interviewed a certain high official. Dr. Lam returned to Canton yesterday." Then follows the reference to the peace negotiations.

The “China Mail” understands that three other gentlemen also came down with Dr. Lam. One of these was a Mr. Lam.

Although Dr. Lam has returned to Canton, the other three are still, as far as is known, in the Colony.

headline: PASSENGERS HELD TO RANSOM? / OVER 80% CAPTURED
text:
Over eighty passengers are alleged, in the "Kung Sheung Yat Fo," to have fallen into the hands of boycott pickets in Chinese territory near Macao, for whom ransoms were demanded.

After a running duel in waters near Chin Shan, a native boat was captured. Several kinds of weapons were used in the fight, it is stated, including machine-guns and cannon. The boat was ultimately boarded by pickets who took all the passengers to their depot. There, the report continues, they were made to communicate with their relatives, making that sums of money, varying from $80 to $120, should be paid to bring about their release.

headline: AMERICAN INDUSTRY
text: Evidently Charles M. Schwab is not to be numbered amongst those who claim that they see no good on the horizon of the near-by future, for he declared before the New York Building Congress the other day that he believed the next twenty years would see the greatest expansion and the greatest accomplishment American industry had ever known. "If I had my choice to be born again, I believe I would choose to be a young man to day," he said. And then he spoke of co-operation between competitors in industry and democratic relations between employer and workingmen. When it comes to be commonly recognized that co-operation is the avenue leading to true success, and that democratic relations between employer and employee constitute without a doubt the key to the business relations of the future, it may be understood why Mr. Schwab has never had a strike among his men.

headline: FAMILIAR COIN
text:
Already this year we have sent another £342,111 in gold bullion or Russia. Russia is a large place, and it is not all under the Soviet Government, so probably there is a simple explanation.

There is, at any rate, no indication in the imports of any Bolshevik gold coming to this country in a solid form.

Travellers tell us that Great Britain is about the only place in the world now in which it is difficult to come by an English sovereign. We have been broadcasting them for a long time past. Should you travel in Albania, you will find the sovereign well represented in the very much mixed coinage of that country. Among the Arabs on the shores of the Red Sea the sovereign is a familiar and highly-prized coin. Already this year two and a half millions have gone to India.

It is, perhaps, the best advertisement this country could have, for the sovereign is always "worth its weight in gold" and can now hold its head up, even in the company of dollars.

headline: BRIFISH CAPITAL IN CANADA. / RAILWAY CHIEF'S ADVICE.
text: Mr. E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, addressing the Quebec division of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, emphasised the importance of encouraging the investment of British capital in Canada. The British investor, he said, both on patriotic and national grounds, would, under proper conditions, prefer this country to any other portion of the world, but Canadians should not create the impression that this was not a country in which honest investments were given proper protection. "Whatever we may do to encourage the introduction of capital, we should see that it is entitled to such a measure of just protection as will place the burden of failure, if failure ensues, on its own administration, and not upon the country's fiscal political policies." Mr. Beatty's reference follows the publication of British Press comment on the Canadian railway situation.

headline: CONTRACTS WE LOSE.
text:
A novel suggestion for stimulating British shipbuilding and shipping industries was made at Jarrow at the launching of a collier for the South Metropolitan Gas Co. by Mr. G. F. Mulherion. He said: "There are many reasons why foreign shipbuilders should undercut British builders, but the way the Government allows British money to go abroad while British workmer are starving is another question.

"In my opinion it is a question whether import duties should not be imposed on ships built abroad rather than allow money to go on contracts abroad which could do so much good at home... It may strike the German mind that if they were to spend £50,000,000 a year they could ruin the industries of this country."

SHAMEEN SHOOTING: -- (Router's Service), Canton, June 25.- Replying to the protott of the Civil Governor of Canton with regard to the shooting of June 23, the British Consul General has omphatically repudiated the Governor's allegation that foreign officials at Carton were responsible for the affair and has requested the Governor to take very complete measures to safeguard the lives of Britons at Canton.

HOML LABOUR VIEWS (Router) London, Juno 25:--- The General Council of the Trade Union Congress on the National Executive of the Labour Party at a joint meeting in London passed a resolution declaring that disgraceful working conditions in Chinese mills are the immediate cause of the present disturbance in China. The resolution expresses the opinion that immediate steps should be taken to carry out in the Treaty Ports the recommendations of the Shanghai Child Labour Commission and to assist the Chinese Government to give general effect to their recent factory act and raise the general conditions of Chinese workers. The extracerritorial regime is provocative and dangerous and should be ended as soon as possible by an international conference on British initiative. The proposed conference on Chinese tariffs gives the opportunity for such initiative in respect of the Treaty Ports.

SHANGHAI STUDENT PLOT (Router) Shanghai, June 25:--- The Police yesterday obtained information of a widespread student plot to hire motor-cars and dash round the International Settlement bombing and shooting. The Police ordered garages not to hire cars except to well-known customers. The special constables were mobilised and posted at strategic points. Young Chinese were searched for arms and other precautions were taken. The shipping situation is becoming worse. British and Japanese ocean-going ships are avoiding Shanghai.

FRANCE PROTESTS (Router) Peking, Juno 25:-- The Fronch Minister has handed the Chinosé Foreign Ministor a note protesting against the killing of a French merchant at Canton on Tuesday and roserving the right to claim reparation. Twenty thousand students, workman and merchants paraded the streets carrying banners, some of which were inscribed "Declare war against England!" Chinese troops and police guarded foreign premises, also the entrancos to the Logation quarter, but there was no sign of any disturbances.

headline: STRIKE MALADY
text:
2 p.m. to 4 p.m.

It is possible to add to established optimism by regarding conditions as they are at the moment in the light of a sickness. There have been the symptoms, then the outbreak leading either to a crisis or a quick suppression; and in the case of the former to convalescence and complete recovery. This view indicates that a resumption of normal Hongkong life is merely a matter of time. This being so the continuation of marking time in strict measure, if it needs not to be urged, can lose nothing by being emphasised. The community has been given a distinct, direct and clear lead by H. E. the Governor. For this let us give due credit. In addition the recognised leading foreign firms and institutions have nobly ridden the storm. No praise can be too lavish in commenting on the arrangements so promptly initiated and so efficiently maintained. It is in the main due to this happy triumph of maintaining the supply of essential service that really matters — the supply of food — that the spirit of equanimity is so strongly evident to which has to be added the knowledge that the Colony has had a pistol placed at its head which, probably to the surprise of those who have held it has misfired. Attention has been diverted to Canton and to the happenings there. As in Hongkong, so in Canton! There is no case to answer and nothing of which to be ashamed. The spirited action of the British Com

sul there has won commendation by its absolute fearlessness and its insistence on the truth. Blood-shed is to be deplored but those who resort to it must expect reprisals. All this but skims the cream of the present situation behind which the evil of anti-foreignism backed by the worst forces of Bolshevism lurk. The simile of sickness suffices for the time being. The disease has spread, but the doctors have the case well in hand and the time seems rapidly drawing in sight when the patient arriving at convalescence will sit up and take n'urishment—of common sense.

headline: A LIVELY CROWD / POLICE DISPERSE CROWD CLEARING A WHARF
text:
Large crowds attempted to board the Tung On as she lay alongside the wharf this morning and they became so insistent in their demands that a certain amount of force had to be used by the police in clearing the wharf.

One man, even then, broke away and taking a flying leap, managed to get aboard. The crowd seemed to be under the impression that the boat was leaving at once for Canton but it only went as far as the naval yard where, it is believed supplies for Shameen are to be put on board.

The Tung On, also it is thought, the Sai On and Charles Bardouin will leave later for Canton.

headline: CANTON QUIET
text:
SAMSHUI

Canton is still quiet, the China Mail learned upon enquiry from the naval authorities who appear to be the only well informed source of information at the present time.

Agitators are reported to have gone from Canton to Samshui in an endeavour to stir up trouble there.

(Samshui is a treaty port further up the West River.)

headline: STRIKE ITEM
text:
House boys and amahs are said to have returned in large numbers in the Happy Valley district and asked to be taken back.

The 'Bus service instituted by the Hongkong Hotel to Causeway Bay and Happy Valley has proved very popular indeed. With two motors on the run a half-hour service is maintained.

PROPAGANDA. RESTRICTED Government and Canton Gazette

A prominent position is given in Thursday's issue of this organ of the Canton Bolsheviks to the alleged resolutions of the American staff of the Canton Christian College and streamer headlines on the front page state that "the massacre has contributed another sacrifice on the altar of foreign imperialism."

Another streamer heading on an inside page announces that the Hongkong Government is “terror stricken” by the general strike.

headline: ANTI-FOREIGN STRIKE ENDS (Reuter's Service.) Shanghai June 26th.
text:
This morning's developments terminate the anti-foreign strike in Shanghai, but do not affect the industrial strike which is virtually a boycott aimed principally at the British and Japanese. The Chamber of Commerce last night formally requested the re-opening of the shops and banks of which 70 per cent. acquiesced.

At 9 o'clock crowds in the streets watched the distribution of Chamber of Commerce handbills which were viewed with some suspicion, but in order to ensure the public confidence in them a delegation consisting of the Foreign Commissioner, the Prefect in Chief of the Shanghai-Woosung Constabulary, the Chinese City Magistrate, and representatives of the Chamber of Commerce and federated unions made a procession through the streets in motors bearing flags inscribed "Shops should be opened. The Government takes full responsibility for negotiations." After this the hesitators opened their doors.

headline: STUDENTS' BIG IDEAS
text:
A meeting of the Shanghai Students' Union yesterday afternoon resolved to appeal to the students all over the country to learn the art of war and be ready to fight for their country, to appeal to the patriotism of the militarists and select lecturers to arouse the people and soldiers.

A programme for wide student demonstrations yesterday was largely a fiasco-owing to official prohibitions, while precautions in Shanghai completely frustrated the student activities. Many Volunteers and "Specialists" have been withdrawn from the streets which appear normal this afternoon.

Two Japanese destroyers from Pescadores have gone to Amoy and Canton.

headline: HOPEFUL AUGURY
text:
For the first time since the beginning of the strike the Central Market stalls were manned with a limited number of workers this morning and meat was to be obtained.

This, the Food Controller, Mr. N. L. Smith, told a China Mail representative, is due to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in placing men at the disposal of the Government. The Government has promised the owners all along that if their men left they would see to the slaughtering and preparation of the animals also the delivering of meat to the market in vans and the owners had replied that it was as much as their lives were worth to allow it to be sold.

The action of the Tung Wah hospital will probably lead to greater confidence, however. The start is only in a small way at present, Mr. Smith informed the China Mail, but there was plenty of beef and pork in stock and the supply in the market he hoped would gradually increase.

Mr. Smith further informed the China Mail that owing to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in selling rice cheaply the Chinese retailers had this morning been forced to bring their prices down and rice was now to be had at almost below pre-strike cost. Notices were now up at the shops that owing to the price charged by the Tung Wah Hospital the price would be reduced to $7.00 a picul. As much as $14.00 had been charged just recently, said Mr. Smith, which was exorbitant as there was a plentiful supply here.

With regard to firewood, the next most important item in the poor man's budget, as Mr. Smith remarked, it had been found upon inquiry that there was about two months' supply in the Colony. Mr. Harold Seth had been appointed Firewood controller under Mr. Smith and the question was being considered as to whether the Government would have to make purchases elsewhere.

So far he had avoided Government purchase of any supplies, said Mr. Smith.

headline: SHAMEEN SHOOTING
text:
Dr. Alexander Baxter, Vice-President of the Canton Christian College, yesterday retracted statements attributed to the seventeen American staff members at the College, in which blame and responsibility for what the statement termed “the merciless and unjustified assault” rests entirely on those who directed the firing from Shameen.

This statement expressed to "our Chinese colleagues, students and friends" deep-felt sympathy and support. The world had been inadequately informed of the Chinese viewpoint, continued the statement, and the signatories were determined to co-operate with the Chinese in the presentation of their case.

The statement attributed to the Shameen troops the firing of the first shots and stated that the parade was proceeding in an orderly manner and was composed largely of students and workmen unarmed and defenceless.

In a statement signed yesterday in the presence of Sir Claude Severn, Mr. W. W. Hornell, Vice President of the Hongkong University, and Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Mr. Baxter said that he could not say whether the translation of which the above is an extract was a correct one of what he and his colleagues had signed. The Chinese masters had informed them of the gist of it and had asked that it should be made available at once for publication.

Students from the College had returned after the firing and had stated that their procession had been fired on without firing on their side. They produced blood-stained clothes. Their story was corroborated in every detail by trustworthy members of the Chinese staff and had been accepted, as Dr. Baxter and Dr. Henry the President of the College, had been unable to get to Shameen themselves.

Since this statement had been signed, stated Dr. Baxter, in his retraction yesterday, he had been entirely satisfied from what he had gathered from eyewitnesses that the firing started from the Chinese side. He had not been aware of the fact that the statement had been directed to the American public with the hope that America would do her best to assist China in securing just treatment and in realising her aims to free herself from foreign Imperialism.

headline: HONGKONG AMERICAN'S VIEW
text:
The following letter expressing the opinion of the American community of Hongkong as to the Shameen shooting has been signed by as many members of the American community as could be reached in a short space of time this morning.

The letter is addressed to the Editor of the China Mail and is as follows:—

Sir,— On account of the serious implications and consequences involved in the statement of the American members of the foreign staff of the Canton Christian College as expressed in the resolutions originally printed in the Canton Gazette, we, the undersigned members of the American Community in Hongkong, desire to place on record our emphatic disapproval of the action of the parties concerned, whose entire lack of judgment and restraint at such a time, we consider deplorable.

Although a retraction has been made and published, which places the resolutions originally printed we wish to leave the Hongkong Community in no doubt as to our attitude.

headline: DURING THE
text:

being done to make the slogan "business as usual" as definite as sounds. If the ferret are able to maintain a satisfactory service suitable to the times and the Peak Tramway also, why not be lower level trams? If the Hongkong Hotel, Wisemans and the Dairy Farm are able to maintain their eminently essential service, why not a few others who, up to a few days ago were doing satisfactory business? The hotel has imported assistance of a type that has made that great concern function so happily. It has met the situation without complaint or exercise and in this way helped not a little in the large feeling of security equanimity and determination which exists. The Colony has placed itself in a position of what may be termed defence. If another week of ineptitude on the part of the strikers is to be our lot, the suggestion of either importing assistance or diverting the time and energy of such workers as the volunteers to some of the essential services indicated, should be seriously considered, and whilst a settlement of our present inconveniences may depend on what takes place in Shanghai, the fact that Canton is not so many miles distant should not be lost sight of. It is to Canton that all eyes should be turned. British equity, justice, and consideration, has again been despised and trodden under root. There is a suspicion of envy mixed with hatred and uncharitableness—perhaps what is known as sour grapes—in the thinking and proceedings which have led to the building of a cul-de-suc which can only be razed by those who have, maus it. This we trust, has not been lost sight of by those who, profiting by past and present experience, should know how to act. headline: WOMAN KILLED
text:
A young Chinese woman Chung Ching-tung received a mortal wounds from two men who attacked her as she was selling pork in the Western district yesterday.

The men are reported to have stopped her and asked the price of the pork and on receiving the reply "70 cents per cattle" the alleged attack was made. The woman's most severe wounds were on the head.

Another attack allegedly on the instigation of men concerned in the trade was that on a man who was also engaged in selling pork. This man was seriously injured.

Today's cables from the principal centres in China inhabited by foreigners should that the situation is "not, although precautions are, just outbreaks are not being relaxed. Foreign women and children have been evacuated from the port of Hoihow. Strikers on land and sea continue considerably to affect shipping, but improvised measures are being taken. Messages from Hongkong state that over twenty ships have been tied up owing to the desertion of the crews. Canton messages state that the Shameen is now plenifully supplied with food, the warship Khaki having brought a large shipment from Hongkong.

Advices from Peking state that the Powers represented at the conference with the Chinese will investigate the events in Shanghai by the American Italian and French Ministers.— Reuter.

headline: STRIKE PAY.
text: On every hand the decision reached by the Hongkong Hotel management on the subject of returning employees is welcomed. It is a clear lead to the rest of the community. There is no suspicion of harshness. The strikers have "dismissed themselves." If they desire to be reinstated they will have to forfeit their wages for June and "sign on" as any entirely new servant would.

The following are the latest reports from the outports:—SWATOW:—The situation is not so satisfactory. Agitators have been attempting to board British ships. Protection from H.M.S. Bluebell has been necessary. The crews of ships are unwilling to strike and are remaining on board. Conditions for strikers ashore are very unsatisfactory. The accommodation is bad and insanitary, causing sickness. Food is inadequate and the strike is unpopular. A demonstration has been arranged for tomorrow.

Later last night a mob broke out and was breaking up foreign hotels and property along the Customs Bund. An armed party was landed on the Customs Bund by H.M.S. Bluebell. The mob quietened down shortly afterwards and moved away. The armed party re-embarked early this morning. To-day all is quiet. The houseboys have decided to come out this afternoon.

WUCHOW:—The women and children are being evaluated and escorted to Hongkong by H.M.S. Moorhen. There is nothing further to report.

CANTON:—The situation has improved. All is quiet.

A new Government was inaugurated yesterday consisting of seventeen members.

HOIHOW:--- The situation is satisfactory. Submarine L.33 has sailed for Hongkong and is due to-day.

KONGMOON & SAMSHUI: Nothing to report.

headline: STRIKE SITUATION. / LITTLE CHANGE TO REPORT.
text:
FEWER PEOPLE LEAVE.

There is no material change to report in the strike situation generally.

"Star" Ferry.

Manned by Mercantile Marine men from ships which are lying idle the “Star” Ferry boats are maintaining a twenty minute service across the harbour.

Efforts were made earlier in the morning to speed things up a bit and to run a ten minute service but the operatives had not thoroughly mastered the workings of their new charges and after one boat had overtaken another and then had to lay to for about a quarter of an hour "so near and yet so far" the twenty minute service was reverted and substantially kept to.

Boys returning from the markets to-day report that there is no meat to be had in Hongkong or Kowloon. They also report a scarcity of vegetables.

Enquiries at the offices of the Food Controller elicited the information that there were plenty of supplies in the Colony but there had been a slight hitch in the sorting and preparation. This would be remedied as soon as possible. The Food Controller was not aware of any scarcity of vegetables.

A Chinese, who was charged with attempting to export a sum of $40 contrary to the regulations, failed to appear at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning. Bail of $50 was estreated, and the other money was also confiscated.

headline: STRIKE ITEMS.
text:
In spite of the teahouse workers being on strike, several places were open yesterday. They were "sold out" in less than an hour.

"Some of the native banking and commercial institutions, including the Sun Co., Ltd., are remitting money to Canton, for the public, at a fee of 2 per cent.

More laundry washermen are reported to be on strike this morning and there are reports of a few houseboys having left after receiving their month's wages.

Chinese shops are closing a little earlier during the strike, including the department stores.

The number of empty flats and vacant sub-tenements in the outlying districts has increased.

Police Reservists are joining up in appreciable numbers...daily. Chinese special police are now on duty even at Yaumati. Others are attached to police pickets and some are on duty at the "Star" Ferry wharf.

That the Shameen are well able to carry on with essential work is instanced by the fact that the services were courteously refused of a detachment of Royal Engineers despatched from Hongkong. They arrived back here yesterday morning on the s.s. Tung On.

Imagine the surprise of a Volunteer who went for his rifle at Headquarters and found that in its place had been left one of which the Army number (running into five figures) was that of the one which had served him throughout his period of war service. A truly amazing coincidence but, none the less, true.

A large crowd of strikers have congregated at Sumchun and it is reported that a party of sight-seers, Chinese clerks, still at work but desirous of seeing what things are like on the border, received a rather hostile reception when it became apparent that they were not new recruits. The clerks are said to have contented themselves by watching from British territory whereupon imprecations and threats were hurled at them from across the railway bridge. Revenue Officers at Hongkong whose duties are in the ordinary way confined to in-coming ships are now dealing with ships going out, thus enabling the police to concentrate on in-coming boats. The police have thus been enabled to prevent undesirables from entering the Colony. Interviewed by a Chinese reporter regarding restrictions on money and valuables taken out of the Colony, Mr. Lloyd stated that jewels and diamond rings can be taken out of the Colony by their side passenger. headline: JUSTICE AND FAIRPLAY.
text:
Sir Oracle hath spoken. That oracle is David Z.T. Yui, General Secretary of the National Committee of the Y.M.C.A. for China, who has the temerity to address an open letter to the public dealing with the situation in China and a possible way out of the tangle in which the Chinese students and rioters have got themselves and the Chinese nation.

Montgomery, Ollerton & Co. 10, Des Vœux Road Central.

The letter is not worth repulsion in full. Some of the points therein do not coincide with facts. Some of them raise issues which cannot be settled by means of an "open letter" to the public. Condensed, his plea is merely for a special commission of inquiry to be appointed jointly by the British and Chinese authorities. He praises the Chinese for their "love"

CUBIC YARDS OF EARTH MOVED PER DAY BY OUR STEAM ROYEL EQUIPMENT

"love of fairplay," which should not stand in the way of Chinese being on the Commission. Lastly, he suggests an invitation to "some other fair-minded nationals" to join them on the Commission which he proposes to create.

Evidently Mr. David Z. T. Yui realises that the Chinese students, rioters, and strikers have done China the worst turn for many a long year, and that it is time to do something constructive to stay the rot. That is the impression gained from his penultimate paragraph in his "open letter," which reads as under:—

May we pause for a moment to think of the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves, the amount of self-sacrifices to no good, the real dangers to peace and order not only in the Far East but in the entire world, and the tremendous damage to the international friendships involved? Do we not desire to free us from all these at the earliest possible moment? We believe without doubt that it is altogether within our power either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify and end it within a very short time. Are we not wise, just, courageous, and large-hearted enough to choose to do the constructive and fundamental and therefore more difficult-ish? That admission from an educated Chinese—“the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves”—is worth noting in any discussion of the situation. Likewise the Chinese gentleman in question believes that it is “without doubt within the power of the Chinese either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify it and end it within a very short time.” If Mr. David Z. T. Yui would go a step further and endeavour to inculrate some of these rational ideas into his compatriots in Shanghai and Peking, he would be performing a meritorious service for China. Propaganda of this kind is really more required in the big central of China than outside them. Let him get on with the good work in this direction alone, and leave international issues arising out of what he terms “the tragic event” or may go to be senior berwer China and the interested Power in the hours.

headline: REGISTRATION
text: hitherto responsible for lesser skilled work had been (unknowingly, of course) re-engaged by the police as coolies to relieve the situation at the docks and godowns occasioned a certain amount of resentment. Those upon whom devolves the duty of selection among the crowds of coolies daily congregating at the police headquarters in the hope of being assigned work at the appointed scale of wages consider that they are entitled to more confidence in their ability to select between the good and the bad sheep. Their claim is not without justification in view of their long experience of that particular type of Chinese mentality—a glance at the hands and features and an experienced officer would probably be able to tell at once whether a man was, for instance, a dock hand or a scavenger, coolie. But such methods are after all not infallible, and unless some scheme of registration is introduced there will always be the possibility of strikers from a poorly paid service seeking more remunerative work which in addition guarantees them police protection on the spot. Such a scheme of registration might even be extended to more highly skilled grades of labour for the purpose of distinguishing strikers and workers. Certificates, with photographs of their rightful owners attached, might be deemed impracticable; but something certainly ought to be done to draw a distinguishing line between those who are helping in this time of crisis and those whose presence is but a burden.

headline: DOSSERS' TRIAL
text:
In the Mixed Court before the Chinese Magistrate and the British Assessor, Mr. Fischer, Counsel for Mr. and Mrs. Dosser, applied for at least a fortnight's remand on the grounds that the first charge (of making preparations to commit a hostile action against certain Foreign States) was incomplete and did not specify the countries; likewise the second and third charges were incomplete because no dates were mentioned.

[The'second and third' charges were of possessing literature likely to cause a breach of the peace and menacing the order of the Foreign Settlement.]

The Court replied that the Shanghai Municipal Police was an international body whose duty was to protect all nations. Therefore the objections would be overruled.

Mr. Fischer then challenged the Court's jurisdiction, pointing out that since the Revolution the Consular Body had appointed the Chinese Mixed Court Magistrates and entirely controlled the Mixed Court, consequently the Chinese Government did not recognise the Mixed Court as in Chinese Court; while by the Sino-Russian agreement of October 1924, Soviet citizens in China must be tried by the Chinese Court. Therefore the Mixed Court had no jurisdiction over the Dossers.

The Court again overruled Mr. Fischer's objection, the British Assessor stating that he had the most definite instructions from the Consular body with regard to hearing all Russian cases, criminal and civil.

Mr. Fischer's third plen was that he had not received all relevant documents from the police. The Court replied that the documents which he had not received would not be admitted for hearing to-day.

Inspector Yorke gave evidence of arrest, and described the documents found in the luggage of the accused, also a telegram which Dosser handed to the Captain of the steamship Mantua, informing the Soviet Consul at Shanghai that he was de-tained in Hongkong to be forcibly deported to Shanghai, and adding an urgent request that Peking should be informed. The Captain refused to wireless this message. The hearing was adjourned until Monday.

headline: APPEAL TO REASON
text:
LETTER TO CHINESE RESIDENTS

SOME PERTINENT FACTS

You are now living under the fairest government in the world. This is no ill-considered statement and if you have visited other countries and studied their government you must admit its truth. There is no place under the sun where anyone has as much personal liberty as here. You can carry on your life and trade with the minimum of governmental regulation and restriction. You are guaranteed and you receive absolute justice without a suspicion of discrimination on account of race, creed, colour, or condition of life. Your customs and religion are respected without interference of any nature. This colony is administered by a set of men who have made a life study of the science of government; without question they are men of education, probity and sound judgment. They and their predecessors have turned a barren rock into a beautiful healthy spot with a superb system of roadways, excellent sanitation, adequate schools and free hospitals. In all of this you share equally yet taxes are so low that they are comparatively negligible.

And yet you listen to cries of British Imperialism! Fraternalism if you will, paternalism if you must, but not Imperialism in an invidious sense. Do you think you might obtain equal benefits in republics such as France or the United States? Though a citizen of the latter country, I am regretfully forced to tell you that you would not; it is not that the American friendship for China is not sincere, or that you would be discriminated against, but not even its own people have the privileges you receive here. If this be true, what are you doing to assure a continuation of your unique condition? You are alive to the fact that this community cannot exist without trade, principally with South China, and if Bolshevism conquers in Canton, depression will follow here with destitution, misery and want in its wake. The burden will fall on you far more heavily than on the foreigner who can transfer his sphere of activity elsewhere.

There is not a single thing that the Hongkong Government or a member of this community can do to settle the Shanghai or Shameen incidents. The unprovoked walk-out cannot assist the settlement, cannot hasten or retard it. Except for a slight inconvenience to some foreigners, this strike appears to be principally directed against you; surely you must realize that in many ways you are the ultimate losers. The time has come for a show of sanity; a firm courageous word from you will stop this silly procedure at once. The Government has guaranteed you safety and you are convinced that you can trust its guarantee. You know or you can easily find out who these cowardly agitators are you alone can curb their activities; you can kill the silly canards passed among the ignorant here and widely quoted in China. Are you willing to protect your future? Your choice is clear—do you wish peace and prosperity or chaos and penury? Do not listen to hard-brained missionaries; pay no attention to irresponsible, poorly posted politics in America and France.

headline: GOLD MEDAL.
text:
HIGHEST REWARD FOR AMUNDSEN.

Amundsen and his companions have arrived by air from Horten. They were accorded a most enthusiastic welcome. The Polar fliers' aeroplane was escorted to Oslo by five Army and five Navy aeroplanes all of which descended into the harbour to the accompaniment of salutes of the fortress.

A Norwegian cruiser, vessels of the British Naval Squadron now visiting the port and steamers in harbour sirened the people aboard. Crowds ashore cheered, the streets of the city were gaily decorated.

Amundsen and his party received a cordial reception from President Storting, chairman of the Oslo Municipality.

The aviators subsequently drove to the Palace where the King presented Amundsen with a gold medal for a patriotic deed, the highest distinction only held by two living persons.

The other members of the party were decorated with the order of Stoslay.

headline: PLAIN TALK.
text:
Earl Crawford, the former Cabinet Minister, speaking at Gillingham, said the time had come for the British Government to give clear and unmistakable warning to Russia that continued organisation of anti-British attacks in China, India and elsewhere would result in the breaking of Anglo-Russian diplomatic relations.

Britain was. tiring of these underhand, underground attacks and was determined to end them.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE / SHANGHAI TRADE.
text:
The result of the year's trade at Shanghai came as a surprise to the mercantile community in general, says Mr. L. de Lana. Statistical Secretary of the Maritime Customs, in his 1924 report. Throughout the year there had been a feeling of depression, trade was reported as dull and featureless, profits as unsatisfactory, and yet the Shanghai Customs Returns show, in round numbers, a revenue collection of Hk. Tls. 27,500,000, an increase on the 1923 collection of no less than Hk. Tls. 3,640,000, the bulk of which—Hk. Tls. 3,470,000—was derived from import duties alone. Furthermore the gross value of the import trade was Hk. Tls. 488,000,000, an increase on the preceding year of Hk. Tls. 65,000,000. It should be noted also that the greater portion of the increase in revenues—Hk. Tls. 2,800,000—was reached during the first six months of the year, which represented a period of comparative peace and freedom from political disturbances. Trade during the September and December quarters was much less satisfactory, in consequence of political complication and fighting in and around the port.

To enter into a minute study of the causes which contributed to the expansion more especially of the import trade and to the discrepancy existing between the good results achieved—from the point of view of Customs revenue—and the general fdeling of dissatisfaction prevailing in the mercantile community would be beyond the limits and scope of this report; never-the-less, a brief enumeration of some of the causes which may be taken as an explanation of the situation will not be amiss.

In the first place, it should be remembered that Shanghai is the principal entrepot of China and that not all the trade that comes to it is for the local market; a good share of it is destined from the outset for other trade centres, principally the northern and Yangtze ports. In fact, the total value of foreign imports re-exported to Chinese ports was Hk. Tls. 174,000,000 which, when the value of foreign re-exports to Hongkong and foreign countries—Hk. Tls. 12,700,000—is added, leaves a net value of foreign imports into Shanghai of about 301 million tnels, and increase on the 1923 figures of about 57 millions.

Secondly, German competition, which had been practically extinguished during the European War and for some time afterwards is now reviving: thirdly, the Chinese are said to be doing more direct trade, instead of through the intermediary of foreigners, and several large Chinese firms have their own buyers in Europe and America; and, lastly, the cessation of the anti-Japanese boycott on the Yangtze and at some of the coast ports has enabled Japan to take a more active part in the import trade of China, which, in her case, was favoured also by the low value of the yen.

The report and accounts having been in your hands, for some days, with your permission I will take them as read. In spite of the continued depression in shipping and shipbuilding during the years under review the net profits is just over Tls. 100,000 more than the previous year. An interim dividend of 5 per cent. was paid and it is now proposed to pay a final dividend of 9 per cent. and carry forward Tls. 172,444,50. It was considered unnecessary to increase the reserve account which now stands at Tls. 1,250,000 or the depreciation account standing at Tls. 750,000, but it is felt that a somewhat larger carry forward is necessary owing to the present strike, which has now been in force amongst the dock company's Chinese staff for over six weeks. With regard to the land belonging to the company, your directors have come to the conclusion, after very careful consideration, that we have a greater area than required and that the land between the International Dock and Cosmopolitan Dock can best be spared. The Cosmopolitan Dock requires lengthening and repairing and two schemes have been considered:

-Lengthening and repairing the Cosmopolitan Dock, leaving for sale an area of 110 mow between the Dock and International Dock with a river frontage of 1,300 feet.

2.—Making a new Cosmopolitan Dock alongside the International Dock, leaving for sale an area of 140 mow with 1,800 feet river frontage.

Both these plots of land have a deep water frontage, in fact as deep as any in the harbour, and we are now prepared to consider offers for either; plans being obtainable from the manager, Mr. Burns. We are not in any immediate hurry to dispose of this land but the decision as to whether we shall remove or merely repair Cosmopolitan Dock will be dependent, to a certain extent, upon the offers received. If necessary we are prepared to consider part of the purchase price being covered by a mortgage. In order to increase our ability to handle every class of work, improve the quarters for employees, and generally improve the value of your property, we have authorized the expenditure of about Tls. 500,000 spread over a year or 18 months; this will considerably reduce our cash on deposit and in current account, and as we do not consider a return of capital under Tls. 25 per share worth while, the matter of reducing the capital will have to be left in abeyance until the land near the Cosmopolitan Dock is sold. On behalf of the directors, and I feel sure I may say the shareholders as well, I should like to thank Mr. Burns and the staff for the able and loyal manner in which they have carried out their work during the year under review and I trust the bonus and the provident fund, which is at last in proper working order, will be appreciated. In this connection we have decided to appoint Mr. W. S. Burns, who has been with the company 26 years, managing director, a step which I am sure will be appreciated both by our clients and staff. Before closing I consider it advisable to say a few words regarding the strike and prospects of future business. That the former is caused by agitators is beyond question and the fact that we have received numerous letters from Chinese employees who have been with us for 40 or 50 years, stating that they are perfectly satisfied with their pay and the treatment they have received, is sufficient testimony to the fair manner in which the company has dealt with them in the past, and the fact that but for these agitators they would never have ceased work. It is difficult to deal with the prospects for the future but a good deal of work is waiting to be done directly the strike is over and our strong financial position enables us, even at the present time, to look forward to the future with equanimity if not with optimism.

headline: GFRMAN CREDIT
text:
Hamburg: July 1.—Moscow reports that Krupps Germain Werft at Kiel, and the Deutsche Werft at Hamburg have offered to the shipping department of the Soviet Government to build ships for Russia on a basis of allowing 90 per cent. of the contract price to be paid out of profits for the ensuing 10 and, if necessary, 15 years.

The full reconstruction programme of the Soviet shipping department is said to provide for the construction of 208 new units, with a total capacity of 733,000 tons.

According to the Russian press it was stúbed at a meeting in Moscow that the present Russian mercantile fleet has inherited from its predecessor, the State Mercantile Fleet, a deficit of 4,242,000 rubles, in addition to which it is notorious that the present working capital has for some time past been quite inadequate. The Soviet administration with its usual optimism hopes to do a great deal with the promise of 1,800,000 rubles placed at the disposal of the shipping board by the council of labour and defence.

headline: Other Credit Inclinations.
text: This inclination on the part of Germany to give credit to Russian customers is also seen in the case of German exports to Russia. According to the Fremdenblatt, practically all the goods bought in Germany for Russia either through the medium of the Commercial Mission in Berlin or by the agents of the various Soviet States trusts and syndicates are purchased on the credit system. The German exporting firms are as a rule content with a cash payment of 50 per cent or in some cases of only 25 per cent of the sum due, the remainder being payable on short term credits. The reality is that the German export trade in Russia rises and falls according to the willingness of the seller to with for his money. It is estimated that on an average goods to the value of 2,000,000 gold marks are as present being exported each working day from Germany.

headline: GET MARRIED.
text:
To encourage marriages and raising families among Moros in P. Islands, a bill will be presented by Representative Jose P. Melencio, from Mindanao and Sulu, providing for rubber land concessions for every married person in Mindanao and Sulu. Each qualified individual would get 24 hectares, the author of the measure believing that a greater area could not be cultivated properly by one family with small capital.

Rep. Melencio said that the bill will be presented without prejudice to whatever measures the legislature may enact regarding rubber land concessions to corporations. He believes however that his bill would do much to stimulate cultivation of rubber. The cost of the rubber seeds as well as the capital advanced to the homesteaders would constitute a loan by the Government; to be paid annually until fully paid, from the produce of the land. The homesteads granted by virtue of the Act could not be alienated or encumbered by its owners, and in case of default of heirs would revert to the Government.

headline: CHINA MISSIONS.
text:
FACTORS LEADING TO PRESENT UNREST

ARCHIDEACON BARNETT'S COMMENT.

No-one is better qualified to write on the present and past situation in South China as it affects missionary work than the late Archidencon, the Ven. E. J. Barnett, who devoted over 20 years of his life to such service. The extent to which mission work is affected by recent disorders in China has already been referred to, also the decision of missionary bodies to hand over supervision, temporarily at any rate, to Chinese, and it is interesting to note that Archidecon Barnett has contributed to the August number of the "Church Missionary Outlook" an illuminating article on the factors leading up to the present unrest. The author of Church Notes and News in the "Telegraph" comments as follows on this article:—

Archdeacon Burnett takes the view that the present serious crisis is more deep-seated than the Boxer outbreak, and more dangerous, because there is recognised reasonableness in certain of the demands. The chaotic condition of robber-ridden China, under so many independent military rulers, doubtless favours the anti-foreign agitator. But the root cause, he points out, is a hideous sense of humiliation which, if it is to be removed, demands (so they are taught) desperate measures. Neither economic nor industrial conditions alone would have produced the present upheaval. It is an attempt to wipe out what is regarded as an intolerable national reproach. The means being used to that end are improper and illegal, but they are prompted by a new and sinister influence which has of late worked its way into Chinese politics.

headline: account for much.
text:
In judging the Chinese today the archdeacon warns us not to forget that they can boast an historic past which is millennium older than that of the Western peoples whom they regard as their oppressors. They are conscious of capabilities and intellectual powers which will well compare with those of others. It is therefore mental agony to the later educated generation to realise that their great country, with all its immeasurable possibilities, hags so far behind Japan and the Western peoples in their forward march. For their backward position they blame (not altogether justly) the Great Powers, who in the past have imposed upon them trenties which they now demand shall be revised. The archdeacon concludes his review of the position by saying that it is not all evil is certain, for the motive is one which all fair-minded Christians must respect. During the past decade we ourselves learned anew what patriotism means. Patriotism is now the dynamic of Chinese discontent. Without belittling the students' serious mistakes, it is through the exercise of Christian virtues—love, sympathy, patience—that we, with unfailing prayer, can best set forward God's own remedy for China's present troubles.

Writing from Shaolisingfu, Chekingu, under date June 30, the Rev. T. Grant ends an account of local conditions by saying: "Our Chinese Christian fellow-workers and friends remain friendly to us; though taking the Chinese point of view in the Shanghai affair. I think they are beginning to see our point of view more clearly now, as the truth comes out. I believe that none of the Chinese newspapers has published, true accounts, with all the facts, of the troubles, and, consequently, a great many lies have been believed by the Chinese, much to the detriment of the good names of the foreign sojourners in the country."

Geneva, September 9.—The Turkish memorandum on the Mosul question has been published. It is largely an attempt to refute the arguments of Mr. Amery and contends that the League of Nations will be acting in opposition to the League Covenant if it prolongs the British mandate. It adheres to the proposal to take a plebiscite in the disputed Mosul region.—Reuter.

headline: SILVER AND ELECTRO-PLATE
text:
Sheffield, July 29. — The Sheffield silver and electro-plate trades are passing through dull times again. The usual summer lethargy has been accentuated by a scarcity of big business from the colonies, which have been good buyers for some years. In the case of Australia the falling-off is most marked, especially in the better qualities of plated ware. Some firms who cater for buyers of cheaper qualities have booked some business with Australia, but from the point of view of value the trade has fallen off considerably. One of the striking features of the trade, both in electro-plate and nickel silver is the collapse at last of the phenomenal demand for spoons and forks. For over three years the resources of the factories have been taxed to meet the huge demand both for the home trade and export. Makers could not account for the extraordinarily heavy demand, and now they are at a loss to understand why it has collapsed. It had been sustained so long that they believed it had come to stay. Sterling silver sells extremely slowly. Best quality: electroplate, because of the relatively high price of nickel, is prohibitive in price to the average buyer, while electro-plate. Britannia metalware seems to meet the demands of the majority in these days of cutting down expenses. Stainless nickel has come to stay although progress with the sale of best qualities is slow. Italy is making a decided effort to increase the number of hebig trans-Atlantic vessels. The Navigazione Generale Italian Company is actively planning the construction of large vessels for passengers and cargo services. The company already possesses two big liners, the "Galliello" and the "Giulio Gessare and a third one, the "Borna" over 30,000 tons. It now read and will start service next year. The Compagnie de Commerce et de Navigation d'Extreme-Orient, of Saigon, in their market report dated September 9, state:—

Our market continues to be very quiet and the prices have made a further drop. Business with Hongkong and China is at a standstill; the demand from other markets is very poor. The ruins continue to be regular and planting is proceeding normally.

The Chilian Government has allotted 37,000,000 pesos for the construction of new bridges in various parts of the country, and 8,150,000 pesos (to be raised by an internal loan) for widening and paving the highways from the capital, Santiago to San Bernardo, one of its more important suburbs.

headline: EXPORTING MONEY / TRAIN TRAVELLER'S EXCUSE
text:
NOT CROHING THE BORDER.

An excuse that he was going in search of an employee who absccaded with $1,600 belonging to a foundry at Yaumati was tendered at the Nowloon Magistracy this morning when a Chinese was charged with attempting to export $15 from the Colony and thus contravening a strike emergency enactment which is still in force.

Sergeant Morton said he did not wish to press the charge as the defendant when arrested on the train yesterday had been quite straightforward and told the same story. In answer to a question, defendant said that he did not intend to cross the border. Another object of his journey was to await the arrival of his wife, who was on the Chinese side.

The money was returned to the defendant and he was discharged with a caution.

headline: EAST RIVER WAR.
text:
TERNITÓico GAINED BY

RAILWAY REPORTED OLEAB.

Considered an indication that the Reds have advanced materially from their original base in the campaign against the Chan Kwingming party, is the announcement by the Chinese section that passengers will again be carried on that part of the Kowloon-Canton Railway from Canton to Samchun, as from tomorrow.

At the height of their success, General Chan's army reached positions from which they could strike at vulnerable points on the railway. Civil transport was interrupted by frantic moves on Canton's part to rush reinforcements to the front. With the full of Wu-how the position—from Canton's point of view—has been eased.

headline: THE BOYCOTT
text:
LATEST UP-COUNTRY NEWS.

Pakkai, Kongmoon, Oct. 8. All firms here, with the exception of British, have resumed trade. The Marion Barclay Hospital (Candjan) and schools are still closed. The situation generally is normal. Business is dull. The harvest has been good. H.M.S. "Moorhen" and H.M.'s armed launch "Kwong Lee" were here during the greater part of

There is a shortage of kerosine and liquid fuel. Merchants have attempted to smuggle the commodity in but their junkshares seldom got through the atrike pickets' cordons. All seized cargoes are confiscated.

The s.s. "Leung Kwong" (formerly on the Hongkong-Kong-moon run) is now plying between Canton and Wuchow. The s.s. "Kung On" was removed from Pakkai to Kong Mei, the owners' village, for fear of being "requisitioned" by strikers or the military.

headline: Pirates Dispersed:
text:
Some of the men of the former commander at this port (Li Yatngok who fled to Hongkong after the first Red coup) have turned pirates, and established themselves at Pa Chung. A combined force of village guards and Kongmoon (Kuomintar) soldiers attacked the outlaws and dislodged them. Three pirates were captured. On his following being disbanded, Li Yatngok retired to Yanping, joining Leung Hungkal's remnants.

Pirates have often been active in the neighbourhood of this port. The Merchants' Volunteers (now known as the "M.F.T.en") have authority to patrol as before the Saikwan Massacre of a year ago. At present Commander Leung Hung-lam (a brother of Leung Hung-kai, the alleged anti-Red general detained at Whampoa) is at Chekhom and Yanping with his troops. General Li Chici-sum, the Red nominee, holds Summing, Kungvick and Sanwui but he himself is absent from the sphere of operations. Kongmoon is in the hands of Brigadier-General Chan Ming-shu.

Many junks have been commandeered to transport troops to Canton and communication with other river ports has been suspended for over a week but is now re-commencing.

During the present trooping season, there have been no pressgangs at work. Coolie volunteers are asked for. Even at $16 a month, there are very few coming forward. Accordingly the magistrate had ordered the prisoners on small offences to be put on to military transport.

headline: Miscellaneous Notes.
text:
The Commissioner of Police (Cheung Cho-wing) has been dismissed and Li Poon is in his place. The Commissioner of Customs is leaving for Home this month.

A Chinese who graduated in an American course of engineering has proposed establishing a waterworks at the top of Kwei Fung hill, outside Sanwui city. He is asking for subscriptions for shares and it is hoped that a modern supply of water will soon be available.

Saltfish is the only-import permitted from Macao but boats are now running here from Shekki.

Rice-mill workers are striking for higher pay. Negotiations have been going on and rice is a little higher. Premium on Hongkong banknotes (in exchange for Canton subsidiary silver coin) is 29 per cent.

It transpires that a Portuguese watchman was killed in the “Kwok Ning” piracy (reported previously in the “China Mail”).

headline: CANTON ITEMS / STRIKE PICKETS ASSIST
text:
FURTHER WEAKENING.

The action of the strike pickets in actually supervising the landing arrangements at Canton for passengers carried by the a.s. "Honam" on her last trip illustrates the general weakening of the strike directed against Hong Kong. The prices changed by the junka and sampans operating under their supervision are considerable and it is doubtless their need of such revenue that has led to the change of front, but the fact remains that no difficulty was experienced by passengers desirous of landing. The “Honam” left again this morning with 400 passengers, nearly all of whom were Chinese. The “Fatahan” will leave tomorrow. No arrangements have to be made by the Steamboat Company for the “special tugs” which were deemed necessary to navigate that portion of the river which the Canton Government has stated is mined; what actually occurs is that the signal to stop is given from the hillside off Bocca Tigris forts, whereupon a boat puts out, questions about cargo and passengers carried are asked and a pilot boat proceeds ahead, deviating but slightly from the usual route.

headline: TO DISARM STRIKERS?
text:
The strikers' executive have acquired considerable power in the absence of troops in the neighbourhood of the East River. The seizure of Annamite clerks in the employ of the Banque de l'Indo Chine is typical of their high handed actions. These clerks had walked through the French gate and presumably had the passes from the French Consul without which they are not allowed to pass through into Canton.

The disarming of the strikers upon the return of the troops from Wichow is looked upon as a certainty, as the Canton authorities are stated to have regarded the strikers' growing power with considerable uneasiness. but they have been powerless as yet to act in the matter.

headline: 1926 FIGURES
text:
Those who have been anxious regarding the position of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation, which has been an object of special attack during the last six months of trouble in Hongkong and Shanghai, will read the preliminary figures for 1925, just issued, with much gratification, states the "China Express & Telegraph".

Especially will they welcome the declaration that the final dividend, namely, £3 per share, with a bonus of £2 per share remains unaltered. This makes the usual distribution of £8 per share for the whole year, and when one considers the extremely chaotic state into which China has fallen and the boycott directed against British interests generally, the result can only be described as a highly satisfactory one for all concerned.

Of course, the Bank did not escape the attack unscathed. While it was able to write off $1,000,000 from Bank Premises Account, as in the previous year, and to carry forward about $3,400,000, virtually the same amount as it brought in it is noted that the new addition to Silver Reserve is to be only $500,000 as against $1,000,000 a year ago. This implies a reduction of about half a million dollars in net earnings, a loss which, in view of the conditions mentioned, comes as an agreeable surprise to many shareholders who feared that the Bank stood to suffer much more heavily.

The announcement of the usual dividend has allayed all fears, and public confidence in the Bank's ability to weather the storm is already reflected in a sharp rise in the shares. Although British interests in China, and particularly in Hongkong, continue to suffer, there are ample grounds for hope. There is a growing feeling in Canton that the boycott should come to an end; the militarists who have so long disturbed the country are inclined to give up the ruinous struggle, and the representatives of the Powers sitting in Peking are most anxious to adjust the country's grievances.

Some time must elapse ere a settlement is reached, but men- time the people seem to be wearying of civil warfare, and of the outside influences that have upset their foreign relationships, and there is the Customs revenue, the one shining star in a beclouded firmament, which reveals that, in spite of all the trouble, China's trade during the past year has reached a record figure. What it might have amounted to had peaceful conditions prevailed there is no saying, but that the China trade field offers wonderful scope for all in the future cannot be disputed.

In the present circumstances, however, it is fortunate for the Bank that China is by no means the only field in which it operates. It is soundly established throughout the Far East, and during the year has, no doubt, been able to recoup some of its China losses from the prosperity prevailing in the Federated Malay States and the Dutch East Indies, while maintaining its record of steady progress in Japan, Siam, Indo-China, the Philippines and elsewhere.

headline: LAUNCH TOLL / BODY FOUND INSIDE CABIN. / "LEE FAT" CASUALTY
text:
The report that no life was lost in the sinking of the local ferry steam-launch. "Lee Fat" near the Wing Lok (Macao steamer) wharf early on Thursday morning proved to be incorrect when the launch was subsequently brought to the surface.

An examination of the cabin revealed the presence of the dead body of a Chinese. The man was identified as an accountant from Whampoa who was sleeping in the cabin at the time of the mishap. It was thought at first that he was not then on board.

headline: STORMY CAREER.
text:
DEATH OF THE EX-SHAH OF PERSIA.

A. Reuter telegrun from San Remo states that Mohammed Ali, formerly Shah of Persia and father of the present Shah, died recently of a heart attack at the Villa San Michele, where he resided. The remains are to be taken to Teheran. Mohammed. Ali," sixth of the dynasty of the Kajars, which secured possession of the Crown of Persia after a civil war extending over 15 years, from 1770 to 1704, came to the throne on January 8, 1907.

Up to the year 1906 the form of government in Persia was similar to that in Turkey before the proclamation of the Constitution. The Shah, within the limitations imposed by the Mohammedan religion, was "an absolute ruler. In 1905 the Nationalist movement arose, and in January, 1906, Muzaffard-Din, the father of Mohammed Ali, gave his consent to the establishment of a Constitution. On coming to the throne Mohammed Ali signed the Constitution and took the prescribed oath: On June 23, 1908, however, Parliament was dissolved and the Parliament building partly demolished and sacked by his, Cossacks.

In the same year an attempt on his life was made by bomb. More fortunate than his grandfather, Nasr-ed-Din, he escaped with his life; but many were injured by the outrage. It did not come as a surprise; for even among moderate reformers suspicion had been felt that

he might not prove entirely loyal to the Constitution which was granted by his father a little more than a week before his own accession. This hostility and this suspicion did not disappear with time. The difficulties of effecting a radical change in the system of government, the intrigues of courtiers who had everything to lose by reform, led to misunderstandings which kept the Shah and his people apart and were a constant source of friction. The fact that the members of the National Assembly were not invited either to the coronation or to the Selameh-Ann, the general Durbar by which it was followed, an omission due probably to the intrigues of the Palace clique, gave great offence; and the delay in the acceptance of the revised form of the Constitution even produced something like a rebellion in Tabriz, the stronghold of the revolutionary societies. The natural

desire of the new Shah to have a strong, man on whom he could depend as Prime Minister led him to recall the Atabeg Azum and to place the direction of affairs in his hands. Unfortunately Atabeg, whose autocratic tendencies were well known, was detested by the people, who immediately jumped to the conclusion that he was brought back to Persia to re-establish the old despotism.

In July, 1909, Mohammed Ali was forced to abdicate. It was arranged that he should live in Russia, and a pension was provided, which was to be paid as long as he remained there. Shortly afterwards it was announced that the ex-Shah had left Odessa, presumably with the connivance of Russia. Twice since then he has returned to Persia. In 1911 he made, with the help of his brother Sarad-ed-Dowleh, vain attempt to regain the throne. His adherents raised trouble in various districts, and threatened to advance on the capital. One of them, Arshad-ud-Dowleh, got within 40 miles of Teheran, with a force consisting mainly of Turcomans. He was defeated by a smaller body of Nationalist troops, and was executed. A second attempt in 1919 to regain the throne failed, and the ex-Shah has since then lived in retirement. His son and successor has been absent from Persia for the last two years, and government is virtually a dictatorship by the present Prince Minister. Riza Khan.

Early in 1824 a Republican movement made such headway that the deposition of the Shah and the introduction of Republican government were to be moved in the Mejlis on March 22. At the last minute unexpected hostility to the proposed change of regime was vigorously manifested, and on April 1 the Premier announced the demise of the movement in a proclamation declaring that a republic was contrary to the Islamic religion and prohibiting all mention of the subject under threat of penalties.

Through the charming residential walls of Wynberg and Muizenberg, past Ceil Rhodes's private Z. which stands in the open air's close to the roadside that lions both tail almost on the footpath, the Prince motored to the naval Biscet Sarnstown and there went abroad the training ship General Pettha, where Dutch boys from the volt, who never saw the sea till they joined her, are trained for the Mercantile Marine.

headline: GIRL'S DEATH. / CORONER'S QUESTIONS TO FATHER. / DENIALS OF CRUELTY.
text:
At an inquest at Westminster on Ellen Jackson, 13, who was found drowned in the Thames, James Jackson, the father, a steel worker, of Latchmere-grove, Battersea, said his wife died on March 6, and since then "the girl had been " trying to run the house." There were four other children at home. Ellen had been going to school every day and the children had their meals at a relative's house.

The Coroner (Mr. Oddie): Can you explain why this girl should drown herself?—No, except worry. There was something else for

her to worry about, wasn't there?—I smacked her because she had only a few shillings left out of £3 or £4 I had given her. She had paid the rent and 12s. 6d. for the children's food.

It was not the only time you have hit her?—Never before that. That is not my information. You have thrashed her frequently and without sufficient cause?—No.

Did you ever threaten to kill her?—No.

Didn't you flog her on Thursday [the day before she disappeared]? —No.

I am told that you used to knock your wife about. What do you say to that?—That is a direct lie.

Jackson said that he only hit the girl with his flat hand on the face.

The Coroner: Why did you do that? She had already got enough trouble, having lost her mother and being left at the age of thirteen in charge of the household. Wasn't it a brutal thing to do? She is dead now, you know, and that is the cause of it. That will do.

Sergt. Nichols, the coroner's officer, said he was informed that before his wife died Jackson was a confirmed wife beater and a very heavy drinker; that on one occasion, when the father had threatened to kill all the children, the girl said she would drown herself, and then few days before her death, when her father was shouting and raving, the girl appeared obviously terrorised.

The coroner said he must have some substantiation of those statements and adjourned the inquiry.

headline: TROTSKY'S RETURN. / "REDS" AND THE PEASANTRY.
text:
The latest advices from Soviet Russia shed some additional light upon the probable effect of M. Trotsky's return to Moscow. While it is true that he repudiates any weakening of his faith in Leninism and its economics, it would seem to be a fact that he does propose to influence the policy of the Soviets in at least one new direction. His intention is, above all things, to improve the conditions of the peasants, who, he considers, have latterly been sorely neglected in favour of the urban workers. Owing to this neglect the State was bound to suffer, especially such a country as Russia, whose staple industry has always been and remains agriculture. There is yet another reason, namely, that the peasant is the backbone of the army; and it is the army first and foremost of which the head of the Red militants is for ever thinking. He means to strengthen his personal position in this way by finding new supporters in the ranks of the country against the extremists, who are chiefly drawn from the towns.

It is gathered that Moscow is by no means enamoured of the quality of the results recently achieved by the Soviet Embassies, Legations, and Trade Delegations abroad. Consequently, what might be described as a kind of diplomatic Cheks in being appointed, a voting commission whose hisiness it will be to pay visits of inspection to the Embassies and Legations in question, and report on their labours. headline: "I WILL" AND
text: "I will" and "I am" were the foundation of our whole human mind life, said Dr. Edwin Ash in a paper on Psychotherapy at a meeting of the Victoria Institute, Westminster. As a child grew up, said Dr. Ash, its sense of "I will" and "I am" both developed. Where strength and vitality were prominent, then "I will" dominated individual mentality. Too great a sense of "I am," with weakness in the sense of "I will," was a foundation for nervous breakdown and mental disorder. Too great a sense of "I will" might lead to physical breakdown. Harmony in the balance between the two made for health, peace of mind, and success. "Will is the moving force in human activity," he declared. "It can be trained and developed to a remarkable degree." The methods in use for exercising the human mind currently were suggestion, auto-suggestion, psycho-analysis, the general form psychotherapy conveniently covering the whole field of mind. At least stable very idea of such a thing as psychotherapy or mind-beating seemed to continue with common sense and the fact that a student is prophète.

headline: WELSH NOTES.
text:
MORE OUTSPOKEN CRITICISM.

Outspoken criticism of “slavish adoration of degrees, the enthronement of financial success as the ultimate object of life, the sports mania which took 54 train loads from the land of religious revivals to see 22 men kick a piece of leather about and the growing professionalism in our religion” has drawn on D Martin Lloyd Jones the wrath of some who have dubbed him a “second Caradoc Evans” but a closer examination of the text of the address in the latest Welsh papers shows that Dr. Jones has been wronged by the extracts which have been published away from their proper context.

Dr. Jones's criticism was a feature of the Union of Welsh Societies Conference, a full report of which has reached me. Dr. Jones was at some pains to explain that what he said about modern Wales could be said with equal truth about England and other countries but what was evil and regrettable in the case of other nations was to him a tragedy when applied to Wales, with a tradition second to none other. A critic who addressed his criticisms to a foreign nation and not to his own countrymen might deservedly call upon himself the assignation of a traitor but his treachery was only equalled by the treachery of those who, while realising that all was not well with Wales, persisted in saying in public that all was well.

The standpoint of Dr. Jones was that of a lover of his country to whom any evidence of deterioration in the object of his love was intolerable and there is nothing in the text of his address to which exception could be taken by any other than the narrow minded who refuse to contemplate the possibility of there ever being in the principality anything calling for a measure of reform.

Striking corroboration of the point made by Dr. Jones as to there being at the present time a kind of ebb in the tide of intellectual activity in Wales is to hand in a statement appearing in a Welsh weekly paper which has had to give up its poetry column owing to the poor and tawdry character of the work submitted for publication. Commenting on the fact, the "Welsh Outlook" states that it is discorparting after all the ferment of years to find so little good brew and hardly any of exceptional quality. In support of its contention that the Welsh fiction of the last few years has almost without exception been lengths below the standard of Daniel Owen, this paper comments as follows:—We still remember the thrill which the Rev. Dewi Williams and Prof. W. J. Gruffydd gave us in their first handling of it. But apart from the lighter and slighter efforts of Miss Kate Roberts, the Rev. R. G. Berry and the Rev. Seymour Rees, the new literary factory has apparently been closed.

On the whole it would appear that Dr. Jones' criticism has not been unfavourably received by the majority of thinking Welshmen who can see a quicker emancipation in a more complete realisation of the difficulties to be confronted. Many of them, too, are placing a firm faith in the ultimate benefit to the principality and its language and literature of the recently constituted departmental committee set up to enquire into the education system of Wales.
