I was searched, put into a carriage with an armed soldier, and driven to the secret police prison. After waiting two or more hours I was deprived of my money, watch, tie, belt, and other articles, and was sent under escort to a cell, which was about 10ft. square by 9ft. high.

It had no windows, but a grat-ing at the upper end of a shaft in the roof. The straw bed was in an indescribably filthy state. There was a table and a stool and a wooden spoon.

There were a Russian and a Chinese in the cell, which seemed to amuse the Bolshevik guard, who frequently reminded me of the fact that the three of us were bunched together in a Russian prison.

On June 16 I went to the court house for what was nothing more than a farcical trial, in which the Public Prosecutor refused to prosecute. The trial lasted from 4 p.m. till midnight. The marriage trated at among the crowd in color and I was tried by three peasants in corduroys with handkerchiefs round their necks.

headline: NERVOUS DISEASE.
text:
HOW CENTRAL BICEAMING ENDFENANT

That Hsu Shung-chi is no longer one of the Canton rulers is confirmed in a report in Tuesday's "Canton Gazette" which concludes thus:

"Owing to the repeated rebellion of his troops, General Hsu thought himself unable to show faith to the Kuomintang and the Government, nor to explain himself, and he became unusually indignant and depressed. His nervous disease returned and he therefore decided to leave for Shanghai for recompensation."

"The closing of the Headquarters of the Cantonese Forces was decided upon some time ago, and so all the matters pertaining thereto will be dealt with by Gen. Chang Kai-shi who is in command of the Kuomintang Forces, and is Chief of Staff in the said Headquarters, during the absence of Gen. Hsu in Shanghai." Gen. Chang has ordered the troops under his command to station in the said Headquarters at the Provincial Assembly Hall since the afternoon of Sunday. The three battalions of gendarmes which were there before, are now put under the command of Gen. Chen Ming-chao, and have been transferred to Shek waiting."

The same issue reports the following:

Tam Yin-hoi to be chairman of the Military Council.

Kwan To (Director of Commissariat) and Li Kee-hung (Finance Commissioner) dismissed.

Generals Cheng Yun-ki and Mok Hang to be dismissed.

headline: SHIPS WANTED. / CANTON ASKS RUSSIA FOR MORE.
text:
Since the participation in the general strike by the seamen, inferrupting communication with Hongkong, the sailing of steamers between Canton, Swatow and Shanghai has been less frequent, remarks the "Canton Gazette," Communication between these places has been, however, maintained with vessels despatched by the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Co. At present, although there are vessels sailing between Canton and Swatow, the sailing time is so irregular, it is most inconvenient to the merchants. In view of this, the Soviet Steamship Co., telegraphed some time ago to Russia requesting the despatched of more steamers to sail between Canton, Swatow and Shanghai so as to facilitate communication and the transporting of cargo.

It is learned that several of these vessels will sail to Canton regularly, and will take passengers and cargo to Swatow and Shanghai. Besides these vessels, there are other vessels, American, Norwegian and German, which will arrive in Canton shortly.

A later issue of the same paper said:—

A German firm has written to the Strike Committee reporting that by the steam's "Hang Fung" of which they are the agents, they have imported a large shipment of food stalls and other candries from Shanghai, on Canton and the steamer is now lying off the Macao Passage.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
While Washington despatches are optimistic in regard to the prospect of the Franco-American debt settlement, Paris is doubtful and some papers even anticipate the failure of the negotiations. The despatches from French correspondents at Washington, however, speak of the new French proposals as possibly providing for initial annual payments of thirty instead of twenty-five million dollars, increasing in a decade to a maximum of approximately a hundred million, payable in fifty-two years instead of ninety. The Americans are now said to be ready to agree to maximum annuities of 120 million dollars. M. Caillaux is said to have assured Mr. Mellon that no payment would be made to Britain and no Franco-British arrangement will be concluded without identical payment and arrangement with America. The incident of the loan to the Bank of France is reported to be settled.

Teheran, September 28.—The Minister of Public works has declared that though the Government urgently supplied provisions in order to remove the general alarm, it has been found that the recent troubles, though based on a pretext of the lack of provisions, had other motives. The Government's have decided to investigate the mutter and to punish the instigators of the riots and to prevent fresh outbreaks.—Reuter.

From a letter appearing in the “Times” from a Robe reader it would appear that the stoppage of the British sugar refineries in China has created a demand for the Japanese product in Manchuria in the boxcott, and in other Eastern countries.

The increased export trade in Japanese goods such as cottons and manufactured foodstuffs is also reported to have reacted favourably on the value of the yen. Japanese grey shootings, again, are reported to have made considerable inroads into the trade with East African ports.

Commenting on the statement with regard to sugar, the "China Express" and Telegraph" thinks that the Taikoo and Jardine concerns in Hongkong are those particularly referred to: The news from Japan certainly indicates activity, of which British interests, seriously affected by the deadlock in China, should take note, it states. Hongkong is not afraid of Japan as far as sugar is concerned. The market lost is not easy to regain. The remark applies equally to shirting and shipping.

Vera Cruz, September 28.—One person was killed and fifty wounded in rioting the municipal elections. It is alleged that Lopez, the Red candidate, abstracted ballotting papers from one booth and that the followers of Galvez, the opposing candidate, began the shooting which became indiscriminate. Troops restored order. Numbers of Reds have been arrested on a charge of inciting revolt.—Reuter's American Service.

New York, Sept. 28.—Crowds of anti-Fascists and pro-Fascists met the steamer bringing the Italian delegates to the Conference of the Inter-Parliamentary Union. Notwithstanding police supervision, an unidentified anti-Fascist shot and slightly injured two Fascist-symptholders, and escaped. Reuter's American Service DRIVER CHARGED WITH MANSLAUGHTER.

headline: LABOUR QUESTIONS.
text:
The statement in the House of Commons by the Labour Socialist, Mr. Ponsonby, that he thought it was farcical to attribute the trouble of China to Communistic agencies drew from the Under-Secretary, Foreign Office, Mr. R. McNeil, the comment that he did not think any proof of propaganda could be so positive as to convince that right honourable gentleman.

In the course of discussion Major-General Knox insisted that the anti-British propaganda in China was engineered from Moscow. Their agent, whose name was Tomski, was now known as Livinski. (Laughter). Mr. J. Jones (Labour-Socialist, Silvertown): Is it in order for a member of this House to refer to the member of another Government as if he had changed his name for some disreputable reason? (Ministerial laughter). The King of this country had changed his name, and they thought none the worse of him for that.

A Labour-Socialist: And so has the President of the Board of Trade. (Labour-Socialist cheers).

A. Knox had referred in any dis- respectful terms to the gentleman he had mentioned. (Ministerial cheers).

Sir A. Knox regretted that he had ruffled hon. members opposite. (Laughter and cheers). In the course of his speech, Mr. Ponsonby asked the Government to give the House some information in regard to China. The problem was one that might smoulder until it blazed up into something extremely dangerous. His Majesty's Government were showing a sort of spineless inertia, and were taking no action. They seemed to have an incorrigible habit of allowing situations, whether at home or abroad, to come to a head before they could be persuaded to move at all. He thought that the suggestion that the disturbances in China were due to Bolshevik propaganda had been disproved. To say that the movement was due to Communist agitation was far critical in the extreme. It was the culmination of events that had been growing in China ever since the Western exploitation of that country in 1840. The breaking point had been reached in the way the Chinese had been treated as inferior people and exploited by the Western peoples. If the Western Powers wanted to deal honestly by China; it would not be long before a strong Government arose in that country. We were throwing Russia into the arms of Asia; we were entranging the whole of the vast population of China; and were raising up a sort of suspicious feeling against Japan. The unfortunate action of to-day might culminate in great catastrophes years hence. In reply to Mr. Ponsonby, Mr. R. McNeil said that Russian intrigue was creating great difficulties and making much missionary and unhelpful, however, believe that in the long run it would do any material damage to the British Empire. (Ministerial cheers).

As regarded the attitude of the British Government there was not the slightest foundation for Mr. Ponsonby's charge that the Government were showing supine inertia. From the first moment the troubles developed, the Government had been very active in trying to bring about a wise settlement of the existing troubles, and to devise and encourage and initiate as far as they could a wise policy dealing with the subject of our relations with China and the internal conditions of that country. He agreed that the condition of affairs in China was not due to Bolshevik propaganda, but he did think that Bolshevik propaganda had been fishing in troubled waters. It had been exasperating tempers and making more mischief where there was mischief to work on at the beginning, and he had very little doubt that it was very largely due to Bolshevik propaganda that, anti-foreign hostility had largely concentrated its animosity upon this country rather than upon others. Chinese interests and British interests there were identical. Trade could only flourish in an atmosphere of peace and confidence, and it was obviously to our interest that China should enjoy those blessings. In spite of all the existing difficulties, he did not think we should be pessimistic with regard to the future of China, and as to what we could do there. He hoped that the coming conference would improve the whole of the foreign relations with China. He did not believe that the present Chinese feeling of animosity against this country would continue.

headline: SNUB FOR REDS.
text: The members of the left wing made an attack on Mr. Ramsay MacDonald in connection with the Zinovieff letter which they say proved a flasco, at the Labour Conference this morning. A composite resolution on the subject was introduced demanding inter alia that an apology be sent to the Soviet Government and Zinovieff, but it was overwhelmingly rejected on a show of hands.

headline: COMMUNIST LEADERS CANNOT THROW STONES.
text:
The Labour Conference overwhelmingly defeated a Communist motion to refer back the section of the Executive Board's report dealing with unemployment. Mr. Gallagher, of Paisley, submitting the motion, asserted that the movement was being handed over to the middle classes. Mr. MacDonald, replying, said that it was a libel to say that the labour leaders had blank cheques from Moscow and that it was time that such slanders were faced. He declared that nobody was less entitled to point the finger of scorn at himself or anyone else from the viewpoint of vulgar display of wealth or riotous living than the present British Communist leaders. (Cheers).

Shanghai, September 30.—When nearing the upper Yangtze port of Tuchow on the 27th the American steamer “Chichuen” was fired on by a large contingent of soldiers ensonced on the heights overlooking the gorges. The firing was kept up for an hour when steamer was struck at least two hundred times. A Chinese member of the crew was slightly wounded. The American gunboat “Palce” was ordered to escort the vessel through the soldier ridden area to Chungqing. The miscreants are believed to be fleeing soldiers of General Yangsen. The “Chichuen,” which was flying the American flag, belongs to the Yangtze Rapids S.S. Co. The skipper was the only foreigner aboard.—Reuter.

headline: ABNORMAL FANATICS
text:
One feels convinced after a few weeks in Russia that only a small minority of the Communists believe in anything but their own power and advancement, writes a correspondent of the "Daily Telegraph." Many of the leaders are, no doubt, genuine Communists. Of the sincerity of Chicherin, for instance, there can be no doubt: he refused a great inheritance in his early years for the sake of his principles, and at that fateful meeting in London, where Lenin split the Socialists into Bolsheviks and Mensheviks, he voted with the former. But not one, looking into his pale eyes with that strange glitter in them, could regard him as normal, Dzerhinsky, too, produces the impression of a cold-blooded fanatic. "You cannot make revolutions in white kid gloves," he answered a more squeamish acquaintance, and the same spirit has carried him through ruthless seas of blood as through fifteen years in a dungeon for the sake of his convictions.

The “screwed-up” expression of the great Bolsheviks, especially of Lenin and Trotsky, has often been commented on, and the galleries of portraits with which Moscow abounds show this phenomenon to be characteristic. Rykoff is almost the only prominent Communist who has the face of an ordinary human being. For this very reason, perhaps, and because of his moderation, his influence is small, and since he gave the Third International some very sound advice on the folly of persecuting the nephew, or private traders, out of existence, he has made himself disliked by the extremists. It would seem that the screwed-up face and glinty eyes are symptoms of abnormality, and no real Bolshevik leader can be regarded as quite normal. Lenin was certainly a great man, of tremendous driving power; yet in the official bulletin of his autopsy it was announced that, instead of grey matter in his brain, they found green slime.

headline: SWARMS OF SPIES.
text:
The extremists now in power have taken the bit between their teeth, and miss the controlling master-hand. None of the moderate men appear to be strong enough to check them, and they are capable of overriding any reasonable arrangement made with a, foreign country by the Government on the grounds of political expediency. Yet the officials with whom foreigners come into contact seem not only reasonable, but civil and courteous; their hands, however, are so entwined in the meshes of an endless tangle of red tape that business is as tedious as it is difficult. Yet this very red tape is necessary as a check, for they cannot trust one another; all are thinking of lining their nests against a rainy day, and survivors of pre-Communistic days are always on the look-out for a chance to recover, regardless of means, some of their lost property.

In Russia the individual dares very little. Spies swarm everywhere, and the more prominent and more responsible the man, the more his actions are watched and recorded. The leaders spy upon each other, and the powerful "Ogpu" spies on everybody. Foreigners are watched, and the inquisitive spoon-fed, so that it is very difficult to form a genuine opinion. In the hotels thecomings and goings are registered, as well as interesting conversations. As a rule this is done without attracting attention, but occasionally a clumsy fellow, when eavesdropping, will betray himself. Natives dare not visit foreigners, and if foreigners visit Russian friends it is certain to bring suspicion upon them. The postal censorship is an old Russian institution, and it is certain that the Bolsheviks have continued this legacy of the Tsars, with many other of the worst features of the old regime, and it is unwise to write from abroad to friends in Russia.

WORSE THAN TSARIST TYRANNY. But the tyranny of the Tsars was liberty, indeed, compared with the tyranny of the Bolsheviks. Then at least one was allowed to live and trade and work, so long as politics were not touched. Russian broadmindedness, the child of their boundless plains, allowed greater freedom of action than does public opinion in Britain. To-day everyone lives in constant dread. Many people never go to bed before two a.m., so as to be dressed when the agents come, for that is their favourite hour. It is characteristic of Russia that the old saying, when a chance silence falls upon a party, it is not that an angel is passing over, but "a policeman has been born."

Intolerance is the keynote of the Communist system, which might be defined as the very anti-podes of the policy of "live and let live." They loathe Democracy, for the Dictatorship of the Proletariat is incompatible with the greatest good of the greatest number, and means exclusive power in the hands of the minority—another characteristic in common with the old régime. They openly treat as enemies all who are not members of the party; they make use of them so far as it suits their purpose, but once they have ceased to be useful they are better dead.

It is told that in 1923 Moscow was a gay city, but in 1924 the swing to the left and the economic distress made themselves felt. Seats at the Bolshoi Theatre, opera, and ballet cost too much. There are few people in Moscow to-day who can afford ten, or even fifteen, gold roubles for stalls, which are patronised chiefly by an occasional member of some foreign mission, a concession-hunter from capitalistic Europe, or nephew who has not yet received the usual short notice of expulsion. Yet, as during the terror in the French Revolution we read that the theatres were crammed, so to-day during the terror which few see, but everybody feels in the air in Russia, the harassed and nervous public flocks to the theatre and the cinemas to forget for a moment their anxieties and fears.

Still, the Russian temperament shows itself often enough in laughing faces in the streets; yet this laugh has a hollow ring about it; it is the spirit of "let us eat, drink, and be merry, for to-morrow we die," that spirit which is truer of the Russian than of any other nationality in Europe, for everybody lives from hand to mouth, nothing knowing and little caring what to-morrow may bring forth. The only man I saw in Moscow who seemed genuinely happy had no legs. Both had been amputated above the knee. He came stumping cheerfully into a grocer's shop, with a healthy glow and a cheerful smile on his bronzed and bearded face. I instinctively drew out a few kopecks, when to my surprise he fished out of a capacious pocket a huge pile of small change, both paper and that not unpleasing "hard valuta" now in circulation, which was evidently his day's takings. He changed it for five and ten rouble notes, for he found begging a lucrative business, he cracked jokes with the salesmen, laughed uproariously, and after a vigorous discussion about vintages, bought a bottle of "port-vin" for three roubles, stuffed it into his pocket, and stumped out into the street, whistling a cheerful air.

headline: FORLORN CHILDREN.
text:
If the other beggars in Moscow were as merry, it would be a cheerful city, indeed, for scarcely even on the Galata Bridge at Stamboul can one see so many maimed and distorted beggars as in the capital of Bolshevism; and not all are cripples; ragged boys are a perfect nuisance, and it is impossible to buy a packet of cigarettes at a kiosk or come out of a restaurant without being persecuted by a batch of these important young ruffians. I was surprised at this phenomenon, and made inquiries, as I thought that under the proletarian regime all the poor were provided for. I was told that many found it a more paying game than working, while others could not produce the indispensable "dokument" which is so dear to the Russian official. Another characteristic feature is afforded by the swarms of forlorn children. The years of social disturbance, mortality among parents, and general life.

moralisation, especially among the youth of both sexes, have produced a big crop of parentless children, who live God knows how, begging a bit, stealing a bit, sleeping huddled up together among ruined and uncompleted buildings. To their credit, the Soviet authorities are endeavouring to cope with this evil, and among the very numerous appeals to one's purse when sitting in cafés and restaurants the one to which one gives with least reluctance is the fund for these poor waifs.

The concentration of the government in Moscow has led to a shortage of lodgings which is probably more acute than in any other city in Europe. Directly the frost breaks building proceeds vigorously. One huge skeleton structure near the Arbat was condemned as unsafe in the Tsar's days, and a lengthy lawsuit ensued. Now the Bolsheviks regardless of the architects' verdict, are hurrying on its completion with all possible speed. The only comment I heard was: "Thank God, only Communists will live there, so it will be a good thing if it does collapse." Rooms are almost impossible to secure, and few are worth having. A limited definite space called "ploshchad" is allotted to every person and heavily taxed. No body is permitted to stay in the city unless he can give a good reason, and many, a family has been deported at a few hours' notice to remote villages in the Arctic Circle. Few flats or lodgings remind one of civilised Europe. The "paradni," or front entrance, is invariably closed, bolted, and barred. No one can afford to keep a dvornik, or hall porter, and all use the "black" entrance, or back door. When calling upon an acquaintance it is necessary to wander about a courtyard, usually immense and always untidy, to find the tradesmen's entrance, which admits to a dark and gloomy kitchen, and then through dingy passages and corridors littered with boxes, stacks of old furniture, broken statues, and musty pictures, all recking and never ventilated, to the single room that is all that most families can boast it. This is usually over-furnished, and always depressing; an old rug may conceal a bed and make it look like a sofa, but a washstand, especially a Russian one, is never an elegant object. Worst of all is the Russia's dread of fresh air.

/orst of all is | "Silly fellow I Now he will hear if fresh air, you all the pluaner."

the result of his climate, which seldom permits him to open the fortochka, or ventilating window. Only when spring timidly shows itself and the earliest flowers are hawked about the streets usually at extravagant prices can the Russian brighten his dingy quarters with a sprig or two of mimosa from the Crimea or lilac from Kieff, to remind him that Nature is still beautiful.

headline: POSITION OF WOMEN. / OVERLAND CHINA MAIL
text: The Municipal Soviet exercises a fatherly supervision over its citizens; as in the old days, it is forbidden to enter or leave a tram when in motion, and the fine of a gold rouble for so doing is enforced; penalties, too are exacted for throwing about those long cardboard cigarette ends with which Russians are apt to strew the country, and big receptacles, labelled "dlia okurok," are placed in all public buildings and in the streets. But the latter are defaced by the shrieking propaganda, which gets on one's nerves until they are dulled; the effect produced by this incessant appeal to the eye is one of insincerity.

A rather surprisingly puritanical feature is the "struggle with prostitution," for which an active propaganda is maintained, visible in great posters. This seems odd, when they have tried to abolish Christianity, and Soviet marriage is a mere formula of registration; as easy and inexpensive to undo as to enter. But woman's position in Soviet Russia is in no way inferior to man's; she serves upon the General Staff of the Red army, and the tripe-woman of Marseilles has found her modern counterpart in the female executioners of the Che-Ka. The Communist women endeavour to distinguish themselves from their bourgeoisie sisters by eccentricities of dress or affection of masculinity, which completely destroys their attractiveness to the eye. It is often hard to tell the sex when one sees a young person with close-cropped hair, check jockey cap with a huge long peak, a cigarette end hanging on the lip, and the hands deep in the trousers pockets. The figure is that of a veritable female apache straight from the variety stage.

headline: BRITAIN'S PRESTIGE
text:
The "Telegraph" regards the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities and minimise personal outrages on British subjects as threatening the prestige of Britain in the War East. The treatment in Canton of two Hongkong journalists is referred to in this connection.

In editorial comment, Mr. Percival Landon's review of the situation in China is regarded as bringing out very clearly the painful fact that the Chinese politicians regard Great Britain and other Powers as their enemies. It is very difficult for British readers to realise this. There is no hostility towards China in England. We are sorry for her; we lament the misery that the collapse of her Central Government has brought upon the oldest of civilised peoples; we are anxious to give her effective help in recovering her ancient peace, though we do not know how to set about it. But of enmity or even dislike there is no trace on our side. Those who concern themselves with Chinese affairs are much readier to blame our Foreign Office for its supposed faults of commission or omission than to denounce the Chinese. It is surely remarkable that the deliberate insult offered to the British Iseigation at Peking by subjecting it to a boycott and constraining the Chinese servants to leave the premises should not have excited public indignation at home, although the Peking Government, in permitting the boycott to continue, has disregarded Treaty stipulations as well as the ordinary diplomatic courtesies. The disgraceful incident at Canton recently, when two British journalists from Hongkong, relying on the Canton Government's assertion that there was no boycott of British shipping, landed on the quay and were immediately seized and thrust into a filthy jail, would have stirred our fathers and grand-fathers to violent wrath. They, in their day, expected British citizens to be treated fairly in every part of the world, and they would have looked for something more than the evasive apology proffered at Canton—an apology not for the unlawful imprisonment, but for the use of the chains in which these unfortunate journalists were led through the city and exposed to the jeers of the mob. But the benevolence with which Great Britain is determined to regard Chinese doings, and the prevalent tendency to excuse the Chinese authorities because all real power is in the hands of military chieftains, may cause even these personal outrages on British subject to be minimised and overlooked, though nothing could be worse for our prestige in the Far East. Yet, in spite of all our resolute manifestations of goodwill towards China, we are reminded by Mr. Landon that the friendliness is all on our side. The Chinese politicians, led by Mr. Wang, who's Moscow's warmest friend at Peking, regard us and the other Powers as enemies, and will enter the coming Conference with the object of doing us harm.

headline: UNPLEASANT FACTS
text:
It is better to face the facts, unpleasant though they are, than to blind ourselves with illusions. China's hostility is bad enough, but the impotence of her self-styled Government is worse from a diplomatic standpoint, because it affords the Powers no hope of remedying her grievances satisfactorily. If President Tuan Chijui and his Cabinet really controlled the Eighteen Provinces the Powers might easily come to terms with him, as Great Britain, America, and Japan are most anxious to restore good relations with their Chinese customers. But the truth is that the President is but the head of a shadow Government, a mere simulacrum of sovereignty, a marionette whose strings are pulled by the inscrutable "Christian" General Feng Yu-hsiang, whose troops occupy the capital, and who receives his munitions by way of Mongolia from his Bolshevik paymasters. Outside Peking and the border Provinces of Shensi and Kansu, which constitute Feng's present zone of occupation, his puppet President is virtually unrecognised, except as the giver of honorific titles to the military leaders who obtain temporary control in the several provinces. The Powers, in negotiating with the nominees of Tuan Chijui, will be dealing with men who have no power to implement their promises, but who undoubtedly will use the Conference as a means of inflaming the anti-foreign movement. As Mr. Tandon points out, the Powers may agree to the proposed increase of the Chinese tariff on

foreign imports, which the Conference has been summoned to discuss. But they will be asked by the Chinese to go further, and to consider the complete abolition of the fiscal treaties and of the extra-territorial rights possessed by foreigners in China. If they refuse to do so the aglators will have fresh material for their propaganda. Yet no discussion of these matters can be helpful while there is no protection for foreigners and their property outside the Treaty ports. Even the tariff question is complicated by the prevailing disorder. As Mr. Landon says, if the Flowers allow the Peking Government to raise some additional millions out of the Maritime Customs they will give fresh offence to all Feng's rivals. He would receive the money, through his obedient servants in Peking, and would spend it in spreading the Soviet agitation. The other Tupans, or Tuchuns, with armies of their own, would want to know why the Powers were thus subsidising Feng against them. We should thus be assisting our bitterest opponent and annoying all the other powerful chiefs. Yet it is difficult to see how the Powers could insist on supervising the expenditure of the new Customs revenue if they agree to its being raised.

headline: CHINA UNITY PROSPECTS.
text: It may be that some Chinese Napoleon will arise and restore the unity of the Empire. But the recent history of China's civil wars warns us that provincial discussions and the lack of moral sense among the generals make the task of a Chinese Napoleon extremely difficult. Chang Two-lin, the Manchurian ruler, still has what is nominally the largest army, a quarter of a million strong, and exercises control, as far south as Shanghai. His chief rival, Feng Yu-hsiang, who was once the leading commander under Wu Pei-fu, the former over-lord of Central China, and who rose to eminence by betraying Wu in his last struggle with Chang, is now, with Moscow's help, at the head of a force almost as numerous as the Manchurian host, and perhaps as well armed. Whether and when these two potentates, Chang and Feng, who depend respectively on Japan and on Russia, will come into collision no one can say. Nor is it safe to conclude that the victor in the duel, if it came, would necessarily gather Central China, to say nothing of the unruly South, into his fold, and make China one again. Chinese domestic politics are not so simple as that; the fierce animosities existing between the provinces are complicated by party feuds and personal ambitions, so that military victories, real or supposed, have hitherto had no definite results. We may suppose that the anarchy which is wasting China and ruining her trade will come to an end sooner or later, and that force will have to be used to restore order. But to assign a date to this consummation, or to suppose that Chang or Wu, or any other personality now prominent in Western eyes, will achieve the desired end would be very unwise. Our chief hopes must rest on the innate good sense and untiring industry of the Chinese people. If they could somehow be persuaded that the foreigner was not their enemy but anxious to be their friend, and to resume the trade which has benefited all parties engaged in it, they would soon bring about a revival, as they have done many times before in their long history. But how this change of view is to be brought about, in face of the persistent Bolshevik campaign throughout China, is the real problem to which Western diplomats need to address themselves in earnest before still worse mischief has been done.

headline: COAL STRIKE.
text:
The country is completely unruffled over the anthracite coal strike which has been proceeding for six weeks. The miners themselves are enjoying a prolonged holiday fishing, camping and touring. Some have taken temporary employment. A number of foreigners are profiting from the opportunity to visit their homes. The owners similarly are unperturbed. They believe that the strikers will return when their money is spent. In the meantime the country is carrying on with accumulated stocks which however will soon disappear with the approach of winter. The Government hitherto has been reluctant to intervene until the placidity has passed off.

headline: CUSTOMS MEETING.
text:
DIFFICUL CIES WHICH MUST BE MET.

Mr. P. LANDON'S VIEWS.

Mr. Percival Landon, writing from Peking, takes the view that the prospects of the Customs Conference are not of the brightest and that the best hope of achieving some success rests in not shutting our eyes to certain obvious difficulties and dangers which if taken in time may be dealt with although they cannot be avoided.

Before dealing with the many parties. Chinese and foreign, whose interests, amotions, and intrigues are concerned with the Customs Conference in Peking, he writes, it is as well to touch upon certain aspects of the approaching congress which deserve attention at home. Apart from the principles involved there are certain material facts which distinguish this conference from any other and must be understood, if the complexity of the task that lies before the foreign delegates can be understood, or indeed the chance of successful issue estimated Events in China move with such rapidity and their changes are so kaleidoscopic that it may be that a new situation—which means a new military situation—will have arisen before the opening days of November. But however political, financial or military considerations may regroup the forces opposed to the foreign representatives; there will be no change in the consistent anti-foreign complexion of Chinese policy during and probably after the meeting in Peking.

I have used the word “opposed” intentionally, as it would be a grave error to suppose that this conference can be either a friendly adjustment of conflicting interests or is one in which terms are imposed by either side. From the first moment to the last it will be a grim struggle, in which on the one side the interests of foreign States, and, indeed, of China herself, in maintaining and developing trade relations are believed to be vitally concerned, while the other side is blindly convinced that nothing less than Chinese independence is at stake.

headline: A Shadow Government.
text:
The first point to be borne in mind is that the Allies—if the term may be allowed, without indicating in any way an identity of interests—are dealing with a shadow Government that has no power either to conclude a treaty or to enforce any part of it, except by permission of and at the direction of a military autocrat. At the moment it is the Soviet Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang—whose outbreakings of war and slaughter against foreigners will be fresh in the memory of Englishmen—who has the Peking Government under his absolute control. Without his assent from Kalgan or Kansu not a clause will be accepted by the Chinese Government or put afterwards into force.

The second point of practical importance is that the conference will be held in a hostile capital. In itself this characteristic distinguishes this conference from any other international discussion in recent years. In the event of a dissolution of the congress without achieving a satisfactory result, this fact is worth while bearing in mind. To judge by the insults already directed against our own Legation and that of the United States, incidents may occur which may seriously complicate subsequent relations. In respect of these insults, the shadow Government has turned a deaf ear to protests, and a similar attitude on the part of the military autocrat might precipitate grave trouble. Such behaviour as sanctioning the action of those who are terrorising the Legation servants into desertion is inconceivable in any civilised Government, but the fact remains that the Government still tacitly endorses this intimidation, and that consequently the strike continues. It will be in an avowedly anti-foreign atmosphere that this debate will take place. The real enemy will not be directly represented, but every move in China's game will have been suggested or sanctioned from Moscow and played across the council-table by Mr. T. Wang, the ablest of Chinese politicians, and the most thorough adherent of the Soviet Government in China. No doubt he believes that he is merely using Moscow as a tool, but the recent experience of the unhappy Hu Han-min in Canton should teach him that he who sups with the devil needs a loor spoon. But for the moment it is only the avowedly hostile driving force behind the Conference that I wish to emphasize. Thirdly, it must be remembered that additional revenues from the increase of Customs distractions, to which the Allies are, of course, pledged, will in itself cause acute

dissension in China, even before a treaty is signed. To give it to Peking is tantamount to giving it through Feng, for the spread of Soviet propaganda throughout the Chinese Republic. The other Tupans would only see in the grant a subsidy given by foreign influence to Peking for their undoing. Among these latter Chang Tso-lin himself must be ranked, unless he manages to obtain at least his full share of the increment by a private arrangement with his inevitable enemy Feng. Moreover, we should not overlook the recrudescence of activity from Yochow, whither Wu Pei-fu has been taken himself. On the one hand, nothing is so likely to arouse civil war as the handing over to Peking and Feng Yu-hsiang of any large share of the proceeds of these increased duties; on the other hand, nothing will exacerbate anti-foreign hatred more than any attempt of foreigners to control or deal in any way with this new surplus. It will be useless for foreigners to pretend that, after securing the loans, the use made of the extra revenue is no affair of theirs. The time has gone by when indirect responsibility can be repudiated in China. Certain European nations who used this excuse for pouring arms and ammunition into China during recent years are now regretting their action. If the Conference uses its unquestionable right to assign these extra revenues to Peking—the prisoner of each military autocrat in turn—it cannot plead irresponsibility if the civil war which it has been the constant endeavour of all foreign diplomacy to extinguish blazes up again more savagely than ever.

headline: Powers Must Agree.
parent_headline: STOPS LEAKS IN OLD ROFS 2555 PRISERVES NEW ROOFS
text: In some ways the Peking Conference presents resemblances to that of Lausanne, the course of which may usefully be studied now. Whether actually on the agenda or not, fiscal autonomy and abolition of the Capitulations will figure as, obstinately upon the Peking programme as at Ouchy. The role of Greece as the only possible armed agent of the Allies in an emergency might—and in the event of a civil war inviting the intervention of Russia, must—be played by Japan. Once more the known unwillingness of some Allies, and the inability of others to interfere, will again be a trump card in the hands of our opponent; and we may be certain that any reasonable concessions on our part will be trumpeted through China as proof of our weakness. It is a knot of which Gordius might be proud. For the Allies in Peking to go outside the exact letter of the terms of reference would be sheer folly: yet to refuse to discuss the matters that China is more intent upon than any mere raising of the tariff will infallibly revive the anti-foreign hatred in an acuter form than ever.

headline: ATTRACTIVE ADVERTISING
text:
The resources of up-agency are great, and it is certain that our action here will vindicate our good faith at Washington; but over this conference there seems to hang the need of a second at a later date, when, to a united China which has proved her capacity to govern without corruption and without injustice, a full measure of independence shall be willingly conceded by the world. Still, it would be a dangerous illusion to cherish the hope that, however generously the Allied delegates may interpret their rights and duties, they will succeed in holding up the present anti-foreign movement which is carrying the red flag of Moscow into every corner of the Chinese Republic.

Last, and perhaps more important than all else, is the necessity of keeping the League of Nations wholly out of this trouble. No conception of the League is more fallacious than that which attributes to it a standpoint based upon universally recognised wisdom, justice, or even expediency. Although its creators were quite unconscious of the fact, neither in concept, on, organisation, nor practice is the League anything but the product of Western civilisation, Western law, and the Western attitudes towards life and even of Christianity. It was, in fact, called together to spread Western ideas, and the presence of such States upon its roll as China or Persia has not availed to broaden its outlook or make its precepts one whit more blastic. There is little in the Chinese outlook upon life which the League would wholly understand; there is even less in the tenets of the League at which in time of stress China would not look askancé. Moreover, in order to preserve the facade of impartiality, the League would draw for its representatives upon precisey those nationality which have no interests in and therefore no knowledge of the East. We have just seen Hogstrangely the Meepotantan situation has been judged by the artists appointed by the League; the display of a similar ignorant point in Chinese affairs, and the Chinese outlook would produce an强的 effect on a certain trouble in this East State.

headline: $ ^{1} $ JAPAN AND RUSSIA
text:
THEIR RELATIONS WITH CHINA.

Whilst the ex-Kaiser chooses to see in the Far East, possibilities of a Russo-Japanese alliance against Europe with particular reference to the development of China, the "Belfast Telegraph" thinks that the end has not been seen of rivalry between Japan and Russia in this area. "If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast tomorrow," states this "journal," she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the possibility of German intervention and possibly that of the United States at a later stage.

The "Bolfust Telegraph" article in full is as follows:—

The strike at the Japanese factories in Shanghai, which has been the pretext for so much anti-foreign irritation in China, has now been settled but the trouble else where is still far from being at an end. A good deal of the unrest which is visible in many parts of the world to-day arises from the stirring up of racial feeling; noticeable in various ways of late years, but specially through the Great War. Some 200,000 Chinese were on that occasion in the service of the Allies in munition work, the manning of ships, or making roads behind the lines. The number of Hindu troops sefting, in the war was very large, and their losses, especially in Mesopotamia, were heavy. Although Britain did not employ African negro troops on the Western front, the French did so to a large extent. It is certain that these members of black or "coloured" races brought back to their homes changed views as to life in general and a certain amount of dissatisfaction with their lot, the desire being felt for a more ample scope for existence. There is a demand for more room, as it were, which finds vent in a blind striking out in all directions. Of this we have examples in China at the present time. There are aspects of the situation which are not wholly to be deplored. There is an undoubted danger to the white race in some parts of the globe, like Australia and California, of being "swamped" by Chinese or Japanese settlement. The Chinaman has always been looked upon as an economic danger whenever his labour comes into competition with that of the European. "The Chinese coolie," says an American writer, "is the ideal industrial machine, the perfect human ox." He can live in almost any variety of climate, and once he gets unchecked admission is likely to drive out the white man. To some extent the same applies to Hindu coolie labour. If Hawaii is being "swamped" by Japanese, the island of Mauritius has been taken possession of by Hindus, who now form two-thirds of the whole population. Only for the enactment of an Exclusion Law recently, something of the same sort would have happened in Natal.

WAR SERVICE RESULTS. During the Great War, as in the wars of the middle of the eighteenth century between France and Britain, the conflict was not waged by whites alone. The "black" races of Africa, the "browns" of India, and the "yellow" of Japan took part in the actual fighting to a greater or less extent, and the services which they rendered in defeating the Germans were not allowed to sink into oblivion. The movement now visible in China is part of a world-wide stirring amongst the "coloured" races against white domination. All the benefits which the European has bestowed are ignored, but it is also forgotten that China is not yet at the stage at which she can dispense with extraneous guidance, whether from the European or the scarcely less unpopular Japanese. The attitude adopted by the Soviet Government at this juncture is true to the traditions of the "Czarist" Government, of which it is in many respects the true heir. Bolshevik intrigues may help to keep alive the agitation against the foreigner, but the real object in view is the regaining of that ascendancy in Manchuria which the Czar's advisers gained only to lose it in battle with Japan. If Britain were driven entirely away from the Chinese coast to morrow she would simply leave a clear field for Japan and Russia to fight in, with the pros-

headline: RESULT OF TEACHING.
text:
That the West is doubly responsible for the present movement for self-determination in China by reason of its touching and its promises and that it must not-in-sympathetic-co-operation is the burden of an article on "The Orient: Awake and Aggressive," appearing in the Christian Science Monitor.

There is hardly anything more certain in our uncertain human world than that a new factor has taken prominent place in the complicated equation of current events. The East—Near and Far: from the Pacific through to Egypt, and so across North Africa to Morocco—this far-flung East no longer is to be treated as was natural enough in those earlier generations when, obviously, it scare more than stirred uneasily in its age-long slumber under the impact of restless aggression from the other side the globe. "It is very much awake, now. It has become distinctly self-conscious; is fast growing as consistently active as for so long it has been persistingly passive. More and more it is playing a part, with increasing resistance to being played upon. Above all, from the Straits of Gibraltar to those of Tsushima, it is insisting on being its own master. In a word then our times must provide immediately some readjustment of relations between the civilisations of East and West, or the smouldering discontent of to-day may to-morrow flare up into the blaze of open widespread trouble.

In the actual fighting Japan won the first round, but the Russia Bolshevik diplomacy is now seeking to revenge the disasters of 1904 by striking at Japan and Britain, whose moral support contributed not a little to the victory of the former country on that occasion. JAPAN'S EXAMPLE:

Whether the Chinese will continue to lend themselves to be used for this purpose long enough to suit the designs of Moscow is a doubtful question. In the case of Japan's awakening she proved her capacity to develop along the lines chosen by her, retaining foreign assistance up to the point at which it could be dispensed with safely. No discrimination was exercised against any particular European nation, and an absence of violence characterised the proceedings. Japan's circumstances were, and still are, vastly different from those of China. The latter country, with her vast area and population of over 400 millions, offers a wide field for industrial development. The construction of railways, the opening up of the great coalfields and other mineral resources would give lucrative employment to many Chinamen now on the verge of starvation, and there are extensive areas in the west which could be made productive by cultivation on up-to-date lines. The men who have made such a tragic muddle of splendid opportunities in Russia are not likely to lead the Chinese along a safe path to national regeneration. Japan could do so with a fair amount of success, but she would be certain to exact a heavy price. Britain, which is being assailed most vigorously of all the supposed enemies of the "New China," is the best qualified to be the friend of that country. If the present attitude of certain sections of the Chinese people is persisted in, it will be a tragic blunder from the point of view of the whole country, and the consequences will be regretted in days to come when it is too late. There is enough intellect amongst the Chinese people to avert such a cost of strenge if it is properly brought and led in the right direction.

headline: PROUD MEMORY.
text:
I have valued my association with you more than I can say and it will always be one of my proudest memories that you have unanimously and repeatedly shown your confidence in me by asking that my term of office should be extend. If your request had been granted I should have been happy to remain, but, as this has not been found possible, I can only express to you my heartfelt thanks for paying me so striking a compliment.

I have also to thank you, gentlemen, one and all, for the invaluable help which you have given me during these years by your advice and criticisms. It has been a cause of admiration and wonder to me that in a Colony such as this, where there is no lessured class, it has always been possible to find able and hard-working men who will sacrifice their time to the gratuous service of the State. Membership of this Council has been no sinecure, and the Colony has cause to be grateful to all of you and to those other former members of the Council, who have been taken from us—such men as my dear friend Alexander Stephen, Montague Ede, Arthur Lowe, Lau Chu-pak, Ng Hon-tsz and Chow Sul-ki.

I owe a special debt of gratitude to those of you who have served on my Executive Council, for I fear that I have on many occasions taxed your patience to an

unprecedented extent by long sitings. I have often felt that, although you did not say so, you must have thought that I was wasting your time in long discussions and by bringing before you matters which there was no statutory obligation to refer to the Executive Council. If so I can only ask you to forgive me for taking advantage of your goodwill. My reason has been that I have always believed that it is better to discuss things before they are done rather than after, and whenever possible to make sure that all aspects of a question are considered before a decision is taken. I am not so vain as to believe that I have made no mistakes, but I do feel justified in claiming that I have avoided many by this policy and that those long meetings have served the public weal.

headline: COLONY'S PROGRESS.
text:
In addition to the messages of farewell to H.E. Sir R. E. Stubbs, reference was also made at yesterday's meeting of the Legislative Council to the services of Sir Claud Severn, the meeting in question being probably the last Council meeting... he will attend and certainly the last at which he will reply to points on the budget raised by Unofficial members.

H.E. the Governor in thanking Sir Claud Severn for the highly efficient manner in which he had served as Colonial Secretary for some 14 years in this Colony, referred to the entirely adequate manner in which he had taken the place of Governor during temporary absences. (Hear, hear)

Sir Claud Severn mentioned that this was the twelfth debate on the Budget in this Colony in which he had taken part, and he had had the honour of introducing the estimates for the years 1914, 1919 and 1923. The progress and development of the Colony and its general prosperity during the 14 years he had been here had, of course, been extremely gratifying to him as well as to the whole community. He had watched the progress of the Colony with the greatest possible interest, and although there was now what he was sure was generally felt to be just a temporary slackening of that development, he felt that if he was able to return to "this Colony" after a comparatively short time he would find all the big works that are in contemplation and had progress in full swing again and ample revenue to make provisions for them.

London, October 22.—Two more alleged Communists arrested by the Scotland Yale! main last night were Phannington and Robert Arnot, both described as members of the Commanist executive. The four Commanist leaders, Murphy, McMarus, Arnot and Flankington were remanded at Bow Street until to-morrow when they will be brought up with eight others and charged with sedition and conspiracy to incite mutiny.—Reuter.

headline: RIVER MINES?
text:
EMPLOYING UNQUALIFIED PILOTS?

A floating object, black, round and smooth, which might have been a mine, is reported to have been sighted by the s.s. "Honam". and to have passed halfway between Sampan Chau and Fish Stakes.

A Harbour Office's notification is posted to this effect and reporting that other vessels passing up and down the river have sighted similar objects, the French gunboat, "Argus" having met two within the last week.

Mishaps to steamers in the Canton river, reports of which have been received in Hongkong, are believed to have been due to the engagement of unqualified men as pilots. As most ships proceeding to Canton to discharge cargo do not call at Hongkong they have been at a loss to secure good pilots and the mishaps are the consequence.

There have been no serious accidents up to the present, the majority of groundings being cases of small steamers touching mud and coming off at the next high water, or after the cargo has been discharged in part. In some cases, however, vessels have been hard and fast for the best part of a week it is stated, and the work of lightening them is proceeding. Two that have been refloated are the "Nanyo Maru" No. 1 and the "Yei Maru," both of which were frequent callers at Hongkong prior to the boycott.

There has never been any opposition in this country to China's desire for a tariff rate higher than 5 per cent, or indeed, for a more scientific and better-distributed scale of duties. If the Central Government will guarantee that each province shall receive from the increased Customs revenue adequate compensation for the protection of trade within its borders, and if identical treatment is guaranteed to all goods, whether Chinese or foreign, the problem can certainly be solved in a practical and effective way. The stoppage of irregular taxes and the protection and security of trade throughout the country would have an immediate effect in restoring confidence among traders and investors all. From Our Own Correspondent.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
TECHNICAL INSTITUTE

Sir,—It is simple and clear that the present trouble has been initiated by some of the Hongkong students and for that various methods (including a contemplation of raising the school fees) have been introduced to punish the defaulters.

But isn't it strange that teachers were made to suffer for the students' fault (if it can be called a fault) because the normal class fee which was already considered rather high has been increased by 40 per cent., while owing to the present circumstances many teachers (normal students) got a reduction in their salary and therefore the above increase is absolutely unjustified.

Is it not that the aim of the Technical Institute is to give a liberal Education for bettering the knowledge of those who can not afford to join a higher school or university? If so, why should its aim be lost? Also certain Educational Institute in Hongkong seems to lose sight of the ends of its founder who devoted all his time to teach the poor children and surely expects his followers to do the same and not to refuse the admission of the poor boys who pay deficient fees under the excuse "no place."

headline: LIES: GOOD AND BAD.
text:
It happened to me the other day, while engaged on the rather sad task of reholding old letters, to come across one about golf, writes the golf correspondent of "The Times." The writer was praising the beautiful turf of a seaside course (the turf there is beautiful and delicate still, though this is 40 years on) and wrote:—"I think a professional could take his driver wherever he wanted to except in the bunkers."

There seems to me something pathetic and ingenious and out of date in that comment; it is a sentence that nobody would write to-day. First, there is the mention of a professional as if he were a god. A professional is a great man still, but not quite so great as when golf was first beginning to spread over England. Then he appeared a wizard or a conjurer. His very manner of waggling a club seemed unearthly to the band of clumsy middle-aged novices. He came, too, from a far country, he was a Scot and they were Englishmen; he had all that stark and formidable quality, that musky glamour, which belong to the North in Southern eyes.

That however, is by the way. What really strikes me as old and old-fashioned is the picture of the professional taking his driver nowadays except on the tea. He tears the ball away with his strong iron, and at long intervals takes his spoon. Once there really was wooden club play through the green. He wanted to use his driver even when playing his own ball. He wanted to use it very often, when retrieving the inept effects of his partner in a foursome. Alas! who takes out the professional to play in a foursome to-day?

And then how eloquent are those few words in the matter of lies, good lies and bad lies. No one to-day exclaims gladly that he has got a good life, nor grumbles at his enemy's luck in having one. We take our good lies for granted and only mention the subject of lies at all when railing against our fate. It is hard to say to what extent this is due to better and more expensive green keeping, and to what extent to the rubber-cored ball. Certainly if we do get a bad lie, the ball flies easily away from it; it also makes it possible to take all iron club with far less sacrifice of distance. The reward of the man who can nip the ball out and away with wood is not what it was. Of all the romantic and splendid things I can remember from my earliest reading in golf, one stands out.

It related to Lieutenant James Campbell Stewart, of the 72nd Highlanders, a great man who played level with Allan Robertson and, with Mr. George Glennie, won the Silver Claret Jug in the grand tournament at St. Andrews in 1858, "thereby," as the records of Blackheath so proudly tell, "constituting this club the Champion Golf Club of the World." Somewhere it is written of Mr. Stewart that he never troubled to see his ball, but threw it down upon the teeing ground; and before that simple statement all the stories of the Morrises and the Parks paled in my youthful eyes. It is true that I have since had doubts, Mr. Stewart must have thrown his ball warily. Perhaps he resembled a man throwing a document dramatically into the fire after making sure that the fire

was out. Or perhaps—well, perhaps, in short, it was a lie. If so, it was at any rate a good one. There is something else which may make our lies seem better today. That is—and I am treading on controversial ground—the comparative parity of crossbunkers.

headline: LIGHT ON CANTON.
text:
EFFORTS TO REACH A SETTLEMENT

SHANGHAI PAPER'S COMMENT.

our Canton correspondent account of how the strike picket had arrested the installation manager of the A. P. C. as hailed from the steam. "Honam," after firing some rifle shots at his launch, says the "North China Daily News. Another correspondent now writes to say that this report was exaggerated, that only two shots were fired, probably from a revolver, and not at the launch but in the air, as a warning only. Our original correspondent quoted it witness on the "Honam." The information received recently apparently was from the installation manager himself. The writer of this letter comments not without reason, on the injurious effect of any exaggeration at a time like this when, he thinks, the influence of the extremists is warning. He says that although the recent negotiation for the ending of the boycott failed, there is a growing party among Cantonese officials and merchants who are working for a settlement behind the scenes. In proof of the better feeling which he believes to exist, he says that the general attitude towards the British is much improved, that they move freely about the city nowadays without interference and that some of them have even visited Whampoa and walked through the cantonments, of the cadets without being molested in any way. "In fact many of the soldiers came to attention and saluted" as the party went by. Furthermore, the Shameen Municipal Council are removing the barricades and most of the barbed wire and the gates of the Shameen are open from sunrise to sunset. All this is very good news, the import of which, as regards Chinese feeling in Cantons, does not lack corroboration in other quarters.

Certain outstanding facts and tendencies may be remembered at the present juncture. Foremost, perhaps that it is not in the kindly nature of the Chinese people to stay in a passion and nourish unkindly feeling. Secondly, that the interests of so many Cantonese business men and shopkeepers are so closely bound up with those of the Chinese in Hongkong, that there is always a strong disposition towards a settlement if only it can find room to act. On the other side, there is the intemperate nature of the extremists, like Chou Enlai, recently speaking at Swatow on the fight against imperialism. As regards this party, there appears reason to think that the dictatorial attitude of Moscow's agents is beginning to be resented even by their most ardent followers. In general, one may take it as an axiom that the Chinese will not submit to outside control indefinitely. It is perhaps not going too far to hazard the opinion that the movement started by the Russians will not subside, but will become less Russian and more Chinese, more genuinely national and less wildly doctrinaires. For the basis of all these manifestations, we cannot forget, is national feeling. That they should in their first operation be extravagant and ill-regulated is not in the least surprising: it is the rule with all such movements. But as time goes on and the first fury subsides, the whole political impetus will gain in reason and popular support. There is undoubted wisdom in one suggestion recently made by a correspondent of this paper that the only possible way of dealing with the new forces at work in South China (and not only in the south) is to recognise that they have come to stay, to wait patiently for the gradual moulding of them which the irresistible influence of Chinese thought, philosophy and sentiment must impart and to endeavour to make friends with them and gain their confidence.

headline: EVOLUTION OF MAN
text:
THE RACE IN ITS INFANCY.

There was a large congregation at the luncheon hour service at Christ Church, Westminster, for an address by Sir Oliver Lodge on the subject of the evolution of man.

Sir Oliver said the order of evolution was first some grade of plant, then water beasts, then land beasts. The first truly land animals were lizards or reptiles, come of which took to the air and became birds, while others developed into mammals, which were in the line of human ancestry and were comparatively late-comers on this planet. It was noteworthy that no special day was allotted in the Genesis story to the creation of man. He was represented as originating in the evening of the day on which the mammals originated, the special distinction given to him being not in a special variety of form but in the soul. His superiority and intelligence were indicated by the dominion, granted to him. Thus man was raised far above his bodily ape-like ancestors and felt like a new creation. We could not really follow the whole process of man's evolution, which must have been very gradual; but at some stage a special kind

It was not easy to specify at what stage the developing creature might be called human, but he thought all agreed that it was only a case of thousands of years—perhaps 50,000, perhaps 100,000, but certainly a short time. So far as humanity was concerned, we were still in the morning of the times and the human race was still in its infancy. The human race began but a short time ago and might have millions of years before it on this planet.

Going on to speak of the development of the sense of free will, Sir Oliver said it probably arose very gradually, but we might conceive its apprehension by some early genius of the race whom we might regard as "the first man," whether we called him Adam or any other name. He said the story of the fall in the third chapter of Genesis was a crude legend, but it contained a great truth. The free will, being was liable to fall from his highest eminence, and, as all Christians believed, a lofty Being ultimately took flesh and dwelt among us to help humanity and share its weaknesses and burden. We could not examine the Incarnation in the light of science. Apart from all puzzles of theology we were immortal beings with a great destiny before us, and were surrounded by a host of helpers with whom, indeed, I know that it is possible to have communion.

Mr. Wu, whose speech was on much the same lines as the statement issued by the Canton Government last week, sought to acquit the Canton Government of responsibility for the prolonging of the boycott. "Our Government had nothing to do with the strike which the Chinese workers at Hongkong started as a demonstration of protest against the British people in China and the British Government of which the Hongkong Government is a part.

"When the first indications of a strike settlement were mooted, our Government made it clear that if the Hongkong Government was desirous of a settlement, it could not be with the Canton Government but must be with the strikers and people. The Canton Government could not add had no right to intervene as one of the principals."

Nevertheless, continued Mr. Wu, "seeing that the aim and object of the popular strike had been achieved as a protest against the British, and mindful of the fact that the Chinese both in Hongkong and Canton were suffering by the continuance of the strike and boycott, the Canton Government placed no obstacles and rather encouraged or welcomed all attempts put forth to bring about an early settlement between the two parties concerned. Unofficial pourparlers were entered into on the distinct understanding that.

1. The discussions between the Government and Hongkong would be informal and unofficial.

2. The Government was not one of the parties in the desired settlement which had to be effected direct between the strikers and the Hongkong Government.

Our Government had to make this abundantly clear, Mr Wu said, because we did not wish to compromise the Government in the eyes of the world.

Mr. Wu then went into details concerning the Canton Government's part in the negotiations. Coming to the appointment of a Canton official to visit Hongkong. Mr. Wu said: —

"On receipt of the Hongkong Governor's letter, our Government deliberated whether we should or should not send one of our officials down to Hongkong. The first consideration was one of prestige, as on the face of it, there was no reason why we should send one of our officials to Hongkong at the request of the Hongkong Governor. However, on careful consideration, our Government decided that as we were desirous to have the strike settled at an early date, the sooner the better, so as to shorten the sacrifices that the strikers had borne, and the losses that our Chinese merchants in Hongkong and Canton were suffering, we would brush aside the matter of dignity and comply with the request of the Hongkong Governor."

The Canton Government, Mr. W. continued, thus showed its sincerity in desiring to have the strike settled. "Because the visit would be entirely unofficial and private, our Government did not send one of its diplomatic officials but sent a high official from another department.

“This official went down to Hongkong and after discussing the situation with the Hongkong Governor returned, accompanied by a high official from Hongkong, who stayed here for two or three days. Our Government showed the Hongkong official every courtesy and met and conferred with him repeatedly.”
