headline: $3 a Day.
text: The statements made in "the course of the prosecution of a Kowloon house coolie yesterday do not give rise to satisfactory thoughts. General conversation has been devoted to the action of servants generally and the treatment to be meted when they returned. Yesterday's case proved that the servants of a prominent Kowloon resident lost no time in leaving his employment and later that he found the lowliest of them in other employment at $3'a day. Such a condition of things seems hopeless, suggests selfishness, and must tend to sour those who are seeking the good of the community by a uniform standard of settlement. Mr. Wylie has done good in taking the trouble to appear in court. It reveals the attitude of certain members of the community who have "money to burn" and also the fact that intimidation does not seem to count where emergency wages can be obtained by a coolie at the princely rate of $3 a day. Something drastic should be devised to meet such a state of affairs.

headline: BEHIND THE SCENES IN SHANGHAI.
text:
With uniform alacrity, press accounts of the serious anti-foreign movement in Shanghai and other Chinese cities have laid the blame at the gate of the Kremlin, says a "Christian Science Monitor" writer. In the news stories of a single day, in fact, one finds the "Rods" held responsible for French difficulties in North Africa; British difficulties in Afghanistan; and this Chinese outbreak in Shanghai. Unquestionably the potency of Moscow's influence has been widely-overestimated; and Communian, too often has been advanced to explain situations for which no other explanation could be found or for which a more accurate explanation was not held to be altogether desirable.

But with all due allowance for the exaggerated menace of Soviet propaganda—activities,—it—still remains most likely that Russian influence in China is the immediate cause of the present difficulty. When Karakhan, the present Soviet Ambassador, came to Peking he brought with him a staff, the size of which was more than passingly significant. The Ambassador, himself, did nothing to conceal his determination to reveal to the Chinese, on the one hand, "the treachery" of the powers in China, and, on the other hand, "the honesty" of the purposes of the Soviets.

As proof of this latter point the Soviets relinquished extra-territorial rights in China and made other promises—most of which have not fully been carried out. The relinquisition of extra-territoriality, however, proved to be a potent argument with the young Chinese and the Soviet representatives soon made a large place for themselves in certain of the intellectual circles of China.

The significance of this achievement cannot be over-estimated. In China the intelligentsia possess a status higher than accorded to them in Western nations. Many, perhaps most, of the great reform movements in China's history have been instigated by the student classes. The most recent example of this is found in the student uprising against Japan in 1919 which resulted in a nation-wide boycott of Japanese goods in protest against the award to Japan of rights in Shantung Province. The Soviets, having won the friendship of certain elements among the students, have allied with themselves one of the most powerful groups in the country. Having thus satisfied large numbers of these students that their purposes were honest, the Soviets proceeded to demonstrate the dishonesty of the Powers in their dealings with China. The hostility that resulted from this effort was apparent before the recent outbreak developed. This hostility took the form of an active anti-Christian movement. The headquarters of this movement were in Shanghai. The ones were established through

outside of them. In Foochow, in Fukien Province, for example, the Anglo-Chinese college was practically forced to close its doors recently because of the reign of terror inaugurated against Christians by a guerrilla student organization known as the "Blood and Iron Band."

It is this developing hostility that has now centered in Shanghai. The exact occasion for the trouble leaves something to be desired, from the point of view of the foreigners in the city. Industrial conditions in the foreign-owned mills of Shanghai are notoriously bad. A strike occurred recently in one of these mills, owned by a Japanese concern. The strikers were arrested, just why has not appeared. They were brought before the Mixed Court—a tribunal composed of a Chinese and a foreign justice to deal with cases affecting the interests of both Chinese and foreigners. The court jailed the strikers—This action—an action which sorely needs explanation—fanned the smouldering fires of re-sentment against foreigners. Students rushed in to infuiliate the labourers. Industry has practically closed down and a virtual state of war exists in the city.

Wheeler or not the Mixed Court was justified in sentencing the Chinese strikers - particularly in the face of the growing hostility to foreigners - is a question that has not been answered. That the Soviets, through their hold on student groups, are utilizing the situation to their own ends is undeniable. Communism thrives where there is trouble. Peace is contrary to the Soviet programme. Every incipient outbreak is hailed in Moscow with great glee, as hemiding the progress of world revolution.

Progress and justice, save in terms of violence and destruction, is invariably regarded with scorn by Moscow's trouble-brewers. That China has not always fared well at the hands of foreigners is undeniable. That progress toward better treatment is being made is equally undeniable. It is unquestionably the Soviet fear that this progress threatens their own programme taint had led them to foster, on whatever pretext presents itself, this anti-foreign uprising in China. A further fact needs to be kept in mind in regard to this difficulty. Neither all—or a majority—of the intelligent Chinese leaders or students are in sympathy with the Communist Party. There may be some basis for dissatisfaction with the decision of the Mixed Court. But reports coming from mission schools in China indicate that a vast number of the students have been awayed by Soviet propaganda and desire nothing more than peace for their country. Let like manner, the roll orders of Chinese life a great many of whom have studied in America and England will not be easily swung from a belief in orderly progress in violence.

"Here I be and here I intends to stay" is not a case that requires elaborate refutation.

As for the legal objections raised, they could easily be overcome, as Lord Hewitt made clear in an article of which the Duke of Atholl reminded their lordships. This is not a question of legality, but of justice and expediency, and against these twin arguments the opposition were hard put to it to make out a convincing case. The most formidable, if not the newest, weapon in their armoury was the argument of procrastination: the House of Lords is soon to be reformed; why, not, then, in the interests of compactness, delay the smaller measure till it can be incorporated in the larger. We are bound to say that this argument strikes us as having about it more than a savour of opportunism. But in any case we have yet to learn by what law of right or reason it must be considered improper to do to day what it will, admittedly, be proper to do tomorrow. It is from such defences as these that the peeresses and their sympathisers have for the moment fallen back frustrated. But only for the moment. Into all other departments of public life, women have won their way, and only by two votes did they fail of their last objective. The battle is as surely won as if the Bill had been read a second time.

Typhoon Wireless.

Referred to by the Colonial Secretary during yesterday's Finance Committee meeting was a matter which was overshadowed by the Governor's strike statement but which has a considerable bearing on the future well-being of the community and the efficiency of a very vital service, namely the commencement of wireless communication between Hongkong and the Pratas Shoal. This statement may not to the lay mind appear of sufficient importance to warrant its being bracketed with a matter of such moment as the strike but the initiated see in it something which will endure long when the strike is but a memory, the commencement of a service which, if adequately maintained, will be a most important safeguard not only to Hongkong but to the shipping trade on the welfare of which Hongkong depends for its prosperity. It is, of course, but a commencement and the present typhoon season may be over before regular notifications of typhoon movements, which alone would be of any material assistance, are made available; but it serves to show that the undertaking given by the Chinese Admiralty was not an empty promise although the project has taken long enough to materialise. It was in 1909 that the Chinese Government first agreed to erect such a station although in justice to them it should be stated that definite instructions had been given, which were interfered with by the Revolution in China and that the Great War was also responsible for attention being distracted from the scheme. The Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce has all along interested itself in the matter and the Chinese Maritime Customs, under the Chinese Admiralty, has more or less made itself responsible for the work. It only remains now for the Chinese Government to see to it that an efficient staff is sent to operate the wireless and meteorological station and doubtless the Hongkong Government will do its part in the matter of despatching of provisions and reliefs—the special tug which was to be for this purpose is well on the way to completion.

question of how long it will take the strikers to come to their senses and decide that a steady billet in Hongkong is, after all, much preferable to what the Governor neatly termed the "hospitality of Canton." Judging from reports filtering through from that hotbed of intrigue, whilst many may be willing to throw up the sponge the leaders of the movement directed against law and order are bent on prolonging their absence from Hongkong as long as possible. If threats and intimidation have played some part in inducing employees to leave their work here, it is quite certain that these mental instruments of torture exist to a far greater extent in Canton. It is true that some have been permitted to return, but the credentials of these should, if at all possible, be carefully examined.

Meanwhile, until “something happens” in Canton, it seems useless to think of the strike here coming to an end so quickly as some would like. All that can be usefully done is to continue with the good work in the absence of the strikers, always remembering, as His Excellency the Governor also did well to point out, that the inconveniences are not all on one side. In fact, the lot of the strikers in Canton may not be altogether an enviable one even when that “something” does happen. Many may find that working peacefully in Hongkong under the protection of the British flag is a thousand times to be preferred to being utilised as “gun fodder” for the rival.

He would be a bold man even at this time of day who would profess to foretell the date of the strike with accuracy. In this respect the strike is remarkable. That is because of the fact, as His Excellency the Governor explained in his speech in the Legislative Council on Thursday, that there are no issues to be settled either by compromise or by agreement. There is not a single point on which the contending parties—the strikers and the employers—can possibly hinge on a excuse for a round table conference. In this respect the strike is unique among strikes the world over.

headline: DRIVER'S NERVES / ACOIDENT ATTRIBUTED TO INTIMIDATION.
text:
Kowloon 'bus drivers report' to the police that they have been intimidated by men, with revolvers. One, who was concerned in an accident near the Orient Buildings on Thursday night, attributes this to the effect on his nerves which this had had. He stated that revolvers had been pointed at him outside the Mongok Police station.

No passengers were injured in the accident in question although the "bus completely overturned." A telephone message was sent to the offices of the "bus Company (also on Thursday evening) to the effect that a "bus driver had been intimidated at Shamshuipo by a number of men who produced revolvers. The driver was afraid to drive back to the garage until the police arrived. When the police did arrive on the scene the intimidators had disappeared and efforts to truck them failed. More than that it may not have been possible for the British Foreign Secretary to have stated in the condensed form of a cablegram. But, it reveals the traditional British policy of trusting the man on the spot and of telling the world that the fullest confidence is felt in his actions. That is one view to take of the Foreign Secretary's message but it is not the only one. There is that rebuff to the Canton Government — a rebuff that cannot be welcomed by it in view of the previous desire expressed by its spokesmen for time "to see what it can do" in the way of setting Canton's house in order after the eviction of the Yunnanese. Three months was asked as a sort of probationary period, but the new Government in Canton was not three weeks in power before it disclosed "what it can do"—witness the attack on Shameen and the countenancing of the strike in Hongkong. Now that the British Foreign Office has seen what the new Canton Government can do it will be prepared for any emergency.

There is yet another view of the Foreign Secretary's message to the Consul-General, and that is the excellent material it affords for propaganda, plain and unadorned, amongst all sections of the Chinese community. The Consul-General has been supported, and will continue to be supported, by all the weight behind the British Foreign Office. That means not merely the British Government but the whole British Empire, which is no less interest

ed in the Shameen concession than the handful of British residents who were subjected to the shameful outrage by the Russian-led troops of the Canton Government. The handwriting is on the wall for the Canton leaders to read—and to heed lest they contemplate countenancing another attack on Shameen. The British lion's tail may be twisted just once too often!

Antichrist.

The voice of professional religion in the Colony has not been very audible so far in the matter of our present troubles: Orthodoxy will go on its steady way, taking no sides but using petitions and prayers for a speedy deliverance out of all our troubles with the usual catchwards of “lasting peace,” etc. Disturbers of the world's peace were wont to be called Antichrists and such one-time prominent individuals as Napoleon and the ex-Kaiser have had this unenviable name thrust upon them. It now remains for some prophet to use the name nearer home and to apply it to “Reds” of whatsoever physical colour they may be. No harm will be done, a little nonsense now and then being relished in the most serious of times. Even so, there are those who take this matter seriously and a spice of today's news deals with the attempt in America to put in their place those whose modern teaching and outlook compel them to discard the fundamentalism of old evangelical Bible teaching and to reach out for the new that, seemingly places reason first and faith next. These latter are being dubbed “antichrists.” The word is likely to assume a measure of importance denied it in ordinary times. To use it in connection with the present condition of things would be ludicrous, although seeing that much of it in China is against Christian teaching, it may well be used in a limited sense.

headline: THAT REBUFF.
text: The cablegram from the Foreign Secretary to the Consul-General at Canton has been the subject of much comment locally, satisfaction being expressed at the fact that, although it may seem rather belated—the attack on Shameen was made on June 23—it administers a distinct rebuff to the Government of Canton. The Foreign Secretary entirely homologates the warning sent to Dr. Wu by Sir J. W. Jamieson, as of course it was expected it would, and, moreover, expresses the hope that Sir J. W. Jamieson will continue to handle the situation with his accustomed skill and judgment.

headline: TIMELY ADVICE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir, — Will you allow me through the medium of your columns to register a protest against the vindictive tone which is gradually creeping into the local Press, and even into official utterances, when discussing the present unfortunate state of affairs. Such a feeling is, no doubt, natural under the circumstances but a little reflection should show us that it is both unwise and unjust to give way to it. We are living, although in a British Colony, amongst the Chinese with whom most of us must trade in order to live. We cannot get on without the Chinese nor they, I venture to say in spite of the Canton Government's opinion, without us. It should be borne in mind that the present agitation has been carefully prepared and fostered by the worst elements of Russia for their own ends, co-operating with a comparatively small clique of Chinese, partly malcontents out to line their own pockets and partly idealistic dreamers. Able countrymen of our own with a life time's experience of China have left on record their opinion that the Chinese generally, particularly the poorer classes, are a kindly, peaceable and industrious people, but the cunning of the professional agitator has given to the present movement the complexion of a great patriotic demonstration and when we remember the power of a patriotic appeal in our own country and the ignominy attaching to those who fail to respond we should surely have at least as much sympathy and admiration for the great many loyal Chinese who are continuing in our midst at their regular duties, as blame for those poor sheep who have followed their leaders into the wilderness. Last I should be taken to counsel leniency to lawbreakers and mischief makers I would urge on the contrary that at present and for such an outrage as that committed recently in Connaught Road, if our criminal code permits, the penalty should be death preceded by flogging. As, however, the perpetrators of even such a crime as this may be sincere, though misguided, patriots, it is unworthy of British traditions to exult in their punishment nor should we make ridiculous rules calculated to make life in the Colony intolerable for those Chinese who remain. No more sedition is talked, for instance on Blake Pier than in the back streets of Wanchai or Kennedy Town, nor is there any more danger of this occurring in the evening than during the day.

Leave the "Canton Gazette" to spit and fume but for God's sake let us keep our sense of proportion.

Yours, etc.,

Northcott. Such homilies as he delivered may be liable to be passed over in normal times, but they deserve all the prominence possible when the agitators are let loose and timid strikers are between two fires. The rev. gentleman uttered a strong condemnation of Bolshevism, the tenor of which, of course, is not in any way strange to those who have the following the teachings of Trotsky since the earliest days of the Soviet regime. But a good story lacks nothing in the telling again and again, especially if in the reiteration there be the remotest chance to make the enemy pause and to inspire pluck into the intimidated Great Britain is their ciner enemy it is a compliment to every Briton. More, it is a challenge that will not go unheeded so long as it continues to be the menace it is to all the traditions of the British Empire and so long as it threatens to disintegrate what it has taken centuries of British pluck, endurance, and enterprise to build up within the confines of our rightful and legitimate domain.

It is well that the Chinese as a whole should learn the truth about Bolshevism, which, as the Rev. R. J. Northcott pointed out, has caricatured the great Christian watchwords of liberty, equality, and fraternity. There is no liberty in modern Russia for anything or anybody, which is a striking contrast to the conditions of freedom obtaining under the Union Jack. Equality is unknown in Russia, for the Reds have shown themselves more despotic and tyrannical than any kings or Tsars. Instead of fraternity there exist bitterness, hatred, starvation and terrorism—an unevitable exchange even for the conditions obtainable in China itself during normal times and still more wretched exchange for the conditions prevailing wherever the British flag is flown. It is well for the pulpit no less than the Press to emphasize that if the Bolshevists consider that Even if the strike lasts but another fortnight the lessons unfolded by Empire teachers and preachers during the present state of emergency will never fall on barren soil or be considered a mere beating of the air.

A Municipal Council.

The Government as a result of its strike experiences will surely legislate for a Municipal Board or Council. Had there been no Kowloon and Peak Residents Association, the present position would not have been met so spontaneously. There is now to be a mid-level Residents Association, so that the only part of the Colony to be unrepresented or without any voice will be the centre and extreme ends of the town containing probably the largest class of residents—and the people who, by being scattered, suffer most whenever there is an upheaval as at present. The Government, as at present constituted, attempts too much and consequently either does not do all it sets out to do, or does a lot of it inefficiently. It has created a Sanitary Board and also an Education Board with limited powers;—and—only—a-churl would argue that these Boards have not proved their worth. They have thrown light on two most important branches of local endeavour and the members of them have taken their duties and tackled them in a serious manner in spite of the fact that their wings are clipped to the most extreme degree. A number of other Boards are highly desirable. The P.W.D., for instance, would function more easily if it had a Board of an advisory capacity working with it. When there is a strike upheaval it is a question of "Tommy here and Tommy there" (if we may so call the Hongkong resident)—but when trouble ends, "Tommy" recedes into the background until the next call comes. We need not labour the point. The Colony possesses organisers of a high order—not necessarily Peak residents or taipans. Soak them out and let them not stagnate in a sea of indifference.

headline: The Shipping Strike.
text:
Like everywhere else we have been subjected to plenty of student agitation, more especially against the British and Japanese, and several times there have been threats of a general strike of servants, but so far, to a large extent thanks to our enterprising Tao-Yin, nothing has occurred in that way.

The shipping strike has, of course, upset things here to some extent as we are more or less dependent on the steamers owing to having no railway connection nearer than Wei-Hsien, which can only be reached by motor car service. Summer visitors have been considerably hindered in arriving here, more especially from the South, but during the last few days several parties have turned up, some by China Merchants' steamers and others by rather roundabout routes. There seems to be quite a boycott of British and Japanese goods by the merchants, although this, too, is probably more talk than actual, quite a number of dealers having bought in considerable stocks from the foreign firms before the boycott was supposed to commence.

I heard to-day that insurance policies are being withdrawn from the British firms, but this also is probably only a temporary measure on the part of merchants to appease the student agitators.

On the whole, however, we have probably been more fortunate than most other ports, partly because of the presence of the U.S.S. Huron and several destroyers, and partly because of firm action taken by the foreign Consuls and the responsible Chinese authorities—the Tao-Yin and the Chinese General.

headline: Mixed Labour.
parent_headline: H. M. HAJEE ESMAIL 2 TIN LOK LANE MORRISON HILL
text: Chinese labour has had the Colony by the throat. Its methods have even been cut-throat. Would the Colony have been partially paralysed if the labour elements had been mixed and not wholly Chinese? Those who discuss the question say it would not. Why not then have cocktail labour—a sprinkling of various nationalities? It would not prevent the consolidation of labour or reduce even the potency of Labour Guilds; but it would reduce the possibility of dislocation caused by freaks of humour and childishness. It is reasonable to assume that non-Chinese would refuse to listen to the voice of intimidation, and refuse also to strike unless there were good grounds for so doing. Is the matter one of practical politics?

headline: Cash Payments.
parent_headline: H. M. HAJEE ESMAIL 2 TIN LOK LANE MORRISON HILL
text: The conditions under which we exist have played havoc with the chit system. Those who have risen to the occasion and continued to cater for our creature comforts have rightly stipulated for cash payments: It has enabled them to dispense with clerical labour and helped that quick passing of money which means good trade and cheap prices. It has been usual to commence certain types of conversation with—“When the strike is over.” When it is over and becomes a set topic of dinner conversation, perhaps a part of the “settlement” will be some drastic review of the chit system. Its entire abolition does not seem possible or desirable. But there should be some diminution in the amounts for which it is possible to sign.

headline: THE DELUGE. / STREETS CLEARED THOUGH INUNDATED.
text:
The number of pedestrians caught unprepared in yesterday's downpour and detained under shelter for the greater part of an hour when there was a temporary cessation was surprising in view of the warning given by the ominous clouds. Whilst it lasted, it was as heavy as downpour as Hongkong has experienced for some considerable time and if it had continued for any length of time there would probably have been serious landslides to record. As it is, however, although the wake of the atmospheric disturbance left by the typhoon which entered the coast near Swatow has not yet departed, the worst that it has given rise to is a little temporary inconvenience, in some cases a slight inundation of the lower regions of the house through drains not having been cleared so regularly since the strike and in many cases of street floods due to the same reason and the tremendous tax placed upon the drains by the enormous volume of water and the refuse carried down to the main streets.

The trite maxim that "Tis an ill wind" applies equally to rain in certain circumstances. and yesterday's certainly did more thoroughly and with considerably greater despatch scavenging work which hundreds of coolies might have tackled in vain.

During 3.30 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. the Observatory registered a fall of 1.82 in.

OFFICIALS DETAINED. As the height of the storm was at the time that the Sanitary Board was due to meet, the only members of the Sanitary Board present were the President (Mr. N. L. Smith), the Medical Officer (Dr. W. W. Pearse) and the Secretary (Mr. G. S. Kennedy-Skipton).

For what is believed to be the first time in the history of the Board, the meeting had therefore to be postponed on account of the absence of a quorum.

Dr. Severn (the Assistant Medical Officer of Health) and Mr. D. D. Davies (the Assistant Secretary) also attended.

headline: TOLERATION.
text:
Toleration seems to be the key-note of the situation in the Colony. There is an effort to exploit that phase to the utmost. There is toleration with the "daily (a-k, the common round)" which have become inevitable in what is tantamount to a servantless city. What may have seemed novel and even irritable in the first week of the strike is now being tolerated. The household chores have to be done. Somebody has to do them, if householders and their families are to eat and sleep and generally live in spite of the strike. The work of the office must go on, and the shell-shattered phrase, "Business as usual" is a fair substitution for sheer toleration, however monotonous it may be becoming. As there are limits to patience there may be limits to toleration, and to paraphrase another phrase much noted when His Excellency the Governor decided to stay on and see this business through "someons will suffer" when both toleration and patience go by the risk. That "someone" almost needless to say is the smite for the

liar who stooped to every fabrication and every device to induce otherwise unoffending, servants to put their employers to the inconvenience of a strike. Even with a certain class of servant there cannot be sympathy. Some of these knew full well what the result of their "downing tools" would mean not only for their particular employers but for the whole community, Chinese as well as non-Chinese. Apart from any withholding of strike pay and the forfeiture of wages earned during June there must be hundreds of "Number Ones" and office assistants who joined in the little jaunt to Canton with their eyes wide open—they required precious little in the way of intimidation to leave, and to induce their fellow-servants to go likewise.

Now that the inconvenience on the part of the employers is being reduced day by day, the position is being reversed. It is now a question of how long there will exist the spirit of tolerance amongst the strikers with the conditions obtaining in Canton, The inconveniences and even hardships to which they are being subjected must by now be teaching them that Canton is indeed a hard-nay a cruel-taskmaster in comparison with the assured steadiness of their billets in Hongkong, with no risks whatever in pursuing their callings or exacting their "squeeze." It was the easiest thing in the world to find five dollars and rush off to Canton. Again the tables are turned, and they are finding that the mere will to return to Hongkong is not by any means sufficient for that will to be converted into power and ability to come back. They have been robbed of their birthright by the very Government whose protection they so rashly sought, and those of them who do filter through and take up billets here will by then have received a lesson that should last them all their lives. But before the great majority ever see Hongkong again their patience and their toleration will have been sadly depleted—and what may happen then is the concern of the Canton

There is a suspicion of Mrs. Beeton about the discussions regarding servants. First procure an egg, says Mrs. B. in dealing with a domestic recipe. Then follows instructions as to beating, ingredients; time, etc. So with servants. First get your servant. Generally it is likely to be someone else's; and generally the tired house-holder is likely to seize him with both hands without enquiring whence he came and whom he has served. The calm-and unbiased onlooker—if such there be in these hectic times—may question if much, if any, good is being done by public discussions on treatment of servants: and he may well question the wisdom of Government servants taking a prominent part in them, as happened at the meeting of the Mid-Levels Residents' Association yesterday. Such proceedings, liberally broadcasted, are likely to strengthen the hands of propagandists in Canton, who are bound to put them in the most lurid manner, and to add to present difficulties. The law is clear as to June wages, and a number of Kowloon residents have made this additionally clear by prosecuting absent servants, and done not a little to impress the servant class with the nature of their offence. It is desirable that there should be unanimity of treatment and not haphazard arrangements that will tend to split the ranks of employers. Servants are necessary. They must be employed—presumably the sooner the better. It should not be difficult for representatives of—the Residents' Associations which continue to multiply, to get together,—and once—and for all solve a not insuperable problem, to the extent even of forming a Registration Bureau.

headline: CHINESE LABOUR.
text:
CHINA'S GREAT BLAME.

The following letter from Mr Gilbert G. Warren appears in the “London Times” of June 12:—

Those who by long residence in China realise what are the actual conditions of industrial life there agree with your Peking Correspondent in believing that in present circumstances it would be the cruellest thing to the working class to comede to any serious degree what the students demand for the factory hands.

The conditions of their work, appalling an hideous as they are, neither are the cause of the disturbances at Shanghai, nor have they, as the I.L.P. states, been "introduced into the Far East by foreign capitalism." They are native to China and are prevalent there and do not reflect specially on the mill-owners whether Chinese or foreign, of Shanghai. On the contrary, those of us who know China from within know that the conditions inside the factories at Shanghai and elsewhere contrast favourably with conditions anywhere outside in providing lighter work, better wages, and shorter hours. As evidence of this, I may refer to two cities, Changsha and Han-kow, in which for the past 40 years I have lived. As far as labour is concerned, these cities are thoroughly typical,—and in both hundreds of children under 10 work 18 hours a day for seven days a week for food only—and a miserably insufficient supply of that—at shoemaking, tailoring, hand-loom weaving, and even as apprentices to metal tinsmiths and blacksmiths. To change economic conditions like these needs something more than revolutions or political action.

As to extrality, as extraterritoriality is better termed, the I.L.P. can have no idea what would be the result to Chinese workmen if they were granted "the fullest recognition of the right of the Chinese people to manage their own affairs." The following incident speaks for itself; and more effectively than argument. In January, 1922, there was a minor disturbance at a Chinese-owned spinning mill at Changsha (a mill in which no foreigner has any part or lot) over the trifling question of a small travel allowance made to the workers to enable them to get home for their Chinese New Year holiday. No damage whatever was done to the property; there was nothing more than a somewhat noisy demonstration by the workers, a disturbance so slight that had it occurred in the International Settlement in Shanghai, the Chinese owners would not have found it possible to bring any action against the demonstrators, or even to have obtained summonses against them. At Changsha, however, within 24 hours two men who were supposed, perhaps rightly, to have been leaders were arrested in the street at dusk; taken to the Governor's headquarters, and in the morning their decapitated bodies were lying outside the city gate. Any trial which they may have had was without any possibility of defence by the accused; no legal help could be procured, no witnesses called, no documents other than what they may have had on their persons could be produced. In the same jurisdiction and at the same time four lads under 20 had been lying imprisoned for four months, not only without trial but without any kind of formal accusation. Their release was accomplished not through process of law, but because the Chinese Governor urgently needed someone to translate into English and send to the "N.C.D. News" a letter in which he defended his action in executing the two labour leaders. This translation I undertook, on condition that he would release the lads within 24 hours. The bargain was accepted and carried out.

The only chance of procuring for Chinese workmen any approach to such social and political liberty as the British workman enjoys is, in my opinion, to refuse to revise the system of extrality embodied in treaties until China has a legal system of her own securing, not also merely for foreigners resident in China but also for the 400,000,000 of Chinese, the elementary rights of personal justice. SENSATIONAL PRICES.

headline: THE PIPE IN POLITICS.
text:
The British Prime Minister knows an anodyne for the worries provoked by a brilliant Chancellor's silk stocking budget, the temperamental incompatibilities of members of the Irish race, the magical appearances of foreign communists in Glasgow and the falling French franc. Mr. Baldwin smokes a pipe. With fine fervour he praised it when he received the Freedom of Dundee. He said he had always found that pipe smokers had a wisdom, calmless of outlook and breadth of vision which were denied to cigarette and cigar smokers. This unwarranted reflection upon fellow-worshippers of "My Lady Nicotine" will be answered, no doubt, by the cigar smokers and the cigarette lovers. It is sufficient here to concede the philosophic importance of the pipe in politics. One can imagine Mr. Baldwin quoting, with a fine air of detachment.

headline: Honneur Aux Dames!
text: Men occupy the centre of the stage in the present production of what may be termed "Strike and Strike" with an indefinite run before it. The limelight is on the men and on the whole they are standing its glare very well. But the work that women are doing is not to be despised even if it is not patently apparent. The general outcry against servants is dictated, unconsciously or otherwise, by the extra-labour, worry and inconvenience, which the ill-natured actions of servants has thrown on the shoulders of many women in the Colony. Households have been left where there has been, and is sickness and where the needs of quite young children have been ignored by the abscending ones. It is in such cases as these that the boss of the house—the man—has risen to the occasion and seen to foodstuffs, and taken a hand in washing up, in addition to doing some piece of Volunteer work outside. Generally he has been heartened by the splendid uncomplaining fortitude of his helpmeet, where the contrary attitude might reasonably be expected. In the ranks of single women, the readiness to be up and doing has not escaped observation. It has been less spectacular than war work, but in that it is aimed at intolerance, selfishness and feelings that know no law of common sense, it is equally valuable. The Colony is not unmindful of the services that women, young and not so young, are performing so willingly, so ungrudgingly and so efficiently.

headline: COAL CRISIS / POLICE CALLED TO DEAL WITH STRIKERS.
text:
GLAMORGAN COLLIERY INCIDENT.

Five thousand strikers surrounded the Rock Colliery at Glynnenth, Glumorgan, where seven hundred men are still working and refused to disperse.

A hundred police who were summoned came into collision with the strikers.

Sixteen were injured.

The miners eventually decided to cease work and the colliery is at a stand-still.

Hankow, July 16.—In connection with the recent report in the vernacular papers that Wu Pei-fu had sent a military officer to interview Tuan Chi-jui regarding the various diplomatic problems resulting from the Shanghai incident and also the statement that Wu Pei-fu was thought to be proceeding to Hankow and when necessary to Tientsin to confer with Chang Tso-lin and Feng Yu-hsiang to discuss national defence against England and Japan, Wu Pei-fu states that such are absolutely groundless and likewise that letters and telegrams alleged to be sent out by him in connection with the Shanghai, Hankow and Canton cases are also fabrications.—Reuter.

Peking, July 16.—It is reliably reported that fighting has begun at Huayin and Shensi between forces belonging to General Sun Yueh, Civil Governor of Honan, and those of Wuh Sin-tien, the Tupan of Shenzhi. Tuan Chi-jui has wired instructing Sun Yueh to withdraw, but it is believed that the latter is unlikely to comply. The Honan Tupan Yush Wei-chun is reported to be supporting Sun Yueh with the object of getting him out of Honan.—Reuter. A message from Peking via London stated: Civil war has again broken out in Szechuan province where General Yang Han is attacking rival generals near Chungking. Forces from Honan entered Shenzhi advancing to Sianfu where fighting is also probable.

headline: TO BE FLOGGED? / INTIMIDATOR AND HOUSE BOY.
text:
A Chinese watchman was yesterday convicted at the Kowloon "Magistracy" of having attempted to intimidate the loyal house boy employed by Mr. "Kid" Marriott and the Magistrate, Mr. E. W. Hamilton adjourned his decision as to the measures to be taken against the punishment to be meted out to the man until he had taken the opinion of the Attorney General regarding the application of the powers of flogging given under the recently passed emergency measures.

As regarded the actual offence the defendant's excuse was that he was asked by another man if he had seen the complainant and was merely telling the latter that such enquiry was being made for him at the time of the alleged intimidation.

The complainant denied this and said that he had never seen the man before until by threats he endeavoured to get him to leave his employment.

His Worship said that h entirely believed the evidence the complainant.

There was the corroboration of Mr. Marriott, who had said that when he saw his boy he was obviously frightened. Complaintant was further given an excellent character by his employer.

Although the Rev. G. R. Lindsay had spoken in the defendant's favour, that evidence, when analysed, was merely that Rev. Lindsay had obtained for him his position as a watchman and had heard that he was progressing satisfactorily. This latter statement was not, however, evidence. The defendant had further made a statement which was not corroborated.

Shanghai, July 17.—Dosser was ordered to be expelled from the International Settlement as an undesirable by Magistrate Zau and the British Assessor at the Mixed Court to-day. The charge of possession of inflammatory literature of a nature, tending to cause a breach of the peace was dismissed. A stay of execution of the sentence for a fortnight was granted on the application of counsel for the defence, who intimated that he might file an application for a rehearing, in which he will raise the question of the Court's authority to expel foreigners. The Court held that the document typewritten on a piece of silk, purparing to be a certificate issued to Dosser by the Arbitration Department of the Russian Communist Party, was authentic.—Reuter

Melbourne, July 16.—The Senate has passed the Coastal Navigation Bill—Renter. "No?" Mrs. Asquith retorted "Well, at any rate, we all try!"

Patrick McCarthy, charged at Willesden with being helplessly drunk: 'It was all owing to the strike. I was tired at walking, so I look a little whisky to help me on my way, and it didn't.' He was fined 5%.

'We are unable to decide which of you two women is speaking the truth,' so we will bind both of you over to keep the peace.' —Magistrate at Tottenham.

An old lady asked the advice of the magistrates at Ongar--Police Court on the ground that a neighbour had called her a "bally" something--or other, and she wished to know the meaning of the word.

The chairman smilingly replied that he had heard the word before, but he was not prepared to explain what it meant—especially in open court.

The proceedings were naturally conducted in Chinese, but it was evident that the majority attended with a real desire to do something to end the present position of stalemate and thus effect a change for the better in the trade of the Colony with which is interwoven the success and prosperity of loyal Chinese who have a large stake here and are determined to do their utmost to bring about a return to normality as quickly as possible.

The discussion was of a protracted nature, various points being mentioned as likely to ease the present position. It was stated by one gentleman that the mechanics at Taikoo, Kowloon Dock and the Naval Yard had already returned to work, and there were indications that others would return as soon as employment could be found for them.

It was ultimately decided, it is understood, to ask the support of the members of the Chamber of Commerce and of masters and men belonging to the various local/guilds for the recently formed Chinese Trading Trade Maintenance Association, of which Mr. Ho Sai-kwong is chairman. The latter body will in turn seek the co-operation of the Chinese members of the Legislative Council in influencing the Government to extend its protection to any measures that may be adopted with a view to carrying on the business life of the Colony independent of the strikers in Canton.

The opinion was naturally expressed that the meeting had no power or influence in the direction of actually ending the strike—this resting not with the loyal Chinese in Hongkong but with Canton—but it was hoped that by doing all possible to return to normal conditions as speedily as possible, a powerful moral effect would be exercised over Canton. Trade Maintenance Association.

It may be stated here that the inauguration of the Chinese Trade Maintenance Association was held on the first floor of the City Hall on Thursday. Mr. Li Yau-chuen, Chairman of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce presided, and there was also present a large number of prominent Chinese merchants, including Mr. Ho Sai-kwong and others. Upon the motion of Mr. Li Yau-chuen seconded by Mr. M. K. Lo, Mr. Ho Sai-kwong was elected Chairman of the Association.

Proposed by Mr. Ho Sai-kwong and seconded by Mr. Li Po-kwai, Mr. M. K. Lo was elected as legal adviser of the Association, and Mr. Lo Woon-cho as its Hon. Secretary. Sub-Committees representing the different lines of business, including shipping, rice, sugar, sundry goods, marine products, brass and iron, tin, piece goods, cotton yarn, etc., were appointed.

It was decided that police protection be applied for from the Government for the taking delivery of and shipping cargo.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
Quebec, July 19. The death is announced of Cardinal Begin.—Reuter's Ameri- can Service.

Hanoi, July 18.—An Annamite revolutionary named Pham Boichau who was recently sentenced to death in Contumacian on a charge of attempting to poison the Hanoi garrison has arrived here under escort from Shanghai.—Router.

Peking, July 18.—Cheng Chen, the Civil Governor of Jiangsu, has wired to the Government stating that the prolonged strike is seriously affecting the workers' conditions and he urges the Government to settle the Shanghai and other incidentes with the Diplomatic Corps as soon as possible, so that work may be resumed. He suggests that larger demands can be discussed afterwards.—Reuter.

Conversely, it was urged that, by merely making the strikers forfeit June wages, employers would be acting fairly and not vindictively. If, it was asserted, they desired to impose any harsh penalty, all that employers had to do was to issue a summons against their servants for leaving without notice. headline: PEAK SERVANTS
text:
As the result of a meeting of Peak residents held last night, it has been decided to fall into line with the Mid-Level Residents' Association in respect of making striking domestic servants forfeit June wages. Thus, the lead given by the Hongkong Hotel—the greatest employer of the domestic servant class—has now been followed: by two of the Residents' Association on the Peak.

Every consideration was given to the "other side" of the case—that is, in favour of paying for wages actually earned before the exodus from Peak houses commenced. It was contended for examples that animals and cookies in particular

THE HONGKONG EXCAVATION, PILE DRIVING & CONSTRUCTION CO., LTD.

that this trait should be remembered by their employers. It was further alleged that at a meeting of the Servants' Guild held before the inauguration of the strike, the cosies and house boys expressed themselves against a strike, but ultimately were compelled to obey the Guilds.

headline: TO-DAY'S POSITION.
text:
Further evidence that strikers who never left the Colony or who have managed to get back from Canton have realised the error of their ways is to hand in the return to work at Kowloon Dock to-day of large numbers of workers estimated at about a thousand and at the Naval Yard of another 300.

That strikers in Canton are anxious to return is the report of many such who have had the good fortune to possess the necessary money or the brains to elude the surveillance kept upon them and who have returned to Hongkong; and it is generally recognised that the duration of the strike in so far as seamen and skilled workers are concerned resolves itself into the problem of how long Canton can keep them from returning. CANTON BOATS.

The restrictions imposed at Canton would, it is thought, hardly be equal to such a strain as would result on a resumption of river steamer traffic—hence the interest shown in the movements of the Charles Hardouin and Paul Beau, which have resumed their wharf position from the Stonecutters anchorage. Nothing definite could be ascertained at the water front this morning, but it was emphatically reported that certain river boats are to resume, whilst it was doubted whether the Tung On will be run again under Government. This private enterprise may now be given a chance again. The Tung On arrived back from Canton this afternoon.

Meanwhile things are shaping in Hongkong on such lines that it is more than doubtful whether many unskilled men will be able to return to their former occupations. The Tramway Company, for instance, have had large numbers of Chinese volunteers come forward who are prepared to learn the duties of drivers, conductors, and inspectors, and to sign contracts as permanent employees of the Company. Their services have been accepted and they are being trained by the Company. The services of volunteers will be dispensed with as the new employees master their duties. The only men that the Tramway Company are likely to re-engage upon their return are fitters and mechanics.

, HONGKONG HOTELS' ACTION. Another instance of independent action is that of the Hong-kong Hotel where latest acquisitions have comprised 50 ex-ships' stewards who have signed contracts.

An interesting feature of the contracts which employees of the Hotel have to sign is that 10 per cent. of their salary is deducted each month for five years, at the end of which period, if their record has been good, it is returned to them and (providing, of course, the employee wishes to remain) the deductions commence again.

There are further signs of the improvement in the local shipping situation and harbour traffic generally, 12 applications for clearances having been granted in respect of ocean-going vessels. Nine of these have actually left. There have been five further arrivals.

Out of 93 ocean-going vessels now in the harbour 52 are British. Of the vessels in respect of which clearances have been granted, five are British, two Japanese, two Chinese, one German, and one Italian.

Junks which have been tied up since the strike were noticed today to have left. The harbour presents a normal appearance with launches, motor boats and Moonraker boats running almost as usual.

Mexico City, July 20.—Spain also beat Mexico in the doubles in the Davis Cup. The Spanish players departed for the United States and will meet Japan at Baltimore. — Reuter's American Service.

Shanghai, July 20.—A wireless message from Luchow, Szechuen, states that two vessels, escorted by H.M.S. Teal from Chungking, have arrived for the purpose of bringing down foreigners from Chengtu and other parts of Szechuen. The vessels were fired upon by Chinese troops on the way. H.M.S. Teal replied. There were no British casualties. Reuter.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
PAYMENT OF JUNE WAGES.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir.—The Peak residents decided yesterday afternoon by an absolutely overwhelming majority that no wages should be paid to servants for June and that no pay should be given to servants whilst out on strike.

It is understood that the Mid Levels Association will follow the same course, and it now remains for the Committee of the Kowloon Residents' Association to call their members together, in which case it seems certain that the same course will be adopted by the members of the Kowloon Residents' Association, and thus that a united front, which is so desirable, will be presented by the residents in the different districts of this Colony.

Enclosing my card, Yours, etc., PEAK RESIDENT. Hongkong, July 21, 1925.

headline: REPLACING THE STRIKERS.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—The management of the Hongkong Hotel has received nothing but commendation for the lead it has given in the matter of the reinstatement of its Chinese employees. That the lead is one correct in law as in policy is borne out by the fact of the announced attitude of the Government—naval, military and civil—towards public servants implicated in the rebellion against law and order in the Colony.

The latest move taken by the Managing Director of the Hongkong Hotel deserves the approbation of the community at large. As an employer of labour myself

my congratulations to Mr. J. H. Taggart on the dilution of labour he has instituted in the big establishments under his capable management. One sees to-day in the tea, lounge sturdy Russian waiters, alert West Indian lads, and courteous Filipino attendants, who are such efficient substitutes for those who have taken leave from an institution that for years has been a veritable gold mine for the Chinese "boys."

Customers of the Hotel now receive civility with efficient service. When the Chinese had a monopoly of attendance in the tea lounge their language, expressed among themselves, in very many instances was vulgar to all who knew and spoke the Chinese language. A welcome change has come over the scene with the recent dilution of labour.

I trust the innovation will not be considered an "emergency measure"; but a welcome change that has come to stay.

headline: CANTON'S WAIL.
text: There is only one thing at stake in the position in China and that is the truth. This the Canton Nationalist Government claims to have found, and as usual with anybody who has made a startling discovery it almost trips over itself in its anxiety to publish it to the world. The sole problems which are causing all the agitation in China, says the Canton Government, are those "inequal treaties," the alleged "inhuman exploitation" of Chinese labour in foreign Concessions, and the temerity of the Powers in seeking to maintain their economic and political domination of China. The poor old Labour Party has fallen into the 'trmp. That can't about "inhuman exploitation" of Chinese labour has done the trick. The rest of the wait matters not a jot. Their poor Chinese brethren are being downtrodden by foreigners in the Concessions—so they choose to believe—and hence they in their turn must rush into print with the cablegram from Canton.

Cares to believe this twaddle from Canton nobody else, in Britain will. It should be treated with the silent contempt that it deserves. Let the Labour Party come to China itself and tour through the Chinese cities and towns where the Power's have not been one inch of power or jurisdiction, and they will weep with sympathy for the Chinese workers who are being ground to death by their Chinese taskmasters. The conditions in the foreign Concessions and in China's own sphere are as different as chalk is from cheese. They will admit, if they are honest men and not mere pains in the political chessboard, that the conditions obtaining in the foreign Concessions are worlds superior to those for which the Chinese authorities are responsible for day after day and year after year, without the shadow of a hope for reform for the labourer. Canton's outburst will fall on deaf ears. It is an attempt to gain friends in a quarter where there ought be open enmity, or at least complete alienation—if the Labour Party only knew the actual conditions of Chinese labour outside the foreign Concessions. Even so, were the position of the poor Chinese workers in the Concessions not as good as it is in comparison with the rest of China, what does the Canton Government hope to gain from fomenting and encouraging agitation that leads to rioting and striking and attacking the British Concession of Shameen? If they hope to explain that, away to the world through the British Labour Party, then they are indeed simple.

headline: CANTON'S LATEST. / STRIKERS AT FOREIGN CEMETERY.
text:
THE UNOFFENDING DEAD.

The Consul-General at Canton, Sir J. W. Jamieson, has addressed the following letter to the Canton Government:—

H.B.M. Consulate, Canton, July 20, 1925.

To Fu Ping-ch'ang Esq., Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, Canton:—

Sir,—I have the honour to bring to your notice the latest instance "bf "frightfulness" committed under the legis of the Nationalist Government.

As you are aware there is on Honam island a cemetery for foreigners of all nationalities, where incidentally the late German Consul General was buried, which is in charge of a Chinese sexton and his family.

This morning a gang of intimidators approached the latter and stated that, unless he took his immediate departure, the graves would be dug up. Comment on such threatened action, more especially from a Chinese point of view, is superfluous.

The sexton has been allowed to go, and I would ask you to be so good as to see that the unoffending dead remain undisturbed.—I have the honour to be, Sir, Your Obedient Servant,

headline: WATCH CHINA
text:
NEED FOR FIRMNESS BY THE POWERS.

BOLSHEVIK CUNNING. ___

Well may attention, be called to the fact that in China serious events are browing. In the Ehr East we

the fact that in China serious events are browing. In the Fur East we are accustomed to minor, disturbances, but the events of the past month give serious cause for un-eignness, fomented as they are by secret societies bearing a markedly anti-foreign character. Further, the rioters and strikers (sic!) are openly countennanced by the provisional authorities, who in their turn seem to rely on the protection of the highest powers in Peking, Britons and others have been assaulted and even murdered without it being possible to obtain the punishment of the evil-doers.

North and South are alike affected. The foreign possessions, in which the art of Government is practised according to European bureaucratic routines, have in their turn become centres of anti-foreign feeling. The growing dissatisfaction turned at first against the weak and rotten Government and there were wars between the rival Chinese factions. Nobody interfered and not the slightest real protection was given to those men who opposed that which the foreigners themselves had preached to China—enlightenment and reform. Unconcerned, the representatives of all the civilised Powers prided themselves on their diplomatically correct attitude of non-interference in internal Chinese questions. Having once taken the retrograde road China is now both to stop. With Bolshevik aid and teachings she has cleverly succeeded in leading general discontent away from how Government, and, it would seem from events that have transpired, is directing it against the foreigners. Seemingly she has given the anti-foreign party to understand that it may count on her support!

- Let us take by a couple of- incidents of recent date. The wun- ton unprovoked attack on Shameen on June 23 Was engineered under the guise of a peaceful sympathetic (sic!) demonstration parade headed by students and other peaceful- looking subjects. What of the core? A diabolical dustardly plot of an organised attack on the British Concession hatched by Bolsheviks and carried out by them as leaders, in The hope that the Concession would be taken by sur- priest. Then we have the murder of Mr. Mackenzie at Shanghai and the wounding of his lady com- pension.

The Chinese Press go so far as to say that the first incident was the slaughtering of unarmed Chinese students by Imperialists and the second, the destruction of Mr. Mackenzie (who was ill) by his Doctor so that no blame could be laid at the door of the Chinese. The Chinese Press is certainly pleaving up to the susceptibility of its nationals and directing its forces against Britain. There are many who may take exception to the last statement, but can the fact be gainsaid that other nationals have received protection in the present crisis's, whereas it has refused, or totally ignored when sought by British and Japanese subjects.

We must now face the situation boldly, and not show the slightest weakness or inconsistency in our dealings. Steps taken can never be retraced, therefore watchfulness and anticipation of all eventualities are now a matter of self preservation. If the present situation is allowed to pass without a check, there may be a catastrophe, in China, such as has never been seen there before. Then indeed would commerce and all enterprises in China be interrunted for years, and we should be driven into complications, expenses, and sacrifices, the end of which cannot be foreseen. It is as well to remember that events of far lesser import than those of the last few weeks caused nation to rise against nation, and the great world conflict of 1914-1918. Let us by prompt and firm action convince not only China but others that it still is "England what" thou wert, thou art.

headline: 1ours, etc., S00KUMP00. Hongkong, July 22. / DON'T FETCH THEM BACK.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir, — Many Chinese today have been suggesting that it would be advisable for the Government to put more steamers running to Canton at usual fares so that strikers can have better facilities to return to Hongkong. May I point out that in this my countrymen who have made the suggestions are wrong. If we sent ships up to bring back the erring wanderers they will still not be convinced that it is foolish to do the bidding of those they cannot see nor hear.

No other policy than that of proving that the loyal ones can carry on will pay in the long run. We are determined to show that those who cannot fend for themselves are a burden on the community. We do not want to welcome them back by sending up steamers for them. If they realise that they have erred, unintentionally I admit, then it is up to them to tell us by deeds that they want to and are now thinking for themselves. To do so they must bring themselves back, by their own means, as was the case when they left so hurriedly and so ignominiously. Yours, etc.

headline: Mixed Labour.
text: The Hotel's experiment will be watched with much interest. At the moment the staff does not consist wholly of Chinese. It is agreeably cosmopolitan, and, working in harmony, should meet all demands made upon it. It is easier to staff a Hotel in this manner than, say, such an institution as the Naval Dock Yard; but where it is feasible to introduce the system, it should be tried. In this way wholesale abstentions would not be the order of any strike, and the Chinese themselves would benefit in having the means to contrast their own line of thought and action with that of other places. They would also take their place in a system in which ability only counted—a system also which would probably sound the deathknell of what is popularly described as "squeeze".

Maintain the Volunteer Defence Corps by all means; but let there be in addition a Police Reserve, and sections in which those possessing technical and other qualifications are enrolled. headline: PUBLIC SAFETY.
text:
We are disinclined to throw cold water on the suggestion which has been adopted to hold a public meeting. There are immense possibilities for good in holding such a meeting if it is designed to plan methods for the future that shall rouse the civic spirit that lies dormant in most people; and that shall tell us something new to provoke thought or action on the political questions which now seem part and parcel of the thing from which we are suffering—a distinctly anti-British feeling. We shall deplore a meeting in which language of a peevish character is likely to find expression, or language even of hostility—hostility even against Unofficial members of the Legislative Council who have failed to make prominent such questions as the registration of servants and the question of our general preparedness to meet the possible contingency of a general strike. On the question of the registration of servants we add nothing to

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
SERVANT REGISTRATION.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir, — Having opened a Domestic Servants' Employment, and Registration Bureau (as per copy of letter attached herewith) I am desirous of improving the organisation as it stands at present.

Before proceeding any further, I may say that a copy of the letter attached was handed to the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoke prior to the meeting, but it was apparently overlooked during the discussion on the subject.

The man, and apparently the only, objection in the minds of the speakers at yesterday's meeting was that a private bureau would make possible the exploitation of servants through the administration of that bureau arranging for or conniving at frequent changes of employment by those servants, thereby bringing in, to the bureau increased fees. It should be fairly obvious that this is a weak suggestion, as there is no doubt it all keeping in view the fact that such a bureau, to be successful, must enjoy a full measure of confidence both from employer and employee, that such a policy would be absolutely suicidal so far as the continued existence of the bureau was concerned.

Thanking you for the privilege of inserting this.

Yours, etc., P. H. Shaw,

Domestic Servants Employment and Registration Bureau. Hongkong, July 28. (COPA)

Sir,—Having opened a Domestic Servants' Employment and Registration on Bureau some short time before, the present strike began, I am jostfully interested in the question of "servants' registration and should like to hay before this meeting a few of my views on this matter. I may say that the organisation is only in an embryo stage, and, although it is in working order, modifications may be necessary from time to time. Registration cards are already available, these being made to contain photo, thumbprint, signature, etc., of the servant. I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible in my remarks.

His Excellency the Governor has pointed out the difficulties likely to be experienced by an attempt to enforce. Compulsory Registration; and it must be apparent to all that the danger of any measures taken in this direction becoming "insupplicable" would be very great. But, whilst anything of a compulsory nature might be impracticable, I am of opinion that a system of voluntary registration would ultimately be of much value. The idea of registration of servants generally has recently been strongly opposed in the Press, some of the arguments against it being that photographs are unreliable and that thumbprints are associated solely with the province of crime. As regards photographs, it is common knowledge that most passports in use rely to a great extent on them, which should be sufficient argument in their favour. If, ferring to thumbprints, I believe it is not unknown that in dealing with natives of the East, to accept thumbprints in lieu of signatures (or in addition to them): e.g., in the case of native pay-rolls in establishments in the Army of India. In addition, I believe many important mercantile firms here us them in connection with pay-rolls, "etc. Surely" such recognised use of thumb-prints ought to be sufficient to dispel their association with crimes. It seems to me that the two objections mentioned cannot be considered to be of a very grave nature.

On the other hand, T' think voluntary registration would be productive of a much higher standard of efficiency amongst servants. My reasons are:

(1) One would stand a much better chance of knowing exactly who one's servants were. "Record cards would be difficult to "fake." Photographs, of course, might be changed, but the same would hardly apply to thumb-prints.

(2) Record cards would encourage servants to do better' work, as these certificates, if satisfactory, would provide them with a greater guarantee of future employment and enhanced wages.

(3) Were a servant, as has been suggested recently as a possibility, to receive an undeservedly adverse conduct mark by an unreasonable employer, he could destroy his card and thus place himself in a position of not having registered at all; though in a case of this kind, the Registration Bureau would take reasonable measures for the reinstatement of apparently wrongfully discharged servants.

headline: THOSE: GUILDS.
text:
If one were dealing with people of balanced mentality it might be said that the logical reasoning of a striker who followed the advice of his Guild and left Hongkong for Canton should be that, once having experienced the folly of putting his trust in Guild officials, he would see to if that in future his monthly contributions should go to some more worthy and personally profitable object. But people who leave situations worth $30-$50 a month—and in some cases considerably more—for the chemical stories of Canton which they

shared with thousands of others, can hardly lay claim to be favoured with that particular class of mentality. It is, doubtful if their faith will be smoker even by a reduction in wages and, in some cases, the entire loss of their employment which has followed the action they were persuaded into taking. The power of the Guilds, then, is not likely to suffer more than a temporary set back and are long the Hongkong Government will be called upon to face again the problem of whether something cannot be done to curb activities which in the present strike have been exercised for evil to the fullest extent.

The present Ordinance allows of interference on the part of the Hongkong Government only when the Guilds are detected in unlawful practices. If the Home Government, with similar powers, cannot place into that category, the action of trade union officials in bringing public services to a standstill, it is doubtful whether the Hongkong Government can act differently in respect of the Chinese Guild officials under their jurisdiction. There appears to be no real reason, however, why the Ordinances should not be amended in order to give the Hongkong Government more control over these pernicious bodies. The trade unionists at Home would kick, of course, and talk glibly about the sacred liberty of the subject—probably it is this more than anything else which has restrained the Government from taking up to the present a step which it certainly is called upon to do in the interests of the foreigner in Hongkong. Were a concensus of opinion possible, it would be found to be in the interests of and in accord with the desire of the greater number of the Guild members themselves. But, after all, why should much notice be taken of a section of the community the ignorance of whom in regard to things Har Eastern the present would maximize least served to throw into minority.

headline: Thế First 100,000.
text: One of the most popular New York City's "The First Hundred Thousand," which graphically dealt with the first big armies raised for the Front at a time when the irksome conditions of war time were novel as well as incommoding. It requires no great strain of the imagination to draw on analogy between that "First Hundred Thousand" and the first hundred thousand meals served during the local strike by the Hongkong Hotels, Limited. The conditions since June 19 have been akin to a state of war in more respects than one; they have to many been irksome, but they have also been novel and likewise incommoding. Looking to the unique circumstances under which the hotels, in common with businesses and households, were left without sufficient labour to "carry on," it must generously be conceded that the supplying of an average of 2,500 meals a day establishes a record of which the whole community must be proud. Whilst the forces behind the strike movement sought—and are seeking—to create an economic blockade of the Colony, they have been dealt a vital blow in regard to the morale of the strikers by witnessing the Hongkong Hotels not only "making good," but even exceeding pre-strike records to the extent of serving a hundred thousand meals, thus incidentally enabling hundreds of residents and visitors to eat as well as to work. The position of the usual state of war has been reversed. An army can only march on its stomach, as some great General once observed in effect. In the case of Hongkong the army of strikers has little or nothing to march on, whilst the peaceful residents have had not the slightest need to worry about the needs of "the interior," so well have those been catered for by Mr. Taggart and his battalion of volunteer workers. Many compliments have already been showered on the Hotels since the strike began, but they have signalised the best compliment to their own services in the feat of serving a hundred thousand meals.

let us hand out the bouquets to others who are probably more deserving of them. Let us hand them out—verbal bouquets though they be—to those Chinese who, as the Hon. Mr. Holyoak reminds us—and reminds us from his own vital experience—have been loyal and proved their loyalty in different directions, all of a practical nature. This section of the community deserves all that has been said of it. It has had to surmount. those inborn feelings of sympathy which come naturally, if unreasonably, when the actions of our nationals are the subject of discussion or rebuke. The national life is akin to the family life. Attack the one, and the members of it fall into either a defensive or offensive line. It is more than likely that in throwing in their lot with the British for either business or sentimental reasons, those who have earned for themselves the right to receive Mr. Holyoak's commendation, retain decided opinions as to the claims of China to be heard on such questions as extr-territoriality, Concessions, etc.; and the desire to have happenings at Shanghai and Shameen probed by an impartial board. If they do not, we shall be inclined to throw doubts on their possession of any sense of loyalty to anyone, and to say that they are merely of that class of opportunities which, of the Machiavellian, are the most Machiavellian. But those who have set themselves the task of assisting in the fostering of trade; the return of the workers, and a desire for right feelings as between foreigners and Chinese, give us confidence that British administration, justice, freedom, education, etc., have not been in vain, and that the fruits of these things are to be seen in this desire of a large and influential body of Chinese to recreate confidence and to set in motion again the wheels of finance and commerce. The two

Chinese Unofficial members of the Legislative Council have been mentioned; and we are glad that this has been done. Their position is no sinecure, and especially so at the present moment when doing good by stealth and without the flourish of trumpets is part of their daily work. Of the work of Dr. S. W. Tso it is difficult to speak adequately, for it has not necessarily been called into play by the frolic of the moment but by a deep seated belief in the principles that have made British justice the envy—and, as in the present instance—the hate also—of different parts of the world. In this particular matter it is good to remember that many realise we are all in the same boat, even if, as Mr. Douglas Jerrold would any, not necessarily with the same skulls!
