headline: Hongkong, Monday, August 24, 1925. / TO-MORROW'S MEETING.
text:
Spirited indeed are the terms of the draft telegram to be submitted as a resolution to the public meeting to-morrow evening, and it is difficult to see how they can be amended. Hongkong can congratulate itself that it possesses the men with the public spirit—and the ability—to state the Colony's case against the Canton Reds so forcefully. The quiet dignity of the telegram which to-morrow evening's public meeting will be asked to send to the Prime Minister will do far more to impress Mr. Stanley Baldwin and the Cabinet with the gravity of the situation in South China than all the heroics in the world. The wording of the telegram must strike the Imperial Government, not as the hysterics of an excited mob, but as the calculated utterance of a responsible gathering. How important this is needs no saying. High officials are apt to regard the resolutions of mass meetings as the products of excited minds and

to discount them accordingly They cannot possibly do that if the present instance. The telegram is one that brooks no disrespect, every argument in being to the point. Not the least telling argument is the on regarding the Colony's military contribution. During twenty-five years not less than $49,000,000 has been contributed as "insurance fund for the protection of rights secured to British subjects by treaties with China." Policy-holders — keeping to the insurance simile—have every right to call upon those who accept the annual premium to carry out the implied terms of the policy. Upon that ground alone Hongkong is entitled to demand immediate action to protect it from the insidious forces that are threatening its prosperity. But of course there are more important reasons than this for the demands which the Colony is submitting to the [imperial Government in the telegram to be despatched to the Prime Minister to-morrow evening. There are reasons of trade and of prestige, not merely in this part of the world, but in every place to which British influence extends. The struggle is really one between Britain and Russia, between honesty and dishonesty. That is why there can be only one result. That is why also the Colony, which has itself individually so much at stake, must strain very nerve to spur the Imperial government into action. To borrow evening's meeting represents a further opportunity for doing that. Every citizen who as the future of the Colony and he future of the Empire at heart should be present to give further eight to the resolution which are confident, will be passed by record gathering with a united office.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir.—The often-talked of “Foreign Intervention” over the disorders of China to-day will, I think, have to bear fruit this time. Rightly, we should take Canton as the chief centre of unruly activities and whatever foreign action to be taken against it, is all for the salvation of the city and her people from the fate of living under Bolshevistic rule. Bolshevism is purely an act of war against trade, and brings terror to right thinking peoples, but the occasion has come for us, as neighbours in friendship and in business, to make a hurried rescue lest a-wreck becomes shattering. China's stand to-day can bring evidence of its weakness through the affairs in Canton with a Government which does not recognise and communicate with the capital Peking, and it falls out altogether from the co-operation and advice of any one but the parliamentarians of her own, whose knowledge of clean politics is naturally low, and thus they sought Bolshevism as a guiding hand. A meeting such as we are having tomorrow is the true spirit of the times, and something must be done. As the friendship between England and China exists as ever, it is the stern hope of her well-wishers that the parliamentarians in Peking would adhere to the counsel of the Powers and they would, as a first and necessary step, place a responsible party to rule Canton and cause redress to be made to all her other territories, and particularly measures be adopted to give full protection to the interests of foreigners. China is old in history and her place amongst nations should have been by far superior. Her population is great, her mineral resources are abundant but unearthed, her citizens are eminent in every walk of life, but the path of glory has been darkened by the fumes of revolutionary parties and caused militarism to stay, and will they have Bolshevism now as the root of all evils. Let us all hope that China as a whole, after the aid of foreign intervention, will make a start for the restoration of peace and tranquillity, and for the restoration of her rights and honour among the Powers of

headline: HONGKONG'S DEMANDS.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—The terms of the revolutions to be submitted at tomorrow evening's public meeting are to the point, and it is difficult to see how they can be added to, although in one respect they might be amended. Sir Henry Pollock has been incessant in his contention that the Canton-Hongkong problem is entirely separate and distinct from that in any other part of China, and the meeting is to be asked to agree. A contrari-wise argument could be advanced; that the outbreak beginning at Shanghai, spreading to Hankow, quickly came to Canton, and as a consequence—this Colony being a British possession and the outbreak being primarily against Britain, Britishers and British interests—Hongkong became involved. Evidently other opinions differ and the Colony is being asked to agree to the view taken by those responsible for the meeting. I trust that events will prove the absolute correctness of the view. I confess to some little doubt on the matter, more so when I remember the capital made out of the Shameen incident, and that Shameen itself is an argument used by the many who so glibly rail against what they describe as "unjust treaties." The promoters of the meeting seem to be strengthened in their line of thought by the prompt action of the Home Government, on hearing of the Canton Government's embargo on British shipping, sending Admiral Sinclair to Canton to enquire, and, if necessary, to take action. This suggests that the Foreign Office is not so supine in its activities to uphold the sacredness of treaties, particularly when they constitute a deliberate insult, but bring ruin in their train.

If there is a weakness about the proposed demands, it is that which asks that steps be taken to "install an alternative and friendly Chinese Government at Canton." I submit this is going outside reasonable bounds. It is not within the province of the British or any other Government to install any alternative or friendly Government. It would be fatal to attempt such a thing, and a legacy for this future, for which the future will not thank us. The people who are fomenting the trouble are those to be dealt with, with whatsoever threats or actions are deemed advisable.

headline: BOLSHEVISM IN CHINA.
text:
The situation in China is a reminder of the limitations of Western statesmanship, remarks the "Outlook (London): Nevertheless, after a century's contact, Chimmun, and European are best at arm's length and at worst—as—now—at daggers drawn. Let us admit at once that the factors which here vote that intercourse which elsewhere is part of the natural habit of mankind are too subtle for full analysis. But at least the obvious explanations will not hold water. It is said that the Chinese are humiliated by the privileged position of Europeans in the Treaty ports. Maybe; but their humiliation is of their own deliberate making. It was they who first imposed upon Europeans their special and exclusive status. If they would abolish it they have only to confer on Europeans those same guarantees of security which Chinamon abroad themselves receive from all civilised States. It is said, further, that the Chinese labourers has been the victim of European capitalists, but for this sweeping indictment there is no shadow of justification. That commercial adventurers have at times thrown over the restraints imposed upon them in Europe is no doubt true. But the populations of Shanghai and Hongkong are evidence enough that European industrialism is compatible with Chinese prosperity, and it is beyond dispute that European factories have set a new standard of labour conditions in the Far East. We must look deeper, and the next point that suggests itself is that in China, at any rate, until quite recently, Europeans have only done business, whereas elsewhere in Asia they have also imposed their culture. The Europeanisation of the East may have been a result of territorial conquest as in India or of self-determined policy as in Japan. But in any event it has occurred, whereas China until now has kept Western influences at bay. At last, however, something Western has impinged upon the Chinese mind and has brought about an explosion of Chinese national pride. That something is Bolshevism. While China would have nothing of European ways, she has adopted Europe's own protest against those ways. For Chinese thought, at any rate, the Russian revolution is a tremendous event, and those very elements which twenty years ago rejoiced at Russia's defeat by Japan are now taking Russia for their guide and help. There, so far as China herself is concerned, we must at present be content to leave it. What still concerns us, however, is

One advance of Bolshevism. That its blow is struck in the first instance at Britain follows from the historical fact that Britain has been preeminent in extending Western culture into Asia. Ultimately, however, Bolshevism aims at the overthrow of that culture itself by working war on the principal of individual initiative by reliance on which, from Greek times onwards, our civilisation has developed. The first attack was made in the West. At one time it almost broke through the weak barrier of Poland, and it is still thrusting into the Balkans. On the whole, however, the Western attack has failed. But the Far Eastern attack, the appeal to the one quarter of the world where Western ideas have not established themselves in any strength, is apparently succeeding. Its success involves important consequences. In the long run, the Western Power which will have to meet the full force of the Bolshevist challenge is not Britain, but America. A realisation of the danger goes far to account for the startlingly aggressive attitude of American opinion towards ideas which it regards as subversive. Political agitation is watched with peculiar alarm, and there is no country in Europe, not even Italy, in which Bolshevist propaganda is so ruthlessly suppressed as in the United States. The situation is, indeed, of a kind to warrant anxiety. The Pacific Ocean is of vital importance to America's future trade expansion and anything that occurs in China is bound to have repercussions in the States, particularly because it involves Japan. The fear of Bolshevism in America amounts almost to a phobia, and the thought that all the Far East may be set aflume is enough to give Washington the jumps. While Japan nominally plays with the Western Powers, the Americans fear that she may desert them at any moment, and take advantage of the disorders in China to establish herself permanently there as she did in Korea. No wonder that in its tentative approaches to the Chinese situation Washington is on the alert for reactions at home. Chinese policy is a sufficiently delicate matter in England: but it touches America more nearly still. For this reason we have not directed special attention to the decisions which this country will shortly be called upon to make—we fear on imperfect data. What chiefly deserves notice is the spectacle of America dragged back into world politics against her will.

headline: A ROVING NOVELIST. STELLA BENSON'S CAREER
text:
Stella Benson, the novelist, who is Mrs. O'Gorman Anderson in private life, is on her way back to England via California after over three years absence in China, where her husband has a post in the Chinese Customs Service. She is very fond of the Chinese—a fondness which dates back to the time when she worked her way round the world and tarried in Hongkong teaching English to a class of fifty Chinese boys for £11 a month and in Peking assisting in the X-ray department of the American Rockefeller Hospital.

This witty woman has capitalised her frail health to the great profit of her experience, for she has spent a good part of her life “travelling rough” to ward off illness. She has worked on a ranch in Colorado 6,000 feet up the Rockies. She has been “help” in a San Francisco boardinghouse, “book agent” in California (trying to sell “Milton for the Babes”), teacher in an American university, shopkeeper in Hoxton, and member of the staff of the Charity. Organization Society. She has been tiger shooting in India, under fire in the Chinese Civil War, in the West Indies, and was the first English woman to penetrate into the Indo-Chinese province of Laos. Mrs. Anderson is a niece through her mother of Mary Cholmondeley, author of the once celebrated novel "Red Pottage."

We are often reminded that a people gets the Government it deserves. If this is so, it may explain matters in Canton. The Cantonese, in their own time—we need to remember Chinese characteristics—will deal with reactionaries in their own way—as the past week has shown. All that Britain can do is to insist on the recognition of existing treaties; and this she will do—public meetings or no—if such things as the embargo referred to are employed. These are friendly observations. If as a preliminary to a settlement, we are compelled to use an Americanism to spill bifurc of talk. Just it be at least based on reason. Hongkong, August 24

headline: OUT THE REDS
text:
Australia has for some time been facing a shipping situation which has elements of similarity to that confronting Hongkong although there is this difference regarding the latest developments there, that in Australia is an alleged issue which can be used as a basis for discussion. The similarity between our plights lies in the nature of the forces at work behind the scenes, which have as their object the infliction of injury to trade and commercial relations within the British Empire. By the Federal Immigration Act (passed about a month ago) Australia indicated plainly that she had at last awakened to the fact that her industrial disturbances were due in no small measure to alien influences and that she was determined to take strain measures to uproot and send from the Dominion at the public expense. If you need to

To quote again "the shipping trouble, which has dragged on for three-quarters of a year, has not been a strike but an insurrection. It was organised and conducted with ferocious energy by men who were certainly not Australians." The opinion appears to be that this Immigration Act will effect the object for which it was passed in spite of the passionate assurances which are being given that if any batch of non-Australian conspirators is shipped. Home under the new law the next Labour Government will recall and compensate them. Mr. Bruce, the Australian Prime Minister, is to be congratulated on the firmness with which he is handling the situation. Hongkong, too, is proceeding along similar lines in ridding itself of "undesirables," and by endorsing the resolution before the meeting this evening, the Colony will signify in clear and unmistakable terms its conviction that only when the root cause of South China's industrial depression has been removed can further steps be inaugurated for a return to stable conditions.

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text: The utility of the Motor-BIKBS. motor-bike was never more shown than in the early days of the strike. It was brought into use early and late; flashed its user to various food depots, and in its side car brought home all kinds of necessities. The owners of them in numbers of cases proved Communists of the right sort. They served lines "of houses, bringing, up loads of ice for distribution: And they were good to those who were compelled to trudge and to gasp and to sweat, by giving them "lifts." Blessings on them all!

in Hongkong—with the exception of the loafer, the intimidator and the lawless—have pursued what may be described as “the eventenor of their ways.” The merchant is not reviled, nor are shopkeepers’ windows smashed. We still hold friendly converse with those of our Chinese friends and acquaintances whom we have learned to regard, and in whose sanity we have every hope and confidence. It may seem strange that this phase of British temperament has not been more effective in bringing things to a state of settlement. Unfortunately it is impossible to get this effect to Canton where the aforesaid juggling of lies, on those all too willing to believe them, is having a contra effect. In the good time which we firmly believe is coming when the lion will lie down with the lamb, there should once more be a resurrection of the various suggestions made to get the Colony’s wide and varied nationalities known more to each other. A League of Fellowship and Service might have done something to that end. But the slingers of hackneyisms, and with an outlook almost blinded by mind instigmatism, found Kipling’s undisputed geographical formulae that East is East, and West is West, with the contentious addendum that the twain were never meant to, or would not meet, a trite saying to bolster up their arguments. The idea that peoples of different hues and creeds are, as a result, unable to meet in fellowship and service, must, to the serious minded, to like the peace that passeth all understanding. It cannot possibly attach itself to the suggestion of an International Club. The very name is so suggestive of its intent, that space need not be taken up in arguing in its favour. Neither a League nor a Club is likely to bring in the millennium, or settle a strike or an outbreak. It would be foolish to make this claim for them. But, in the case of a Club, it would afford a means for those who, in the main, are responsible for the "life-blood" of the Colony—its trade and commerce—getting into touch one with the other, and so lessening the feeling of cold and studied isolation, making one party lean to the opinion that so far as business is concerned, he and his conferees, were all right, but after that they faded from the scheme of things. Quite striking is the characterisation of the Canton Christian College, at Canton, China, by Philip N. Youtz, a former member of its teaching staff, in Current History Magazine, as a “powerful broadcasting station for modern thought, as well as a model of higher living.” The college is not entirely a foreign institution, as it is conducted jointly by Chinese and American educators, the professors on the faculty representing no less than fifteen denominations, thirty American and European universities and two races. It is hence with no little interest that one reads that in this institution may be found “many of the finest traditions and customs of American university life adapted to the needs of awakening. headline: AMERICA AND CHINA.
text: Try as she will to hold aloof, America is becoming more and more involved in the European situation. Her isolation ceased when she entered the war, but at its close she studiously avoided entering into European politics, although appeals to join the League of Nations were made on all hands. Theorists may argue that as a looker-on America is more likely to be a moral force than she otherwise would be. But while the looker-on may see most of the game, the help-that an active worker can give is too obvious to need comment. America is not likely to be a submissive onlooker so far as things in China are concerned. There is official warrant to emphasise this fact. There may be no American Concessions in China; but there are many Americans resident in the treaty ports and elsewhere. Nor is the volume of trade America enjoys with China to be despised. headline: ASIATIC BUILDING.
text:
◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇

be pardoned for failing to understand. The trend of Chinese politics since the revolution, has been bewildering. The revolution which should have led to unity, led to disintegration. Whatever corruption existed before was exceeded by those engaged in the selfish task of feathering their own nests. Each province of the republic bears witness to a regrettable feature of Chinese official life. Trite maxiums, glibby uttered, disappeared when money came into view. The foreigner had sent his missionaries, his medical men, and his educationists, to show the way. His own standard of conduct approximated as near the golden rule as it is possible to get in competitive days, and if example is better than precept, he had supplied it. The bewildered foreigner is probably open to conviction. If he is to be convicted of sin, he would like the evidence. So far there is none. From a bewildering sense of the strange flights of Chinese politics, he comes to the knowledge of warring bands of militarists, and those periods of boycotts and hates levelled at "certain foreign nations." In South China—in Hongkong—the isanse of bewilderment is as evident as it is elsewhere. The foreigner wonders what the real cause of the trouble is: if it is to be laid at the door of Russian Bolsheviks, or those Chinese extremists who have imbibed the vices of unreason and hatred—refused to regard the lesson of history, and are as far from the standards set up by the old guard of Chinese as it is possible to be. Simple morality is absent. The Canton directors state they are not responsible for the embargo on shipping recently issued from their city. It is true no doubt. But they are silent on the fact that a Taw issued by a labour body has Government sanction behind it in that it is allowed to operate with.

Even Brigham Young, the Mormon found it impossible to do anything in the matter in his day. The following is taken from his "life," one of many striking paragraphs in the book:—

In the effort to standardize the dress of the Mormon women and to prevent the extremes which he dwelt upon so often, of a dress which was so short that it revealed tops of the stockings, Brigham Young designed a costume for the Mormon women, which consisted of a modest sunbonnet and a simple cape, but only a few of them wore it for a short time and he was compelled until the last years of his life to continue his propaganda against the extravagant. absurdities of fashion. He had been successful in dictating to his people on almost every subject, but this was one on which he was destined to fail, because of the force of personality arrayed against him.

A force against which all men are destined to fail, always. It is one of the rare facts of life and we recognize it not alone through intuition.

Here is another extract from a book bearing on the subject, which should interest Hongkong. It is the sister of Louis XIV., writing on June 16, 1716, to Caroline, Princess of Wales:—

The late King once said: "I confess that I feel rather annoyed when I perceive that with all my royal authority as King of this country, I have cried out against head-dresses being too high, and no one had sufficient regard for me to make them lower. Then an unknown woman, a baggage from England, comes along wearing a low head-dress, and immediately all the "princesses rush from one extreme to the other."

The “baggage” was Lady Sandwich, wife of the English Ambassador, and, of course, she proved only one thing, and that is, the only way to change fashions is to change them. But how to do it remains with the gods.

headline: Hongkong, Wednesday, Sept. 2, 1925.
text:
If any doubt existed that the position of Hongkong in relation to Canton is a separate thing, and has nothing to do with the general position in China, it must be dissolved in the latest news. The "Anti-Imperialist Joint Union" and the Seamen's Union express their wishes to those in power at Canton, and those wishes, becoming practically a demand, are ordered to be observed. Thus shipping embargoes, strike pickets, and all the rest of disorderliness, gain Government protection, and become part of the present Government's policy. How long this will last remains to be seen. Successful coups have placed the "Red" element in control of the situation in Canton. Though flushed with power, there is a suspicion that those in office are not yet prepared to exert that power in the quarters that must fit

does not help matters much, except that it strengthens the arguments of those who urge direct action of no uncertain kind. The bearers of olive branches find their occupation almost gone. Sober-minded Chinese in Hongkong urge that, "something" be done, and are quite clear what that "something" should be. We were disposed at one time to suggest that the situation at Shanghai had some bearing on that in Canton. But it is a position which now is far from tenable. The olive branch has been held out by the Shanghai British Chamber of Commerce and the branch of the China Association there. It seems to us to be full of olives. The sentiments expressed are not merely those of Shanghai Britons, but of Britons in Hongkong and in other parts of the world. They may have been late in coming; but they are none the less sincere. We might argue that if there is an excuse to explain the delay, it is that the possession of such sentiments has been taken for granted. In Hongkong our olive branch has been shown in the exercise of much patience, a vast amount of tolerance, and a desire to end an unnatural state of things. It is almost impossible to deal with petulance and pettiness. The legitimate strivings of another people after good Government nationalism, equality of treatment in international politics, must excite interest in others, even when methods of reaching such things may be questioned. But Canton has yet to prove that she is doing these things. The unholy alliance, she has contracted with the worst forms of modern anarchy show how dangerous the holding out of an olive branch may be. It Moscow money is calling

with general approval. If it is the least they could do, it is the best they could do. Self-respect can go no further. If the Shanghai situation becomes a settled fact, what then of Canton? Ever since the revolution, Canton has been the stormy petrel of Chinese politics. She cannot always remain such. If the north returns to sanity it is possible she may attempt to put the strait-waist-coat on the erring province in the south. This is probably the direct action that would give more satisfaction than, any other. China's weakness has been in having so many warring elements, instead of one united front. Canton has been the offender. Shanghai settled, let us hope for the olive branch from Peking. Perhaps we hope in vain. The "Red" stain will need some labour ere it is obliterated.

headline: GLENCOE.
text:
Why is the nine of diamonds called the curse of Scotland? There is more than one answer in tradition. But we have to note that the phrase came into use about 1700, and though it does not seem in the least likely that the Master of Stair used a nine of diamonds to write on it the order for the massacre of Glencoe, there is no denying that the arma of his House were on, on a saltire azure, nine lozenges of the first. This Glencoe business is infernal, Macaulay confided to his dairy when he was working on the details, The Master of Stair is a perfect fago. And Macaulay was tempted to make no light of it as he could, for the guilt of the massacre involved his hero, William III. The world has by this time made up its mind that the slaughter in Glencoe was one of the most disturdy crimes in history, convicting its perpetrators not only of callous brutality but of a treachery and meanness of spirit rare even among the brutal. The orders upon which the executive officer of the massacre acted have now come into the market, and an attempt, to which we wish all success, is being made to secure the document for the National Library of Scotland, says the "Daily Telegraph" (London). What is the natural inference from such querely-phrased instructions? Glenlyon must have seen that his major did not like the business, and meant to put it on him. In fact, Duncanson did not reach Glencoe at five, not till six hours later. But Glenlyon accepted the ugly task, and murdered the men and women whose guest he had been at the appointed time. There seems to be no doubt that he did a brutal thing in a wantonly brutal way, but we feel no inclination to absolve that respectable gentleman, Major Duncanson, who passed on the order. The obvious hesitation of Duncanson, however, is a crushing refutation of the plag that the butchery of Glencoe was but an ordinary episode of clan warfare. A strict observance of them and all the rest of the things worth having, will be added as a matter of course. Some Cantonese will admit all this. They will see in the sending of the "Honam"—and the promise of regular sailings—not an act of bravado or of provocation—but one of peaceful commonsense. It is not designed—we are quite convinced of it—to take any sort of "war into the enemy's camp." Hongkong, on general lines, has no quarrel with Canton. It has provoked none, and desires none, unless vital issues are at stake. The Colony has been somewhat helpless in being in what may be termed a state of sinlessness! Reiteration of the obvious is a dreary business. Having once testified to our spotlessness, it is best left at that. The Seamen's Union may, or may not resent, the sailing of the "Honam." The Union has made the mistake of prostituting labour to a spurious form of politics designed to turn out Robots. It has not helped the cause of genuine labour one whit. It will find that out soon, and it may be that the familiar lines of the "Honam" will help to a state of thought leading to the reign of reason. We certainly hope so. The tentacles of friendship are too far outspread for them to be entirely cut off from their hold. Certainly, they have been strained and weakened, but it has been difficult to think that they would cease to hold, and that the future had nothing in it but hate and ruin. We speak of the "Honam's" sailing in that spirit of optimism we have kept since the days of June ushered in an intolerable situation. Municipal Council and the remedying of irregularities connected with the Mixed Court. It is doubtful if the decisions of these important British bodies will find general favour in the Settlement, however, for if articles in the leading journals and correspondence columns are anything to go by, the attitude throughout the strike and subsequent boycott has been that to negotiate on matters other than the shooting affair of May 30 before the judicial enquiry had been concluded, would be an act of weakness. We have already stated reasons for our approval of the action of the two bodies in question. In holding out the olive branch in this manner and we fail to see in what respect it may be said to amount to desertion of Hongkong. The gesture, however, must be interpreted in the spirit in which it was made if bitterness is not to be engendered which will render impossible of creation the necessary spirit of goodwill and co-operation. The action of the Chinese Minister of Justice in Shanghai, for instance, in telegraphing to leading politicians and others in London that the Mixed Court has no legal foundation and that it is due to its existence that the local Chinese Court is prevented from co-operating in a judicial enquiry into the shooting incidents can only be described as foolish and reprehensible since it has no foundation in fact. Although in practice it appears to have given rise to certain irregularities, the Mixed Court has a solid enough legal basis for its existence in the Regulations governing the foundation of the Settlement—these, in fact, providing that the municipal authorities "shall arrest offenders of the public peace, hand them over and prosecute them before respective authorities, Chinese or other as the case may be." An argument often advanced against this practice is that a settlement for foreigners is not the proper place for trying one whose Government is outside that Settlement; but it must be borne in mind that punishment, although indicated, is not carried out in the Settlement and that whatever anomalies the working of the Mixed Court gives rise to (divided consular jurisdiction appears to be held chiefly responsible) some laws must be made, respecting the conduct of the ever increasing numbers of Chinese who since the Taiping rebellion have found protection within the Settlement borders. Similarly, if there is to be smooth working within, the Chinese committee which already advises on matters relating to the government of the Settlement must be replaced by actual Chinese representation on the Municipal Council. Far from being a disturbing element in the present negotiations the association with requests along these lines by responsible British bodies in Shanghai should be all for the good and should lead to the creation of a more favourable atmosphere for the hearing of other matters of more immediate importance.

headline: OUR RENTS LAW.
text:
Those who have petitioned H.E. the Governor in behalf of the 7,000 members of the Hongkong Tenants' Protective Association, which represents upwards of 100,000 residents of Hongkong, to suspend the Rents Ordinance permitting an increase of 15 per cent. on the standard rent, seem to have made out a good case. The arguments advanced affect primarily the Chinese community, although one or two might well be used to represent conditions amongst the foreign community. Since the outbreak of the "strike" over 500 distress warrants have been issued for rent in arrear, and, as a result, there is a great deal of empty property. Statistics at the moment of writing are not available, but we may take it for granted that the number of warrants devoted is exceptional and, in the main, due entirely to the unnecessary and harsh conditions forced on the

has been made for rent in arrear only in the "strike" months, it seems to reflect hardly on Chinese property owners who have not been moved to grant a sort of moratorium. The looker-on has to remember that property owners generally are liable for rates and Crown Rent, and very often for interest on mortgage: The situation is difficult for all concerned. If the suspension of the 15 per cent, order is likely to make a change for the good, public opinion will fervently hope that H.E. the Governor will listen favourably to the petition. The petitioners are decided in their opinion that Chinese tenants affected by the Rents Ordinance cannot afford to pay an increase of rent above Standard Rent until the trade conditions within the Colony resume a normal state. The alternative to a suspension seems to be simply one of overcrowding into other premises, to create a spirit of discontentment, to convey a wrong impression to the evil-doers at Canton, and to put the Colony's administration into a bad light. A suspension of the Ordinance giving the powers referred to should do some good. Property owners should be glad of postponement which at once cancels the main argument for the non-payment of rent, and strengthens their hands in seeking lawful demands. Tenants will be encouraged to meet their contracts, and the spirit of unrest will be killed at its birth. The signatories to the petition state that the great majority of the proprietors of small businesses and shops, and wage earners, are permanent residents and are law abiding and peaceful persons. Recent events seem to bear out the latter part of this contention. Police patrols were, in the main, singularly free from the capture of many undesirables, whilst a feature of the work of the cordons was the relatively small numbers of unwanteds they caught when compared with the total population of either the districts concerned or the Colony as a whole. It seems to us that the temporary suspension of the 15 per cent increase on the Standard

whether as tenants, owners, mortgage holders,—to say nothing of the Government as rate collectors—are so vitally interested in property.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I crave for a little space within your columns to express my appreciation for one whose untimely death has cast a gloom over the entire Colony. It has been my privilege and fortune to have known the late Mr. Ho Cheuk intimately for well night twenty years, as a promising youth, as a devoted husband and as an affectionate father.

Genial in disposition, he had always a good word for someone; quiet by nature, most of his many good deeds were done quietly; unassuming in manner, he was "tender towards the bashful, gentle towards the distant and merciful towards the absurd."

A devoted husband, he never returned home without a parcel or something for his wife. A tender father he spared no pains to inspire his children with the highest and taught them the best. A filial son, he loved his father and mother dearly. An ideal brother, he was ideal to the end: A helpful neighbour, he was always a friend in need. Since the beginning of the strike right up to a week before his regrettable end, he was up early every day to get ice and food and attend to the needs of his neighbours. Throughout his short but serviceable life he had no enemies while the record attendance at his funeral amply justifies the highest esteem in which he was (and still is) held.

In expressing my deepest sympathy to those who are his dearest and nearest, let me also mention that though it seemed cruel that such a promising life should be abruptly end, yet heaven hath endowed us with his spirit which will never die but will always be present to inspire his friends to a nobler living and his loved ones to a more perfect trust in the goodness and mercy of Providence.

Thou art gone but not forgotten, Never shall thy memory fade; Sweetest thoughts shall ever linger Round the place where thou art

Under Educational and Artists objects: To grant a sum of $1,000 to the Hongkong A.D.C. to encourage it in its effort to produce Classical and Shakespearean plays." It would be money well spent. The suggestion is prompted by the news that the Irish Free State has voted $14,500 toward the endowment of a national theatre. This is the first time a State subsidy for the encouragement of the drama has ever been granted in Great Britain or Ireland, and it is hailed as another gratifying outcome of the autonomous powers conferred on the Free State by the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The endowment probably will be enlarged in future years if the results justify such a course. The grant to the Abbey Theatre will be specially useful in enabling it not only to make larger payment to authors but also to retain promising actors and actresses against the inducements offered to them by British and American managers. An Comhar Dramiochta, which came into being a couple of years ago, also produces its plays at the Abbey Theatre, but is managed separately. Already it has presented a number of quite excellent plays and the company, which is composed exclusively of amateurs, includes several actors of decided ability. The audiences are steadily increasing, and high hopes are entertained for the movement, particularly in view of the intensive teaching of the Irish language now in progress in all the public schools.

headline: STRIKE THREAT.
text:
FRENCH MINERS WANT MORE WAGES.

REFERENDUM TO BE TAKEN.

The National Council of the Federation of French Mine Workers has adopted a resolution declaring that unless wages are increased by January 21, to compensate for the increased cost of living, a referendum will be taken on the question of a general strike of French miners.

MOSCOW'S VERSION.

headline: CARGO SEIZED.
text:
How Canton watermen dived into the river, rather than face the strike pickets, is related by passengers who have come down to Hongkong.

On Saturday night, or in the small hours of Sunday morning, a number of shots were fired. It appears that two native boats, loaded with about 20 tubes of (fresh water) fish, valued at over $1,000, were making for the s.s. "Lungshan." An allegation has been made that "permission had been arranged," whatever that may mean—and it is given only for what it is worth.

When 500 feet or so off shore, the boats were fired at; presumably by boycott pickets. One of the first shots hit a helmsman who either fell or jumped into the river. Another fokl was also struck, and he went overboard. When the fire got within range, several others followed.

The foreign warships trained their searchlights on the spot. One report is that a boat was lowered, and two of the refugees were thus saved. The fish boats and the cargoons are stated to have been seized by the pickets.

Negotiations between merchant organisations in Canton, and the boycott executive, relative to cargo owned by Messrs. Kwong Sang Hong, have been given publicity in the "Kung Sheung Yat Po" (published in Hongkong).

It appears that some cargo shipped from Shanghai to Canton, for account of the firm, has been seized by pickets.

headline: SPIRITED AWAY.
text:
There was an enthusiastic and dramatic scene at the Communist conference at Glasgow when it was announced that in spite of the Home Office ban on foreign Reds, Dr. Stocker, the fraternal German delegate, was present.

Dr. Stocker went on the platform amidst tremendous enthusiasm and the singing of the "Internationale."

He declared it was childish and absurd of Sir William Joynson Hicks (the Home Secretary) to think he could stop the British revolution by endeavouring to prevent the Communists of different countries from meeting.

headline: LIEUT. LIVOCK. / KEEPS WICKET FOR MIDDLESEX.
text:
INTERPORT CRICKETER.

Flight Lieut. G. E. Livock, R.A.F., who played for Malaya against Hongkong and Shanghai in the triangular interport cricket matches here last year, has turned out for Middlesex at Home this season.

Prior to coming to Hongkong on the seaplane carrier Pegasus, Lieut. Livock already had a big reputation as he had. "kept" wicket for Lord Cowdray's XI against an England XI which included some of the best players in the Old Country.

In the interport series he batted first for Malaya. Though his average was not big his batting was certainly very impressive and his work behind the sticks was brilliant. Against Kowloon he made a century. When Mr. Ezra Abraham. Vice-President of the K.C.C: presented him with a bat, Lieut. Livock hinted that he would have preferred a golf club.

However, his inclusion in the Lord's team seems to indicate that he has not deserted the summer game. A Home paper, in mail week, mentions him as an amateur from Chiswick. He was ninth on the batting list and scored 20 not out after some of the opening batsmen had failed. Only the first day's play was given and Warwickshire, who were playing at Lord's had only started their innings so it is not known if he did anything spectacular. According to a Reuter cable at the time, Middlesex eventually won the match.

Lieut. Livock's progress now that he is at Home will be watched with interest by cricketers who have seen him in the Far East.

headline: FRENCH RETIRING.
text: A War Ministry communiqué referring to “pessimistic reports on recent military events in Eastern Morocco in the direction of Tazza,” says that “certain loyally tribes partly failed us, opening a breach in the first line of defence, through which the Riffs passed and attacked our regular troops, who are now taking up the best positions to repel the enemy. Public opinion must not be disturbed by these inevitable episodes in colonial warfare.” The communiqué refers to the difficulties of the French forces, owing to the improvement in the enemy's numbers, equipment, and tactics compared with ten years ago and adds “Their attacks are more frequent, and better co-ordinated on a wider front. They are constructing trenches, dug-outs, and barbed wire entanglements, whereas the tactics of modern armies, concentrating to strike decisive blows, if employed too systematically, are bound to result in the disaffection of abandoned loyal tribes, with a consequent infiltration of enemy contingents. We must not be surprised or alarmed if, on a vast front difficulties should lead locally to retirements, regroupings, and concentrations of our forces that, however, prepare the way to more vigorous counterblows.”

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
dateline: Hongkong, July 8. OLD HAND. Hongkong, July 7.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Some people do not care one way or the other whether the remaining river boats continue operations or not. Others do care. There are yet others who, by virtue of long contact with the crews, are able to throw light on one aspect of the trouble as the men concerned themselves are far too much scared to do anything.

Strike Executive are calling on the No. 1's of the crews. On introduction they take considerable pains to explain that they are volunteers, duly empowered by the Executive, the members of the latter having had to make themselves scarce. I have recognised one or two of these "volunteers" as former No. 1's on river and coastal shipping. As they are out of work themselves they are anxious to see all colleagues idle. After a brief hurangue on national honour, they emphasise the claim that if all shipping was to cease the trouble would soon be over. As is characteristic of the Chinese worker, the men approached put off the agitators by promising that if vital lines shut down, they will also stop themselves. In this manner, one has been waiting for the other and the service has continued till now. If a visit were paid to the ships an hour or two after arrival at the wharves here some of these "volunteer" delegates could be seen actually making their daily rounds. To those who have been ap

To those who have been approached I would say that it is difficult to see how the situation up North can be affected by making the shipping stoppage an entire one.

Thanking you for inserting this letter.

Yours, etc.,

(To the Editor of The China Mail)

Sir,—Perhaps the thought may have struck others or the suggestion I am about to make has already been put into actual practice. With regard to the letter published in your issue of yesterday, from “An Americann Friend,” I beg to propose, with all deference, that the Government have the letter translated and re-published (1) in the vernicular papers which are still being issued and (2) as circulars as was the case with a speech of Mr. D. Lloyd George at a critical period of the last War. Such publication may do a great deal to commenter pernicious propaganda from sources beyond the control of the Colony.

About the question of reward for arrests and/or convictions of agitators. There are some of us who may think twice about performing a public duty because a wrong impression may be gained, viz. that of going after the monetary reward. Such people would consider a medal or other tangible remembrance a much more suitable reward.

Yours, etc.

headline: HELD UP:
text:
INCIDENTS AT SHANGHAI

Shanghai: July 7.

The shipping situation remains the same and the concentrated intimidation of the last few days resulted in a number of tramwaymen failing to turn up this morning, but the Tramway Company is determined to carry on. Specials guarded the trams to-day. There was no incident. Otherwise, however, the situation is quiet, though forty thousand are out of work due to the cutting off of the bulk of the power supply of electricity. In many cases resumption is believed to be taking place owing to the inadequate dole which is being given out.

The bulk of the power supply of electricity has been discontinued. A number of mills are installing their own motors.

Agitators are taking advantage of the discontinuance of the electricity supply and are furthering unrest, but no serious trouble has occurred.

The intimidation of tramwaymen is being carried on without abatement. Last evening, a crowd of a hundred, including a number of former tramwaymen, held up a car conveying thirty tramway fitters from the repair shops. They forced the fitters to accompany them to Chinese territory.

About half the telephone operators have resumed work.

The body of an American member of the crew of the s.s. President Pierce has been found in a creek, whilst a British blue-jacket has been missing for sixty hours and has not yet been found.

At the inquest on the man who was shot by the American seaman Dizik, it was stated that the deceased was shot by the sailor when the latter was protecting a Municipal officer. Two men who were arrested were charged at the Mixed Court, one for inciting to riot and the other for firing crackers. The first was remandied on bail, and the other nominally fined.

The Japanese community is raising subscriptions for the purpose of making a presentation to the Volunteers and naval landing parties in recognition of their services. So far, nearly ten thousand dollars have been subscribed.

headline: Dosser Trial.
text:
Shanghai; July 7..

The Mixed Court dismissed three of the four charges against Dosser who was allowed bail on Tls. 20,000 security (which the Soviet Trade Mission is alleged to be furnishing).

Dosser, was remanded for a week. All charges against his wife were dismissed. The remaining charge against Dosser is that he made preparations to openly incite disorder.

The Court dismissed the charge that accused was making preparations to commit a hostile-act against certain foreign states, because the text of an article in the Chinese Criminal Code, whereon the charge was based, meant "declare war" and not "hostile act." Two other charges were dismissed as they rested upon the above mentioned charge.

headline: THE HONGKONG & WHAMPOA DOCK COMPANY, LIMITED.

headline: THE STRIKE.
text:
JIONG KONG'S EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.

Elsewhere in this issue (says the "Shanghai Mercury" of July 1), will be found an extract from a private letter received from Hongkong under date of June 21. We would particularly commend this article to the careful perusal of our readers. There can, we think, be little doubt that the Governor of Hongkong is acting with the full approval not only of all foreign residents in the "Colony", but also of all foreigners in this country. The policy of the Hongkong Government can only be regarded as an excellent example—an example which the local Authorities would do well to follow.

There is of course, a certain amount of difference between the Shanghai and Hongkong cases. That of Hongkong was brought about solely by the inischievous activities of the Kuomintang Reds. As Sir Reginald Stubbs pointed out at last week's meeting of the Legislative Council, there is nothing to discuss or adjudicate or on which to compromise. There is no shadow of grievance to justify this strike. In regard to the Shanghai incident, it will be readily admitted that there was something to discuss. It must also be admitted by Chinese and foreigner alike that the interested Powers took prompt action with a view to settling the affair. Six delegates were sent down from "Peking-fully empowered to come to terms, but the Chinese persisted in demanding matters entirely irrelevant to the incident of May 10, with the result that the foreign delegates did the only thing possible—they returned to Peking. The question of these irrelevant matters and also that of the Nanking Head affair will be settled in the course by the responsible parties in Peking. Neither have any legitimate hearing upon the present state of affairs in Shanghai, and neither have any claims upon the attention or consideration of China's school boys, and others responsible for prolonging the strike.

After practically a month of dislocated commerce it seems to us that some concerted action should be taken by the foreign employers. There can be little doubt that the strikers have been led to believe that their employers will pay them strike pay. Is it to be seriously thought that any soldier-minded tapan would agree to such an action? We think—and certainly hope—not. Such being the ease, is it not tim that the attitude of the employers was made known. Surely such a step would expedite the return to normal conditions, but foreigners must follow Hongkong's example and present a united front. Any dilly-dallving would be fatal, but we are firmly convinced that the time has come when the foreign employers should make known their attitude.

The following is part of the letter quoted by the “Shanghai Mercury”:—

'You will already know that Hongkong is in the throes of another disgusting strike. The Government is determined this time to fight to a finish, and we have no Prince of Wales' coming to prepare for. Already the Chinese have asked to be taken back, but the Government is going to decide that matter. It will be a case this time. May I and will you take me back? You must have read of the drastic action already taken by the Government, and honestly, I am proud to be under the Union Jack here. We can and are showing the Chinese what we can do. No money exceeding $5 can be taken away from the Colony, no rice, no flour, and practically all foodstuffs are strictly forbidden to be exported. The Chinese are already feeling the 'pinch,' but the Europeans have plenty to eat and drink. No rioting or disturbances of any sort have arisen, and the military have charge of the whole situation. Thousands daily are going to Canton, but what they think they are going to do with $5 and shortage of rice in Canton, remains to be seen.

headline: CUSTOM'S. DECLINE.
text:
Reuter learns that owing to the Shanghai strike and other disturbances and unrest all over the country, the net Customs revenue for the six months ending on June 30 declined by 1,500,000 taels compared with last year, out of which there was 1,000,000 taels decline during June. It is considered, however, that the decrease need not cause undue alarm to bondholders.

Washington, July 8 It is announced that Mr. Kellogg has appointed Mr. MacMurray and Mr. Silas Strawn Layer as America's Commissioners at the Shanghai Customs Conference.

headline: AS OTHERS SEE US.
text:
A FIGHT TO A FINISH.

The Red wing of the Kuomintang who are again in control in Canton five chosen to make war on a neighbouring and friendly Colony, says the "Peking and Tientan Times" of June 20. There is no other meaning attaching to the "spontaneous" outbreak of the strike and other disturbances which followed the return of the Reds to authority in Canton. Whilst the whole of China was in an uproar, and anti-foreign demonstrations had occurred in such distant centres as Chungking, Hongkong remained normal and quiet. But within a few days of the re-establishment of the Reds in Canton all was changed. The strike, fomented and engineered by the Canton Government, and the unprovoked attack upon the Shameen, form the culmination of a long series of provocations during the past two years. The Governor of Hongkong has expressed his determination to "see this thing through." We are

"See this thing through. We are confident that the entire British community are with him to a man and to a woman in their will relentlessly to prosecute this struggle to a victorious issue."

The sermen's strike and the manner of its Termination have taught us all a bitter and unforgettable lesson. There can be no discussion of terms this time. As Sir Reginald Stabbs publicly declared at a meeting of the Legislative Council: "There is nothing to discuss or adjudicate, or on which to compromise." It must be—a fight—to—a finish.—There is "no shadow of a grievance" to justify this strike. It is purely political in complexion and hatched in malice and ensoy by the Kuomintang Reds. The demands published by the agitators who have brought about this crisis are essentially political. The Chinese have some reason to complain of the refusal to give them representation on the Shanghai Municipal Council. It was a counsel of perfection, not of higher wisdom and tact, which denied the Chinese this participation in the administration of the "Molel Settlement." It will unquestionably be remedied when reasonable conciliation on our side is commended by a similar spirit on the part of the Chinese, and when the acceptable compromise regarding representation of foreign taxpayers on the Municipal Council of the ex-Russian Concession in Hankow is adopted in the case of similar foreign areas in "Tientsin," in accordance with an undertaking that has hitherto been utterly ignored.

But in Hongkong the Chinese have no such grievance. The demand for the popular election of the Chinese representatives on the Legislative Council is inadmissible while a similar right is denied to the British and foreign community. There is no discrimination. The British community have been conducting a perfectly legitimate campaign for a limited electoral representation during the past few years. They have of course, not sought to enforce their demand by disorderly processes. If and when their desires are met probably similar rights will be conceded to the responsible section of the Chinese taxpayers. But at present we are all on the same basis in the principle of representation. The Chinese members of the Council have always been high-minded and able men, and truly representative of the Chinese interests. That is more than can be said of the self-styled authorities in Canton. If there were a genuine popular election in that city nothing would be more certain than the overwhelming repudiation of the Kuomintang extremists. It is a characteristic feature of Chinese inconsistency in their disputes with the foreign authorities, that they demand rights under foreign auspices which they do not enjoy, and apparently do not even make any serious attempt to acquire in their own country. The Chinese taxpayers have absolutely no voice in the administration of the native city of Shanghai; and even the inchongta and futile effort to secure the popular election of a Tupan after the civil war soon died out of initiation. What voice have the Chinese taxpayers got in the municipal administration of the native cities of Peking, Wuchang, Tientsin.

For very many years the relations between Hongkong and Canton were of the most cordial description. There was no common recognition of the essential unity of interests, and the one co-operated with the other in a fine spirit of mutual helpfulness. The Semmen's Strike, openly supported and sustained by Dr. Sun Yat-sen's administration in Canton, by whom the strikers were housed and fed and subsidised, was the first really serious breach. With the exception of a brief interval the relations between the two Governments have been progressively worsening. This most deplorable break with the past is the solely to the intrigues of the Polshevists and to the amazing influence which Moscow's agents came to exert over the left wing of the Kuomintang. While Red Army instructors have been imported and have played a large part

in the military campaigns since Sun Yat-sen returned to Kwangtung in 1923, the Hongkong Government has been reviled for its sympathy with the great commercial class. It has been accused of subsidising the revolt against the appalling exactions and tyranny of the Red regime in Canton. But this may be said for the Colony. If it had lent British officers to Chen Chiung-ming or to Chan Tim-pak, and had actually given them financial and other support, if it had actually turned its very natural and proper sympathy for the sufferers from Red rule, in Canton to active help of the opponents of that regime, and backed the moderate section of the Konfrontung against Hu Hun-min and his gang, it is safe to say that the Canton Bolsheviks would not be where they are today. If it is right for a section of Chinese political extremists to accept the aid of one Power, why should it be improper for those with real material interests,—the merchants, not the politicians—to seek and to be granted the help of another?

But in point of fact we have not given material aid to anybody so far. We have scrupulously maintained our traditional policy of non-interference, in the face of intense provocation, though in the many crises that have arisen during the past two years as the result of the appalling military situation in the province, when the Red Kuomintang's late hung by a thread, a slight departure from that neutrality would have decided the issue. What would the Soviet have to say if Chang Tso-lin imported British or Japanese officers into Harbin? There would not, merely be a protest. There would be another concentration of Red troops on the frontier. We have not even protested against what is unquestionably things being as they are, a deliberate-ly Fostile action. If the British or Hongkong Governments wanted to interfere they could do so, and to some purpose. If they wanted to associate themselves with the Yunnanese they could transport not 600 but 6,000 troops by sea from Yunnan and turn them loose within striking distance of Canton, and they could keep them in power. They could do the same in the case of Chen Chiong-ming, who has apparently re-taken Swatow. We are becoming tired of these preposterous and childish charges of interference. It is inducing a feeling of exsperation, and that attitude of mind which is a temptation to do the very things we are wrongfully accused of doing. If we lent a handful of officers, money and munitions, to Chen Chiong-ming, and rendered him a little unobtrusive. Naval support, he would have no difficulty in cleaning up Canton. Such help has undoubtedly been solicited on many occasions by one or other of the factions hostile to the Kuomintang extremists, and the fact is that such overtures have always been refined. Could we have a more convincing pretext than the attack on the Shameen and the officially-inspired plot against the Hongkong Government if we really wished to interfero.

Finally, let us quote the tribute paid to the British Administration in Hongkong by Sun Yat-sen when he was about to resume power in Canton in February, 1923:

“The difference between the Governments in China and Hong Kong impress me so much that I begin to wonder why the British

could do so much on the barren rock of Hongkong within 70 years. China during a thousand years has been unable to accomplish the same things as Hongkong. In the administration of Hongkong corruption is the exception and purity the rule. On the contrary, in China corruption is the rule. In China we have not got a Government. We have been misgoverned for many centuries. You (the Hongkong University students) must learn the English example, and we must carry the example of good Government to all parts of China. That is the best advice San Yatsen has ever given to his countrymen. In its fulfilment the Hongkong Government are undoubtedly prepared to offer any assistance that may be welcome, and that does not involve us in a breach of the policy of neutrality. Even in the present crisis, though the British have been provoked beyond measure, that policy will be and should be maintained. But we hope that the Kuomintang will take warning from the situation their avowedly and consciously hostile policy has produced, and will forthwith cease from further provocation, lest they make desperate remedies inevitable. We shall continue to defend our lives and property on the Shameen, but we shall go no farther unless Hu Han-min, and his fellow-despernades forces us to abandon our neutrality and to intervene, as the only means of self-preservation.

headline: NOT YET.
text:
ABANDONMENT OF TREATIES UNSUITABLE

WHAT MUST BE DONE FIRST.

In the House of Commons, the Laborite Mr. Johnston asked whether Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) would advise British initiative for the abandonment of extra-territoriality in China similar to Britain's action to Japan. Mr. A. M. Samuel (Foreign Under-Secretary) replied that it was self-evident the present position in China as regards orderly administration, the safety of life and property compared very unfavourably with Japan in 1894.

The Government regarded as important regards China that the Treaty Powers concerned should act together in this matter. He said "we are ready to abandon the rights when conditions are suitable but they are unsuitable for so doing."

headline: Washington Treaty.
text:
Reuter understands now that the French Parliament has ratified the Washington Treaty as regards China; it is expected the ratifications of the various Powers will be shortly deposited.

The Washington Treaty will then come into force, clearing a way for the Tariffs Conference which the British Government regards as an opportunity for doing something to co-operate with China. As regards further Treaty signed at Washington providing a commission to enquire into the abolition of extraterritoriality, this commission is not yet appointed owing to request for postponement by China and other Powers.

headline: FIVE DEMANDS. / ORDER OF PRECEDENCE LEADS TO DEADLOCK.
text:
The situation continues a deadlock. While nothing has been officially announced it appears that the Chinese Government desires that negotiations regarding the last eight of the thirteen demands, as well as the revision of the so-called unequal treaties shall be taken up simultaneously with the first five demands. It is understood that the Powers insist that the five demands arising directly out of the Shanghai incident be discussed first. Meanwhile agitators continue to urge negotiations with Britain alone.

The Chinese Chamber of Commerce has hitherto handed to the bureau distributing strike pay $620,000 but it is believed that it is insufficient to last much longer.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE
text:
CHINESE SPORTSMEN

(To the Editor of the China Muit.)

Sir,—It is now perfectly clear that the agitators are out to cripple and, if possible, to destroy the business life of the Colony and that the incidents at Shanghai and elsewhere were used as a cloak to conceal their intent. Having served their purpose, these incidents are no longer referred to at all. This being the case, the path for the Hongkong Chinese to take is also clear. The peace of the Colony is threatened and the sporting thing to do is to rally round the Government to help to preserve law and order and thereby protect their own families. All the foreign sportsmen are doing essential service in some form and it is up to the Chinese sportsmen to fall in line. It is true that Dr. Tso and his helpers have gathered together about a thousand Chinese to volunteer but this number is disproportionate and the South China Athletic Association alone should be able to enlist a few hundred amongst its members to serve as Volunteers or Special Constables. This possibility should be immediately considered by Messrs. Li Yih-tong and Ng Szew-kwong, the energetic Chairman of the two most important Chinese sporting organizations of the Colony.

Are Chinese sportsmen cowards? The next week or so should provide mple opportunity to show that hey are not.

headline: ORDER TO TROOPS.
text:
TO AVOID BOLSHEVIST PROPAGANDA.

According to the Ching Pao, Feng Yu-hsiang has issued an an order to the troops directing them to avoid Bolshevist propaganda and to oppose it to the utmost, pointing out that Kalgan is on the borders of Mongolia and Russia, but that there is a vital difference between the habits and customs of the Chinese people and those of these countries and, moreover, the national spirit differs. He concludes by urging the Chinese to adhere to the teaching, and practices of their own ancient sages.

Russian aeroplanes, it is reported, are arriving here to-day. The Finance Ministry has been requested to provide $20,000 for the reception of the aviators.

The Secretariat of the Chief Executive, it is reported, has sent a circular by telegram to the provinces saying that the Government has maintained a firm attitude from the beginning in regard to the Shanghai affair. A popular movement based on patriotism is to be commended, but the actions of bad characters, such as the destruction of the homes of foreigners, is to be avoided as it will be prejudicial to the progress of the negotiations. It concludes that henceforth the popular agitation must be carried on by peaceful means only.

headline: CHINA'S DISORDERS.
text:
HOME PAPERS' STRONG COMMENT.

Contemplating a long struggle, with not a few complications, the Times, in a leader, expresses the opinion that the time has come for British policy toward China to take a clear and definite shape, and declares that if this policy leads to effective common action so much the better, but the responsibility for defining threatened British interests dies first and foremost with the British Government.

The Times considers the British are now hampered by past neglect, particularly in allowing the Washington decisions to remain in cold-storage, but the fact of the stimulation of anti-British agitation may be the outcome, directly of indirectly from the report of the Commission of Enquiry into the Shanghai disorders.

The paper emphasises the necessity of a clear renewal of British initiative and adds that the situation is intimately connected with the recent discussion of the cruiser programme. We must be unfettered in the disposal of means whereby British nationals and trade in the Far East can be continually protected.

headline: Bungled”？
text:
The "Daily Telegraph" diplomatic correspondent says there is a strong feeling among certain members of the Cabinet about the manner in which the proceedings, relating to the Shanghai incidents in regard to the action of the British police there, have been "bungled, to perhaps the serious detriment of British prestige," and adds that the anxiety of a section of the Diplomatic Body, whether through undue nervousness or for reasons connected with their countries' material advantages, to placate the Chinese agitators is indeed regrettable.

The writer suggests that a British veto should from the first have been placed upon the foreign project of a "Diplomatic investigation" to be carried out in an atmosphere of Chinese intimidation, and adds that firmness on the subject is needed in London and is likely to be forthcoming, judging by the recent statements of Mr. Austen Chamberlain and Mr. Samuel.

headline: NOTICE
text: Subscribers of the China Mail not receiving their paper every evening owing to the uncertain delivery as the result of the strike are invited to notify this office if they would prefer to purchase their paper from the street news-boys direct and have the amount credited to their account.

headline: “ALL POWERS.”
text:
PEKING'S NEGOTIATIONS

SOVIET PLANES.

Yesterday's evening vernacular papers state a proposal was brought forward at to-day's meeting of the Foreign Relations Committee that negotiations regarding Shanghai be with Britain only, but the majority, rejected the proposal and decided that negotiations will be with all interested Powers.

After rejecting the proposal to conduct negotiations, regarding Britain only, the Foreign Relations Committee decided negotiations were to be carried on with all interested Powers.

Three Soviet aeroplanes have arrived from Russia. A fourth aeroplane has broken down en route.

headline: LUCKY ESCAPE.
text:
ALARMING STUBBS ROAD ACCIDENT.

CAR STRIKES PARAPET.

Mr. H. S. Bennett, manager of the Hongkong Telephone Co., and two friends had a lucky escape from serious injury on Monday afternoon. They were proceeding to the Peak by Stubbs Road when their car met with a nasty mishap. They were approaching the second bend after the hairpin bend when a tyre burst and the car ran into the granite wall at the cliff side. Mr. Bennett was flung violently against the wind-screen but luckily escaped with nothing more serious than a few scratches and bruises. His two friends were thrown from the car by the force of the impact, also fortunately without serious injury. That all three escaped so lightly, when they might easily have been involved in the gravest consequences, was largely due to the fact that the car was travelling at not more than 15 miles an hour.

headline: RIOT SEQUEL. / QUESTIONS IN HOUSE OF COMMONS.
text:
LABOURITES' TRANSLATION.

Replying to questions by Labourites, Mr. Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that he had not yet received a full report of the evidence before the Mixed Court at Shanghai in regard to the shootings, nor a report of the Commission of Inquiry.

Mr. W. M. Adamson (Labour) said that Chinese newspapers had arrived in England and a translation showed that an inspector had admitted in evidence that he did not know a warning must be given before shooting.

Mr. Chamberlain was of the opinion that the report to which Mr. Adamson had referred was the report of the commencement of the Enquiry on people who were killed. The mail which brought the commencement of the report had not brought the end of it.

He was of the opinion that he ought to see the whole of the evidence before he expressed an opinion.

Replying to Mr. J. Beckett (Labour), Mr. Chamberlain said that he did not know the exact nature of the divergence in views in the recent discussions between the Diplomatic representatives at Peking in connection with which the French Minister withdrew.

Meibourne, July 15.—Major di Pinedo took off on his flight to Japan but was compelled to re-land owing to a leakage. He will re-start at eight on the morning of July 16.—Reuter.

Paris, July 15.—The National Fête was celebrated brilliantly all over France. Paris witnessed an imposing ceremony at the Unknown Soldier's tomb and the finish of a relay race from Verdun whence runners bearing the symbolic torch came by way of the battlefields to lay the symbol on the grave. In the Moroccan towns impressive military parades took place attended by huge crowds of natives and at Habat by the Sultan with his Viziers Hayes.

headline: “NOT UNDERSTOOD.”

FRANCE AND RIGHTS REVISION.

WASHINGTON POINTER.
