text: Subscribers of the China Mail not receiving their paper every evening owing to the uncertain delivery as the result of the strike are invited to notify this office if they would prefer to purchase their paper from the street news-boys direct and have the amount credited to their account.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE / DEPARTATION ORDERS MADE. / RAILWAYMEN THREATEN.
text:
Deportation summonses are being issued against four persons connected with the Seamen's strike.

Two hundred and sixty-six thousand tons of British shipping are now idle in Australian ports.

The Governments of Tasmania, Victoria and South Australia, replying to Mr. Stanley Bruce's request, have promised to take necessary steps to protect seamen remaining loyal to agreements.

A general railway strike is threatened at Brisbane on, the 31st inst. unless a demand is met for the restoration of the recent five per cent, reduction in wages.

headline: Vladivostock Myth.
text:
The whole morning's sitting, the Advisory Committee on Opium devoted to discussion of the British proposal regarding the export of opium from the Persian Gulf.

Sir John Jordan gave us his opinion that import certificates had done more harm than good. He declared that unless the Committee could take more effective measures to prevent the large export, it had better abandon the matter. He hoped other Governments could follow India's practice of not attaching importance to import certificates. Sir John Jordan added that nearly the whole of the exports from the Persian Gulf were nominally destined for Vladivostok but in reality had been landed elsewhere.

a British Consular report showing the Soviet authorities at Vladivostok to be exercising more strict control on opium consignments, but Sir John Jordan attributed the fact to the Soviet's endeavouring to protect the Siberian monopoly.

An American observer, Mr. Tuck, former United States Consultant to Vladivostok, agreed with Sir John Jordan.

Dr. Tsurumi (Japan) remarked that many Japanese vessels from the Persian Gulf, bound for Vladivostok, did not touch Japanese ports. The Japanese Government had taken steps to prevent the transhipment of opium at Japanese ports.

Sir John Campbell (1904) urged the Persian Government to control the export of opium to illicit destinations. Sir John Jordan was not optimistic with regard to action to be taken by Teheran. He remarked that the Japanese Government was capable of coping with the situation and proposed that the League Council call the attention of Persia to the subject; also to induce all Powers to prohibit transnipment at their ports and to take action to control their shipping.

Later.

The afternoon session of the Advisory Committee on Opium opened with the reading of a letter by the American financial adviser to Persia stating the country favoured the restriction of cultivation when the financial situation permitted and welcoming the proposed European commission of enquiry into the opium situation in Persia.

The remainder of the session was devoted to the discussion of illicit traffic. Sir Malcolm Delevingne and Sir John Campbell paid a tribute to the efforts of preventive officials at Hongkong in the matter of discoveries and seizures. Sir John Jordan's opinion was that the question of amuggling was relatively of minor importance. The best means of curtailing "opium consumption" was the limitation of production in which co-operation with the Japanese will be most effective. He said he hoped the Press would note Sir John Campbell's statement. They could not rely on the measures of some Governments dealing with the opium problem. The remainder of the sitting

headline: FOREIGN VESSELS GAIN.
text:
Local representatives of overseas shipping companies believe the unofficial strike is ending and consider work will be gradually resumed when the strikers realise their lack of unanimity and the owners' determination.

Meanwhile, foreign vessels and ships of the Commonwealth Line are benefitting from the enforced idleness of British ships, an instance of which is the German motor ship Konigsberg, sailing with full cargo.

The Commonwealth Government has appointed a board to consider the question of deportations.

Labour Premier's Stand.

The Labourite Premier, Mr. Lang, stated he is of the opinion that the Deportation Act is the most iniquitous ever passed. He firmly refuses to permit State instrumentalities to be used for the purpose of deporting political and industrial leaders.

Mr. Walsh, the strike leader, visited Mr. Lang to-day. It is understood the discussion concerned an early settlement of the dispute.

headline: 18,000 MEN.OUT. / QUEENSLAND RAILWAY STRIKE.
text: Apart from serious inconvenience throughout the State, the strike of 18,000 railwaymen is having very bad effects on the sugar industry. Thousands of tons of cane are deteriorating.

headline: ANTI-BOLSHEVIK
text:
REPORTED MOVEMENT IN SHANGHAI.

This morning's "Kung Seung Vat Po" publishes a report to the effect that the Chinese masses in Shanghai are joining together to resist Communistic influences.

That the Shanghai trouble had its origin in Canton intrigue is alleged. Bolshevism now threatens the whole of China, the sponsors are said to have declared, and concrete plans are being advanced for repelling the sinister tenchings.

A mass meeting of seamen at Southampton under the auspices of the Marine Workers'. Union decide to refuse to sign on except at the old rate. The meeting decided to form a strike committee and to approach other seamen with a view to a general strike.

headline: DEATH FOR THEFT. / RUSSIAN MILITARY OFFICIALS SENTENCED.
text:
At the end of a 48-day trial, nine officials of the military supply'depot were sentenced to death on a charge of misappropriation of goods.

Thirty-three officials received varying terms of imprisonment, the maximum being ten years.

Peking, August 29.—The students of the Peking Government colleges have decided when the new term begins in September to return to their studies and not continue the strike.—Reuter.

Paris, August 29.—The Police have been busy this evening Trustrating Communists' efforts to form processions in various parts of the capital to demonstrate against the Polish execution of Communists. One hundred and forty were arrested, twelve of whom are detained in custody.—Reuter.

text:
Tokyo, August 20.—The Foreign Office has selected Hioki as chief delegate to the Tariff Conference with Yoshizawa, but it is not yet formally announced. Odagiri Masunosike is appointed adviser. Tokyo, August 30.—Burojs Hioki and Yoshizawa have been formally appointed delegates to the Tariff Conference.—Reuter.

Shanghai, August 29.—The strike movement is gradually spreading to Chinese concerns. Following a settlement of the strike at the Commercial Press the employees of another prominent printing concern have walked out and there is unrest among the employees of Wing On's and Sincere's department stores, and the printers of Chinese newspapers.—Renter.

Tokyo, August 29.—The Navy Office announces that Canton's reply to the Japanese protest against the shooting of their marines expresses profound sympathy with the killed and wounded, and assures that they have no hostile intentions. It explains that the incident was caused by the darkness preventing them distinguishing the Japanese flag, as the fortress had been ordered to forbid boats passing at night time, though no notice had been served on the Powers to this effect. —Reuter. Interviewed on board a steamer on route for Paris, M. Lyndsey, is reported to have stated that the recent operations against the Brunes were more severe than was anticipated they would be owing to the presence of a large number of Riffian regulars, and he added that an examination of the situation after a visit to the front had convinced him of the impossibility of a general offensive before the rainy season.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
MEN STILL REFUSING TO WORK.

The crew of the Royal Mail liner Arlanza, which was due to sail to Buenos Aires from Southampton on September 4, refused to day to accept the wage reduction and left the Board of Trade Office without signing on. On the other hand the captain of the “transport Derbyshire which opens the autumn trooping season on Wednesday by taking reliefs to India said he had obtained practically a full crew.

headline: RAY OF HOPE.
text: The decision of the "Strike Council to attend the compulsory conference of all unions summoned by the President of the Arbitration Court has aroused hopes that the strike will soon end.

headline: LASCARS RECRUITED.
text: Bombay, August 31. The first batch of Indian Lascars numbering 700 has been recruited for service in connection with the shipping strike. They are proceeding to South Africa shortly. More are expected to snill later.

headline: RIVAL UNIONS
text:
A meeting of seamen at Avonmouth passed a resolution stating their intention to hold up the New Zealand liner Piako, due to sail on Wednesday, until the wages reduction has been restored.

The secretary of the Amalgamated Marine Workers' Union, the rival to the Sailors and Firemen's Union, stated to-day that his union was not officially backing the seamen's strike.

He claimed to be responsible for the Arlanzás crew refusing to sign on. He declared that the crew of the White Star liner Majestic, who signed on last week, had decided to go: 24 hours' notice to terminate their articles. The men on the trooper Glamorganshire had also refused to sign on.

The Secretary of the Sailors and Firemen's Union declared the trouble at Southampton had been engineered by another union with small membership which was trying to get a new lease of life.

A meeting of Hull seamen tonight, after hearing an official of the Marine Workers' Union, decided to join the strike. A committee was formed and pickets were detailed to visit the docks. The meeting represented only a portion the seamen at Hull

headline: CARLIER CABLES
text:
Important developments are likely to result from the secret conference at Sydney last week-end between the labour leaders and the trade-unionists. It is understood that labour is endeavouring to settle the strike preferring to fight the deportation issue in connection with which there is talk of a federal election.

A leading member of the Cabinet is of the opinion that an election will be held in a few months. Several applications have already been made to the Government to join the special police although the bill has not yet been approved by the Senate which passed it on a second reading after a strenuous debate. Summonses have been served requesting Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen to appear before the deportation board on September 3. —Reuter.

headline: THL STRIKE IN SOUTH AFRICA.
text:
The shipping strike has extended and five vessels are now affected. —Reuter.

Johannesburg, August 31. The Transvaal labour conference has passed a resolution recognising the justice of the semmen's strike and calling on the Government to refuse to support the shipping companies against the strikers. Colonel Cresswell, the labour minister, opposing the resolution, deprecated the notion of the men refusing to carry out the agreements centered into by their unions.—Reuter.

headline: PRAYA SMASH.
text:
RECKLESS DRIVING CHARGES FOLLOWS.

TRUCK STRIKES RICHSA:

As a sequel to an accident which occurred at 2 p.m. yesterday at Prayu East, the driver of a hand truck was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Magistracy this morning with having no licence and driving recklessly.

Mr. N. M. Bux, giving evidence, stated that he was travelling in a riesha from east to west when he noticed a loaded hand truck come out from Landale Street at a fast pace and stand in the way of a trum car proceeding to Causeway Bay, the driver of the latter narrowly averting a collision by applying his emergency brake and pulling up with a jerk. The truck people then turned the truck round so suddenly that the shafts and one of the wheels of the riesha on which he was seated were smashed and the coolie slightly injured.

Sergeant Roberts said that the damage to the ricsha was estimated at $20, but he was not pressing for compensation as it was found that the coolie had been using a private ricsha for public hire.

The accused stated that in attempting to avoid a collision with the trum car he swerved the truck round and in doing so struck the riesha.

Fines amounting to $15 were imposed on the two counts.

HULD STTUAITION MORE THREATENING

VARIOUR DOCKS PICKIFIED.

The various docks were pickoted. The steamship "Melville" engaged in the West African trade was unable to obtain a crew. The situation is generally more

Capetown, Sept. 1. The British seamen's strike has affected twelve steamers, the majority at Durban where the strike is spreading.

headline: MEN WHO WILL WORK.
text:
The strike situation at Rome ports is stationary.

The "Melville" obtained a full crew at Hull in spite of the efforts of pickets. The ships signed on previously suited according to schedule. The crew of the liner "Bristol City, due to sail to-morrow, refused to sign on. The "Bristol" is at Avonmouth where the "Piako" is in a similar plight.

A party of over forty ex-Service-men, some former Navalmen, left Plymouth for the "Majestic" at Southhampden. A batch of men left South Shields for the purpose of signing on for vessels lying in the Thares.

Troubled, has not been experienced in scurfing crews at the Tyne where there are more applicants than borths. Nearly a hundred seamen signed on at Cardiff and Barry for steamers whose crews at Bristol refused service.

The liner City of Alexandria has sailed for England with a Luevar crew.

The South African Udian Congress has strongly protested against the importation of Tascars from Bombay, expressing the opinion that such a policy is calculated to intensify the anti-Asiaic campaign in South Africa.

headline: EARTHER CAIRNS.
text:
Th3 Victorian Seamen's and the Butchers' Unions have decided, on a levy of five, shillings per member to assist the strikers. The Victorian seamen resolved to strike if an attempt is made to report Messrs. Walsh and Johannsen.

The Secretary of the Trades Council is urgently appealing to the unions to provide funds to feed the strikers.

headline: DANES AND SIAM.
text:
The Danish Foreign Minister and the Siamese Minister have signed a treaty of friendship, commerce and navigation based on the principles of reciprocity and the most favoured nation. The treaty must be ratified within six months.

Peking September 1.—It has been decided to start the so-called Christian College for those students of the five British missionary schools in Peking who do not desire to return thereto. Vernacular papers state that Feng Yu-hsiang has promised $10,000 to that end.—Reuter.

headline: NOT A DULL CITY. / SIR ROBERT HO TUNG'S ADVICE.
text:
The thing that strikes me most forcibly each time I visit London is the amount of traffic, and the hurrying crowds of people intent upon business or pleasure, and the splendid manner in which those crowds and vehicles are regulated by the ever-courteous police stationed at all crossings, making it quite safe to wend one's way where one lists if only one follows the traffic regulations, writes Sir Robert Ho Tung in the "London Evening News."

Year by year I notice changes and improvements in this great city; some old landmarks swept away to be replaced by wider streets and splendid buildings.

If London Men Wore Silk.

Englishmen's clothes are as sombre as some of the grey old buildings which I love to see again and enjoy visiting. Perhaps if your men adopted a Chinese dress of flowered silk it might help to brighten the appearance of streets — but, notwithstanding, I do not find London a dull city. It is in my opinion a serious, a busy one.

Some streets and houses look gloomy, but others are gay and pretty, especially at this time of the year.

You must not change London very much, or else visitors like myself and my wife and daughter, who enjoy coming here so much, would not be pleased!

But to return to our subject, the everlasting, much discussed one of clothes. I think Chinese garments are more picturesque, warmer in winter, cooler in summer, easier to put on, and very comfortable for the wearer. They have one disadvantage, they make more luggage, for so many suits are required for changes of climate.

A Chinese wears satin clothes on all formal occasions. viz.:—a blue robe reaching to the ankles, and a black riding jacket which is quite short.

In the day time, and for tea parties, etc., our robes and riding jackets are made of any bright coloured silk, like English ladies' summer gowns. We rarely wear overcoats, but if the weather is very cold we have a lining of fur or cottonwool padding under our robes.

I do not see why Englishmen should not wear brighter colours such as we use, although in my humble opinion no European costume is more becoming than the frock coat worn with light trousers, and also the light grey frock suit with hat to match. I am sorry it is no longer fashionable to wear a black frock coat; the morning coat which has taken its place is a poor substitute. Skirts too long. Then too short.

English evening dress, with the white bow tie and waistcoat, looks beautiful, but the dinner jacket is in some respects better than the tail coat.

As I am asked to express my humble opinion freely, I think the tails are a little bit clumsy, and the pockets bulge in an ugly fashion if anything is put in them.

Ladies' dresses are so grand and graceful I cannot help admiring them. Sometimes I think the skirts are a little too short, and I wonder if the ladies' calves are not cold!

In China short dresses would be more economical, because we pay for clothes in accordance with the amount of material that is in them. So I asked a friend if short dresses are cheaper, and he told me "No."

Perhaps the ladies like them short?

But I think they put up with them because they are the fashion

And if the shorter dresses are not cheaper for the ladies who buy them they must be cheaper for the dressmakers. I remember when European dresses reached to the ground: then they were too long and I pitied the poor ladies having to hold them up. It must have been fatiguing.

London streets are very well kept and clean, in spite of the great amount of traffic there. But some of them are not wide enough and many houses might be more artistic; though houses may be beautiful within, they are often ugly outside.

If the people who live in these houses made the outside beautiful would that not. conduct to a Brighter London? London is much cleaner than it used to be. Thirty years ago you could not go out without getting your hands and necks dirty. Perhaps London is so much less smoky that brighter-coloured point could now be applied to the TRUCK CRASHES INTO GARDEN WALL.

headline: MOTOR MISHAP.
text:
A motor truck owned by a Chinese transporting firm crashed into the side wall of the Botanical Gardens facing Garden Road yesterday morning, both the vehicle and the wall sustaining damage.

A Chinese who was seated beside the driver stated to the Police that the driver changed his gears on ascending the slope past Kennedy Road. The truck then ran backward, uprooted a gas lamp post, and was brought to a sudden halt by striking the wall.

The occupants of the truck escaped injury except for slight bruises sustained by a cookie woman.

headline: WALKED THE PLANK? FATE OF A TOWN.
text:
THE WINGFUNG'S CAPTAIN.

Reading like an episode of walking the plank from pirate craft a hundred years ago is a report in the "Wah Tsz Yat Po" concerning the flagship of the Canton Government.

Two messages were received yesterday by the vernacular paper stating that the Russian commander had been thrown over the ship's side into "the middle of the sea." Considerable interest has been manifested in the unusual action of the vessel.

The Wing Fung is called a cruiser. One of several of its type, it is supposed to have migrated to Canton from Peking when the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen came south to establish opposition to Yuan Shi-kai's monarchy. Admiral Ching Pik-kwong, whose statue now faces down the Canton River on Dutch Folly Island, took the "First Northern Cruiser Squadron" down with him. All have since gone back with the exception of the Wing Fung. This boat has been re-named the Chung San in honour of Dr. Sun whose other name—best known to the Chinese—was Sun Chung-san.

Recently Russian officers were placed in command of 'Canton's fleet'. As reported at the time resentment was alleged. It is now reported that a mutiny has taken place and that the warship has sailed for Hainan Island which is in the hands of General Tang Punyan, a pro-Chan leader.

When sighted the Wing Fung was flying neither the Bolshevik ensign nor her commander's pennant. However, this may have been only a blind as the Wing Fung has previously been on expeditions to the south of the province, on one occasion taking back the s.s. Hok Canton as a prize for alleged smuggling. She may be on one of those errands now or her movements may be in connection with the more recent political developments. Another point—reported in yesterday's "China Mail"—has been the pronounced naval activity in Canton harbour this week, both day and night.

headline: CAPETOWN SITUATION.
text:
The strike situation remains unchanged.

The crews of twelve steamers at South African ports, totalling over 2,300 men, are now definitely on strike and other ships are being held up.

The cross-Channel service from Southampton was partially resumed to-day, The Royal Mail Tiner Glamorganshire has all-ed.

headline: EARLIER CABLES
text:
The Steamers Piako and Bristol City both "sailed on scheduled time. The Piako obtained nearly a full crew from Bristol, and picked up the remainder in Barry Roads. The Bristol City similarly shipped the remainder of her crew in Walton Bay.

The latest move of the Liverpool strikers is for pickets to sign on Liverpool liners and when aboard to threaten the union men who refused to join the strikers.

The Cunard liners Carmania and Aurania and the Canadian Pacific Liner Montcalm are held up, firemen and seamen having struck, but officials are confident that new crews will be forthcoming. Men are arriving at Liverpool from all over the country in the hope of finding employment.—Reuter.

headline: HOLIDAY MAKERS STRANDED.
text: At a mass meeting 150 seamen of Middlesborough decided to join the strike and appointed a strike committee and pickets. Holiday-makers are stranded at Jersey where no mail arrived today.—Reuter.

headline: CHINA POLICY
text:
AMERICA AND PRIVITEGUE QUESTIONS

SPECIAL COMMISSIONMB

Mr. Kellogg, Secretary of State, in his speech yesterday evening, intimated that Mr. Silas Strawn had been appointed special commissioner to the proposed commission on extraterritoriality, treaty revision and other special privilege questions for which the date had not yet been fixed.

Mr. Silas Hardy Strawn is a lawyer who began his career at the Ottawa bar and later took up practice in Chicago. He is a director of the First National Bank of Chicago and several big commercial concerns. He has been President of the Chicago Bar Association and has held other similar distinguished honorary positions in connection with the legal profession.

headline: CHINISSE AGAINST BOYCOTT.
text:
It is understood that Sir Ronald Macleay is likely to depart from London to Peking shortly in order to resume his duties in connection with the conference on the Chinese customs, at which he will be supported by fiscal experts, one of whom, the "Daily Telegraph's" diplomatic correspondent says, is of considerable professional eminence.

Sir John Jordan, in a letter to the “Times,” welcomes Mr. Kellogg’s declaration of policy as regards China, but asks why the conference of the Powers on October 26 meets at Peking. He says the conference has a unique opportunity of appealing to all sections of the Chinese nation and therefore to achieve any prospect of success it must meet at Shanghai or some other neutral centre, where the provinces may take an active and untrammelled part in the negotiations.

The “Times,” in an editorial, says practical sympathy with the Chinese, collaboration with friends of law and order and adaptability to the changing conditions will give the keynote to British policy in China. Progress along the road to reform will be checked not by British reluctance but by Bolshevik intrigues and Chinese chaos. The fact that American policy accords with the British is shown by Mr. Kellogg's speech.

Special Committee.

Peking, September 5. — The Cabinet decided to issue a mandate this evening appointing twelve members as a special committee connected with the Tariff Conference.

"British Are a Just People." Peking, September 5.—Tsai Ting-kan, in a letter to the "Peking Leader," urges the dropping of the anti-British agitation and says, inter alia: "I have always maintained that the British are a just people. The joint resolution of the British Chamber of Commerce and the China Branch of the British Association of Shanghai is a splendid gesture, proving that the British will meet us more than half way."

Mr. Tsai Ting-kan quotes Mr. Chamberlain's reply to Mr. Chu's note concerning the judicial enquiry. He says that with the joint resolution of the British at Shanghai and Mr. Chamberlain's replies, "We are justified in changing to a new front. With the coming of the conference before us, we should meet with a smile and a warm handshake."

United States Representative.

Justice E. Finley Johnson of the Philippine Supreme Court, is expected to be appointed to represent the United States at the proposed International Commission of Judges to investigate the causes of the Shanghai riot on May 30, according to a cable from the State Department to Governor General Wood.

headline: REGULAR RUNS.
text:
STEAMBOAT COMPANY'S DEIERMINATION.

"HONAM" AND CANTON

The s.s. "Honam," which returned yesterday from Canton, was again unable to discharge its cargo there on account of inability to obtain lighters.

Passengers who went up from Hongkong were able to land, but few desirous of returning to Hongkong were able to elude the strike pickets and sampun owners at Canton have evidently been threatened with severe measures if they convey anyone to the ship. Thirty-five Chinese managed to give the pickets the slip and board the ship.

The Steambont Company have announced their determination to maintain a regular service between Hongkong and Canton.

Another sign of the gradual return to normal times is the announcement that the sale of cheap rice to relieve the poor will be discontinued by the Kwong Wah Hospital, Yaumati's leading Chinese institution of philanthropy.

According to the vernsacular papers, strict orders have been issued to police officers in regard to possession of toy platols. It is understood that the sale, manufacture or keeping will be subject to regulation.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE
text:
OVER 2,000 PASSENGERS HELD UP.

CAI'ETOWN EXPERIMENT.

The owners of the “Sophocls” decided as an experiment to test the strength of the men's feeling and ordered the vessel to depart, but the “Sophocles” returned shortly afterwards in consequence of the crew intimating sympathy with the strikers.

Two thousand passengers for Australia are held up at Cape town.

The Minister, Mr. Creswell, meets a delegation of strikers tomorrow.

Wellington, Sept. 6. 'Failing the strikers' acceptance of the shipowners' offer to return to work, the authorities have decided to prosecute for disregard of legal contracts.

headline: LABOUR'S AMBITIONS
text:
PROPOSALS FOR GIGANTIC ALLIANCE.

MOMENTOUS CONFERENCE.

Proposals for a gigantic Labour alliance coupled with shadows threatening to becloud the relationships of several big industries promise to provide a momentous session at the Trade Union Congress which has opened at Scarborough.

Mr. Swales, in his presidential address, referred to the increasing seriousness of the economic and social conditions of the past year and dwell on the soundness with which the Trade Union movement had emerged from a period of unparalleled crisis since 1920.

Mr. Swales urged employers who think the organised workers can be still further driven back to take warning therefrom. He declared the demonstration of the solidarity of the Trade Union movement in connection with the miners' struggle had given hope to the whole movement.

He drew attention to the amalgamation as shown by the fact of a 15 per cent. reduction in the number of separate unions in five years.

Mr. Swales demanded an extension of trade with Russia. He expressed sympathy with the workers' struggles in India and China and regretted that an international front had not yet been secured, though the differences of Amsterdam and Moscow were small.

Mr. Swales concluded by declaring that a new phase of the development which was worldwide had been entered. The next would probably be the last stage of revolt. He appealed to the workers to solidify the movements and to be prepared with machinery and men for the final struggle to destroy wage slavery.

Mr. Swales said the General Council had started an inquiry into labour conditions in Eastern countries, including China.

headline: AFRICAN STRIKE.
text:

headline: MAIZE SHIPS.
text:
The strikers have agreed with Colonel Creswell, the Labour Minister, that in order to prevent congestion of the maize export and consequent unemployment of dock labourers, maize vessels shall be taken from the jetties into the roadstead, provided a guarantee is given that the ships will not put to sea without the crews' consent.

The shipowners decline to give a general undertaking.

The strikers by arrangement with the Government ballotted regarding the sailing of the fruit ship "Roman Star." The ballot resulted in 432 to 352 votes against sailing.

headline: RUSSIAN LABOUR. / INDO-CHINA / STEAM NAVIGATION CO LTD.
text: British workers, who imagine that Russian labour conditions are ideal, will find a good deal to interest them in the report which Mr. Tomsky gave to the 14th Congress at Moscow of the Communist Party. Mr. Tomsky, who is chairman of the All-Russian Council of Trade Unions, says, for instance, that, in principle, strikes in State undertakings are prohibited. A strike in a proletarian State is a proof of some defect in the State machinery, or of the weakness of the trade unions, or of lack of education on the parts of the workers. The trade unions must do everything in their power to settle disputes in State undertakings by means of conciliation or arbitration, and at all costs to avoid strikes. There have recently been certain irregularities in the settlement of disputes. Instead of being settled by conciliation and arbitration, some of these disputes have been referred to the Communist party organisations. Such action impairs the authority of the regular institutions, makes non-party workers lose confidence in their union and in the impartiality of the decisions taken, and ends by embittering disputes and disorganising the whole labour movement. In private undertakings, or the other hand, any form of dispute is allowed; but a strike may be declared only in the event of the failure of conciliation and arbitration. In no case should the trade unions exercise any administrative pressure on the private employer, for this tends to weaken the worker's notion of the class struggle and the power of the trade union. The trade union should rather strengthen the authority of the Commissariat of Labour as an impartial arbitrator.

headline: Assassination.
text: The Continent is the cock-pit of Europe. They grow bitter weeds there, and the result is death and the thing that leads to death—war. As the number one Robot said—"Read History." Why certain parts of Europe should breed the pestilential trait of mind to be found in unholy and senseless anarchy no one seems to know. It may be that minds brood more deeply than in the colder clime of Britain where the motto might be said to be—"Be slow to anger." Why should there be a desire to "remove" Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the British Foreign Secretary? What object would be gained in taking away a life which it would be generally admitted, is and has been, stainless? There is no sensible answer to such a question. The present Government has seen fit to reverse its predecessor's arrangement with the Russian Soviet Government. It might be said that the electorate gave it a mandate to do so. It may be that certain elements in Russia see in this a just cause for "direct action." Such a line of thought is beyond understanding. That it exists on the Continent is obvious. That Governments are not able to guard against it has already been proved. All the more reason then why the persons of those who serve the nation so ably, conscientiously and well should be guarded with the utmost care; more especially when the exercise of their duties call them to "foreign parts."

headline: FRANCE AND MOROCCO.
text:
Although to-day's cables from Morocco report that the Riffs have "infiltrated" into the French zone, the position need not be viewed with any due alarm. Marshal Lyantey is confident he can deal with the trouble with the troops at his disposal. The intentions and dispositions of the French Government, there is every reason to believe, are as pacific towards the Riffians as they are conciliatory towards Spain, and considerate of her susceptibilities. France, it is true, maintains her legal interpretation of the Franco-Spanish Agreements of 1904 and 1912 as investing Spain with the duty, as well as the right, to control effectively the Moroccan zone entrusted to her protectorate, i.e., to ensure by a military occupation that no troubles shall occur within that zone such as might entail any danger to the adjoining French zone. Juridically, therefore, France would claim for herself the right to occupy militarily any areas evacuated by the Spanish army with resultant difficulties to the contiguous frontier regions of the French Protectorate.

But this claim, which is contested by Spain on the ground that the latter's Protectorate can be legitimately exercised without necessarily involving a complete military occupation (as a matter of fact, within the French zone the military frontier does not everywhere extend as far as the political frontier), is to be upheld, for the time being, rather on abstract than on practical grounds. headline: May Day:
text: It is not clear why the organised forces of Labour have selected the first day of May on which to celebrate their existence and to voice their grievances—fancied or real. The Morris pole is, presumably forsaken, and processions of drabness and speeches of spleen, take its place. London's labourists march to the Bulgarian Legation and protest against the alleged persecution of Bulgarian workers—a persecution which is denied. Moscow's "joy" is more militaristic than Labouristic. There the garrison is reviewed, 50 aeroplanes participate, the while members of the Government and Diplomatic Corps look on. Canton provides the humour, although it is stud and sorry stuff. "Down with foreign religion," and "Down with capitalism" are the cries, whilst there is a word for the "progressive Soviet." The Cantonese dearly love a procession. The one at Canton was three miles long. There is something pathetic about these processions—in London, Moscow and Canton. We do not seem to have progressed very far even in China with its boasted civilisation, when a three-mile long procession can give vent only to parrot like cries the purport of which, it seems very likely, at least one and half miles of the procession does not understand.

shire, and on this day even yet with some the method of proceeding is for some member of the household or family to go the first thing in the morning, with no thought of any particular rowan tree—rather, it might be said, till some rowan tree is fallen in with of which no previous knowledge had been possessed by the seeker. From this tree a supply of branches is taken, and (a different path homewards having been taken, by the strict observers, from that by which they went) on reaching home twigs are stuck over every door of every house in the homestead, and scrupulously left there until they fall out of themselves. A piece is also always borne about by many in their pockets or purses, as a prophylactic against witching. Not so very long since either the farmers used to have whipstocks of rowan tree wood—rowan tree-gads they were called, —and it was held that, thus supplied, they were safe against having their draught fixed, or their horses made restive by a witch. If ever a draught came to a standstill—there being in such cases no rowan tree-gad in the driver's hands, of course—then the nearest witchwood tree was resorted to, and a stick cut to flog the horses on with, to the discomfiture of the malevolent witch who had caused the stoppage.

headline: THE MODERN GIRL.
text:
A CONFIDENT REPLY TO HER CRITICS.

That the modern girl is not a distinct improvement on her mother was the timidly worded motion debated recently at the Forum Club. Yet the debate was interesting because the attack was opened by Lady Barrett, who certainly has a wide experience, and countered by the Hon. Emily Kinnaird, who perhaps has a wider and more understanding knowledge of the modern girls than any other woman in England because, verteran as she is, she will always be a girl of the day.

The modern girl, said Lady Barrett, has numberless advantages which her mother did not enjoy. She has an education that constantly moves to bring her into touch with real experience, her games bring her into competition with other girls, and with boys. She may have friendships with men free from emphasis of sex. She has a hundred different choices of work with adequate rewards and always the possibility of striking out some new line untouched before by man or woman. It was almost impossible to believe that she should not reach some higher level than the previous generation had reached, and, indeed, some of today's must arrive at places far beyond what any woman had yet reached.

But the very fact that the modern girl reaped the fruits that other women had toiled for placed her at a disadvantage, for it was effort that developed consciousness and strength. "Does not the girl of to-day," asked Lady Barrett, "luck vision and is she not therefore less keen, less dependable, less devoted to work as work, and is not her sense of values false?"

The Turkish refugees, numbering 390,000, have come chiefly from Greece in the exchange of populations, and about 79,000 of them are established in Eastern Thrace, while 64,000 have gone to Smyrna. These figures convey no impression to the average man of the mountainous mass of misery and wretchedness which they represent. It would be interesting to learn the number of refugees who have found a safe haven in Hongkong as a result of fleeing from Canton during political and militarist upheaval and who decided to remain here.

headline: Hongkong, Wednesday, May 27, 1925.
text:
Still no word comes over the cables as to the fate of Captain Ronald Amundsen, the famous Norwegian explorer, who has disappeared into the unknown North to reach the Pole by air. First to reach the South Pole and second to navigate the North-East Passage, Amundsen has been hoping to make this new undertaking the crowning achievement of his career. And indeed, unless the manifold perils prove too great, he will have accomplished a voyage fit to rank with the world's epic feats, for his plan has been described as the greatest venture into the unknown since Columbus set out from the shores of Spain.

Polar exploration has many heroic tales to tell—who will ever forget Scott's undying story of Shackleton's deathless man, but not since Andre, a Sweden engineer, tried to discover the North Pole twenty-five years ago by means of a specially constructed balloon, has such a daring plan as Amundsen's been tried. Striking right across the "Unknown Region," which Stefansson describes as "The Zone of Comparative Inaccessibility," Amundsen must, unless he is able to land, keep his adoption going steadily for eighteen hours. Accompanied by two plots—one a German army, a monitor and the other a Norwegian surgeon—has met out with enough gasoline for barry over two tons and there are also oil, food, cameras and scientific instruments. However, experts affirm that flying conditions in the Arctic are ideal in the summer time, and, we are told, in the latitude of Point Barrow the sun never sets between May 9 and August 4. Other advantages are the constancy of the prevailing north-easterly winds and the presence of large icefields which tend to keep the surface of the sea comparatively smooth.

To the Communist Party must be assigned the sensation of the moment. To have smuggled into Britain two of its most noted continental leaders to attend a Conference at Glasgow, in defiance of the Government's restriction, speaks itself of the strength of the movement, and the power and determination of those who control it. How this feat of smuggling has been done, will doubtless soon be revealed. That smuggling into Britain has been going on of Communists generally has been known for sometime. It is alleged that the whole weight of the second International has been transferred from Germany to England. Not only are the Bolsheviks sending their own countrymen to Britain, but they are pressing into their service people who arrive from America travelling with United States passports. It has been found that these people are Russians naturalised as United States subjects. The incident under review is perhaps the most direct challenge which has been made to British authority—an authority which distinctly ordered that no foreign Communist was to be allowed admittance to the country to attend the Glasgow Conference. The Communist peril is directed at undermining the Constitution of the British Empire — at all costs. These "costs" include red revolution which the heart and soul of the Empire detests and is determined to subdue. Nowhere under the sun is there a more just constitution than that under which British subjects live. There is freedom and liberty for all and right means of redressing known grievances. It is not likely that the present Government will sit down lightly in face of the challenge now issued to it. It may be childish to think that a Home Secretary in his own person can stop a British revolution by preventing the Communists of different countries from meeting; but it is not childish to believe that a Home Secretary with a free Government behind him—and better still a free people—will effectively take measures to stop any undermining of such a Constitution as the British people possess, by means of anarchy. It looks very much as if the British Communist Party at any rate has voluntarily committed suicide.

headline: Hongkong, Thursday, June 4, 1925.
text:
From all accounts the position in Shanghai is, if anything, worse. The student elements are still excited and frenzied, and therefore at present beyond the realm of reason and sense. For the first time the rioters have had resort to arms, and there is no saying at present where a very ugly situation will end. The one hopeful ray remains—that the Municipal authorities are determined not to give way to the frantic outburst of the irresponsible students, many of whom are still only in their teens. In that attitude the authorities will have the solid backing of all the foreign Powers, Soviet Russia, of course, excepted.

There can be no question of discussing “peace terms” until the students first of all return to their classes, and refrain from inciting the rioters to violence against the foreigners. Tolerably safe guesses can be made as to the real force behind the outbreak, but these are in a sense beside the point at the moment when hot-headed youth is running amok. The “North China Daily News” rightly sums up the position when it states that “there is only one way in which peace can be brought back and that it by the unconditional surrender of the students and other agitators.” Any middle course would be as dangerous as it would be futile. strued, and in the end do more harm than good to foreign interests. There cannot but be great inconvenience to foreign employers of labour whilst the trouble is acute. There will also be some embarrassment through scantier food supplies. But, in comparison with the vital issue at stake, these are mere details that must be cheerfully tolerated.

Ugly — and 'even' critical—though the situation be, nothing is to be gained by fanning the flames of passion amongst the Chinese in general. Once they are convinced that no parley is possible until the students return to their classes and the strikers to work, there is still a hope that wiser counsels will prevail before the anti-foreign ebullition spreads further.

Dinosaurs were reptiles which flourished in the Secondary Period—the middle of the three great divisions among which geologist distribute the fossil-bearing rocks. At a time when mammals were small and inoffensive, the dinosaurs were the dominant group of land animals, particularly in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods, the latter including the age when the chalk was deposited. They are divided into four groups. The first consisted of animals which walked on all fours and included the largest land animals ever known. Among these giants are Diplodoons, already referred to, and Gigantoosa, the principal object of the British Museum Expedition. The dinosaurs of the second group were remarkable for bearing a Balliff, formerly prevailed at Wenlock, in Whitsun week. It consisted of a man who wore a hair-cloth gown, and was called the balliff, a recorder, justices, and other municipal officers. These animals differed from the members of the other two groups in walking on their hind legs in the attitude of a kangaroo, no doubt making use of their well-developed tail as an aid to locomotion.

The most familiar of this section (which includes small dinosaurs) is the remarkable Iguanodon, first discovered in this country, but best known from the descriptions which have been published of the bones of about thirty skeleton found together at a depth of 1,000 feet during coal-mining operations at Bernissart, Belgium. The fourth of the main groups of dinosaurs included the carnivorous forms, which, no doubt, preyed, on their herbivorous relations. Most of them seem to have walked on their hind legs, and some of them, such as Tyrannosaurus, already mentioned, were of very large size.

headline: A DIRECT CHALLENGE.
text:
At the moment of writing there is a lull in the position in Shanghai so far as actual riots are concerned, the students concentrating their efforts on extending the strike. However well organised a simple strike movement may be, it is better than intermittent outbursts of frenzied madness, leading to bloodshed on both sides and to a bitterness of feeling that will take years to die out.

The latest Shanghai papers to hand to-day make it clear that the disorders are a direct challenge to the foreign government of Shanghai. That being so, it must still be open to doubt whether the students will really confine their future activities to extending the strikes. Time will tell. But there is this to be said in favour of the Municipal authorities, as pointed out by the "North China Daily News": "The fact that over a million Chinese are content to dwell under the rule of the Municipal Council, vastly preferring it to that of their own officials, is sufficient proof of the beneficence of that authority." And again, there is this to be remembered, in the words of the "Shanghai Times": "The interests of the Chinese merchant classes coincide with those of the foreigners, Peace and good government are essential. We cannot tolerate any movement toward that anarchy which prevails elsewhere in China. The foreign authorities have the support of responsible Chinese in this matter, and their duty could scarcely be clearer."

It is certainly to the influence of the responsible Chinese, that the Municipal Council in Shanghai must look for any betterment in the situations. A perusal of the Shanghai papers makes it clearer than ever that the riots of last Saturday were prearranged by the students at a time when the whole city was given over to its usual Saturday afternoon's sport. It is also demonstrated beyond doubt that whilst the Police exercised most admirable restraint in the face of the oncoming hordes of riofers, the outbreak would have led to even more disastrous and calamitous results had the order to fire not eventually been given. Amongst any other mob in any other place the Riot Act would have been read and the order to fire would have been given long before the Police were being driven headlong back to their station. Elsewhere than in an international settlement in a Chinese city, there would have been resort to firearms, as a means of defence, long before the rioters got so far out of hand as to endeavour to wrest the weapons from the Police—weapons given to them for the express purpose of maintaining law and order.

Then, added to the riots themselves, there was the broadcasting of inflammatory leaflets attacking the “Imperialism of Great Britain, the United States of America and Japan.” No nation with any sense of its dignity, and with due regard for the safety of its nationals, could tolerate for a moment an exhortation to “unite and defeat Imperialism.” Thus, there must be perfect agreement with the “Shanghai Times” when it declares that “we cannot regard this document as containing the vapourings of semi-educated youths which could well be passed over. These leaflets were part and parcel of a carefully laid scheme to challenge foreign control in Shanghai by stirring up animals against all foreigners.” It may be early to predict the result of any general inquiry into the “disturbances.” For the moment the attention of the Municipal authorities is tiller occupied with coping with the position as it stands to day. They are

as determined as ever to stand by their Treaty rights is what every sane man, Chinese or foreigner, fully expects. In the maintenance of that determination lies the only true solution of a very difficult problem.

Aviation Research.

Whilst the Empire was recently thrilled by the adventures of the R33, which broke away in a damaged state from her mooring mast, was blown 130 miles across Europe, and yet returned safely, it is apparent that there are two schools of thought in aviation. The “heavier than air” section is inclined to make capital out of the airship's misfortune. The fact is, however, that both the ship and the mooring mast are obsolete and only retained for experimental purposes. The Ministry declare that experience was gained as a result of the mishap that would not otherwise have been obtained. Although worked by a skeleton crew and at the mercy of the wind, owing to the fact that she was so damaged that the engineer did not dare to put on her cruising speed, the airship was able, with the aid of meteorological science, scientific positioning, and wireless communication, to circumvent the storm, to find a region of merely stiff breezes, and to await a favourable moment to run home. The real danger to an airship is that her fuel should become exhausted; then, sooner or later, she must land, which for a helpless craft is a most difficult task. The Air Ministry intend to persevere with the construction of airships. The R36 is to undertake a series of experimental voyages to Egypt and atmospheric exploration of the air route to India. The demand has arisen for more money for research, and a new training ship or two may be put into commission before long. A suggestion has been made in one quarter that a scheme should be drawn up under which some of the wartime airship personnel of all ranks and departments, who have now returned to civil life, should be induced to keep in partial training and made acquainted with new developments — forming, in fact, an Airship Reserve. For long distance journeys, the airship must remain supreme.

headline: SHANGHAPS - CRISIS.
text:
With the despatch from Peking of a Diplomatic Mission to Shanghai to examine the position on the spot, hopes are entertained of at least a temporary lull in the disturbances. The beginning of "discussions" always is regarded as a hopeful sign by those in the wrong. They set out to demand the impossible, in the expectation of exacting some concession which never would have been dreamt of before.

The only thing that may tend to upset an optimistic view of the position is the likelihood of outbreaks elsewhere throughout the country strengthening the irresponsible students in Shanghai. In that event, even the arrival on the scene of the Diplomatic Mission from Peking may not be attended by immediate beneficial results. So long as the Chinese Foreign Office takes for granted that the Police in the International Concessions are culpable in firing upon “unarmed students”—without pausing to enquire into the nature of the attacks upon the Police—half a dozen Diplomatic Missions will accomplish little. There is a time for everything, and the time for an enquiry into the part played by the Police has not yet arrived. It is obvious that the duty of the Chinese Government is to influence the students to return to their classes and the strikers to return to their work. Until that is done it cannot be expected that the foreigners will make the first move toward either compromise or settlement. To weaken in this respect would merely be the signal for more serious disturbances not

the Union of Chinese Associations in London have held a special meeting and solemnly adopted a resolution protesting against “the use of armed forces by interfering Powers to suppress the strike who shot down defenceless workers and students” and recording “full support” of the strikers.

The very wording of the resolution condemns those responsible for it. They have only received garbled and inspired versions of the origin of the disturbances, and read into these just what they were pleased to believe. They have taken their cue from the Chinese Foreign Office, which straight away also "protested" against the use of arms against the frenzied students, little knowing that those who had resort to arms were fighting with their back to the wall and only fired in self defence of their own lives and in the hope of saving the truculent Chinese themselves from a more terrible disaster. The members of the Union of Chinese Associations in London may know something about the traits of their compatriots in Shanghai, but obviously they can know as little of the actual cause of the outbreak as the natives of Timbuctoo. And even were they to be placed in possession of the facts, it seems too much to expect them to appraise these at their true worth and refrain at least from comment and protest until such time as the inevitable inquiry is made by an impartial tribunal.

Even if it be admitted, for the sake of argument, that the members of the Union of Chinese Associations in London have a certain right, by virtue of their nationality, to give expression to their views on the disturbances in Shanghai, what is to be said of the “sympathy” expressed by the International Labour Conference in Geneva? That conference comprises delegates of nearly sixty States, and although the Governments are entitled to send two delegates the representative organisations of workers may be expected to take greater advantage of their right to be represented by two delegates each. It is a labour affair pure and simple. What do workers' delegates from Sydney or Brussels know of the facts of the Shanghai disturbances? It is all very well for them to sit in conference twelve thousand miles away from the actual scene of the strife and adopt resolutions of “sympathy” with the Chinese workers—“sympathy,” be it noted that is impliedly a vote of censure on the foreign authorities in Shanghai.

headline: Sir Charles Eliot.
text: The Colony has had as its governors' soldiers of distinction and administrators of ability, but never, so far as we know, one whose shone as a man of letters equally as a diplomat. Should Sir Charles Eliot be appointed to this. For eastern "plum"—surely persimmon and li-chee would have been more appropriate—the Colony will gain in having a man whose towering height is "only exceeded by the many qualities he possesses. At the University it was not a pleasant thing to be "on the mat" before the Vice-Chancellor: there was a something about the ordeal which made you—if you were a somewhat wayward student—vow that the thing would never be repeated. The Vice-Chancellor exuded personality of a potent kind. Since those days Sir Charles has done a number of things entitling him to respect. There is his work in Siberia at a peculiarly vital time. There is also his ambassadorship at Tokyo, also during critical times. In the world of letters there is his recent monumental work on Buddhism. But behind everything is a distinguished career in many walks of life, entitling him to such a "plum" as Hongkong is now semi-officially described.

headline: THE CHINA OF THE PAST.
text:
Reviewing "The Chater Collection" of Pictures relating to China, Hongkong and Macao, 1655-1860, "The Times Literary Supplement" says that Mr. James Orange was happily inspired when he persuaded Sir Paul Chater to acquire this interesting collection of pictures, engravings and books relating to the early days of European traffics and discoveries in China, with a view to presenting it to the Colony of Hongkong. Like Hakluyt, Mr. Orange in compiling this collection set himself to bring to light antiquities smothered and buried in dark silence, and to preserve certain memorable exploits, of late years by our English nation achieved, from the greedy and devouring jaws of oblivion; to gather likewise, and as it were to incorporate into one body, and torn and scattered limbs of our ancient and late navigations by sea, our voyages by land, and traffics of merchandise by both.

To the fulfilment of this evidently congenital task he has brought a wide knowledge of the subject and the discriminating taste of m connoisseur; the result is a volume worthy of the object in view and of Sir Paul's munificent gift to the Crown Colony.

Of the 430 paintings and drawings in the Chater Collection, 261 are reproduced in colour and half-tone plates by the Nickeloid Electrotype Company's "Ultimatt" process. Mr. Orange has divided them, chronologically and geographically, into twelve sections, each separately catalogued and annotated with numerous quotations from the works of contemporary authors, the whole supplemented by biographical lists of the artists and authors represented, and an excellent Index. For the student the interest of these beautifully printed pictures is intensified by their association with important events in the early history of foreign intercourse with China; for the general reader, the elusive charm of the works of Chinnery, Allom, Alexander, Borget, and other artist adventurers in the Far East is emphasized by extracts, admirably selected, from the descriptive writings of Robert Fortune, George Wingrove, Cooke, Bernard (of the Nemesis), Laurence Oliphant, Robert Swinhoe, Sir George Staunton, and many other authors. Their combined effect is as of "magic dasements" opening on the whole fascinating panorama of life in China, as Englishmen knew and lived it, from the beginning of the seventeenth century to the middle of the nineteenth century.

Even those who reckon themselves fairly familiar with the early days of British diplomacy and trade in the Far East may find their memories refreshed by this delightful book concerning many things which, in China itself, have long since been devoured by the greedy jaws of chilion. How many inhabitants of the Treaty Ports to-day, remember anything of our four years' military occupation of Canton, from 1857 to 1861, or the

fact that, by order of the Chinese Government, no white women were ever allowed to visit that city before 1841? How many underpaid diplomatists at Peking are aware that Lord Macartney's allowances as "Ambassador to China" (1793) were £15,000 a year? How many of Hongkong's prosperous citizens know that at a critical moment, just before the birth of the Colony, the now insignificant island of Chusan seemed destined to become the local habitation and base of British power in the China Sea? Or, to go still farther back, how many of us remember anything of the hazardous adventures, which these pictures recall, that led the Portuguese to plant their outpost of empire at Macao and to establish their trade, early in the sixteenth century; in rivalry with that of the Japanese, at Ningpo?

To those who have lived in the East these pages, that bring to mind so vividly remembrance of things past, will naturally suggest the reflection that, on the whole, the instincts and impulses which determine the attitude and actions of the Chinese, in the ever-recurring phases of their history, are far more consistent and persistent than our own. He who compares, for instance, the attitude towards the Opium Question of China's present representatives at Geneva with that of Viceroy Yeh at Canton in 1857 cannot fail to be impressed by the continuity of unbroken traditions which underlies Chinese statecraft. As far back as 1834, just after the arrival of Lord Napier at Macao, we find the Cantonese officials "burning some chests of opium in public, but still, in private, continuing to connive at and foster the opium trade." The words and gestures of a Sun Yat-sen may appear to be very different from those of the Imperial Commissioner Lin, who ruled over Canton eighty odd years ago, but their ultimate purport: and the racemind behind them, remain unmistakably the same.

Another unfortunately neglected lesson which these pages teach—amply demonstrated by Parkes at Canton in 1857 and clear for him who runs to read today at Hongkong, Shanghai, and Tientsin—is that no people on earth are more ready than the Chinese to accept and support quiet and orderly government, even though it be administered by foreigners; furthermore (a truth of vital significance to day), that the force required to establish and maintain law and order, in any city or province, need not be large. Nevertheless, as it was in the days of Macartney so it is today—China's rulers and leaders prefer pleasant fictions to unpleasant realities, and are still ready to jeopardize life, property, and the future of their country in blind adherence to their unchanging devotion to "face-pidgin." Any wealthy philanthropist concerned with the welfare of China might do good work and sow rich seeds of wisdom by sending a copy of this book to each of her Tuchuns, and to those of her modern Intellectuals who hold forth so eloquently on the abolition of extra-territoriality.

headline: LASH. FOR THIEVES.
text:
No comment on a sentence on a convicted man can be just unless it takes into account, firstly, the adequacy of the punishment, and, secondly, its deterrent effect on others criminally disposed. The use of the “cat” for bag snatchers has not for the first time been the subject of comment here, but both the Bench and the Press have been agreed that there are times when even a comparatively trifling offence such as snatching hand-bags from ladies or earrings from Chinese children is perfectly justifiable.

Flogging may be objected to by those who profess more than an average proportion of humanitarianism as being brutal and degrading, but ethics and ethics alone cannot prevent an isolated case leading to an epidemic. Were the criminal records of the Colony of the last six months, to go no further back, to show a white sheet in respect of bag snatching from foreign ladies, there would naturally be not the slightest need to invoke the aid of the lush either as a punishment or as a deterrent. Unfortunately, cases of this kind have been fairly numerous. Some of the delinquents have escaped, for they have been cowardly enough to commit their offences in secluded parts of the Peak or, paradoxical though it may seem, in crowded streets which afford an all too easy means of escape amongst their own compatriots. To the coward and the bully nothing is ferred so much as a good flogging. One need not enter the realms of criminology to establish that. The most elementary student of human nature knows it to be a fact. It requires no labouring.

headline: HOW LONDON PROVIDES LIBRARIES.
text:
Although it seems a truism in this generation that libraries must play an important part in any good system of education it was not many years ago that they were neglected in London, writes the London correspondent of the "Christian Science Monitor." Now the London County Council, which controls public education within its area, has evolved a system for the distribution of books, which, if still imperfect, is a long way ahead of the pitiful libraries of half a century ago.

It must feed the 665,000 children in the elementary schools; 120,000 students who attend evening institutes, and 30,000 teachers.

Books for elementary education are drawn from four sources; the requisition list, the circulation scheme, the loan collection, and the education library. Up to a limit fixed by per capita allowances an elementary school may requisition books once a year. From a catalogue of many hundreds of books the head teacher selects his list.

Under the circulation scheme books are also requisitioned from the County Hall at Westminster, but they remain at the school for only six months. They are supplied in sets in order that pupils in class may each have a copy. Forty thousand sets are now in use, with a total number of volumes amounting to 2,000,000. They are not text-books, but standard works by famous authors. At the end of each half year the books are collected and sent to another school. The Wand of Mercury, the Rod of Healing and of Peace, in powerful mascot healing quarrels, driving away sickness, giving cloquence and youthfulness to its possessor. It was a very mystic talisman, and its influence was all for good. Apollo gave Mercury a staff surmounted by a plane cone-symbol of healing—with wings to represent the flight of man's thoughts to the higher things. The god added that whoever carried the rod would have a marvellous gift of speech and would be able to smooth away all quarrels by bending his hearers to his will. Armed with this magic wand, Mercury went forth and presently saw two serpents in deadly fight. He laid his rod between them and exerting his newly bestowed cloquence ended the bitter feud. From that time the serpents were added to the rod; they typify regeneration, that as a serpent casts its skin and emerges in a new and glittering form, so man may rid himself of his lower nature and rise to the heights, whither the mystic wings will bear him.

THE LOAN COLLECTION: The town collection of 65,000 volumes is kept at the County Hall. The majority are English classics. To these must be added 145,000 copies of port songs and other song music, and 25,000 copies of instrumental selections. This music library is in large demand by music classes at evening institutes. The Education Library contains reference books of value to teachers. By a system of circulation it enables each school to have a small reference library. Membership of this library has grown since the war. In 1012 there were 1,300 teachers using 6,700 books. To-day 12,000 teachers use 25,000 books. In higher education secondary

libraries are more individual. Governors of secondary schools may decide the amount of money which should be spent on books stored in a room that becomes the library. Though these schools do not benefit under the circulation scheme they may obtain from the Education Library books too expensive for them to buy. These books are retained for a year.

headline: IN FIGERN EDUCATION.
text:
Students in a training college buy their own textbooks. This means that the authorities usually have sufficient funds for keeping the library well stocked. One important college has a library of 8,000 volumes, and another of 7,000 Technical institutes form their own libraries for their own particular needs, a policy also pursued by the art schools.

The literary institutes form one of the most interesting branches of the council's work. They offer to men and women over 18 years of age the opportunity for general culture which will take them from the monotony of their daily work into an atmosphere that stirs their imagination and makes them feel the beauty of life as expressed in education.

Naturally, books play an important part in this education. The loan collection, with its 170,000 musical selections, is available to them. Arrangements are in progress by which the institutes will be able to obtain sets of books on different subjects on the lines of the circulating library that feeds the elementary schools. Thus, a set of books may be on the appreciation of music, or on economics, or, again, on architecture.

Finally an effort is being made to bring schools and public libraries in closer association with each other. This important work has in the past been spusiodic, depending on the initiative and energy of the librarian of a particular public library. Various schemes have been adopted in different areas. In some special facilities are given schools which wish to use books in class, in another district the librarian permits selected classes from schools to use the library for reference purposes. The children attend in school hours.

headline: Hongkong, Thursday, June 11, 1925.
text:
HAPHAZARD EDUCATION.

It is a striking commentary on the haphazard methods of education to find that during the past three years no fewer than 126 private schools have been registered for the purpose of teaching English to the Chinese, whilst as many as 103 were closed during the same period. The Chairman of the Education Board—the Director of Education—in reply to questions at yesterday's meeting of that body, stated that there is no fixed standard of qualification for the teachers of these schools, but the suitability of the teacher is always considered before registration of a school is granted. There is no doubt that in the absence of a sufficient number of Government schools, both for day and night tuition, a number of schools are established that are first and foremost out-and-out commercial ventures. All that matters is not the quality of the education imparted but the amount drawn in month by month in the shape of fees. The danger of some of these schools developing into centres of propaganda inimical to the Government is when it was disclosed yesterday

that the only Government supervision consists in a visit once a year—whether a surprise visit or not was not stated. It would be easy to imagine a teacher with the necessary qualifications for imparting a knowledge of English to Chinese of the artisan class being subsidised by, say, Bolshevik interests, running his school for six months, and then closing down after sufficient, mischief had been done by way of undermining Chinese workmen or servants. The insidious methods of propaganda introduced by the Bolsheviks make anything possible. It would not be like their paid agents here to miss such an obvious opportunity of spreading the cult of Bolsheviks under the cloak of an innocent night school for teaching English to practically inarticulate Chinese whose enthusiasm to learn English provides an ideal inlet for the inculcation of any kind of modern thought on any given subject. It is admitted that there are insufficient Government schools to cope with the demand. There is likewise a paucity of voluntary schools of the type associated with certain well-known religious bodies who keep the teachings of their particular creeds always in the background. There does seem a necessity for a tightening of the control of all other schools. Formal registration and informa visits once a year are surely quite inadequate to cope with the obvious requirements of the position. If there is a genuine demand for more schools, either for the teaching of English or fo imparting the elementary rudi ments common to a public school at Home, that demand must be met by the Government. If, for any good reason, it is unable to provide the necessary accommodation and the necessary staff, the Government must ensure that such inability is only temporary. As the greatest fault found with present day education is the tendency to turn out a super abundance of "half baked students, so the greatest danger in the Government, not being practically the sole dispenser of education lies in the grave risk it is running of a certain proportion of day and night scholars in private schools developing into firebrands and Communists. That risk is too great for any cheese paring policy of any British Government in respect of education. Let the Government-here think it over!

Likewise, it serves to heighten the grave suspicion that the origin of the present trouble can be traced back as far as the refusal of the British Government, on taking office, to have any truck with the Soviet on the lines proposed by its immediate Labour predecessor. An outbreak of the kind that occurred in Shanghai on May 30, attended by the broadcasting of Communistic and anti-foreign literature, is not planned in a day, nor in a month for that matter. It was only to be expected that the obvious remedy for the present troubles and a preventative for any recurrence would be pointed out in the House of Commons. That remedy lies in the attempt by the Treaty Powers to carry out the decisions of the Washington Conference in regard to co-operation in China. The assurance was also reiterated that the British Government is considering the best means of overcoming the difficulties arising largely from the absence of effective Government in China. It may be that the forthcoming conference on the internal tariff in China will afford an opportunity for removing such obstacles, dissipating the present atmosphere of mistrust, and inaugurating an

Thus, it will be conceded, the real solution lies not with the Powers but with China herself. Let her—as has been pointed out so often of late—put her own house in order. The co-operation of the Powers is there for the seeking!

headline: THE OBYIOUS REMEDY.
text:
In the House of Commons the Labour Party are to be thanked in no unstinted measure for their inquisitive spirit, regarding the Shanghai troubles, for, far from putting the British Government in a quandary, they are eliciting replies of a nature calculated to place the British position in its true light. It is not likely, of course, that translations of these statements by the leaders of the British Government, if circulated amongst the Chinese students, would accomplish very much by way of counter-propaganda just at present. But they must serve the most useful purpose of revealing to the industrial workers at Home, to the Chinese heads, and to foreigners outside China generally, the bona fides of Great Britain. From this point of view such official statements are doubly welcome, even though they are made in the nature of replies to questions in the House of Commons. Take the point made by Mr.

Take the point made by Mr. A. M. Samuel, Parliamentary Secretary to the Department of Overseas Trade, that no Chinese

headline: The Chinese Parent.
text: It would be interesting to have the views of the parents of the three or four hundred boys on the action of their offspring in deliberately absenting themselves from the Saiyingpun School on a matter of dispute over routine regulation. It is charitable to infer that either they do not understand their parental duties; are bewildered by the actions of their children, or evince no interest whatsoever in what they do. For years now it has been the desire of the young student to act as a tail wagging the dog. And often, it has to be admitted, the wagging has succeeded. The person whom one might expect to take an active interest in such matters—the male parent—is something like Brer Rabbit. He lies low and says nuffin'. Presumably if a boy is filial at home—or seems, so—nothing else matters. And yet K-Ung Fu-Tzu (Confucius) enjoined that in addition to such piety, a youth should be respectful abroad; earnest and truthful. He should overflow in love to all, but cultivate the friendship of the good. "Then, whatsoever of energy may be left to him, he should devote to the improvement of his mind." It may be that just as many Christians do not read their Bible, so many Chinese do not read the Master's words. This may account for the apparent "decline and fall of the Chinese parent." Which is greatly to be pitied.
