Government so strong morally that there is no limit to the good it might not accomplish for the provinces at present under its control, and—who shall say?—for the whole vast republic, if not by example only, perhaps also by actual sway. The vision is a rosy one, but it is by no means fanciful. Armed with the sinews of state in the shape of increased revenues and supported by the goodwill of the Powers, the Canton Government, possessing intellect and youthful vigour, would soon acquire the seasoned experience of settled administration, and would thus become the really stable and progressive government the country has been wanting so long. To make all this come true the Canton Government has only to muster up the courage or exert the force needed to end the illegal activities of the strike pickets. When it can do that its star will begin to rise. That Hongkong's star will also rise is an incidental which, so far from discouraging the Canton Government from seizing the present opportunity should spur it into yet quicker action, for apart from the benefit that would accrue to nearly a million Chinese in the Colony, the fact stands out as clearly as ever it did, that the prosperity of the two places goes hand in hand.

headline: CANTON AND THE STRIKE.
text: The Canton Government, in a reply to the Hongkong Government's statement regarding the strike negotiations, declares that it is "still animated by the same sincere desire to see an early settlement and is ready to continue its efforts to assist the two sides." This makes welcome hearing. Without the goodwill of the Canton Government, the Hongkong Government could hardly hope to achieve success as mediator. That much is certain. Whether the Canton Government is in a position to grant a settlement if it chose, as some aver, or whether its hands are largely tied owing to the strength of the strike pickets, as others maintain, must remain to some extent a matter for dispute. Perhaps the Canton Government does not itself know how it stands in this respect. Thus it is hard to judge the Canton Government's statement as an index to the prospects of an early settlement being reached. The chief hope in that regard is the golden opportunity the Canton Government now has of turning the present trouble to good account by having it settled out of hand. Such a success as that, besides bringing welcome relief to hundreds of thousands of Chinese who are suffering loss and hardship owing to the boycott, would establish the Canton Government in the eyes of the world in a way it could not otherwise hope to establish itself, save only by years of unremitting effort. Thus in a single stroke the Canton Government would make itself recognised by the Powers as the one governing body in China willing to combat disorder—for nobody can say the boycott is not grossly illegal—and strong enough to enforce its will. That would be a gesture such as few young governments have been able to make, and an opportunity which few would not seize with alacrity. For what would be the result? The very lifting of the boycott would give such an impetus to South China trade that the Canton Government would be able to enjoy revenues ten times greater than those it commands to day. Then the prestige that would accrue to both among the

"Must stop" would have a longer reign than it is likely to. Still we must thank Mr. D. G-M. Bernard for it if only for its indication that the Star Ferry Co., Ltd., is taking action in a matter that long since needed attention. Generally speaking, the ordinary person needs saving from himself, and this is shown in the disregard of ordinary precautions which is often noticed at the ferries. But are there not other things in Hongkong to which the phrase "must stop" might be applied? Not many perhaps, but still a few. The littering of the slippery sidewalks with such things as orange peel should certainly cease. The sight of little children in charge of edibles for sale, or being used as sympathy movers, or touters for cumshas, strikes the onlooker as something which might also cease. Avoiding trick cyclists going at full speed is now an almost common occurrence. There will be general agreement that "must stop" should apply to the misapplied ingenuity or bravado that finds outlet in riding furiously on two wheels. It needs no Board of Directors to remedy such a matter as this. At one time the sight of numbers of members of the Guild of Beggars was fairly common in the Colony, and their importunities were as aggressive as the odour which came from them. But the police indicated that the practice must stop, and the evil as a consequence has almost entirely disappeared. The same applies to the custom which at one time prevailed of infirmities—natural and otherwise being made open to the gaze of the passer-by. The decidedness of the two words gains them the attention they deserve. Government, public utility, companies, and even individuals might take them into consideration and see in what way they can be applied to any abuses which may exist. Apply it to the present situation. Let representative bodies from both sides get together and decide that the tendency to prolong the unnecessary must stop, and stop it soon will. A start might be made by the individual, with persistent Coueism repeating a must stop formula. The daily repetition will not be in vain. Differences will diminish, until one day the Colony awakes to find itself, buzzing about its activities and not caring about it of hurrying ferry-riders are imperilling their immortal souls in taking the risks some of them do.

headline: FIGHT FOR RUBBER
text:
In America the anti-British rubber faction has not been getting its own way. With typical frankness American agitators, including Mr. Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, himself, have been told by their own compatriots that, if the control of rubber cultivation outside American soil savours of commercial morality, Americans are not guiltless by controlling the production of other products when deemed necessary. Moreover, whilst rubber manufacturers are growing at the alleged effect of control on prices—which must surely hit the rubber industry in Britain as well—a timely exposure is made by American politicians and writers of the mammoth profits being made by American motor and tyre companies last year.

That the outlook for the plantation rubber industry is of the brightest cannot be denied. There is, or will be, a demand for all the rubber that can be grown both within and without the British Possessions. Without in any way impinging on British preserves there are ample acres for cultivation in other parts of the globe by Americans and all others who look with pardonable envy on the growth of the rubber planting industry in Malaya, Ceylon, Burma, and India.

One fact stands out in the rubber controversy in America, and that is the remarkable lack of enterprise on the part of usually enterprising Americans in not awakening to the vital importance of rubber cultivation years ago. The pioneers from America in this field can be counted on one hand, those from Britain, would require a whole volume to record their names. Hence the unrivalled position of the British to day. The more the demand grows for a thorough investigation into the profits made in America from rubber, the greater will be seen the hollowness and the sham of developing British rubber control. The dream of the public rubber cultivation has been outlawed by British Operations.

headline: HOME POLITICS.
text: Distance from the scene of events does not entirely eradicate an inborn interest in the Homeland's politics. Every infant born into this world is now something more than Gilbert's Liberal or little Conservative. Political thought has moved since "Iolanthe" first graced the boards. Labour has raised its head and there are such "by-products" as Communists. These divergences of thought, if it can be so regarded, should be hailed with a show of reason. Like religious denominations they are steering to the promised land, differing only in the methods employed in getting there. The country has had samples of Liberal, Labour and Conservative direction — loving them each with the durable consistency associated with the mind of the voter. We had a war coalition Government with Mr. Lloyd George at its head. That was "wrecked" and Mr. Stanley Baldwin enjoyed a brief innings. This was followed by a short-lived Labour regime, which in turn was followed by the present consolidated Conservative rule. The Labour party is the main opposition with the Liberal party a mere shadow of its former greatness. There are signs of dissension in the Liberal ranks—common to parties whose only work is to criticise—and it may soon be said of the Liberals—Ver is not party now! headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, Feb. 2, 1926.
text:
CANTON TAKING RISKS

Yesterday's local papers chronicled, quietly and briefly, the fact that Canton strike pickets, seeking to prevent the fish dealers putting their wares aboard, fired a number of shots at the river steamer "Kinshan." There is no doubt about the attack having been made—scarred and chipped paintwork tell the tale. This incident is fresh proof, if such were needed, that the boycott is not a patriotic movement organized by the Chinese people but is simply a piece of mischief-making carried on by lawless gangs to serve their own ends. Presumably the Canton Government knows its own business best, but quite apart from the ethical side of the matter, we think it is making a grave mistake in allowing these outrages to continue. For the moment we are not referring to the possible international trouble which might be invited by prolonged attacks on the trade of a friendly nation, but more to the internal dangers the Canton Government is likely to provoke by allowing the strike pickets to pursue their lawless course. Unless the situation is taken in hand without further delay one of two things is likely to happen. Either the strike pickets, growing in power and insolence, will challenge, not merely the authority, but perhaps the very existence of the Canton Government, or the long-suffering merchants and tradespeople, goaded beyond endurance, will seek their own remedy, or turn to the first

them relief. "The Canton Government" may feel that it can accept these risks without anxiety, but it would do well to remember that China, politically, is a land of sudden changes.

The dangers of the present position seem to us so patent and the promises of peace so alluring, that we quite fail to understand why the Canton Government does not suppress the strike pickets out of hand. This would be no betraying of labour to whom we are told the Canton Government feels so beholden. With the exception of the actual strike leaders, labour is suffering as much as anyone through the boycott and would be among the first to welcome relief.

There can be no middle course. There can be no mediation between the Hongkong Government and the Canton Strike Committee. There can be no waste of words respecting a settlement with an organisation that has avowed its desire—at the instigation of the Bolsheviks — if possible to ruin Hongkong. The first word and the last word must lie between the Hongkong Government on the one hand and with the Canton Government on the other hand. The sooner that fact sinks into the mind of the Canton Government the better it will be for all concerned.

The policy of the Hongkong Government has been determined. It "requires and expects the Canton Government to put an end to these illegalities." The next move lies with the Canton Government.

An opening for such a move seems likely to be presented to it on the initiative of the British Foreign Office. As the outcome of discussions between the Foreign Office and the China Committee—a new organisation formed in London at the end of January under the chairmanship of Lord Southborough—it is alleged that Sir Austen Chamberlain may send a Special Commissioner to South China to make a full report on the situation and attempt a settlement of the trade crisis. The appointment of a Special Commissioner, were such to be made; would only establish more firmly than ever the bonafides of the British to come to a fair and honourable settlement with the Canton Government. To-day Reuter denies the London newspaper report of the probable appointment of the Special Commissioner. Thus, again, let it be repeated, the next step lies with the Canton Government.

In the well-reasoned speech of His Excellency the Governor there is one important phrase that may be liable, in the numerous eulogies of his statement, to be overlooked: "Only the unlawful activities of the Canton Strike Committee, instigated by Bolshevist intrigue, prevent the resumption of normal relations between Hongkong and Canton on the old familiar footing. We expect and require the Canton Government to put an end to these illegalities." That statement is well worth emphasising. It is an echo of what the whole Colony has been saying for the last seven months. It is a true reflection of public opinion as reiterated in the columns of the local newspapers—the only outlet, save by the medium of public meetings, for the expression of the voice of the community.

"This nonsense must cease," said Sir Edward Stubbs at the very outset of the strike. "We expect and require the Canton Government to put an end to these illegalities," says Sir Cecil Clementi to-day. The Hongkong Government for its part is perfectly ready to negotiate a settlement, but it can obviously negate it with none other than the Canton Government itself. The Hongkong Government has not the vestige of control over the Canton Strike Committee.

headline: AN EXAMPLE
text:
It is not possible for many of us to found universities, or endow them, or even to direct their activities. One of these three things has been done by Dr. Lim Boon-keng and Hongkong at any rate should be particularly proud and interested in his achievement. The Cantonese, and the Chinese people generally should also be not a little interested in one of India's nationalities. For here is an example of a Chinese working in the true field of "Imperialism" without losing an lot of his love for his country and his people,ஜெய்க்கு, in the fact that he is a Chinese, and continuing

work among his own people for their moral and educational advancement Dr. Lim Boon-Keng gave up large business interests in the F.M.S. to devote himself to educational work and the glorious success at Amoy is the result The lighthouse description which he gave to our own Universit, may aptly be applied to the one which he directs. Dr. Lim's desire for his country is that it should become uplifted and thus help other countries. When the Chinese—Republic came it was natural that there should be many schools of thought. Communism was tried in China 2,000 years ago and proved a failure, the Doctor reminds us. "There were radicals and others all pulling in different directions, but it would not last, and he was confident the position would right itself." The opinions of such cultured Chinese must have great weight with those called upon to deal with the present chaos. Unfortunately not all those who have imbibed Western ideals and gained from Western education the best that it has to give are prepared to discuss, dispassionately or in spirit, of forbearance, or to face facts as they should be faced. It needs honesty, no less than courage to do as Dr. Lim has done—to acknowledge the benefits of a Western education and to apply those benefits to his own country. The world loves honesty. It hates the subterfuges of wordy arguments that obscures the real issues. Before it is too late, those who see no shame, and no sense of immorality in such a procedure, should consider what they are about. Let China "save face" by all means, but let the saving be done by means which will bring her honour and respect, and not those others for which she is deliberately asking.

headline: A Still Tongue.
text: Sir Cecil Clementi's speech in the Legislative Council last Thursday has naturally been the chief topic of comment in the Colony among all classes. Public opinion has been unanimous in supporting His Excellency's views regarding the boycott, but there has been some diversity concerning his remarks about a possible new strike. This diversity, let us hasten to add, does not relate to the duty of standing by the authorities loyally and steadfastly should fresh trouble break out — the Governor's confidence in that respect is not misplaced—but simply as to whether the workmen will again leave their posts. The "China Mail" agrees with Sir Cecil Clementi that the prospects of another strike are remote—the workmen would have to be incredibly foolish before they went out again after all that has happened during the past eight months—but there is of course no absolute guarantee that they will not once more succumb to intimidation. Here it is that a word of warning is needed. The more the community talks about a possible strike and the more it gives the impression it is expecting one to begin any moment, the easier it makes the task of the agitators from Canton. Therefore nobody can be too circumspect during the next few months, and the policy of every loyal citizen should be to discredit idle rumour and abstain from repeating gossip which may possibly help to create an atmosphere helpful to the Colony's enemies.

A Midnight an unusual experience, Companion and I wonder if any of your readers have had a similar one? It happened on my first night in the hotel that is up the hill above Penang. I was in black darkness with the knowledge that some big animal was in the room. With the alert mind of the suddenly awakened I knew the size of the animal by the distance from the floor of its two gleaming eyes. I also knew that it was something from the jungle that had somehow strayed on to my balcony, and that it had got lost in my room and was waiting for the dawn to find its way out. But, being tired and longing for more of the delicious sound sleep of the East. I tucked in my mosquito curtains, and knew nothing more until the movements of the animal again awakened me.

This happened three or four times, and when I finally awoke in broad daylight I was, of course, alone. The house boy told me that from the traces a musang, a species of wild cat, had been my companion.

headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, February 9, 1926 / OUR VOLUNTEERS.
text: His Excellency the Governor did the cause of the local Volunteers a good turn yesterday evening when he carried out an inspection of the Corps and afterward delivered a brief but telling address. The days for Volunteer duty and the Volunteer spirit are far from past. Wherever he may be situated it is the first duty of an able-bodied citizen to offer his services for the defence of his own town or port or Colony. It is one of the finest forms of insurance for the preservation of the community's tranquillity and peace of mind. Volunteering duties, however, cannot be learned at one drill or even in one year. There must be constant training for any undertaking that may arise, otherwise the whole aim of the movement may be destroyed when the call comes for something more than pleasant parades on the drill ground or enjoyable practices at the rifle range. Moreover, in a floating population such as Hongkong it would be non-sensical to expect the strength of the Corps to be maintained year in and year out at a given ratio. There is always a demand for re-cruits, and just because of that demand and because the service is voluntary, the Corps must be made as attractive as possible for our young manhood. It was only to be expected that His Excellency the Governor would dwell on that side of local Volunteering arising out of the anti-British boycott. It is common knowledge that the mobilisation of the Corps last June had an excellent moral effect, and during the period of "carrying arms" our citizen soldiers earned the gratitude and pratise of the entire community. To get work well done voluntarily is often the precursor of a request for yet more. headline: VOLUNTEER CORPS
text:
With four hundred and thirty on parade, the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps marched from Headquarters to Murray parade ground yesterday evening for the annual inspection by the Governor.

Lining the banks and in the assembly in the pavilion on the parade ground were friends and the generally interested public. The Corps was drawn up in companies forming a hollow square, the Artillery, Machine guns, Armoured Car section (together with the mobile column), being at the northern end the Scottish and Reserves at the southern, the Infantry and Engineers at the eastern and the saluting point at the western. The Corps was called to attention when H.E. the Governor, accompanied by His Excellency the General, Major-General C.C. Luard, alde-de-camps and Fun-jabis officers, entered the ground promptly at 5.45, the royal salute being given with the Corps at the "present" when the saluting point was reached. H.E. the Governor in the course of his inspection was accompanied from front to rear of each company by the respective platoon and company officers, exchanging

The march past, which followed, was most impressive, particularly at the saluting point where company after company swung past, nothing being heard but the skirt of the pibroch and the drums, the steady tramp of the marchers and the orders for marching acknowledgment when the actual point was reached by the leading files. With the Corps drawn, up in close order, His Excellency, an impressive figure in levee dress, addressed them as follows, his words being plainly audible to all: — Officers, N.C.O.'s and Men of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps, in addressing you my mind instinctively travels back to the days when I myself stood in your ranks as a private in what was then known as "A Machine Gun Company". A great impetus had at that time been given to volunteering, because owing to disturbances which occurred when the New Territory first came under British rule the Volunteer Defence Corps was mobilized. To-day the call for volunteers is even more imperative because of the anti-British boycott in which, for no fault of curs, we find ourselves involved, and I am glad to see so fine a muster on parade. I congratulate you all on your soldierly bearing and I desire especially to compliment the newly formed Medical Section, a unit of great value to the Hongkong garrison. It is most reassuring to see the civil population volunteering in such numbers and with such efficiency for military duty in connection with the defence of the Colony and I thank you for your services and for the splendid spirit in which they are offered.
The Soviet Embassy says that the blood transfusion with which Mr. Krassin (Soviet Ambassador-elect to Great Britain) is being treated is producing the desired effect, but a long rest is necessary.

headline: A FOOL'S VIEW.
text:
Signor Mussolini trailing his coat is not an 'edifying spectacle. Some day, some one will stand on it, and the consequent rent will be great. Let not this obscure the saner side of Italian politics or desires. There is a story that Italy was considering suggesting to the League of Nations that certain cities be considered as cosmopolitan monuments of art, and as such be declared immune from bombing attack in war. Italy would present as such cities Venice, which suffered the loss of historical edifices and frescoes by Titian and Trepolo in the late war, Florence, Pisa and Rome. Here is a sensible suggestion. It should appeal to every art lover, every student of history, every admirer of the ancient and the beautiful. If adopted, the idea would seriously affect the practice of war. In war your object is to do as much damage and destruction as possible. The chasteness — if we may so describe it— of our own immaculate City Hall would have no effect or appeal on an invader. It would probably go. St. Paul's Cathedral, the Abbey, and other historical monuments also would disappear in the application of a programme of frightfulness. The last war demonstrated that and there is no need to enlarge on it. The suggestion is not likely to have a universal appeal. Florence is a small town packed with art treasures, while Paris is a great city with quite as much to arouse the reverence of the art lover. If one is given immunity, so should the other. If the plan for granting immunity to some is adopted, it is likely to spread immensably—and war-makers would not desire that. Common sense is not usually allied with war. Petrarch illustrates the way in which the wise ones regard war. "A fool in Florence, seeing troops issuing from the city asked why all those movements. Don't you know," he was answered, "that war has been declared on Pisa? But said the fool, will not

How can you talk of peace? O fool, since the war is now beginning?

None the less, said the fool, peace must return some day. Well, no war is eternal; there will be peace some day, but now its war.

"Since we must needs come to that," said the fool, "why would you not make peace just now, before beginning the war?" Which proves that even a fool can be wise.

headline: AWAITING A NEW CHINA.
text: On a former occasion the opportunity was taken in this paper to single out for comment some pertinent utterances by Mr. Silas H. Strawn, the American delegate to the Conferences on Tariff and Extraterritoriality — utterances that rise far above the popular conception of representative American opinions on Chinese topics. Less than a month ago Mr. Strawn delivered a striking address to the students of Tsing Hua College, Peking, in the course of which he spoke with the engaging frankness characteristic of his countrymen. His words formed excellent propaganda material in every sense of the term. He told his hearers, for instance, that he has "thus far seen no convincing evidence that China's present-day troubles are in any degree attributable to the so-called unequal Treaties or to the Imperialistic attitude of the foreign Powers". On the contrary, Mr. Strawn stated that "the evidence seems to be overwhelming that the troubles of China are internal rather than external, and that unequal Treaties, extraterritoriality, tariff autonomy, and Imperialism are political slogans which are availed of by the agitators to excite the people of China into a frenzy of criticism and unrest." Tactfully, Mr. Strawn proceeded to warn the students against accepting any of these slogans without a most careful study of the facts, and next referred to the part that America is prepared to play, quoting the U.S. Secretary of State's Note to the Chinese Foreign Office on September 8, 1925, which expressed a desire to assist China to realise her aspiration, but emphasised the necessity of giving concrete evidence of China's ability and willingness to enforce respect for the safety of foreign lives and property and to suppress disorders and anti-foreign activation which embittens

headline: PIRATES TO DIE
text:
FOUR DEATH SENTENCES:

Shanghai Feb. 10.

The French mixed Cour pronounced sentence on the eight Chinese who were charged with having taken part in the piracy of the C. N. s.s. "Tungchow" at the end of last year.

The remaining four were hand- ed over to be dealt with by the Chinese authorities and outlawed from the Concession. It will be recalled that these eight men were arrested on board the O.N.S.S. "Soochow," on in- formation received by the French police that members of the gang were returning to Shanghai to com- mit another atrocious crime. Four of them were identified in Court by Mr. Nisbet first officer of the "Tungchow," and Mr. Scott, the second officer. Several of the pass- engers in Tientsin, to whom photographs of the prisoners were sent, also recognised accused. Their evidence, sent by post, was accepted by the Court.

The prisoners' defence was complete denial that they were on board the pirated vessel. Four of them pleaded that they were in Waichow at the time. Those who put forward this plea declared that they had been officers in the anti-Bolshevik forces and had been reduced to poverty.

M. du Pac de Marsoulies, who with Mr. A. E. Seddon prosecuted on behalf of the "Tungchow's" owners, the China Navigation Co., after describing the piracy, said that four of the men had been identified by two of the officers and several passengers. In the case of the other four they had an allib. Yet they all returned to Shanghai. In the same vessel and embarked at the same place. Waichow, from which four came, was well known to the Court as a nest of pirates.

headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text: Quiet and featureless may best describe the happenings of the past week. Locally, the Chinese New Year celebrations have been indulged in, giving food for thought as to how many similar festivals will dome and go before chaos yields place to order in China. The holidays associated with the Chinese New Year passed equally quietly, only the interport golf fixtures, and the Fanling Hunt Club steeplechase meeting serving to break the motonony the while our local footballers were losing the big interport game in Shanghai by the narrow margin of a goal and winning a secondary encounter by five goals to nil. Socially, the interport golfers' dinner and a dancing display by Miss Daisy O'Keefe's pupils aroused a certain amount of interest and enthusiasm, both functions being tempered by the regret felt at the news of the passing away in London of Mr. D. K. Blair, whose activities whilst in the Colony earned for him universal admiration and appreciation. In other respects all that has occurred to "mark the calendar" has been another daring burglary in the heart of the city. Altogether, the week, as indicated, would have been more or less flat, stale, and profitless but for one redeeming feature—the statement of His Excellency the Governor at the Engineers' dinner respecting the determined attempts made by the Canton Strike Committee to persuade the members of the Chinese Engineering Guild to "down tools." As His Excellency remarked, the Guild, in refusing to obey the behests of Canton, had set a fine example which others had followed. Chinese New Year had well begun, and the victory over the Canton Strike Committee was complete.

Outside the Colony, pride of place may be given to the acceptance by the House of Commons of the Treaty with Irak. Great Britain's case was ably presented by the Secretary of State for the Dominions and the Colonies (Mr. L. M. S. Amery). He literally pulled to pieces the Labour amendment, the adoption of which, he declared, would mean that "we should make ourselves ridiculous in the eyes of the League of Nations," contemptible in the eyes of the Turks, and odious in the eyes of the people of Irak whom we should have, betrayed." No less interesting in this connection was Sir Austen Chamberlain's disclosure of his refusal, at Turkish bidding in March of last year, to barter away Irak's welfare to British capitalists—thus giving the lie to the Labourite allegations that British policy in Irak had been solely actuated by sordid oil concessions.

Statesmen and politicians of all nations interested in the League have been freely expressing their views during the week on the extension or otherwise of the League Council as soon as Germany's application for admission is granted. The consensus of opinion is that, for the moment, at any rate, any extension of the membership of the Council, beyond Germany, would be inopportunement. The most reasoned pronouncement on the subject comes from that veteran South African statesman, General Smuts, who states that for Germany "Locarrio means the voluntary, deliberate, and final renunciation of Alsace-Lorraine. Is this nothing to France? Is this to be lightly treated, and are others, then, to be asked to guarantee the frontiers of France in the future? Surely the situation between Germany and France specially calls for honourable dealings and a scrupulous regard of all the proprieties. Locamo began as a gentleman's business. Let it be completed in that spirit." Another event worth recording is the completion of the flight from London to Capetown by Mr. Alan Cobham — an accomplishment that again brings British progress in the realm of aviation well to the fore. As a minor occurrence may be mentioned the end of the marine wireless operators' strike at Home, which has been in progress since last November. The employees have resumed duty at a reduced rate of pay, but all their demands are to be made the subject of negotiations and, failing these, arbitration. Next there comes the news of the Soviet negotiations with Austria for minitions and explosives, including the whole equipment of the Vienna, arsenal and the Danube boat building works at Fischamand. If this report be correct and the negotiations succeed, the Powers may well keep their

eye' on the Soviet and her intentions toward her neighbours in the not very distant future. Finally, the franc has fallen to a new low level owing to the financial deadlock and the fears of M. Briand's Cabinet being wrecked.

For several days before Chinese New Year determined attempts were made by the Canton Strike Committee to persuade the members of the guild to down tools. They refused to do so and behaved with sound common sense.

Chinese labour was deserving of special praise for their courage in spite of and in face of attempts of threats and intimidation. Those responsible had been taught the worthlessness of Bolshevik propaganda.

The Guild had set a fine example which others had followed. Chinese New Year had now well begun and the victory over the Canton Strike Committee was complete. He hoped that this marked the beginning of the end of the trouble which through no fault of ours we had been involved in. It was only right that the engineering and shipbuilding guilds should have shown the way. Mr. J. Ormiston proposed the toast of the visitors and coupled with it the name of Mr. Reid.

The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, *replying, said it had been stated that the shipbuilding and engineering industries were the life blood of the Colony. From personal observations during his time in the Colony he had seen, in 25 years, ship after ship launched which succeeded each other with improvement upon improvement, until some of the recent ones had equalled ships which could be made in any part of the world.

He would not hesitate to prophesy that the greatest future of the Colony was still to come, and that the present circumstances would quickly die awny. The present position, due to circumstances over which we had no control, was merely a passing one.

He believed Hongkong was destined to be greater in the next ten years than anyone could dream of. Ships were being built beyond contracts, and this was due to the fact that the workmen devoted themselves to the defeat of the conditions with which they had to battle.

There had been ships launched from both yards which surpassed ships ever built in the history of the Colony. He did not speak as an expert, but he believed the difficulties through which we were passing, would be of a very short duration, and that permanent progress had not been interfered with and that the principles which had made the Colony great would make it greater still.

Sir.—It is a matter of great regret to me, as the person who aroused John Beall's wrath, that he should have taken my comments on his remarkable experience of what he terms Eastern Magic, so much to heart. Perhaps I was carried away by my great interest in the little I know of his remarkable experience in connection with his friend All.

I do feel that a man who has gone through what John Beal has, should give these experiences to the Public—particularly as some of these are known to many people in the Colony, in a more or less garbled version. It is hardly fair to the Public to lift the veil so little—as John Beal does, and then refuse to proceed any further, thus leaving the Public guessing.

At the risk of rousing his wrath again I feel bound to re-count the little I know of this episode; in the hope that John Beal himself will realise the interest aroused by his experiences, and will consent to give them in full.

John Beal states that "by means unfathomable by our material philosophy" he was taken back to the time as mentioned in my previous communication and actually caught the train which ten years previously he had missed. As a result of catching his train, it is stated that perfectly natural events led him to some Eastern country where he assumed, or arrogated to himself, the position of an Eastern Potentate. It is at this point that the story trails off into speculations which only John Beal himself can deal with.

To the every-day man the suggestions of what happened in these circumstances are too fantastic to be credible, and he needs authoritative guidance from the man who has actually been through them before he can ever begin to conceive that such happenings could ever have taken place.

It seems therefore, that one is perfectly justified in making an appeal to John Beal to come out into the open to recount to a sceptical public just exactly what his experiences were. Everybody is an “earnest enquirer into these esoteric questions” therefore everyone is entitled to request John Beal “to enlarge on my experiences.” Yours, etc., THE ORIGINAL CORRESPONDENT

headline: LITERATURE IN SCHOOLS.
text:
Ever since the school began to take modern languages seriously there has been searching of heart among the pedagogues as to what French and German books should be read in class. It was not unnecessary. Some of us (says, the "Daily Telegraph") can remember being set down to volumes of elegant extracts from authors whose works we have never met since. There were, when Plancus was Consul, schools in which certain innocuous tales of the late M. Zola were chosen by an inscrutable Providence as the best introduction to French literature. Stalky and his young friends, it is recorded, had to wander through the sands of the "Roman d'un Jeune Homme Pauvre." Many generations since Major Pendennis was a child have been fed upon the edifying pages of "Télémaque." In the learning of German the works of Schiller, verse and prose, used to loom so large that he seemed to be the only German author. They have changed all that, or most of it, but even yet the headmasters cannot rest and be thankful Mr. H. Nicholson has been telling their assembled Conference that much of the stuff which is being read in modern languages is merely amusing and of no high literary value. He demands that every book chosen should be first rate; "not only should it be good literature, but it should deal with the history, art, and social conditions of the country whose language they were studying." This is hard saying. What is "first rate?" The world has agreed to consider certain things

in the grand style, the "Inferno," for instance, and "King Lear," as the supreme achievement of the human mind in literature. But it is not every language which has an Eschylus, a Dante, a Shakespeare. Perhaps Mr. Nicholson asks only that whatever is read should be first rate of its kind. This is in itself a sound and sufficiently practical principle. But we do not know how to reconcile it with the condition that the book must deal with "history, art, and social conditions." This would let in almost any good novel, but seems to exclude most of the best poetry. Whether Ronsard is writing a ballad or Racine a tragedy, their verses have nothing to say about social conditions or history, or any art but their own. There are, of course, schemes of education which would condemn such poetry. Dr. Arnold never could understand why people wanted to read poems the subjects of which seemed to him undignified. But though a schoolmaster must in the nature of things act on the assumption that he is always right, he had better not erect his private taste into a universal law. The most difficult problems in the choice of foreign books for class reading are not in excluding whatever is not valuable. The riches of those modern languages which are taught in schools are ample. But to choose such books as will rouse and stimulate children's interest in reading, while providing such mental exercise and discipline as their minds need and a store of knowledge and thoughts which will endure—this is none too easy in a world of unequal brains.

headline: WELCOME. RELIEF. / HELP FOR BRITISH SEA OFFICERS
text:
EFFECT OF BOYCOTT

The following, posted on the Harbour Office notice board, speak for itself:—

It has been brought to the notice of Government that, owing to the strike and boycott, certain officers of the British mercantile marine have been greatly reduced in circumstances.

Government has therefore decided to afford assistance in reasonable cases, either in the form of a loan or relief as may be considered to be the most desirable. Applicants should communicate in writing with the Harbour Master, such letters to reach the Harbour Office not later than noon on Tuesday, and will be required to state their cases and produce their papers before a Committee at 2.30 p.m. on the following Thursday. The Committee will sit weekly and consider applications received during the previous week.

Amongst the events of the week ending to-day two stand out as of paramount importance locally—the Canton Customs imbroglio and the annual meeting to-day of the Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corporation. The pros and cons of the Canton Customs inciden have been fully threshed out since the announcement last Monday of the Commissioner of Customs in Canton not to issue further permits for the loading and unloading of cargo until such time as the armed boycott pickets had returned cargo seized in contravention of the Customs regulations. The dispute could only have one possible ending. The authority of the Chinese Maritime Customs has been upheld, and guarantees have been given by the Canton Government against future interference with the functioning of the Customs by the boycott pickets. Incidentally, it is worthy of note that when it was really up against a trial of strength the Canton Government asserted itself at long last and put the boycott pickets in their place. What has been done in regard to the Customs incident can likewise be done respecting the ending of the strike and the boycott if the Canton Government would only evince the slightest desire to govern the pickets instead of being governed by them. By the business community of the Colony the annual meeting of “the Bank” holds a place second to none in its degree of importance. With the prosperity of the Bank is interwoven the prosperity of the whole of the Far East. The Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corporation is the barometer of trade and commerce; the Chairman's review of the part and present position is always an able exposition, eagerly awaited and eagerly read by shareholders and non-shareholders not only in Hongkong but in every centre of British trade in the Orient. At the moment of writing

we have not naturally the Chairman's speech before us, but that will appear as supplement to our second edition this afternoon.

Affecting a large section of the community a resolution was carried in the Legislative Council yesterday by which relief in the shape of rebates of rates will be granted to owners of tenement houses that have been partly or wholly vacant. This is not the kind of legislation that can be termed "hasty." A request for such relief was made several months ago, but the Government has waited, before acting, until it was satisfied that a prima facie case had been made out by those owners on whom the recent overbuilding of tenements and the exodus of Chinese from the Colony pressed hardly. In Empire matters interest is attached to the Air Estimates submitted in the House of Commons by the Minister for Air, Sir Samuel Hoare. With pardonable pride he pointed to the British Air Force as the most efficient in the world, and he looked forward to making the British a "people of the air." Equally vital was his reference to the development of the Empire's airways and to the finding of markets abroad for British aircraft machinery.

Once again the subject of the Council of the League of Nations has been kept well to the fore. China is the latest spoken of as demanding a seat on the Council should any extensions be made additional to the admission of Germany. Sir Austen Chamberlain, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, appears to have drawn a hornet's nest over him by a striking speech at Birmingham in which he enunciated the theory that, even although Germany were elected on the Council, there is absolutely nothing against the Council being still further enlarged by the admission of other Powers. This is no new contention, for it was adumbrated upon in a British wireless service message a few weeks ago—at a moment, too, when many considered that British policy would be found to be opposed to any extension of the Council's membership at present beyond Germany.

headline: MARINE INQUIRY. DOUBLE STRANDING IN HAINAN STRAITS.
text:
After our report had closed yesterday of the Marine Inquiry into the stranding of the s.s. "Hunan" and "Kweiyang" Captain W.G. McKenzie of the first-named ship continued his evidence.

The "Hunan" grounded on February 1. On February 8 the "Kweiyang" anchored two miles away to give assistance. Cargo was jettisoned on February 6 when the water on the starboard was 16 feet and 22 feet on the port. Witness said that the stranding was due to striking a sunken wreck or other submerged object. The bottom appeared to be of sand or gravel.

Mr. O. G. Jones (2nd officer, "Hunan") gave corroborative evidence.

Captain D. H. Martin of the "Kwelyang" said that he had been through the Hainan Straits 50 times since returning from War service. He described in detail how his ship ran aground on February 8 in trying to tow the "Hunen" off Cargo was also jettisoned from his ship. Mr. A. McDonald (chief officer of the "Kwelyang"), also gave evidence and the hearing was adjourned till this morning. COBHAM'S FLIGHT. (Reuter's Service.) Capetown, Feb. 26. Alan Cobham has started on his return flight to England. A further shortage in supplies has necessitated water restrictions in Kowloon as from Monday when the public made will be turned on during hours mentioned in an advertisement.

headline: The Chieftain's Speech
text:
It is a great pleasure to us to entertain our friends of other nationalities on festive occasions of this sort, said the chieftain, and I think it is a good thing for you to be with us at these times. It gives you an opportunity of seeing for yourselves how truly modest we really are. We as Scots, fully realise that all men are equal and if there are times when down in the bottom of our hearts we are a little more than equal it is only at a time like this that you have the opportunity of seeing how strenuously we strive to disguise this fact from the world. (Applause and laughter).

After thanking the committees for their hard work in co-operating in the arrangements for the Ball, the Chieftain said that they had met to do honour to the memory of the patron. Saint of Scotland.

Much of St. Andrew's life-was surrounded by legend but it was known that he was a heroic man who suffered death rather than betray principles which appeared to him as true and the spirit which inspired him was the spirit which had inspired the lives of those whose names adorned the pages of Scottish history.

I believe thoroughly in celebrating these national festivals, or national memorials if you wish, said the Chieftain, to hand down to our children and our children's children our glorious traditions and to keep alive the spirit which has made Scotland what she is, and has given her her place in the Empire and in the world.

In conclusion, the Chieftain again expressed to Their Excellencies and the other guests the great pleasure the Society felt in welcoming them and reminding them that the history of Scotland was now and had been for all time, one with the history of the British Empire. “Hark the pibroch's martial strain, Ca's the Clan to Lothian Plain, Scotland has her King again, Welcome Royal Geordie.” (Applause). The haggis was played into the dining hall with all the honours.

Local Insurance Associations notify that during race-days, offices will be open till noon. The Stock Exchange will be closed during the four days. Mr A, Brearley, the sub-manager of the Chartered Bank of India, Australia and China, has returned to the Colony and will relieve the present acting sub-manager, Mr. N. J. Austen, who is going on home leave next month. Although it is partly correct to say that the Chinese waitress in Hongkong is a “product” of the strike—and the trouble is to all intents and purposes not over—it seems that lady attendants are already losing favour.

A few years ago, some enterprising people brought down a number of teashop girls from Canton but the scheme never took shape. After about a month or so of the strike, local restaurants which had lost their staffs obtained permission to employ women and girls instead. It was not long before practically every teahouse, middle-class restaurant, and Chinese cafe had a waitress or two. Really capable girls brought an immense patronage with the result that there was keen competition for services. Very good wages were paid but with the advent of the more genteel domestics into the business, rates began to be cut.

To-day there are about 140 establishments in Hongkong which find work for about 600 waitresses (in addition to the male staffs).

Long before China New Year, a rumour went round that the authorities would forbid the employment of waitresses as nearly all the strikers had returned and there was no shortage. Such did not come to pass. Other events followed and it has now been announced that a number of Wanchai teahouses have mutually agreed to save trouble and out down expense by dispensing with their female employees.

Wages ranged from $1 to $3 a day, in addition to tips (nothing found, on fairly long hours, but on very light work). It is difficult to say exactly what class of girl has been attracted but the average income would exceed that of professions in which the members have to go through a course of systematic training.

Practically every day of the week sees a skit or two in the vernacular papers. It may be that the Chinese temperament can only look on the waitress askance. Generally speaking, no concession has been made that Oriental womenfolk will one day compete with the sterner sex for work.

However, other reasons have led to the thin end of the wedge being inserted at Wanchai. There was a case, if I remember rightly, at which some sordid facts were brought out about a waitress who had left her husband some years ago. It was not her return that the man sought so much, as she openly said that he was ugly. Rather, he may have persisted in his attentions as he knew that his erring spouse was in funds and therefore in a position to buy him off. Ultimately, it seems, rowdies were introduced by both sides, scrap followed and the police were called in. This sort of thing was of no use to the master of the teahouse.

Then again members of the local underworld have attempted to prey on the earnings of waitresses. Threats were sent and the poor girls were induced to join some secret society which would accord her full protection—at a fee. She had done nothing wrong beyond having found lucrative employment. To make her pay rather than lose her situation, the rogues would assemble at her shop at the busiest hour, bay a cup of tea each (thereby spending the smallest amount of money possible) and keep up a barrage of small talk while prospective customers were kept out. This would get a waitress into bad favour with her employer as it would be made out that the roughnecks were her personal friends.

Many other similar instances could be chronicled but they are of similar nature. Wanchai has taken the lead but others have not followed suit. One teahouse in Queen's Road Central is still doing an enormous turnover because it has the biggest and prettiest staff of waitresses. There, it is still possible to turn round and say the Chinese equivalent of "Miss," feeling certain that one's request will be answered by a smile. The favourite slang term for tipping (to tremble the hand) is also believed to have originated in that shop.

Notice has been given by the Canton Harbour office that, owing to breakdown of mechanism, the fog gun at Sampanchoy lighthouse is out of commission. Pending repairs, a bell will be sounded at intervals of two minutes during fog or this weather. The bell being of small size, mariners are warned to navigate the vicinity with caution.

headline: A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.
text:
ESTIMATES FREELY GIVEN.

In things that matter — by which are now generally accepted questions relating to the strike and the boycott—Hongkong has had another quiet week. "Nothing new" is the order of each day, although there is gradually arising a quiet under-current of greater confidence than has been known for some months. One important piece of intelligence is that the Finance Committee of the Legislative Council is to consider on Monday the advisability of re-opening the Statistical Department of the Imports and Exports Office, the closing of which some time ago was decided upon by the Government in connection with its economy campaign. Strong representations have been made by the General Chamber of Commerce in favour of re-opening the Department. There are other factors than the mere momentary saving of a few thousand dollars to be taken into consideration. It is known that the Colony has suffered trade losses through the strike and the boycott; but naturally it is impossible to assess these properly without a Statistical Department, nor can comparisons be made in the current year with previous periods unless that Department is functioning. In short, it would appear to be nothing short of false economy to delay the re-opening. In other purely local affairs, the annual Race meeting has, as usual, been responsible for good displays of sportsmanship, not to mention the attraction to thousands of the inevitable cash sweeps. And mention may also be made of the latest success of the Hongkong A.D.C. in its staging of "If." In the domain of Imperial questions a good start has been made with the flight from Cairo to the Cape undertaken by the Royal Air Force, but it was, unfortunate that the aeroplane flight from Karachi to London had to be abandoned on the Persian coast owing to acute fatigue trouble after a struggle against sand storms and mist. We may soon expect to see the establishment of a Naval Volunteer Defence Corps, a fact accomplished. We should like to say the same of a Police Reserve. The absence of this Reserve has been a minor wonder. During the war the then Reserve did a magnificent work. It accomplished more than it set out to do. It proved how the interesting units of our cosmopolitan life could combine for the common good and meet on the common ground of service. The Reserve was in commonly well directed. It was not merely served by patriotism. Efficiency was aimed at and achieved. It gave interest to those who patrolled, and by its lectures on police law, the problems it put at various examination on procedures in certain circumstances, added to knowledge. It ceased on the conclusion of war to be somewhat half-married. It is directed during the two upheavals which have affected the Colony. headline: LORD WILLINGDON. / CORDIAL WELCOME FROM ALL CHINESE
text:
The "N.C. Daily News" of last Monday reports — Lord Willingdon, Chairman of the delegation to advise the Statutory Committee with regard to the disposition of the British Boxer Indemnity funds, left yesterday morning about 11 o'clock by the "Haishing". Lord Willingdon was accompanied by Sir Francis Aglen, Inspector General of Customs, and by Mr. R. F. Johnston, secretary of the delegation. It is expected that they will return about the middle of March to meet the other members of the delegation, Dame Adelaide Anderson and Professor Soothill, who are arriving by different routes. Whether the delegation will make Shanghai or Peking the main base for its deliberations is undecided, but it is probable that it will at least open its sittings here.

When seen by a representative of the "North China Daily News," yesterday Lord Willingdon expressed great satisfaction with the results of his visit in Shanghai. "While three days is a short time on which to base an opinion, and while my activities here have been entirely social and not official," said he, "I cannot help feeling that the spirit of kindness and cooperation everywhere manifested is a very happy augury. I have been privileged to meet a great many prominent Chinese gentlemen and personally I have not been able to discover any of that anti-British feeling which has been so widely advertised.

The Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce very graciously gave to luncheon for me, the Chinese Commissioner of Foreign Affairs gave us a dinner party, I had tea with Mr. Tong Shao-yi, and also with Lord Li Ching-mei. At the Consulate-General Mr. Barton has given luncheons and dinner parties at which I have had an opportunity to meet many of the Chinese and I have had interviews with four or five of their prominent leaders. The feeling I have in all these instances is that I have formed contacts with people who are anxious to assist the delegation in making its inquiries and who will be willing to place all their sources of information at its service. Besides all this," he added, "I attended the races and saw for the first time that famous institution, the China-pony, Really, this has been a remarkably pleasant three days." On Thursday, a Chinese case of enteric fever was found in the Victoria district. His Excellency the Governor has, under instructions from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, recognised Mr. John Theophilus Bagram as Vice Consul for Siam at Hongkong. Taking this report in conjunction with Réuter's message today regarding the discovery of Bolshevik literature addressed to farmers and labourers, it would certainly appear on the surface that the Allied war lords have not exposed anything in the nature of a mare's nest. The "Christian General's connections with Moscow have long been under suspicion, apart from the mere fact of a purely commercial transaction involving the purchase of arms from Russia, and although his henchmen have always strenuously denied that he is pro-Bolshevik, the average individual can form his own conclusions. The sinister plot of the Reds to dominate the Capital, as revealed at the Russian Red Conference, cannot but strengthen the arguments of those who have before now vehemently denounced the "Christian General's coquetting with Moscow.

Apart from the reasons actuating the Allied war lords in participating in the continuance of civil war in China, the best friends of China cannot but hope that, provided the connection between the Reds and Peking is an accomplished fact, Feng Yu-hsiang and those who would sell their country to Moscow may be eliminated for all time as the result of the present struggle.

headline: Hongkông; Mơndng, March 8, 1926.
text:
A striking revelation is reported to-day to have been made by Wu Pei-fu and the allies, although it may be discredited by some as a form of counter-propaganda common to the Chinese rival war lords. It is alleged that, after the retreat of the Second Kuominchan Army, Bolshevik pamphlets were found by the successful allied troops addressed to farmers and labourers; thus proving, it is asserted, that the Kuominchun and its leader, "the "Christian" General, Feng Yu-hsiang, are pro-Bolshevist. In the face of this important discovery—which, of course, has yet to be proved beyond the shadow of a doubt—the Allied military leaders declare that they "will fight the Red Government until it is destroyed."

There may be a semblance of truth in the story. Prominence is given in the "North China Daily News" of March 3 to a message from Mr. Rodney Gilbert from Peking, who reports that "the Russian Red Conference held in the Capital resulted in a decision to "extend all possible support to the present military patrons of the Peking Government." It was also reported that Moscow had agreed to make further advances of men, money and arms. The conference, to which many Chinese were admitted, opposed "Comrade" Sverdloff's coming and the establishment of a branch of the Third International at this juncture, since the time was not thought of to withdraw support from the Kuominchun politicians and military. In an arresting paragraph Mr. Rodney Gilbert says:

Moscow has been told that since anti-Red slogans were the war cries of Peking's opponents, the collapse of the Kuominchun would mean the suppression of all Soviet work in North China. Hence it must make every effort to save the cause by supporting Marshal Feng Yu-hsiang, A-sum of $6,500,000 has therefore, been made available together with some arms. The Embassy also asked for 7,000 troops, including 800 men, half in uniform and half in mufti, to control Peking, but it is unknown whether the Soviet has agreed to this.

headline: MID LEVELS
text:
The Committee of the Mid Levels Association has issued to the members the report of the first period of the Association's existence. (July 31 to December 31, 1925).

Since the formation of the Association 89 members have been enrolled. The present membership is 83, the reduction being due to departures from the Colony, etc.

The Hon. Secretary and Hon. Treasurer's statement of accounts shows a balance in hand on December 31, 1925, of $113.61.

Four meetings of the committee have been held since the general meeting on July 21 last.

Apart from matters connected with the strike, the Committee have brought to the notice of the Government several matters which they considered would be for the benefit of members, such as the provision of a children's playground near May Road Station, the unsatisfactory Chair service at the Robinson Chair Stand and the question of Traffic Control.

In response to representations by the Committee the Peak Tramways Company, Limited, have met the wants of residents using the May Road Station by altering the time to suit their convenience. It is hoped that the request which was also made that an adequate shelter be provided at this station will be acceded to in the near future.

The Committee extends their cordial thanks to the Committee of the Ladies' Recreation Club for the use of their Club room on several occasions, to Mrs. Harman for allowing the Committee meetings to be held in her flat, and to Mr. E. J. R. Mitchell for auditing the accounts.

It is hoped that members will help the Committee by inducing their friends to join the Association and that they will bring to the notice of the Committee any matters which they consider can be usefully dealt with by the Association. The report is signed by Mr. A. S. D. Cousland, as Chairman.

Colonel Tomlin's humour was delightful. On one occasion, on going into the 'billard-room' after dinner, he declared that there was a smell of escaping gas. He rang for the butler and asked him if he could smell it. The butler said "No, Colonel," to which he replied: "Then go away and send somebody else who can."

A musical student gives further instances of revised versions.

headline: LONDON STRIKE
text:
CRISIS ASSUMES SERIOUS ASPEC1

PUBLIC SERVICES MENACED:

The engineering crisis has assumed a more serious aspect as the result of a meeting in London of the representatives of all the Engineering. Unions in London deciding to press the claim for a separate wage advance of $1 weekly in London and to ask the authority of the Unions to take a joint district strike ballot and a national ballot on the question of ending the agreement, which embraces provisions for avoiding disputes, which the employers declare was broken by the unofficial stoppage at Messrs. Hoe's Works.

The meeting endorsed the action of the District Committees of seven Unions in backing Messrs. Hoe's strikers and resisting the proposal of the National Executive's Unions that the strikers should be instructed to return to work in order to place the Unions in a constitutional position. The meeting also threatened to hold up the public services if the threatened lock-out occurred. Song: "The Yeoman of England" has twice been revised. Before the war the chorus ran:—

It is always interesting, if not sometimes exactly refreshing, to obtain a fresh view of the position in Canton. This is provided in the course of a pen picture of General Chiang. Che-sak contributed to a Shanghai contemporary by a Chinese, who incidentally takes up a deal of space with an “essay” on the situation in Canton. He makes a rather forced effort to warm up to his subject; he appears to aim at reaching the summit of eloquence but falls very flat at the first hillock. Thus, after reviewing Canton's military campaigns, he expresses the opinion that these “rapid-fire victories” have given Canton “such a thorough house cleaning that she is now having some semblance of peace and order”!

The reader of this sketch of the situation is constrained to pause. A “semblance of peace and order!” If the position in Canton today is worthy of being called “a semblance of peace and order,” then all that can be said is Heaven help Canton. It is a curious type of “peace and order” that goes hand in hand with illegalities by strike and boycott pickets, that permits the Guilds to rule the Government, that allows sacred Treaties to be literally torn to pieces, and that countenances outrages against foreigners. Surely the writer of the article possesses quaint ideas of what really constitutes “law and order.” Or, was he speaking with his tongue in his cheek or simply playing to the gallery of the constituents, of the particular newspaper to which he was contributing? That he has got hopelessly fogged in his ideas is discernible when he subsequently remarks that “there is no doubt there has been great unwisdom in some of Canton’s policies, but she has been as good as her word.” In which case it must be admitted that her word has not been good at all. Less hopelessly mixed is the writer of the article in question when he comes to the “Red” stigma, although he is rather mild in his declaration that “Canton is unfortunate to have admitted Russian participation.” The presence of a Red agent, he says, is difficult to explain: “it discounts much of her achievement, and, what is worse, gives an impression to the world at large that she

is merely an instrument as such to the propaganda of an anomalous faith." His phraseology is inclined to be crude, but his meaning can be guessed, particularly when he asserts, in effect, that if Canton has laid herself open to the reproach of Bolshevik sympathy she has only herself to blame.

Unfortunately for the logic of his arguments, “Russian participation” and “law and order” are not hand-maidens. They are as opposite as the poles. On what possible basis, therefore, can he lay his eulogy of Canton for having indulged in “such a thorough house-cleaning, that she is now having some semblance of peace and order”? His logic is as weak as his effort to whitewash Canton is puerile.

headline: Hongkong, Thursday, March 11, 1926. / A BOMB OUTRAGE.
text:
It is a welcome sign of the times of the placid mood of the community that, beyond the usual feeling of horror associated with bomb butrages, there has not been the slightest concern as to the safety of the public generally as the outcome of yesterday afternoon's regrettable incident at Hunghom. The nerve of the Colony are not on edge. The strikers shot their bolt months ago so far as law and order are concerned. The machinations of the intimidators were short-lived. The raids on certain areas by the Police, with the co-operation of the East Surrey Regiment, succeeded in ridding the Colony of undesirables. The criminal records soon began to testify to the efficacy of the drastic measures enforced, even armed robbers finding for a time that the last place in South China to ply their nefarious calling was Hongkong. With the relaxation of vigilance on the part of the pickets in Canton, it was inevitable that there should creep through the cordon and drift back to their old haunts some of the criminal classes—hence the occurrence now and again of an armed robbery and of a series of burglaries in city stores. But, knowing the desperate nature of such criminals, the only wonder is that outrages of this nature have not been more frequent. It is evidence in itself that the preventive work of the Police has not been permitted to slacken in the more demonstrative duty of protection of the public from crimes with or without violence. To revert to the incident at Hunghom it is the easiest thing in the world to place it at the door of intimidators, but all the circumstances point to exactly the opposite; and only unimpeachable evidence secured eventually by the Police will convince anybody that the motive was not personal revenge for some real or imaginary wrong. The setting of the crime was too crude in the extreme for it to have been the work of anyone but blundering amateurs unaccustomed to be entrusted with the execution of political offences. The bomb itself, if such it could be called, was a "home-made" product, although powerful enough to cause a fair amount of damage to a crowd. The sole professional touch—if such it can be described of the whole business lay in the fact that the assailant had the will

to make good his escape, but even this is not a promising in view of the panic naturally created in the vicinity of the explosion. Nor would it be the first time by a long way that an amateur bomb thrower, as compared with a professional political malcontent, has succeeded in eluding the vigilance of the crowd and of the Police subsequently.

In short, the whole outrage can be ascribed purely and simply to malice or revenge, outside the realm of which it is not worth comment, beyond regret that a number of innocent persons were injured and congratulation that other persons, including Europeans, escaped from the effects of the explosion.

headline: DIOCESAN BOYS SCHOOL
text:
Without much crashing of cymbals, the transference of the Diocesan Boys' School from the island to the mainland has been accomplished. If “this” are progress” is always going on, it is always going on in connection with institutions—and particularly with educational institutions. The old quarters of the Diocesan Boys' School had outworn their usefulness. The methods were new, but not so the buildings. And so this move has been made; and from cramped quarters with little or no outlook—not even the hackneyed fine view of the harbour—a number of very fortunate schoolboys find themselves in the midst of spaciousness where, indeed, every prospect pleases. The schoolboy of the future in this Colony—at least that section which decides to place itself in the disciplinary and educational care of the Diocesan School, will give thanks—if the modern schoolboy ever gives thanks—for the commendable foresight, and wonderful initiative which has produced the most modern block of school buildings in this part of the world. The move has been a wise one—and having made it, perhaps other institutions who gasp for lack of space will consider copying such an excellent example. For in Kowloon and beyond, there is ample space. The youthful vision is not clogged; the mind has a pleasant prospect before it and the chance of producing mainly and independent young men should be more easy of accomplishment than under the conditions which are more or more extensions, makes, or developments, are to be encouraged. We owe it to the University to encourage them. They serve not merely a local purpose, but a purpose outside the boundaries of the Colony in that they attract the youth of other parts who find here educational advantages not to be had in the district from which they come. Such schools as the Diocesan Boy's form a feeder to the University—and they send students to the University of whom they may well be proud. This is one of many aspects. The good name when the Diocesan Boys' School has borne since its inception, is likely to increase as this year go on. It has always been well controlled and perhaps never better under its present spirited head whose independence of outlook and modern convention of the things necessary to elicit

Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eton, many a boy may in the future decide that his soul's salvation was gained on the playing fields, and in the classrooms of the Diocesan Boys' School. The school, in its new quarters does not begin a new life. It merely continues a life that has always been new.

headline: LONDON STRIKE / UNIONS' RECOMMENDATION REJECTED.
text:
A lively mass meeting of the strikers at Messrs. Hoe's factory rejected the recommendation of the Executives of the Unions to return to work, and resolved not to resume work until the non-Unionists were removed and a substantial increase in wages assured.

The Executives of the Union have called a meeting to consider the taking of disciplinary action against the strikers.

As a result of a meeting of the members of the executives of the seven Unions concerned in the dispute at Hoe's factory and Sir Allan Smith, Chairman of the Employers' Federation, the employers have agreed to defer the operation of the lock-out notices until Thursday, March 18.

headline: TO AVERT STRIKES.
text: The Senate has approved by 138 votes to 26 the Fascist Trade Unions Bill providing compulsory arbitration in labour disputes. Signor Mussolini described the measure as the most revolutionary yet produced by the Fascist Government.

headline: Fascist Discipline. Rome later
text:
Signor Mussolini, in a speech in the Senate on the subject of the Fascist Trade Unions Bill, emphasised the disciplinary character of the measure pointing out that Fascist Syndicalism now comprised 2,000,000 agricultural and industrial workers, a formidable and obedient force completely controlled by Fascism and the Government, and fully appreciating the value of the function of capitalism as a necessity for cooperation.

The Fascist conception was that that all must be within, and none outside. The State was above all and nobody must be against the State. The struggle of life was such nowadays that no nation could indulge in luxury strikes.
