headline: Vines May Curve to the Right or to the Left, But the Twining is Uniform—Trees Have Similar Habits.
text:
[By NORMAN C, McLOUD.]

In climbing a pole does a vine twist to the left or to the right?

To the left or to the right? To Nature Lovers the question is full of interest; and since most of PB find pleasure in the curious workings of natural laws the answer is worth the seeking. Close observation reveals striking individuality in the twining habits of plant growth.

Some vines twist to the right after the fusion of the hands of a clock in circling the dial. Others turn to the left and seem to grow backwards. In most cases the habit is fixed throughout an entire group or family. In others there is variation, even among vines of close kinship.

Climbing Vines are interesting forms of growth, which depend on outside help for their meats of support. In fact, that they may realize their ambition to rise in the world they avail themselves of any upright object available, whether growing or otherwise. The support may be the trunk of a tree, the post of a fence or the wall of a building. Any object, according to the chants to climb is welcome, to the climbers.

More Than One Way To Climb. In establishing themselves on their supports the vines have notions of their own as to the ways and means to be adopted. Most climbers attach themselves by coiling. With others the contact with the tree or post is effected by means of adhesive disks, as in the case of the widely distributed Virginia Creeper. Another type of vine attaches itself by means of tendrils which are thrown out in all directions to take hold of anything in reach. In this latter class are the gourd and the grape; the grasping tendrils of which are familiar to everyone.

Whether twinning or otherwise fastened to its support, the vine has a definite object in view when the upward journey is undertaken. To the Nature student the climbing habit is essentially utilitarian. Ascending growth is necessary to the fulfillment of the vine's life mission of displaying its flowers to the flitting bees and offer the seeds to the winds and the birds. Enough enabled to escape from the crowded plant life of the surface the vine would be submerged and hidden, and would meet with failure in its efforts to provide the bees with material for the making of honey and the birds with a valuable source of food supply. In similar fashion the plant would be cheated of a chance for reproduction through the scattering of its seeds by birds and breezes.

An Engineering Feet. The Highway is one of America's newest pathways for the recreationist. It is a great pathway for everyone who visits our North-west. Its scenic beauties have been likened to a combination of the Alps, the Rine and Southern Italy with the wild grandeur of the American Cascades but it is also not worthy its great engineering project. Going west it reaches Astoria and Seaside on the Pacific and running east it pierces and enters the historic gorge of the Columbia and passes sixty miles of etis and tailing waters. This wonderful road hangs on cliffs in many places hundreds of feet above the stream; in other points it is virtually at the level of the waters. Picturesque bridges span turbulent streams which sprawl many feet beneath and for miles of its length the road is supported by quint walls of dry masonry. As one drives along the magnificent reenery on both sides of the Columbia is unfolded mile by mile, and within ten miles of travel there are eleven beautiful waterfalls, including Multenmah, the highest waterfall in our country. IN A SOUR-WOOD TREE THAT IS TWISTING THE GRAIN ALMOST INVA-RIABLY WINDS TO THE RIGHT

Covered a wide field and brought to light many interesting points which the average person easily overlooks. In discussing the subject for the American Nature Association, Dr. Frederick Brooks has pointed out peculiarities in which most of us will find suggestions for surprise breeding observations of our own.

The case of the climbing bean of the home garden is one of the striking examples of individuality in vines. This form of vegetation always twines to the right. Wild or tame, sturdy or poorly nourished, in sunlight or in shade, the bean twists in the one direction. No allurement of nature seems to influence it to the left. The bean rises in a right-hand spiral with a persistence not to be overcomed. The hop vine is similarly constant This plant the growth is always to the left, and Dr. Brooks reports that his observation has never revealed an exception to this dominant rule. Among the right hand twines we find the climbing buckwheat, dodder, h 线 and Dutchman's pipe. Among those twisting to the left are the wild yam and the Japanese honey-suckle. With any of these plants the amateur will find an interesting field of experiment in trying to force the growth in the opposite direction. Efforts of this character develop the full stubbornness of the vines and bring ultimate failure of the human effort. In this respect the vines seem to know what they want and to defy the efforts of mankind to divert them from their course.

IN PRACTICALLY ALL THE TWISTING RED MAPLE TREES THE CURVATURE IS TO THE LEFT THE MOONSEED VINE ALWAYS CLIMBS BY WINDING TO THE RIGHT

Legend Of A Great Bridge. Shortly after attention is riveted on the Washington shore for Castle Rock which Lewis and Clark called Beacon Rock looms up. It covers thirteen and a half acres and can be seen for miles. No wonder Lewis and Clark used it for a landmark. The Indians, too, play their part in the stories of this inspiring river. In one place, on the Washington side is seen the north abutment of the "Bridge of the Gods." The legends say that at one time the great stream was spanned at this point by a natural bridge, but Mt. Hood and Mt. Adams quarrelled and in their rage the great bridge was shattered. Still more romantic is the story that an Indian brave from the Oregon side married an Indian maiden from the Washington

side in spite of the opposition of their tribes. As they started across the bridge to his home they were pursued by her disappointed suitors and kinsmen. Hardly had they reached safety than the bridge fell, carrying with it their advancing enemies. At any rate the bridge fell and formed rapids in the river.

Indians play a prominent part in legends of this river. Castle Rock, 1,140 feet high, whose summit has only recently been sealed by the white man, was an Indian lookout, and Memalooose Island was used by the Indians for many years as a burying ground, the dead being placed in pine huts. On this island is the grave of Vicor Trevitt, a pioneer river man whose wish was to be buried with the Indians. "If there should be such a thing as a resurrection," this sceptic said, "I will take my chance with the Indians."

Fish wheels in operation gather the sufficient salmon in many places and there are the Dalles and the falls of Cadillac—thirty feet high—and the locks which lift the boats to the level of the Middle Columbia. All these are a part of the enjoyment of a trip on the Columbia. Above the Dalles the river becomes unnavigable, caused by balastic formations and this stretch is a favourite spot among the Indians, many of whom live near by. During the fishing season they can be seen far out on the rocks, speaking salmon which are dried in the sun and used as food. This mighty river with a flow of over 1,800,000 cubic feet of water every second — greater than either the Mississippi or St. Lawrence—fed by overlasting snow fields and glaciers, winds its way through the Pacific North-west and at the mouth the tide reaches in for one hundred and fifty miles. Its crags, cascades, cataracts and falls are worth going many miles to see. If Neolithic man chose this water way to enter this continent he is to be congratulated on his good taste and forenight. At any rate present-day man can see no more picturesque river.

Study of the spirals reveals curious variations. While a particular species will stick to its habits with staunch insistence, other members of the same family will strike off in the opposite direction. The morning glories offer good example of this pecuniary of family tendencies. Most of the plants of this group twine to the right, with no departure from the established rule. In at least one species, however, the custom meets with complete reversal and the vine is always found twisting to the left. Just why this variation should occur has never been determined although the tendency is widely recognized by students of natural Science. headline: CONGRESS SOVIETS.
text:
EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE ELECTED:

THREE HUNDRED STRONG.

Three hundred members of the Central Executive Committee of the Federation of Socialist Republics were elected to day at a congress of the Soviets.

They include Kalinin, Rykoß Stalin, Zinovieff, Trotsky and Tomisky.

ECONOMIC CHANGES. Moscow May 11

The All-Russian Soviet Congress has ratified the revised constitution, particularly the changes introduced in consequence of the present economic conditions. It has also noted that the Republics of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan have left the Federation.

Peking, May 11.—The Japanese aeroplanes flying to Peking are expected to leave Tokyo on the 23rd and to arrive on the 26th. They are due to return on the 28th. — Reuter.

Peking, May 10.—The students' delegates, who failed to see Tunn Chi-jui yesterday, were seen by his aide-de-camp, who promised them that Lu Ching-Jin, Commandant of the Precautionary Force, would see them on Monday and give them a reply from the Government. Pending this reply, the students are not agitating to-day, but the police are still taking precautions. It is reported in judicial circles that five of the arrested students have been released on bail.—Reuter.

headline: THE OLD MAN AIR
text:
After the presentation of a bouquet by Dr. Luther's young daughter, Marshal von Hindenburg left for the Chancellor's palace. The 5-mile route was lined the whole way by cheering crowds which von Hindenburg acknowledged. Nationalist organisations were very prominent, but the Republicans adhered to their earlier boycott decision.

Throughout the drive von Hindenburg exhibited the air of an old man well pleased with the cordiality of his reception.

At the conclusion of the drive the crowds dispersed quietly the Monarchists marching off singing patriotic songs.

To-night the President dines with the Chancellor. He takes the oath to-morrow.

Marshall von Händenburg in a statement before his departure for Berlin, earnestly pleaded for unity.

He said that he would bear in mind those who were "poor and distressed and would try to act as peace-maker. His aim was for a happy Fatherland.

As the train started amid the strains of “Deutschland Ueber Alles, von Hindenburg called for three cheers for Germany. The crowd enthusiastically responded.

headline: PIRACY ECHO / ALLEGED RINGLEADER ARRESTED:
text:
TRIAL IN COLONY

A former member of the crew of the s.s. Tai Lee was arrested this week, at Whampoa by the Canton authorities. The man is alleged to be one of the ringleaders of the piracy committed on that vessel in January last year when Captain—Willcox—was—brutally murdered.

A photograph of the accused sent to the Hongkong Police by the Canton authorities is alleged to have been identified by officers of the s.s. Tai Lee as that of the wanted man.

It is understood that the man will be brought to Hongkong for trial.

headline: WAR DEBTS.
text:
It transpires that the United States took the initiative in seeking a general refunding arrangement with all America's principal war debtors. It is indicated that the United States Government virtually circularised the debtors, including France, Italy, Belgium, Czecho-Slovakia, Greece, Jugo, Slavia, Estonia and Latvia, expressing the opinion that the time had come to strike a general balance. Russia is the only debtor nation not addressed, as she does not possess a Government recognised by the United States. Furthermore, the French Government has been informed that the United States will be pleased if a French Debt Commission is sent to America. It is possible that M. Caillaux will come personally to Washington.

Sofin, May 17.—It is officially announced that the police have discovered a large secret store of arms and explosives, supposedly intended for an armed insurrection and blowing up bridges and railways. Considerable money was also found. Several arrests have been made.—Reuter. ready, the largest being the £4,000,000 debenture issue of the Niger Co., guaranteed by Lever Brothers.

headline: SOVIET INJUSTRY.
text:
Moscow, May 16. Replying to some opposition from the industrial districts expressed at the Congress of Soviets to the scheme to increase imports, M. Dzjerjinsky, chairman of the All Russian Council of National Economies, pointed out that increase of machinery was unavoidable in order to effect the quickest possible revival of industry, whose production was approaching the pre-war figure. The peasants' demand for agricultural implements had increased to such a degree that the Soviet factories were unable to satisfy it. Seventeen million roubles worth of agricultural implements must be imported during the current year.

The Hague, May 17.—The Permanent Court's ruling in connection with the Danzig letter-boxes gives the opinion that no ruling was made in connection with the disputed point by the Danzig High Commissioner, but the Polish postal service of the port is entitled to install letter-boxes outside its premises, though the service is not reserved for Polish officials and authorities but is for the public use.—Refer.

London, May 16.—It is officially announced that the attendance at Wembley cup to Friday night was 350,000, as compared with 302,000 for the first six days last year, the latter including Cup Final day. Therefore it is evident that the attendance has this year hitherto greatly-increased.—Reuter.

headline: HOME FOR WAIFS.
text:
Stanley peninsula may not be chosen as the site of the proposed Home for Waifs and Strays as a result of the visit of the promoters of the scheme to the industrial home at Macao.

“Let justice be done though the heavens fall” was the axiom of the Deemster as portrayed by Hall Caine. Let justice be done to the sub-tenants of houses here though the principal tenants fall. That, in a nutshell, was the plant put forth at the meeting of the Legislative Council yesterday afternoon by the senior Chinese member, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shouson. A lessor, be he the principal tenant or a lessor under the principal tenant, has no equity or right to increase his rental charge to a sub-tenant if his own principal rent is not increased by the owner himself.

An equally vital point raised in the discussion at yesterday's meeting was the right of the sub-tenant to give notice to quit without being called upon to pay the higher rent during the period of such notice. In the case of a tenancy for an indefinite period it is obviously not the intention of the Legislature that a sub-tenant should be placed unwittingly in a position to be penalised after giving due notice to quit. This point was very rightly strongly emphasised by the Hon. Mr. Alabaster, and generally supported.

That there are Americans with a soul above pelf can easily be proved. That there are those who regard the possession of wealth as connoting obligations can also be proved; whilst a number can be produced whose patriotism—a love of country and a high sense of ideals—is beyond reproach and worthy of emulation. headline: WORTH COPYING

His independence was not only mental. His enjoyment of life required so few of the ordinary creature comforts. The simplicity of his habits and of his tastes, at once fastidious and austere, remained singularly free from any inclination towards luxury or magnificence, which he nevertheless painted with such delight, whether expressed in splendid architecture, or in interiors where fine proportions were� accentanted by the surface beauty of lovely material, over which his brush lingered. During one holiday before the war, while painting at the Carrara marble quarries, he slept for weeks in a hut so completely devoid of all ordinary comfort that his companions, far younger men, fled after a few days, unable to stand the spartan rigours tolerated by their senior with such serene indifference.

All his life he remained the student, absorbed in this work, sleeping himself in it, atta mpting always some new development, some fresh experiment. During the last few months he had found extraordinary pleasure in sculpture and small sculptured groups remain to show this fireless exploration of another field. To his indefatigable energy, a holiday means simply a change from the work of the moment to work of another description. The brilliant sparkle of his water-colours conveys perfectly the relaxed tension of his holiday mood; yet even, in these guy records how disciplined was the eye that chose a subject how controlled the hand that held the dripping brush, dipped it seemed, in dazzling light!

Hongkong and the whole world was startled by this outrage on the occasion of M. Merlin's visit to Shaneen, after calling here on his return to Indo-China from Japan, M. Merlin was the guest, with members of his staff, at a dinner given by the French community of Canton, at the Victoria Hotel. Shortly after the gathering had sat down, a young Oriental throw a bomb at them from a window. He was pursued and fired at and was seen to have dived into the creek. Subsequently a body confidently believed to have been that of the assassin, was found in the river. It was stated that the assassin who caused the deaths of several French residents and wounds to others, was an Annarnite. A memorial is said to have been erected to his memory by Revolutionaries. Mr. Merlin escaped without injury and came down to Hongkong to aid for Indo-China.

London, June 4—It is now announced that contracts for £3,500,000 have been placed in Britain for two 10,000 ton cruisers and two submarines for the Royal Australian Navy. The cruisers will be similar to the British "County" class.-Reuter.

Sofia, June 4.—The police are very active against the Communists. They arrested 450 person on the ground that they had no identity papers and no fixed occupation. The authorities in Varna have arrested 140 alleged Communists.—Reuter.

√

Lisbon, June 4.—In the Chamber, the Minister for the Colonies explained the reasons for the resignation of Dr. Rodrigues, Governor of Macao. He read a document referring to the works of the port of Macao, showing that the Governor was of the opinion that 60 per cent. of the capital of the company constructing the port works should be Portuguese and the rest divided among British and Chinese. The Governor, who is also a Deputy, defended his attitude.

[Last week a court with three judges began the trial of nine men charged with having been concerned in the murder of the Sirdar. The two student brothers. Enaial nervously recounted their participation in the crime. Another prisoner. Mahmoud Rashed broke down and wept while repeating his confession. Five of the prisoners denied complicity in the murder.]

The ex-convict Negui-Bhel Bawi, the chief agent employed by the secret police in their investigations, who was largely responsible for the success of the police enquiry, received the reward of £10,000 Egyptian offered by the Government for the apprehension of the murderers.

[Last week the ex-convict told a hushed court how he gained the confidence of the prisoners and extracted the story of the murder from them. He induced them to flee; thus leading to their arrest in the train.]

Plotting the Crime.

The judicial authorities have published a summary of the confessions of some of the accused, Abdel Fatah. Enaiat, aged 22, a

Zaglul Pusha who was head of the Government of which the two arrested former Cabinet Ministers were members. Zaglul is no longer Premier of Egypt.

student, declared in the course of his statement to the police that following the failure of the conversations between Zaghloul Pasha and Mr. Ramsey MacDonald in London, he, Abdel Hamid Enaiat, Shafik Mansour, and Mahmud Ismail, met at the house of Shafik Mansour and decided to commit political murders. They chose the Sirdar as a victim.

London, June 6.—The silk section of the London Chamber of Commerce has passed a unanimous resolution of protest against the amended Government proposals. Reuter.

headline: BACK TO RUSSIA. / AND. BACK TO THE LAND.
text:
A large party of Russian emigrants who were converted to Bolshevism while in the United States have arrived at Libau en route to Russia bringing tractors and other agricultural machinery with a view to reconstructing the agricultural life of the country.

Paris, June 6.—A "Temps" correspondent in Morocco learns that the Spanish will begin operations in ten days' time against Abd El Krim's capital, Adjur. An expeditionary force is landing in the neighbourhood of Albucernis, covered by the fleet and airforce. It is stated that General De Riveri will personally direct operations from aboard a cruiser.—Reuter.

headline: SOVIET ENEMIES.
text:
THREE DEATH SENTENCES SUSPENDED.

MOSCOW June, 9.

The execution of General Belavin, M. Ivaroff and Madame Kizeczkovska has been suspended. [The Kieff Military Tribunal concluded on June 6, the trial of the members of an anti-Soviet organisation called “Russia for the Russians,” headed by an ex-Tsarist General Belavin, who is accused of military espionage on behalf of Poland. General Belavin and M. Ivancoff, who was an official on the Staff of the Ukrainian Red Army and a woman intermediary, Nina Kizeczkovska, were sentenced to death. Twelve others were variously imprisoned and one acquitted. General Belavin is alleged to have described himself as the ideological enemy of the Soviet and to have admitted the charge.]

text:
(Renter's American Service.) Hendaye, Pyrenees, June 10. It appears that young students of the school of engineering were responsible for the attempt on the royal train on June 5.

Messrs. Morgan's are offering $50,000,000 Belgian Government loan at 7 per cent. interest, issue price ninety-eight.

Toonones, June 10.—M. Painlevo has arrived on route to Morocco. In an interview he said he was going to the front to comfort with General Lyasley on the position in Morocco and the possibility of a Franco-Spanish understanding to secure peace with a minimum of force and risk. He is returning to Paris on the 16th via Spain—Renter

A court martial has sentence the ringleader to twenty years jail and nine others to term ranging from four years to ten

Travellers from Barcelona persistently reported an attempt to blow up the train in which the King and Queen of Spain had arranged to go to Madrid. A bomb weighing eighty kilograms was said to have been found in a tunnel, and nineteen arrests were reported to have been made. Their Majesties were said to have postponed their departure and to be remaining at Barcelona.

The Spanish Embassy in London discredited the story of an attempt on the Spanish Royal train and said the report is merely a part of a campaign to discredit Spain.

headline: MOROCCO—FIGHTING. / CIVILIANS EVACUATE TOWN,
text:
TRIBESMEN PRESS FORWARD.

A message from Wezzin states that owing to enemy pressure which resulted in many penetrations of the French line along the Wadizess, the French command decided precautionarily to remove the civilian population of Wezzin to the south. The evacuation was carried out very calmly.

Moscow, June 10.—An aerial expedition consisting of six aeroplanes, including — four — constructed — in Russia, left this morning for Peking in the presence of thousands of people including members of the government. Many other aeroplanes escorted the expedition on the first stage of the journey, the object of which is to survey an air route across Siberia by may of the Gold desert to China. It successful is proposed to form a Soviet Chinese company to establish permanent communication between Burma and China by this route.

headline: Patterns In Moth Cases.
text:
"Without leaving its cause the larva makes a slit halfway down one side and inserts a triangular gore of new material. A similar insertion is made on the opposite side, and the larva then reverses itself without leaving the case, and makes corresponding slits and additions in the other half. The case is lengthened by successive additions to either end. On the exterior the case appears to be a rattled mass of small particles of wool; on the interior it is lined with soft whitish silk. By transferring the larva from time to time to fabrics of different colours the case may be made to assume as varied a pattern as the experimenter desires, and will illustrate, in its colouring, the peculiar method of making the enlargements and additions described."

What a chance for an experiment. Here is a scientific research in easy reach of every home.

First find your lava. If the creature changes to be feeding upon your red sweater you will note the bright, red colouring of a portion of the housing. Now transfer the builder to a garment of brilliant yellow. In due course the case will show the new colouring in sharp and striking contrast to the earlier red. Then give him a posture of green clothing, and follow his with blue, purple, orange and carise. The colour scheme will be riot. Even more destructive than the assembling clothes moth is the webbing type, which disensues with the housing equipment and goes in for the creation of tunnels. This creature has a habit of spinning a cobwebby mass of silken thread; apparently as random, in its crawling journeys along fabric surfaces. This webbing is a frequent sight on unprotected clothing and gives the moth its name. Sheet Lived Creature Mochis are short-lived creatures who solidified lives on long as Chity plays. They seem to take no nonintelligent misuse. A female begins to live in a life that emerges from her chrysalis and she keeps at it with a persistence which explains the multiplication of the species in the clothes closest. Suspension of egg-laying is a sign of, approach-big, death. Entomologists have found as many as 50 eggs laid within a 24-hour period by a single female.

To scientists and tourists the volcanous hold a strong appeal. As the entire group of islands are the result of the "labour of lars and the coral polyp," both are very prominent features of the land.

During the Mixed Court trial of alleged rioters in Shanghai a Chinese physician gave evidence that the students were not shot in the back.

A Chinese physician's testimony that the student rioters killed at the Louza station on May 30 were not shot in the back, and the admission of a missionary, who saw the shooting that under the circumstances the police action was inevitable, were the outstanding incidents in the hearing of 19 students charged with participation in the riots in the International Mixed Court before Mr. Jacobs, American Assessor, and Magistrate Kwan. Forty-six students were scheduled to appear, but 27 forfeited bail ranging from $10 to $100.

Dr. O. Fischer watched the case on behalf of the Chinese Commissioner of Foreign Affairs. Mr. E. T. Maitland, police prosecutor, conducted the case against the accused, one of whom was defended by the Chinese lawyer, Mr. Ho Fei. In the afternoon Dr. H. C. Mei was called in to defend some of the students.

The evidence was most important in correcting statements which have been made repeatedly not only by agitators but even by the Peking Government in notes directed to the "Legations. Dr. H. C. Chen, a Chinese physician attached to the Woosung Road police hospital, contradicted the unsupported statements which have been circulated throughout China and in foreign countries that the students were shot in the back. Dr. Chen examined seven of the slain men when they were brought into the hospital after the riots of Saturday and Monday.

Dr. Chen said one of the victims was wounded in the left scapule, the second in the chest, a third in the right side, a fourth in the neck, a fifth in the right shoulder, a sixth in the chest and the left shoulder-blade, and the seventh in the left eye and skull.

The Chinese physician added that any wounds which might have been received in the backs of other wounded men might easily have been received while turning around to beckon the rioters to come on.

Mr. Harry "Westnidge, a Szechwan missionary attached to the China Inland Mission, who has lived for 15 years in China, in giving the evidence, upheld the necessity of the shooting. Near the Town Hall the mob were striking the foreign police with their fists, and witness particularly noticed how forbearing the police were in endeavouring to maintain order. When they were being overwhelmed and had to protect their lives he saw one Sikh policeman draw his baton while the foreign officers drew their canes.

"I noticed," continued Mr. Westnidge, "that when the police had their backs turned to any of the attackers the mob seemed to gather more courage. Crowds from the side street began to flow into Nanking Road. The side of the tram car held up in the vicinity assisted the police in their manœuvres to make a more hurried return to the station. The crowd ran on the other side of the tram in an endeavour to intercept the police, and were by this time rushing forward from all direc

Geneva, June 15.—General Habibullah, the Persian delegate, withdrew from the arms conference owing to the adoption of articles dealing with the supervision of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman which Persia considers derogatory to her sovereign rights and dignity. —Reuter.

tions to the Louza police station. I rather feared what would take place, and suddenly heard the shooting. The police seemed to be inside the entrance, and appeared to come out to meet the throng.

Asked what would have happened if the police had not then opened fire the witness replied:

“I am used to Chinese crowds, and at first this one appeared to be simply the grinning ‘look sees.’ They appeared to be a lot of boys who never expected to run into so serious a matter. I think the students started out without ever dreaming of so serious an ending. If the police had hesitated a moment they would have been trampled down unquestionably.

Cross-examined by the Chinese lawyer as to what nationality he was the witness replied that he was born in England, but that in Szechwan he was called a China-man. After the shooting occurred he rendered assistance to the wounded. The surging mass were yelling so much that he only heard the sound of the shots.

Witness in answer to a question put to him replied by asking the Chinese lawyer if he realised what the students were doing at the time when “they were yelling and screaming and rushing at the police station from three directions in a mixed mob.”

Asked if he would have shot, he replied to the Magistrate that "he would have hated to as a missionary, but that as an officer of the law there was no option. If it had been a foreign crowd at home we would have got the same. I believe that the students were looking for trouble, and not the police."

Witness told the court that some of the older students he saw in the street appeared to be the leaders, and that one man who ran along the side streets shouting and waving a flag appeared to be acting as a warner and a collector of the crowd. Inspector Everson then elaborated the evidence he gave at the inquest, describing how the mob had “made a blind rush at the gates.” When the mob were within six feet of the police he gave the order to fire. The crowd in the opinion of the witness were by no means composed all of students, and by the look of most of them they appeared to be loafers.

The afternoon session was occupied until 6.15 in hearing the evidence of the other foreign police who drove the crowd back to Wing On's and were then attacked near the Town Hall. The case was adjourned, bail being granted to all the accused.

London, June 15.—The considerable anticipations of the Budget duty are reflected in the trade returns for last month, the imports of silk goods totalling fourteen million yards, as contrasted with eight/and a half millions for April. Goods under the category of the McKenna duties, excluding motor cars, tofalled £1,000,000, compared with £580,000.—Reuter.

Brussels, June 15.—In an effort to solve the crisis which has deprived the country of a Cabinet for nearly three months, the King summoned a conference of the Catholic leaders Vaudevyvere, the Socialist Vandervelde and the Liberal Masson. He urged the subordination of party considerations to the need of forming stable government.—Reuter. INDIA'S LEAD.

text:

TALUTAO ISLAND—LIGHT ESTABLISHED.

The light-tower, which is round, built of steel, and painted white, is situated on the small island at the eastern end of Talutao Island, and is 28 feet in height from base to lantern vane.

The illuminating apparatus. is Dioptic, of the Fourth Order, and the character of the light is group-flashing, showing two white lightning flashes every 10 seconds. The light is elevated 248 feet above high water and should be visible in clear weather at a distance of 22 nautical miles.

Approximate position:

Latitude 39° 44′ 40″ E. Longitude 123° 44′ 50″ E. British Admiralty Chart No. 1256.

headline: STRIKE LOOTING / INCENDIARIES ACTIVE.
text:
SYDNEY, NOVA SCOTIA, June 16. The disturbances in the Cape Breton coalfield continue, in spite of the presence in the strike area of over seven hundred troops.

The incendiaries, who are active at several points, last night destroyed a number of buildings near Sydney, including a powder magazine. The Federal Labour Minister the Hon. James Murdoch, arrived, and, is endeavouring to mediate.

Ottawa, June 16.—Further looting has occurred in the Nova Scotia strike area. The Officer Commanding has requested immediate despatch of additional troops, although during the past few days practically all the available permanent forces in Ontario Quebec and Nova Scotia have been sent to the scene of the disturbances. The Labour Minister, Mr. Murdoch, at the request of the miners and employers, has gone to mediate.—Reuter's American Service.

In the House of Commons in answer to questions, Sir W. Mitchell Thompson, Postmaster General announced that all the postal administrations of the Empire and abroad, with a few exceptions, which accepted parcels not exceeding 11 lbs. weight had been invited to exchange with Britain parcels not exceeding 22 lbs. weight.

Sonia, June 16.—The latest victim of the Macedonian ventelite in M. Milhalloff, formerly one of the leading lieutenants of Todor Alexandroff, famous Macedonian chieftain, who was assassinated last year. Two suspects have been arrested.—Reuter.

Parish, June 16—M. Palabtharur arrived from Morocco

Please remain silent and do not smoke.” In facing-death by a 2,000-volt current the three desperadoes showed great courage. headline: OUTLOOK GRAVER.
text:
The situation is unchanged. The removal of negotiations from Shanghai to Peking has not caused any outward excitement.

It is reported that the Japanese have handed in a Note of protest as regards the affair at Kiukiang; on June 18, but both the Chinese and Japanese authorities are maintaining complete secrecy.

The Union of Labour, Commerce and Education, which came into being in consequence, of the events of May 30, have decided to insist on the continuation of the strike of shops, despite the decision reached at the meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, which decided that the banks should re-open on Sunday.

headline: Terror Gang.
text:
The students yesterday terrorised the shopkeepers, bankers, and members of the Chamber of Commerce in connection with the decision to re-open the banks and shops to-day.

Two special meetings were held in the Chamber yesterday, at which the extremists contended that foreigners would view the re-opening as a sign of weakening. The business members pointed out that the closing of the banks and shops was not materially affecting the foreigners but was causing tremendous Chinese losses, instancing that enormous supplies of tea and cocoons were piling up in Shanghai, which were at present unfinanceable and not movable.

Yesterday morning the meeting resolved to postpone the opening until June 24. Last night's wholly rescinded the resolution of June 19, and resolved to postpone settlement day until the end of the lunar month, namely July 21.

headline: Chairman Attacked.
text:
During the discussions, the extremists bitterly attacked Yu Ya-ching, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, charging him with having received $500,000 from the Imperialists to re-open the banks and shops.

Yu Ya-ching vehemently denied this. He hurried to Shanghai from Peking, and since worked day and night in the interests of China and her people. He had not influenced the voting, and he had sufficient money for his few remaining years on this earth.

The attack on Yu Ya-ching silenced other solid business men, and the rescission was carried by a huge majority.

While a definite split between the business members, and the extremists has not occurred, each group is attempting to justify itself, and the outcome will depend largely on the attitude of the Chinese Government.

headline: More Bluster.
text: Delegates, representing 48 colleges, met at the Law College this morning. They sent a deputation to interview the Foreign Minister and War Minister, this afternoon, demanding severance of diplomatic relations with Britain and the impeachment of the Hankow Tupan. The situation, however, at least outwardly, is becoming quiet. There are no signs of the boycott or strike. Numerous students have left for their homes during the past week.

headline: Chungking Trouble.
text:
A message from Chungking yesterday, states that after student agitators worked up popular excitement, rioters on the 17th. attacked foreign customs, employés and assaulted Britons on the streets, though none were seriously hurt. Meanwhile a demonstration occurred at the British Consulate, where the rioters-threatened-the-consular Chinese stuff. The Consul, thereupon, requested the city commandant to furnish a consular guard and restore order. As there was no response, the Consul evacuated the Consulate and went aboard a gunboat.

He sent messages to all Britons, advising them quickly to assemble on the gunboat. The community, on June 18, found accommodation at the riverside, under the protection of gunboats where they are remaining. Order has

been restored in the city, but excitement has not subsided. It is unsafe for foreigners to appear in the streets, though no danger is apprehended under present circumstances. The British Consulate is damaged to an extent unknown, and troops are now guarding it. At Chungking, as at many other centres the rivalries of the militarists have proved an important factor in the situation. Leaders, who are inclined to restore order feared popular ill-will and held aloof at a critical period.

The Foreign Office Note, in reply to the Powers' note regarding the riots against foreign sentiment in China, states that the accounts of different incidents given therein are not in accord with the local Chinese authorities' reports.

The Note gives a lengthy Chinese version of the recent occurrences. It says the Hankow British Volunteers suddenly opened fire on an entirely unarmed crowd and the British authorities should assume full responsibility for their violent action.

At Kiukiang, during an altercation between the police and a small number of workmen, fire suddenly broke out at the Taiwan Bank. During the confusion at the time of putting out the fire slight damage was "caused" to sundry articles in the British and Japanese Consulates. Such damage was accidental. Regarding the killing of a British subject at Shanghai, the Note says that he was outside the Settlement, where the Municipality has built roads without China's consent. The motives of the criminals have not been ascertained. It is regrettable for the above reasons that the incident occurred.

headline: Peking "Stands Firm."
text:
The Note goes on to say that with the exception of the killing of a British subject at Shanghai all the incidents happened as a result of failure to obtain a prompt and fair settlement of the Shanghai case.

There never existed any anti-foreign tendency.

Since the Shanghai occurrence, the Government has issued mandates ordering the people to exercise self-restraint, and has instructed the provincial authorities to maintain order. In view of the present circumstances, the Government hope the Ministers of the Powers will promptly settle the Shanghai case, then the present indignation will be appeased and- excitement subside. The Note, in conclusion, declares "I declare the stand I have taken in the previous protests will be insisted upon."

headline: The Chinese View.
text:
Responding to the diplomatic commission's statement, the Chinese delegation have issued a statement in which they express the belief that a permanent basis of settlement could only be achieved by solving certain questions which have been sources of misunderstanding between the Chinese and foreigners in Shanghai, including the rendition of the Mixed Court, the amelioration of conditions of labourers and the participation of Chinese ratepayers in the Municipal Council.

These points were presented at the first meeting when it was intended to apply for authority to discuss them. But, at the subsequent two meetings, the commission evinced a desire to shift onto the Chinese authorities, the responsibility for indirect causes which led up to the shooting. The commission further stated that not having authority to deal with questions of an international nature it must leave immediately for Peking. The conference was thus brought to an end: The Chinese delegation much regrets that its sincere efforts hitherto have failed to bring about a satisfactory solution.

The statement is signed by Messrs. Tsai Ting-kan, Cheng Chien and Tseng Tsung-chien.

headline: From Afar: EDINBURGH, June 20.
text:
Over a thousand delegates, representing sixty countries, attended the opening of the World Women's Christian Temperance Convention. The Conference opened with a devotional session, at which delegates from South Africa, Australia, Denmark Canada, India and China gave short addresses.

Miss Tinling from Shanghai said that in the present trouble the Chinese should not be blamed for the effects of Bolshevik influence. The rest of the world was threatened with the same changes. The Chinese were only doing what mobs do elsewhere.

headline: Shanghai Position.
text:
Shanghai is quiet, but there is no cessation of anti-foreigo propaganda. The decision to reopen the banks and shops is favourably affecting the general situation; but merely reflects the necessity of the Chinese to end the phase of the situation causing them much severer losses and inconvenience than foreigners.

The shipping strike, which is a strong anti-foreign weapon, is not weakening. Strikers are beginning to kidnap Japanese employees who are taken to Chapei, robbed and beaten and only released on payment of money and promises to quit employment.

A wireless from Chinkiang says the strikers have resolved that coal will not be sold to British or Japanese.

No danger is now apprehended t Anking.

At Swatow anti-foreign demonstrations continue.

At Foochow an anti-Japanese boycott has been decided upon but no date has been fixed.

Ample Strike Funds.

The extremists are not concerned in the deadlock, for sufficient funds for strike purposes continue to flow in from China and abroad.

The strikers' programme includes a huge demonstration in the native city to-morrow, which together with the growing activities of organised bands of ruffians, is giving rise to additional precautions. Chang Hsue Liang is bringing a second brigade to Shanghai of Fengtien soldiers and is taking up strategic positions in the vicinity of the native city.

The vernacular papers all published Mr. Chamberlain's speech, some commenting on it as nonsense, and others treating it impartially.

headline: Outroges Continue. SHANGHAI Tura
text:
The strikers yesterday afternoon attacked the wharf coolies coaling the Blue Funnel liner Pootung. Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's assistant compradore, intervening, aroused the ire of the strikers who set upon him and chased him to the river-side, where failing to reach a sampah, he fell in and was drowned.

A Briton, Mr. Moalem, a driver of the Volunteer Machine Gun Co., was going home in uniform last night by way of Lord Lane when he was struck between the shoulders and the neck with a meatchopper. He was seriously wounded and taken to Hospital.

[A message received later in correction of the foregoing states that it was the younger brother of the Holt's Wharf compradore who was killed, not Messrs. Butterfield & Swire's compradore]

No damage resulted from the wharf incident which was quickly over. A British warship is protecting the wharf to-day.

Mr. Moalem is progressing satisfactorily.

headline: Santiago de Chile. June
text:
Santiago de Chile, June 21.—In order to stop Soviet propaganda in Chile the Government has ordered that the Russian ship Vorovsky shall not be allowed to enter Chilean ports.—Reuter's American Service.

Moecow, June 21.—The Russian Batic fleet made for the open sea this morning for manoeuvres, with Admiral Frunze abroad a battleship.

Paris, June 20. The Main announces 20 arrests in Paris and the provinces in pursuance of the measures of suppression of Communist propaganda in regard to Morocco. M. Painlevo will early raise a question in the Chamber raising Parliamentary immunity in respect to two Communist leaders, who are deputies, to enable prosecution.

Tangiers, June 20th—situation in the Western Spanish Zone is becoming serious. The Rif contingents are concentrating at various points along the Court Torcan Larache line.—Reuter.

headline: BOYCOTT DENIED. / SHANGHAI CHAMBER'S DESIRES
text:
SPEEDY SETTLEMENT

The Chinese General Chamber of Commerce denies that it has decided on a British and Japanese boycott.

The Chinese General Committee of Commerce has requested Reuter to deny the report in the local Press to the effect that the Vice-Chairman of the Chamber, at a meeting last Sunday, announced that goods purchased after June 30 from British and Japanese sources would be seized and confiscated after discovery by the students and that the boycott should be maintained for a year. The Chamber states that the report is unfounded, as the meeting was convened exclusively to discuss steps to urge the Chairman, Yu Yah-ching, not to retire. Hostile foreign criticisms have here been aroused and various retaliatory measures are proposed in letters to the foreign Press, all calculated to do harm to Chinese and foreign relations. This Chamber wishes all foreign business men to understand that no action of an illegal nature has been or will be contemplated by the Board of Directors, whose only hope is that a speedy settlement on the lines of international justice of the May 30 affair, may be effected and the moral support of the foreign friends of China abroad is earnestly solicited and will be heartily appreciated.

headline: Wharf Coolies Resume.
text: The majority of the wharf coolies have resumed. Many indignation meetings are being held as the result of the closing down of the Labour Unions. Agitators accused the Fengtien General of accepting foreign bribes. A female speaker endorsed the suggestion that efforts to compel the General to modify his policy should be made.

headline: SECURITY PACT. / FOREIGN SECRETARY'S SPEECH.
text:
British interest in the settled Continental situation, was emphasised by Mr. Austen Chamberlain at Birmingham. The Foreign Secretary expressed a little disappointment at the character of the German Reply with regard to the mutual pact, as it would involve a continuance of written communications instead of a personal conference to hammer out the agreement. Nevertheless he recognised the German desire to advance their own proposals. He was hopeful of a settlement of the question, which would remove a sense of fear of renewed peril and afford sensible relief throughout the world.

It must not be supposed that we have no interest in the relations of our neighbours, in their security or in the peace of Europe. Some people objected to our giving any form of guarantee regarding the existing French and Belgian and German boundaries, but the sanctity of those frontiers was the groundwork of our own protection. We had it in our power, by associating ourselves as guarantors of that peaceful settlement, to give a measure of confidence to France, Belgium and Germany, which they would never find in any instrument to which we were not the parties.

headline: A NEW BURRIS.
text:
The first instalment of a series of hitherto unpublished letters written by the late Mr. Walter H. Page during his American Embassage in London, and now obtained from the private files of the late President Wilson, appears in the June issue of "The World."

In a letter dated February 22, 1914, Mr. Page declared that the feeling was strong in this country that the United States Government wished to prohibit European financial adventurers from exploiting Central and South America because we wish to exploit them ourselves!" "Men who have looked on at the parcelling out of the world and have taken part in it don't all at once think of the people that dwell on a land before they think of the land itself," the letter continued. "This is one interesting test of the great distance that the Old World thought is behind our thought in all matters of popular welfare. I am constantly surprised to discover how far ahead of them we have travelled.

"I told the German Ambassador (Prince Lichnowsky) here the other night that we wished no more territory, and didn't want Mexico as a (free gift of the gods. He looked at me—a mere glimpse of one one hundredth of a second—and I saw this flit across his mind: 'You are a consummate liar or an impossible idiot.' In this kingdom the Tories do not understand the vocabulary that the Liberals use, and the Liberals wouldn't understand our democratic vocabulary. They have no idea of our notion of freeing men."

HISTORIC THE GOVERNMENT. Writing on May 1, 1014, Mr. Page described a conversation which he had at dinner with "a remarkable old lady, the daughter of one earl and the wife of another," who was "full of the notion that a democracy was necessarily vulgar and venal." "This old Tory notion of the corruption of the United States," Mr. Page's letter proceeded, "crops up oftener than you would think, and there lurks in it a sort of aristocratic hope that it will yet fail. But this is not an active anti-American feeling. It is rather a social resentment of the success of a democratic order of society. It is, I am sure, becoming more and more merely a subject of historical-interest—a curious survival that has no important meaning now."

Of a conversation with a Welsh bishop, who spoke "with shame and grief and horror of the wicked effort to disestablish 'God's Holy Church' in Wales and thus strike the first blow, towards the dethronement of his most gracious Majesty himself, Mr. Page wrote: "I swear he almost persuaded me to be a Tory." He continued:

"When the appeal is made in the name of English history and of your vision of this conquering race sending its soldiers and sailors and bishops and adventurers to blazo ways for civilisation on all sens and continents, it was that sort of an appeal that almost persuaded me to be a 'Tory'—till I got out in the open air and drove over the bridge to Westminster Hall, where, at 11.30 at night, the political partners of the bishops were hectoring and insulting the Government in a way that ought to have put the Tower in commission again."

"They use this historic appeal—they use everything—to cling to their privileges, often you feel with all sincerity. They are English history; they are England; they are the Empire; and they point to all the strength and glory of the past to prove it—for all the world exactly as our own tariff nabobs used to point to every good thing in our land as of their bringing, and as Wall Street used to prove that the prosperity of Yuda Dam in Arizona was of Wall Street's creation."

Nobility not "played out." "In our country," continued Mr. Page, "there is nothing noble or convincing in the beneficiaries of civilize: as a role, they are more sponges, with no more moral quality than sponges. Here they are in many respects the finest flower of British civilisation. Physically they are remarkable. The noble families of this kingdom have practised engenies pretty well for centuries. Now and then there's a dirty duke's (I know one who is the biggest liar in England) now and then a noble lord marries a chos girl or gambles away his ancestral vectrals. But, after all, they are few.

"The race isn't degenerating: I imagine that the noblemen of this generation on this island include more first-class men than those of any preceding generation. The error they make is to conclude that they owe their vitality to their special privilages. If you look at the House of Commons, the Opposition believes show more men of chity, of good mettle, of individual power than they. Governments you have they have every adornment of newspaper rights in the House of Commons and stock in the same reservation."

headline: SHANGHAI APPROVES / MURDER DONE?
text:
SEQUEL TO HECTIC NIGHT.

HONGKONG'S FIGHTING STRIKE MEASURES.

SIMILAR POLICY REQUESTED:

MILLIONAIRE AND POLICEMAN.

The emergency measures adopted in Hongkong for dealing with strikers have aroused the ire of the Labourites at Home, but judging from editorial articles and the correspondence columns in the Shanghai newspapers, they are looked upon as the very thing for bringing the Chinese involved to their senses.

Donald Parsons, a millionaire member of the Stock Exchange, was celebrating so industriously amongst the cabarets that a policeman had to see him home.

Parsons invited the policeman inside, and the officer later retired with the members of the household, only to be awakened by the smell of smoke. He quickly phoned for firemen, who failed to arrive before Parsons and his son Vivian had been burned to death. The police are investigating what promises to become an amazing murder mystery, committed right under the policeman's eyes, even though they were closed.

"We adhere to our opinion that, if the strike can die a natural death, it had better be allowed to do so. If it can be broken by means of passive resistance, there will be the less heart-burning and bitterness afterwards. And if General Shing will act up to the threat of his own proclamations, put down the unions and suppress the intimidation, the workers would go back to their work with alacrity. Welcome news was received last night that he had caused six agitators to be arrested and there are other indications that his forbearance is reaching its limit. It needs only that he should shoot one intimidator, to make the rest understand that their game is up. But if he does not take action on resolute lines, then it will become necessary for the Settlement authorities to do so. Already it begins to be felt by persons in a position of responsibility that the strike and boycott can only be ended by a display of force. And if that line is reluctantly decided upon, there are plenty of ways in which it can be adopted. Why, for example, should the Settlement continue; by means of volunteer labour replacing the strikers, to supply water and light to Chapel, the headquarters of the strike? And why should the Chinese workmen who will not allow their fellows to work—every office probably knows whom it has to thank for this among its own former employees—be permitted to reside in the Settlement free to carry on their silent terrorization? As for those convicted in the Mixed Court, we cannot unfortunately use the "cat" but there are plenty of other more appropriate punishments for them, as Hongkong has shown.

The putting of agitators to "useful if unpleasant duties" in connection with the sanitation of the Colony has particularly met with approval as a fitting punishment, also the campaign conducted against intimidators and the banishment of idlers.

"One of our correspondents to day has obtained some extremely interesting information as regards Hongkong's way of dealing with strikers and intimidators, writes the North China Daily News." A good deal more might be told, but the censorship imposed in Hongkong is very strict and since the Government of the Colony does not wish to let out such information by the usual channels, we have no wish to defeat its policy by divulging what has been obtained from travellers. In a word, however, it may be said that the strike in Hongkong is being fought; not just played with; and the results of this were seen a day or two ago in the brief telegram saying that the volunteers for essential services had been demobilized, implying that regular labour was now available.

headline: CHINESE PROCLAMATIONS.
text: Simultaneously Mr. Arthur Sowerby returns to the charge with his demand for a forward policy, asking if we are still in the same mind as when a week ago we deprecated the line he wished to take. And yet another correspondent details a number of measures which might be taken to break the boycott. The answer to Mr. Sowerby is that a week ago things may have been different from what they are to-day. In point of fact they were. At that time it appeared that the strike funds were running out and that General Shing Shi-lien's proclamations might be expected to have an effect on the intimidators. With regard to the latter we have been waiting patiently. It is difficult to belliave that a man in General Shing's position can speak so plainly as he has done and not give effect to his words. Surely he must "lose face" by falling to do so to an extent far worse than any unpopularity he might earn with the riff-raff by acting sternly in defence of law and order. headline: SAFE TO RETURN.
text:
ANTI-FOREIGN FEELING OVER?

LATEST CHINA COAST NEWS.

Conditions in Hainan Island have been quiet during the past month. When the Canton trouble occurred it was feared that an outbreak against foreigners might happen here. All the English and American women and children left for Haiphong where they have since been. It is now thought safe for them to return and the present week will see most of them back. They have appreciated the hospitality of the Hotel de L'Europe even if the weather there has been hotter than that of Hoihow.

headline: (official) Extortion.
text: While writing the above I was called out to see a Chinese friend who came to tell about a raid on a small village by some soldiers near Sivuni. The local leader of the militia was in need of funds. These leaders are in many cases friends with the government and the robbers. The soldiers robbed the village and found no one except a few men and women who did not run. Ten of the men were taken to the yaman and they will be released if $1,000 is paid. Being poor farmers they could pay no such sum. Yesterday two were taken out and shot and the eight men were taken out to view the execution. For the past ten days the men have been fled up and beaten thrice daily and almost starved. To-morrow four men are to be taken out and shot unless the thousand dollars is forthcoming. Of course no trial was held, but the officials must get money even if a few poor people are killed! How can our Chinese friends expect foreigners to give up extraterritoriality when some Chinese people have no law or justice?

headline: Motor Car Progress.
text: The boycott against English and Japanese goods has not made much headway. The merchants are permitted to sell all the goods they have in stock and there are few steamers to bring in new goods. The merchants have exempted machinery, matches, cotton thread, kerosene and gasoline from the boycott. The auto companies have been concerned lest their cars would have no gasoline. During the past three years there has been great progress in the making of auto roads and there are at present over seventy motor cars in Hainan. At the present rate it will not be long before there will be roads all over the island. The official of Kheng-Dong, Oang Dai-fong, has been a leader in the building of motor roads. He has been a district official for the past four years and built the road to Kachek. He has also constructed modern markets and public schools. It is reported that he has lost his position and that a Mr. Kiang, a native of that district, is to take over the duties of "magistrate" this week. headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
CHINA AND THE WEST.

(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I read in yesterday's papers that Dr. Tso expressed his doubt as to whether Western Education was good for Chinese students. Western Education carries with it what we understand as Western Civilisation, and as I feel that Western Civilisation, as it stands to-day, does more harm than good to China, I agree with Dr. Tso that the Chinese have not benefitted from Western Education.

Yet, though firmly convinced that China was a happier but weaker nation when her own peculiar civilisation was uncontaminated by Western influence, I say that China has to move on with the rest of the world and has to try her best to adapt herself to a civilisation which is as different from her own as West is from East.

No country to-day can keep to herself, much less China whose vast unexplored resources exercise a magnetic influence on people saturated with Western Civilisation. She has to learn to be as “Civilised” as her visitors and acquire what knowledge she can of Western Science, the concomitant of Western Civilisation. Western Science with its modern implements of War, is an invaluable asset to a nation in an age when, in spite of all that the advocates of Western Science can say, “Might is Right” holds as strongly as it did in the days when our ancestors dressed in animal skins stalked about with heavy clubs.

headline: JAIL SANITATION. / BERI-BERI OUTBREAK DUE
text:
TO FLIES

STRIKE DELAYS IMPROVEMENTS

Insanitary conditions at Lai-chikok Prison were referred to in the course of hearing of an enquiry yesterday into the death of a prisoner from beri-berl.

The spread of the epidemic in May and June throughout the prison was attributed by Dr. G. W. Pope, Medical Officer of Victoria Gaol Prison, to flies. The jail was badly constructed from a sanitary point of view, as in the main building, only ten yards separated the latrines and cookhouse. Buckets were used as containers in the former and it was almost impossible to keep flies from these and from subsequently contaminating the food. The flies probably had their breeding place in the village below the prison.

Capt. H. F. Bloxham, Assistant Superintendent of Prisons, spoke of the measures taken by the authorities to cope with the epidemic. As a result of a visit the P.C.M.O. paid with him to the prison, he received a minute from the P.C.M.O., attributing the outbreak to infection of food by flies and making recommendations with regard to moving the cause. Among them was the removal of the Chinese village at the foot of the hill on the eastern side of the prison which was responsible for the number of flies in the first place. In connection with this Mr. Bloxham said the resumption of the village would take place in September and steps were already in hand to fill in the swamp surrounding it.

As regarded the putting in-hand of other, improvements, an order had been placed locally for the manufacture of more sanitary-receptacles in the latrines and as it could not be fulfilled because of the strike, they were being made in the jail as fast as material could be obtained. Approval for the putting in work of adequate fly-proofing had been received and the D.P.W. had been requested to have it put in hand as soon as possible. A reply had been received that it would be commenced immediately labour was available.

The verdict returned by the jury regarding the death of the prisoner was in accordance with the medical evidence. No rider was added.

headline: "FIERY CROSS."
text:
ARRESTS ALL OVER GERMANY.

FRONTIER INCIDENT.

Berlin; Sept. 10.

The police have unearthed a complete list of members of the Fiery Cross mentioned earlier and have instructed the authorities all over the country to arrest all of the members.

The arrested include the well-known Nationalists ex-Lieutenant Hildebrandt, Dr, Huebner, and ex-Captain Klipproth.

The last-named was apprehended on the point of crossing the frontier into Holland in a motor car.

It appears the order was found-ed two years ago and played a great part in the revolt of the so-called Black Reichswehr which started in 1923 in the fortresses of Cuestrin and Spandau.

Thirty "Knights of the Fiery Cross" were arrested by the police who claim that they have discovered a dangerous extremist organisation of a thousand members. The founders of the new order are three Americans who are among the arrested men. They came to Germany to create an organisation on the lines of the Ku Klux Klan in order to liberate Germany from persons not "100 per cent. true Germans."

headline: URGENT NEEDS
text:
THE POLICY OF DRIFT CONDEMNED.

READER'S STRONG VIEWS.

From a correspondent who signs himself "J.C." we have received a letter dealing with local problems of the first importance. Owing to the pressure on our space to-day we are unable to publish the letter in full. Referring to the growing atmosphere of "tiredness and drift," J.C. writes:

"There is no excuse for any policy of drift, or for any easing down of our standards as regards the governance of the Colony. In one's wanderings round the city in the course of the day, one seems to notice everywhere a slovenliness and a slackness in the way that public work is being carried on. For example, the streets, before the strike, were always clean and well swept. Now, particularly at tram stops, they look as if they were never swept, or as if the cleaning up and washing away of rubbish depended on the wind and rain. Let one cast one's eyes up the side streets when going along the Praya East on a tram, and notice what a fearful state some of them are in. Not to spin out, what I have said about street cleaning, applies to most of the jobs that are in progress."

"Now let us leave the present and take a long view of the future of Hongkong. Surely by now the Government must have realised the public are not children and that it is quite safe to take them into their confidence as regards the broad outlines of their policy. We all applauded when the rounding up policy was inaugurated, and we can all see what a beneficial effect it has had, particularly in the criminal courts. What we would all like to know—and undoubtedly we are entitled to know—is what the policy is going to be in the future. Are we going to drift back to that miserable policy of admitting the lame, the halt and the blind, the criminals and Bolsheviks, who all make of Hongkong a happy hunting ground? Or are we going to continue the policy of frequent cleanups, followed by the deportation of undesirables? What is the real objection to a poll-tax?"

J.C. points out that the French and Americans are both able to collect a poll tax in neighbouring colonies and suggests that the revenue, amounting to millions even with the poll tax as low as $2 per head, would go a long way to fill “the nasty gap” the depression will make in the Colony's revenue.

"Is one a pessimist if one assumes that British business houses, both old and new, are going to be very badly hit in some cases, perhaps, even to drop out?" J.C. asks next. "Granted that, it means a big reduction of staffs, from top to bottom. One knows, also, that a very large proportion of British coast shipping is laid up, and that Norwegian, Japanese and others have got such a footing that it will be a long time before British shipping is running again at any profit. That means, in conjunction with the starvation wages paid in Norwegian and Japanese ships, that there will be any number of Britishers out of jobs on the China Coast."

Is it not time that some notice was taken of the increasing numbers of Russians who are flocking into the Colony? There was a time when Russians were forbidden to land here on the ground that Hongkong did not wish to have to face the problem that Shanghai was up against. It is quite time that our own problem of what is going to happen to our own people, who will be axed, during the coming winter, were thoroughly gone into. After pointing to the fact that Russians are doing work which could be done by Britons, J.C. remarks: It is quite time that the Government began to get busy on this problem of unemployment. They have the example of Singapore before them, and there is at present nothing to show that Hongkong may not have to endure just as long and severe a storm as Singapore faced, with practically the same problems. "Turning to another side of the problem, are the public not entitled to know what the Government are doing to trim ship and shorten sail, to meet the storm? After the recent inquests, with the summings up and the Juries riders, we all know that things in the P.W.D. are pretty rotten. Is the Government going to ignore the suggestion for an expert's inquiry into the working of the P.W.D.? With the lean times ahead, such inquiry should be extended into the whole question of whether the Colony is getting anything. headline: IN ROYAL ESTATE.
text:
KARAKHAN'S ARRIVAL IN HARBIN.

V SUMPTION'S CAR FROM C. H. R.

Just two years ago, Mr. L. M. Karukhan was met in Harbin, on his arrival from Moscow, by an enormous crowd of people. He was yesterday greeted by the Soviet citizens's of Harbin in such a manner as Kings and Emperors are accustomed to. A special train of eight cars, including the now celebrated No 56, was sent specially to Chingchun to bring him to Harbin and many representatives of the Russian Consulate and the C. B. R. went to meet him. Thousands of people crowded the roads to the Harbin railway station and literally hundreds of motor cars fought their way through the crowd. As the train steamed into the station, the symphony orchestra played the strains of the "International" and all eyes were fixed on car 56, where, however, only a Russian soldier was to be seen. Mr. Karukhan and suite happened to be in the observation car at the end of the train. As he descended from the curring, the air was rent with motor sirens and horns and the hurrabs of the thousands of people. He entered the large arrival room where fruit and champagne were served and he was introduced to heads of the Railway Departments and to the Chinese administrative chiefs. During this reception the brass band from the Railway Club played selections. After a quarter of an hour, the police made a road for the Soviet ambassador and his family, who entered motor cars and drove to a railway house which has been put at his disposal. Last night a banquet was served at the Chinese Administration quarters, and to-day there are three special fetings to Mr. Karakhan. The first is a lunch at the Railway Workman's Club, the first that this Club has ever given, the second a five o'clock ten at the Railway Club for the hands of all the railway departments and this evening a grand banquet at the Railway Club. To-morrow morning Mr. Karakhan leaves for Moscow, travelling in the special train as far as the frontier and in his special car right through to the end of the journey. The fitting up of this car has cost the C. B. R. a sum of thirty thousand dollars and no crowned head, has ever had such a sumptuous carriage to travel in.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE. / SHAMEEN SCUTTLE
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail.

Sir,—A paragraph is going the rounds of the papers to the effect that Shameen merchants, other than British, have been considering moving their offices from the Shameen to the Chinese City. This is the outcome of the strike committee's announcement that the boycott would be continued against British goods only. Furthermore, a meeting of consuls was held on Shameen from which only the British Consul was absent, to go into this question of removing. Now to put an item of news like that into the paper with no explanation as to what the real significance of the news is, shows a lack of consideration on the part of the paper towards its readers.

Perhaps you could elucidate whether my interpretation of this item is correct or not.

To begin with, is it, as it certainly appears to be, a case of gross discourtesy toward Sir James Jamieson?

Let it be remembered that Sir James is not only the Doyen of the Foreign Consuls at Canton, and head and shoulders, in ability and experience, above the rest, but he is also—as Representative of Great Britain who, with France, owns Shameen—in the position of the landlord by whose act of grace the nationals of all Foreign Powers are privileged to rent a single foot of land on Shameen at all.

Again, is it, as it appears to be, a case of the rats leaving, what to them appears to be a sinking ship?

If it is not that, what is the reason of this unseemly anxiety on the part of the foreign firms to make a very undignified scuttle out of Shameen at the crack of the Bolshevik's whip?

Whatever the reason may be, the fact apparently remains that such a course is contemplated by these chicken-hearted merchants, who seem to have lost all secrecy of dignity and decency in their hurry to disassociate themselves from Great Britain, and to scramble for such crumbs of her Trade as their Bolshie friends will allow them to have.

And these are the people, who Mr. Baldwin informed us he is trying to work with in straightening things out in China, and on whose convenience and consent we are all waiting.

No wonder it has been a long wait.

When will Great Britain awake to the fact that she has to fight for her own hand if she wants anything in this world?

All the other nations are quick enough to profess undying friendship when they are in need, but when the shoe is on the other foot, they pass by on the other side like a certain well-known character in the Bible.

General Smuts states the case in his usual succinct way. "Why not go forward to the uncertain future hand in hand with the young nations of the Empire, rather than with the spectres of Europe."

If this China business does not open the eyes of the Home Government to who are our friends, and who only pretend to be, for their own purposes, they must be singularly slow and unspicious.

In any case, let us, sincerely hope that if all these people do leave Shameen and set up in Canton, they will be clearly made to understand that the hospitality of Shameen is not open to them the next time that trouble comes along, and when they come begging at the gates to be admitted into safety.

Finally let us recognise the fact that there is was deadly a form of warfare being waged to-day as that we call The Great War. The difference, as far as we Britons are concerned, is that in the Great War we faced the unpleasant facts, took our coats off and got down to it. In this "peace war" the majority of us don't seem to realise that there is anything happening out of the ordinary, and while John Bull peacefully doses and dreams of perpetual friendship with all and sundry, these same "friends" are working overtime to grab the heritage that has been built up through the centuries and handed on to us.

Oh! For a Palmerston! Yours, etc.

A notable visitor to Falkirk (Scotland) in mall week was Mr. Robert Dollar, the San Francisco millionaire and shipping magnate, who was re-visiting the scenes of his boyhood. Mr. Dollar has been a great benefactor to his native town of Falkirk, and on this visit was entertained to lunch by the Provost.

headline: WHO'S WHO.
text:
SWATOW PERSONALITIES

CHAN KWING-MING'S HELPERS

General Chan Kwing-ming's army in and around Swatow is estimated to be from 15,000 to 50,000 strong. Canton places the rival strength at the lower figure whereas pro-Chan adherents claim the bigger one. It is difficult to say what the actual fighting numbers are but from 20,000 to 30,000 would not be far off the mark.

Of this army from which much is expected the major portion is not actually subordinate to Chan but is under Lin Fu, a Kwangsi general who is allied to Chan in that they are both opposed to the Kuomintang at Canton. At least one of Chan's armies—the sixth, according to the last official designation—is now under Yeung Kwan-yu at Waichow and Yeung nominally surrendered to General Hsu Shung-chi a few months ago. At any rate, the pro-Chan faction is inferior to the Canton forces in equipment, arms, ammunition, artillery and the other important attributes of modern warfare.

Ip Kue is Chan's Chief Director of Operations. He it was who successfully carried out the coup of June 15, 1922, which finally resulted in the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen fleeing to Hongkong on a British gunboat. To suit Lin Fu, Chan Kwing-ming had to make Ip Kue's title relate only to the "East River territory." Ip does not have more than a few thousand bayonets but Lin's strength is over 10,000. Lin is Chief Director of Operations in the Chiu-Mui area and Hung Shiu-lun is the assistant. Hung is a native of Hunan. Years ago he was the defendant in a protracted extradition case in Hongkong when he was sought by Tuchun Lung-Chai-kwung and was not released till the proceedings had reached the Supreme Court. After the disappointments of a few years ago he was alleged to have become a monk. If that was so, he has since renounced ecclesiastical orders. The ex-monk also has a few thousand soldiers.

Hung Leuk is another of the senior officers and like Ip Kue and Hung Shiu-lun, he is considered one of Chan's personal subordinates. His army suffered heavily in the last campaign and has since been resting. During the absence of Ip Kue, he has really carried on for Chan Kwingming, having occupied the post of commander of the Yuet Kwan (pro-Chan army) headquarters.
