headline: THE IMMEDIATE PROBLEMS.
text:
First, with regard to Shanghai we are about to hold a public judicial inquiry into the riots. This is not an attempt to whitewash anybody, but is designed to bring all the facts out and ensure that justice shall be done. We have tried to get the Chinese Government to appoint representatives, but, much to our regret, the Chinese Government has refused.

Secondly, negotiations have been begun between the diplomatic bodies at Peking and the Chinese Government on subjects connected with Shanghai though not in connection with the actual riots. One of the subjects so discussed is the representation of the Chinese on the Municipal Council of Shanghai. At present the rate-payers elect the Council, which in practice means the Europeans. The Council consists of Europeans, Americans, and Japanese, and its present chairman is an American.

Thirdly, the British Government seeks to arrange a collective answer by all the Powers to the various Chinese Notes that have been presented, and particularly to the Note of July 24, in which the Chinese complained of the unfairness of the various treaties. Our wish is that this Note should be a declaration of policy by all the Powers. The first thing is to carry out the conclusions of the Washington Conference, and the first step is the Tariff Conference, which is now very soon to be held. At the same time there follows the setting up of a commission to inquire into the whole subject of extraterritoriality.

The collective answer of the Powers to the Chinese Notes is still under consideration. It will be a slow business, because a complete consultation involves sixteen Powers with a right to be consulted. The British Government lays the great stress upon this collective action, and has the greatest interest in any action being collective, because there is an attempt in China, largely due, as the Foreign Office believes, to Russian Influence, to isolate Great Britain and represent her as the villain of the piece. headline: YEAR'S TOUR.
text:
HONGKONG'S INTERESTING VISITOR.

An interesting visitor to Hongkong is Dr. Maurice Parmelee, Ph.D., the well-known sociologist, psychologist and author, who is making a year's tour of the East to study the political problems of Japan, China, India and Egypt as they affect his special subjects.

Dr. Parmelee is one of the most distinguished of the younger thinkers in the field of social and psychological science.

His books are lucid expositions of subjects of the deepest human interest. His principal lifework is a series of treatises, of which his "Science of Human Behaviour" is the first, upon the evolution of human nature and culture culminating in our civilisation.

He is a graduate of Yale and Columbia Universities and has been professor of sociology, economics and anthropology, at the Universities of Minnesota, Missouri, and Kansas, and the College of the City of New York. He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science and a member of the Institut International de Sociologie.

His lectures before scientific and lay audiences both in Europe and America have, for years been models of ease and clarity, combined with sound scholarship and stimulating originality.

A representative of the United States War Trade Board in London and taking part in the administration of the Blockade, Dr. Parmelee was the only American who was Chairman of an Allied committee—the Allied Rationing Committee. From 1920 to 1923 he was an economic adviser in the Department of State and conducted investigations for the Department, travelling extensively in Europe. His new book, "Blockade And Sea Power," is the result of this unusual experience. Dr. Parmelee's book is of great historical importance and a valuable contribution to the discussion of the problems of sea power, imperialism, and the evolution of a world state which are of the utmost significance for the prevention of war and the promotion of harmonious international relations.

Among the subjects on which Dr. Parmelee lectures are: the development of "personality, the conflicts in human nature, art and the natural life, the modern Humanitarian Movement, the abolition of poverty, the influence of civilisation upon crime, sea power and the world state, and the economic collapse of Europe.

Described by Havelock Ellis as possessing "a temperamentally cool, judicial, deliberate mind, with a seemingly instinctive impulse to balance and weigh all the considerations that are brought before him, Dr. Parmelee's books include "The Science of Human Behaviour," "Criminology," "Poverty and Social Progress," and "Personality and Conduct," all of which have been highly praised in the Press, especially his book on criminology which presents a comprehensive survey of the whole field of criminology from the point of view of Social Control. A recent issue of the "Times Literary Supplement" mentions that Dr. Parmelee's "Blockade and Sea Power" will be published in London during the autumn by Messrs. Hutchinson.

Dr. Parmelee, after visiting Japan, went to Peking, and there met most of the outstanding personalities in the present situation including Karakhan himself. Dr. Parmelee went to Kalgan to see General Feng Yu-hsiang. Other places he visited were Shanghai, Soochow, and Hankow. In Shanghai he narrowly escaped being involved in the rioting of the 7th — had he been two minutes earlier he would certainly have shared the fate of the American who was brutally assaulted—and in Soochow he narrowly escaped serious trouble through a ricsha-coolie trying to exploit the strong anti-foreign feeling to extort exorbitant squeeze.

Dr. Parmelee leaves Hongkong to-morrow for Java, whence he goes to Malaya, Burma and India. He proposes to spend several months in India and then to go to Egypt, returning to America after nearly a year's absence travelling. As soon as he returns to America, in February, Dr. Parmelee will begin a lecture tour in which his Impressions of the East will play a large part.

headline: Rensons for Acquisition.
text:
The reason why the Tug and Lighter Co., Ltd., is willing to sell and we are desirous of buying is that the tendency is for more and more of the lighterage business to come to us, as, since the boycott and scarcity of labour, storers of cargo have begun to rely on us to do the whole business of landing and storing in one transaction rather than lose time in going to the one Company for the landing and to the other for the storing. headline: CAPETOWN INCIDENT. / AUSTRALIAN PREMIER'S FIGHTING SPEECH.
text:

The departure of the “Arundel Castle” wirelessing “This is the way to go home” had an immediate effect on ports in South Africa, especially Durban.

The crews of several other ships are conferring on the position as a result of the sailing of the Arundel Castle.

headline: SEAMEN'S STRIKE.
text:
TRADE UNION CONGRESS DECISION.

STRIKERS GETTING TIRED.

The General Council of the Trade Union Congress has declined to interfere in the Seamen's strike.

Seventeen shipyard trade unions were invited to participate in the conference which decided to approach the Council, but the communication forwarded to the Council emanated from only six of the smaller unions. The remaining eleven refused to be parties to the request.

There are indications, as a result of the cumulative effect of the departures of vessels from Capetown, Durban and Delagoa Bay that the strike is rapidly breaking.

The majority of the men admit that they are sick of idleness, and are anxious to alleviate the sufferings of their families.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text:
The early end of the shipping strike is predicted, the only outstanding point being the strikers' demand for full pay during the strike which is likely to be waived. It is believed that the unanimous decision of the waterside workers to work all ships even if the strikers have been replaced will profoundly affect the situation.

-Reuter.

The steamers "Portcurno" and "Largolaw" have sailed from Durban. The steamer "Garth Castle," which was held up at Lourenco Marques, owing to the refusal of the crew to take the ship to sea unless the strike is settled, sailed with her original crew.

headline: TRAIL OF A PIN.
text:
BOY UNDER X-RAYS FOR TWO DAYS.

For two days doctors at the Metropolitan Hospital, Kingsland-road, N., have watched, by the aid of X-rays, a pin passing through, a five-veurs-old boy's body.

Albert Smith, of 4, Watson-place, Kingsland-road, swallowed the pin, which he was using as a toothpick, on Tuesday when he was left in the house alone. He went to a neighbour's house and told what had happened.

He was taken at once to the Metropolitan Hospital, where he was kept without food for two days, while the doctors watched the progress of the pin.

He was discharged cured and he went home to a big meal. If he had eaten anything after swallowing the pin, a "Daily Mail" reporter was informed, he might have pushed the point into the wall of his stomach and set up peritonitis.

headline: SAYINGPUN SCHOOL
text:
QUARTERLY REPORT.

Asked at the Legislative Council meeting yesterday by the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyonk as to when the work on the new Sayingpun School was expected to be completed, the Director of Public Works said he had not the papers with him to refer to the date on which the contract had to be completed but as work had been delayed two months because of the strike it would probably be two months later.

H.E. the Governor suggested that the hon. member should put a question down in order that the Director might answer it at the next meeting.

The following quarterly report on the work on this new school was laid before the Council.

Satisfactory progress was being made until the commencement of the present unsettled labour conditions; workmen have left the site and the work is necessarily proceeding very slowly at present.

The brickwork has been completed to the roof level and the tower has been carried up to a few feet higher than roof. The floor to top storey and also the verandah roofs are completed. Steel trusses over Science Block have been fixed and the roof timbering to both N. and S. Blocks is practically finished. Roof tiling has been commenced on the South Block.

The steel roof trusses over Assembly Hall are in position and internal plastering has progressed favourably.

The standard of work is good.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text:

To night and tomorrow there is screened at the Queen's Theatre a first National feature which was well received last night by reason of the finer points of appeal which those favourite screen artists, Anna C. Nilsson and Milton Miles, were able to do full justice to—"Flowing Gold," a drama of the oil fields.

The vindication of the honour of an ex-army officer to whom attaches the stigma of dismissal and his victory over his enemy in the struggle for supremacy in the oil fields plays an important part in the development of the story which is concerned with the fortunes of a family which after years of labour eventually hit it rich.

There are some fine scenic effects which are a triumph of the film producer's art, that, for instance, when the lightning strikes an oilwell and it disappears in a cloud of smoke comprising within wrecked timber those with whose fortunes the story is primarily concerned. Again there is the thrilling rescue scene when a cloud burst carries death and destruction with it by reason of the burning oil borne on the surface of the floods.

headline: “DISTRESSING.” / "NEED FOR CAUTION."
text:
The need for caution in dealing with the South China problem is stressed in a "Times" leader of August 21 which terms as "only too distressing" Hongkong's particular difficulties and the "effrontery of the Red Government of Canton was hardly to be borne." For that very reason great circumspection is necessary, states the article, as the Bolsheviks in Canton are obviously anxious to provoke some action by Great Britain which would turn the uncertain situation throughout China more definitely in their favour.

The river—that dreary river, on which so much has been done with British aid to suppress piracy and to make profitable navigation secure for all the nations—flows out from Canton, the chief commercial centre of South China, to Kowloon and to the island that not long ago was the very prosperous British colony of Hongkong, states the "Times." Hongkong and Canton are mutually complementary. Each depends in a large degree upon the other for its prosperity and even for its existence. Canton commands the trade of the interior, Hongkong is the highly organized medium for transforming that trade into an international asset, increasingly valuable alike to Chinese and to foreigners. One of the very serious features of the present phase of the Chinese crisis is the practical severance of normal communication between Canton and Hongkong.

headline: BOLSHEVISTS IN CANTON.
text: Through a movement engineered from Canton, the trade of the British island colony at the mouth of the river is paralysed, and the daily losses now amount to several hundred thousand pounds. This movement is associated with the general anti-British movement in China, of which the Whit-suntide incident in Shanghai was made the pretext. But in Canton the opportunity was seized to give it a specific direction. Canton happens to be the birthplace and the home of the Kuomintang Party, which, in the declining years of its late leader, Sun Yat-sen, established a very intimate connection with the Russian Soviet Government. The extremist wing of this party, after strange vicissitudes during the chaotic civil war of the last few years, succeeded, also about Whit-suntide, in recovering control in Canton with Bolshevist aid. A confessedly Red Government is now established in Canton. It is supported by Soviet Russians who act as instructors in the Wham-poa Cadet School and as advisers in administrative and revolutionary technique. Steamers from Vladivostok have passed Hongkong conveying to Canton Bolshevik agents and Bolshevik supplies. The Canton merchants probably object to the present régime and would like to side with the more moderate but now apparently helpless wing of the Kuomintang. But the merchants can do little now, less even than when, in the days of the civil war, the Volunteer Corps financed by them was thrust aside. The Red faction, reinforced by Russian revolutionary and military aid, is in complete control of Canton and the Kwangtung region. The activities of this Government are now violently directed against Great Britain, the immediate object being the British colony of Hongkong at the mouth of the river.

headline: THAT DECREE.
text:
The general strike among the large population of Chinese workers in Hongkong and the irregular boycott of British goods have already done great harm to the colony. The Canton revolutionaries have something to show for their efforts. Now they have been emboldened to take a new step. They have published decrees forbidding the approach of British and Japanese ships to Canton and permitting other foreign ships to come only if they have avoided calling at Hongkong on their way. The penalty for infraction of the decree seems to be some activity of labour pickets and the prevention of loading or unloading. The decree is an open challenge. It is tantamount to defiant repudiation of treaties that have governed for decades the relations between the European Powers and America on the one hand and Southern China on the other. What can the Powers do about it, for if Great Britain and Japan are defied directly, all other Powers are indirectly condemned by the prohibition of access to any foreign ships that may dare to call at British Hongkong on their way up the river? This typically Bolshovist challenge must be confined warily. The Admiral Commanding the

China Station has gone up the river to investigate, and in the British concession on the island of Shameen, facing the city of Canton, we have a very gallant Consul-General, Sir James Jamieson, who knows his Cantonese through and through and is facing the extraordinary situation with great courage and unruffled humour. It would be the simplest thing in the world to retort by blockading the mouth of the river, admitting those who may be our friends and refusing access to declared enemies. But it must be remembered that the real object of our enemies in issuing these decrees may be to provoke Great Britain into taking exactly some such step as might be construed as a war measure. The Nationalist extremists in China, the Bolsheviks, and their friends throughout the world are using all their resources of propaganda to demonstrate the ridiculous thesis that Great Britain has aggressive, military or imperialistic designs on China. Our Australian Correspondent reported that even a broadcasting centre in Queensland has been used for this purpose. The situation in Hongkong is only too distressing. The effrontery of the Red Government of Canton is hardly to be borne. For that very reason great circumspection is necessary. While the Admiral investigates and while Sir James Jamieson remonstrates with Dr. Wu, the Canton Foreign Commissioner, son of the well-known Dr. Wu Ting-fang, it will be well to let ships of all nations go up the river and test in practice the actual efficacy of this impudent decree.

headline: PROVOKING.
text:
There is the more need to proceed cautiously since the Bolsheviks in Canton are obviously anxious to provoke some action by Great Britain that would turn the uncertain situation throughout China more definitely in their favour. Canton is practically independent, and its military forces are pushing out into Yunnan and Fukien. But the Yangtsze Governors seem to be combining to maintain order and to check the dangerous and destructive anti-foreign agitation. In the north, so far as Chang Tso-lin, the Lord of Manchuria, is disposed to exert his influence, the situation is comparatively favourable for the moment. But near Peking, Feng Yu-hsiang, the general of Christian professions, Bolshevik associations, and violently anti-British sentiments, is steadily strengthening his position, securing control of Shensi and Kiangsu, pushing out towards the Musulman West, and all the time vigilantly maintaining his communications, not alone with Karakhan and Borodin in Peking, but along the roads for the supply of munitions of war that lead down from Soviet Siberia through Kalgan. General Feng is in close sympathy with the Government now in power in Canton. The success of a provocative manoeuvre there might give him the opportunity, for which he is perhaps waiting, definitely to seize power in Peking. He dallies yet. In the meantime the wavering Peking Government, after having subsidized the Shanghai strike and given direct and indirect encouragement to the anti-foreign agitation, has found it possible to yield for once to an impulse of common sense. It has decided to invite the Powers to the Tariff Conference provided for in the Washington Treaty of 1922. The probability therefore is that the Conference will actually take place in October, and the Powers may at last have a real opportunity of concerting their policies in regard to China. It must be admitted that Great Britain and Japan stand somewhat alone in the intensity of their concern in the present dangerous situation, and it is something for us in these difficult days to have an old friend at our side. It must, however, be repeated again and again that while little that is effective can be done without the co-operation of all the Powers, a wise and vigorous British initiative is necessary above all. It is good news that Sir Ronald Mackay, our Minister in Peking, is so far recovered from his illness that he will shortly be able to return to his post. Mr. Austen Chamberlain came up to town specially to deal with the Chinese problem. In such a crisis as this we cannot afford for a moment to be off our guard.

Sydney September 26. — The Prime Minister, Mr. Bruce, addressing the Convention of the National Association, said Australia was faced with a greater menace than Prussianism, namely the destruction of law and order. He added that the Federal Government met with a flat refusal when it called on the New South Wales Labour Government to carry out the Community Depotation laws, which meant that the State was arrogating to itself power the law which was the Federal Government should pass.

headline: “THE SEA HAWK.” / BABATINI'S MASTERPIECE
text:
A fleet of five large vessels of sixteenth century design was built for First National's screen version of Rafael Sabatini's "The Sea Hawk," which comes to the World Theatre to-morrow. The picture, which has been given a great reception in America, was shown in the Albert Hall, London, on October 15. In other sea stories on the screen, schooners or steam vessels have been rented or purchased. But in "The Sea Hawk," the ships, which ranged from 90 to 192 feet in length, were specially constructed in the shipyards of San Pedro, California, under the supervision of Frederick Gabouri, an expert. Mr. Gabouri was assisted by more than 300 draftsmen, mechanics, riggers, carpenters, electricians, sailors, and labourers. With poop decks, grotesque figureheads, gaudily coloured sails, and old-fashioned cannon, the fleet affoated recalled the Pacific expeditions of Balbón, Megellan, and Cabrillo, three hundred years ago. Many of the scenes in "The Sea Hawk," as those who have read Sabatini's book will appreciate, had to be produced on the high seas. All the vessels were made seaworthy and equipped with motor power. One of the ships was a replica of an English frigate of 1500; a second, a Moorish galleas, and a third, a Moorish frigate. There was also a Spanish galleon and pirate craft. The Moorish frigate was propelled by over 200 men, four to six chained to each oar, and the other vessels had oarsmen in proportionate numbers. In order to accommodate the sailors, galley slaves, fighting men, principals, and technical workers required for the big battles at sea, Frank Lloyd producer-director, who, by the way, is a native of Glasgow, established a camp near an Algerian village on the west coast of Santa Catalina Island. Three naval speed boats and two large barges were used to carry supplies to the camp, which at times numbered as many as 750 men. Rafael Sabatini has been called the modern Dumas. His "Sea Hawk," as everyone interested in literature knows, has met with great success as a novel. Briefly, the narrative tells of a seventeenth century English baron, whose brother, seeking to divert suspicion for a murder, has him placed aboard a ship and carried to sea in the hope that he will be accused of "the crime." The British ship is captured by the crew of a Spanish vessel, and all on board become galley slaves. Later, the Spanish vessel is attacked and taken by the Moors, and among the latter, Milton Sills, leading man in a score of big productions, becomes a great chieftain and is known as "The Sea Hawk." This account falls a long way short of justice to the story, which embodies great sweeps of action, too full of detail for recital in limited space. Incident after incident of dramatic significance follow one on the other. The picture represents First National's most ambitious undertaking, which is a big statement to make on the heels of the wonderful reception accorded "Abraham Lincoln" by London and provincial newspapers.

headline: FRANCE'S DEBTS.
text:
The joint session of the Franco-American debt funding commissioners only lasted twenty minutes, the Americans indicating that they considered the French proposals inadequate and unsatisfactory.

The Americans handed over data, which the French spent the afternoon examining and preparing further proposal for presentation at next session.

Although the members of the American commission are not at all optimistic, it is understood that the majority feel that considerable progress has been made towards reconciliation of the divergent Franco-American views.

The "Journal" publishes a report from Washington that M. Caillaux has telegraphically informed M. Painleve on the state of the debt negotiations and the concessions he reckoned on making. He stated that the American counter proposals claimed maximum annuities of $120,000,000 compared with the 80,000,000 contemplated by M. Caillaux.

The “Le Matin” publishes a report for the same capital stating that the Americans presented a totally unexpected claim for the payment of interest on $245,000,-000 which the United States treasury advanced to the Bank of France which it demanded should not be regarded as a political loan but a commercial loan, similar to the Bank of England's credit to the Bank of France.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
STREET TRAM NOISES

(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—Exercising — that's the word describing the noise the street cars make when turning the corner, out of Russell Street into Persicival Street. I said 'What for', to a car conductor one morning. headline: HOCKEY.
text:
CLUB'S TRIAL MATCH.

Yesterday afternoon at the Marina Ground, Kowloon, a trial Hockey match was played between two teams of the Hongkong Hockey Club.

The Match was fairly well contested, although "Whites" captained by J. Lammert had the lead throughout the whole game, and eventually won by three goals to one. The late start made play towards the end very difficult owing to approaching darkness.

The match started with Whites pressing and after ten minutes' play, from a good forward movement Faers opened the score. The game then settled down to a very evenly contested match, neither side adding any further score before halftime. The second half opened with a brilliant rush by Vallack and Lammert, the latter netting, giving Whites an additional lead. This woke Colours up and they pressed hard with the result that they scored. Lammert, however, once more got going and put through another goal five minutes later. Lammert had the misfortune to lose a fine opportunity just before the end when after a fine run down, owing to the failing light, he just missed an open goal. The whistle blew shortly after.

headline: OPEN LETTER. / CHINESE ADDRESS TO SOLDIERY.
text:
THE CANTONESE PEOPLE.

Mr. Leo Chung-jun's second letter to the soldiers in Kwang-tung has been translated and sent to the "China Mail" for publication, inter alia, as follows:—

Since the arrival of Red Russians in Kwangtung through the invitation of Cheung Kai-shek, Wong Ching-wai and others, they are regarded as “wolves getting admission into the house.” The Cantonese version that Cheung and Wong are fond of Communism which would menace Kwangtung does not sufficiently describe their faults and disclose their secrets. Speaking truly, they are taking the country's goods to be changed for. Soviet Russia's money and they are under the shelter of Soviet Russia. They are obeying the order of aliens.

Though I am not a wise man, I cannot keep in silence. I have repeatedly applied to my elders and brethren for their prompt action to save themselves from the fire and the deep and have earnest expectation towards the forceful soldiers. I have urged them to expel the bad elements by united strength and to relieve the villages without taking discrimination.

Now the Kwangtung Army of Chiu Yeung and Mui Yuen is advancing westward. The dawn of light appears in the clouds of East Kwangtung and the evil mist will soon dissipate. Then the thirty million people of Kwangtung will come to life again. The Kwangtung Army will not hesitate to relieve their brethren from danger and the Kwangtung people will prepare to welcome them having for long hoped to do so.

My elders and brethren, you should get up quickly to follow them. Do not put your hands into your sleeves and look on. If every man can exert his ability, the campaign to expel Reds will be successful. It is the action of self-salvation and not helping others. My elders and brethren are aware of this idea, of which I need not say any more. What I want to state is that all soldiers in Kwangtung, whether hosts or guests, who are being supplied by the Kwangtung people, have to do their duty by protecting the people. Seeing that the people are in such a wretched position, how can you delay your operations to relieve them? Moreover the Reds are pressing forward to exterminate the dissenters. Can you bend down your head to suffer; the rough treatment of Russian officers? To fight for the Cantonese who will extol your merit is better than to serve under the bad elements who are hated by many persons. It is unnecessary to argue which is right or wrong. To relieve Kwangtung is to relieve your country and to help others is to help yourselves. Our military officers must have understood this point. I hope you will rise up quickly to help the soldiers in the East River and to expel the bad elements from the Five-Rams City. You may attack them from different directions or start the battle in an inner part. The present time is the only opportunity of settling the whole province of Kwangtung and it is also the day on which the Cantonese are applying for your relief. If you still take no notice of their supplications, you will not be allowed to keep your present position on the other hand you will be eventually exterminated by those whom you keep company with. Every person beags the responsibility of the rise and fall of his province. You cannot force the public to follow your opinion on your certainly can choose the way of popularity. I expose my views for your decision.

headline: HONAM DEATH / SECOND ENGINEER IOST OVERBOARD.
text:
A EONCKONG RESIDENT

A distressing fatality involving the loss of the second engineer of the s.s. "Honum," Mr. David Mason, was reported on the return of that ship to Hongkong from Canton yesterday afternoon. It occurred in the early hours of yesterday morning as the "Honum" was lying at anchor off Shameen. The Second Engineer had attended ashoro n. performance of the "Broadensters" and was at the time (shortly after 1 a.m.) about to make fast to the "Honum" the painter of the sumpan which conveyed him from the shore. He is stated to have lost his balance and fallen overboard, disappearing from view at once.

As soon as those on board were aware of the disaster the alarm was raised and gunbouts in the vicinity trained searchlights on the spot, without, however, resulting in any sign of the missing engineer who, it is presumed, was drowned.

Mr. Mason had not been long in the employ of the Steambolt Company but was an old resident of Hongkong and has many friends here. The deepest sympathy is extended to the relatives, who include Mrs. D. Harvey, of Kowloon.

Apart from this distressing mishap the voyage of the s.s. "Honum" was without untoward incident. The same conditions prevail as heretofore, namely the strike pickets continue to patrol with vigilance in the vicinity of the steamer and prevent passengers being taken off. Chinese merchants and others who had made their own arrangements were able to leave the ship but some of the poorer class Chinese passengers were unable to do so and were obliged to return. 22 Europeans and 61 Chinese were carried on the voyage to Hongkong.

headline: EMPIRE NEWS.
text:
A complaint of insufficient Australian news published in Britain was the burden of a resolution moved by Sir Hugh Denison, New South Wales, advocating co-operation between Australian newspapers with the object of supplying the British Press with a service similar to the present service from Britain to Australia. Mr. Holtz, Victoria, in second-ing, advocated that other Dominions should be similarly linked up. Mr. Turner, Britain, moved an amendment pledging his conferees to do their utmost to secure the publication of more Empire news and stated that agencies and correspondents already gave British papers more Dominions news that they could use.

Several delegates argued in the same strain.

Mr. Woods, Canada, in supporting the amendment, agreed that this was the most that could be done. Lord Burnham lengthily explained the difficulties of British newspapers as regards cabled news and showed the difficulty of giving effect to the scheme embodied in the resolution. Sir, Denison accepted the amendment and as a substantive motion it was finally carried that in view of the growing importance of overseas Dominions, and in order to promote a better inter-Empire knowledge and understanding, members of the Conference pledge themselves to the utmost efforts to secure the publication of more Empire news than hitherto. Douhing with the release of Swatow from Red control and the probable effect that the success of this section of the Kuomintang will have on the prospects for settlement of China's political dissensions and disunity, the "Peking and Tientsin Times" comments as follows:—

moderate advance will be made in the direction of Canton, A great dent of preparation and re-organisation will be necessary before the anti-Bolshevist troops in eastern Kwangtung can hope to challenge the more efficient and well-armed units under the direct control of Borodin and his henchmen. The Peking Government, for various reasons, of which fear of the expansion of the influence of the present regime in Canton is the foremost seems anxious to help the moderate wing of the Kuomintang, and to give Chen Chiang-ming the assistance his army needs. But there are difficulties on both sides. The separatist tendencies of the Kuomintang have not been eliminated. Even though so-called moderates seem to be determined to continue this policy to compel the Central Authorities to give them a large share in the Government. The Citizens' Conference is obviously the faintest means of a settlement of China's political discussions and disunity, but the Kuomintang are not more sincere than the Anfuities in the proposed use of this instrument. Each wants to pack the Conference with arbitrarily chosen nominees who will serve the interests of the respective parties before they will consider the higher concerns of the nation. Peking cannot very well co-operate with the Kuomintang in a war on the Bolsheviks and refuse to co-operate in the Citizens' Conference. On the other hand, many of the Kuomintang leaders, who dispute the authority the Central Committee, have to walk warily. Both extremists and moderates are courting the favours and support of the numerous branches of the party in the provinces, and the Right Wing apparently feel that even a temporary alliance with the present Peking Government would deprive them of much of the sympathy they might otherwise obtain from the provincial committees. The tradition of separatism which has developed since the Republic—partly political and partly psychological—is not an easy thing to break down, in spite of all that the province has suffered since it broke away from Peking. There are internal differences, for which handicap prompt and effective action by the moderates. We cannot understand the hostility that still exists to Chen Chiang-ming, whose action in refusing to participate in Sun Yat-sen's much-mounted but fantastic Expedition against the North was perfectly right, as same as his chief's course was insane. But the hostility is there, whether it be justified or not. The Party leaders have done their best to make his name anathematic throughout the rank and file, and they cannot very well turn round admit they were wrong, and openly support his campaign. This attitude is based on no punctilious moral grounds. The stigma they have attached to Chen Chiang-ming others have attached to Marsha Feng Yu-hsiang, but that has no prevented the Kuomintang from carrying favour with the latter.

The whole situation is very complicated, and it is probable that the Kuomintang moderates will conduct their own propaganda campaign against the Reds, persuade Peking to keep its own counsel, and, if help must be given the troops now at Swatow and other parts of the province not directly under Canton's authority, to give that help secretly. If there were any evidence of disinterested and patriotic statesmanship, we might look to the Citizens' Conference to provide an amicable solution, but he Tuan Government, which has cunningly used the anti-foreign agitation to perpetuate its enjoyment of office, is not likely—without pressure from abroad—to use the instrument it has created for unselfish purposes. Every approach to unification hitherto has been marred by sordid motives. It will never be achieved that way.

headline: CHINA CABLES.
text:
TELEGRAMS TO INLAND PLACES

The Eastern Extension Telegraph Co. notifies that:—

Telegrams to Amoy, Fooahow and Shanghai as well as to all places in North China (Chihli, Shantung, Manchuria, Mongolia, etc.) are accepted and transmitted as usual.

Telegrams to Hankow will be accepted either with abbreviated telegraphic address or with full address and will be forwarded by wire to Peking and thence posted direct to addressees.

Telegrams to other places in Central China than Hankow and to Inland places via Shanghai, Amoy and Foochow will also be accepted and will, if fully addressed be posted direct to addressees from Peking, Shanghai, Amoy or Foochow respectively but if bearing abbreviated address may be retained until normal conditions are re-established.

All telegrams to places affected by the dislocation of the Chinese Telegraph Administration's service are, however, accepted at the senders' risk-only.

Warsaw, September 30.—The visit of Chicherin who is en route to a health resort in Germany was marked by a notable reapproachment between Poland and Russia. Chicherin was received and entertained by the President of the Republic, the Presidents of the two Chambers and the Prime Minister. He had a two hours' conference with the Polish Foreign Minister. The German Minister who was suddenly recalled from leave tried on several occasions to see Chicherin, but calls at the Soviet Legation were fruitless owing to Chicherin's other engagements.—Reuter;

London, September 30. — The Bakers' and Allied Traders' Association has sent a letter to Sir Kingsley Wood asking for an extension of time before the enforcement of the new regulations in regard to the use of boric acid in egg yolks imported from China. The association say that they propose to try out two new methods of preservation by packing in England and sending to China and then re-shipping here in order to see the effect of the various climatic conditions on the contents of the barrels. Sir Kingsley Wood, in reply, regretted that he was unable to hold out any hope of a further extension of time.—Reuter.

headline: MISCHA LEVITZKI. / WORLD FIGURE AT THEATRE ROYAL. / TO-NIGHT'S CONCERT.
text:
To-night at the Theatre Royal Hongkong has the opportunity of hearing a young man who has come to be regarded as a great figure in the pianistic world,—Mischa Levitski. From an obscure Russian boy, then a student of tender years showing exceptional talent, M. Levitzki has risen to the position of a great artist, being claimed as such by thousands everywhere.

At the great festival which was held recently in New York under the auspices of the Beethoven Society, to which all the great artists of the world belong, Mischa Levitzki was one of the two chosen to perform on that evening, the other being the great interpreter, Heifetz, and then as on all occasions his thoughtful and intellectual interpretations completely enthralled his audience.

Writing of Mischa Levitzki in the "Shanghai Times," "Tomasso" has the following comments to make:—

Two nights ago Mischa Levitzki played to a select company at the home of Mr. Strok, under whose management he appears in the East, and the impression he made then will last until he returns to give three concerts in November after a tour of India and Java where his arrival is, eagerly awaited.

I do not want here to dilate on the artistry of this young, debornair yet thoughtful interpreter of the world's greatest musical composers for the piano, but this I will say: Some time ago I took occasion to call the Shanghai lander's love of music to task, and for this act was overwhelmed with an avalanche of wrath which, somehow, affected me very little.

I still retain, the impression I had then, but will willingly deny the stability of it if Shanghai will show to Mischa Levitzki a tenth of the appreciation New York alone has shown to him since his debut there less than a decade ago when, for all his immature years, he showed the strength and vigour of a Hoffman, almost the brilliancy of a Paderewski and all the grace and delicacy of a Percy Grainger, the greatest musician which my own country, Australia, gave to the world.

headline: JAPAN'S ALARM.
text:
Plans which Chang Tso-lin, the Mukden warlord, has in hand for developing Manchuria and opening up rich land for more direct trade are thought by Japan to be a menace to its hold on Southern Manchuria and, incidentally, by Russia to constitute a menace to its hold on more northern districts.

The Tokyo correspondent of the "Daily Mail" states:—

While China, from Peking to Canton, is racked with anti-foreign rioting, boycotts, and demands for “freedom” from foreign supervision, Manchuria is proceeding calmly in its development, with the aid of foreign capital as well as foreign engineers and the use of foreign material and machinery.

Chang Tso-lin, the Ruler of the Three Eastern Provinces that go to make up the vast dominion of Manchuria, is boldly carrying out a scheme of railway construction that will treble the wealth of his provinces and give him an independence of communication that will double his military strength.

One line is to connect Mukden, Jehol, and Kalgan, and to consolidate under his rule the territory he gained in his recent war with Wu Pei-fu, which made him paramount in China. This line will furnish a new route into Peking. British engineers are now laying out the line, and material for a start on its construction has been purchased.

Take a map of North China and the two main Manchurian railway lines are seen to form a great "T" with the Chinese Eastern, from Manchuli, on the Siberian border, running south-east to Pogranitchafa, on the Ussuri border, forming the upper line of the letter, and the South Manchurian running south-west from Changchun to Dairen, as the vertical stroke.

headline: Rich Land.
text:
The traffic of this richest section of China, one of the greatest undeveloped corners of the globe, has been shared so far between Russia and Japan. Now its owner, ruler, the progressive Chang Tsollin, proposes to run a series of lines east and west, connecting with and feeding into the Japanese line, but capable of being linked up ultimately as an independent, self-sufficient system.

Two new lines are under way, one being the Taonan-Tsitsihar spur, to tap the territory of the Chinese Eastern, the other an extension of Chang's own main railway from Mukden north-east to Tungliac, via Changwu.

It can also later be linked up with the Chinese spur lines to the north and give Chang'an independent connection with the Chinese Eastern. Thus his plans not only threaten Russia's hold on North Manchuria but also Japan's hold upon South Manchuria as well.

The Taonan-Taitsihar line is one the Japanese desired to exempt from inclusion under the Consortium, claiming priority in any loans made for it.

Another line Japan fought to retain but ultimately abandoned, on the surface at least, is one to connect Mukden and Kalgan to the north of the Great Wall. This line will, besides opening up a vast territory of rich land, said to be particularly valuable as a poppy-growing country, yielding a superior grade of opium, be of the highest strategic value.

Through the Great Wall

When the line is built it will command all the roads from the north into Peking through the mountain passes and the Great Wall. It will also give control over the routes from Urga, over which now is believed to be passing Soviet military supplies for the "Christian General," Fang Yushian, alleged to be Moscow's ally against Japan, who, at least is playing Moscow's game to-day in China against Great Britain. It must necessarily be years before this line can be built, under present financial conditions in China, but the first link has been completed in the spur running from Chinchow, on the main Chinese Mukden Tientain line to Chaoyang, over which trains will be operating by the end of this year. headline: SHANGHAI COMMENT
text: One of our Hongkong contemporaries is waxing righteously — indignant in regard to a practice that is becoming increasingly prevalent in the Crown Colony as a result of the strike which has affected Hongkong so much, notes the "North China Daily News." When the general exodus of Chinese employed by foreigners took place in June, the house servants at Hongkong were among the first to go and, as it is now much easier to get into Canton than out of it, many of those who left Hongkong so light-heartedly three months ago cannot get back if they would. A certain number have, however, returned, but by no means a large proportion, and the shortage of servants—or at least trained ones—is still neutally felt. Now there come complaints that people whose servants have not returned are enticing away other peoples' servants who have either managed to get back or did not go away at all, and it is stated that even Government staffs are being preyed upon. The process adopted is an eminently simple one, and one that is most likely to make appeal to Chinese of the servant class—the offer of higher wages. The practice is strongly being condemned in Hongkong, where in view of the special circumstances of the Colony, it appears to be a lowdown practice and one that must be condemned. With those remarks, no reasonableண்டு can find fault, as also the statement that if things go on in the same manner wages will soar and domestic economies remain seriously on of joint long after the boycott bus finished. Certainly the practice of persons able to pay high wages, enticing the servants of people who are not, perhaps, able to pay as much is a mean one. Apparently, however, it is one of those things that nothing will ever stop, whether conditions be normal or otherwise. Servant-enticing is by no mean an unknown sport in Europe and America, and appears to be one of those phases of the Tenth Commandinent which will be violated so long as there are desirable men-servants and maid-servants for people to covet.

headline: “RED” MENACE.
text:
In an article appearing in "The Pubriot," Harriet Osgood Taylor, whose name is well-known in Hongkong through her former residence here—she is the wife of a former Harbour Master—and her appeals in connection with the work of restoring devastated areas in France, urges the Governments concerned to combat more resolutely the insidious influence of Bolsheviks in China, which she terms as the gruesest possible menace to China and civilisation itself. "The various wars between North and South," she states, the constant strikes (far too friendly handled by the British Government in Hongkong, as those who know say there) are all symptoms of the same disease—the virus of Revolution injected into body already disordered.

The article is headed "Renping the Whirtwind in China" and is as follows:

It is small satisfaction to one who still owns a house and other interests in the British Crown Colony of Hongkong and sees their value deteriorating steadily under the weight of trade depression caused by Chinese strikes and British Governmental weakness to be able to say, "I told you so," as regards the cause. But eighteen years residence in the Far East, in the Philippines, Japan, and Java, as well as in China, has shown me that until the several Governments concerned meet the challenge of the insidious force which is making for disintegration—often than not in the guise of wished-for reforms—civilisation itself as well as same government is threatened.

headline: ROOT TROUBLE.
text:
In one way or another the whole East is smouldering, ready to blaze. In the Philippines the United States now understand that they must clear out or govern. Unable at such a distance to do the latter, they will probably retire without loss of face —so important in the Orient—by selling the islands to Japan. This would be excellent for everyone, especially the Filipinos, who would be governed firmly and unsentimentally, while the Japanese, overcrowded to bursting it home, would here find room for national expansion, causing to arouse suspicion in America's, Australia's, and Holland's neighbourly breasts. The Dutch in Java live on the oversizzling lids of political as well as physical volcanos, and China's complete Bolsheviks would doubtless destroy them more effectively than even another Krukton eruption would. The French in Indo-China, the British in Singapore and Burma are equally threatened. Japan, the only Eastern nation which has realised the danger, but who, owing to the success of the sinister plot which ruptured the Anglo-Japanese Alliance and betrayed the British Navy in Washington three years ago, has at last been forced into the arms she wished to escape—of the blood-smeared Bolsheviks. The writings in China, as at home, have been many. Bolsheviks are now working openly where formerly they acted through secret societies. Flabbiness in dealing with the dangerous situation which has been permitted thereby to develop has hastened the crisis. Much nonsense is talked and written about "National Aspirations," "Reenochment of Foreigners," "Factory Conditions," "Child Labour," and all the rest of the formula to incite and excuse revolution. There may be some de-hided people who really believe in them, just as there were when Ireland was dismembered and the veins of the British Empire opened to ensure her slow but not painless demise. No one worth arguing with...believes it is anything but Bolshevism that inspires this trouble, which, wittingly or not—again as in Ireland, Egypt, and India—our own Government has complacently helped. In spite of a truncated navy, an unbuilt base at Singapore, a weak army, without our ally Japan, and, I fear, with false friends working against us in China, we must nevertheless act. Bolshevism must be destroyed, or it will destroy us. In finding a remedy for all ills, physical, moral, or political, the first thing to do is to discover the cause. Does China's history show any previous outbreaks of the virulent disease now ringing there which would suggest a remedy? The answer is overwhelmingly affirmative. The revolution now commencing there is like cancer; and just as the two men who recently announced the discovery of a virus which, in conjunction with an already-discussed state, in-line probable cause of that world scourge, so Mrs. Webster, in her remarkable series of books dealing with revolution, has discovered the germ by which, in conjunction with an already-discussed system, revolutions may be propagated. ALLEGED PREMATURE PUBLICATION.
surviving civilisation in the world, but it is not civilised to-day—it is barbarous. Its unnumbered millions are ignorant, superstitious, and oppressed as no other people; except Russians, are oppressed. China's whole history—in spite of its contributions to art, literature, and philosophy—like that of Egypt, is of a succession of conquests. She has been eternally ruled by aliens, who, conquering as much by the weakness and corruption of her own people as by force of arms, have in turn themselves been displaced by the same combination of degeneracy and venality at home, force and guile from outside. Modern history in China, as elsewhere, has been repeated itself, and although, after the Opinion Wars of 1840 and 1860, the war with Japan in 1894 and the Boxer rebellion in 1900, her nominal ruler was allowed to remain on the throne, her inner monde steadily deteriorated, and the secret power, silently working like poison in the body politic, prepared the unhappy country for its worst rule of all—the Republic and the brigands and Bolsheviks who have succeeded it. China's only honest rule in recent years has come from outside. The extraterritoriality granted to foreigners—briefly, that they should be tried by their own and not by corrupt Chinese Counts—has been, and more than ever now, a vital necessity. All her recent troubles have been propagated through secret societies, and, although this is well known, there seems to be a conspiracy of silence in the Press regarding it, especially in the present crisis. The Boxer Rebellion, with its outbreaks of anti-foreign feeling, was in itself as factitious as it was fatal to the policy it advocated of turning out foreigners. The Revolution, of 1911 was, from the Chinese point of view, braving of view-breaking up by civil war an empire which had existed for thousands of years—even more stupid. The nation has been warring against itself ever since—helped always by agitators working through trade guilds as well as through secret societies. As for the ostensible reasons for the present crisis, they can be dismissed as absurd and in China's own interest, should be. No one who knows conditions in China itself, as well as in the foreign concessions, believes in them. But things are too serious now for further yielding and sentimentality. If the Bolshevik agents who are organising this business are not destroyed, China itself will be. If any foreign States concerned, through apathy, jealousy, self-interest, or blindness, refuses now to face the ngry facts, yields in the smallest degree to the preposterous demands of the agents of that secret controlling force, Bolsheviks will slowly but surely triumph over the whole world. Not Treaty Ports and Crown Colonies will go down but whole civilisations. It is a world issue.

headline: CHICHERIN'S OUTBURST.
text: Signs of the Soviet's anxiety at Germany's participation in the Locarno conference are forthcoming in an interview with M. Chicherin published in the "Berliner Tageblatt," wherein the strongest anti-British sentiments are expressed. Chicherin said the present situation in European politics was the result of British enmity towards the Soviet and that England's Pact policy was part of her fundamental anti-Soviet activity. That was why Russia watched with growing concern how Germany was falling in the wake of the British plans. No doubt it was against the wish of the German Government, but it was questionable whether England would not succeed in forcing her anti-Soviet policy on Germany. So far as the pact campaign was concerned, England's aim was to obtain the position of arbiter of the Continent. Chicherin said he found comfort in the belief of the impending signature of the Russo-German trade agreement, which was clear proof of Germany's determination not to deviate from the principles of the Rapallo treaty.

The political police have arrested at Voynia, near the Soviet frontier, 80 persons belonging to a widespread spying organisation alleged to be acting in behalf of the Soviet, including government officials and soldiers.

headline: A THORNY TASK.
text:
Messages from Berlin and Locarno indicate that Dr. Luther and Herr Stresemann's task at the Pact Conference is rendered more difficult by the critical attitude of German newspapers and political parties.

The former particularly are protesting at the report of a possible German abandonment of objections to France's standing guarantee for the Eastern Pact in return for French concessions as regards the occupation of the Rhineland.

The Nationalists have even sent a prominent Reichstag supporter to Locarno, apparently to apply a, restraining influence on the German delegates' actions, if deemed desirable,

A Locarno message says that the German delegates are prepared to accept clauses dealing with general arbitration on all Franco-German questions of a. politico-juridical character.

headline: SNUB FOR REDS. / AMERICAN LABOUR'S SENSE.
text:
HOLDING ALOOF.

(Keuter's American Service.

The position of the American Federation of Labour in regard to the Russian labour movement was vividly indicated in a reply by Mr. Green, President of the American Federation, to an address by Mr. Purcell, M.P., representative of the British Trade Union Congress, who criticised the Americans as being the slowest in accepting the new social and political ideas, and hoped the American Federation would send delegations to Russia to establish close and fraternal relations with the Russian workers.

Mr. Green, amid the greatest enthusiasm, announced that the American Federation would never affiliate with the present Russian labour movement, and added: "We are not willing to pay the price of casting in our lot with a class that would destroy us if it could."

headline: FASCIST GRIP.
text:
BLOW TO RIVAL UNIONS.

The Fascist Grand Council has resolved that only Fascist Unions should be legally recognised as representing all classes of employers and workers; also that an industrial court should be established to regulate labour disputes, and that action by any one class should not be permitted, and any strike of State employers or political strike intended to intimidate the State should be punished as a crime.

headline: LINERS SAIL.
text:
CAPE SEAMEN'S STRIKE BROKEN.

DEPORTATION QUESTION.

Cape Town, October 7. The "Kildonan Castle" left for England leaving behind the men who deserted the ship.

The “Edinburgh Castle” and “Kenilworth Castle” are leaving for England on the 12th and 16th inst. after which there will again be a regular mail service to England.

The Supreme Court has granted an order restraining the deportation of 16 of the crew of the "Kildonan Castle," pending an appeal.

The strikers' attorney states that the Minister of Justice has undertaken that nobody will be deported before he is afforded an opportunity of showing that if he remains in South Africa he would not be a burden to the State.

A magistrate has sentenced 130 strikers on the steamer “Ballarat” to a month's imprisonment, but has granted bail pending an appeal.

headline: STRIKER KILLED. / COMMUNISTS' FUTILE T.ACTICS.
text:
FORENCH FIASCO, V (Reuter's Service.)

While the strike is a substantial failure, the Communists profited by the occasion to demonstrate and harangue their followers, leading to sharp scuffles with the police.

The strikers had a few casualties in several places, one man being killed at Suresnes where the genèchnes attacked the strikers who were trying to force an entrance into a factory.

A meticulous flight in the north-east of Paris ended in the arrest of a Communist. Doriat who was "wanted" on a charge of trying to seduce the troops at Morocco for which he was sentenced to 13 months' imprisonment and fined 3,000 francs in default.

headline: THE DISCORDANT NOTE.
text:
While the European delegates are doing their utmost in the interests of peace at Locarno, the German monarchists are striking a discordant note.

General Von Arninn, unveiling a regimental monument, referred to the "loyalty to our military oath which we swore to our war lord" and alluded to Germans' gratitude and unswerving loyalty towards the Kaiser.

Later, President von Hindenburg in field marshal's uniform drove up to the monument and took the salute of the Reichswehr Company of the nationalist organisations, regarding which the Republican Press is most indignant.

Meanwhile the German National extremist organs deplore the meagre results of the Locarno Conference and express the fear that the German delegation may be satisfied with vague promises from the Allies regarding Germany's vital demands.

headline: "VIA SIBERIA"
text:
One of the signs of the return to normal after the war was early considered to be the "Via Siberia" mode of travelling to the East, or the direction to this effect written on correspondence Only this week is it given as a piece of interesting news that a mail from Home arrived in a record transit of twenty days. Information of this sort was fairly common before the war, and the Via Siberia route was becoming a fairly popular one with those who either were "no sailors bold," or with whom time was of some consequence. As a mail route, the Russia way has yet to be equalled—unless it will be equalled and surpassed, as seems probable by air mail routes—for it has meant the early confirmation of cables, contracts, and orders, and has made home seem just round the corner. It is only recently that the line has again been open for traffic and there is on record the interesting experiences of those who have essayed the journey since the Soviet became responsible for the control of the line. These experiences were interesting to say the least, but not encouraging to those who contemplated a journey across Europe. The news now cabled out will effectually dampen any andour that would be

travelers had in this connection. A judge, the son of a judge, feeling the restraint of Soviet hospitality, freely acknowledged, feels called upon to recount his and his fellow-passengers' experiences during a journey home. Three times held up by the overheating of an axle, may not be a matter worth complaining about; but a considerable delay due to the work of bandits, is a reasonable cause of complaint, more so when the work of these outlaws results in the loss of lives of railway workers, and is likely to do so in the case of passengers belonging to different countries. The incidents mentioned by Mr. W. W. Grantham, K.C., point to serious facts which cannot be blinked. Russia's internal affairs are by no means settled or secure. Counter-revolutionaries appear to be carrying on a sort of guerilla warfare, and this suggests that "Red" activities now so well known under the word Bolshevism, are not generally appreciated. Nor are they, we imagine, likely to be appreciated. Thus we may still expect the removal of bolts and pins from railway-lines, more or less as a matter of course for some little time to come. The statement that the railway track and rolling stock are both in a "shocking state," suggest a laxity of control due either to indifference, or to what is probably more correct, to the fact that the Government has it hands too full as a result of its interference in things which it can be argued do not concern it in the least. Oh! to be scrambling among those rocks that have with stood the storms of countless ages or to be investigating again that cave at Ness, where the pigmies used to dwell, and where the dauntless sea-rievers of old were wont to conceal their plunder!

The sea is a great leveller of men as well as of things that have no being—there is neither disdain or class distinction about the sea. Senfuring is a calling whose watchword is internationality. Nothing could be more pleasingly instructive in these days of imperialistic tendency than to inspect those stringently different visitors from many lands that are berthed in the docks of a modern seaport town.

Seafaring is a calling where all men are men and nothing more; And what higher praise can we bestow upon a human being in this age of artificiality than to say that he is a plain, unaffected man?

The local Police Department should have just reason to be proud of their efforts when the statistics for the year come to be published as the measures taken since the commencement of the strike four months ago have resuited in a remarkable falling off in the number of serious crimes which in normal times fill the daily register. This happy result has been achieved by hard work on the part of the officials of this department and to some extent through other causes. These latter include the vlaublé assistance of special constables, the quietening effect on evildoers by the presence of the mobilised Volunteers, and the stoppage of the Canton traffic, which enabled the authorities to exercise more efficient control on Chinese passengers by ships. Added to these is the good which resulted in eliminating the lawless element by periodical raids on suspected houses and dwellings in general.

headline: FRANCE'S REDS.
text:
COMMUNIST MAYORS SUSPENDED.

ARHESTS IN PARIS.

A Communist demonstration outside the Bolshevik Pavilion at the Decorative arts exhibition was forcibly dispersed and 40 arrests were made.

The Communist Mayor of Saint Denis has been suspended for a month for grave dereliction of duty in allowing public services to be held up on the 12th inst., when the Communists attempted a general strike.

The Communist Mayor and Deputy Mayor of Halluin in department Nord have also been suspended for abusing the privileges of their office.

headline: JUDICIAL INQUIRY. / INSPICTOR EVIDENCE.
text:
At the Federal Equipment Design, the report of Hanson, replying to Mr. Dusnee Dindley Johnson, said that he did not believe that the events of May 20 would have been averted by detailing the original mob of students who thronged the charge room when the first four were arrested. He did not believe that they were preventing them from joining the outside mob the temper of the crowd would have been better. He had no special instructions from his superiors to take precautions against risks previous to May 30. An American missionary, Mr. Cities, giving evidence said that he was among the crowd at the time of the shooting. The mob was excited, waving banners and throwing leaflets in the air. From his position in the crowd witness did not realise any necessity for shooting.

Sub-Inspector Shellsworth said he was on duty at the Ninking Road and Chekiang Road corner. At about three o'clock he saw a "howling mob" surrounding a policeman on point duty. Witness, accompanied by three foreign police, attempted to break up the crowd, whereupon the mob pulled down. Unstable Cole and Stevens to the ground. Witness then ordered badons to be drawn, and the police slowly retreated toward the Station, pressed by a violent crowd. Witness heard the cry "Kill the foreigners," and was of the opinion that both volleys were necessary to repel the crowd. Had witness been in charge of the Station he would have done the same as Inspector Elverson.

headline: NEW AIR FEAT.
text:
London, Oct. 15. The first experiments in England with the use of a dirigible ax can aeroplane carrier were carried out at Pulham this morning. The R 33 left her mooring must with a light aeroplane fixed by a special apparatus under her hull. The R 38 cruised for a quarter of an hour and then a 1553 monoplane, piloted by Flight-Lieutenant R. L. Haig, chief test pilot of the Royal Aircraft establishment, was released from a trapeze slung beneath the airship, but in attempting to re-attach itself to the dirigible the aeroplane was slightly damaged and the pilot decided to land.

It transpires that the aeroplane unhooked from the airship and flew for some time. It then re-hooked but tie propeller of the aeroplane was slightly damaged by striking a wire. The pilot then unhooked successfully for a second time and descended.

headline: THREE OPERATIONS.
text: Richard Carless, Swayne, Dr. Swayne's son, repeated the story he told at the inquest regarding the shooting of his father, and replying to questions he said he knew that in consequence of having been gased in the war, his brother-in-law underwent three mastoid operations, and that he still had discharge from a wound which needed constant attention. He knew that his brother-in-law's father had been in a lunatic asylum.

headline: STRIKE OVER.
text: The southern's strike at British ports is now definitely ended. The unofficial strike committee at London decided to call it off. Mr. Shinwell of the Marine Workers' Union said so far as his union is concerned the strike ended over a week ago.

headline: FARLIER CABLES.
text:
Interesting comments are made on the results of the Locarno Conference by the newspapers.

... "Petit Parisien" says that the most exacting critics must be satisfied with them.

L'Echo de Paris" says that the complexity of the contradictions in the agreements are disquieting, and that there is a possibility that the Anglo-French defensive accords no longer exist.

“Le Journal Gaulois” says that the entente cordiale is re-born and is again the pivot of European equilibrium.

The “Taeglicherundeschau” says that the German conception triumphed completely and that a peaceful revision of the Treaty of Versailles is not altogether out of the question.

"Germania" says that Locarno proved that Germany is again regarded as a world power.

The "Berliner Tageblatt" says that "the western Pact is the Magna Charta of the future life of European nations, and that never before has Great Britain so bound herself.

“Vorwaerts” says that the idea of a lasting peace has been realised.

The “Diplomatisch Politische Correspondenz,” which is the official mouthpiece, emphasises the importance of article 20 on arbitration treaties which it believes makes almost all the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles subject to arbitration.

Even the Nationalist journals acknowledge that much has been achieved at Locarno though they condemn the various details of the treaties.

M. Krassin, who has arrived with M. Kharkoff to participate at the session of the all Ukrainian Central Executive Committee, in an interview in regard to the results of the Locarno Conference, declared that the Security Pact was a means of drawing Germany into the "sphere" of anti-Soviet policy and preventing her rapprochement with Soviet Russia.

Sydney, October 20.—The compulsory conference called to settle the scumens' strike failed, the men adhering to their decision not to participate in the proceedings as long as any of the strikers remained in goal.—Reuter.

"Mine are," answered the tired-looking man, "but hers are perfectly horrid."

headline: JUDICIAL INQUIRY. / EVIDENCIÓN BRITISH DOCTOR.
text: a British doctor and his wife related the spectacle of one Chinese traditionally heading himself into a fury to incite others on Nanking Road on May 30. Dr. Burton said that some of the crowd shouted at him and spat at his car. Another Briton gave similar evidence. The manager of the Nagaiwailkaisha Japanese mills told the court of the disturbances at the mills prior to the May 30 incident. The British solicitor, Mr. Covey, said that Nanking Road up to the time of the shooting was in a comparatively normal state. He said he had attributed the reason for the shooting, which he did not witness, to the presence of armed robbers as he saw no other reason why any firing should have taken place. Witness, cross-examined, admitted that he held a retaining fee from a certain Chinese Union and also had acted in a legal capacity for the acting-president of the so-called Bolshevik Shanghai University—Fanter

headline: BRITISH TAXIS.
text:
An announcement that the directors have under consideration the purchase of a new fleet of British made taxicabs of an improved design and the sale of the present fleet of vehicles was made at the second annual meeting of the Hongkong and Kowloon Taxi-cub Co., Ltd. held at the registered office of the Company yesterday afternoon.

Mr. H. Birkett presided. Others present were Mr. A. H. Rowe (managing director), Messrs. Fred Ellis, E. M. Raymond (directors), C. A. Fulcher, D. McNeill, A. A. Alves (shareholders).

The Chairman said:—

Gentlemen.—The report and accounts for 1924-25 having been in your hands for some days, I will, with your permission, take them as read.

Before proceeding to deal with the Company's affairs, I desire to refer to the great loss we have sustained in the death, under the tragic circumstances which you will all remember, of the late Hon. Mr. Chau Su-ki, who was a director of the company from its inception and always took the deepest interest in its affairs. Mr. T. N. Chau has been invited by the directors to fill the seat thus vacated, and I am sure he will carry on his father's excellent work.

You will note that the balance sheet shows a loss of $46,680.14, but it has to be borne in mind that $62,303.41 has been written off for depreciation, in addition to the $45,915.04 written off last year, making the total amount written off for depreciation, $108,215.45, which represents about one-third of the paid-up capital of the company and more than half the original cost of our taxicabs, and this has been accomplished in a period of only fourteen months' finding, as the bulk of our taxis did not arrive in the Colony until March, 1924, and further it shows that your directors have pursued a hold policy and made ample provision for depreciation, which I feel sure will meet with the approbation of the shareholders.

A Farming Scheme.

You will also note that the balance sheet before you refers to the period ending April 30, 1925, and since that date the affairs of the company have been conducted on a different plan: the loss of $46,680.14 is to be attributed in a large measure to the fact that our drivers, working as servants of the company, grievously abused the taxicabs, a fact which is borne out by the item in the profit and loss. account of $46,937.85 for workshop and garage charges. Furthermore, by various ways too complicated to describe here, the company was deprived by the drivers of a considerable part of its just receipts. Your directors, therefore, decided to begin the present year with a system of farming out the taxis to a syndicate formed by the drivers themselves. The syndicate pays a fixed rate for the vehicles and they have to meet their own running workshop and garage charges, thus eliminating from our accounts, the items running charges, workshop and garage charges, and trading expenses, which together amount to $210,910.87—an item which will not occur at all in the next statement of accounts to be presented to you. Furthermore, the item "office administration and expenses" has been greatly reduced as the company now employs a much smaller staff. In future, apart from these reduced office expenses, the company has only to meet the cost of depreciation, and is at the same time in receipt of a regular income from the hire of its taxis.

I would also call your attention to the item in the balance sheet of calls in arrear. These shareholders have been served with a notice under registered cover to pay the third call with interest due and informing them that in default of payment within 14 days their shares will be forfeited and sold in accordance with clause 36 (a) of our Articles of Association.

Your directors have under consideration the sale of the present fleet of taxis and the purchase of a new fleet of British made vehicles, for which purpose a visit home to England by your managing director is under contemplation, in order to select the most suitable taxicab, and you may rest assured that the result will be the putting in commission of a greatly improved type of vehicle, especially adapted to hill climbing and generally suited to local conditions, and which will last much

Longer with lower training expenses and smaller repair till than our present fleet of cartoats and for which the directors are of the opinion that there will be no need to make any further calls to meet the cost of the new fleet of taxi-cabs. Although the balance sheet shows a loss, the results of our trading since May 1 under the new system of farming out the taxis has been very profitable and when the books are closed at the end of this month, which will be just six months' trading under the new system, your directors hope to declare an interim dividend.

I have now pleasure in moving the adoption of the report and accounts, and after this has been seconded I shall be glad to answer to the best of my ability any questions which any shareholder may desire to ask.

Shareholder's Questions. Mr. McNeill desired information on a sum of over $60,000 appearing in the balance sheet for office administration and "expenses—a sum which he considered too large.

Mr. Rowe explained that this was due to having to upkeep three branches and pay rent. The expenses over a period of six months had entered the balance sheet figures. Formerly the Company had an office in the Asiatic Building, which cost $2,000 in rent. This had been vacated, and the expenses now amounted to only $2,000 a month.

In querying the expenses for cushion covers and drivers' uniforms, Mr. McNeill said that he had not seen a driver at any time in uniform.

It was explained that each man had been supplied with two suits, but it was difficult to get them to wear the uniforms, and they never kept them clean, so the uniforms had to be withdrawn.

Mr. Rowe also explained that the cost of uniforms was a small one, and that the total included the cost of taximeters, which represented a large sum.

A sum of over $7,000 for furniture was explained by having to fit up the old office at the Asiatic Building.

Mr. McNeill said that he had looked over the Kowloon office; but did not consider the whole place worth more than $50.

The Chairman said that the large expenses was in a large measure due to the showroom at Pedder Street which it was thought necessary with a view to larger sales. The results did not justify the expense, and as soon as the opportunity presented itself the premises were vacated. To another query by Mr. McNeill as regards the hiring of the taxis, it was explained that three men were responsible under the scheme and that the money was collected every day.

Condition: of Vehicles.

Mr. McNeill drew attention to what he termed the bad state and filthy condition of the cars for months and months. There was no inducement to the public to engage them, as he had found for himself after spending hundreds of dollars by riding in them, and he considered that they should be looked after better by the Company. As a small shareholder he would certainly like to see the Company get on. He knew the Chinese were careless when the expenses did not come out of their own pocket, and he thought that the drivers should be pulled up a bit.

The Chairman said that the Company was being constantly pulled up by the Police: They made a thorough inspection periodically of the gears, mechanism and other things, and any cars not in order were not allowed to run.

Mr. Rowe added that prior to the strike they had 30 mechanics on the Hongkong side. They now had only about eight men, and were consequently working under great difficulties. Under the hiring scheme, the farmer has to look after the cars and do everything. He said that all the taxis are now running, and in respect of any vehicle that is not running the farmer has to pay $600 under the contract, which was for three years.

This concluded the questions and the Chairman's proposal that that report and accounts be adopted was seconded by Mr. Raymond and unanimously agreed to.

Election of Officers. The re-election of Messrs. Sam Pak-ming and Chan Lim-pak as directors was proposed by Mr Rowe and seconded by Mr Fulcher Carried unanimously.

It was also unanimously agreed to re-appoint Messrs Lowe, Bingham & Matthews as auditors for the current year on a proposal made by Mr. Filcher and second
