headline: MOTORIST CHARGED. / MR. WERSCHKUL'S EVENING RIDE. / REPULSE HAY INCIDENTS.
text:
The greater part of three hours was taken up at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon with the hearing of the case against Mr. Howard T. Werschkul, a young American flour broker, who was charged with causing bodily harm to an Indian watchman in the employ of the Repulse Bay Hotel by wanton and furious driving.

The case for the Crown was that he drove a car in a zigzag course past the entrance to the Hotel on the night of Saturday, June 6, that he had not full control of the car and that as a result he knocked down the watchman who was standing outside the Hotel.

Witnesses called all attributed to the defendant's car a dangerous speed for such a spot. Mr. F. G. H. Haslam, who watched the car's progress from the main flight of steps leading up to the Hotel while he was waiting for his own car, said that the occupants were laughing and singing. The car was zigzagging along the road at a speed of about 20-25 miles an hour. He did not see the watchman but heard the crash. The car did not stop. Mr. M. M. Maas, of the A.P.C. gave corroborative evidence.

Mr. C. Edwards, of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, who was waiting at the foot of the steps to the Hotel in the main road said that the car was travelling at considerable speed and cut in on another car in such a manner that it caused simultaneous exclamations of surprise from himself and others who were with him. He should think it was going at 18 miles an hour when it passed the Hotel.

Mr A. Grimmett, of the Revenue Office, who was outside the Hotel at the time at the top of the steps said that he thought the car was going to run over the spot where he and his wife were standing. He pushed his wife out of the way and jumped clear himself. The car swerved and hit the watchman on the opposite side. Witness called to the driver to stop but the latter took no notice. The car was going at about 25 miles an hour in his opinion. He noticed that the number was 175.

Mr. Graham, of the Colonial Secretariat, said that the Indian watchman seeing his danger jumped in an attempt to get clear but was caught and carried for some yards.

The injuries sustained were a fractured thigh bone and abrasions, said Dr. W. L. Paterson.

The case for the Crown having been closed the defendant went into the witness box.

On the night in question he had dinner with some friends, among whom were M. Dupre, the boxer, and after watching the dancers it was suggested that they should go for a ride. They got as far as the Hotel garage in the car when it was found that no one had any cigarettes so they returned. On driving off again witness (who was driving) felt something strike the front of the car but thought they had struck the rail. Later when they stopped for a puncture near Tytam Tuk reservoir they found that the front head light had been broken and that it was no longer functioning. At Shaukiwan they were stopped by a police officer who told them he had been warned to keep a lookout for a car of their number.

Mr. Werschkul said that the first drink of an alcoholic nature he had on the day in question was a cocktail or two before dinner. He was going at a speed of fifteen miles, an hour at the time he passed the Hotel which he admitted was faster than he ought to have been travelling at that spot. When he drove down the hill after returning to procure the cigarettes the car was in first gear and he changed into second at the bottom as he took the turn to approach the hotel for the second time.

Mr. Andre Dupre gave corrosive evidence and said that in his opinion the car was travelling at a speed of about ten miles or fifteen kilometres an hour.

The case was adjourned until this afternoon.

The Coroner's Inquiry into the death of a coolie as the result of a motor car running into the pavement at West Point, which, as stated yesterday, opened at the Central Magistracy, concluded in the afternoon when a verdict of manslaughter against the driver was returned. Britain is the staunch friend of China—would she, for instance, forego the Boxer Indemnity were it otherwise?—and every effort that she can make to put the country on its feet will be made. headline: A Strike-Moral.
text:
The general recognition of the greater benefit to be derived from close personal contact between pupils and those who have devoted their lives to the training of the youth and adolescent is shown by the increasing growth of public boarding schools throughout the world and the, even greater demand for the amenities they provide. The parent who made his own way in life looks back on a youth devoid of friendship with others older and more experienced than himself and is actuated by the resolve that his children shall have the opportunity of availing themselves of what he missed; while the parent who experienced it himself realises its value too well to think of denying to his children a privilege to which he owes the formation of habits of mental exercise which are an ever increasing source of enjoyment to himself. There are boarding schools in Hongkong modelled on English public school lines and there are in these and other schools here as the type of master as the staffs of the best public schools in England are made up of. It is more than likely that it is the feeling of loyalty to these masters which has resulted in so much comparative restraint having been exercised among the students of Hongkong during the present crisis and it is significant

that the only trouble of any magnitude has been at the chief Government School where there is no hostel, and where the application of the authorities for the provision of boarding accommodation has been persistently refused. It is no reflection on a staff which is well known to be as fine a mentally equipped body of educational enthusiasts as one could hope to meet in a college of its kind to state that it is not surprising that the seeds of disaffection should have found richer soil in the minds of youths who are free (so far as college supervision is concerned) to roam the street at any hour of the day or night when they are not actually engaged in their studies. No great harm has been done up to the present, however, and as they have not received the support from other schools they are believed to have been led to expect it is probable that a few days will see the main body of students back at their studies; if not there would be little difficulty in making up the numbers of even as large a body of the students as are affected judging from the waiting lists. The trouble should not have been without its lesson, however, and for the reasons stated above the Government might well reconsider their decision regarding the provision of a hostel for Queen's College.

headline: TO GOLF OR NOT TO GOLF.
text:
For some time past serious persons have objected to the game of golf, notes the "Daily Telegraph" (London.) Mr. Leo Maxse, who has just matched himself against the Earl of Balfour to denounce it, is not original or lonely in that occupation. Men may be heard at it any day and upon any links, and they are far more fervent and free than Mr. Maxse's courtesy permitted to him. But he argued his case, which they do not. Britons, he urged, should never be slaves to golf, first, because it was made in Germany; secondly, because it has a debilitating influence upon the younger generation. The evidence which Mr. Marse has been so fortunate as to discover that the Teutonic Knights played golf in the intervals of breaking the heathen Prussians we shall be glad to see. Meantime, we propose to continue to blame Scotland. The second part of the indictment lacks the element of surprise. Five hundred years ago it was discovered that golf was doing Scotsmen a lot of harm. The state of that unfortunate nation must by this time be deplorable. In 1457 the Scottish Parliament "decreted and ordained that the fute-bal and the golfe be vtterly cryit downe and's noet vsyt." It was desired that the youth of the country should give their time to military training and particularly shooting. For Scotsmen have always, with strange modesty, held that the English were superior to them in the use of the long bow. But the ancient Parliament was no more convincing than Mr. Marse. Nobody seems to have taken any notice of its decree. It tried again, and "ordت in that in no place of the realme there be usit fute-ball, golfe, or uthar sik unprofitabil sports." Thus early was the horrible seductive power of the game made manifest. Mr. Maxse thinks that its essential vice is proceed by the kind of men who are attracted to it, "politicians, journalists, international financiers, mugwumps, mandarins, bureaucrats, and highbrows." We could go on in this strain for years together, "dinners and suppers and sleeping times excepted." What game was it that Mary of Scots was found playing after her husband had been in suspicious circumstances, blown up? Golf, of course. Who brought golf to England? Not Lord Balfour, but that "wlest fool in Christendom," James I. They were great golfers in that unhappy House of Stuart. Obviously that accounts for their misfortunes, and perhaps also for their fatal charm.

But there is, after all, something serious in Mr. Maxse's charges. Golf, he contends, is a good game for the elderly and the sedentary, but it is not good enough for anyone else. Boys and young men have taken it up, and thus surrendered our old English supremacy in sport. To this Lord Balfour replies that golf is not largely played by our public schools, and that so far as we have ceased to be supreme in games it is because the other nations have now at length learnt to play. The answer is not wholly adequate. Though golf is not played by a large number of boys and young men who are perfectly fit to play something faster and more strenuous. Most people who know anything of the training of physique and character would allow that young fellows ought to have a course of some hard team game. No other sport, however good for muscular development, for adroitness of body, and quickness of eye, will supply the place of vigorous team work. We have, of course, many current examples that golf and other games are not, mutually exclusive. A man may, and, in fact does, get his blue for "Rugger" or "Soccer," and play golf for his University. But probably there is some truth in the suggestion that golf tempts a good many boys to desert "the flannelled fools at the wicket and the muddied oafs at the goals." Why should a lad not play the game which he likes best, which, in general, will be that most suited to him? We fear that it is vain to call, as Mr. Maxse would, all the young golfers back to cricket in order that we may recover the ashes. It is confusion of thought to assume that we play games in order to beat other nations. The object of playing a game is not "international supremacy," but amusement, exercise, health of body and mind. We send our best men to make a match with the best of other nations in order to keep the game strenuous and skilful. It is surely plain that a nation which gets about the winning of international games as if that were a chief object of sport may easily achieve supremacy without a high general standard of skill or physique or sportsmanship. A concentration of interest on a few matches and a few players is not necessarily good for a game or a nation. What we should rather aim at is that every body should be playing something, and playing it for sport, not as a prescription or a task or a business. It does not seem likely that for the years in which one is a trifle slower or foot and stiffer of shoulder and shorter of wind a better game will be invented than golf.

headline: RUBBER BOOM.
text:
The India Manufacturers Association, representing ninety-five per cent. of the British manufacturers of rubber articles, has issued a manifesto protesting against the continuance of the operation of the Stevenson scheme and the present form for the restriction of the exports of crude rubber from Malay and Ceylon, and demanding that the scheme be abolished or so drastically amended that it will provide quick releases as and when the price of rubber goes beyond the limits aimed at by the scheme.

At Mr. Coolidge's suggestion a delegation representing American rubber interests has interviewed the Secretary of State, Mr. Kellogg, and explained the unprecedented difficulties of the industry owing to the high cost of rubber, which is attributed to British restrictions though it is not alleged that there is unfair discrimination against America especially.

Mr. Kellogg promised to consider a "memorial left on behalf of the Rubber Association.

Warsaw, July 18.—After an exciting, Wild-West type of chase in motor cars through the main streets, the Police captured three Communists in the outskirts of the city. Two Police and one Communist were killed and fourteen pedestrians and the remaining two Communists wounded.—Reuter.

headline: CONCILIATION.
text:
DO STRIKERS UNDERSTAND

A correspondent writes to the Editor of the North China Daily News as follows:

Sir,—A week ago, in reply to correspondence in your columns advocating stronger measures in Slaughal against strikers and others, you published an editorial on "Repression versus Conciliation." In it the withdrawal of emergency measures was advocated, it was said there were signs that the strike was about to collapse, and the pious hope was printed that the Chinese would readily respond to conciliation.

It is admittedly easy to criticise, especially prophets; but there is reason to do so because it is more than probable that such sentiments as the above, expressed in a foreign newspaper, do much to strengthen the hands and inspire the courage of the strike leaders and signators, and even more to cause such men as the vice-president of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce to come out but-footed for strike and boycott, when before they wavered between two opinions.

There is one characteristic that every foreign student of the Chinese character has commented upon. The Chinaman is ever and always on the side of the strong: he never sides with the weak. He is, according to his idea, on the side of the strong now, and it still remains to be soon whether he is right or not.

Cold waters has been thrown on many suggestions that have been made here of a retaliatory nature—a deterrent nature if you like it better. The consequence is that worker, agitator and striker are equally welcome in our midst, as far as essentials go. They use our light, gas, water, transport, and other public utilities with equal ease. The members of this Chinese Chamber whose utterances we frequently read in your columns can say what they like about us, injure us, boycott us and what not. Let us conciliate rather than repress them then! The "Shun Pao" and "Sin Wan Pao", publish matter that foreign newspapers would never dare do, and there are a host of smaller fry who are only coincளred in insulting the foreigner and intimidating his employees.

Hongkong's strike began after ours and was more severe at the beginning. It is, however, nearer its end because the Hongkong authorities have acted. They often a reward of $1,000 for the apprehension of any intimidator or agitator; when convicted he is not fined or cautioned; he is placed at public sanitary Work (the collection of nightsoil to be exact), is clothed in convict's garb and works in the public streets; or he may be flogged. To carry on waterfront work Malays are being imported and are working well. But the regulation that has had more effect than ally other is one that requires the expulsion of every striker from the Colony. A Chinese to live in Hongkong has to work; in Shanghai he can do as he pleases. The effect of this places every worker in Hongkong of Chinese nationality in a dilemma. He has the option of relinquishing the advantages of life in a foreign settlement with all its amenities, and not least its protection to his life and property, for life in Canton or some other Chinese city. Your previous correspondent suggested several schemes for bringing the strike home to those who are responsible for it. Here are others that have been tried out, and not found wanting, for in Hongkong many of the strikers, the printers among them, have returned to work and are trying to forget. Is it too much to ask our Council to take a leaf out of Hongkong's

A STRIKER'S SUBSTITUT. Shanghai, July 22, 1925.

headline: A WITHDRAWAL.
text:
CANTON CHRISTIAN COLLEGE STATEMENT.

PREBIDNT AND RESOLUTIONS.

At the request of the South China Morning Post, who wrote asking whether he wished to answer the criticisms levelled against the Canton Christian College because of the resolutions passed by members of the staff regarding the Shameen incidents of June 23, Dr. Henry, President of the College, has made public the following statement:

It is a matter of sincere regret that it has not been possible to make the following statement long before this. No outbiter can appreciate the feeling on the Canton Christian College campus upon the part of foreigner and Chinese alike which it became known that a much honoured teacher and one of the students had been killed and at least two others wounded. In a very intimate sense it was a family affair.

The next morning, June 24, I spoke to the students and Chinese staff, at a meeting surcharged with the tensest feeling, and where even I was looked upon with a certain degree of distrust. I said—and I spoke not only from a full heart, but with deep misgiving for the future—that I would rather have lost an own brother and one of my owii children.

Immediately after this, having with one of my colleagues, to attend to getting some people off to Hongkong, I had, just before leaving, suggested that the few remaining members of the foreign staff frame some resolutions suitable to the occasion. There certainly was no Chinese pressure of any sort in this.

It was six thirty that evening when we got back to the campus. The problem of getting the rest of the foreign staff away the next day plus the various pressing problems at such a time on a campus where over one hundred and fifty students were marooned and whose non-student population is over eight hundred, kept one more than absorbed. It appears from what I have since learned, that the resolutions had already been drafted and sent out before I had returned to the campus that night. It was not until they appeared in the Hongkong papers, which arrived some days later, that I read them for the first time. It is therefore evident that these resolutions can only be regarded as personal expressions of opinion, and not as an official statement from the College.

"In order to make any sort of statement it was necessary to get in touch with some of those present when the resolutions were drawn up. Being scattered and the maila irregular this was not easy. Meanwhile, different ones in Hongkong, realising how completely, as will appear, their intentions had been misunderstood, were on several occasions on the point of making statements, but were persuaded that at the risk of considerable delay and even further misunderstanding it might be better to wait until one final statement could be made.

I have now satisfied myself that, regardless of the wording of the resolutions, no one had any idea whatever of suggesting which side fired first or of singling out any particular nation. In so far as the resolutions indicate or imply otherwise, they are definitely at fault, and on behalf of those who drew them up I wish hereby in these respects to withdraw them. No one had had any chance to hear from the Shameen side, but what was definitely and foremost in every one's mind—was a protest against what seemed, according to the information available on June 24, to be unnecessary severity in the Shameen defence and the apparently indiscriminate machine-gun fire. “Had the wording of these resolutions been as clear in this as I have satisfied myself was the intention of those who drew them up, I am confident so much misunderstanding would not have arisen, nor so regrettable and, I beg to say, undeserved bitterness evoked against an institution which, despite every assertion to the contrary, has been striving steadily to promote international goodwill, and as an institution with Chinese, British and Americans on its staff and on its Board of Trustees has, we believe, been to no small degree successful in this and we hope will continue to be.

We yield second place to none in our keen desire for the early adjustment of Chinese and foreign relationships. It is our belief that the only settlements of China's external difficulties will be on a wherewith mutual rights are mutually recognised, and where the foreigners are willing to do what has been so well-suggested recently by a group in London,—put Chinese interests first.

President, Canton, Christian College

headline: SECRET SOCIETIES.
text:
UNDERWORLD HELP FOR STRIKERS.

It is reported that two secret societies, the membership of which is largely of the criminal class, have joined forces with labour agitators in the Chinese city and sworn allegiance to one of the most notorious labour leaders. It is believed that their intention is to blackmail Chinese firms and shops dealing in foreign goods, and Chinese in foreign employ.

A Japanese paper asserts that the Far Eastern Committee of the Third Internationale recently petitioned Vladivostok for 50,000,000 roubles for propaganda purposes in China, which petition was duly granted by the Bureau of Asiatic Propaganda.

MILL WORKERS STABBED. Five strike breakers from a Japanese mill have been stabbed in a teashop by loafers, who are probably strikers. Two of the injured men have been removed to hospital.

headline: COAL DISPUTE.
text:
SIX MONTHS INTERIM CONTRACT

Halifax (Nova Scotia), August 3. —With a view to terminate the dispute between the British Empire Steel Corporation and the striking coalminers, which has completely stopped work in the coal industry for the past five months and caused much distress and disorder, the Premier, the Hon. H. N. Rhodes, P.C., has proposed that the parties immediately arrange an interim contract for six months to embrace the 1924 working terms and the 1922 wages. Thid Provincial Government will grant a rebate of one-fifth of its coal royalties for a year, and institute a full enquiry. The Executive Pedy, representing the workers, has already recommended that the Unions should accept the proposals.

Stevens, engineer who is well known throughout the Far East and in Siberia in connection with his railway building, was recently unveiled on the crest of the Continental Divide in the United States. Furness shipyard on the Tyne has achieved a remarkable feat in rapid ship construction. Fifteen weeks ago the keel was laid of a 2,500-ton vessel for service on the Canadian Lakes. She is now loading her first cargo in the Tyne, having successfully passed her trials.

The new Chinese Minister to Moscow, Mr. Sun Pao-chi, received a letter wrapped round a live cartridge. The letter said that on arrival in Moscow he must demand that the Russian Government make good to the Chinese losses through depreciated roubles, or he would be shot. It is reported that Dr. C. T. Wang received a similar postal packet, says the "Central China Post."

More Women drive Buicks than any other car because of the striking appearance of this famous motor car. Then comes Buick dependability. A woman knows when she starts out with her Buick that she will "get there and back." Other reasons are—the comfort in driving a Buick—the velvet clutch action, easy steering; then the power and quietness of Buick's Valve-in-Head engine and the safety of Buick mechanical four-wheel brakes.

Eels when they come down the rivers to the seas " swim at once to the Atlantic Ocean to a secret rendezvous near the Antilles, between longitude 48 and 60, and there lay their eggs. This statement was made to the French Academy of Science by Dr. Schmidt, of Copenhagen University.

Another witness has come forward to testify to the reality of the much-debated sea-serpent. This is Sir Henry F. Woods, K.C.V.O., who, while serving in the British Navy in the old sailing days, distinctly saw the monster at close quarters while cruising off the Javanese coast. In the newly-published book, "Spunyarn," he describes it as being fully 50ft. long, and of girth proportionate.

Dublin saw its busiest and gayest week in its annual Horse Show. Visitors came from all parts of Ireland and Great Britain, for the Dublin Horse Show is now a national event. The decline in popular favour of this animal has made no appreciable difference to the show, nor, so far as one could judge from the congested condition of the streets, in the attendance. The effects of the troubled political times of recent years have worn off, and the city has regained its wonted gaiety.

Undiscouraged by the failure of their campaign to banish alcohol, the Soviet authorities are now tackling the problem of profanity—a large scale task. Under a new ordinance the use of a curse in public is liable to a fine of one gold ruble for each curse. Students of Russian swearing are inclined to believe that the Government will have to compromise by introducing the ration system. Managers of the telephone system have placed a taboo on "Miss" as a term of address to the telephone girls on the ground that this is a bourgeois title.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Two of the public bathing beaches, those at Stonecutter's and Kennedy Town, are to be closed at the end of the present month. Launches will not be available to these beaches after Wednesday evening. September 30, and the matsheds will be dismantled. Other public beaches remain open.

At a dinner given at Wellington to delegates of the Empire Press Union, who are visiting New Zealand, Sir Harry Brittain mentioned the increasing fact that New Zealand's 1,250,000 population did more trade with Great Britain than the 400,000,000 of China. This must not however, be taken as underrating the importance of certain branches of China trade to England and of China as a field for British manufactures.

Malaya and Hongkong "are both represented in a large Empire's delegation which is visiting Hull to see for themselves how comprehensive are the quays for handling fruit, the warehouses for storing grain and meat, the sheds for holding wool, and how expeditiously, with the aid of the London and North-Eastern Railway, can large cargoes be unloaded and transported over the greater part of northern England.

At the annual meeting at Auckland on August 4 of the New Zealand Insurance Company, whose local agents are Messrs. Holyoak, Massey and Co., the shareholders were informed that the directors felt justified in recommending an increase of the rate of dividend, and they accordingly recommended that a sum of £118,750 should be distributed by way of dividend for the year, being equivalent to a dividend at the rate of 1/7 per share. In order to meet this increase in dividend it would not be necessary to draw on the underwriting profits for more than £7,154, as the income derived from investments was only short of the dividend by that amount.

The case against a Chinese revenue officer, who is charged with attempting to obtain by threats a sum of $100 from a distiller, was continued before the Kowloon Magistrate and again adjourned. A scheme was alleged to have been suggested to the distiller by which he could defraud the Revenue Department.

Since the recent unpleasant incidents due to the appearance of sharks and crocodiles at favourite bathing resorts, the increase in the number of bathing pagars at Port Dickson is very noticeable. Nowadays scarcely any bathers are seen in the open sea. A very striking addition to these pagars is that adjoining the fine new bungalow recently erected at the fifth mile on the Coast Road, by a well-known Pasir Panjang towkay.

Among interesting items referred to in an article in the "Ice Cream Trade Journal" are the following: If the ice cream consumed in the United States in one year were put into one cone, it would tower over the Washington Monument; that more than 700,000 cows supply the cream, and that most of the eggs used in the trade come from China. All of which is highly interesting; comments the "N. C. Daily News," but are we to draw the conclusion from these latter facts that honest-to-goodness cream and eggs really enter into the composition of everything sold as ice cream? Alas, we wish we could believe it.

The cruiser “Diomede,” Captain C. E. Kennedy-Purvis, arrived at Portsmouth on August 29 from China, where she has been serving since her completion in 1922. The vessel was commissioned for the first time for service on October 2, 1922, so that by the time she is paid off her term will have extended to nearly three years instead of the normal two-and-a-half. The place of the “Diomede” has temporarily been taken by the “Concord,” Captain A. R. W. Woods, D.S.O., from the Mediterranean, until such time as the large cruiser “Vindictive,” Captain G. F. Hyde, R.A.N., arrives on the station. The “Diomede” will be transferred to the New Zealand Government, which a year ago offered to maintain a second cruiser of the same type as the “Dunedin,” already out there.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Joseph Conrad is the inspiration for the new library and reading room in the annex to the Seamen's Church institute at 25 South Street, New York. The memorial room will cost approximately $100,000 (G.) It is planned to make it a shrine for all Conrad lovers.

Mr. F. J. Benton, formerly of the E. E. A. and C. Telegraph Co., Ltd., in Singapore, is now settled in Sydney and is a director of the Rural Estate and Development Co., Ltd., and the Federal Building Loan Co., Ltd. He writes to say that if any Straits men require information regarding real estate in Australia he will be pleased to answer letters addressed to the offices of the companies, 251, George Street, Sydney.

A wedding of especial interest to the younger set was solemnized at St. Joseph's Church, Shanghai, when Miss Marguerite Tahaney, of San Francisco, became the bride of Mr. Lewis Jackson Peoples, of Townsville, North Carolina, who is Han River manager of the British Cigarette Company. The bride was given away by Mr. Otis D. Terell, and Mrs. C. F. Wolsiffer attended as matron of honour, while Miss Ramona Gray acted as brides-maid. The Very Rev. Dean Symons has been elected an honorary life member of the Shanghai Football Association. Dean Symons has always been a keen patron of sport, and on most Saturday afternoons is to be found at the Race Course, watching the games.

Three men who in the last few years have been unofficial advisors to Herbert Hoover, Secretary of Commerce, and the Administration at Washington regarding Russian affairs, are going again to Soviet Russia. They are James P. Goodrich, formerly Governor of Indiana; William N. Haskell and Dr. F. A. Golder of Stanford University. Colonel Haskell, who directed the American relief administration in Russia, already has sailed from New York.

Mr. A. H. F. Edwards, who was Commissioner of Customs, at Canton at the time of the attack on Shameen, and was shot in the knee, has been undergoing medical treatment at home. It was found inadvisable to extract the bullet which was in the centre of the bone, but success was attained in the difficult and painful process of joining up the severed portions of a tendon which had been shot away. Mr. Edwards is shortly returning to the Far East via Siberia together with Mrs. Edwards, but his future sphere of activities is not yet known.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL. GREEN ISLAND CEMENT CO LTD
text:
"Messrs. Mackintosh & Co., Ltd. issue an attractive folder called 'Dress of To-day.'

、Subscriptions to the local Garrison· Recreation Club, per quarter, are:—Officers $2; other ranks 20 cents.

During the weak ended Sept. 26, the only case of notifiable disease was of enteric fever, a Russian (imported). There was a clean sheet for Monday.

According to latest reliable information the employees of Chinese Telegraph Administration in Canton went on strike on the 28th inst. in support of their fellow-workers. in Shanghai to enforce their demands for increase of wages and better treatment.

. Reuter cables that the Peking Government has received a telegram stating that the telegraph strike at Tsingtao has ended. The Cabinet to-day discussed the strike but it is understood that it is left to Chiao Tung-pu to decide whether or not to accept the strikers terms.

A meeting of the Legislative Council will be held to-morrow when the following resolution will be moved by the Colonial Secretary: "Resolved by the Legislative Council that the percentages on the valuation of tenements on the following lots on Kowloon Bay Reclamation shall be 13 percent: New Kowloon Inland Lots Nos. 132, 227, 228, 238, 239 and 251." The following questions will be asked: By Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird.—"Has the Government considered the advisability of establishing a Labour Bureau for the voluntary registration of domestic servants and others? If so with what result?" By Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak.—"Will the Government state when it is hoped to complete and open the new 'Saiyingpun' School?" The Orders of the Day contain the second reading of five Bills which were introduced at the last meeting of the Council. “The Motion Picture Industry in China” was discussed at the last weekly meeting of the Shanghai Rotary Club held at the Astor House by Roturian Luther Jee of the Pencock Motion Picture Corporation.

Messrs. Wm. Powell, Ltd. announce the engagement of Mr. E. Broadberry as a cutter in charge of their tailoring department.

The annual general meeting of the Hongkong Philharmonic Society is announced to be held on Monday, October 5 next at 9 p.m. in St. John's Cathedral Hall.

Babies' finger prints are to be taken in Ireland when they leave workhouses. This decision was made by the Union Commissioners in consequence of large increases in the number of babies, living and dead, found in the streets, shops, and elsewhere in Dublin. It is hoped that the finger prints will enable the police to trace the mothers or foster mothers abandoning children.

A peculiar incident was brought to light at Vigo when a girl of 18 jumped into the sea. Her act was in consequence of apparently insuperable obstacles to her marriage to a youth who was wrongly registered as a girl at birth. The authorities refused to certify him as anything but a female, and it was thus impossible to obtain the necessary documents for the marriage. Two sailors saved the would-be suicide.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Reuter cables that Wu Kuang-hsin has arrived at Hankow to interview Hsiao Yao-nan.

The leave granted to Captain L. W. Smith, R.A. has been changed to "from October 5 to October 11."

Professor Danenberg cables from Tokyo that the recital given by young Emil has been a great success. Emil is to play in Osaka, Kobe and Shanghai.

The marriage of Mr. Chia Powhin, of the Hongkong University, formerly assistant master of St. John's Institution, Kuala Lumpur, to Miss Lye Nyon Keow, eldest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lye Ah Yew, of Singapore, has taken place at Singapore.

News to hand from Liemchow indicates the collapse of part of the roof of the C. E. Church outside the city, through the work of white ants. The Church was the gift of Miss A. M. Bakewell, so well known in Hongkong, who is a C.M.S. missionary at Liemchow. The foundation stone was laid by Miss Marguerite Bradley, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Bradley, of Yunnanfu, also well known in the Colony.

Lieut. G. H. Sloane-Stanley, R.A., Lieut. E. L. E. Davies, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. H. C. Gould, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. B. Aucott, H.K.S.B., R.A., Lieut. G. M. S. Webb, 5/2nd Punjab Regt., and Lieut. E. A. S. Cope, 1st Batt. East Surrey Regt. will be examined for promotion on Friday; Captain L. D. Joll, M.C., R.A., Captain P. H. Drake-Brockman and Captain D. J. Allfree of the Surrey Regt. will be examined on Thursday week.

Justice E. Finley Johnson, member for the United States at the International Commission, was the honour guest, with Mrs. Johnson, at a notable dinner given by Consul General for China Mr. Lingui Wang at the Manila Hotel Mr. Wang's other invited guests were the Honourable Robert M. Bacon and Mrs. Bacon, Admiral and Mrs. W. Bullard, Colonel, and Mrs. Arthur W. Yates, Colonel and Mrs. C. M. National Dr. and Mrs. H. Sugeno Stafford Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Zoninger Mr. and Mr. C. G. Brinsney Mr. and Mrs. W. The Hongkong Technical Institute re-opens next Monday. Students joining classes held at Queen's College will be enrolled at the Education Department only, but those joining classes to be held at the Central British School, Kowloon, may be enrolled at the school. Entry forms can be obtained from the Education Department or the Central British School.

Mr. D. F. Dunn of the Hongkong Taxi Cab Co., Ltd. returned to the Colony from Manila yesterday by the "President Madison."

Mr. R. J. Farrar, President of the Municipal Commissioners, has arrived at Singapore by the "d'Artagnan" from home leave.

H.E. Major-General Sir T. Fraser, K.C.B., arrived in Kuala Lumpur on the morning of September 20, and is staying at the British Residency.

Reuter cables that Messrs. Abe and Kawachi, the Japanese aviators "who are flying from Japan to London, have arrived at Le Bourget.

The engagement is announced between Mr. Lionel Van Geyzel, son of Dr. Van Geyzel, of Seremban, and Miss Dorothy Marks, eldest daughter of Mr. John Marks of Digwarah group, Sungkai.

The Rev. P. B. Clayton, the founder and the first padre of Toc H, who is now in Australia is expected to arrive in Singapore on October 2 and will be in Penang on the 14, 15 and 16, leaving following day for Calcutta.

The following were among the candidates declared successful at the recent examination by the Civil Service Commissioners for admission to the Police Force of Ceylon, the Straits Settlements, the Federated Malay States, and Hongkong: T. D. Ogier, F. O. Mell), A. R. H. Anderson, H. P. Waights, L. F. Knight, H. R. Bond, L. R. Barnett-Smith, O. E. M. de Bretton, A. R. MacKillop, H. M. Smith, and L. A. Ives.

Mr. G. W. King, O.B.E., Registrar of H.M. Supreme Court (Shanghai), who wound up the estate of the late Mr. Patrick Reilly who died on February 22, 1925, has received a letter from the deceased's alster, Mrs. Downie, expressing appreciation in the following words: "I wish that you could thank the many friends of my late brother for the lovely wreaths and the interest they look in him," only wish I could thank each one personally but may be your could not some way to thank them for me. The late Mr. Reilly was employed in the Shanghai War. Mr. A. B. M. Mr. F. A. Walls, of H.B.M. Consulate-General, accompanied by his wife, is on a trip to Baguio for his health.

Uniformed interpreters for the convenience of tourists have been stationed at the three principal terminals in Berlin. They are on hand at the arrival and departure of all trains and their services are given to the travelling public without charge.

In spite of unrest and anti-foreign agitation, more books are said to have been sold in China lately by the British and Foreign Bible Society. Out of every ten books sold in 1924 about four were sold in China. Half of their increased circulation last year took place there.

Among the passengers who arrived Home by the "Mantua" was Mrs. Mackenzie, widow of the Englishman who was shot dead by Chinese rebels while motoring outside Shanghai. She has gone to London with her little daughter. Another passenger was Sergeant Gavan, of Shanghai Police Force, who has been invalidated home as the result of wounds inflicted by women who, armed with knives, were in the front of the strike crowds.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
The Exchange Banks will be closed to the transaction of public business on Monday, October 12.

For cheap living Timor is to be recommended since a man is passing rich on £50 a year there, according to a recently returned traveller.

Admission prices for the 9.15 performance of Harold Lloyd's great comedy "Hot Water" at the Queen's Theatre to-night are $1, $1.50 and $2 (not $2.50 as erroneously stated in one announcement).

The Chinese Government is about to publish a de luxe edition of the Chinese classics. There will be a few copies for sale at $6,000 (Chinese currency) each, and the rest will be donated to libraries in China and abroad.

"We offer a cordial welcome to the claw of the British Eastern squadron,"—so reads the legend on a packet in which picture postcards are being sold at Amanhashidate. It is rather doubtful whether the honoured crew would recognise itself as the "claw"—presumably of the British lion, says the "Japan Chronicle."

A thirsty tourist drank copiously from a roadside spring in Oregon. A sign that read, "The water is contaminated," had been placed beside the spring. An official of the Oregon Highway Department, driving by, saw the drinker and stopped to warn him; only to be met by the question, "What sort of mineral water is this? I never heard of it before." The authorities have now replaced the sign with one reading: "This water is not fit to drink."

Jacob Epstein's eighteen sculptures on the building of the British Medical Association, which opened his career as the stormy petrel of contemporary British art, will not be transferred to the association's new building, now nearing completion. These figures nearly a generation ago caused a furore in staid England and were the reproach of all academicians and were even important enough to bring down the condemnation of the churches. The doctors, apparently, do not wish to mix up with controversies over art. They will not lose on their investment, as they paid $10,000 for the sculptures and already have received offers of $30,000 for them.

The news that one of the new cruisers is to be built at Devonport has been received with great joy, for although the work is unlikely to involve the taking on of any additional men, it guarantees the constant employment for several years of the existing staff, now numbering about 12,000. It is expected that the new cruiser will be up to the Washington limit of 10,000 tons, and that she will be laid down upon the slip at present occupied by the cruiser "Cornwall." The latter vessel in all probability will be ready to leave the slip in February next, in which event the keel of the new one will be laid down in the following month.

The question, What is the queerest address in London? has brought forward an interesting article on the subject in the "Post Annual," the organ of the postalworkers of London. Probably the queerest one given is: "XXplace, Globe-road, E.I." Others nearly as original are:—

Shoulder-of-mutton alley. Frying-pan alley. Farthing fields. Pickle-herring Stairs. Crooked Billet-yard.

The complexity of the postman's problem may be understood when we learn that there are 105 Park-roads, 77 Grove-roads, 56 Victoria-roads, 13 Tennyson-roads, and 12 Shakespeare-roads, in the London district. There are also 112 Church-roads, streets, and crescents.

“The average American film is by no means an accurate portrayal of the American people. For that matter, it is not an accurate portrayal of any nation or race of people. Most of the characters presented in our photoplays are not human beings at all, as they are known, and found upon this earth. It is not the American film producer who is responsible. It is the American public. There is only about one film in every hundred released which dares to transgress, the walls of artificiality and absurdity which the American motion picture public has erected. The American public does not wish to see the truth on the screen. It does not want realism. It wants unadulterated herum. The American producers being caterers, not artists, are giving it to them. From “The Film Mercury,” a Hollywood technical newspaper.

The Australian-Oriental Line, Ltd., Captain Gambrill and owners of the S.s. "Changte" sent out invitations for a reception on board that ship from five to seven p.m. on Friday last at Manila.

Apparently the fame of our popular songs is reaching to as far as the West Coast of Africa. An “educated” native writes to a Midland firm: “I want be happy, make me happy so too. Popula song say well. Do it now. Me, big, black bess man, want plenty size gold ring for beloved. Send so long an valuable present you go.”

If Ken Wood had been in China, the King would not have had to make his moving appeal to the public to avoid littering our parks with paper and other rubbish. The Chinese regard paper as one of the "four precious things," the other three being pens, ink, and ink-slabs. They pick up every loose scrap of paper they see if it bears printing or writing upon it, and the remnants are solemnly burned.—Candide, in "The Sunday Pictorial."

A good story about that man of astonishing memory, “Datas.” Some ten years ago a friend asked him if he liked eggs to which “Datas” readily responded “Yes.” The other who frankly disbelieved in his powers, thinking his marvellous answers were a mere trick, made a careful note of the question. Then, some time ago, he met “Datas” again, and, before anything else was said, hurled at him “How?” Without the least hesitation “Datas” answered “Fried.”

The Liberal Party, which is widely regarded as almost extinct, won a striking success in a debate at the Union Society of Cambridge University recently. The motion before the house was "that this house, rejecting Conservatism, wishes to express its unqualified approval of the Liberal Party and its aims." The motion, of course, was one upon which both Conservatives and Labourites could unite against the Liberals. In spite of this, the Liberals won through by 146 votes to 152. Lord Hugh Cecil, brother of the more famous Lord Robert—now Viscount Chelwood—championed the cause of Conservatism, while the Liberal stalwart was Ramsay Muir, the historian, who edits the "Weekly Westminster."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. and Mrs. A. G. Hewitt are due to leave England for Hongkong on November 8.

The forthcoming weeding is announced of Mr. John Walter Harris, of the Kowloon Docks, to Mrs. Adola Camino, widow, of Jordan Road, Kowloon.

Dr. William Peek, the Managing Director of the London Congress of 700 American doctors, says: "The whole tragedy of modern life is that all the best citizens, the greatest men, are killing themselves before their time." He denounces the mania for overwork, overplay, and the indulgence in night life. The modern hustle is just suicide, and a return to the simple life would do away with the necessity for many doctors.

Bulletin No. 200 of the Canadian Pacific contains the following: — Canadian Pacific—As Others See Us.

1. From Sir Claud Severn, Colonial Secretary Hongkong Government, to E.F.I. Sturdee, General Passenger Agent, Hongkong:

I am most grateful to you and to the representatives of the Canadian Pacific Railway Co.—at Vancouver, Montreal and Saint John for all the kindness and attention shown to Lady Severn on her journey.

“I have been told by her how much she appreciated what was done for her, and how easy her journey was made thereby.”

The scantiness of women's costumes at the recent Ascot meeting was widely commented on. One smartly dressed woman made the admission that the hat which she wore at Ascot as a debutante fifteen years ago weighed only an ounce more than the entire outfit she wore to day. The woman who was the first held by an evening newspaper held the recall of weighing the hat at the time because it gave her a leadsche. She put her chiffon-gown silk underwear, hat shoes, stockings and handbag of the sales and found they weighed quite an ounce more than the hat.

A Consulate-General for the Argentine Republic was opened in Kobe on October 1, at 100, Yedo-machi. Mr. Francisco Ortis has been appointed Consul-General.

Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister has now withdrawn his resignation as President of the Board of Trade as a result of pressure from the Premier. Sir Philip tendered his resignation over the Government's subvention to the coal industry, thinking it the proper thing to do, because of his wife's large interests as a coalowner. Mr. Baldwin and his Ministers felt strongly that there was no reason whatever in the circumstances why he should resign, and Sir Philip has now come round to their point of view.

Sir William Joynson-Hicks, British Home Secretary, in an interview with the London “Morning Post” last month, characterised as “premature” the report that a special constabulary was to be recruited to safeguard the public against unrest fostered by the Communists. He admitted, however, that such a plan was under consideration, together with other “safety measures.”

During his stay in Chile, the Prince of Wales received many reminders of his grandfather's association with the Republic. Nominally King Edward acted as arbitrator between Chile and the Argentine, and his name is greatly honoured throughout the 38 degrees of latitude over which the State extends. Conventional boundaries only exist in the south, where by the award of King Edward in 1902, as a result of the examination of the disputed territories by the Commission, led by Sir Thomas Holdie, limits were established to lands where the ownership was not otherwise definable.

The annual dinner of the London Critics' Circle allows the tables to be turned for once and the critics themselves to be criticised by those whom they are in the habit of pillorying. Lord Darling, who presided, said that in proposing the health of the critics he was compelled to do a painful and unpopular thing. He asked anyone who had ever been criticised from the cradle upward to tell him whether he had ever benefited in the slightest degree from it. He quoted Coleridge as saying: "Reviewers are usually people who would have been poets, historians, biographers, if they could they have tried their talents at one or the other, and they have failed; therefore they turn critics." He inquired whether any of the critics who had potentially commented on the world of Miss Still Thorndike as "Joan of Arc's but " are attempted to play the GREEN ISLAND CEMENT GO., LTD.

Messrs. Vernon and Smyth in their share reported dated October 30, comment as follows: —Since the boycott and strike in the Colony and the stoppage of credit, the Stock Exchange has been closed since June 22 and reopened on 21st inst. With the exception of "Banks" and "Insurances" which show a slight drop in prices, all other stocks almost without exception show a capital depreciation of between 30 per cent. and 40 per cent.; and in some cases as much as 50 per cent.; with the exchange closed there was small enquiry for investment Shares at bargain prices but with the re-opening this enquiry appears to have ceased, and the market closes practically without buyers or sellers. Calls and New Issues on several stocks could not be met and the dates have had to be postponed.

The floating dock at Southampton has now lifted successfully all the biggest Atlantic liners except the "Leviathan".

Ships arriving with cargo at Hamburg during the first half of the year represented a million-and-half tons more than in the corresponding period of 1913.

Ireland owns more than 50,000 cottages erected at the expense of the local authorities, to provide housing for labourers. The policy of their erection dates from as far back as 1883 when T. P. O'Connor secured enactment of a bill for that purpose by the British Parliament, and it has since been largely extended. The rent of one of these cottages in the Cork rural district is only 42 cents a week.

The court-martial of the officers and soldiers who were implicated in the April military rising at Lisbon ended in an absolvatory sentence, the generals who formed the jury deciding after five hours' deliberation that it had been proved that the revolt had been inspired by patriotic motives. Exceptional interest was attached to the court-martial throughout the country, owing to the high moral and military status of the accused, some of whom rendered distinguished service in the war. The sentence was received with public approval.

Col. J. Obed Smith, Commissioner of Immigration in London for many years for the Dominion, on a trans-Canada tour, expressed the view that the Government should undertake the work of finding new markets for the grain products of Canada. Colonel Smith made the suggestion that it would be a good thing to distribute millions of loaves of wheat bread in China to accustom the Chinese to eating white bread. Mr. Smith predicted that if proper steps were taken to enlarge the Oriental market, it would within 10 years absorb a large percentage of the wheat grown on the prairies.

headline: KOWLOON SHOOTING.
text:
ACCUSEID COMMITTED TO SESSIONS.

The three men arrested in connection with the shopping affair at Chatham Road on Friday night were again before the Kowloon Magistrate yesterday, when evidence of the shooting at Sergeant Clarke was taken and details were given as to the arrest of the two men at the residence of Captain Joll.

Mr. Leo d'Almada appeared for the man charged with unlawful possession of a revolver and shooting at Sergeant Clarke. Another man was charged with unlawful possession of the revolver. The case against the third man was one of unlawful assembly, and this was adjourned for a week to be dealt with summarily.

Capt. L. D. Joll, testified to being the owner of the revolver, which when he went to camp he left in a drawer. The second accused was previously engaged by him as cook, and had borne a very good character.

Mrs. Joll gavo evidence of handling, over to the police the revolver which she found in a drawer, after a second search. The weapon was at the rear of the drawer and witness could not say whether it was there when she first searched but was of the opinion, after the arrests of the two men in the house, that the revolver was put in the drawer after her first search.

Lient. Aucott, R.A., stated that on being asked by Mrs. Joll, on their return to the house, to close the doors and windows, before leaving, in case the servants should gain admittance through them, he noticed a leg protruding from under a bed in a spare room. The man was pulled out and was followed by the second and third.

The two accused were committed for trial at the Criminal Sessions.

headline: REDS ON TRIAL.
text:
SEDITIOUS CONSPIRACY DENIED.

At the resumption of the trial of the 12 Communists at the Old Bailey, the case for the prosecution closed.

Sir Henry Slesser opened the defence and submitted that the documents or extracts from defendants' newspapers cited by the prosecution did not constitute seditious libels, and said defendants had not conspired to publish them.

AMERY ANCO BURBERRY RESTRICTION (Ractor's Service).

headline: POOR CHILDREN'S EDUCATION.
text:
Another branch of work in which the Society is particularly interested is that of educating the children of the poor, to ensure the efficient management of which, an Education Sub-Committee has been organised by the Council of the Society, their chief duties being to examine and sign the weekly school reports of the students, to look after their moral and intellectual improvement and to provide them with clothes, shoes, books, stationery, etc., when required. It is gratifying to note that this new branch has been working very successfully to the satisfaction of both teachers and parents.

Owing to many of the poor having to live in small premises and congested areas constituting not only a danger to their own health but a grave moral danger for their children, it is gratifying to note that improvements have been effected and flats and cubicles in less overcrowded districts have been secured.

Other works of mercy under-taken by the Society are in connection with temporary relief and passages to Europeans and other destitutes from outside the Colony, the relief of the aged poor of the Colony at the Home in Kowloon Tong, general medical help and supply of clothing and shoes, and finding for the children under their care suitable employment. In this connection most valuable emergency work was done in the strike for which the Society has been especially thanked by the Government.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
The International Traders, Ltd., hope to make arrangements for the reopening of the Boa Vista Hotel, Mucao, by Christmas or early New Year.

There will a Public Lecture at the Helena May Institute this evening at 5.30 p.m. given by Professor J. R. Shellshear, D.S.O., entitled: "Early Man in Borneo." Admittance free.

The Infantry Company, Scottish Company, and the Mounted Infantry Company of the Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps participated in a field day at Fanling yesterday. A strong muster turned out and field firing practices and other training was carried out.

The Cathedral Architect reports that St. Peter's Church, West Point, is in an unsafe condition. The council of the Church have recently sanctioned urgent repairs costing almost two thousand dollars. An appeal is to be made immediately to raise this sum.

Messrs. Lane, Crawford, Ltd., have just published their general catalogue for 1926. It is a book of 225 pages and a regular mine of useful information for all householders. Without it one does not realise the wide range and variety of the goods on offer by this big departmental store, and, moreover, it is an exceedingly useful publication for checking prices. A copy should be in the possession of every family and Messrs. Lane Crawford will be pleased to supply them on application. The catalogue covers all sections of the business with the exception of the grocery department. The groceries price list, owing to the constant fluctuations, is issued monthly.

A final dividend of 5 per cent, free of Income Tax, for the year ended June 30, 1925, has been declared by the Kallan Mining Administration.

The Second Concert in aid of the Organ Fund will be given in the Cathedral Hall on Wednesday, next December, at 6 p.m. (sharp). The Hongkong Male Voice Choir--(Conductor, Mr. Stanley Collett), will assist and the soloists are Mrs. Minney, Mr. Li Chor-chi and Mr. H. E. Gardner. Tickets (one dollar) may be obtained from the Organist, at the Cathedral Hall.

Messrs. Vernon & Smyon, in their weekly share report, say: During the week under review business in the Local Share Market opened with some enquiry and rates generally took a turn for the better though only a small volume of business resulted; sellers holding off for better prices which still show a large capital depreciation; during the latter part of the week enquiry has not been so much in evidence and although the market closes firm very little business has been negotiated. The money market still appears to be tight in spite of a possible lifting of the boycott in the near future, when this becomes a fact we believe all stocks will show considerable advancement or at least nominal rates to-day will revert to buying prices.

"The Shanghai Market has been active during the week especially in 'Rubber' and 'Cpttons' where a huge volume of business has been done both for cash and forward delivery.

With “Rubber”. And up again in Singapore the market there has been active throughout with still an upward tendency, business has been done in almost all local stocks and the market closes firm with buyers predominating. “Tin” closes firm with less business passing.

The Chinese press reports that Marshal Sun Chun-feng proposes to reorganise the Shanghai Chinese police and to increase their number to 5,000, strong in order to preserve peace and order locally.

A certain busy City man in London has a very good method of dealing with barbers. As soon as he is seated in the chair he says: "Cut the whole three short." "What three sir," asks the barber. "Hair, whiskers, and chatter," replies the busy man.

One really extraordinary achievement of the Mormons was the erection of a great building with absolutely perfect acoustics. This is the vast Mormon Tabernacle at Salt Lake City, with its egg-shaped auditorium and seating accommodation for 9,000 people. The splendid acoustic properties of the building greatly impressed that keen observer, the late Lord Leverhulme, and he declared that it was, for once, no exaggeration to say that the dropping of a pin on the platform of the Tabernacle could really be heard at the other end of the building.

Dr. Temple, Bishop of Manchester, speaking at the luncheon of the Manchester Publicity Club, last month, warned his hearers that religion could not be worked by "stunts." Giving an example of the kind of publicity he de-precated, Dr. Temple said: "You see in America this sort of Church announcement: 'If you will come inside here you will hear a Church yell'by mussed choirs.' "The chief evil from which our age is suffering (the continued) is restlessness and dissipation. We are not sufficiently quiet at any period of life or for any length of time, to strike deep roots. In consequence we have, comparatively speaking, practically ceased to grow great individuals."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Rev. E. K. Quick of St. Stephen's College, leaves on the 16th inst. He is not returning. His going will be a distinct loss to local cricket.

Father José Algue, whose name is so well known throughout the East for his work at the Manila Observatory, is reported to be retiring from the Directorship of the Weather Bureau owing to failing eyesight. It is stated that in that event he will receive a life-long pension under the Philippines Retirement Act. Father Selga, the present Assistant Director, is mentioned as his successor.

The second gramophone concert was given in the lounge of the Hotel Metropole yesterday, at 9.15 p.m. The Anderson Music Co. kindly lent one of the recent Grafonola models and some of the new process records for the occasion. The programme included numbers from the operas Othello, Carmen, Rigoletto and Pagliacci and instrumental items by W. H. Squire and others. Madame Clara Butt was also represented, and the famous 850 voices record was included. The recital was under the direction of Mr. R. Wilson of Messrs. Trollope and Colls Ltd. The seventh ordinary yearly meeting of shareholders of the China Light and Power Co. (1918), Ltd., is advertised for December 21, at 11:30 a.m.

It is an interesting fact that the Chief Scout Sir Robert Baden Powell is an artist of considerable ability. At the recent show, of pictures and sculpture by Army Officers, one of the most striking exhibits was a modelled figure of a Boy Scout. This was one of Sir Robert's productions. To the same exhibition he contributed several paintings. Sir Robert is a great believer in the educational values of art in general and modelling in particular, and at his Hampshire home his children are encouraged to follow the paternal example in a large sandpit specially prepared for them.

A large portrait of King George, by Mr. Charles Sims, Keeper of the Royal Academy, who was commissioned by the Council of that body for this one of its series of "Royal Patrons," has been rejected. Exhibited at the Academy last year, it provoked controversy because of the rather odd pose of the slight figure within mountainous robes. Sir Frank Dicksee, President of the Royal Academy, told the "Westminster Gazette" that the rejection was quite an amisable affair. "There was considerable difference of opinion," he said, "when the proposal for the purchase was brought before the Academy, so Mr. Sims decided to withdraw it rather than reopen a controversy."

Miss V. M. Aspinall leaves for home this month after your years of service at the Diocesan Girls' School, Kowloon.

Chaliapine's appearance at the Albert Hall reminds a reader of a conversation which he overheard on the occasion of his last visit. Two ladies listened with great attention to his first song; then one turned to the other and said, tentatively: "He's a tenor, isn't he?" The other looked at her, in surprise. "He sounds like a baritone!" she affirmed. Hastily they turned to the programme, and naturally discovered that the great singer is a bass. That is the result of having a voice of unusual range.

Out of Russia has come a strangely designed flat gold box, studded with precious jewels, reputed to be the cigarette case of Rasputin, "the Mad Monk," who wielded a powerful influence over the Czar and who was assassinated during the war. The case is now in the possession of M. Milan of Boston, who purchased it from Jacques H. Jopkeen. Jewellers have appraised the value of the metal, stones and workmanship at more than $2,000. Evidence that the case was the property of Rasputin is said to be good and, it is said, is strengthened by the story of a gift by the Czarina of such a case to the monk.

headline: HONGKONG HOTEL / A CHINESE NEW YEAR'S EVE
text:
WILL BE HOLD

FRIDAY, 12th FEBRUARY, 1926.

One British case of diphtheria was reported in the Colony on Wednesday.

The steamship "Angiolina" has arrived at King George Dock, Hull, with a cargo of 10,165 tons of cotton seed from Alexandria, the largest cargo ever imported into Hull docks.

Visitors to the Zoo to the end of November this year numbered 1,796,470. Gate money was £57,871, a decrease of £10,537 compared with the corresponding period last year.

A big fire in the heart of Bangkok destroyed about fifty houses, most of which were small ones. Several fire brigades combined to suppress the conflagration, which was witnessed by over 10,000 people among whom was the King of Siam.

Glowing tribute to the progress made by the Philippines Islands since American occupation was paid by Bishop Charles Bayard Mitchell, bishop of the Methodist Episcopal church of the Philippine Islands, in a recent sermon at the first Methodist Church in Los Angeles.

The Shanghai Municipal "Gazette" gives the figures of the foreign population of the Settlement taken at the recent census. The outstanding feature of the census is an increase in this population of over 6,000 as compared with 1920, while turning back to previous years the striking growth of the Settlement is well illustrated. In 1900 the foreign population was under 7,000, and it was not until the 1920 census that it went over the 20,000 mark. Up to 1910 the British led the foreign community in numbers, but from that time onwards they were surpassed by the Japanese. The ever greater number of Japanese there is a striking point about the census figures, for while they were a community of 736 only in 1900, they now head the totals with 13,804. Their increase during the last five years is practically 40 per cent.

headline: ORTHOPHONIC VICTRO LA
text:
IT IS WONDERFUL III

Victor Distributors

◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇◇

ON

when it remarks that "no one can govern and organise China but the Chinese themselves." The wish is obviously the father of the thought. Were the Chinese to set to work and govern and organise China the entire picture would be altered. Those ideals handed down by age-old sages would at long last be revivified. Those principles that formed the common platform on the creation of the Chinese Republic would come into active practice. China, in short, would gain that "place" in the sun" which has so far been denied her by her own mistaken leaders and by her subtle Bolshevik advisers.

No greater encouragement to govern and organise their own country has been given to the Chinese than by the British. Even in difficult and embarrassing times there has not been the slightest deviation in the British spirit of help and co-operation. Circumstances have arisen from time to time to cloud that spirit, but the right of doubt has ever yielded place to the dawn of the "entente cordiale." Viewed from this angle—and this angle alone,—the "Times" is right in its endorsement of British policy at the moment. And, of course, it is ever so much easier to be an optimist ten thousand miles away from the scene of conflicting and trying events.

headline: CAFE INCIDENT. / IMPRISONMENT SENTENCE REVISED:
text:
It was submitted by Mr. Lo that there was conflicting evidence in the case. The complainant alleged that the defendant attacked him with a knife and that, in self defence he tried to ward off the blow and then hit the defendant. An independent witness, a Portuguese gentleman, who was sitting at the adjoining table, said he saw the complainant strike the defendant after ordering him to remove some dirty knives. Having regard to the evidence that the defendant had a knife in his hand, His Worship might find that complainant was hurt as a result of holding a knife.

He further said that the injury was superficial and was not deliberately inflicted. He agreed that perhaps defendant should not have had a knife in his hand. Major Willson said he agreed to a certain extent with Mr. Lo's submissions, and holding that there was no deliberate intention of stabbing, imposed a fine of $25.

headline: THE PASSING OF LUNCH.
text: There comes from Paris the strange story that lunch is passing away. The Parisian working day, like all else in Continental life, has ever been organised upon the basis of a large and a long midday meal. Whatever else was reformed, this, call it déjeuner or Mittagessen, seemed secure, and nowhere else safer than in Paris. The Parisian at least, we thought (says the "Daily Telegraph"), we could rely upon to place the comforts of life above the "base exactions of business, never for the sake of livelihood to sacrifice what makes life worth living. The plea is that both the senses of comfort and business unite in voting for the abolition of the déjeuner. To go home to lunch was well enough while Paris was compact. Now that everybody has to live miles away from shop and office an unconscionable time is wasted over lunch, to nobody's satisfaction. The mere thought of going home to lunch strikes the Londoner as antediluvian. What he would say to the common Paris hours of a working day that begins at nine and ends at seven, with some two hours or more of a luncheon interval, is beyond imagination, but certainly he would prefer his tea shop to all the flesh-pots of Paris. A number of large business houses in Paris have lately been making experiments with a working day on the London pattern, ending at five, broken only by a short interlude for lunch. Everybody is said to be pleased, and business people consider that the knell of lunch is sounded. We must suppose that they intend to fortify Nature with a more substantial or English breakfast. So time offers us the prospect of an interesting experiment to prove whether the difference between Continental meals and ours is mere chance or the expression of a natural incompatibility of temperament. It is to be observed that there is nothing permanent about the time of our meals or even the distribution of quantities between them. Not to go back into the dark ages, which would afford overwhelming examples of variety, let us be content with the food of one poor century. When Macaulay went to breakfast at Holland House, a temple of luxury, there was nothing to eat but rolls and butter.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
A movement is on foot to organise a debating society in connection with the Hongkong University.

"Don't kiss the Book—that superstition is done away with."—Murlborough Street magistrate to witness.

Fire: enused considerable damage to the Prince of Wales's stables at Tor Royal, Farm, Prineetown, in Dartmoor Forest. But all the Prince's horses were safely removed.

When at Port Tilbot it was said that the inhabitants of one street had paid neither rent nor rates for some years the magnitude remarked. "This seems to be the real Utopia."

"Don't come any further or you will be sitting on my lap soon."—Judge Furtitt to woman who failed to see the witness-box and advanced on the judge's bench at Clerkenwell.

A Chinese boatman charged at the Kowloon Magistracy yesterday with participation in an armed robbery on board a junk at Deep Bay, clavigged that he was kidnapped by the other, robbers and forced to accompany them to the boat. This story was believed and the man was discharged.

One of the attractions in Japan is the Tokyo fish market. It is the longest in the country and occupies 480,000 square feet. The market is an association of 750 wholesalers and 552 brokers who operate under the supervision of municipal authorities. Two thousand fish mongers and buyers from numerous hotels and restaurants assemble at this market every morning between 5 and 10 o'clock and carry away with them from 800 to 1,200 tons of fish.

As a result of carefully planned newspaper publicity, Brighton is enjoying a "boom." During 1925-74, 327 more tickets were taken between London and Brighton, than were booked during 1924, while the number of passengers passing through the barriers of the Central Station, Brighton. During the first six weeks of 1925 was 660,000. This is an increase of 27.8 per cent, as compared with the corresponding period last year. In all no flower than 16,000,000 passengers passed in or out of the station in 1425. "I am a mere home."—Husband. at Police Court.

The four Dutch submarines visiting Manila were opened for public inspection.

Moscow is to maugurate an air post service between European Capitals on May 1.

"I know he's a har but you can't help loving him," said a woman of her husband the Bow County Court.

A. Blackpool Corporation workman, engaged on street work, stuck his pick into a cable composed of 1,600 telephone wires, and 532 subscribers were cut off from the Exchange.

Wholesale prosecution of municipal officials in Passay as a result of failure to enforce the anti-vice ordinance in force in that municipality since 1920 is expected to begin during the next few days.

A gift from Trinity House has been received by the National Lifeboat Institution, as a mark of gratitude for the saving of one of the keepers of Godrevy Lighthouse, who was dangerously ill during a gale.

France has successfully prohibited absinthe as a beverage and accomplished it in a single day. The absinthe habit was rooted in the French people. Up to the first days of the war the Paris boulevard and all France had its "hour of absinthe" or its "green hour" every afternoon at 5 o'clock.

"The University of California baseballteam's proposed tour of Japan this summer has been cancelled, say cables from America. The reason given for this action is that the University wanted a guarantee of $20,000/year for the expenses of the tour, whereas the Japanese organisers offered only a part of the receipts from the games. The California baseballers will," however, tour Hawaii for six weeks.

A new Roman Catholic Society, supported by Cardinal Bourne and many Catholic Arch-bishops and Bishops, is launching an organised campaign throughout Britain against spiritualism, which is described as a dangerous cult, aiming at the root and branch destruction of Christianity. The late Bishop of Salford (Dr. Casartelli), claimed that spiritualism was responsible for a large leakage from Roman Catholicism.

Judged by the prosperity and peace which it should promote through opening to cultivation 3,000,000 acres in the Sudan, "Makepeace" would seem more appropriate than Makkwa as a name for the great dam recently opened on the Blue Nile.

Women pickets in a textile dispute at Kirkenton have adopted music as a “persuader.” As the non-striking operatives leave the factory the pickets “chorus” sings. “Onward, Christian Soldiers” The heads of the firm are also “serenaded” with hynns. About one hundred women are affected

Bethesda, in Curnarvonshire, is tired of its Hebrew name, but is having considerable difficulty in selecting one in Welsh. A subcommittee submitted four possible names to the urban council to-day. Glynogwen, Giltorowen. The for-wen and Naitogwen. None of them was sufficiently attractive, and the special committee was asked to meet again and try to invent a better one.

An influential delegation, representing 300 chambers of commerce: and several important national trade organisations visited Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer to make a vigorous protest against the present tax methods by which business is done by co-operative societies, which receive more favourable tax treatment than private trading. Co-operative societies have reached an enormous size in Great Britain, and it was pointed out that they are profit-making organisations and do not deserve preferential treatment as against heavily-taxed private trading.
