headline: Exodus: Continues.
text:
Long before sunrise, in fact within a short time of the incoming river steamers discharging their passengers, hundreds of Chinese had swarmed on to the wharves determined to obtain a passage for Canton or the native village. At daylight this morning the vessels due to leave this evening were absolutely full of passengers. Little or no cargo was worked, but a constant stream of men and women, all carrying luggage, were turned back. A conservative estimate places the number shut-out at 10,000. Many of those going down were domestic' servants, ostensibly from foreign households.

This morning some households still had their servants and were able to get their meals, but the majority of the more fortunate employers were informed that their employees would, reluctantly, as in nearly every case, have to leave about tiffin time.

headline: Scouts Helping
text: The Hongkong Boy Scout's Association is doing its "bit" and arrangements in hand by which this help will be considerably extended if necessary. At present there are several qualified Scouts working in hospitals and many others are holding themselves in readiness for all sorts of other work, down to working in lifts if necessary. The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave, Commissioner, informed us on enquiry that all Scouts had been asked to report to Headquarters. The parade arranged to take place at Government House on Wednesday had been cancelled.

headline: Rumours About To-morrow.
text:
Many are the rumours about tomorrow. Those who correctly predicted on Saturday night that the trams would stop on Sunday now say that the beef and other stalls at the market may have to shut down tomorrow and that the engineeringers and firemen on harbour ferries may stay away.

Vernacular papers suspended publication this morning but extras were issued.

Hundreds of workers are crossing the Territories to travel by train to Canton, A China Mail reporter was informed that had it not been for the rain yesterday and to-day, a much larger number would have trekked miles but refrained for fear of weiting their personal effects.

headline: Earlier Developments.
text:
The strike which commenced on Friday has now developed considerably and affects all classes and almost all industries and businesses.

The boys at the Peak Hotel began to leave shortly before tiffin on Saturday and the remainder went after tiffin. The exodus, from the Peak Club took place on Saturday afternoon, but this did not interfere with the dance in the evening, refreshments being served and the necessary washing-up done with skill and dexterity, by the members themselves.

The Chinese staff at Repulse Bay did not leave until tiffin on Sunday. It was stated that between four and five hundred Chinese engaged in the two hotels—the Peak Hotel and the Repulse Bay Hotel—had gone. A few of the boys from the Hongkong Hotel left during the course of yesterday morning, and last night all but one or two had left. At all the hotels, however, careful and well-planned arrangements have been made to "carry on" as well as is possible in the circumstances.

The boys began to leave the houses in the Peak district on Sunday morning. Previously there had been no suggestion of a strike.

During the night, however, the following notice, in Chinese, was stated to have been left at a considerable number of residences:—

Gentlemen,— I his is to inform you that in consequence of the recent incidents in Shanghai, causing workers and students to suffer cruel deaths, our corps has determined to carry out a general strike on and from Sunday next. Anybody who fails to join the strike will get from our corps extraordinary treatment.

This precious document is said to have been found on the doorsteps of the houses early in the morning. Its effect was extraordinary.

When the employees of the Tramway Company finished their work at Saturday mid-night, there was no reference to any possibility of a strike. The drivers and conductors, however, failed to put in an appearance on Sunday morning and consequently yesterday no trams were running.

At the tiffin given in honour of H.E. the Governor at the Hongkong Club on Saturday, His Excellency made a passing reference to the possibility of his approaching departure being postponed on account of the strike. "If this nonsense continues," H.E. declared, "I am going to see it through, and I do not think the arrangement will be a comfortable one for those responsible for my delay." In view of the developments, since this speech was delivered it seems highly improbable that H.E. the Governor will leave on Saturday as arranged.

headline: Further Details.
text:
About 11.30 a.m. to-day, a Japanese was shot near the French Bridge by an unknown person who is said to be a Chinese. Two shots were heard. One bullet went through the man's left arm into his body and the other struck his leg. He was carried into the Concession by French sailors and Dr. Reynolds of Shameen. Later on I was informed that the man had succumbed and that he was connected with the Japanese hospital at Nam Kwan.

All the Hongkong and Macao boats to-day were anchored off Shameen with the exception of the s.s. Charles Hardouin. The Honam did not sail for Hongkong this morning and is anchored in the same place.

The Canton Government has issued an order that all former gambling houses and Yunnanese holdings are to be used as strike quarters and that the merchants are to contribute to strike funds.

Although the Chinese employees on Shameen have declared that they do not wish to strike but it seems that they will ultimately yield to the inevitable.

What the World is Being Told. Below will be found the Reuter messages broadcast from Hong- kong:—

The motormen and conductors of the electric Tramway Company have struck. The service is temporarily suspended. The strike of Chinese servants is spreading. Many boarding houses, some hospitals and hotels are affected. Boy Scouts are mobilising for the purpose of assisting the hospital. The Government has offered a reward of $250 for information leading to arrest and conviction of persons endeavouring to disturb the peace of the Colony. Numbers of Chinese are leaving the city for Canton. Chinese crews on several more British steamers have deserted.

The Volunteers have been mobilised. Boy Scouts have replaced the striking Chinese attendants at Hospital. Six steamers of the Indo-China Navigation Company are tied up.

Later.

A number of British and other foreign women and children have arrived from Shameen whence they were advised to leave. Police re patrolling the business quarters of Shameen precautionarily.

headline: Canton Shooting.
text:
An unknown Chinese shot dead Mr. Nakadai, the Japanese treasurer of the Japanese Hospital, just outside Shameen, and carried off a bag with five thousand dollars with which Mr. Nakadai was returning from the Bank of Taiwan.

The Japanese Consul has strongly protested to the local authorities, reserving the right to claim indemnity, and asking for police to be posted outside Shameen. He advised Japanese subjects in Canton to come to Shameen.

Many foreigners are going to Hongkong.—Most of the others residing outside the European quarter are now coming to Shameen.

The strike at Shameen began this morning. The Chinese are (ielty leaving the Concession.

There are no disturbances. British Marines are operating the ice-plant and are ready to operate the waterworks.

Later.

The Civil Governor of Canton has requested the merchants to contribute to strike funds. Gambling houses closed before the war have been taken over as quarters for strikers who number approximately 1,500. Shameen has an extra supply of food. Another Japanese destroyer has arrived.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Comm. Maxwell Scott, the Senior Naval Officer at Canton, has been promoted to the rank of captain.

Says Dr. Inge (the Gloomy Dean) on his visit to America:—I met with nothing but courtesy from high and low. The good American is a great gentleman; and this quality seems to be widely diffused, irrespective of differences in social position.

It is not without significance that, when a procession of Chinese paraded the streets the other day in Kobe in order to encourage the strike of Chinese semmen, some of the most prominent in the procession were employees of British firms, and these prominent patriots were not themselves on strike.

A Naval flight is projected from Yokosuka to Maizuru and across the Japan Sea to Vladivostok, to take place in either July or September. The return trip is expected to take a week. The seaplanes will participate.

The British American Tobacco Co. (China), Ltd., announces that as so much unjust pro-paganda is being directed against it by competitive interests in an effort to boycott the products of the Company, the Company has felt justified in calling the attention of the public to the great quantity of charitable work it has done in China. A list of its charities follows, making a very large total.

President von Hindenburg has objected to the paintings hung by President Ebert in the rooms of the Presidential Palace. President Ebert, who was a great lover of nature, had decorated his rooms almost exclusively with landscape pictures. In his working room hung a large landscape, a woman's portrait by Rembrandt and two small water colours. President von Hindenburg, however, declared they were not cheerful enough for his taste, and has chosen several new pictures at the state picture galleries.

A Biblical ballet has been holding the attention of the Moscow public for some time. It is entitled "Beautiful Joseph," and depicts the incidents of the persecution of Joseph by his brothers, with his sale into Egypt and subsequent adventures there, through the medium of a rich Oriental ballet, with a weird, bizarre musical accompaniment by the modern Russian composer, Vassilenko. A "more conventional ballet entitled "Teodelinda," a story of bandits transformed into fauns, with musical accompaniment by Schubert, is given along with "Beautiful Joseph," and the double attraction has, for many weeks drawn large crowds to the Experimental Theatre, where it is given.

headline: 一
text: The Chinese Communists, arrested after the attack on the Chinese Legation at Paris, were taken to the frontier of Belgium to be dumped in that friendly State. As a rule, the Belgian police do not object, but these undesirables were too much for them. John Chinaman was promptly pounted back into France. A French Commissary tried several points along the Belgian frontier; but each time the yellow Reds were returned to him (without thanks). He resolved to try Germany. From Strasbourg he took his proteges to the nearest point of the frontier beyond the Rhine, and told them to go straight on. They did not return. The new Chinese puzzle was solved.

A driver of a taxicab goes to the Chamber of Deputies in Paris, and when he arrives he places a black cover over the flag of his taximeter. This indicates that he is not soliciting fares. He puts his cwb on the rank and enters the Chamber. He takes his seat on the parliamentary benches, listens to the discussions and sometimes intervenes. When the sitting is over, or when he considers that his presence is not required, he leaves, returns to his cab, takes off the black cover, and plies for hire. For the taxi driver is a Deputy, but because he is a Deputy he does not therefore cease to follow his occupation. For a number of hours every day he drives for a living. The cab is his own property and he is therefore under no restrictions as to hours. His name is Monsieur Adam, and he sits as a Communist in the Department of the Seine.

headline: HOCKEY PROSPECTS. / DISCUSSED AT ANNUAL MEETING.
text:
Confidence in the prospects for another successful season was expressed at the annual meeting yesterday of the Hongkong Hockey Club. - This took place at Volunteer Headquarters, and was presided over by Lieut. Col. L. G. Bird, D.S.O., the attendance not being large owing to the coincidence of the Rugby match between the Volunteers and H.M.S. "Hermes."

After a balance in hand of $238.88 had been reported, last season's excellent record was read and the revival of meetings between the Club and Shameen was referred to. As regarded the future, the Club would have three representatives at a meeting on Monday of the Recreation Grounds Committee which would consider a request for a double plot to serve as sports ground for the Volunteers. During the coming season there would again be three teams and playing days would be the same. The resignation of Mr. Bower from the Club was received with regret and for his organisation which had made possible the playing by the A team of 18 matches the thanks of the Club were recorded.

Present officers willing to serve again were Hon. Secretary, P.W. F. Mills; Captain, E.J. R. Mitchell; and Vice-Captain, W. Woodward. Mr. J. Wedlake was elected Captain of the second XI. and Mr. L. H. Kearne of the "A" team. Mr. G. H. Piercy who had signified his inability to continue in the office of Hon. Treasurer was succeeded by Mr. L. H. Ralphs.

The thanks of the Club were recorded to the United Services Recreation Club for the use of grounds and entertainment of visitors.

headline: S.S. "WAH SHAN."
text:
CANTON ACKNOWLEDGES SEIZURE.

POLITICS BLAMED.

In connection with the seizure of the s.s. "Wah Shan," the "Canton Gazette" of Monday says:—

A special correspondent reports that the steamer "Wah Shan" was found transporting provisions to Hongkong. "She was seized by the pickets immediately. Several officers under Tang Poon-yan were arrested on board the steamer. They were brought to the Strike Committee at Canton.

The Nationalist Government has ordered the Strike Committee to transfer the case, including criminals and steamer, to the Government for judgment, as documents relating to political matters were found on the criminals when their arrest was effected.

[Commander Tang Pun-yan is the pro-Chan Kwing-ming ruler of Hainan and the Lui Chow peninsula. The "Wah Shan" did not touch his territory nor is it a passenger steamer. The only ports of call were Hongkong (British), Kwong Chow Wan (French) and Macao (Portuguese).]

headline: RUGBY RULES.
text:
INTERNATIONAL BOARD'S CHANGES.

SCRUMS, OFFSIDE, THROW-OUT.

In order that all players may familiarise themselves with the changes in the laws of the game recently passed by the International Board, the Home Rugby Union have just issued a resume of such changes.

In regard to a scrummage, the team not responsible for the stoppage now has the right of putting the ball into the scrummage on either side, and the ball is not to be considered fairly in the scrummage until it has passed a player on each side.

An offside player is not to be put onside when the ball is touched by an opponent, but only when the ball is intentionally so touched. No charge is to be allowed when a penalty kick is taken.

Another interesting change is in the throw-out law. The ball must now be thrown out so as to alight at least five yards at right angles to the touch-line.

What is the best of all exercises from the point of view of health and fitness? The Lord Mayor of London (Sir Alfred Bowar)

headline: TRADE ROMANCE
text:
The enterprise of these responsible for the founding of the English India Company and the patented and bravery of those responsible for carrying on its work forms the subject of an article in the Scottish Educational Journal. The story whilst being of educational value, it states, is also sufficiently colourful to attract the youthful student. After dealing with the first efforts of London merchants to secure a portion of the profitable business which was being carried on in the East India by the Portuguese and Dutch and the bestowal on them by Queen Elizabeth of a special monopoly, the efforts of the leading members of the association to obtain funds for the equipping of a commercial squadron are referred to. Large numbers shrank from the risk, and at last there was nothing for it but to create a separate association of the more enterprising and start business on much smaller scale than was originally intended.

On February 18, 1601, therefore, five small ships, the largest of which was only 600 tons, weighed anchor at Tor Bay, and steered on that amazing course which was to lead to the conquest of an empire. Of the many adventuring banks that have left our shores, not one has opened a story to equal the strangeness, the romance, the magnificence, of the events that were ushered in by the sailing of those five ships. Patience must have been one of the finest assets of the little group of merchants who undertook the first expedition, for they had to wait two years and seven months before their ships came home. Captain James Lancaster, under whose command they had sailed, had already been in India, but so slightly was he acquainted with the geography of the regions into which his argosies were sailing that he did not reach his destination. Acheen in Sumatra, till June 5, 1602—one year and a half after leaving England. In spite of successful business done, the wake of his five ships was not followed with much enthusiasm, the result being that for about ten years no great advance was made. Then, in 1812, a Captain Best secured privileges from the ruler at Delhi, which included the right to establish a factory at Surat, and the connection with the mainland thus made, was greatly strengthened three years later, when James I. sent Sir Thomas Roe as his ambassador to Delhi. He was received with the highest honours, and English trade with India was much encouraged. But in viewing the story of the advance of the British in the land of the Moguls, we have always to bear in mind that the distance between the two scenes of the Company's activities, together with ever changing circumstance in both places, did much to dislocate their arrangements. While the pioneers, far from the home base, were opening up fresh sources of prosperity, the Governor and his Directors in London were facing and overcoming a variety of difficulties. Increasing success (somewhat slow, however), brought competitors into the field who sought to ignore the Charter which James I. had renewed; and these competitors were not discouraged by Charles I. In spite of the monopoly that the Company legally possessed, the King last named—doubtless on account of his own need for money—granted a second Charter to a separate association, and the trade thus divided was of little profit to either, till they were finally amalgamated into one company.

headline: HELPFUL PHYBIO
text:
One of the most important factors in the peaceful means of progress referred to in the article was the help which the medicine chest of a ship's surgeon was in vastly extending the dominions of the English merchants. The Emperor Shah Jehan was touring in the neighbourhood of Surat when a fire borke cut in his camp, causing serious injury to a favourite daughter. He sent express to the English factory for a physician, and Dr. Boughton immediately set out for the scene of the accident. His skill was so effective that the princess was quickly cured, and Boughton was invited to name his fea. He asked nothing more than further concessions to the English traders, and these were readily granted. A little later, this diplomatic doctor was similarly rewarded for services rendered to one of Shah Jehan's sons. Thus the English influence gradually spread in India—so far as the natives were concerned—by peaceful means. He only resort to arms being against their European war. However, these had won to the fleet of 17, carry out a business to prepared by a capital of $140,000. In spite of ever recurring difficulties,

frequent changes in the plan of management, and of having to satisfy parliamentary demands, the trading connection between England and India continued to grow stronger. As a commercial body only, the Company were not supposed to take sides in any agreement between the native princes, though they had the right to use arms in defence of their various factories. But, with the passage of years there rose a circumstances which was to force upon the Company the fullest possible interpretation of their right to draw the sword. A French trading association, supported by their home government, appeared in Indian waters, and, under the management of very able leaders, sought to destroy British prestige. But we are now upon the threshold of common history. All the works known that there was at this time in the service of the Company, a young counting house clerk of Madras who quickly proved himself a great soldier, and who, with very indifferent military resources, destroyed the pretentious of the French; and by the victory of Plasay, rendered British influence beyond dispute.

headline: C.S.C.C. MEETING.
text:
NEW OFFICIALS FOR NEXT YEAR.

Sir Claud Severn (President) presided at yesterday's annual meeting of the Civil Service Cricket Club, held in the club house, Happy Valley.

In proposing the adoption of the report, and accounts Sir Claud referred to the Club winning both divisions of the cricket league last season. The Club was grateful to Messrs. Gipson and Wood for their work on the ground, and to Mr. Squibbs for work on the green.

The balance in hand was $1,436 as against $105 last year.

The following officers were elected. (Cricket) Captain of first XI, Mr. F. J. de Rome; vice-captain, Mr. B. D. Evans. Captain "A" team, Mr. W. H. Edmonds; vice-captain, Mr. F. Squibbs. Cricket representative, Mr. F. H. Holdman; Bowls representative, Mr. R. Smith; Tennis representative, Mr. R. R. Wood; Steward, Mr. Gregory.

Hon. Secretary, Mr. R. S. Vergette; Hon. Treas., Mr. B. Maughan; Greenranger, Mr. H. Rose.

General Committee, Messrs. Deacon, Lamble, Alderman, Brawn, Harrison, Longbotham and Strange.

Proposed by Mr. Maughan and seconded by Mr. Vergette, a motion was passed authorising the committee to draw on fixed deposit account up to $2,000 for repairs and alterations to the club-house. Sir Claud presented Mr. Gregory and Mr. Rose with inscribed silver cigarette cases in recognition of their services in looking after refreshments while the club boys were on strike.

Referring to the impending departure of H.E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs), Sir Claud suggested that a letter be sent to him, as Patron of the Club, thanking him for the great honour he had bestowed and the work he had done while in the Colony. The meeting expressed approval and then Sir Claud mentioned his own departure, speaking of the pleasure it had been for him to be associated with the Club.

Mr. E. W. Hamilton spoke of Sir Claud's services since his arrival here in 1912. They were grateful for all that he had done and trusted that Sir Claud and Lady Severn would be spared to enjoy many years of retirement. Mr. Hamilton said he hoped that among Sir Claud's many recollections of Hongkong not the least pleasant would be his connection with the Civil Service Cricket Club. Replying, Sir Claud said that later, he would take a more formal leave of them.

Proposed by Mr. Alderman, the usual honorarium was voted to the hon. secretary, treasurer and steward, a member having raised the question at an earlier stage of the meeting.

Mr. James and Mr. Williams were re-elected auditors for the year. Votes of thanks were passed to outgoing officers and to Mr. Maughana.

The following will play in the second round of the Kowloon Golf Club summer competition: K. S. Robertson v. F. X. Ramsford, R. Meldrum v. E. A. Beaumont; A. Brookshank v. E. A. de Blanc, F. Oliver v. A. W. Brown.

headline: DF NEED ARISEH
text:
That the members of Hong Kong's mass meeting were not alone in their opinion. that Canton's challenge to British treaty rights called for immediate and prompt action is shown by editorial comment in the leading Home newspapers and journals at the time news reached there of the embargo on British shipping. Instancing the need for direct action, the “Telegraph” refers to the “useful, precedent” which America set a few months ago when the American naval commander threatened to use force if there was any attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America in the light of this and more weighty facts could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese of similar measures should the need for it arise.

Discussing the regulations emanating from Canton, the "Telegraph". states:—

The first is clearly designed to prevent steamers of all nationalities, "other than British and Japanese," from touching at Hongkong, under penalty of being denied an entry to Chinese ports. Does this prohibition also apply to the Chinese vessels, mostly junks, to which goods are generally transhipped from British ships at Hongkong for conveyance to Cantonese river and other southern ports? It is difficult to resist the impression that we are here witnessing a deliberate conspiracy to destroy the economic importance of Hongkong as a great commercial distributing and transhipment centre.

The various inquiries and surveys now in progress will enable a decision to be postponed by London for yet a few days, until the whole situation has been cleared up. But it is now admitted that, once the official review thereof has been completed, prompt action will have to be taken. The feeling is also gaining ground that, in such an emergency as this where the exercise of our specific Treaty rights are directly challenged, and may be denied to us by violence, there is no reason why we should consult the dozen Powers or more, whose rights are unaffected. An exchange of views between London, Tokyo, and Washington should suffice.

As a matter of fact, Washington would be unlikely to raise any substantial objections to such naval measures as we and the Japanese may be constrained to take for the protection of British and Japanese merchantmen and merchandise from physical interference by the Canton: "Reds," to judge from an American precedent a few months old. This was during the struggle for mastery at and around Shanghai between Generals Li and Chi, and the defending commander sought to restrict the freedom of foreign vessels, including American, in the estuary. The retort of the American naval commander was that he would not hesitate to frustrate, by force if necessary, any such attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America, in the light of this and other more weighty facts, could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese naval commanders off Cantonese ports of a similar line of conduct, should the need for it arise. For Chinese labour to refuse to unload British vessels is one thing; for the Chinese central or local authorities to enjoin upon Chinese labour such a course would be a totally different thing — a serious and unfriendly act, contrary to the Treaties. As for any physical molestation of our merchants or seamen, the only suitable retort would be the intervention of the British Navy. The British communities in Hongkong and South China have once more appealed to London that our naval forces in China should be strengthened and allowed greater freedom of action.

The Chinese Government's invitation to the projected Customs Conference claims the right for China to demand complete fiscal autonomy. The demand that made will probably still further prolong the exchanges of views on the subject already is not more than between the numerous Treaty Powers. The view of the British commercial leaders states the Daily Mail is that, whatever policy is adopted by the Foreign Office, it must be one of firmness and the offensive act on such as the Trading of Customs of the Five Months by excluding Chinese shipping. Could be made the all-time value to the total value of the

The serious nature of the crisis in Canton and Hongkong is revealed in messages reaching. London headquarters of firms which trade in the Far East. They indicate that the agitation has now resulted in what is virtually a national rising, and show that British trade has nowadays come to a complete standstill.

In almost every cablegram in the last few days, commercial correspondents are appealing for representations to be made to the British Government not to delay definite action further.

Their unanimous recommendation is that the position will be best dealt with by the Foreign Office immediately sending an eminent person to Perking armed with a measure of authority to negotiate an agreement.

The trade representatives declare that the want of evidence of the intention of the British Government to act has become exasperating and is depressing morale in Hongkong. "Every day's delay," states one telegram from Hongkong, "results in increasing financial exhaustion."

Reports from Hongkong and Canton state that the daily financial loss being incurred in both places is about £250,000.

Trade correspondents' messages all allude to the unfortunate absence in Britain, where he is on sick leave, of Sir J. W. R. Macleay, the British Minister to Peking.

A representative of "The Daily Mail" was informed that Sir James Macleay hopes to have recovered sufficiently to enable him to return to Peking in about three weeks.

headline: WAR NOT WANTED.
text:
We do not, of course, want to go to war with China, further states the "Daily Mail," or if we can possibly help it with any one of the domestic or alien tyrannies which usurp authority in that distracted country. With the toiling Chinese millions we have no quarrel, and we do not believe they have any hostile feeling towards ourselves; the majority are scarcely aware of our existence. Our difficulty is with the "students" and other Westernised agitators who are stirring up the mobs and rowdies of the cities at the instigation of the Russian Soviet. These persons care little for the sufferings they may bring upon Chinese peasants, by cutting off their chief source of foreign supplies, provided they can inflict loss upon Great Britain and add to the industrial depression in this country.

That they can do so, if they are allowed to maintain, the boycott they have declared, is obvious. China is one of the great markets for British manufactured commodities. For some of these products it is the greatest foreign market of all. It is Lancashire's largest customer for certain classes of cotton goods, and many mills will have to close down if the Far Eastern trade is arrested. Yorkshire will be no less badly hit. A most substantial portion of the worsteds, woollens, and dyed cloths manufactured in Bradford and the neighbourhood has been prepared for China. The woollens alone came to £8,387,000 in 1924, and the total export of these classes of goods for the year was little short of ten millions sterling.

headline: VALUABLE "LINK." / PATIENCE REWARD:
text:
The Rev. Chapman Andrews, leader of the Third Asiatic Expedition to Mongolia, reports that priceless discoveries have been made of skulls, the discoveries of the dunia dwellers and their culture, also of what might be termed the link between the age of cold blooded reptiles and warm blooded animals through the multituberente lute skull.

The following article is an appreciation of the persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending these repeated expeditions to Mongolia, with such eventual rich reward.

The persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending repeated expeditions to Mongolia appears to have been richly rewarded. Two years ago Mr. Roy C. Andrews and his scientific colleagues found fossil dinosaurs with their eggs, but this summer they have also found many traces, though no remains as yet, of paluolithic man. The reason why Professor H. F. Osborn has for many years past advocated an exploration of the fossil deposits of Mongolia may be stated very simply. That vast country is a lofty and arid plateau, with no mountains and very few rivers. Consequently, there is a good chance of finding the fossilised remains of animals in a comparatively undisturbed condition. This prediction was confirmed two years ago, when Mr. Andrews, working at a place five hundred miles within the Gobi Desert, came upon the complete skeleton of a dinosaur with the nine eggs that she had just laid before a sandstorm came and buried her. This sand, falling gently, killed but did not crush, and the great reptile, with her eggs, remained slowly fossilising through perhaps ten million years.

In Professor Osborn's view, these Mongolian dinosaurs were ancestors of the still larger land reptiles found in Western America, such as the famous diplodocus that we may see at the Natural History Museum. Indeed, he inclines to regard Mongolian as "a centre of dispersal" of animal life—as the region, that is, where the main kinds or orders developed first, and whence tuoy spread to other parts of the earth. To establish such a during hypothesis we need, of course, infinitely more evidence than is yet available, but the American scientists who have repentedly braved the tigers of the Gobi Desert in the search for fossils have, at any rate, made the theory seem plausible. This summer Mr. Andrews has discovered six mammalian skills—and the remains of a giant rhinoceros, orbitally in strata above those containing the dinosaurs.

But special interest attaches to his finding of arrowheads, spear points, drills, and the like relics of man of the Old Stone Age, because very little is known of man's presence in Mongolia in the remote past, long before the Mongols lived there. Mr. Andrews's finds should throw welcome light on the migrations of those remote ancestors of ours in the Glacial Period, who apparently roamed over the whole earth, since their weapons and tools are much the same wherever they are found; whether in England or Egypt or Turkestan. Thus the New World through Mr. Andrews and his generous porters, is helping to elucidate the earliest history of the Old

headline: SHIPPING BOYCOTT. / RELATION TO CHINA'S SINCERITY.
text:
PROOF OF THE PUDDING

The statement of one of the Chinese delegates to the Tariff Conference that it was China's wish to walk and not run; to follow Japan's, not Turkey's example, leads the "North China Daily News" to the belief that China is trying to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any power. "But," states the "N. C. D. News," the past will no, be effaced while the present shipping boycott continues.

Why is the boycott of British shipping allowed to continue? Let us use correct terms. There is no strike. Except, perhaps, for a negligible handful, the Chinese crews would gladly go to their ships. Intimidation keeps them away, the outcome of a boycott which is being actively pushed by certain parties. And we ask, why are they allowed to continue in this nefarious, wholly illegal work?

In other directions the passive warfare of the past four months has to a large extent been stopped. General Shing Shi-lien has done much for the restoration of order by closing labour union headquarters and pro-scribing strike-leaders. But no attempt to touch the Seamen's Union, the most powerful of all.

headline: CHANGE OF SPIRIT.
text:
There is no question but that General Shing Shi-lien's suppression of the agitators had the approval of Peking. In the recent past a change has come over the spirit of the capital. True, it has refused to take part in the judicial inquiry. But it has exchanged letters of a markedly conciliatory tone with the Diplomatic Body. It has sent messages to the provinces recommending the students to go back to school and instructing their betters, if the young men do not heed the advice, at least to see that there are no more demonstrations. And within its own walls Peking has even repressed such demonstrations itself. It has sent out other messages to the provinces, ordering hurried reforms in respect of likin, justice, prisons and opium. It lets it to be known that its attitude towards the Tariff Conference is entirely reasonable: China does not wish to run before she can walk; her model is to be Japan, not Turkey. In a word, everything is being done to efface recollection of the past, to make a good show, to prove that China is civilised, organised, the political equal of any Power.

But the past will not be effaced, while the shipping boycott continues. There is no parallel that we can recall of a civilised Power permitting such an act—which only open warfare could justify—against a friendly people? It is true that some British ships continue to ply, but under no conditions even approximating the normal. Within the past few days two British vessels have put in to Swatown one from north to south there other from south to north. Swatown has recently been delivered from the Reds by General Cher Chilung-ming and it might be supposed that the boycott would have ceased. But though Swatown is bursting with cargo, not a pound of it might these two vessels take. Here, clearly, was no influence of Canton at work. Whose, then, was it, and why is permitted?

We are willing to admit that what Canton chooses to do, Peking cannot prevent, although that fact does not exactly fit in with the semblance of a civilised and organised China which Peking is so anxious to present for the delusion of the Tariff Conference. But there is no practical doubt that Peking could close the Semmen's Union in Shanghai, could throttle the agitators, could lift the boycott from British shipping, if it wished. Some, at least, of the men who are promoting the boycott may easily be guessed and they are not the men who would dare to disregard such an order from Peking. As for their bullies, a file of Fengtien troops would make short work of them. It may be said that merchants cannot be compelled to ship cargo by any particular line of ships. That is, of course, true enough. But let the boycott be called off and the intimidators put down, and there will be no lack of work for any ship. Repress the minority of ringtoners and British shipping will be quite willing to take its chance with merchants in general, as it is fully entitled to do by treaty, by custom and by every written and unwritten law that governs the mutual dealings of friendly Powers.

We believe that Peking can stop the boycott and allow British ships to trade freely. Will it dare to reply that it cannot? Then here is the alternative before it. Either it can do so, and then we ask, Why does it not? Why does it aid and abut on unlawful, hostile and unparalleled act of aggression against a friendly and innocent Power? How can it have the effrontery, while openly guilty of such conduct, to be asking of that Power all sorts of concessions and privileges? If, on the other hand, Peking speaks the truth, and is unable to stop the boycott, then know can it claim to be a sovereign Government? If it cannot co-peel one section of its people to assist from conduct injurious to the prestige of the whole country, how shall it keep others in subjection on larger issues? What is the use of any Power entering into agreements with such a poor, nerveless imitation of a Government, which all the time is confessing, by unmistakeable acts, that it has no power to perform its part of any bargain?

In shipping boycott strikes at the rezoos of the tariff reform, the�arraterritoriality and every effort of conference imaginative with China. If Peking can stop it, why does it not? If it cannot, where is the sense of entering into negotiation with a thing so helpless?

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text: Comediently with Sofia amminging the signature to the Turco. Bulgarian Treaty of friendship and arbitration, Athens reports a Greece. Bulgarian frontier incident, namely that Bulgarian regulars attacked a Greek outpost at Belles, shooting a sentry and a captain dead. It says that subsequently the Bulgarists hoisted a white flag and explained that the firing was due to a misunderstanding. The Greek Government, however, despite the Bulgarian expressions of regret and the explanations made, is determined to throw full light on the incident and has ordered the Greek forces to advance to occupy certain points, whence it will be possible to ascertain the strength of the Bulgarian force.

headline: GERMANY'S EXCITING ELECTIONS.
text:
CANTON STRIKERS GROWING UNPOPUARITY EVIDENCED LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

The growing unpopularity in Canton of the strikers has been emphasised in earlier reports, one of its outward manifestations being the driving away of strike pickets attempting to interfere with the landing of passengers from the "Honam". From later reports it would appear that now the military have barred the landing of passengers, but this is not indicative of antagonism between the two factions having been dropped. The Canton authorities have decided to make a determined effort to make their section of the railway pay, now that the anti-Red forces are away from the railway area, and the banning of "Honam" passengers is part of this scheme.

In other directions the Canton Government is expressing its determination to curb the power of the strikers, the merchants having made representations of indignation that they should be called upon to pay so much in taxes while the strikers make a good thing of the strike in the matter of squeeze. A cargo of considerable value which was confiscated by the strikers had to be returned by them on instructions from Dr. C. C. Wu.

The class of strikers who in Canton itself have by far the greater power is curiously enough that of the barbers and cooks. It will be recalled in this connection that on Central Black Wednesday slightly over a year ago the barbers' guild was largely responsible for the conflagration and massacre which followed. When Saikwan was held by the merchants and Dr. Sun's Red forces could not get in, the barbers inside the western suburb are alleged to have let in the Reds and started tires themselves in many places. The power of the barbers and cooks at the present moment is confined, however, to Caiton whilst at Shekki, Kongmoon, Namtau, Taiping, Chinshan and other outlying places power is in the hands of the seamen, trans-Pacific seamen being the more active section and the coastal, seamen more passive.

A publication entitled "the Empire Rebel" was mentioned in the resumed proceedings against twelve Communists at Bow Street. A police sergeant who gave evidence of finding literature at the Communist headquarters, including "a circular" to which the "Empire Rebel" was attached, declared that apparently it circulated amongst factory workers.

The witness produced another circular addressed to Losovsky, Moscow, also to the secretary of the Berlin branch of the Moscow International, complaining of the non-receipt of promised funds. Counsel for the prosecution declared the letter related to money promised to be sent to England, but not sent.

The cause was adjourned until to-morrow.

headline: DUD AEROPLANES.
text:
Reverting to a phase of the military situation—that relating to the aeroplanes in the possession of Canton, a local resident on a visit to Canton was informed by one of the two German officers who have acted as tutors that the planes are in a very bad condition and need constant repairs even for short flights. The crashing of one at Tungshan a short while ago reduces the number to two. The officers in question are engaged purely for commercial purposes by agents other than the Government and have acted merely as tutors for prospective fliers. They themselves are said to be as opposed as any of the Bolshevik régime and together with others are observing critically events in the north. If Bolshevik control continues in the South until the Spring it is thought that the danger will be that it will receive an impetus as a result of the departure of Fukien troops which in the event of War in the North will leave to join Wu Pei-fu. The possibilities of active developments in the North this winter are considered remote.

headline: CLUB GO DOWN.
text:
SUBMARINES' HOCKEY VICTORY..

YESTERDAY'S MATCH.

Playing on the U.S.N.C. ground yesterday afternoon, the Submarine Plotilla defeated the Hongkong Hockey Club 2nd XI by five goals to three.

The teams lined up as follows: Hongkong Hockey Club 2nd XI: —O. Eager; J. Wedlake, Hearne; E. F. Stewart, A. A. Dand, J. E. Noronha; A. S. Exell, J. Prior, H. J. Armstrong, G. R. Vallack, G. P. Lammert.

Submarine Plotilla: — Sherwood: Emley, Conway; King, Simpson, Brooms; Armstrong, Slade, Hill, Majendie, Garwood.

The play for some time from the start was mostly in the Club territory, but the Club forwards got away, with Lammert prominent on the wing. The first raid ended in off-side. Two further moves were pulled up by Conway. Play being transferred, Eager was called upon to save twice. From a corner King obtained possession and scored, the ball striking the post and bounding in, making the Navy one up. The Club broke through again, Vallack scoring a fine goal. Half-time arrived with one goal each.

In the second half the sailors were soon one up again, through Armstrong, who was successful with a cross shot at long range. headline: END OF STRIKE
text:
SIGNIFICANT CANTON MEETING

PEACH NEBLERS NIRST

Considerable significance is attached to a meeting of all four commercial associations (or chambers) in Canton on Monday when the subject discussed by the Chinese merchants was again the end of the strike.

The meeting, which was informal, agreed that something must be done to end the present situation. A proposition was carried that a working committee, composed of two members of each association, sound all classes of opinion in Canton, and report to a mass meeting which will decide the steps to be taken.

News of Strikers

According to a special report to the "Wah Tsz Yat Po," the Canton Strike Executive has forbidden (Canton) pressmen to attend their meetings or call at headquarters.

Another message concerns the corps of "special investigators" of strikers formed to supervise the pickets. Apparently discord has set in between the investigators and the pickets.

headline: COTTON TRADE.
text:
To transpires that only an informal exchange of views occurred between Mr. N. U. Wadia, Chairman of the Bombay Mill Owners Association, and the Manchester trade representatives. It is understood that the object of his visit is to secure, if possible, the co-operation of the leaders of the Lancashire cotton industry with the Bombay millowners in legislative action against Japanese competition and the depreciation of Japanese exchange which is said to have created havoo with the sale both of Lancashire and Bombay cotton goods. It is alleged that the Japanese are disregarding the hours and conditions of labour agreed upon in the Washington Convention. The Bombay millowners say that this has compelled them to reduce wages 11½ per cent., which has led to the present strike. It is understood that Mr. Wadia will continue his discussions in Lancashire during the week. In this connection it is noteworthy that a suggestion has been made for the abolition of the 3½ per cent. excise duty on Indian woven cloth which it is said suffers competition with Japanese coarse counts but does not compete with Lancashire's finer counts. Lancashire, however, appears to favour a simultaneous similar reduction of eleven per cent. in the Indian import duty on Lancashire cloth.

Portland, Maine, November 10.—An Army steamer, laden with explosive powder, suspected to be a rum runner by a coastguard patrol boat, found one pound shells being aimed at her before she was able to signal her identity. Not recalling that she was pursued she had veered off and put on steam. The commander of the patrol boat explained later that the circumstances looked most suspicious as the vessel had cases piled up on deck and appeared to be fleeing.—Reuter's American Service.

headline: POSITION IN NORTH. (Reuter's Service.)
text:
Fengtien cavalry have occupied Hsiangho-hsien in addition to Sanhohsien and are advancing on Tungchow.

The Kuominchun (People's Army) is apparently prepared to evacuate Tungchow without fighting.

The Chief Executive, Tuan Chi-jui, is still striving to maintain peace between Fengtien and the Kuomtuchun.

He called a Cabinet meeting yesterday afternoon and urged Mr. Mo Teh-hui, who is an adherent of Chang Tso-lin, to wire to the Marshal, stating that the Kuominchun entertained no hostility towards Fengtien, and asking why the Fengtienites were penetrating the metropolitan area. Mr. Mo Teh-hui accordingly telegraphed to that effect.

Confirmation is to hand of the evacuation of Hsuchowfu by the Fengtien troops.

The town has been occupied by the allied armies, without fighting.

It is notified in Command Orders that Captain G. A. Clements restless, receiving a gratuity, October 7, 1925. Captain Clements is now head of the Shameen police. Also that Captain H. J. Hardiman restles on retired pay, October 8, 1925.

Shanghai, November 10.—The International Commission of Judges investigating the Shanghai affair of May 80, has closed its report which has been forwarded to Peking and the Commissioners will return home at the earliest opportunity.—Reuter.

headline: BORDER INQUIRY. / VERDICT OF JUSTIFIABLE
text:
JURY AND QUESTIONS

In the course of cross-examination by the Coroner (Mr. R. E. Lindsell) yesterday, Sub-Inspector Barnett said with reference to the two Chinese he shot near the border recently that there was no doubt but that they would have got away had he not fired. When one of the men ran down the hill he fired two shots and witness replied with two. His idea in firing was to stop them and not to kill.

In reply to Mr. Brayfield, foreman of the jury, witness said that he believed all three men to be armed at the time but he had reason to believe now that only one who fired at him was armed.

There was reason to believe from the notebooks found on the men who were shot that the latter were members of a strike picket, stated Mr. W. G. Gerrard, A.S.P., in answer to the Coroner.

headline: NOT ONE-SIDED.
text:
BOARD OF TRADE AND WIRELESS OPERATORS.

At question time in the House of Commons, Sir Curlife Lister said that since November 28, in consequence of the strike of wireless operators, 500 ships had sailed without operators (including 47 passenger ships).

The Labourite, Mr. Ammon, asked if the action of the Board of Trade in refusing to detain ships was not participating in one side of the strike?

Sir Cunliffe Lister replied in the negative adding that the Board was maintaining complete

Sir Steel Maitland said that at a meeting at the Ministry of Labour yesterday, a conference of both sides had been arranged for today.

headline: Viennan_Uneasy. Vienna, Feb. 8.
text: Uneasiness and much comment have been caused by a passage in Mussolini's speech in which he declared that Italy never would remove her flag from Brenner, but would carry it farther if necessary. The leading daily paper, the "Neue Freie Presse," considers that Mussolini's menaces open the threat of war. It concludes: "The policy of customer cannot successfully be employed in foreign policy especially in the present Locarno era. Germany cannot be intimidated by such threats as Mussolini uttered in the Chamber. The fight for the most primitive rights of mankind cannot be suppressed by decrees."

headline: Germans' Angry
text:
The German newspapers are up in arms against Signor Muosolini on account of his speech in the Italian Chamber, the Nationalists describing him as a "megalomuniae" and amateur politician," and declaring that Germany, being disarmed, is unable to give the reply which the speech deserves.

The Democrat papers are also very bitter. Whilst not trying to excuse the Bavarian Premier, whose incussions into foreign politics caused the attack, they declare that the Italian Premier was not justified to indulge in "such insulting attacks on the German nation." They caustically remark that the speech is scarcely calculated to do. Mussolini, honour as a signatory of the Locarno agreement and the spirit of Locarno appears to be gradually waning. It is generally felt that Mussolini is making a mountain out of a molshill as the German Government itself does not approve of the Bavarian campaign.

Dr. Stresemann (Minister for Foreign Affairs) is expected to reply in the Reichstag on Tuesday.

headline: Cabinet Gets Busy.
text:
The German Cabinet spent most of its time to-day discussing Mussolini's speech, and its decision to reply in open session in the Reichstag on Tuesday is generally approved.

The speech is unanimously described as an unjustified attack on Germany. The opinion is reported to be that it expressed such words which would formerly have been regarded as a threat of war.

The Daily News correspondent in "Berlin states: — As a result of Mossolini's anti-German speech shopkeepers and housewives at Munich have begun a boycott of Italian oranges and the following notice has been posted in railway stations "Germans who propose to visit Italy are traitors."

headline: ITALY'S DEBT. / NO TRADE CONCESSIONS IN AGREEMENT.
text:
DEFINITE STATEMENT.

The Prime Minister (Mr Stanley Baldwin) stated in the House of Commons, in reply to a question, that no political or commercial arrangements or conclusions had been entered into with the Italian Government in connection with the war debt settlement.

Li Po, the famous bard of the Tang dynasty, is depicted translating the first ultimatum received by China from a "foreign" country in a (Chinese) calendar issued by the Canadian Pacific S.S. Co. The "China Mail" acknowledges receipt of a set with thanks. Mr. L. S. Amery, Colonial Secretary, spoke at Leeds on Britain's position in the Middle East. He said that Great Britain could not get out of Egypt. Sir Austen Chamberlain, the Foreign Secretary, had found it necessary to make it clear that whilst Great Britain desired to encourage Egyptian national life, she wished Egypt to understand that she must pay regard to Great Britain's Imperial rights and responsibilities both in regard to the safety of British communications through Egypt and the British position in the Soudan.

headline: SOVIET SILENT.
text:
NO REPLY TO CONFERENCE INVITATION

OBJECTION TO GENEVA

Questioned in the House of Commons, as to the attitude of the Soviet Government toward the preliminary discussions on disarmament, Sir Austen Chamberlain (Foreign Secretary) said that so far as he was aware the Soviet Government had not yet officially replied to the invitation to take part in the preparatory commission for the Disarmament Conference. He understood that it objected to Geneva as the place of meeting, as it was not in diplomatic relations with the Swiss Government. The British Government had not had occasion to express an opinion on the subject. He hoped that any difficulty would be removed before the date of the meeting.

Peking is now completely cut off from Tientsin, neither telephone nor railway communications functioning.

The Kuomintang have established important lines of trenches at Huang Tsun, with supports two miles behind, in readiness for strong resistance.

All foreigners in Fengtai have gone to Peking. The Mukden troops are now moving across country to Peking, and it is expected that these with Li Chinglin's army will attempt to capture Peking.

headline: APPREHENSION RELIEVED.
text: General Lu Chung-lin, the Commandant of the Kuominehun Garrison here, has emphatically disclaimed his intention of disarming the Chief Executive's (Tuan Chi-jui). Bodyguard, thus greatly relieving, apprehension since General Feng Yu-hsiang's telegram of March 20, blaming the Premier for the shooting of the student demonstrators by the guards through failing to keep order.

The strike of the Kyogo Printing Works, which has remained unsettled for the last two months, has been settled. As a result of negotiations conducted between representatives of strikers and the management of the printing company, it has been decided that the sum of ¥120,000 will be paid as allowances for the diamissal of half of 2,400 strikers in addition to ¥10,000 as consideration money. The management states that though half of the workmen have been discharged, they wish to re-open the works as soon as possible.

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Mr. and Mrs. Tully (A. P. C.) leave for a holiday at Home tomorrow.

The next fortnightly dances of the Peak Club will be held on May 9 and 23, starting on each occasion at 9.15 p.m. Sure indication of the advent of spring is afforded by the work of the Floral Committee of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Thousands of packets of seeds are being distributed to all country stations along the three thousand miles of tracks. Between now and May very large numbers of trees, shrubs and other perennials will be shipped out, while at the end of May bedding plants will be sent out in hundreds of thousands. These will include allyssum, asters, cannas, coleus, geraniums, kochia, lobelia, marigolds, petunias, phlox, ricinus, sulvia, verbena, trailers, pansies.

The Empire's Mother and Boy Competition closes on June 13, 1925, by which entries from overseas must reach London. The silk shipped per s.s. President Madison, which sailed from Hongkong at 11 p.m., April 3, arrived New York at midnight on April 27, having been 24 days in transit.

Mr. W. A. Jordan who has contributed to the "China Mail's" correspondence columns on "Bible Fact" leaves the Colony for Home on Saturday next.

Three gramophone records autographed by Paderewski and auctioned for the Polish White Cross were knocked down to Mr. H. H. Bowles, South Woodford, for £26. The invention of the French engineer, M. André Citroën, of a type of motor car capable of crossing the hitherto formidable Sahara has produced a remarkable result. Timbuctoo, that mysterious place which even today some people think to be imaginary, has been brought within twelve days from London. The journey can now be made in perfect comfort, from the moment of leaving London in the ease of a Pullman to the final stage in a river motorboat from Gao to Timbuctoo on the Niger.

The Bishop of Manchester has accepted the invitation sent him by the students of the Y.M.C.A. and Y.W.C.A. associations to visit China next year, and an itinerary is being arranged for a series of visits to many centres in the country. The Bishop is spoken of as the possible next Archbishop of Canterbury.

Among the passengers on the P. & O. Morea, which arrived from London yesterday were Mr. J. P. B. Eastwood (Jardine, Matheson & Co., Swatow) and Mrs. Eastwood; Mr. A. E. B. Lamble of the same branch of the Firm and Mrs. Lamble, Mr. R. B. Orr, of Messrs. Boyd & Co., Tamsul, and Mrs. Orr.

Mr. Oliver T. Breakspear, who was formerly manager of the Hongkong Daily Press. Ltd., and of the Publicity Bureau, returned to the Colony yesterday from London on the Morea, to succeed the late Mr. H. A. Cartwright as managing director of the Company. Mr. B. A. Hale, who has been recently in charge of the business, will shortly be proceeding. Homs on leave. Mrs. Hale is already on her way Home.

... The Hon. Mr. Kotewall is to distribute the prizes at the Gap Road School on Tuesday next.

Chief Inspector J. E. Wheeler, who has been Acting Registrar at the Shanghai Mixed Court, was the recipient of a handsome cigarette and cigar box, on the eve of his departure for Home on leave, the presentation being made by Major F. L. Wainwright.

Mr. M. W. Pett, Chief Officer of the Shanghai Fire. Brigade, goes home shortly for a well-earned rest. Under his eggs, the Fire Brigade has been completely reorganized until it is now second to none in the Far East, and the benefits of the protective measures adopted by Mr. Pett are now accruing to the community.

A farewell luncheon was given at the American Club to Dr. Jacob Gould Schurman, former American Minister to Peking but now Ambassador-designate to Germany, by members of the American Association and the Chamber of Commerce. In the course of his address, Dr. Schurman said that he was greatly impressed by the friendliness subsisting between the Chinese and Americans, and urged everyone to stimulate and encourage that feeling to the utmost.

A farewell dinner was given to Mr. E. F. Mackay, retiring head of the firm of Butterfield and Swire, at the Union Club of China, Shanghai, by the Chinese members of the Club and friends. Eulogistic references were made by several speakers to Mr. Mackay's sterling qualities and his services to the community. Mr. Mackay has been the recipient of many valuable gifts from his Chinese friends, including some beautiful pieces of porcelain, bronze vases and urns, some said to be 2,000 years old. From the merchants connected with the Taikoo firm he has received a richly emblazoned scroll bearing some 100 signatures which will be a pleasant reminder of his sojourn in China. Confronted with bound feet on all sides of him, the Tao-tai of Suiyuan, following a personal investigation of homes, has issued new instructions urging the magistrates to enforce the rules that the feet of women and girls must be unbound at once.

Mr. C. C. Hickling left yesterday by the St. Albums for Sydney.

Mr. Mrs. and Miss Hughes left for Melbourne yesterday by the St. Albums. Mr. and Mrs. J. R. Way are passengers by the same steamer.

Captain J. J. G. Patterson, who is to take over the command of H.M.A.S. Brisbane arrived in Hongkong by the Moren yesterday.

Mr. E. M. Moffatt and Mr. G. D. Meude arrived on the Morea yesterday to join the staff of the head office of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank.

Viscount Fitzd�in has been appointed a Knight of the Order of the Garter, 'The Viscount has acted as Viceroy of Ireland and was also a Chief Unionist Whip.

Major Nathan, who is Chairman of the Kuilan Mining Administration in London and the Director of the Peking Syndicate, arrived in the Colony yesterday by the s.s. Morea. He is staying at the Hongkong Hotel, and will remain here for about a week. He then proposes to go North for the purpose of reviewing the position in connection with the two Sino-British Coal Companies.

Mrs. Jacob Gould Schurman, wife of the retiring American Minister to China, was entertained to tiffin by the American Women's Club in their rooms, when covers were laid for about 75 members and guests. The tiffin was in charge of the Social Committee, and its Chairman, Mrs. Lunt, acted as Mistress of Ceremonies. Among the guests who delivered impromptu speeches was Mrs. Lee Meriveather of St. Louis, Missouri, who, with her husband, a well-known author and lawyer, is visiting China. The Club's President, Dr. Anne W. Fearn, was, as usual, the afternoon's most effective speaker. Mrs. Schurman, in thanking the Club members for their hospitality on that and previous occasions, assured them that they would not be forgotten.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
Two and a quarter tons of gold were carried by two aeroplanes from London to Paris recently. The bullion was carried in, speeding metal-bound cases and was grounded from the time it left the banks there until its arrival in Switzerland, its eventful destination.

The aerial passenger service between Sydney and Aldaide, established in conjunction with the regular mail service, was inaugurated on January 10. The fare is 621, or slightly more than 60, a mile. As the time, the regular airline service between Sydney and Aldaide was established one of the conditions was that passengers were to be carried after an experimental period, as well as mails and goods. Experimental work with mails and goods has now been carried out for six months, and in this has been satisfactory, the conditions in respect to the carriage of passengers have now come into operation.

President Kalinin has recently been visiting the newly-formed Central Asiatic Soviet Republic of Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In establishing these republics the old Tsarist administrative lines have been redrawn in a manner calculated to correspond better with the distribution of races in this region. For some time after the Revolution the Central Asiatic Soviet Governments were harassed by insurgent natives, known as Easimachi, who resented the introduction of Communist ideas and the accompanying economic dislocations. This movement reached its height in 1921 and 1922, when the Turkish statesman, Enver Pasha, assumed the leadership of the Easmachi. Now law and order have been largely restored and one of the few remaining Basmach leaders sent a message to one of the Soviet congresses addressed by Kalinin, proffering submission and asking for pardon.

In Jardow, this one is great in industrial towth one the Tyne. famous years ago for its shipbuilding and steel works, there are 5,700 workers out of a population of 36,000 drawing the date. There is only one ship on the stock of the yards, and many firmness have been closed down for three years. Lack of trade, shortage of money and lessened demand for war vessels and armaments are mainly responsible for the present depression.

In the Medieval Officer of Health's return for the week ending May 2, there were five cases reported, four of small-pox and one of diphtheria. All were Chinese with the exception of one imported Indian case. Deaths numbered four -- two small-pox, and one each of diphtheria and puenperal fever. All the small-pox cases occurred in Kowloon. Monday's return showed one case of enteric fever, and one of cersbro-spinal fever, both Chinese. There were no cases of paratyphoid fever as this been erroneously reported.

Error in the inscription beneath a "fresco in the Parliament buildings" corridor — first pointed out by a schoolboy of the Royal High School, Edinburgh, when visiting the House of Commons with his fellow scholars—was admitted by G. L. T. Locker-Lampson for the Government in the House. The fresco depicts Montrose's execution in Edinburgh in 1650, and the inscription which has been up for 30 years says that the occurrence took place in the Grassmarket, where the boy said, "That is not, the Grassmarket, that's High Street," and this is now confirmed. The correction, Mr. Locker-Lampson said, is to be made, and the commissioner of works will consider handing over the existing version to the Edinburgh High School for a memento.

A special general meeting of members of the Hongkong Philharmonic Society is advertised to be held on Monday, May 11, at 5.15 p.m. in St. John's Cathedral Hall. Business of an important nature is on the agenda.

Chinese boys and girls are evincing a strong interest in the cause of tenipemence, Miss Amy Spoulding, executive secretary of the Chinese Womup's Christian Temperance Union, reported to headquarters of the World's Union in an article published in the national organ, the Union Signal. More than a thousand essays on temperance subjects were submitted in contests conducted recently by the Chinese Union, Miss' Spoulding stated: Oratorial contests were held in many cities and a quantity of literature distributed. Activities of the Chinese Union covered a wide field, including maintenance of a day nursery in Shanghai, for the babies of factory women, a daily vacation Bible school, and support of a home for women and girls founded about a year ago by the Students' Temperance Region.

As an outcome, of the visit to England last year of an Australian Boy Scout contingent and the jamboree, there has been the resolve to establish a camp in New South Wales, similar to that at Gillwell Park, in Essex, England. This camp was presented to the Boy Scouts Association by Mr. McLaren, who comes from Scotland, and has been found very useful for the training of scouts in woodcraft. A block of land between Narrabeen and Pymble, comprising 80 acres, hks, been placed at the disposal of the scout authorities in this State by V. Roineland Mr. and Mrs. Danvers Power; and the erection of the various structures required is due to the generosity of the chairman of the executive committee, Kelso King.

"What a fine chance for that fizzing kind of noise we used to make at school by putting it in the ink" pot," remarked Judge Cluer when a chemist complained at Shoreditch County Court of iodide of potassium being damaged by water.

Tsuchiyu Shin, aged 19, committed suicide by hanging himself from a tree in his garden in 'Hungo, Tokyo, recently. The direct cause of his rush act was his failure at the entrance examination of the First Higher School, Tokyo. Incidents like this ought really to be headed, "Another murder of a student," says the "Japan Chronicle."

There took place recently at the Goldsmiths' Hall the very ancient ceremony known as "The Trial of the Pyx." The first record of this ceremony is during the reign of Henry III. in the thirteenth century. The trial is of the coins issuing from the Royal Mint and takes place every year. Originally it was carried out in the Pyx, a chamber in Westminster Abbey, which was first the abbot's treasury and later the depository of the "pyx" or chest which contained the trial plates of gold and silver used as standards of reference. The error admissible on the weight of coins is very small, 1.26 grains in a half-crown and a little over half a grain in the shilling. More than this is an "error" and seldom occurs, the last entry being in 1919. The Royal Mint simply sends up a selection of all the different coins made there.

Mr. S. T. Mann, stationmaster at Windsor (Great Western) for 22 years, and well known to every member of the Royal Family, is retiring after 50 years' service.

Mr. J. Jackson, of Arlington square, South Islington, who at 94 still plays the violin and viola, performed in the orchestra at his daughter's 71st birthday celebration.

To a woman with a baby, Judge Cluer, at Shoreditch recently remarked, "I wish I could take your case at the beginning of the day, but if I did everybody would hire babies and bring them here." (Laughter.)

Mr. Jacob Millhoff, of Willesdenlane, N.W., founder of the De Reszke Cigarette Co., a native of Russia, left £130,431. Bequests include:—

±250 to the London Hospital. £250 to the London Jewish Hospital.

£100 to the Jewish Board of Guardians.

21,000 is left to his brother, Haskel Mirowsky, of Odessa.

Richard M. Hall, secretary of the American European Y.M.C.A. at Manila and Sergeant A. Fridman, steward, better known to his hundreds of Manila friends as "Sarg," will leave Manila on June 25 for the United States via Europe. Mr. Hall will be accompanied by Mrs. Hall and his son, Richard, now in Bagulo and a student at the Brent School for Roys. Both Mr. and Mrs. Fridman are going to the United States on vacation and plan to return to Manila in the fall.

General Dunsterville, the original Stalky of Rudyard Kipling's antidote to "Eric; or Little by Little," has written a novel called "And Obeyed." Funsterville and Kipling were schoolboys together at Westward Ho! and have been friends ever since. The greater part of the General's life has been spent in India. During the war he did great deeds.

Lord Derby's family, one by one, are turning to labour in one form or another as a help to livelihood. First, Mr. Oliver Stanley, Lord Derby's younger son and Lord Londonderry's son-in-law, went into the City, where he joined the stock-broking firm of Montagu & Co., of which his uncle, Lord Charles Montagu—who is likewise the uncle of the Duke of Manchester—is a member. Now Mr. Frederick Stanley, the eldest son of Lord Derby's brother, Ferdinand, has departed to Canada to become a farmer.

headline: there are more than a million Buicks
text:
There would not be more than a million Buicks in active use today if Buick had not, through the years, produced a motor car of unvarying and superior quality. In every detail, every Buick is an example of how well a motor car can be built.

Mah Jong, says a New York message, has gone the way of all prizes. It has felt the "cast wind" of cross words, and now sets are selling at give-away prices. The last word is the bankruptcy of the £40,000 'Pung-Chow Company' in New York, the makers of Mah Jong sets.

Referring to the bamboo folding chair so defly made by Cantonese rattian workers, which is now being imported into England, a contemporary says it is nothing very extraordinary to look at, but folds up into quite a small space with all the neatness of a Chinese puzzle, although without any of its complications. There are a good many folding chairs of one kind or another, but the Chinese have managed to combine comfort and strength without adding weight.

headline: BARGAIN PRICE
text:
Among the successful candidates for the degree of Bachelor of Commerce of Bombay University is a Parsi lady, Miss Yasmin Surveyor. She is the first lady to get through B. Com. examination, with banking as her special subject, since the Faculty of Commerce was started in Bombay University. Well-known Shanghai residents who left on Home leave by the R.M.S. Empress of Canada included Mr. and Mrs. W. Wakeford Cox, Mr. G. D. Coutts and Miss Coutts.

Lots of Good Things Here

Opportunity Does. Not Wait.

It was a quiet race day at Shanghai as far as the ladies' costumes went, no especially striking outfits being seen, the favourite colours being easily browns and beiges. A wide range of fabrics was noted running from airy yoiles and silk's at one extreme to heavy for costs at the other. One emotional young thing who shrieked with excitement as the ponies swept round the bend and wept tears of joy as her choice nosed in first was afterwards heard to lament at the Fari-Mutuel window: "All that commotion for 30 cents, and now I've no enthusiasm left for the Champions."

headline: SOCIAL AND PERSONAL.
text:
Captain and Mrs. Clairke returned to the Colony today by the s.s. Empress of Russia.

Dr. W. T. Grenfell who recently visited Hongkong called at Kobe on the last lap of his world tour and delivered an address.

Mr. F. A. Wells, late of Hongkong, is a subscriber to the Congratulatory Address to be presented to the Emperor and Empress of Japan by the Kobe International Committee on the occasion of the celebrations of the Imperial Silver Wedding.

On April 10 (Primrose Day) a number of beautiful wreaths were laid at the base of Lord Beaconsfield's statue, in London, among them being a shield of primroses from the representatives of the well-known Hongkong patriot, the late Mr. R. E. Belilios, upon which were the words, "Peace with Honour."

The eldest son of Dr. Lim Boon-Keng, Dr. Robert K. Lim, M.B.B.C. Ch., Ph.D., D.Sc., F.R.S.E. formerly lecturer in Histology, Edinburgh University and Rockfeller Fellow, Chicago University. was appointed to the chair of Physiology at the University of Anioy in 1923 but by request of the China Medical Board. his services were transferred to the Peking Union Medical College, where at present he is teaching Physiology as a visiting professor.

An Empire Day celebration is being planned by the Tokyo British League. The celebration in Tokyo will be held on the lawn of the British Embassy, which has been offered to the League by Sir Charles Eliot, the British Ambassador to Japan. As Empire Day (May 24) falls on Sunday this year, the gathering in Tokyo will be held on the afternoon of Saturday May 23. A committee of the League is now busy arranging the details of the programme of entertainment.

Business men interested in the opening of a Club and Recreation Town for the use of Foreign Season of all Nationalities at Kobe were invited by the British Consultor to meet Rev. Gurney Goldsmith, M.A. (lately Chaplain Superintendent of the Missions to Seamen in Melbourne, Australia) in the Super-room of the Gymnasium on Thursday. May 14 at 5:30 p.m. by kind permission of the K.R. of A.C. Mr. Goldsmith's representing the London Committee with a view to re-organising a Branch of the Missions to Seamen in Kobe.

The 'Interport Billiard players returned to the Colony to-day by the s.s. Empress of Russia.

Mr. B. G. M. Bernard of Messrs. Jardine, Matheson Co., Ltd., takes the place of Mr. B. D. F. Beith on the Court of Directors of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank. There were 98,215 street accidents in Great Britain, caused by various types of vehicles, an increase of 15,114 over the previous year. Of these accidents 3,631 were fatal—652 more than in 1923. Of the fatal accidents, 258 were caused by horse-drawn vehicles, 459 by omnibuses and motor coaches, 113 by trancars and trackless trolley vehicles, 241 by pedal cycles, and 2,560 by other vehicles.

The Shanghai Chinese Admiralty House has received orders from Peking to welcome Prince George when he arrives and to give him a royal salute. Officials have been ordered to make arrangements for the welcome of the Italian aviator, Col. di Pinedo, who will pass through Shanghai on his flight to Tokyo. Work is rapidly drawing to completion on the new artificial silk plant at Cornwall, Ontario of Courtaulds, Limited, the well known English manufacturers of artificial silk and it is now anticipated that the plant will be in operation about July 1. In connection with the operation of this plant it will be necessary for the company to secure from England a number of highly specialized operatives, and in order to properly house these employees on their arrival the company has decided to construct 150 new houses in Cornwall to accommodate them.

There was a large gathering at the residence of Mrs. J. Macbeth, Shanghai, when representatives of various Christian circles and a host of friends, met to wish "Bon Voyage", to Mrs. A. N. Rowland, wife of the Rev. A. N. Rowland, pastor of Union Church. The Rev. and Mrs. Rowland have left for the Homeland and carry with them the best wishes of a large circle of friends.

A London wire of May 5, says: Mr. George White, Chairman of the National Press Association, at a dinner at the Procedero, after speaking on the text "Let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die," asked. "Do I say that?" and replied: "No, I say shake hands and help for to-day we live." He immediately fell back in his chair and died. The dinner was abandoned.
