The bride is, so to speak, a native daughter of Tientsin, while Mr. Cumming has been a resident at the port for some two or three years.

Heater cables the death of Marquis Huirin Tokugawa, former daimyo of Kishu. He was a brother of Prince Tokugawa. The late Marquis Raimyo Tokugawa was a descendant of one of the three great Houses of Tokugawa, which further enjoyed the help of the Kishu, founded by Yornubù, tenth son of Yevash. The late Madus was He, fifth son of the Elysius branch of Tokugawa. He was born in 1873 and studied for several years in England. He founded the Naki Library. The Hongkong Club will mark the King's Birthday (June 3) as usual, by opening the Club premises to the wives and lady friends of members. The health of His Majesty will be drunk in the main hall at noon. A special tiffin will be served and a band will be in attendance.

headline: AND GENERAL.
text:
The cabin boy from the s.s. President Cleveland who was tried at the Criminal Sessions for possession of arms, was found guilty yesterday afternoon and sentenced to six years' imprisonment with hard labour.

Bolshevist Russia, which last year began organisation of a fishing fleet in northern waters, has begun to extend its business to foreign shores. The first Soviet steam trawler to be seen in a British port arrived in Grimsby recently and attracted much attention. The trawler brought a load of fish caught off the Murmansk coast.

Exports of potatoes from St. John, since the opening of the season to date show a considerable increase over shipments for, the same period last year. Up to April 1, 1924 shipments totaled 729,327 bags and barrels, as compared with 327,762 bags and barrels in the corresponding period of the previous year. The majority of shipments were made to Havana and Bermuda.

Alberta's population at the end of 1924 was approximately 640,000, according to an estimate made by the Provincial Government. This is an increase of 52,000 as compared with 1921, when the last official census was taken. It is also estimated that some 60 per cent of the province's population is of British origin.

In order to encourage the farmers of eastern Ontario in better breeding of live stock, the Canadian Pacific Railway is operating a Better Farming Special Train over its Ottawa-Pembroke branch. The train consists of fifteen cars specially built for the purpose, having exhibits of pure bred cattle, swine and poultry. Some of these animals are to be sold during the trip, but the majority are for exhibition and instruction. Attached to the train are demonstrators and lecturers. After the train concludes its tour in Ontario it will move west and be used for similar purposes out of Winnipeg.

A-new form of lunacy, commented the Stratford magistrate in sending a wireless enthusiast to prison for a month for stealing apparatus.

Beach undertakings at Bournemouth brought £37,823 to the corporation coffers. Some of the items included in this sum are:—£8,000 from beach licences, £5,000 from bathing, £9,000 from beach cakes, and £7,600 from beach chairs. All receipts were down on the previous year owing to the wet summer. Municipal concerts showed a loss of £5,700.

During two pleasure cruises 40 millionaires figured in the passenger list of the White Star Line steamer Megantic. On her journeys the liner covered 19,000 miles and visited:—

Jamaica, South African Coast Windward and Leeward Islands

And other places, thence back New York.

headline: THE WING ON CO., LTD Des Voenx Rd. / SOCIAL & PERSONAL.
text:
While visiting friends at Belper (near Derby) Horace Bent, of Luton, died in tragic circumstances. He was out for a walk with his financee, a girl from Luton, when he collapsed and died in her arms. The banns had been published at Luton, and all the arrangements for the wedding were in hand.

Preaching in St. Paul's Cathedral the Bishop of London referred to his own early scepticism. After taking part in a Lent mission, said the bishop, he felt how completely all our hopes for eternity hinged upon the fact of the Resurrection. If the Resurrection was not true, he idea of a life-long friendship with the Son of God was any empty dream. "The consciousness of this, declared the Bishop of London, kept me from taking Holy Orders until the age of 26."

Dr. Carvalho, late of Hongkong, has been showing his picture in Shanghai, described as "Treasures," one of the most striking exhibits at the recent exhibition of the Chim Society of Science and Art. In the portrait of his daughter, which he adds "Treasures," the light comes from behind the figure, flooding the vivid Chinese tapestry and throwing a reflected glow upon the face of the young girl. The human forms a golden aureole about the expectant face. Below the firements and a temple lion, balanced with a cloisonne vase at the right. The beauty of this work lies in the final combination of colours. The brass of the temple lion, with a child against of the red drapery and a light at the back, makes a great interest in a striking composition where the subjects are well spuced in their respective positions, giving good a most strategic effect.

There is a possibility that Lieutenant-Colonel Zanni may have to delay his intended flight a few days later than he had expected, it is learned, in order to give the vessels time to prepare his landing places along the northern route after he gets out of Japanese waters. However, no previously mentioned, he was to, hope of from Kasunigimura not later than the middle of May. Mr. Murphy is to return to Tokyo at once now, it is understood. The aviator's plane is still at Osaka. He expects to fly back to Kasunigimura in a week or two, at the latest. He will be accompanied from there on, by his navigator, Lieutenant-Etsriato Velo, and the mechanic. Sergeant-Major-Brittany. The route to be followed will be that of the American fiers and British airmen. The Tatter have arrived to the Antentino flyer, use the petrol and other shipments, dumps prepared at Zani, ngo by the Col. E. Broome of the British flight.

headline: TRUTTE TO MR. LAUDER.
text:
You will no doubt join with us in your appreciation of the able and tactful manner in which our General Manager, Mr. Lauder, conducted these negotiations and brought them to a successful issue.

Mr. M. G. Burnie, the General Manager of the Yang-tsze Insurance Association, Limited, and who was, for many years in the Society's employ, and in whom we have full confidence has been appointed Branch Manager of the Society at Shanghai and General Manager of the North China Insurance Company, Limited. Mr. W. E. Smith who was, until recently, in charge of our Shanghai business has been appointed inspector to the Society and its affiliated Companies. Mr. Smith has had lengthy experience in the Society's service and we are sure this appointment will prove most beneficial to the Society's interests.

Our office in Shanghai has been transferred to the Yangtze Insurance Association's Building and our old premises on the ground floor of the Union Building have been let on satisfactory terms.

Considering the adverse conditions of trade I think you will agree that our present position reflects credit on the Society's staff and will heartily approve our following the usual custom of voting a bonus of 15 per cent on salaries to the credit of those members holding Provident Fund Agreements.

You will have learnt with deep regret of the passing of our late General Manager Mr. C. Montague Ede, who was so long and honourably associated with this Society and who played so large a part in its development. I am sure you will desire me to convey to Mrs. Ede and his family the sincere sympathy of this Meeting in the real loss they have sustained.

He was a man of strong and striking personality the charm of which was felt by all who came in contact with him. His admiration for Hongkong and faith in its future were boundless. He continually worked for the public weal and the Colony is the poorer for his death. Before concluding my remarks I would also like to express the deep regret your Directors feel at the death of Mr. A. R. Lowe who acted as our Auditor for a considerable number of years. Mr. Lowe's wise counsel and ability were of great assistance to us and the Colony has lost one of its most valued citizens.

I have further to record with deep regret the death of Mr. John Prentice who at the time of his deceased was the Chairman of The Yangtsze Insurance Association Limited. He was kindly, generous, and public spirited and his death has been keenly felt not only by his friends in Shanghai but by his many friends in this Colony also. Since issuing the present Balance Sheet the Society has received telegraphic advice of the death of Mr. Harry Maitland who was a member of our London Committee. This news has been received with great regret.

I now propose the adoption of the Report and Accounts and when this has been seconded. I shall be glad to answer to the best of my ability any questions you may wish to ask.

headline: RAILWAY DISPUTE. (Reuter's Service).
text:
MOSCOW; May 28.

Commenting on the conflict over the Chinese Eastern Railway owing to the Chinese President of the Board of Railway Directors cancelling the order of the general manager, Mr. Ivanov, dismissing railway employees who were neither Chinese nor Soviet citizens, the "Izvestia" suggests that behind the activity of the Manchurian administration violating the interests of the railway as well as general political interests of the Soviet, is Chang Tso-lin's hostility to the Soviet whom it suspects of alleged support of Feng and the Kuomintang and also incitements of foreign powers.

Reactionary circles in Japan are striving to drive out the Soviet from Manchuria, particularly from the Chinese Eastern Railway. Britain also has lately favourably changed her treatment of Chang Tso-lin.

If Chang were against Feng and the Kuomintang the Chili forces would again be regrouping. He chooses to forget that he has the Soviet in his rear. The worse for him. "Izvestia" recommends the Japanese Government to use the influence of its Marichuria agents with a view to negotiations for the restoration of normal Russia.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:

"Because he wanted to see what would happen," he told the magistrate, Victor Reed, aged 17, put three baulks of timber, on a road near Castor, Cambidagshire frequented by motorists. He was fined.

A well-dressed clerk of the Eastern Telegraph Co., delivering cables during the messenger boys' strike went to a London hotel. A porter took his hat and umbrella and showed him into a room. Then a woman came in, exclaiming, "It's so nice of you to have called. Will you come up and see the wedding presents!" In spite of the fact, a considerable number of farm hands from Great Britain and European countries are being distributed on western Canadian farms, the supply is not equal to the demand and shortage is becoming more pronounced as spring work develops more extensively. Wages are averaging from $30 to $40 (gold) per month and board.

A small army of Paris shop girls are wearing wigs, which they discard on leaving, the premises where they work. Shingled heads have been banned by their directors, under threat of immediate dismissal, and there was nothing left to do but to make the best of a bad job—which the pretty wigs they wear show they have done.

Contests for the Canadian typewriting championships were held simultaneously in five cities of Canada. Miss Irma Wright, of Toronto, won the one-minute contest with a speed of 117 words a minute. This says the "Daily Mail," is far behind the feat of the 29-year-old Miss Millicent Woodward, of Mansfield, England, champion typist of Europe, who, in December, 1922, typed 276 (memorised) words in one minute. She was credited then with receiving £1,000 a year as chief demonstrator for a firm of typewriter manufacturers.

Teachers are wanted for French, Spanish and shorthand classes in Maidstone Prison.

Now celebrating its 100th birthday, the Wesleyan Chapel, St. Germans, Cornwall, owes its origin to a false pair of butcher's scales. By means of the scale a servant to the Earl of St. Germans unjustly accused the butcher of fraud. The Earl, in reparation, offered the man anything he liked to select. He chose a site for a chapel.

I'll taste the luxury of woe, —THOMAS MOORE All for a shilling, a London police-woman was informed that Her life would be full of trouble. Her home would be broken up. Her mother was on a bed of sickness, and

Her sister was mentally afflicted. For making these gloomy prophecies Mrs Charlotte Gentle, a fortune-teller, of Liver-road, Parsons Green, was summoned at West London Police Court. "To me, the astonishing thing is that she should have so many customers, considering she tells such a gloomy tale to them," said the magistrate. Mrs Gentle was fined £3.

A rabbit in flight near Elm Spring, Arkansas, led to the discovery by a shpoting party of a man's skeleton in the hollow of a giant oak (says the "Central News"). When the rabbit took refuge in the hollow, whose opening was only a few inches wide, the "hunters" enlarged the entrance and found the skeleton, also an old flintlock rifle and a buckskin pouch of gunpowder, Foresters judge that it must be over 60 years since the opening was large enough for the man to creep through. Perhaps he took refuge when pursued by Indians. Perhaps he could not so turn as to get out again. Or he may have been wounded and died in the tree, which has since grown up around him. James's Payn's story of the "Lost Sir Massing-berd" is recalled by the discovery.

The engagement is announced of Miss Muriel Stanhope, of Melbourne, Australia, and Seremban, to Mr. L. V. J. Laville, of the Malayan Civil Service.

Mr. Eina V. Schou, the millionaire margarine king, has died in Denmark. In 1889 he began business with one ton of margarine which he invented, and was soon manufacturing 1,000 tons a week.

Mabel Normand, the film actress, has accepted an offer of £500 a week from Mr. Norman Lee, revue producer, connected with the Gulliver circuit. He will present her in a musical play to be produced in Manchester and London in the autumn. A feature will be a film studio scene. Mr. Lee has also engaged Mr. Bryant Washburn, Miss Normand, has not appeared in films lately. Her name was mentioned in connection with a shooting affair nearly two years ago.

A most successful dance, to which the officers of the warships were invited, was given by Sandakan Club in the Club premises on the 13th May. We congratulate the organisers on the excellence of the Arrangements and of the supper. Dances in Sandakan do not unfortunately occur very often, but when they do they go with a fine swing and this one was no exception to the rule, its success being enhanced by the presence of the Carllale's jazz band, which was kindly lent for the occasion.

headline: THE HONGKONG & WHAMPOA DOCK Co., Ltd.
text:
NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that an Extraordinary General Meeting of the above Company will be held at the Registered Office of the Company, Queen's Building, Victoria, Hongkong, on TUESDAY, the 2nd day of June, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon, when the subjoined Resolutions which were passed as Extraordinary Resolutions at the Extraordinary General Meeting of the Company held on the 18th day of May, 1925, will be proposed for confirmation as Special Resolutions, viz.:

(1) That the Articles of Association of the Company be altered in manner following that is to say by the deletion of Article 17 and by the substitution therefor of the following article, namely:— “17. So long as the issued “capital of the Company” shall not exceed $6,000,000 “no member shall be entitled to be registered as the “holder of more than 8,000 shares of the Company.” Should the issued capital “of the Company be increased,” “ed beyond $6,000,000,” the “number of shares in respect of which a member shall be entitled to be registered shall be increased,” “proportionately, but no member shall be entitled to be registered in respect of “a fraction of a share.””

(2) That the authorised Capital of the Company (which is now $3,000,000 consisting of 60,000 shares of the nominal value of $50 each the whole of which have been issued) be increased to $10,000,000 by the creation of 140,000 additional shares of the nominal value of $50 each ranking (subject as herein-after mentioned) for dividend and in all other respects pari passu with the shares constituting the Company's present issued Capital.

(3) That 60,000 of the said 140,000 new shares be offered in the first instance (in the proportion of one new share for every old share held by them respectively) to the members of the Company who on the 10th day of June, 1925, are registered in the Company's Share Register as the holders of the said 60,000 old shares at a premium of $10 per share.

(4) That the aforesaid offer be made to members by notice specifying the number of new shares to which a member is entitled. That a member whose registered address is situate in the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of October, 1925, and such member or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, will be deemed to have declined. That a member

situate outside the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of July, 1925, until the date of receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and a further instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of December, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of October, 1925, until the date of actual receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and such member outside the Far East or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest as aforesaid will be deemed to have declined. The Directors shall have the right to reject any nominee.

(5) That such of the said 60,000 new shares as shall be accepted by members both in and outside the Far East shall be a-vis the said 60,000 old shares rank for dividend as from the 15th day of July, 1925, to the extent of one half of the nominal value of such new shares and as from the 15th day of October, 1925, equally with the said 60,000 old shares.

(6) That any of the said 60,000 new shares which shall not be taken up by the Company's shareholders in manner aforesaid and the remaining 80,000 unissued new shares may be issued and disposed of in such manner at such time or times and upon such terms as to ranking for dividend and otherwise as the Company's Directors shall in their absolute discretion think fit.

The TRANSFER BOOKS of the Company will be closed from WEDNESDAY, the 10th day of June, 1925, to WEDNESDAY, the 17th day of June, 1925, (both days inclusive) during which period no transfer of shares can be registered. Dated the 20th day of May, 1925. By Order of the Board of Directors, R. M. DYER

headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, June 2, 1925.
text:
To-day's news from Shanghai is only reassuring to the extent that it emphasises the determination of the Police and the Municipal authorities to subdue the disturbances at all costs. Within a few hours the vapourings of a few students of Communist tendencies have been responsible for the creation of an international crisis which may drift along a course diametrically opposite to that intended by the first few demonstrations.

Not even the best friend of China would desire a replica of the Boxer Riots and of the humiliation that these eventually brought in their wake for China. But hot-headed youth inspired by sources that know not lav and order—and in fact are "up against" it—cannot be expected to stop and think of the consequences. But at the same time they themselves must share the suffering of these consequences. They cannot expect sympathy. They cannot be raised to the status of martyrs. Law and order must prevail even in China when the lives and the interests of foreigners are menaced.

It matters not at this distance from the scene of conflict whether the riots originated in the killing of a Chinese workman by a Japanese during the recent-cotton strike, or whether the primary cause was a desire on the part of Chinese students to escape examinations and get promotion without them. What does matter, and matter very much, is the fact that the rioters have shown their hands by the inflammatory posters they have issued broadcast over the city denouncing Imperialism and foreigners. That is proof positive that they have only been waiting for the flimiest excuse to break out of bounds and foment what really is tantamount to an anti-foreign rebellion. That is both a stupid and a dangerous policy to pursue. It must recoil on the heads of the Chinese themselves and on the Chinese as a nation.

If those who have the authority and the influence do not step into the breach and assist the Municipal authorities and the Police in Shanghai in the speedy restoration of order, they will assuredly regret it. There must be no weak-kneed measures or sentiment. The riots must be quelled and the originators and participants severely punished. And if that is not done within a reasonable space of time the duty of the British and the other foreigners whose interests are menaced is obvious.

The growing amount of motor traffic is revealed by the amendment of traffic regulations published in the last number of the Government Gazette. Seldom, if ever, does one see a truck in charge of a number of screeching men. The Government has wisely initiated or encouraged a system of motor haulage in keeping with modern conditions. This is all to the good and a further aid to safety, for it is admitted that proffemoving vehicles are less a danger to traffic than the slow moving kind. The speed of 15 miles and 12 miles per hour assigned to various trucks is reasonable. What is of vast importance to the efficiency with which the road haulage is used. The additions covering ordinary vehicles are sane. A licensed driver is not to allow his vehicle to be driven by one who is unlicensed; whilst public motor vehicles are to carry a spare wheel and a serviceable kit of tools to the satisfaction of the head of the police. There should, it appears to us, be some rule covering those roads where there is either no sidewalk for pedestrians, or one of narrow dimensions making it almost impossible for it to be used. In this class of thoroughfare the pedestrian is in extreme danger of injury. A word of caution to drivers should not be out of place.

headline: HONGKONG AND THE CHATER COLLECTION.
text:
Reviewing the Chatter Collection: A Catalogue of Pictures Relating to China, Hongkong, and Macao, 1655-1860," with descriptive letterpress by James Orange (Thornton Butterworth. £7.7s.), Mr. J. O. P. Bland writes as follows in the "Sunday Times," (London): Of the many benefits conferred by Sir Paul Chatter on his fellow-citizens of the Crown Colony of Hongkong, assuredly none will rank higher in times to come than his gift of this collection of pictures and books descriptive of the early days of the Colony and commemorative of the events which led, and the men who contributed, to its making. This handsome volume, with its eighteen plates in colour and 243 in half-tone, constitutes a very fitting and felicitous monument, not only to the public-spirited munificence of "Sir Paul," but to the memory of the stout-hearted mariners, pro-Consuls, and merchant adventurers of England who, against heavy odds, opened up new and great highways of commerce in the Far East. It contains, moreover, much more than the customary catalogue of an art collection, for Mr. Orange has done his work as editor and commentator with a through knowledge and enjoyment of his subject and much scholarly discrimination. The arrangement of the work, in appropriate sections provided with exhaustive indices, should make it of real and permanent value to students, while the numerous quotations from contemporary authors, which accompany each section, enable the casual reader to form a very vivid and accurate impression of the events and scenes they describe.

It is a wonderful pageant of stirring days and captains courageous which these pictures present, beginning with the earliest attempts of the Portuguese Spaniards, British, and Dutch in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries to secure a footing for trude on the coasts of southern China, and to penetrate beyond the barriers of the Celestial Empire's splendid isolation. After the entry upon the scene of the stately orgosies of the Honourable East India Company, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, the European figures in the pageant become conspicuously British. This was to be expected, for, from 1678 onwards, when the Company established its direct and regular trade with Canton, Amoy, and (Later) Chusan, the long and often disbearing task of opening up commercial relations between China and the rest of the world—of sowing, where others have since helped fall almost entirely upon England.

headline: SOCIAL
text:
Mr. H. R. Harling, the Hon. Mr. E. E. Brodie, and Mr. and Mrs. Gordon Yates are' passengers on the President Madison which left for the north yesterday.

With the return to the Colony of the G.O.C. from North China, Lt.-Col. F. S. Montague Bates, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., relinquished command of the garrison in South China.

An interesting wedding took place at Brompton Parish Church when Mr. George R. A. Mills, son of the Rev. Barton and Mrs. Mills, married Miss Vera Beauclerk, a granddaughter of the late Sir Robert Hart, who did great work in China. Young men have become so feminized in their clothes, according to West End tailors, that they are now wearing "divided skirts." At least the new trousers affected by the young blades at Oxford and Cambridge can scarcely be told from divided skirts. "Look at this pair," said a Savile Row tailor mournfully. The waist is 30 inches and each leg is 25 inches around the knee and 22 inches around the shoe top. Those are practically the measurements of a divided skirt. "But it is the latest style and the young men demand them. They go even further. They have now begun cutting their sport shirts low-neck—a purely feminine fashion." Dr. Percy Hall of Hull, speaking at a Rotary Club luncheon, defended the new style of open-necked shirts. "If men can survive the new style, they will benefit from it," he said. "It will harden them. Women nowadays are much more sensibly dressed than men and their styles could be imitated by men to advantage."

Mr. J. T. Pratt, C.M.G., who has been acting British Consul-General at Shanghai during the absence of Mr. Sidney Barton, C.M.G., with Mrs. Pratt and daughter passed through Hongkong on the s.s. Morea during the week and for Home, on leave. London's long-awaited light two-seater taxicab at last promises to materialize and thus bring the British metropolis into line with New York and other important cities. The police commissioners have received numerous applications for services for such vehicles and the Home Department has now announced the appointment of a committee to settle designs and fares. London streets are at present encumbered with a multitude of heavy four-seater taxicabs whose tariff is so high that passengers who can afford to use them are not numerous enough to support them. Moreover, the drivers demand gratuities over and above the face, thereby lengthening the already disproportionately long lines of idle vehicles. The new two-seater, by providing an intermediate form of transport between the two expensive taxi and the cheap but tardy street omnibuses and underground trains, should supply a real need.

Sir William Murison has been appointed to be Chief Justice of the Straits Settlements. Sir J. W. Murison has been in the Straits Settlements since 1919 when he was appointed Attorney-General, being created a Kt. Bachelor in the same year. He is a B. A. and LL.B. of Trinity Hall, Cambridge, where he took honours in classics and law and won the Latham English Prize. He was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1806 and was at the Chancery Bar Hill 1902, when he went to East Africa, rising to be chief judge of Zanzibar in 1914. He was arbitrator in the dispute between the Sultan of Zanzibar and the E. A. P. governments as to His Highness's mainland properties. He is a Hindu student and was examiner in Swahili to the Zanzibar Government. In the Straits has acted as Colonial Secretary and administered the Government. Sir William is fifty-three years of age.

text:
Mr. J. Calliers, a carpenter, of Shrewsbury, lost more than £500 in notes, burnt in a fire in his workshop.

Renter cables that Admiral Leveson, in the "Morning Post" calls attention to the lack of a suitable Seamen's Institute at Shanghai and hopes contributions will be forthcoming from Britain to supplement the anticipated generous provision by the small community of Shanghai people.

Less whisky is being consumed in Scotland and less alcohol generally, Dr. J. D. Comrie told the Royal Commission on Lunchry. Dr. Comrie, who is superintendent of the early mental ward at the Edinburgh Royal Infirmary, said that the percentage of alcoholic cases had fallen from 50 per cent. in 1913 to 26 per cent in 1923-24. He did not think the decline in drinking was due to legislation, but was voluntary. People were more abstemious because of the price of drink and unemployment had something to do with it.

A New York message records the death of Mrs. Mary Saunders, who claimed to be the first demonstrator of the typewriter, 50 years ago. She opened a typewriter school in London in 1891 and retired in 1906. Mrs. Saunders, who died in her home in Leonardo, New Jersey, went to New York from Nova Scotia, hoping to obtain a position as church organist. She was selected from 300 applicants in response to a newspaper advertisement for a woman to take an easy and remunerative position: a musician preferred. Proceeding to an address in Broadway, she was shown what looked like a sewing machine. In two weeks Mrs. Saunders was writing at the phenomenal speed at that time of 70 words a minute, her achievement being a source of great-joy to G. W. N. Yost, the inventor.

Dr. Purvis's paper on shipbuilding in Japan, read to the Institute of Naval Architects at their annual meeting in London in April, was well received and an interesting discussion followed. Admiral Toyoda, Japanese naval, attached, spoke highly of Dr. Purvis's valuable services as professor of naval architecture at the Imperial University, and Commander Taji (an old student, now in civil life), testified in the same strain. Sir Philip Watts, formerly chief, constructor at the British Admiralty, was unable to attend but sent a written contribution. Sir Archibald Denny, of the famous Clyde firm, and Sir John Biles, lately professor of naval architecture at Glasgow University, also took part in the talk, Dr. and Mrs. Purvis are still in London but probably will take up their permanent residence in the south coast before the end of summer. British osteopaths (bone doctors) are to wait on the Minister of Health to claim official recognition.

A wedding, in which all who took part, including the bride, bridegroom, and bridesmaids, were connected with the medical profession recently took place at Christ Church, Hendon. The parties were Dr. John Wallace Mann, of 2, Avenue Gate, Upper Norwood, and Dr. Margaret Alwen Howell, lately on the staff of the North-Eastern Hospital, Tottenham. The bride, was given away by her uncle (Dr. J. B. Howell, medical officer for Hammersmith). The two bridesmaids were Dr. Hsie Mann, sister of the bridegroom, and Miss Nancy Howell, the bride's sister, who is a medical student.

The appearance of Sir Sidney Lee's biography of King Edward recalls a little incident that happened many years ago in the smoking-room of the Marlborough Club. One of his most intimate friends—the late Lord Farquhar, if memory serves bright—was rallying King Edward upon his well known habit of making notes on the backs of envelopes or any other stray piece of paper that came handy. "Think of the trouble you are causing your future biographer," laughed the King's friend. "Yes," replied, "His Majesty, with a smile, "I fear that anyone who attempts to write my life will have very little material to work upon." And such boyish in the case, King Edward's papers were very sorry indeed while he never kept a diary in his life. NIGHTLY (Sundays excepted). Unless otherwise advertised for special occasions,

The return of notifiable diseases for the 48 hours ended Sunday shows one case of paratyphoid and two cases of cerebrospinal fever—all Chinese.

Eels to growing quantities are being taken from the coastal and inland waters of the Canadian Dominion each year. During the 1923 season 1,114 cwt were caught by sea fishermen and 13,753 wertaken in inland waters, as compared with 1,434 cwt and 11,710 cwt., respectively, during the previous year.

He is a neat and dapper little man, but distinctly tough and bubbling over with national and civic patriotism, and of course it was only natural that when the Shanghai Municipal Council called for emergency volunteers, he was amongst the first to present himself at the recruiting office. He had visions of the handing back of the Light Horse sword and carbine which years ago he kept as neat and clean as the contents of his wardrobe. Imagine, then, his feelings when a business like Controller put to him as the first question. Can you stoke?

Peking, which has proved fatal to so many tourin companies saw the break-in of Sgr. Carpi's Italian Opera Company. The capital is sometimes enthusiastic over performances of no particular merit, but when anything really good comes along, Peking is almost always unkind, not to say frigid. This appears to have been the case with the Italian and Russian artists. The company accordingly dissolved. Mr. Scamuzzi and Mr. Ambrose have gone to Australia and Mr. Corbetto is on the way to Italy via Siberia. The rest appear to be going home via Shanghai, and some have already gone. Mr. Carpi's last tour also came to an end in Peking. St. Paul's Fund now amounts to £248,482 19s. 10d The latest Far Eastern subscription is £17 12s. from Foochow (per the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank), vlz., £12 12s. from Mr. W. Muller and £5 from Mr. J. C. Parkin.

The War Office has informed the authorities at Australia House, that tenders have been invited for the supply of brandy for the Army. The specification includes for the first time Australian brandy, as well as French and South African.

Prevalence of betting among schoolboys has set British head masters to wondering what "the world is coming to." One teacher told the national conference of board masters that in one class he had: found nineteen boys out of forty-five bet on horses. The average age in this class was under twelve. In a North London school, where the boys were to write an essay on what they did on Saturday, one boy wrote that the first thing he did was to "make up" his book. This led to the discovery that he was "bookie" in embryo, handling 460 a week.

The port authorities at Melbourne were puzzled recently by the unexpected appearance of the strangest sailing craft they had ever seen. "She had four schooner-rigged musts, but the rear one seemed to have been snapped, off near the top," said it was thought she might have put into port to refit. "The vessel turned out to be the Danish auxiliary schooner Danekonge (1,688 tons gross), en route from Auckland to Port Pire, which put into Melbourne for oil supplies and engine repairs. One of her propellers was disabled. The Danekonge was built in 1920, and is one of the few ships of her type. She is one of the most economically run cargo carriers afflated. Her main means of propulsion are four huge schooner sails, but two auxiliary Diesel engines of 160 h.p. each have been installed for use in calms and head winds.

A traffic regulation stand is being erected at the corner of Pedder Street and Queen's Road. At the moment it does not appear that it will afford much protection from sun or rain to those called upon to use it.

That the Shanghai strike situation has aroused considerable attention abroad is indicated in instructions which correspondents in Shanghai for newspapers to America and Great Britain, have received to send all news possible.

It is an old saying that the House of Commissions is the best club in Europe. The Members are this year to have golf competitions, tennis competitions, cricket competitions, shooting competitions; and some of the Labour Members are arranging for pigeons races for their constituents. The birds are to be set free from Westminster.

Timber scaled in British Columbia during February of this year amounted to 274,681,607 F.B.M., according to a statement prepared by the Department of Lands and Forests. Douglas fir, with a cut of 131,198,732, was the most important specie cut. The cut of red cedar amounted to 61,003,298; spruce, 22,150,947, and hemlock, 36,377,022.

On the occasion of the three hundredth anniversary of the establishment of the Order of Baronets of Nova Scotia, on May 6, a tablet was unveiled in Fort Anne, Annapolis Royal, Nova Scotia. The Historical Society of Annapolis Royal had charged of the proceedings and a lecture was delivered by Rev. W. Bruce-Muir. Beneath the tablet was hung a beautiful drawing in colour of the Badge of the Baronets of Nova Scotia.

In the second round of the Parliamentary Golf Handicap Mr. F.G. Penny (14) beat D.P. Fleming (14) and I. and Lord Donoughmore (16) (who, as Viscount Suerdale, was A.D.C. to Sir Henry Blake when Governor of Hongkong) beat G. Griffith (12) up. Mr. Penny fell in the third round to Mr. James Stuart (12) I down, but Lord Donoughmore kept up the running, beating Lord Massarene by 3 and 2.

A Home writer says:—It is good to see the Royal Standard flying again from the roof of Buckingham Palace. Never since the King's accession, with the exception of the royal visit to India and His Majesty's annual holidays at Balmoral and Sandringham, has the flagstaff been bare for so long a time. The King's message to the Lord Mayor of London speaking of the "sympathy and affection of our people" puts the relations between the King and his subjects in six words.

Mr. C. C. Nieh, the wealthy Chinese cotton mill owner who has (says the "North China Daily News") just tendered his resignation from the post of general secretary of the National Associated Chinese Chamber of Commerce, is a prominent Chinese Christian who has come under the influence of the undoubtedly Buddhist revival. Formerly well-known to the missionaries as an ardent member of the Methodist Church and chairman of the Shanghai Chinese Y.M.C.A. he is now an ardent student of the Buddhist faith.

Prince Chichibu, second son of the Emperor of Japan, who is coming to England for a stay of two years, will arrive in London during the early part of July. The members of the suite will be Viscount Keinin Matsudaira and Count Toshio Mayeda, Secretaries of the Imperial Household; Captain Seizaburo Okazaki, of the Japanese Army; Lieutenant-Colonel Jun-ichi Waka-mura, of the Medical Corps of the Army and Physician-in-Waiting to the Imperial family; and Mr. Hachiro Watanabe, Equerry-in-Waiting to the Prince. headline: SOCIAL
text:
Reuter announces the death of the French explorer Agusté Pavie.

Mr. C. J. Wang, general secretary of Chinese Y.M.C.A. at Amoy, China, is in Manila on a pleasure and business trip. English drama is well represented on the Russian stage. Bernard Shaw's "Saint Joan," despite the false report of its suppression, is enjoying a long run at the Kamerny Theatre, Moscow. Last season this enterprising and original company put on G. K. Chesterton's "The Man Who Was Thursday." "Hamlet" and "Twelfth Night" have both attracted large audiences for many performances. The Little Theatre (so called because of its proximity to the Big Theatre, or State Opera House) includes in its repertory John Galsworthy's "Silver Box." Eugene O'Neill's "Anna Christie" has encountered an enthusiastic reception, and a rather oversentimental play of Dickens. "The Battle of Life," is being played by one of the studios of the Art Theatre.

Major J. Mucready, D.S.O., D.A.A. and Q.M.G., China Commend, proceeded to North China on inspection duty per s.s. Huichow on Friday last.

Reuter's American Service cables that Professor MeElroy of Princeton University has accepted the Professorship of American History at Oxford University.

Major A. L. Cruickshank, D.S.O., R.A., has assumed command on the British Heavy Batteries, Royal Artillery, vice Major W. P. A. Huttersley-Smith, D.S.O., R.A., who has been granted leave. King Alfred's legs, as represented in a painting hung on the walls of one of the committee rooms in Parliament buildings, have been figuring in House of Commons debate. The matter was raised by a facetious Unionist member, who took exception to the picture as being out of drawing, though it was subsequently described by the Government spokesman as a very fine example of the early work of Watts, "who is one of our most distinguished artists." It shows King Alfred a thousand years ago waving on the Saxons with his sword to repel Danish raiders from the sea. The offending leg is twisted as the King looks over his shoulder at the men who are following him. The House of Commons laughed, but the picture is to stay where it is. A proposal by another member to remove it to the lunch room, in honour of King Alfred's connection with burnt cakes, failed to draw the chairman of the kitchen committee.

A meeting of past pupils and all interested was held at St. Joseph's College yesterday evening for the purpose of discussing the arrangements for the celebration of the Golden Jubilee of the College. It was stated that the Golden Jubilee would be celebrated on the 8th; 9th and 10th of November, and after the preliminary arrangements had been discussed, committees to deal with the various details of it were appointed.

H.E. the Governor (Sir Edward Stubbs, K.C.M.G.), will perform the opening ceremony on June 24, of the nearly completed new four-storeyed building which has been erected close to St. Joseph's College. This building which has been admirably planned on generous lines and has plenty of space, light and air, has been erected to meet the social and recreative requirements of the pupils of the St. Joseph's College generally. Among the sections it will house are to be found a gymnasium, laboratory, reading and writing rooms and other rooms suitable both for games, recreation and study.

headline: AND PERSONAL.
text:
The “Sunday Express” publishes the story of a young Englishman, said to be a “wealthy” planter in Singapore a few months ago, who, being jilted, threw up his job, squandered all his money and is now hidden among the stewards of the C.P.R. Empress of Scotland with the intention of making enough money to take him back to the land of rubber. He spent the bulk of his fortune in France en route. In London he woke up one morning to find himself robbed of all that he had left, £40. Penniless, he arrived in Southampton by lorry-jumping, and went into the workhouse. He left these hospitable shores as a third-class steward on May 3, and has undertaken to serve the company for six months.

Reuter announces the death of Mr. Robert Anderson Mowat. Mr. Mowat was educated "in Edinburgh and at the University College, London." He passed a competitive examination and was appointed a student interpreter in the China Consular establishment in 1864 and was acting Interpreter at H.B.M. Consulate at Hankow during part of the year 1866. He was acting Law Secretary of H.B.M. Supreme Court for China and Japan at Shanghai in 1867 and 1868. He was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple in 1871, the year of his marriage. He later occupied the following positions: — Acting Assistant Judge of the Supreme Court, 1876-78; Acting Judge, 1878; Assistant Judge and Registrar, 1878; Acting Chief Justice, 1879, 1881 and 1888-89; Judge of H.B.M. Court for Japan, April 1891, but remained at the request of the Secretary of State, at Shanghai as Acting Chief Justice and Acting Consul General till October, 1891, when he took up his post in Japan. He retired on pension in 1897 and had been residing since at Hove. The Admiralty have decided to substitute cups and saucers for the basins at present in use in seamen's messes, and it is proposed to effect this change gradually as the stocks of basins in His Majesty's ships and at the victualling yards become exhausted. Cups and saucers will be supplied first to home ships and establishments, including the Atlantic Fleet, being subsequently extended to foreign stations.

The P. and O.: Company do not apprehend any difficulties. All the China shipping is held up here.

headline: Students' Trial
parent_headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / SHANGHAI TROUBLE. / CABLES
text:
The students trial was concluded to-day, the accused men being ordered to furnish a bond guaranteeing their good behaviour. The American Assessor, Mr. Jacobs, said that he deeply regretted the case which had much embittered the Sino-Foreign relations.

There was no demonstration by the big crowd. The Court was heavily guarded by police and an armoured car.

Following a coolie dispute, last night of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's upper wharf in which a good deal of stone-throwing took place, a liquid of Chinese Police fired over the crowd, which scattered. A dozen arrests were made. The trouble apparently was purely Chinese, but this morning, when the upper wharf coolies attempted to resume work, they were mobbed and prevented from doing so.

A strike has been declared, and students are at present haranguing the coolies.

Fengtian Troops Arrive. Special trains are conveying to Shanghai upwards of a thousand Fengtian troops from Nanking this evening. Chang Hsueh-Jiang, Chang Tao-lin's "star" commands these troops whose mission is ostensibly to maintain order on the borders of the Settlement.

The movement derives an extra importance from the identity of the commander, who will doubtless personally report the Shanghai situation to his father. It is also believed that Chang Tso-lin is taking advantage of the situation to strengthen his grip on the Shanghai region.

It is reported that 600 students led by Peking aglintors demonstrated at Mukdan, whereupon the Education Bureau warned the students not to harm foreigners or cause disorders.

The students' efforts to cause general strike failed owing to official precautions

Pelong Students

The students, on reaching the Walchiaopu, sent in a, deputation. It is reliably reported that the deputation demanded the despatch of troops to Shanghai, and similar steps.

Not being satisfied with the Minister's replies, the students, on his departure, smashed a large mirror and several windows, and did other damage before leaving the building.

The students make the same demands to Tuan Chijul, who saw the deputation personally, and he promised to bring up the demands at a Cabinet meeting to be held tomorrow.

As far as can be ascertained, no attempt was made to molest any foreigner throughout the demonstration.

headline: INCIDENT OF THE FLAGS.
text:
A circular has been issued by Mr. E. C. Lobenstine, Secretary of the Council of Higher Education of the Chinese Christian Educational Association, reviewing the outbreak from the Christian viewpoint, containing a warning against coming to erroneous conclusions before the result of the enquiry is known, and enclosing a statement by Dr. Potts on the closing of St. John's University.

The students who took the chief part in the demonstration of Saturday, May 30, came from four radical colleges, two of these were the Shanghai University control of the student movement. Within the last two or three days, largely owing to the valuable work done by the Young Men's Christian Association, a change has taken place within the Student Union and every effort is being made to keep the more conservative element in control of the Union's activities. The Union is coming out in opposition to the use of force, although still active in the promotion of a general strike. The strike situation is serious and is growing. Foreign nations have brought in marines who are assisting the regular volunteers and those who have volunteered for temporary service.

The students are still in Shanghai College although they are not attending classes. The faculty of the College passed two resolutions the day before yesterday; one lamenting the events of May 30 and the other calling for a thorough investigation of the entire situation.

It seems to us here that the present is a time when all in Church and Christian institutions need to exercise the utmost caution when careless remarks may, because of the present tense feelings, be unduly magnified and receive wide publicity. One incident from an institution in another city is being widely circulated here, namely, that a foreign professor said the institution was supported by foreigners and therefore was a foreign institution and that if students did not like the way the institution was run the thing to do was for them to leave it.

The issues at stake in this incident are very far-reaching indeed, and raise for us, as Christian workers in China, fundamental questions both to our own Christian attitude toward justice and fair dealing and our methods of working in a country where there may justly be differences of opinion as to what course of action a Christian should choose.

We trust that the information that a thorough investigation is assured will be helpful to you in dealing with your own students and will help to convince them that the best thing for them to do is to continue with their studies, believing that the solution of the questions at issue can best be worked out by those who have access to all the facts, and that the publication of the exact facts is the surest first step toward securing strict justice.

President's Statement.

The President of the St. John's University, in his statement in regard to the sudden closing of the term; gives a brief chronicle of the events leading up to the present situation, in which he says:—

Owing to the excitement caused by the killing of some students by the municipal police in the riot on Saturday afternoon, May 30, an organization called the Students Union was formed by the student body at St. John's. A communication was received from this organization asking that the students might be allowed to suspend their studies indefinitely and also containing the following clause:—

"During the period of suspension, it is our express desire to make sure that no student is unnecessarily absent from the campus. For this reason, we beg to request you to refer all letters to us that are from the students parents or guardians asking for leave. We have a special committee to attend to this matter."

A joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held on Monday evening, June 1, and it was decided to appoint six members of the faculty (three Chinese and three foreign) to meet with six members of the student body (four elected from the College and two elected from the Middle School) for a conference. This conference was held on Tuesday morning, and an endeavour was made to get the students' point of view. Another joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held at seven o'clock (Tuesday). The faculty then adopted the following regulation:

The University has decided to allow the students to suspend their studies until next Monday morning 7.40 a.m. If at the end of that period, they are not ready to resume their regular duties, the University will be closed and all students will be requested to return to their homes. Students living in the vicinity are allowed to return to their homes now. “Letters will be sent to parents and guardians informing them that the University disclaims any responsibility for the students' welfare or safety while they are off the premises.” Students remaining on the grounds and occupying the College dormitories will be expected to observe the regulations put on by the administration.

Chinese flag could be flown at half mast. As it was late, the President had no time to confer with anyone and gave the permission. On Wednesday morning two flags were raised on the flag poles, the Chinese flag at half mast on one pole and the American flag at the top of the other pole. Bishop Graves requested that the flags be taken down, giving his reason that the flying of the Chinese flag at half mast indicated that as an institution we considered the action of the municipal police to have been wrong, which we were not prepared to do. The President promised to comply with his request and sent for the Assistant Scoutmaster. Owing to the fact that the Assistant Scoutmaster did not come immediately, the President decided to take down the flags himself which he proceeded to do. Both flags were taken down at the same time. When the students came out from their mass meeting which they were holding in the Assembly Hall they were surprised to find that the flags were down and sent a deputation to wait on the President to ask why they had been lowered. The President informed them that he himself had lowered them and that owing to the objection made to their being raised, he thought it was better to follow the rule which had been made by the Administration that flags would only be raised when the College was in session. A short time afterwards, hearing a commotion he went out from his office and found some of the students about to raise another Chinese flag. No permission had been asked for doing this and no expiration had been given to him. It seemed to him that it implied that the student body was in such a state of excitement that it was unwilling to abide by the regulations. One of the conditions upon which they were allowed to remain in residence while suspending their studies was that they would observe the regulations put out by the administration.

The President came to the conclusion that the only way to avoid conflict with the students was to close the institution for the term, and it will not be re-opened until next September. The students were not expelled. No threats were used, but they were requested to return to their homes.

headline: Strike at Nanking.
text:
Following the two mass parades of last week, the students have been spending their time in meetings or in speechmaking on the streets. Schools are combed for contributions and a house-to-house canvass on the streets is being conducted for the aid of the striking workers.

On Friday, 5,000 workers of the International Export Company struck and formed a huge parade. The students are working sympathetically with them. Servants in British homes and employees of British Companies have also struck. The agitation in Nanking is centering against the British and Japanese, and the student leaders are advocating no violent measures but the weapon of boycott. Even richness are placarded with the sign "We do not carry British or Japanese."

headline: THEFT OF RICE.
text:
Six Chinese were charged before the Kowloon Magistrate this morning with the theft of ridemenal from the s.s. "Tea." The Magistrate discharged four of the men, who were fokis employed by the other two, as he considered that they were acting under orders from their masters, and sentenced the latter to two months' hard labour each.

A section of the students in Peking this afternoon started a campaign of intimidation against shopkeepers. They warned them of the consequences if they did not support the boycott against the British and Japanese. They have posted notice all over the city call-up for a united stand by the populace. Their apprent was illustrated with photographs of corpses said to be those of the victims of the war in casualties. Another postcard denies income being used to support their own business. They are the campaign's most popular

headline: AND GENERAL
text:
A fire engine served as a wedding coach at a volunteer fireman's wedding at Bournemouth. Man changed at Lambeth with drunkenness: "I met a Scotsman I had not seen for two years' and he gave me a drink." Ordinary life insurance written in Canada shows a decided increase this year so far, as compared with that of the corresponding period in 1924. The increase in March over February was from $28,000,000 to $35,000,000. The beautifully wooded town of Bingley in the West Riding of Yorkshire claims ruefully to have the biggest number of unmarried women, relative to its population, of any town in the Kingdom. The following is the matter in a nutshell: 4,000 females married. 6,500 females unmarried. 8,500 males. So that though the females outnumber the males by 2,000 there are 4,500 males without spouses. These include 355 widowers. Of 1,000 girls between the age of 20 and 24 only 195 are wedded, and only half of those between 25 and 29. Last year Bingley's birth rate was lower than that of any other year recorded, out of war time. Reasons advanced for this unsatisfactory state of affairs is the difficulty in getting houses and the slackness in the textile trade. Is hanging the best method of execution? Earl Russell thinks not. The question has been discussed at a meeting of the Medico-Legal Society, and "The Lancet" reports that Earl Russell thought a better method, giving less unpleasant anticipation for the victim, would be the introduction of coal gas into the prisoner's cell at night during sleep. This would be painless and not disagreeable. Lord Jntsioe Atkin opposed this suggestion. He pointed out that if the prisoner did not know on which night he was to be poisoned he would lie awake many nights expecting death. If, however, he was forewarned he would certainly not sleep on the given night, but would be slowly suffocated while conscious. Lord Justice Atkin added that the public should feel assnerd that judicial hanging was painless, and that complete unconsciousness, if not death itself, was instantaneous. Sir William Wlicox agreed that it was the best method of execution, and more reliable than electrocution. A letter from a boy asking for the provision of a sailing pond for his model yacht has been received by the Mayor of Watford. The executive committee of the Berks County Humane Society has indorsed a movement to prohibit the use of live birds as targets in shooting matches. It plans to conduct a county campaign against the use of birds for this purpose. Recent investigations in Genocals archives have disclosed that the entire cost of Columbus's fleet was only 14,000 lira, or about $5,600. The expenditures on the trip to America amounted to 22,000 lira more, bringing the total cost up to about $14,400. Columbus's annual salary was 1,600 lira, about $640. The captains received half this amount and the monthly pay of seamen was $5. In two parts of the British Isles, Eastbourne and Dublin, there has been observed from time to time a particularly vicious ant known as "The Argentine Ant," which in its native region attacks small chickens, bees, and small birds, which it consumes, and has even been known to attack and kill children, subsequently eating their flesh. Rubber corsets are being banned by the medical profession. “Rubber corsets transgress every principle of modern clothing interfere seriously with the functions of the skin, which must be kept at a high level if we are to be healthy and last, but not least, are moss, uncleanly.” This is the verdict of Dr. R. King Brown, chairman of the executive council of the Institute of Hygiene and lecturer on public health at Guy's Hospital. O'Callaghan, Mr. L. H. Saint, Mrs. Saint, Vice-Admiral Sir Edwyn S. Sinclair K.C.B., M.V.O., and Secretary to the Vice-Admiral.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
A receiver has been appointed for the Pung Chow Co., Inc., of New York, formerly one of the largest domestic manufacturers of mnb-jongg sets. The company encountered financial troubles with the advent of the cross-word puzzle eraze, which resulted in a decline of interest in mnb-jongg.

The return of notifiable diseases in the Colony for last week shows 1 Chinese case of small-pox, 3 cases of enteric fever (1 English and 2 Indian), 2 cases of paratyphoid fever (1 American and 1 Chinese), and 5 fatal Chinese cases of cerebrospinal fever (3 imported).

A District Court Martial will assemble at Murray Barracks, at 10 am, to-morrow for the trial of Duffadar Daulat Khan, Hongkong Mule Corps and Private George Webb, 1st Battalion, the East Surrey Regiment. The President of the Court will be Major R. C. Campbell, 1st Battalion, the East Surrey Regiment.

The American Consult-General at Hongkong is authority for the estimate that a sum equal to 250,000,000 silver dollars is sent annually to that British Colony by Chinese living overseas as remittances to relatives, investments, and for the fulfilment of obligations. Another estimate reckons a total of $100,000,000 in remittances from Cantonese abroad to Canton. Swatow is believed to receive annually about $30,000,000, and Amoy, $20,000,000. American contributions to missionary and other philanthropic work in China are said to aggregate at least $25,000,000 a year. The maintenance of foreign-diplomatic missions, foreign men of war in Chinese waters, foreign expeditionary forces, and foreign shipping in China's probably amounts to $20,000,000 a year. Tourists' expenditures annually may be reckoned at about $10,000,000. The aggregate of these invisible imports would probably net at least 300,000,000 silver dollars per annum. To this sum must be added the investments of foreign capital in business enterprises in China.

Great excitement prevailed in Liverpool Chinatown on May 9, when plain clothes police swooped down in motor-vans on three separate premises in connection with alleged gunning offences. Five Chinese and another coloured man were taken into custody.

At the opening on May 16 of the Printing Trudes International Exhibition in London Prince Henry referred to the presence of visitors from China and Japan, and said that printing ranked in importance as the sixth industry in this country.

Everything served at a luncheon given on May 18 at the House of Commons by Lieut. Commander A. C. Rawson to inangurate an Empire shopping week in Brighton and Hove, was produced within the British Empire. Singapore was represented by tapioca, Malaya by pineapple and Hongkong by preserved ginger.

Writing of queer ways of reckoning time, a correspondent mentions an interesting custom that prevails in the Philippine Islands, where they reckon distances in cigarettes. If you ask a Filipino how far such-and-such a place is, he will reply: "Senior, it is so many cigarillos." If it is one cigarillo, you may reckon it at five minutes' walk.

The last Annual Report of the Missions to Seamen records encouraging progress at Shanghai and Hongkong as well as in over 100 other ports of the world; and it concludes "In looking back at the steady and continuous growth of our work we muv indeed thank God and take courage for the future. But we are also most fully aware that no executive growth can be obtained except at the cost of pain and stress. At this very moment we are considering plans for even greater extension and the opening up of new fields of work." Statistics are given showing that 670,488 seamen unveiled themselves of the Society's Institutes for Social Entertainment and Ambulance classes as well as Religious Service during last year.

"Not guilty," said a deaf prisoner at the Old Bailey when asked if he had any money.

The annual general meeting of the Victoria Recreation Club is to be held on Friday next at 6 p.m.

St. Paul's Fund now totals £218,763. No donations from the For East have been acknowledged this week (May 21.)

"What, and me been here all these times," exclaimed a woman prisoner at Willesden, when the magistrate said he did not know her.

Our Finance and Commerce columns give particulars of a proposed winding-up resolution in connection with Pantal Ltd., Singapore.

"Pity poor, pedestrians," exclaimed the Highgate magistrate. "They can't walk on the roads because of motors, and now cyclists come on to the footway."

headline: SOCIAL
text:
Mr. Andre Dupre, the French boxer, attended an exhibition of Chinese boxing at the rooms of the Chinese Boxing Association, Caine Road, last evening.

Will Hender's jazz band played at a Press luncheon in the Stadium Restaurant a few days before the opening of the Exhibition at Wembley. Mr. Hender will be remembered by the jazzists of Hongkong—and—Shanghai—of 1922-23 season.

New York University has chartered an 18,000-ton liner for a students' experimental world tour. It has been rechristened the University and will sail on September 25, carrying 450 students, as well as a number of professors from cooperating universities. The term in this floating college will last eight months, during which period the ship will visit 50 ports in 35 different countries and in five continents. The ship will visit the Far East.

To little Jean Molison, aged 5, grand-daughter of the head of J. P. Molison and Co., of Yokohama, belongs the honour of having sat with the King and Queen in the boy railway on Treasure Island at Wembley on May 14. The King it appears, chatted with Joan on the trip, and soon overcame her shyness. Some members of the Molison family were lost, it will be remembered; in the earthquake at Yokohama in 1923, and the survivors, including Joan, obtained succour at Hongkong on the way home as refugees.

At a meeting of the board of directors of the Shanghai Rotary Club, it was voted that copies of a telegram received from the Tientsin Rotary Club and the reply of the Shanghai Rotary Club be sent to the foreign and Chinese newspapers in Shanghai. Following is the copy of the message received from the Tientsin Rotary Club: "Roclub, Shanghai: We members Tientsin Rotary Club convey fraternal greetings Shanghai Rotary Club and wish tender our sympathies in present troubles deploring as we do any occurrences which tend to mar the happiness of international relations or run counter to the principles of service. We hope that the principle of mutual respect and confidence for which Rotary stands will be quickly re-established." The following message was sent in reply to the above: "Roclub, Tientsin: Greetings. We share your views. Members Shanghai Rotary Club are doing all possible to re-establish mutual respect and confidence."

The Shanghai stork has not gone on strike, at least not at Dr. Anne Walter Fearn's Hospital, 30 Route Pichon, French Concession, where three babies were born yesterday morning (June 8). They were a son to the Rev. and Mrs. Clifford M. Drury of the Community Church; a daughter to Prof. and Mrs. L. H. Schultz of St. John's University and a daughter to Mr. Mr. N. W. E. Clarke, Mr. Clarke is Assistant Engineer in the Public Works Department of the Municipality. It was reported yesterday that an attempt was made by members of the Students Union to induce the Chinese staff at Dr. Fearn's Hospital to strike, but up to yesterday they were still on the job.
