headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL.
text:
A branch of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. has been opened at 347, Nathan Road, Kowloon.

"The Aim of Humanity" was the subject of a lecture given at the Chinese Y.M.C.A. last night. The speaker was Mr. Lun King sang.

"The Art of Entertaining" is to be the subject of discussion at the English-speaking debating club at the Chinese Y.M.C.A., this evening.

Thanks to the prompt and admirable firmness of the Hendmaster of the Saiyingpun School, the "strike" at this school came to an end yesterday with the return to classes of practically all the boys.

The use of the motor bike in rounding up criminals is not unknown. Shepherding alleged lawbreakers by the same means is probably also not unknown. At any rate the unusual sight of a man being "walked off" to a police station with an inspector behind on a slow-moving motor cycle was witnessed this morning at Causeway Bay. The man was carrying baskets of green stuff and was probably an unlicensed hawker. The usual crowd quickly gathered with amazing rapidity.

The Shanghai Yacht Club have been trying hard to “carry on as usual,” but with the Commodore out with the Twelve-bore Company, the secretary doing duty with the Shanghai Scottish and the blue burgee with a Maltese Cross being represented in every unit of the defence forces, it has been found quite impossible to muster enough skippers for a race. During a spell in between polishing his spornan strap, the hon. secretary compiled an optimistic programme for the current month but he has now been compelled to announce that, owing to the prevalent wind-up, all racing has been suspended until conditions again approach the normal. Jolly and Merry were the names of two men fined 10s., each at Thames for drunkenness.

"What is the good of a wife if she can't mend trousers?" said Mr. Mead, 'the magnisirate, at Marlborough-street.

For the 24 hours ended Wednesday the return of notifiable diseases showed a clean bill of health.

A drawing for 140 Debentures in the Hongkong Cricket Club will take place in the Club's pavilion on Wednesday, the 24th inst. at 5.16 p.m.

The total output of the Kailan Mining Administration's mines for the week ending June 6, 1925, amounted to 73,739 tons, and the sales during the period to 61,705 tons.

The 1st Battalion, the East Yorkshire Regiment, is to take the place of the 1st Battalion, the East Surrey Regiment, on arrival here from Egypt in the next trooping season.

"The is rews for Pussyfoot," said Mr. H. R. O. wald on being informed at a Hammersmith in quest that an ex-soldier who contrac ed malurla" in Salonika would have a bad attack if he drank beer or spirits.

The clerk at Willesden, after reading the formal charge to a prisoner, concluding "—and on divers other dates," asked him if he had anything to say.

"Yes," said the man, "what date was divers dates?"

The Shanghai Teachers' Union formally states that the Union has no connection whatever with Soviet Russia, but on the contrary, the sole object of this Union is to furnish due guidance to the students and to prevent violent action on all sides.

Colombo shippers have made made complaints of pilfering from cases lying in Government bonded warehouses. An old cannon ball, a relic of the days of the Dutch occupation, and quantity of coal were found in certain cases which had been tampered with.

headline: LOCAL
text:
Two hours after an appeal appeared in a local paper, a British Legion branch received a bath chair for a crippled ex-Service man.

Those familiar fictional characters, Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, are making their appearance in a Moscow motion picture house. Mark Twain has always been a popular foreign author in Russia and "Tom Sawyer" was successfully dramatized and produced at the Moscow Children's Theatre.

Mrs. Lane, wife of Sub-Inspector Lane, was forced from her ricsha when approaching the Star Ferry, Kowloon, yesterday morning. Her aggressors were a party of Chinese and as the nature of their intentions appeared decidedly unfavourable it was fortunate that the police were near at the time. Mrs. Lane was taken to the Water Police station not very much the worse for this very unpleasant incident.

Kagawa Toyohiko, a Labour leader of Kobe, Japan, arrived in London recently to study the workings of the British Labour Party as an aid to organizing a Labour party in Japan. Mr. Toyohiko said the Socialist and Labour leaders of Japan had combined in efforts to further the movement and that while the Japanese Labour Party would be modelled after the British system it would function in some ways along the lines of the Social Democratic Party of Germany.

A new kind of "death ray," exceeding in its destructive capacity any previous device, rumoured or realised, has been reported to the Commerce Department Washington as the claimed accomplishment of a German inventor; Mr. William T. Daugherty, Trade Commissioner at Berlin, forwarded a summary of an article describing the invention, which is called "heliotneub," with the startling assertion that its mysterious waves are capable of paralyzing life for six hours over a distance of forty miles and to an altitude of more than 45,000 feet. The highest elevation reached by an airplane as yet is about 39,000 feet.

When Prince Henry visited the Infants' Hospital, Vincent Square, Wesminster, Dorothy Gulliford, a tiny mite of two, kissed her hand as a good-bye to the Royal visitor.

A. E. R. Gilligan, the captain of the British team that lately visited Australia, and F. C. Toone, the manager, have, according to Mr. Kirby Hewlett, joined the British Fascists.

To swell the funds being raised locally for St. Dunstan's Hospital for the Blind, a competition was held at Rokkosan, Kobe. Conditions were, 18 holes against Bogey under handicap, first round of the day, entrance fee Y2.50 to go to St. Dunstan's.

What are claimed to be "record" tiger-shooting performances duly authenticated have just been announced. Mr. N. V. Watson, 21st Field Battery, R.A., stationed at Mhow, bagged three tigers in ten minutes near Harda, in Central India. Even better was the achievement of Colonel on the Staff R. J. Collins, Director of Military Training, who during a recent visit to Gwalior shot three tigers with four shots in two minutes.

The search for a fourteenth guest at the Lloyd George luncheon at the House of Commons, at which it was found that only thirteen guests had been invited, threatens to become historic. But this superstition is even more rife in stage circles, of course. The box-office keeper at the Hay market was saying that many patrons refuse to take a seat numbered 13. Yet at the Savoy Hotel, a little while ago, having deferred to this belief and substituted 12a for the fatal number on a room door, the management was told by so many people that 18 was their lucky number that it has now been restored. Mr. A. G. Warren, late lecturer in Engineering at the University, is now engaged in research work at Woolwich Arsenal. Mr. T. W. Mathewsman, late lecturer in Physics, is now in India.

headline: i
text:
The Imperial Family entertained Mr. Kopp, the Soviet Ambassador in Tokyo, to a luncheon party in the Homeiden Hall of the Imperial Palace on the 29th ult. at noon. Her Majesty the Empress and the Prince Regent were present, and Baron Shidehara, Foreign Minister, Dr. Ichiki, the Imperial Household Minister, Count Makino, Lord Keeper of the Pivy Council, and Mr. Tanaka, Ambassador to Russia, were also invited. At the dinner the Prince Regent expressed his thanks to the Soviet Ambassador's present of coins in gold, silver, and copper, now current in Russia.

A letter of protest was sent to the "Treasury" by the London General Shipowners' Association against the loss and inconvenience which would result from the King's birthday being celebrated on Wednesday, June 3, as a public holiday at London docks, Whit-Monday fell on June 1, and with a second public holiday on the Wednesday there would be very little business done at the docks before Thursday. The Treasury sent a reply that the date fixed for the celebration of the King's birthday cannot be altered without "grave inconvenience," to which the shipowners replied that commerce and shipping interests would suffer for greater inconvenience and financial loss.

headline: PRISONER'S STORY.
text:
Mencia Carniciu presented a striking figure when she appeared before the Chief of Police to be examined. She is 26 years old and is the daughter of one of the richest families in Macedonia. She is a young woman of extraordinary beauty, tall and svelte, with jet back hair and blazing black eyes. She was utterly defiant in face of the murder charge. She told the examining magistrate she vowed two years ago to take the life of Todor Dimitroff as retribution for the lives of two Macedonian patriots whom, she declared. Dimitroff betrayed to their death, Telling the story quietly and proudly, she related how she came to Vienna and contrived, through a woman who knew the Dimitroff's, to arrange the exact seating for both parties in the Municipal Theatre for the performance of Ibsen's "Peer Gynt." Deliberately she told how she had visited the theatre and witnessed the performance earlier in order to judge the best moment to open fire.

"I knew he was always expecting attack, and always ready to attack, Mencis Carniciu declared," So I schemed to sit behind him, and as soon as the chance was right I fired"

Apparently Madame Dimitroff threw herself between her husband and the line of fire at the crack of the revolver, which explained how the second bullet found its mark in the skull of the dead man's wife. Dimitroff's companion, a man named Bagatinoff, had just been able to get his pistol from his pocket when Mencia fired again, killing Dimitroff.

The murder occurred at the moment when Peer Gynt was supposed to be drowned in the Sea. The Viennese actor, Herr Tressler, who was playing the part, emerged from the waves and came back to life, and addressed the audience from the stage, urging them to remain in their seats.

Police investigation establishes the political character of the dramatic murder. From the history of his past activities in Balkan politics the police have confirmed that Dimitroff was responsible for the death of two Macedonian leaders, Boris Sarafoff and Ivan Garbanoff, in Sofia seventeen years ago. Dimitroff, who was 50 years old, had been living in Vienna during the past few months at the apartments of a prominent Macedonian patriot, Philip Attanasoff, but the latter was recently driven from Vienna by the police. Recognised as a sworn enemy of the present Bulgarian Prime Minister, M. Zankoff, Dimitroff went in fear of his life. He was always accompanied by three or four Macedonians armed with automatic pistols, ready to protect him from assassins.

According to a number of Mencia Carnici's friends, an element of mystery in the case is now presenting itself. Her intimate friends declare she was madly in love with the man she killed. When the police arrested her immediately after the tragic murder she had a smoking pistol in one hand and a razor in the other. She admitted that she intended to commit suicide, but she was either too stunned or had no time in which to do it.

In the files of the Vienna police head-quarters officials have found an old Bulgarian extradition paper drawn up against Dimitroff, charging him with being a member of the Macedonian Revolutionary Committee.

The victim of the tragedy in the Burgtheater has now been ascertained to be the notorious Todor Panitza, the founder and leader of the Macedonian Federalist organisation, who twenty years ago murdered two leaders of the Macedonian movement, Sarafoff and Garbanoff in the streets of Sofia. Panitza then fled to the mountains in the Macedonian regions of Bulgaria, where he organised revolutionary bands and lived like a prince, though he was always in dread of assassination. He came to Vienna a few days before to adjust differences which had arisen between Bulgarian emigrants there. He was always attended by heavily armed companions to guard him against attack and murder, and his presence occasioned much irritation in Austrian political circles, which represent such abuse of the rights of asylum being extended to Bulgarian emigrants.

headline: TIENTSIN MILL STRIKE.
text:
The "Perking and Pfeiss Times" states that the workers at Paocheng Mill, outside Tientsin, struck work on Saturday and other mills ceased work on Sunday.

It is reported that trouble arose over the fining of two men for being late, though the authorities state that the workers are demanding an increase of wages. The Chinese Police acted promptly; and there were practically no disturbances beyond the early breaking of windows.

The student delegates played a prominent part at meetings of workers, last evening.

headline: MISSION SCHOOLS.
text:
Considerable interest and importance attaches to the various Missionary Conferences to be held at summer resorts, near Shanghai and elsewhere, this month to discuss the future of Mission Schools in China, in view of the widespread movement among students not to return to such institutions owing to nationalistic and anti-foreign agitation.

It is understood that some missionaries favour opening next term, hoping that a good number of pupils will return.

returning will probably be subjected to considerable annoyance and persecution by students of non-Mission Colleges; and possibly forced to leave. Many Missionaries, therefore, advocate the closing of the schools for 8 months, a year, or more; others suggest the handing over of the schools to the Chinese for a period of one to three years so as to give the native Christian teachers an opportunity of conducting them. The problem not only concerns education; for there are numerous cases of Chinese withdrawing from the Mission. Churches and forning Independent Churches of their own. The question there was also a crisis whether to hand the Chinese to native.

headline: SYRIAN FIGHTING.
text:
General Surrail's despatch, regarding the fighting in Syria was read to a party of pressmen by M. Painlevé, late last evening. It stated that the Druse attack on the French troops originated in discussions among members of the family of the aggressor. Some of them wanted a French Governor: others, favouring independence, clamoured for a Native Governor. As the agitation grew more lively, small columns were sent to inspire respect and order. One immediately entered Jebeldruse and was enveloped, and submerged by the flood of aggressors. The troops fought most valiantly, but were crushed by numbers. Sixty managed to escape massacre.

A large column, commanded by General Michaud, was sent to exact reparation. This action of General Michaud's column was followed by a convoy of mule and camel transport, protected by Mulagasy and Syrian Tiraillens, who fled in the face of a violent Druse attack. The convoy was captured and the officer in command of the convoy was wounded and committed suicide. The infantry column was thus deprived of ammunition, but was able to retire fighting.

M. Painlevé added that he was unable to state the losses of General-Michaud's column as General Serruil's despatch was unfinished.

“Le Journal,” commenting on the above, says that the despatch throws an expected light on the Jebeldruse incidents, their causes and effects, and demands a full and impartial enquiry.

headline: PEKING'S TROUBLES.
text:
Peking, August 10. Two-thirds of the British Legation employees are still on strike, though a few of the office staff and servants returned this morning. The lighting was yesterday linked up with the Legation quarter supply and little inconvenience was caused.

Some instances of subotage were discovered, including damage to the pump providing houses in the Legation with artesian water.

Mr. Pulariet, is interviewing the Chief Executive, His Excellency Tuan Chi-jui, with regard to the strike this afternoon. Legation officials are optimistic that the interview will result in ending the strike.

The British and other foreigners are daily growing more indignant at the seeming'indifference of the Chinese Authorities with regard to the strike which, it is felt, they could have ended promptly if they had desired.

headline: FOOD RIOTS.
text:
SHANGHAI CHINESE CITY OVER-RUN.

Bands of striking wharf and godown coolies this morning overran the Chinese city creating a riot during which they looted the foodshops.

The demonstrations were the result of strike pay not being forthcoming.

The police were helpless. They fired once, wounding one man.

The afternoon was quieter. A mob of a few hundreds started for the Settlement and demonstrated at the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. They were pacified by labour officials. The municipal police prevented trouble.

headline: BOLSHEVIK MENACE.
text:
A reduction in the population of St. Petersburg from two millions before the war to 400,000 and 500,000 now and its ruined state were also referred to by the lecturer, the matter arising out of a question by the Hon. Mr. C. G. Alabaster.

In reply to another member of the audience who quoted the "China Mail" and asked the lecturer if he had heard the rumour with regard to the opening of the gates of Shameen, Mr. Hellstrom said that he had, but it was only a rumour. When the rumour had got about before the Bolsheviks had caused to be re-erected some kind of barrier outside the Chinese's Customs and had warned the Chinese that they were liable to be killed if they had anything to do with Europeans.

His reference to barricades was challenged by a member of the audience and the lecturer admitted that it was perhaps too strong a term to use in indicating duck and pig baskets near some newly laid cement although they had been strengthened somewhat after the rumour about the gates being opened. He did not think Shameen would be attacked by the Bolshevik Government as they preferred to kill trade rather than risk defeat by war.

The meeting applauded an answer given by the lecturer to Mr. M. Manuk who asked what remedy he would suggest for the present state of affairs. A voice interpolated with "British intervention" but Mr. Hellstrom answered that it was not for him to tell Britain how to put her own house in order.

Conditions in Swatow were referred to by Mr. A. Macgown of that port. He referred to the taxes imposed by whatever military leader happened to have control at the time and said that the taxes were collected by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce whose representatives were accompanied by military. Up to the present house rents (one method of taxation) had been collected three years in advance (ltr.) Mr. Macgown referred to the impossible treatment of the British Consul at Swatow who received no replies to his despatches to the Chinese representatives and was not received when he called personally. Examples were given of the intense anti-British feeling in existence there.

More questions were invited at the end and speaking from the audience, Sir Henry Pollock was received with applause when he remarked that the time for drift and inaction was past. A minority in Canton were defying treaties by which it was stipulated that Canton was an open port to Great Britain for trade not only with Canton but with the interior. He felt he was expressing the feelings of those present when he said that they would be grateful to the Committee of the Chamber of Commerce if they would at an early date call a public meeting with a view to definite action being suggested to the British Government.

Thanks to Mr. Hellstrom, the Chairman and the Hon. Mr. Holyoak for getting into touch with Mr. Hellstrom, concluded the meeting.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE. / SPECIAL CONSTABLES:
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—There were some men (foreigners), brave and bold (?), who could but would not help in any capacity during the strike. Now these gentry are vexing sarcastic about the Special Constable's work, who, besides doing office work, had to go on picket duty. These men, (Specials) offered their services willingly and smilingly, without pay. I call such remarks as: "The Specials" are brave and useful, aren't they? Not half," and "When a shot is fired you will see the Specials run to the nearest tree for shelter" caddish and disgraceful. My only conclusion is that the speakers speak from experience. I presume that during the 1922 strike these men were enrolled as Specials and when danger threatened them they, brave men, funked!

Although we have not done anything extraordinary we deserve, I think, more than such sarcasm. We thank God that we have done, and are still doing, our "bit," which is more than what our satirists can say.

A SPECIAL CONSTABLE Hongkong, August 18. HOW MUCH LONGER? (To the Editor of the China Mail). Sir,—How much longer are we Britons going to stand being insulted by a lot of schoolboys and coolies? How much longer are merchants both British and Chinese going to sit down and twiddle their thumbs, while Bolsheviks flout them right and left and stop all their trade? How many more years of our lives are we going to waste out in China waiting for the country to settle down? China has been trying to settle her own affairs ever

It is time Britain intervened and showed a lead to other nations. A large body of influential Chinese should welcome British intervention to help China put her house in order. We can intervene with every justification. Now is our opportunity. Wake up England and fight this blasted Bolshevism. Let's have War and occupy Canton to start with. We have a wonderful record. Let's live up to it and be men, not cowardly politicians.

Will all who want to join an Anti-Bolshevik Association whose objects are to forcibly eject all Bolshevism from China and every other part of the world, send their names in to me care of the "China Mail" as soon as possible, with a view to a mass meeting to ask the Government to declare war on the present Canton Government. This is the only possible solution to the present situation, and the only way to restore our prestige in China.

headline: SHIPPING STRIKE:
text:
NEWS FROM ALL OVER

AUSTRALIAN EMERGENCY

The Federal Cabinet, at a special meeting to consider the difficult situation arising out of the strike of British seamen, subsequently issued a proclamation declaring a serious industrial disturbance exists.

This empowers the Federal authorities to deal with those who continue to obstruct the conveyance of goods and passengers.

Later Melbourne August 24

Highly important developments are expected to follow the issue of a proclamation which sets in motion the machinery of the Immigration Act, empowering the Government to deport persons not born in Australia who are responsible for obstructing transport.

headline: Ten Ships Held Up.
text:
Ten British steamers are idle. Their crews total 2,000 of whom 1,600 are practically nomiess and the remaining 400 are allowed aboard pending a settlement.

Spreads To New Zealand.

A mass meeting of British seamen and firemen at Auckland decided to strike to-morrow.

headline: (Earlier Cable.)
text: At the headquarters of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union it was said to-day that all the ships effected by the trouble at the London Docks sailed and no men left their ships. An official of the Tibbury branch said "our fellows are good men and are acting very decently. There is nothing Bolshevik about them."

headline: POWERS REPLY.
text:
IDENTICAL NOTE TO CHINA

"UNEQUAL" TREATIES.

It is expected that the Powers within a day or two, will send to the Walchisopu an identic note in reply to the Chinese Government's note of June 24. The subject of the so-called unequal treaties is understood to be the substance of the reply agreed upon and the document is now being drafted to Peking.

headline: HONGKONG SAFE.
text: on that "very damaging weapon" the boycott does not convey very clearly what was in the mind of the writer, and those who delight in our "confused British ways" have waxed profanely playful on the subject, remarks the "Peking and Tientsin Times." It is stated that the boycott "is maintained by an idea or an obsession, and it should be the definite object of British policy to dispel the obsession by all possible means." It is not always easy to suppress an idea, and still harder to dispel it when it comes out of the chrysalis and becomes an obsession. But the boycott idea is not among the difficult category. It usually suppresses itself, and it will do so as it has done before, because it is essentially contrary to self-interest. It is pre-eminently the boomerang of economic politics, inflicting hardships quite as severe on the boycotters as upon the boycotted.

headline: RETAILATION?
text: which the dispelling of the obsession may be assisted. Some of them have been openly discussed in Shanghai, and in a restricted sense practised, with notably healthy reactions. There is an unexploited field for retaliation in the Straits Settlements, for instance, where many thousands of Chinese are making their fortunes, and, instead of distributing most of their incomes in the country wherein they are made, as the vast majority of foreigners do in China, send large sums annually to their native land. Enormous sums of money in the aggregate leave the United States in this way for Europe. The same circumstances apply in the Straits. Life could be made very uncomfortable for the large Chinese population in these Settlements. We do not suppose it would ever be made as impossible and, in supportable as in Soviet Siberia, where Chinese traders who have not been kicked out of the country have to carry on under extreme difficulties. It would not be necessary to go farther than the Government of the Philippines, whose book-keeping laws, directed wholly against the Chinese traders, aroused a storm of indignation among the latter. It is not to be supposed that the indigenous population of the Straits is less jealous of the Chinese than are the Filipinos. When the representatives of the British Government in the Peking Legation are boycotted, and attempts are made to starve them out, countermeasures of a salutary description are unquestionably warrantable. However, we do not suppose such reprisals, which are entirely against our traditional Colonial policy, will ever be necessary, or adopted. But some of the fanatics, who, like their ancestors, think they can do without foreigners, the trade they bring, and the employment they afford to thousands of Chinese, and would yell with diabolical glee if they saw the last of us embark for our homelands, might occasionally give a thought to their own countrymen, vastly outnumbering us, who obtain their livelihood and amass wealth — some of which found its way to the coffers of the Kuomintang before the Party went over to the Communists — under the British flag.

headline: HONGKONG EXAMPLE.
text: The crazy swashbucklers, who were rattling their sabres of brass so violently, the other day, and still talk of crushing the economic backbone of Britain in China, might consider what would be the consequences of a war not only to themselves, but to their compatriots abroad, who are carrying on their business and occupations as usual, unmolested and unafraid, because they at least have learnt to place their trust in British patience and fair play. We hear of no panicky deputations from the Chinese residents of the British Colonies to Canton or Peking, to improve the two Governments to think of the possible results of the anti-British movement upon the welfare of the Chinese overseas. Neither fear nor a generous recognition of their indebtedness for fair treatment has impelled them to take such a course. Yet, to quote the page-wide heading of the Canton Gazette, "H.M.S. British Imperialism" can claim no watertight compartments. Under that daunted caption was "History of how a powerful colony of a powerful Empire using its�ive itself. Daily at 2.30, 5.15, 7.15, 9.15. Change of Programme Tuesday—Thursday—Sunday Sundays at 6 p.m., 7.30, 9.15

authorities to Sir James Jamie-son's protest against the former's decision to drum up an agitation, and organise a strike, against Hongkong. And when the Governor of Hongkong declared that he would stay and see it through, he was promptly declared, not a coward, but a bully. We think that Hongkong will prove to be quite able to take care of itself, and will crush once and for all this officially engineered assault upon a Government that has always treated the Chinese perfectly fairly, and to whom Sun Yat-sen paid a glowing tribute in a rare moment of fair-mindedness.

headline: CANTON'S LOSSES.
text:
The strike and boycott are slowly killing themselves. Hongkong has been put to great inconvenience, but Canton has suffered no less. The great silk trade of the city is at a standstill, together with most of the foreign trade. Many large consignments of silk warehoused in Canton for shipment to foreign markets have had to be sent back to the producing districts, and a city whose commerce is thus temporarily ruined has, moreover, to support a veritable army of unemployed, intimidated into leaving their positions in Hongkong, and terrorised into remaining away. The boycott and the nationalist agitation have points of peculiar similarity. A constructive policy could make China independent of those facilities whose withdrawal, as the result of her own action, has paralysed her commerce. A constructive national policy would with for the Chinese people all that a nation of such vast proportions could desire. In the present at in previous agitations, the Chinese are simply kicking with blindury against the pricks. An educational boy, out with last no longer than a trade boycott. The students will are most involved in the movement have decided that they will never return in the foreign educational institutions whose principal adopted the only course consistent with this principle and

duty. Some of them undoubtedly will not, though the choice will not always be theirs. But no serious effort is being made to expand native facilities for education. The thousands who have been receiving their education at the Mission schools will have to go back to them, or consider their education completed, and set out on a fight for existence, already hard enough in this undeveloped and over-populated country, that can have but one result. If only a tithe of the effort devoted to destructive movements, from the civil wars of the Militarists to the rabid ravings of the babus, were given to creative and constructive effort, there might be some hope for the immediate future of this country, and a corresponding respect and generosity among foreign nationals. There is no better or surer way to win the goodwill of the West—or to command it—than by earning and deserving it, and that can only be done by a solid, determined patriotic national effort to introduce order and good government. The world can only respect those who respect themselves.

London, August 26.—St, Paul's Restoration Fund has reached £250,000.—Reuter.

headline: CANTON MISSION WORK.
text:
NESTERDAY'S INTERESTING CONFERENCE DEVISION.

A 'WITH DRAWAL-TEMPORALITY'

The decision come to yesterday at a Conference held in Hongkong to consider the immediate future activities of the U.M.S. in Canton and throughout Kwangtung, marks an epoch in the history of missionary work in China.

Reuter has already cabled with regard to conferences held throughout China recently the opinion that had been expressed by missionary bodies that schools and missions should be handed over to the Chinese at any rate temporarily, because, in the first place, parents of pupils would hesitate to expose their children to possible insult at mission schools, and, in the second, that it would give an opportunity to test whether the time was opportune for Chinese effort alone to carry on with the work.

The decision at the Conference held here yesterday was that the schools in Canton should re-open as under the aegis of the C.M.S. but with no foreign teachers, and as it is the first actual decision which has been reported to the "China Mail," its results as an experiment will be awaited with interest. An important member of the C.M.S. body at present in Hongkong who conversed with a "China Mail" representative this morning said that it should be made clear that the foreign teachers and missionaries were shirking nothing. In leaving and abstaining from visiting the scene of their work they were acting merely in accordance with consular instruction and they were prepared to return at any moment if it were possible and if it were thought that such action would serve a good purpose.

The Chinese masters had in the great majority of cases noted splendidly at the various missions and schools, said the "China Mail" informant, and the Mission had every confidence in them. A few, left but merely as a result of intimidation and not out of sympathy with the forces of disorder.

Missionaries whose sphere of activities have been at Foochow and Pakhoi are awaiting consular instruction before returning

The schools at Canton affected by the decision come to yesterday are Holy Trinity, St. Andrew's Hall and St. Kildn's Girls' School.

headline: KATHERINE MACDONALD in WHITE SHOULDERS / INTIMIDATION.
text:
COOLIE BRAWLS HEARD IN COURT.

ACCUSED FINED

Two Chinese were charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy yesterday with intimidating a coolie foreman.

Mr. R. E. A. Webster, defending, said that certain witnesses he wished to call had dropped out of sight, and that apparently one of the men had been threatened by the complainant not to give evidence against him.

A woman who was in Court at the last hearing was called, and she stated that she heard the complainant threatening a man outside the Court.

One of the accused stated that he had entered into a partnership with the other accused and that they went to the Ping On wharf to unload cargo. They met complainant here and had a dispute as their appearance on the wharf was resented. They were later arrested on a charge of threatening the complainant, which was denied.

The accused were each nned $25.

A similar charge against the two men in which a coolie stated that they threw stones at him and threatened to kill him if he continued in his work was dealt with by Mr. H. R. Butters.

-Both the accused were bound over on a bond of $25 to be of good behaviour for six months.

headline: DR. GREENTELL REOBENT CHINA VISIT
text:
CHRISTIANITY AND BOLSHEVIEM Dr. Wilfred Greenfield, the famous missionary and explorer, who recently visited China and spent a short time in Hongkong, writes on his impressions as follows: The Bolshevik element is various menaces. At present it is mainly among students. But the prop成一 at the end of his life it made an impression upon on Dr. Sun Yat-sen. The Reds are, moreover, now sending forty Mongolian students to Moscow, and have actually fully away in outer Mongolia. The resistance to it is another indication of Chinese character. For there is no question that Chinese have much reason to complain of foreigners of sorts, and of imperialism that has been cruel, repressive and reactionary. Grin and bear it, or keep smiling, is, so some think, too much a characteristic of the Chinese. It might well be said of China today that she doesn't yet know what she wants; but, unlike what was claimed for the Irish, she seems to the stranger too content without it, though she has sense to know that Bolshevism is no way out.

The first great fact that strikes any rational human being with a soul all along this crowded cadre of humanity is the extraordinary depth to which already Christian missionaries have dug themselves into the hearts of the Chinese. It is to some extent true that a so-called anti-Christian, really a Bolshevik and anti-foreign movement, is going on—but in any case that could only mean that the power of Christianity really is being felt, and is an excellent proof of a fact which any man cannot help seeing, if he looks, and as the Scotch say, "uses his powers of observation." Still travellers easily miss the ways in which this is coming about, come to wrong conclusions about missions, and carry away wrong impressions altogether of their immense value in the struggle toward world peace. It is scarcely possible, however, to blame round-the-world trippers, who can barely be classed as travellers, as their time and opportunities available are so limited. Even those in business do not take time as a rule to make their own observations, and this has also been one's experience of many even in political life.

Dr. Grenfell is of the opinion that Union Colleges, Union Hospitals, Union Churches and other Christian efforts are giving new strength to the drive for "peace on earth" in all parts of China and thinks that the public school spirit which is taught in Christian educational institutions is a good ground for the gradual absorption of more civilised ideals.

What, however, surprised us perhaps most was that we couldn't get off at a city anywhere, however primeval looking or snelling, without finding a mission hospital, or school, or Christian effort of some sort, sweetening the atmosphere. Don't let anyone at home worry about things they read in the papers re anti-Christian efforts. The men in the field are not a bit disturbed. No one knows better that God is on His Throne. Most of these reports are like those of Mark Twain's death, " greatly exaggerated. Anyhow, no one expects the way of the Cross—which by the bye is the way all real evolution of every kind—to be wheeling a perambulator down the sidewalk any more than it was formerly, or will be in the future. The wagging of the devil's tail is the best sign manual of Christian activity—it won't hurt the real spiritual Church, of which George Adam Smith said, "There is no danger that it will be destroyed by being blown up, but only from being sat upon by endless numbers of indifferent nobodies." Moreover, the Chinese are a wiser race than many take them for—and their hearts are human and can tell the real thing from the false. Or, in other words, they know a good thing when they see it, as their attitude to missions has amply testified in the past. The Boxer outrage was an anti-Imperial political movement, cleverly switched by the reactionary Empress-Dowager into an anti-foreign and only so an anti-Christian one.

headline: SLOW CHANGES.
text: The pitails have mostly gone from the heads of Chinese but are only going slowly from their minds. The walls which obscure the light and air from people's houses, though originally put there to keep spirits from getting in, for the latter can't burn corners, are falling down nowadays; one seldom sees the scaffolding of a new house ornamented with branches at the top to make spirits, trying to get into the house, think it is a forest. Here, as in India, I now international language is springing up, because even when five generale came down to Shanghai to discuss a campaign they couldn't understand one another—the Cantonese and Pokinese dialects being as different almost as French and English. So one finds English hers in India and Palestine and Mesopotamian and Malaysia spring.

headline: BAG OF REDS.
text: Following a police raid on the British Communist Party headquarters in London, three lorry loads of literature were removed and six prominent Communists arrested, including the secretary, Mr. Irkpin, Mr. Harry Pollatt, who is the "Party's principal operator," Mr. Campbell, Editor of the "Worker's Weekly" who became notorious last year dutying the Labour Government's regime when the prosecution abandoned a sedition charge against him.

headline: ARREST AT GLASGOW.
text:
Two more communist leaders, Thomas Bell and William Gallacher were arrested this morning at Glasgow and Paisley respectively. The six arrested last evening were charged at Bow Street with conspiring to incite sedition and mutiny, and remanded for a week. The three in addition to those mentioned are Thomas Winningham, a member of the staff of the "Workers' Weekly," Ernest Cant, of London, an organiser of the Communist party and William Rust, secretary of the young Communist League.

The communists charged at Bow Street have been released on bail of £100 each.

Paris, October 15.—Replying to a member of the Finance Commission M. Painleve stated that the French losses in the campaign in Syria up to July last were 10,042. He promised to supply the figures of losses up to September 30.—Renter.

headline: QUILUTION OF PRIORITY
text:
The Tokyo correspondent of the Observer has the following comments to make on the wireless triangle in China brought about by the action of China in selling identical interests to three countries.

Information has been received from China reporting a wireless triangle which is of international importance, especially with the Conference in sight. According to apparently, authoritative newspaper reports from Peking, the American Minister has demanded confirmation of the American Federal Wireless Company's concession as a condition of the American Government's favourable and sympathetic attitude at the Conference. On the other hand, the "Japanese Minister demands that the Chinese shall demonstrate their good faith by confirming a similar prior concession to the Mitsui Company.

One outstanding fact is clearly that China sold identical concessions separately to two, and possibly three, firms, representing Mitsui, the Federal Wireless, and the British Marconi. Each in turn protested through its respective Government, but China became in different when the transactions were completed. Now the day of reckoning has arrived, and Peking proposes to compromise by a merger of the Japanese and American interests, so that wireless in China would be conducted by the joint management of the three countries, and, for American loan would be secured by the proceeds of the money policy.

Despatches from Peking, announce this proposal as having remained from America, but Japan apparently does not favour it. The situation contains elements of humour, and also of serious danger. Continuous propaganda from China spreads suspicion of the American motive. Some newspapers assert that Britdin and America have combined against Japan's and are seeking to "steal valuable concessions" for which Japan has already found and capitalised heavily.

Seed in cunning little inserts, bindings and hondings, and furnishes smart collars and cuffs in many different styles. The sleeves are long and tight, as a rule, the sleeves of the dress beneath being either long or wholly missing. There is no half way about it. Occasionally a cape intrudes itself, but they are in the minority. It has been a long time since a mora practical fashion has been launched. For the woman who needs a wrap, but serves a costume suit, may have both in the one.

The long coat, that reaches almost to the hemline, or at least well below the knee is a becoming garment, for it makes for height, and there is nothing about the dress beneath that changes the effect, when the coat is removed. If the costume consists of skirt and tunic, the latter is so very long that the appearance of height is retained, even though there be a contrast in colour or fabric. This beltless silhouette must be watched, however, for it is becoming only to the slender woman. A suggestion of a waistline, correctly placed, is much better if one is not reasonably slight of figure. And a tendency to round-the-hemline trimmings, recently developed, is another detail that must be watched, since it cuts height, if too conspicuous.

Four of the pictured models feature the long coat and dress, or the coat, skirt and tunic. The latter iden is expressed in a woollen fabric that has a decided sheen, and recognizes the value of fur in a decided contrast. The collar is large and the cuffs unique, distinguishing an otherwise plain coat that links itself to the tunic by the trimming, the latter not so striking that is will clash with any other tunic that may be chosen for variation. You will note that the same braid is used to edge a band of the fabric of the garment. A one piece dress, of the same fabric as the coat, is noticeable for its high collar, its vestce, and the smart ball buttons that trim the latter. Both fur, and embroidery edge the hemline, and cuff the straight line cont, that has a collar of the fur.

A tunic dress, very straight of line, uses crepe de chine in contrast to the wool material, and it makes the tunic effect and lines the coat. Fur edges the pocket and outlines the sleeves—fashionably wide at the wrist—and the stand-up collar. It should be noted that appearance of height is aided by the square crowned hat with narrow brim that so amirly complements the costume. Several unusual features are to be seen on the suit that seems to prefer the more striking sports fabric is a modest plaid weave to the more conservative materials. Machine em broidery trims the crepe de chine tunic and the coat has both belt and novelty sleeve, as well as a fur banding on the collar.

A short-contad- suit of the more tailored typo—really a between-season affair—has only its smart, simplicity to recommend it, but it shows a trend away from the O'Rossen type of tailleur. It is distinctly a two-piece affair and with one might wear either a dark or light-coloured blouse. Suits of this type will be seen in recent erous numbers, but they will not be as generally popular as the enable costume suit of much charm and many Who says it is a "new" fashion, the time? It may be in way to many, but it is really a legacy to us from the Saxon women who were wearing it long before the Normans, one, nearly a thousand years ago, a lacy for which we should be most devoutly thankful, so charming and adaptable has "it proven to be. We have in ad it before, so it is really only a revival of other revivals, adapted each time it returns to the mode of which it is art. But never has it assumed the dest

seen laid down for mode—"Straight, " "short" apply course. New if long, it is quite how negligible

the slip or skirt would really be in the combination, and so it is that blouse departments are looking ahead to busy days, for the possession of several tunies will mean several costumes, if one's single skirt or slip is neutral in its tone. One may have a tunic that matches the slip; another that contrasts in colour; a third in plaid that makes use of the same shade as the slip, and yet another with embroideries, linking skirt to tunic by fabric or embroidery, either one. It is quite useless to consider a suit of skirt and coat without visualizing the possibility of the blouses that may complement it and change it into a complete costume.

Because of its general becomingness, length is the prevailing characteristic of the tunic. It really should reach below the knee, and it will be even smarter if it reaches almost to the edge of the hem. In general, the straight, silhouette is more becoming than the flared one, but at times the flares are so subtle that they do not, appreciably, detact from the general appearance of slenderness. There is a choice between belts and the beltless line, but the latter is the smarter, if one finds it becoming. Many do not, and it should be a question in one's mind until the yes or the no of the matter is proven.

The neckline is, of course, varied, but the V-neck is smart, especially when trimmed with tiny revers of lace or the fabric; there are square necks; and the round and hateur line have their following. Georgette, crepe de chine, satin, the newer ribbed silks and velvet, as well as inany novelty materials are featured in the smartest tunics, and trimmings range from appliques and embroideries through to bandings of the material of which the tunic is made. Buttons, headings and braiding are all popular, and at times one meets a model that has no trimming but the fabric itself. Such a tunic is pictured, although it really makes use of two fabrics, or, more specifically, two colours, black and white. Extremely clever this lace affair, with its V-neck that shows satin bound revers of the material; undersleeves that have the appearance of cuffs; white lace set in

under the founce, and a wee collar of the white. The shoulder is kimono and there is a smart little tie belt, in the back, if you please.

Whorever there is a demand, there one will find supply. That is the raison d'etre of the hip-length blouse, which is not nearly as new or as smart as the tunic. There blouses are nearly all gathered into a hip band, though some models maintain their straightness to the end. Only a slight fullness at the hips marks the joining of blouse to band in the model pictured, a very smart model indced, that has its novelty fabric smartened appreciably by the band of lace insertion down the front; the frills of Val. at neckline and sleeve edge; and the whimsical rosette on the waist band. It would seem that fashion interest is bound to centre on the blouse its coming season; for already the tunic is an accepted fashion fact in the costume, and the tunic is, in its original form, a blouse.

headline: STRICTLY BUSINESS.
text:
SOVIET REQUESTS TURNED DOWN

In the House of Commons, Ltd. Col. W. Guinness, Under Secretary of the Treasury, in the course of replies, stated that applications by the Soviet trading organisations Arcos and Centro soyus in Britain for guarantees of £2,000,000. and £100,000, respectively; under the Trade Facilities Act last June were turned down purely on their business merits. He added it was the Government's policy to refuse credit facilities to the Soviet or its agents, until they had restored their creditors' confidence. If as asserted the Soviet's difficulties were complicated by the fact that it had to pay 24 per cent. on the money market this credit be attributed to the Soviet's financial record of lack of security.

headline: FOE OF BOLSHEVISM. / EORIS SAVINKOFF COMMITTS SUICIDE.
text:
Boris Savinkoff has committed suicide in prison.

A few hours previously he wrote to M. Djerjinsky, head of the Police, bagging for his liberation. He received a hopeless answer and threw himself from the fifth-floor window, being killed instantly.

[Foris Savinkoff was a well-known anti-Bolshevik who was alleged to be the leading spirit of the most counter-revolutionary plots, in recent years, operating outside Russia.] He was arrested on Russian territory on August 20. He was tried and sentenced to death, but recommended to energy in consequence of a remarkable statement, in which he said that he considered all his counter-revolutionary activities were mistaken. He recognised the justice of the revolution and acknowledged that he was guilty of the charges brought against him, adding: I recognise the power of the Soviet and say, 'He who loves the Russian nation must recognise the Soviet power.' I do not ask for pity.'

headline: TCHEHOV'S NOVEL
text:
MALTREATED NEWSPAPER SERIAL

The first and only novel by Anton Tchehov, hitherto unknown, "The Tragedy during the Hunt," has just been issued by the Paul Zsolnay Verlag in a German translation. Tchehov wrote the story in his twenty-fourth year. Originally it appeared in 1884 and 1885 in a little Moscow journal, but it treated the work badly leaving, for instance a month's interval between one instalment and the next. Many alterations were also demanded, to which Tchehov would not agree, and finally be eliminated whole chapters. Later he lost all interest in the technique of "novel-writing" in general, and with the exception of his plays devoted himself entirely to the writing of the short story. Curiously enough, Tchehov never mentioned his novel in his numerous letters or in conversation.

headline: KIDNAPPING CASE
text:
The sequel to the alleged kid- napping of Mr. Harry Pollitt, secretary of the Communist or- ganisation known as the National Minority Movement, was heard at Liverpool. Assizes before Mr. Justice Fraser. Five local men, William P. Cochrane, 30, garage proprietor; George F. McGachen, 30, cotton salesman; James B. Owen, 30, commercial traveller; James H. Browner, 35, tailor; and John H. Rowlandson, 26, commercial traveller, were charged with con- spiring to assault and unlawfully imprison. Pollitt.

Mr. A. E. Griffith, who prosecuted, said that Mr. Pollitt, a boilermaker by trade and a trade union speaker, professing Communist beliefs and opinions, was to have addressed a meeting in Liverpool on Sunday, March 15. On the Saturday he was met at Edgehill Station, Liverpool, put into a motor care, and taken to the Liver Hotel, Rhyddalog, a village on the Flintshire moors.

Mr. Pollitt stated that at Edge-hill Station Rowlandson and Owen entered the railway compartment where he was and asked him to address a meeting at Marnaduke-street at the Communistist headquarters. He refused, but was pulled out of the train.

He was, he said, bustled through the barrier into a waiting motorcar. He made no protest at the hotel. He was asked what his financial loss had been, and he replied that he had suffered none. He did not accept any payment.

headline: FAME AND ADVERTISEMENT.
text:
Cross-examined by Sir Henry Curtis Bennett, K.C. (defending), Mr. Pollitt said he was a Communist speaker and had been convicted in 1921 for making alleged seritious speeches.

Sir Henry: "In fact, I might describe you as the famous Mr. Politt -Yes, and I am only quite young."

Do you find advertisement is something which is apt to make you become famous?—No. I find one becomes famous and then gets advertisement.

When Mr. Pollitt described how he was pushed into the motor-car with five other men and said one of them sat on his knee, Sir Henry Curtis Bennett asked: "In an ordinary Ford car, with six persons, somebody had to sit on somebody's knee?" "Yes," replied Mr. Pollitt, "but I don't see why it should have been my knee."

How did you recognise that these gentlemen were not comrades directly they came into the compartment at Edgehill?—First, because I had a definite understanding with my comrades to meet me at Lime street; and, second, my comrades never meet me dressed as hooligans with their caps down over their eyes, mufflers on, and their coat collars turned up. (Laughier.)

Regarding a bottle of mustard oil with which Mr. Pollitt's chest was rubbed at the inn because he had a cough, Sir Henry asked: "Was it famous because some of it got on your chest?"

Mr. Pollitt: Rowlandson rubbed my chest with it—and did it very well.

headline: FALSE NAMES. / SAILORS WHO CREATED TROUBLE.
text:
Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, three "American seamen were charged on two counts of evading payment of tramway fare and obstruction.

There was some delay in the accused being brought into Court after they had been removed this morning from the custody of the Police by an escort from the U.S.S. Sacramento as it was found that they had given false names and stated that they belonged to the U.S.S. Pampanga. Their proper names were Jeff Cantrill, Harry A. Thorne and Irvine Coulter, all of the U.S.S. Helena. A traffic officer of the Tramway Company giving evidence stated that he first saw the three accused in a car near the Ming Yuen gardens. They refused to pay the fare when called upon and gave him and the conductors considerable trouble, as well as causing inconvenience to the passengers by changing cars at Causeway Bay and again at Tin Lok Lane. Witness stated that at Bowrington bridge the third accused threatened to strike him. Witness and a Chinese constable kept up with the men after they had alighted near the bridge, and the latter went ahead later and laid information at No. 2 Police Station which resulted in the accused being taken into custody when they reached that point.

The third accused denied that he threatened to assault witness. Asked by His Worship why they gave false names, all three said that they did it in order to hide their movements from the ship. His Worship said that the evidence he had taken was sufficient to prove their guilt and fined each of the accused $10 and $25 on the two counts respectively.

headline: MYSTIFIED SCIENTISTS. / A MAN WITH SIX SENSES.
text:
一

What is the strange occult power possessed by Louis Kahn, the "Man with the Sixth Sense"?

His case is inexplicable to the foremost French scientists, and a former French Premier. Academicians, High Court judges, and detectives have been mystified by a display of his uncanny power. He is able to read a letter written by another person without seeing or touching it.

Kahn, who is 53 and a German who disarows German nationality, has just demonstrated his powers before an audience including M. Louis Barthou, a French ex-Premier; M. Loucheur, a former Cabinet Minister; and M. Morain, the Prefect of Police.

There were twelve persons in all present and each wrote in an adjoining room a phrase on a slip of paper which was folded eight times and kept in the closed hand.

He left the room while the ships were exchanged, and on returning said: "Though you have been exchanging your slips each one finally came back to its author." This was correct.

Then he told those present what they had written.

With the exception of an error in one word, which did not alter the sense of the phrase, Kahn faithfully rendered the contents of the twelve slips.

Striking proof of his telepathic powers was shown when, at M. Barthou's suggestion, a woman in the company wrote on her slip of paper a declaration of affection for a well known politician.

Madame, please burn your slip, far away from me so that I cannot possibly see it," said Kahn, and when the woman had done so, he pointed to M. Barthou, remarking: "The gentleman there dictated the phrase to you, so he will be able to certify if I renter it correctly." And, amid laughter, he read word for word what the woman had written.

headline: STOP PRESS. / SHANGHAI RIOTING.
text:
The students here held a meeting yesterday afternoon in the Central Park to discuss the Shanghai affair.

The speakers declared that the affair was a national one affecting the whole of the Chinese people.

Further meetings were arranged for to-day at which it is expected resolutions will be passed demanding the restoration of the foreign concessions, the abolition of extra-territoriality and the Mixed Court in Shanghai, also of the foreign police stations in Shanghai, and the punishment of the police who shot the students.

headline: Strike Begins.
text:
Prisoners were taken to the Mixed Court this morning heavily escorted. The route was guarded by Volunteers and police. There were no disturbances.

It was a subdued looking group of 45 rioters who appeared before the Chinese magistrate and American assessor.

Evidence of arrest was given and the case remanded. Light bail was accepted.

There were a few unimportant isturbances in the outlying districts this morning, including the mobbing of a Japanese constable whom the rioters threw into a creek before assistance arrived.

The strike is taking denite form insomuch as the fresh food markets did not open to-day.

Moscow, June 6.—The Kieff military tribunal has concluded the trial of the members of the anti-Soviet organization, “Russia for Russians” headed by the ex-Tsarist General Belavin, who is accused of military espionage on behalf of Poland. Belavin Ivanoff who was an official on the staff of the Ukrainian Red Army, and the woman intermediary Nina Krzeczkovska are sentenced to death. Twelve are variously imprisoned and one acquitted. Belavin allegedly described himself as the ideological enemy of the Soviet and admitted the charge.—Reuter. BEST PORTLAND

headline: ' INVISIDLE EMMARE."
text:
The representatives of the "Invisible Empire" have already poured upon me the vials of their wrath. They have often threatened me with death; they have used every method of boycott, intimidation and character assassination; all because I realised the evils of secret and masked order that sought to dictate men's religious beliefs and to direct the political and moral conduct of those not identified with what they brazenly called an empire. That was what they organised in a free Republic—an empire with a throne, a kingdom with an emperor, a secret power dictating to an irony of obedient subjects and inflicting punishment upon those who dared to disobey its midnates, whether inside or outside the Order.

It was started by one William J. Simmons, a visionary, who was imbued with harmless ideas. He wanted a great brotherhood of white men who could resist the encroachments of the foreign element, and would purify and extol the race, especially the natives of the country. He forgot that America is new that all our ancestors were from foreign shores, only a century or so removed and that it was these men who had made the United States possible and powerful. He forgot that freedom of religion is part of our constitutional guarantee and that racial hatred could not be maintained in a country which owed its very existence to immigration. His idea made little progress until one Clarke seized upon it for a "get-rich quick," campaign. It was Clarke and his coterie of high-powered salesmen who perfected the organisation that made Atlanta, Georgia, its headquarters, and from that point established various realms, appointing men to positions of supposed honour, giving them a certain territory in which to get money for the Order and always paying liberal commissions.

headline: CANTON FIGHTING.
text:
SHOTS FIRED AT LOCAL STEAMERS

BLOCKADE ATTEMPT?

ELEVEN FOREIGN WARSHIPS AT CANTON.

"Usual heavy machine gun and rifle fire in the early hours of the morning—no big engagement"—these and similar messages are all that Hongkong firms with interests in Canton have received this morning. The ferry between the Oriental Hotel (West Bund) and Honam is no longer in operation but the ferry between Shameen Bund and Honam is carrying on a limited service. Special police from the European offices are on duty on Shameen Apparently, the condition of stalemate continues in Canton city. Troops stationed on the opposite banks of the Canton River are remaining under cover and taking pot-shots at their adversaries when opportunities present themselves. Of most concern to Hongkong is the firing on river steamers in Chinese territory. In the early hours of yesterday morning when the Canton-bound vessels were passing Whampoa, fire was opened at them from the shore. All the steamers successfully ran the gauntlet but a "boy" on the Sal On was wounded. He was brought back to hospital in Hongkong. The Sai On and Paul Beau bear bullet marks and one shot went through the Kwangsi's galleys.

The firing is from territory in the hands of the Cantonese. The Cantonese are trying to keep up a blockade and it is believed that they wish to prevent shipping from going to Canton or, at least, to search the vessels for so-called contraband and possible recruits for the non-Cantonese holding the city.

headline: Sniping Danger.
text:
Except for the boom of a few heavy guns in the distance, the eastern suburb and Tungshan appear to be quiet at present.

Fighting continues along the Bund and extends all the way to Shameen; also further up the River at Shek Wai Tong.

Practically all the women and children (foreign?) have moved from Tungshan.

The Railway station at Tai Sha-tau remains vacant. A few soldiers are there but a strong camp is on Taishatau island which faces Honam and the Cement Works.

Both sides are still sniping away across the River.

headline: Russian Officers.
text:
Neither side has yet ventured on a big offensive to land in enemy territory and firing from machine-guns, mausers and rifles continues practically day and night.

The Cantonese reinforcements at Shek Wai Tong have made “feelers” to test the strength of the Yunnanese outpost at Wongsha but are remaining under cover.

Other reinforcements, comprising mostly “Cadet” detachments under Russian officers, have arrived at Honam and it is believed that as soon as conditions are favourable, the Reds will try to cross the River. On the Canton side the Yunnanese remain on the quivive.

Now that the withdrawal from exposed points have been completed, the Yunnanese hold a small area comprising the city on the North side of the River, the heights overlooking the approaches and the eastern and western lines of communication. They have the advantage of being able to move their troops from side to side, rapidly and without interference. However, they are not besieged as they have ample supplies.

Hongkong's food supply is only slightly affected by the Canton fighting and the Shanghai trouble.

As very little fresh-water fish and Canton vegetables can be sent down, prices for these commodities have gone up. A portion of Hongkong's egg imports is from Shenzhou.

headline: JUDGE AND A WOMAN'S LANGUAGE. / HOTEL SCENE.
text:
Miss Enid Violet Annie Orrell-Kelly, daughter of an officer (now dead) of the 7th Hussars, claimed damages for alleged assault and false imprisonment from Mrs. Mary Ellen Thurby, pronietress of the Gore Hotel, South Kensington.

Mr. Croom-Johnson, for Miss Orrell-Kelly, said his client, who was 24, had lived at the Gore Hotel with her mother for some time before Mrs. Thurby purchased it.

In August 1924 they went on a round of visits, locking their furniture in the sitting-room and paying £3 3s. a week during their absence.

When, in passing through London, they called at the hotel Mrs. Thurby. Intimated that Mrs. Orrell Kelly would have to pay £5.5a. in future for the room. A notice to quit was also handed to Mrs. Orrell-Kelly, who, on completing the visits, decided to accept the notice. She made arrangements for their goods to be removed, but Mrs. Thurby declined to allow the workmen to remove a sofa before some account was paid.

Miss Orrell-Kelly went down-stairs to make arrangements for a man to remove their electreliter, but found the front door locked and the key missing. The hall porter told her he had instructions to keep it locked.

Mrs. Thurby told her that she was not to be allowed to leave the hotel until the account was settled.

Miss Orrell Kelly said that if they had not let out she would force her way out and picked up the ylators' book and hurled it through the glass panel of the front door. She then took a chair and was about to get out through the hole she had made, but Mrs Thurby's son and the hall-porter forcibly held her. Ultimately however, she got out. At that moment her mother was upstairs writing out the cheque for the account.

Mrs. Thurby had declined to apologise and was actually counter-claiming for the cost of repairing the broken glass panel.

Miss Orrell-Kelly gave evidence and in cross-examination denied telling the hall-porter that if he did not give her the——key she would give him a—thrashing, but in reply to Mr. Justice Rowlatt she admitted adding the word when she described the affair as an insult.

Mr. Howard (for Mrs. Thurby): When you went to Mrs. Thurby did you threaten to smash her face in?—Quite probably. Didn't you lift your hand as if to strike her?—I don't remember it.

Did you say: "If I cannot smash your—face I'll smash your—house"?—I certainly don't think so. I should have some difficulty in smashing up the house.

Did you say when your mother asked you to give Mrs. Thurby the cheque: "I'll see Mrs. Thurby in—first?"—No.

Miss Orrell Kelly admitted that by that time she was madly enraged.

Miss Orrell-Kelly said she did not know there was another exit which she could have used.

Mrs. Thurby said she asked Mrs. Orrell-Kelly for the cheque because she had lost a good deal of money through people going away. She heard Miss Orrell-Kelly told the hall porter she would give him a—good hiding if he didn't give her the—key. Afterwards she threatened to smash her—face in. It cost £155 to repair the panel.

The hall porter, to reply to Mr. Justice Rowlatt, said he had instructions to lock the door against the furniture and not against persons, but Miss Orrell-Kelly only asked for the key. She didn't ask to go out. When Miss Orrell-Kelly climbed through the broken panel she rushed back again into the house by the door. (Laughter.) Mr. Justice Rowlatt, giving judgment, said Miss Orrell-Kelly, had been using language which a gentleman did not use generally and which a lady should never use. She was wholly wrong from the moment when she used threats, violence, and heat. Otherwise she might have been able to claim heavy damages. As it was he could give her no more than 40s. On the counterclaim Mrs. Thurlby was entitled to the cost of repairing the panel. Mr. Justice Rowlatt was told that 40s had been paid into court, and he informed Miss Orrell-Kelly's counsel that he would be able to take a out of court. Miss Orrell-Kelly would have costed no to the date of payment in. Thurlby would have the costs subsequently incurred. headline: GEORGE III AND A PETITIONER.
text:
No higher authority than Sir Edward Trump, who was Permanent Under-Secretary of State in the Home Office from 1908 to 1922, could have been found to write, for the first time, an account of the history, during, and organisation of the Home Office.

The duties of the Home Secretary are very various.

The Home Secretary is in the position, as it were, of a residuary gate: all that is not assigned by law or established custom to some other Minister falls to him.

All addresses to the King by public bodies are first submitted to the Home Office and are examined to see that they are a proper order. The relies to these addresses are drafted in the Home Office, sometimes with a previous indication from the King as to what he desires to say, and the drafts are always submitted personally to his Majesty and not infrequently altered by him.

Petitions to the King pass through the Home Office. The following account of what happened to a high-born petitioner amusing:

In 1774 the impoverished Duke of St. Albans presented a petition asking for a pension adequate to his rank. The usual form of negative reply to a petition is that "The Secretary of State regrets that he has been unable to advise his Majesty to issue any commands," but in this case there is a refreshing variation from the usual terms. The secretary of the state wrote: "I have obeyed your grace's

commands by presenting your memorial to the King. His Majesty George III] put it in his pocket without expressing His Pleasure one way or the other on the occasion.

Many formalities and ceremonies attend the appointment of a modern bishop.

They stand in striking contrast to the simplicity of the ancient method of handing over the pastoral staff and ring to the new bishop, and even to the Secretary of State's own appointment, which is completed in five seconds by the Kiug's placing three seals in his hands.

Such questions as the use of troops in civil disturbances, the herogative of mercy, the administration of justice, police organisation, prisons, and so forth are authoritatively dealt with.

The Criminal Lunatic Asylum at Broadnoor "is under the direct control and administration of the Home Office aided by a local board of supervision"

The Superintendent of Broad- noor occupits, perhaps, the most dangerous post in the Civil Service. Every lunatic believes the Superi- dent to be responsible for his continued detention, and within the last 40 years two have received permanent injuries from attacks by inmates who appeared to have recovered their sanity, and two have retired worn out with the inxieties of their position.

The power to put first offenders on probation is one which appears not yet to be fully made use of. If in Kent 5½ per cent. of cases tried summarily are put on probation, why should Bedfordshire and Cambridgeshire put on probation less than one fifth per cent. and Monmouthshire none? It 75 is the proper proportion for Birkenhead why is it only 18 in Liverpool? The staff of the Home Office is 76 This figure does not include to charwomen."

headline: ACTRESS
text:
COMING ATTRACTION

How many foreigners living in the Far East have ever taken the trouble, on have even had the opportunity, to make the acquaintance of the Chinese theatre and Chinese acting?

Amongst those of the more venturesome sort who have penetrated into Chinese localities, the impression has generally been a confused mixture of noise, glare and discomfort.

Now we in Hongkong are to have opportunity to-morrow week of seeing, under comfortable conditions, the one actress in China who, by her personality and wonderful command over her art, can take her place on the same plane as the famous Mei Lan-fang.

Miss Pik Wen-ha is coming to the Theatre Royal in response to numerous requests from those who have paid a visit to the Taiping Theatre and have been impressed by her wonderful acting. Having come under the spell of her charm themselves, they wish others of the foreign community, who do not care to go to West Point and sit through the long hours of a complete Chinese play to have the opportunity of seeing for themselves just so much of the wonderful acting of this charming actress as will give them an insight into a world undreamed of and unexplored by the great majority of foreigners in the Far East.

The usual Chinese play is a matter of hours, and often days. What Miss Pik Wen-ha is going to do is to select scenes from three of her most famous plays, representing tragedy and farce, finishing up with a scene from a comedy which introduces a famous dance composed for the beautiful Yang Kuei-fei, the favourite concubine of the Tang Ming Emperor, of the Tong Dynasty.

These scenes will take about thirty minutes each, and in between, in the 15 minute intervals, the audience will have another surprise. We all have an idea that we know what Chinese music is—a mixture of discordant and ear-splitting noises accompanied by the banging of drums and the beating of cymbals. On this occasion we shall be introduced to a form of Chinese music that, except to those foreigners who are privileged to be admitted to the real Chinese life, is absolutely unknown to us. A really wonderful orchestra of stringed instruments, played by leading Chinese amateurs, will give a selection of old and most interesting Chinese music. This in itself makes the performance one that will stand (Reuter's Service.)

— Malbourne, Nov. 14.

A record poll is assured at to-day's election owing to the compulsory voting.

Mr. S. M. Bruce's final appeal to the electors, particularly the women, declares:

"The paramount issue is the maintenance of the supremacy of constitutional government."

Though bitter class-feeling has been aroused the campaign has generally been very orderly.

The main points of Mr. Bruce's platform are a promise of national insurance legislation, insistence on secret ballots in trade unions before a strike is decided upon; a proposal to subsidize road construction in order to facilitate the transport of farm produce, and a proposal that Parliament vote twenty millions to build cottage homes for city workers.

The Labour Party devoted its energies to denouncing the Red menace as an election bogey, declaring the constitutional Labour Party is more qualified to deal with extremists than the reactionaries.

Both sides especially appeal to the hitherto unpolled non-Party electors, the Ministerialists asking for a mandate to deal with alleged dangerous elements in the community and the Labourites warning the electors not to be influenced by side issues.
