This Company is being formed for the purpose of taking over the lucrative business hitherto carried on by various private concerns with their head offices on Mount Hewitt. In Bias Bay.

All the concerns which are being taken over have recently been doing a most lucrative business. It is estimated that the expenses of the new Company will be extremely low, and the profits extremely high. Apart from allowances to the dependants of any of the Company's employees who may fall into the hands of the Shanghai Mixed Courts, no salaries are payable, the employees all being perfectly satisfied to work upon a commission basis. The amalgamation of the present private enterprises will eliminate overlapping, and the waste caused by rival institutions covering the same ground (or water). With the recent increase in business, and the proposed amalgamation, it is reasonable to expect enormous expansion in the future. The travelling population (foreigners and Chinese) is constantly increasing, as also is the movement of bullion and other valuables by sea, and no fulling-off is to be expected while the Government Railways remain in the hands of the Militarists.

The services of the most experienced of the Bias Bay Chiefs have been engaged as Managing Director, and the Board will include a number of Bolshevik agitators, Kuomintang extremists, and Tuchuns, all of whom can be relied upon to do their utmost to further the objects of the new Company. The books of the two principal private companies for the past three months, show that the total turnover amounted to $110,000 in cash, in addition to large quantities of valuables, including silks, furs, watches, jewellery, etc. These form the proceeds of the seizures of the ships "Tungchow," and "Jade." After making liberal provision for commission for the Company's employees, and for the reserve fund for the pensioning of orphans and widows of deceased pirates (whether they meet with a violent death, or succumb from natural causes) it is estimated that these two venturer alone produced a net profit of $50,000. The Directors are confident that even more lucrative business can be done in the near future, and that the economies affected by the amalgamation of competing interests will produce an even higher percentage of profit on every venture. The assets of the new Company consist of goodwill, which is valued at $10,000; from the ammunition stocks ($10,000); opium store, $9,000; one Chinese gunboat book value $17,500; and Pension Fund $3,500.

In addition to the Board of Directors an Advisory Committee has been formed, which will include Comrade Borodin (who is an expert on the subject of China's Sovereign Rights); a Prominent Missionary (yet to be selected) who is convinced that everything that China does is right, and everything that any foreigner does is wrong; the Chairman of the local Students' Union through whom arrangements can be made for the disposal of British or Japanese goods which might otherwise be boycotted; and a Brazilian Chinese, who will manage the Company's Bias Bay Casino.

In addition to piracy, ordinary and extraordinary, the Company will as opportunity offers, engage in other potentially lucrative business. It intends, for instance, to promote a system of anti-piracy insurance under which payment of a substantial fee will render the persons or property insured immune from search or seizure. Holders of these special Bias Bay policies, even if they find themselves on a pirated vessel, will be treated with every possible consideration. It is confidently expected that Foreign and Chinese Banks will avail themselves of these policies for the protection of shipments of bullion.

The Company also believes that there is lucrative business to be done in kidnapping and in the sale of arms and opium.

Part of the new Capital will be used to erect a commodious Hostel for the accommodation of kidnapped passengers, equipped with a modern crematorium and other conveniences.

Being incorporated in Hongkong the Company comes under British protection, and will have nothing to fear from the British Navy.

Shareholders will receive a monthly list of seizures by the Company's employees together with a price-list of articles for sale, which will be marked down to far below their market value. Registered shareholders will perpetually enjoy all the immunities in respect both of their persons and properties, which are granted under the Bias Bay Insurance scheme. The Company has obtained the services of a fuel expert, who will report from time to time upon the suitability of various kinds of cargo as a substitute for coal, in the event of the bunkers running low.

The following documents may be inspected in the original, at the Company's temporary Head Office:

Further information regarding the Company may be obtained, and certified copies of the above documents may be seen, on application to our local representative, Mr. Talkoo F. "The Seillonian" is the first publication to be produced in the Scilly Isles.

Tauenshire County Educate Committee is to assist in organising village concerts.

Three cyclists involved in a collision in Islington were named Lark, Linnett and Sparrow.

Birthrate of Salcombe, Devon, which is half the death rate, is said to be the lowest in the world.

A milliards team of the more skillful Portuguese's exponents of the Colony left for Shanghai in connection with the can interport tournament today.

Competitors blazing away in the revolver "pool" at the Hongkong Rifle League's meeting. Kowloon City, last Saturday and Sunday.

It is interesting to learn that even clean play are paying, and have paid, in London. "Saint Jean," the last weeks of which have been announced, has celebrated its anniversary. It has been seen by half a million people, and has made as much profit as, if not more than any other production in London including the salicious ones.

The idea of having a competition between dogs to decide on the best performer of tricks must be somewhat of a novelty for a Dog Show. It is understood that the committee of the Shanghai Dog Show to be held on the Bund on May 16, contend that a dog in amateur ownership who can do clever tricks must be particularly well trained and cared for and they want to encourage owners of that type. Post entries will be accepted, only from dogs on exhibition at the Show. An Alsatian who dances the Highland Fling and provides her music simultaneously is to be a challenger.

Two cases of small-pox (Chinese) were notified for the 24 hours ended Thursday last.

Electricity plays an important part in what is claimed to be the world's largest clock. This is the new clock of a manufacturing firm which takes the place of one that for many years called attention to their Jersey City factory. The new clock, wound by a quarter horse-power motor, has a dial diameter of 50ft. The minute hand is 38ft. 3in. long, and the hour hand measures 27ft. 6in., the hands weighing together 3,825lbs. More than 200 lamps placed at regular distances around the hands make it as easy to tell the time by night us by day.

The new statistics of the advance of the foreign missionary enterprise in the world since 1900 are very interesting and make for great hopefulness. They are to be found in the World Missionary Atlas, just about to be published, a stupendous compilation of data, of Protestant missions, says the "Western Christian Advocat." In 1860 the total annual income of all Protestant missionary societies was $4,000,000. In 1900, $20,000,000; in 1923, $70,000,000. Of this later figure, i. 1923 the United States contributed $45,000,000. In 1900 the number of whites men and women missionaries was 15,000. In 1923 it was 29,000. The converts have increased from 1,235,000 in 1900 to 3,640,000 in 1923. The British Isles undoubtedly raised the larger portion of the 45,000,000 left from the American total.

At a meeting of the C.M.S. General Committee in London, a letter was read from Dr. Henslett, Bishop of South Tokyo. In it he said: "It is now generally acknowledged that Christianity in Japan has taken its place as one of the permanent religions of the country. It must be considered in the future as a native force. Whilst on a visit to Kyoto last afternoon, the Empress expressed a desire to visit three religious institutions. She therefore paid three arranged visits to a Buddhist Temple, a Shinto Shrine, and a Christian School. At the school (the famous Doshishu) her Majesty gave audience to the faculty. Then the whole body of students assembled in the School Chapel, the Empress taking her place on the rostrum. The students sang the National Anthem and a hymn. Then the Principal ascended the rostrum and while her Majesty stood with bowed head, he offered a prayer.

Devotees of the hair bobbing fashion now are complaining of single, headache. This is nothing but a form of neuralgia, medical men say caused by sudden removal of hair from the tender hair of the neck, which is thus exposed to the blustery March winds. Hats which fit close and very low at the back are said to be an effective safeguard. The death of W. E. Henley's widow at the age of 71, went practically unfoticed in the London papers. The closing years of the lady, a Scot, were spent in Glasgow, but to the last she had a London house, given to her husband by Lord Northelife. Henley never wrote for any of the periodicals of the newspaper peer, but Northelife had a profound admiration for the man and his work. Mr. Maxwell H. Hamilton, American Vice-Consul at Canton, who is at present on a mission to Kuingchow, Hainan, in connection with the killing of an American missionary there last year; has been promoted to Shanghai, where he will serve as Junior Assessor of the Mixed Court under nomination of the American Legation, says the "Canton Gazette." Consul Hamilton was appointed Student Interpreter in China on May 20, 1920; and has served as Vice-Consul and Interpreter at Canton since October 9, 1922. He was promoted to be Consul in July, 1924. He is at present on special duty from the Canton Consulate-General, but as soon as the work in hand has been concluded he will return to Canton and thence proceed to Shanghai, where he will take up the duties of Junior Assessor at the Mixed Court. He is regarded by the Service as one of the very ablest young men in the Interpreter Corps. Reuter cables that Viscount Milner's condition gives rise to grave anxiety.

headline: NOTICE / THE HONGKONG & WHAMPOA DOCK CO.,LTD.
text:
NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that an Extraordinary General Meeting of the above Company will be held at the Registered Office of the Company, Queen's Building, Victoria, Hongkong, on MONDAY, the 18th day of May, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon, when the subjoined Resolutions will be proposed as Extraordinary Resolutions, viz.:—

(1) That the Articles of Association of the Company be altered in manner following that is to say by the deletion of Article 17 and by the substitution therefor of the following Article, name-ly:—

"17. So long as the issued 'capital of the Company' shall not exceed $6,000,000," no member shall be entitled "to be registered as the "holder of more than 8,000 "shares of the Company." Should the issued capital of "the Company be increased "beyond $6,000,000 the "number of shares in respect of which a member "shall be entitled to be "registered shall be increased "ed proportionately, but no "member shall be entitled "to be registered in respect of a fraction of a share."

(2) That the authorised Capital of the Company (which is now $3,000,000 consisting of 60,000 shares of the nominal value of $50 each the whole of which have been issued) be increased to $10,000,000 by the creation of 140,000 additional shares of the nominal value of $50 each ranking (subject as hereinafter mentioned) for dividend and in all other respects pari passu with the shares constituting the Company's present issued Capital.

(3) That 60,000 of the said 140,000 new shares be offered in the first instance (in the proportion of one new share for every old share held by them respectively) to the members of the Company who on the 10th day of June, 1925, are registered in the Company's Share Register as the holders of the said 60,000 old shares at a premium of $10 per share.

(4) That the aforesaid offer be made to members by notice specifying the number of new shares to which a member is entitled. That a member whose registered address is situate in the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of October, 1925, and such member or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, will be deemed to have declined. That a member whose registered address is situate outside the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or

before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of July, 1925, until the date of receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of December, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of October, 1925, until the date of actual receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and such member outside the Far East or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest as aforesaid will be deemed to have declined. The Directors shall have the right to reject any nominee.

(5) That such of the said 60,000 new shares as shall be accepted by members both in and outside the Far East shall vis-a-vis the said 60,000 old shares rank for dividend as from the 15th day of July, 1925, to the extent of one half of the nominal value of such new shares and as from the 15th day of October, 1925, equally with the said 60,000 old shares.

(6) That any of the said 60,000 new shares which shall not be taken up by the Company's shareholders in manner aforesaid and the remaining 80,000 unissued new shares may be issued and disposed of in such manner at such time or times and upon such terms as to ranking for dividend and otherwise as the Company's Directors shall in their absolute discretion think fit.

AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN that a further Extraordinary General Meeting of the Company will be held at its Registered Office aforesaid on TUESDAY, the 2nd day of June, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon for the purpose of receiving a Report of the proceedings at the above mentioned meeting and confirming, if thought fit, as Special Resolutions the above mentioned Resolutions.

The Transfer Books of the Company will be closed from WEDNESDAY, the 10th day of June, 1925, to WEDNESDAY, the 17th Day of June, 1925 (both days inclusive) during which period no transfer of shares can be registered.

Dated the 4th day of May, 1925. B) Order of the Board of Directors, R. M. DYER, Chief Manager.

By way of celebrating the recent consummation of the treaty between Russia and Japan, the Shochiku Theatrical Company in Japan has invited a number of Russian musicians who, being assisted by the Japanese musicians, will give a series of concerts at leading Japanese cities. These Russian musicians have been selected among the members of the Moscow Marynsky Theatre Orchestra, the Leningrad Symphony Orchestra, and the Kieff Conservatory. Their musical tour was commenced in Tokyo, where several successful concerts were given last month.

If Shaw can have his season in Paris, why not Shakespeare? English players headed by Mr. Ben Greet have opened a Paris theatre and it will be interesting to see whether Shakespeare proves to be as attractive for the Paris public as was Shaw. The repertory is a long one, and it is not only English-speaking residents who welcome the opportunity of hearing their tongue spoken on the stage, but the students of the Paris colleges and schools will frequently be in attendance. Special arrangements have been made through Dr. Appel, the rector of the university, with the Shakespearean Players for the admission of those French boys and girls who are learning English. Thus the Shakespeare season will have an educational as well as an entertaining value.

It Miss Jewell Carmen, moving picture actress, can prove she was born in 1897, she may collect $44,500 for which she is suing two movie companies. Miss Carmen broke a contract and she claims they tied up her services so that she lost a $450-a-week contract. She says the contract was illegal because she was under twenty-one when she sighed it.

Mr. Winston Churchill, Chancellor of the Exchequer, announced Great Britain would return to the gold standard immediately. Samuel Untermyer, noted lawyer, in speech, assigned Professor Philip Marshall Brown of Princeton University, for his attack on the Jews as lacking patriotism. Senator Moses, president pro tem of the Senate, declared Vice-President Dawes would get no aid from him in his campaign to change rules of the Senate. Brigadier-General James F. Fechst, who succeeded Col. Mitchell as Chief of America's Air Service stated that the air forces should eventually be separated from army and navy control.

headline: LOCAL AND GENERAL
text:
The members of the "Our Cabaret" Company were again in fine form last night and submitted another change of programme to the immense liking of the audience. The Company complete their Hongkong season this evening with a complete change of programme and commence a short season to-morrow at the Star Theatre, Kowloon.

The remarkable experience of suddenly losing his power of speech befell an Edinburgh man residing in the South Side of the city. I seems that he was reading a newspaper at home shortly after ten o'clock, when he suddenly became conscious of the fact that he could not utter a coherent word. On Sunday the man was able to say a few words, and hopes of his recovery were entertained. The only cause to which the man's misfortune can be attributed is an experience of shell-shock during the war, when, it seems he was thrown a considerable distance by the explosion of a shell.

Glasgow Town Council has decided by a large majority in favour of the demolition of the steeple along with St. Enoch's Church. During the discussion Treasurer Graham pointed out that it was in the interests of the city to take this step and deal with the congestion of traffic. They had no option, he said, but to clear the square and make it of some use to the citizens. Councillor Stark Broun argued that they had bought the church and the steeple at £36,000 simply for the purpose of getting rid of them. All the protests which were made now bought to have been raised at the time negotiations were taking place. It was not the Corporation who should be spoken of as vandals. It was the Church of Scotland, who for sordid gold sold the church and steeple. "The Teachings of Mohammed" will be the subject of this week's public meeting of the Hongkong Lodge. The Theosophical Society, 16, Queen's Road Central, on Wednesday June 3, at 5:45 p.m. The Public are invited.

A specimen of Depmeptera alivacea, a rare species of Sphingidae (Hawk Moth), was taken recently by Mr. G. F. C. Woodlett in a Sandakan bungalow. It has been presented to Mr. Preston Clark of Boston, Massachusetts, who is reputed to have the finest collection of Sphingidae in the world.

In view of the return of M. Callaux to office it is interesting to note that a short time ago he published a book entitled "Ou va la France"? Ou va l'Europe?"—a work which is a challenge to all thoughtful students of European politics. This book was translated into English and published by Messrs. T. Fisher Unwin, Ltd., under the title of "Whither France? Whither Europe."

There has been in Hankow recently the representative of a strong British firm, says the "C. C. Post," on the mission of ascertaining from the Municipal Councils whether they would sanction a scheme for supplying Hankow with a tramway service. The firm is prepared to face the whole expense of the undertaking. What sort of reply will be given there has not yet been time to learn.

American motorcar statistics are always interesting and an authority quoted in the "Literary Digest" (New York) treats them in a new way. California, it appears, in the matter of automobile density, stands in a "class by itself, having one vehicle for each three inhabitants. Next comes Iowa with 41, then Nevada 42, and Kansas, Nebraska and Oregon, 44 each. New England seems to lag far behind these wealthy Western States, Vermont being the nearest with 5.7, while there are some States in the South so impoverished that they can only muster one car to every ten inhabitants.

Sakhalin, the northern end of which has just been handed back to Russia by the Japanese, is as big as Scotland and has a population of about thirty thousand, mostly convicts or ex-convicts, and is also inhabited by bears, wolves, hairy Ainus, and pelagic seals. Its value is purely strategic, for though not uninhabitable, the climate is anything but Mediterranean. Doubtless the Soviet Government will restore its ancient fame as a convict settlement.

A special commissioner of the "Observer." in the course of a series of articles on "Scotland To-day," describing the "Glasgow Sunday," says: — The "Glasgow Sunday" was much as ever—a day when the stimulus of work was withdrawn and the combined weight of dreary architecture and negative morality—sat heavy upon the soul. "Glasgow is not a city to dream in, and when its industry imported the Irishman, who must have his dreaming-time, it took to itself a full cargo of social discord. A scheme of life based on "gear and grace" ("Let Glasgow flourish by, the preaching of the Word") could not assimilate a race touched to lighter, if not to finer issues. The Irish submission was a slow and sour one, mitigated by shebeening and its crude consolations. But there were others who could not fill the void of the Sabbath with gluttonous "diets of worship," and became the sullen prisoners of the inelastic code. Unction and ugliness turned many a mild and harmless bohemian into a social malcontent.

For the 24 hours ended Thursday, a clean bill of health was shown, there being no return on notifiable diseases.

A young Chinese gentleman is advertised for, who can devote some time to studying at the works in England, so as to be prepared to take up the representation of a large firm on his return to China.

A Bazaar and Fair are being held by St. Stephen's College, on June 19th and 20th, in the Great Hall and the grounds of the University, by kind permission of the Vice Chancellor. The object is to raise funds for the New Buildings which they hope to erect at Stanley. A feature of the Bazaar will be useful and ornamental articles from the Southern Seas and from various parts of China where St. Stephen's boys live. There will be tea and refreshments, and various indoor and outdoor amusements.

A public meeting of the C.M.S. was held on May 5 in the Royal Albert Hall. The Bishop of Chichester presided, and the great building was crowded. Rev. G.T. Manley, the secretary, presented a report in which the troubles in China were attributed to the spread of materialism and to Bolshevik influence. Bishop Hind, of Fukien, spoke of his 23 years' work in China. Since he first went to the country, he said, things had greatly changed. There were then hardly any causes for fear, but now hundreds of soldiers were met in all directions. The country was under military chiefs who were raising armies as fast as they could. They had to support a large army of idle men who lived mostly by pillage and looting. Many more men and women missionaries were required to help distracted China at the present moment. Miss A. M. Henty (Japan) also addressed the meeting.

Some sections of the city of Jerusalem ironically draped themselves in black flags on the arrival of the Earl of Balfour to dedicate a Jewish university there. He had been practically boycotted by the Aral natives, who resented his declination fostering the recolonization of the Holy City by the Jews. His residence at Damascus was stoned during a riot over the issue, and the military had to be called out to quell the disturbance.

The “Shanghai Mercury” has met the difficulties of the present position by cyclostyting its issues—an interesting feat.

The list of notifiable diseases for the 24 hours ended Wednesday shows one case of small-pox and three cases of cerebro-spinal fever—all Chinese.

The total output of the Kailan Mining Administration's mines for the week ending May 30, 1925, amounted to 75,121 tons, and the sales during the period to 81,468 tons.

Clubs in the Lawn Tennis Association are requested to send their representatives to a meeting to be held in the Cricket Club Pavilion on Thursday next at 5.30 p.m.

The local branch of the Netherlands Trading Society is in receipt of telegraphic advice from its Batavia office that the dividend for the year 1924 is declared at 7% (seven per cent.) for the Bank.

The latest issue of the "China Press"—suffering like other Shanghai papers from the effects of the strike—has the following:—As this edition of "The China Press" is being sent to press without being proofread, the reader is supposed to use his intelligence.

The Hongkong University Union Magazines says: — One hundred and ninety-two volumes of new books have just arrived from England amounting to the value of £66. These are up-to-date books, carefully selected, and cover a large range of subjects. They will be available in the Library soon. The Council wish to publicly thank Mr. B. G. Birch, formerly a tutor of English at the University, who has very kindly purchased these books for us at Bristol, and seen to their safe arrival at Hongkong.

Where and when did the rumour originate that the authorities will play an exhibition game of "hide and soek" in the City Hall? We are also asked to deny that the official and unofficial members of the Court will play at Tug-of-war during the Long Vac.

When, when asked by the professor about the smell of ozone, answered, "It has an ozone smell."

Is it true that our lady undergrads maintain that women should "attend to human beings instead of nursing puppy dogs?"

If roaming with young chicks does not pay

"I wasn't behaving in a disorderly manner, sir," said an offender at Govan Police Court. "I am a bird-man, and I am in the habit of making professional noises." Constable—"He was shouting and bawling, and gathered a crowd." The Bird-Man—"No, I was imitating a cuckoo."

Most of the commentators on the Royal Academy appear to have missed what is certainly the most fantastic picture in the show. Orpens' "Man and Beast" notwithstanding. It is entitled "Whither?" and depicts a scene in a churchyard. Into a grave, surrounded by sorrowing relatives, a coffin is being lowered, while, at the back of the clergyman, there appears the ghostly figure of a girl rising from the ground. Two children are playing near by, a loafter is leaning against a tombstone, and in the middle distance a football match is in progress. The trees in the churchyard—cypresses

and curious growths with guarded, leafless branches—add to the grimness of the picture, which, incidentally is contained in a black frame with a thin-silver line.

The Prime Minister has addressed the following message to the "Imp," the new journal of the Junior Imperial League, the first number of which has been published: Nothing in the political situation to-day is more encouraging than the zeal with which young men and women are devoting themselves by study and discussion for their responsibilities towards their country, their Empire, and the world at large.

Asked why he took the cath in the Jewish fashion (wearing his hat) a Bow County Court witness replied, "The last witness was sworn that way, and I thought I had to do the game.

The Rev. H. Hayes, addressing a Tee H meeting at Melbourne, said he had visited houses in the Melbourne industrial area where the off and filth flowed out of the doors. He was astounded that such deadly places existed in a new city. They were worse than London slums, and it was not surprising that boys became criminals in such surroundings.

Between Perth and Derby, Australia, two cities 1,500 miles apart, what is asserted to be the longest regular passenger air service in the world is operated by the Western Australia Airways Limited. There are six intermediate calling points, and a weekly schedule is maintained.

Miss W. J. Jack was a passenger from Sydney on the Arafura which arrived yesterday.

Dr. J. B. Fearn, who has been on Home leave in Europe and America, has reserved passage on the Empress of Russia, which is due in Shanghai on September 4.

Mr. A. Crawley, Assistant Naval Store Officer, now serving at H.M. Dockyard, Sheerness, has been appointed to Singapore for duty at the R.N. Fuel and Store Depot.

Among the passengers who arrived by the s.s. Arafura from Australia yesterday were Lady Cruise and Rear-Admiral Sir Guy Gaunt, M.P., who came from Sydney to Hongkong.

Miss M. Bernard, Paris; and Mrs. W. P. R. Harrison, from Manchester, were passengers on the President Lincoln which arrived yesterday. Mr. and Mrs. Roberts Dollar travelled with the boat as far as Shanghai.

News has reached the Colony of the death of Mr George Willis, a former Inspector of the Hongkong Police Force, at his residence, Heathfield Avenue, Dover, Joining the Force in October, 1902, he rose to the rank of Inspector two years before his retirement on pension in August, 1923. Mr. Willis was 57 years old at the time of his death and is survived by a widow and six children.

The Bishop of Victoria and Mrs. Duppy expect to be absent from the Colony from June 11 to the early part of September. The Bishop is visiting Pakhol, Limchow and Yunnanfu for confarms and other work. During his absence the Rev. C. B. Shann, St. John's Hall, University of Hongkong, will be in charge of the Bishop's correspondence.

St. Andrew's Cathedral, Singapore, has been the scene of a very pretty and interesting wedding. The contracting parties were two well-known members of the American community of Singapore, the bridegroom being Mr. John Byron Ingle, of California, director of the Orient Company, Ltd., and the bride, Miss Ethil Rassala Garer Waterhouse, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Fred E. P. Waterhouse.

Mr. A. Dyer Ball returned to the Colony by the -Kashimir yesterday.

Mr. H. L. Pearce of the “North-China Daily News” staff is in the General Hospital suffering from pneumonia.

A crowd of rowdy students including—boys—and girls, and augmented by a number of men and women, demonstrated before the C.M.S. Hospital in Hangchow on June 3 and tore down the Union Jack flag which was flying in honour of the King's birthday. It is to this hospital that Dr. H. G. Thompson, brother of Mrs. Lindsey, Kowloon, has been appointed.

The following tribute to Mrs. Fenton appears in the current issue of the Hongkong University Union Magazine: — Mrs. Fenton has always been a popular figure in the University and has rendered pronounced services. Not long ago, she was the guardian of the Union's piano floral decorations, and other properties, and she always gave the Union a smart appearance. Lately, she was kind enough to act as Hostess at the Eliot Hall. "At Home" For the players she made the pretty costumes, but she did greater service by encouraging them in her own charming and sympathetic way,

The following seems a tribute to Mr. A. H. Barlow, Manager of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation:—The home papers publish the portrait of Sir Frank Nelson, M.P. for Stroud, as among the early arrivals at the House of Commons to hear Mr. Churchill's Budget speech. Sir Frank is the only Bangkok man in the House, says the "Bangkok Times." He was a young man in the Hongkong Bank away back in 1906 to 1910, under Mr. A. H. Barlow. He was then a bachelor, with a taste for amateur theatricals and lawn tennis. On his first leave he got married and was transferred to Bombay. He left the Bank's service and saw his future in the cotton market. In the course of time he became chairman of the Bombay Chamber of Commerce and his services in that position brought him in due time his neighborhood. Sir Frank in a letter recently acknowledged under Mr. A. E. Barlow's train when while in great use in the attributed his later successful career.

Mr. B. M. Ede, son of the late Mr. Montague Ede, arrived in the Colony yesterday by the Kashimir.

Sir Walter Gilbey, at New-market, presented Mr. Richard Marsh, the former King's trainer, with a cheque for £23,435 and an album containing the subscribers' names, but not the amounts subscribed, as a mark of appreciation of his career as trainer for fifty years at Newmarket.

Lieutenant-Colonel John C. Faunthorpe, C.B.E., M.C., V.D., A.D.C., of the Southern Regiment of the United Provinces Horse at Cawnpore, is to compete at the N.R.A. meeting at Bisley in July. This officer, who has been commanding the Auxiliary Force at Lucknow, is a well-known big game and sporting rifle marksman. He captained the British team which competed at the Olympic Games in France last year. He has shot for India with the Service rifle and is the 1924 champion at the Running Deer Singles.

The University Council at its meeting on May 21, accepted with regret the resignation of Professor R. K. M. Simpson from the post of Associate Editor of the Union Magazine. The Vice Chancellor duly appointed Mr. George Keeton to the post. The Council on March 31 appointed Mr. Ong Chong-keng to succeed Mr. M. B. Osman as Editor of the English Section of the Magazine, and Mr. Lau Mo-tsung as Editor of the Chinese Section of the Magazine. Mr. Lau subsequently tendered his resignation, and the post was filled by Mr. Lee Pak-hung, who was appointed on June 2.

They will want to bring actions, get damages, and put them into their own pockets. The equality of the sexes demands this change in the law."

The Lord Chancellor, Lord Cave, replying for the Government, said that the old rule that a husband might beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb had gradually disappeared, but another injustice had been caused by the retention of the liability of the husband. If the husband was liable for his wife's torts, at all events in times past he had her money, but to-day the law was that no part of the woman's property went to the husband on marriage. It was an unjust state of things.

"We have heard much of the rights of wives," concluded Lord Cave, "but I think in this case we ought to consider the rights of husbands." The Government proposed at a convenient time to introduce legislation, to remove this grievance, but it might not be possible to find time during the present session.

headline: BOYCOTT IDEA.
text:
TIMES' URGES EXPERT REPORT.

Drawing attention to a "most damaging" weapon," namely, the boycott of British goods in China, the "Times," in a leader, says it is maintained by an idea or obsession, and a definite object of British policy should be to dispel the obsession by all possible means. It urges the Government to send out to China, simply to investigate and report, a very competent expert on Chinese affairs.

headline: CORRESPONDENCE.
text:
To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—Arising our our murder trials in the Supreme Court this week, it strikes me as rather astonishing to find that very little or no interest is being taken by the public when these criminal trials come up for judgment. I was a spectator in both of the trials and noted that in the first case which two Indian guards stood their trial for the murder of another guard, there was only a fair number of their class as spectators, while in the second case when a Chinese stood his trial for the murder of an Indian policeman, neither Chinese nor Indians were in Court at all, those present were only witnesses and Police officers. I raise this matter because there is importance attached as far as our Jury System is concerned. I would strongly advise those who are Jurors and especially those who have not been called for at any time, that they should not ignore the seriousness of their duty. They must not wait till called to know the procedure of their duty in Court. A man cannot possibly claim that he knows everything, and here I think I am in a safe position to refer to that well-known old saying that “a little knowledge is a dangerous thing,” and my sympathy will not be extended to those who have no knowledge at all of a subject when full liberty is at their disposal to acquaint themselves of. I was more than satisfied to find that in both of the trials the foreman of the jury in each case asked questions. In my opinion, I should say that it is indeed essential, as after all a Jury has as much right as the presiding judge to cross-examine when evidence is not satisfying. When I raised the question of Jury Reform in your columns of last year, you also had remarks made on the subject and you referred to the utter silence of jurymen during proceedings, but it is now pleasing to note that a fault has been corrected and it is to be hoped that for the sake of upholding the true characteristics of British law and order, a foreman of jury should not fail to ask questions when the duty calls there is another question which I should like to take up and that is the privilege that should be accorded to prisoners on trial—a seat in the dock even during the proceedings. The Court does not sit for a matter of an hour or two and to see a prisoner standing up all the while for days does arouse my sympathy, if not others. We know what mercy is and it is only right that we should act upon it. Even God's mercy is solicited by the Judge for a murderer. That can rightly be said of what the true version of British Justice is. Jurors, see that the right course is to be taken!

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / COLLEGE ATHLETICS.
text:
Domination by athletics of the activities of American colleges and universities was deplored by Dr. Henry S. Pritchett, president of the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, in his "annual report" just made public.

Dr. Pritchett expressed hope for educational development in the United States. "Whatever may be the weakness in our American system of education," he said in the report, "there is sincere ground for the belief that our people will find their way to a system of schools that will make for good citizenship and that will promote a high quality of human life." Discussing college athletics, he said:—

To-day the outside activities of the college overshadow and run counter to the intellectual life. Athletics, in large measure professional in its methods and organization, fills a larger place in the eyes of students and even of the public than any other one interest.

"No scholar "in the undergraduate life of one of our universities or colleges would expect to receive the recognition or appreciation given to a successful football player." A dozen new activities call for the time and energy of the students. The college is no longer distinctively an intellectual agency.

“No reasonable man will object to the employment of these activities—for example, athletics—in their due perspective. But when they are allowed to dominate the intellectual life of the colleges they become abuses. The paid coach, the professional organization of college athletics, the demoralization of students by participation in the use of extravagant sums of money, constitute a reproach to American colleges and to those who govern them.” He asserted that schools and colleges, to-day pretended, to do far more than they actually accomplished. “The one sure way of progress,” he continued, “is to follow the path of intellectual sincerity, and to go only so far and so fast as we can go with certainty.”

“The test of intellectual sincerity is the one by which our overloaded educational machinery is to be simplified. The school is primarily an intellectual agency. Intellectual sincerity is the ideal by which its course must be determined.”

headline: PRAISE NON PBLKY.
text:
'Solay Plexus,' writing in the Sydney Referee, has a good word for Young Pelky. He says: After watching his smashing methods against Bill Thurbon (who was knocked out in the tenth round). I aim confident that with an ounce of confidence and a little more polish to his boxing Tomario Pelky would be the most formidable lightweight seen in Australia for many day. Were he to make more use of his left in jabbing and shorten up his right he would be right there. In the gymnasium he is a champion, and it does not matter who his sparring partner may be. But the glare of the footlights and the crowd flurries him. "Pelky is quick to learn anything shown him by his manager Baillieu and puts it into practice," but at this stage only in private. He is exceptionally tall; has no longer reach than most 9.9 men and can hit with the weight of many in good middleweight."

After a long and very successful career as lightweight champion of Australia, Sid Golfrey had to unclnowledge defeat at the hands of the tough and strong Harry Collins at the Sydney Stadium on April 11. A perfect right to the point put Golfrey down for the count in the tenth round.

The contest is described as the best seen in Sydney for a long time. With hanging on eliminated it was all fight, fast and furious, with victory to the fittest and best man. The man who had tried to win in every one of his hundred and more fights, and succeeded in 96. percent. of them, was forced to strike his colours to a more youthful and better conditioned opponent, who fought a better and more crafty fight than ever before.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / SOME HOSPITAL EXPERIENCES.
text:
Phil Scott, the English heavy-weight boxer, in the opinion of the secretary of the Middlesex Hospital, "one of the finest specimens of manhood in the country," acted recently as a model for the anatomy class at the hospital. He was also the subject of a number of medical tests. His costume consisted of a pair of boxing shorts. He stood on a table in the theatre like class-room, very much as a model would pose for an artist. With his body tanned a light mahogany shade, and with the muscles rippling beneath a satin-like skin, he looked as fit as it is possible for an athlete to be. "A minor edition of Hercules" and "a muscular Apollo" were two of the descriptions applied to Scott by the students.

Armed with a long pointer, the professor indicated the points which he was describing by touching them with his wand as a teacher in a geography class indicates points on a map.

The two central figures were a curiously contrasted couple—Scott big and powerful and the professor small and looking very scholarly in his eye-glasses and long white operating gown. Scott fell into the different poses with perfect self-possession. Often he appeared very much like a figure in a Parthenon Frieze. A grim little touch was provided by the bones which lay on the tall desk behind the table. During most of the time the lecturer stood clutching one in his left hand—seeming to draw some inspiration from its "feel."

A certain amount of dry humour relieved the lecture. Once in demonstrating the muscles of the arm, the professor, commenting on the fact that one was not well marked, said in a matter of fact tone. "With all due deference to this gentleman I have better marked muscles than he has."

This was received by the students with roars of laughter and cheers. Scott afterwards said that he quite enjoyed the experience. "It was very interesting," he said, "and I have picked up certain little things in anatomy which will help me in boxing.

"I have had two courses of first-aid training," so I followed a little of what was being explained."

"The professor remarked on certain of my muscles not being well marked, but, of course, these are intentionally covered in fat for protection in the ring."

After the demonstration to the students, Scott went through many of the hospital departments and underwent a number of examinations. His blood pressure, breathing and eye-sight were all tested, and various "reactions" recorded. One of the tests included a sprint round the hospital garden.

headline: SUCCESSFUL EFFORT AT THE UNIVERSITY. / TODAY
text:
From three p.m. to ten p.m. are very comprehensive hours, but the whole time would well be spent at the bazaar at the University, inspecting stalls stocked with a choice variety of goods and enjoying the excellent variety of games and competitions.

That, at any rate, was apparently the opinion of those attending the initial day's proceedings yesterday which were opened by Sir Claud Severn who reminded his hearers that the proceeds were to go to the Building Fund of St. Stephen's College. A site had been granted at Stanley on condition that a certain amount was raised in a given period. A large amount had been raised but a lot still remained to be secured. In formally declaring the bazaar open Sir Claud Severn congratulated all who were instrumental in decorating and arranging the various stalls and anticipated that the function would realise quite a large sum for the building fund.

The Principal of the College, the Rev. W. H. Hewitt, responded on behalf of the students and Mr. Li Chor-chi, an old boy and secretary of the Bazaar Committee of the College, presented Sir Claud with a Chinese engraving on glass as a memento of the occasion.

Sir Henry Pollock presided over the opening ceremony, among others present being Lady Pollock, Mr. E. B. C. Hornell and Mr. W. L. Pattenden.

Quite a brisk business was done at the stalls, most of which were under the superintendence of separate College forms but there is much yet left for intending purchasers this afternoon. The articles are useful and ornamental suitable for use in the home or for curios to be sent to friends.

On the tennis courts are competitions of all kinds and a sliding shoot, but most popular of all are shooting ranges with miniature rifles, in connection with all of which prizes are to be won. In convenient corners are to be found drink and refreshment stalls and sit down teas may be obtained at any time. This and all arrangements for refreshments are in the hands of ladies from St. Stephen's Girls' School who were also responsible for the provision of the good sold.

The services of talented amateur performers had been obtained for a concert held in the evening together with a cinema entertainment which proved a great success. Evening performances are also promised for to-night.

headline: PRISON FOR MOTORIST. / CONVICTED OF WANTON DRIVING.
text:
MAGISTRATES SERIOUS VIEW

Convicted of driving wantonly and furiously outside Repulse Bay Hotel, Mr. Howard T. Werschkul, a young American flour merchant, was yesterday sentenced by Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy to two month's hard labour.

On June 6, a car driven by the defendant knocked down and seriously injured an Indian watchman in the employ of the Hotels Company.

After Mr. Laitle, one of the occupants of the car, had given evidence at the continued hearing yesterday afternoon, Mr. M. H. Turner who appeared for the defence, addressed the Bench and said that the sum and substance of the contentions of the prosecution was that the defendant had driven round the entrance to the Hotel for a joy ride and then went round again. He would submit that the evidence was not definite and that the car had been up the delivery path.

The Magistrate interposed that he was satisfied that this was what actually had taken place. O) the question of speed, Mr. Turner commented that it was impossible to drive at more than 15 miles an hour along the drive passing the hotel after turning round the corner from the delivery entrance. Regarding the striking of the Indian watchman by the car, Mr. Turner said that before His Worship could believe the defendant saw the Indian he would have to come to the conclusion that he deliberately told the occupants lies when he felt the bump and when they asked what had happened.

Finally, Mr. Turner said that he agreed that defendant should not have gone past the Hotel at the speed he did but he could not agree that the driving of the car was wanton and furious. On the question of compensation his client was willing to pay.

In passing sentence the Magistrate said it was necessary for him to take a serious view of any such case that came before him. He could not do less than pass that sentence. He agreed that the defendant did not see the Indian and said that he was taking into consideration all the points raised by Mr. Turner.

The prosecution throughout was conducted by Inspector Kent.

Mr. Teh. Yok-chee Nethersole Hospital, and Mr. Teo Kah-tok, Government Civil Hospital, both of Hongkong University, have been admitted to practise medicine in the Colony.

headline: SERIOUS CHARGE. / SOLDIER WITH BAD RECORD
text:
Private George Francis Webb, of the 1st. Battalion East Surrey Regiment, pleaded guilty at a court martial yesterday to having deserted and taken with him to Canton-three. Webly revolvers. He was arrested in Canton by a Shameen police officer on March 13.

headline: A WAR DISCLOSURE.
text:
GERMAN THREAT TO INVADE AUSTRIA.

How Germany nearly added one of its own Allies to the countries already bringing against it in the World War is revealed by Dr. Otto Elover, the Austrian Socialist leader and Foreign Secretary in the first Republican Government, in his just-published book, "The Austrian Revolution" (Teomird Pursons, 10s. 6d.).

On the thesis that the whole modern history of German Austria is coloured by the opposition between German and Austrian mentalities, Dr. Bauer argues that this antagonism was only neutralised by the fact that, from 1897 onwards, Austrian patriotism saw its Empire threatened by the financing agitation of the Slav races within its frontiers.

How artificial was the apparent resulting unity, and how fundamentally different the outlook of German and Austrian, was clearly shown in January 1918, when, following the Brest-Litovsk Treaty, the Austrian people demonstrated against the continuance of the war against Russia to fulfil that Treaty, and, by a great general strike in Vienna, presaged a revolution that would enforce peace.

headline: BOOKS
text:
RAMSAY'S RAMBLINGS

EX-PREMIER'S TRAVEL

"The wanderlust is perhaps the most precious of all the troublesome appetites of the soul of man. It makes him keep in his cupboard a friendly old suit of comfortable wear that has paled under the fervent eyes of the sun and been matured by dust and mud and rain, and with that a pair of honest boots, nailed like the oak door of an ancient keep, which of themselves direct one's way of'er moor and fell and bog and by-path away from the offence and clamour of cars and trains."

—MR. RAMSAY MACDONALD. in Wanderings and Excursions. (Jonathan Cape, 68. net.)

"The ex-Prime Minister gets so much colour and gaiety and romance out of a single drop of ink, when describing his journeys—especially those through the countryside where so much of his youth lies buried—that we are glad he has had a selection made and put forth of his travel papers." says the "Morning Post" in a generous tribute of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's new book, "Wanderings and Excursions."

"The spirit of adventure awakens in him as he passes by Tortuga, the den of the bucaneers, or skirts the coast of Hayti, with its one hero, Toussaint, or sees the unmatched, unearthly blue of the Central American mountains, or enters the decaying, ghost-haunted Halls of Jamaica," adds the "Morning Post." "The past becomes alive again for him as he view the outposts of the Isles of Greece, dim but flushed in the morning light," or visits Constantinople ("The meeting of many waters flowing from the East and the West; the No Man's Land between Europe and Asia, where all men gather"), or reads a Latin epitaph on a gravestone in the museum at Brindisi, or wanders through the Holy Land, every name in which is written on the heart. "But we like him most, he is the best of travel in g-companions, when he roams on shank's nag through his own country and talks with grey-haired derelicts about the wild doings of his boyhood, and surdes uphill to the magic lilt of

'Sure, 'by Tummel and Loch Rannoch and Lochaber I will go, '

y heather trucks wi' heaven their wides.

"As a politician we have no use for him—but as a wayfarer in Broad Scotland we like him fine, and are not afraid to confess it."

"In his sketches, of political activities Mr. MacDonald has a lightness of touch and a humorous outlook which may well surprise the bourgeois reader of this book who has not been accustomed to read his article in Labour publications," says the "Times Literary Supplement."

"His amused contempt for the proceedings of the French Chamber," his racy accounts of the meetings of the Berlin Socialist Conference with its clash between Socialist moderates and Bolshevik extremists, his sober warnings against political violence and legislative over-haste, and his dictum that one of the weakest things in the world is an Act of Parliament which does not embody public opinion, his recognition that in Republican Germany it is the capitalist who has succeeded to the throne of the feudalist and that German capitalism is now more strongly entrenched than ever, will all seem very strange to the average political opponent in this country, who has been apt to judge Mr. MacDonald rather from his own party posters and headlines in his own morning newspaper."

headline: JOHN KEATS.
text:
What is most striking about Keats in all the matters and relations of life is the richness and splendour of imagination with which he transfused and interpenetrated even the commonest things. All readers of his poetry are familiar with this quality, and the poetry would apply suffice to illustrate it. But his letters are at once less known and more personal, and the glow and glamour of imagination, touches them everywhere as it does the poems. Often in the middle of a letter he burst right into verse. Or he brings in his memories of Shakespeare and other poets till it is difficult to tell where they end and he begins. He himself marks this element of his correspondence and enlarges upon its delightfully: "If I scribble long letters I must play my vagaries—I must be too heavy, or too light, for whole pages—I must be quaint and free of tropes and figures—I must play my draughts as I please; and for my advantage and your erudition, crown a white with a black, or a black with a white, and move into black or white, far and near as I please."

"Bare Souls": Critical Portraits, by GAMALIEL BRADFORD, 128. 6d.

headline: Motor Traffic Advanced
text:
On the credit side there is painfully little to set, but mention should be made of the development work carried out by Feng Yu-hsiang in the North-West frontier districts, including the roadbed for the projected prolongation of the Suiyuan line to Ninghsia. Actual railway construction has been limited to work in the Lunghai railway and certain extensions of the Manchurian system, but the building of roads for motor traffic has advanced considerably in various parts of the country. The Customs administration has, as in the past, remained happily immune from the effects of civil disturbance, except to the extent of a large diminution of revenue during the summer months from the check to trade caused by political strikes and boycotta.

I must now turn to the anti-foreign movement which has been so momentous a feature of 1925. It is unnecessary to refer to the events leading to the outburst of June. I should like, however, to remark in this connection that the charges of exploitation of Chinese labour by foreign employers are thoroughly dealt with in the papers published by H.M. Government showing that foreign-controlled factories compare well with Chinese, and that both our own authorities and the municipal government of the Shanghai international settlement had been keenly concerned for some time past with practical steps for improving labours conditions.

In its early phases the movement threatened the safety of foreign lives and property at various points in China. From an agitation set on foot by students, it rapidly developed into riots in foreign concessions, organized strikes and boycotts, attacks all foreign institutions, hostile mob demonstrations and virulent press abuse combined with a strong propaganda in favour of the abolition of the socialist equal treaties. The British were the chief object of attack owing to no doubt, to our leading position in Shanghai where

the trouble had taken its start, and to Great Britain's historical connection with the origin of foreign privilege in China. On the part of the officials very little was done in most places to hold the extremists in check, and the agitation was left in the main to run its own course. The economic effects of the movement were felt most acutely at Shanghai and the South China ports.

headline: Foreign Powers' Sympathy.
text: The events of the summer have proved the growing political power of the national movement in China. In spite of the lamentable record of the last few months, one cannot but feel that this movement, if the patriotism which its supporters profess is genuine, should have in it the seeds of what the country urgently needs, namely, an organised public opinion among the educated classes, which would break the back of the present system of militantism. For the moment the excitement, engendered by the unfortunate "Shanghai affair," and the instigation of Balsheyist agents, backed by Balshevist money, have shaped the movement into a blind, crusade against the foreigner and foreign rights in China. It is reasonable, however, to hope that a sober view of the facts will in time prevail. The partisans of the movement have now tangible proof that their legitimate aspirations for bettering the international status of their country have the sympathy of the foreign Powers, and that the latter are ready to take practical steps in this direction, so far as conditions admit. It cannot, then, but be obvious that the general obstacle lies in the internate state of China, which at present fails to provide the most ordinary guarantees of order, justice and safety of person and property. Realising this, may they find the courage to attack the root of the evil and attempt to rid China of the military despotism, which is blocking all progress and steadily ruining the country. Of the Tariff Conference, which assembled in Peking at the end of last October, it is yet too early to say very much.

text:

The prosperity arising from the successful export trade of the country induced a corresponding increase in the demand for imports. Trade conditions in the Islands may be said to be good and the prospects for 1926 promising. It is largely owing to their loyal support and hard work at the head office and all branches that our chief manager has been able to carry out his policy, which during a period of unprecedented difficulties, especially in the Far East, has enabled us to put before you such fine results for the year 1925. I now beg to propose the adoption of the report and statement of accounts. After the proposal has been seconded and before placing the motion before the meeting, I shall be pleased to answer to the best of my ability any questions which shareholders may have to ask.

On rising to second Mr. D. J. Lewis said: — Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, — We have already observed from the telegrams which have appeared in the local press of the deep interest taken by financial circles in London in the preliminary announcement which was made by our directors before the balance sheet itself was published and I venture to think that our chairman's speech today will evoke greater world-wide interest than ever before in the history of the corporation.

For many years past it has unfortunately been necessary for the time being to refer to the political unrest, to the wars and rumours of war in China, and to the exploitation of the provinces by successive warlords. The past year has probably been the worst within the experience of any of us here present. All the usual troubles prevail and in addition the outbreak of anti-foreign and particularly anti-British feeling has added to our difficulties.

It may be as our chairman has stated, that this outburst is partly due to a growing spirit of nationalism amongst certain sections of the Chinese nation, but it is most certainly largely fostered by Bolshevik emissaries who can only attain their own ends through others' misfortunes.

It has often been stated that a nation has the Government which it deserves. This is certainly not the case in China. We know that the bulk of the Chinese people are cultured, industrious, and peccating, but the various Governments foisted upon them are self-elected, and self-imposed, totally self-interested and in no way representative of the people whom they oppress, whilst professing to govern.

headline: Spirit of NationaHsm:
text:
"It is to be hoped that this growing spirit of nationalism will soon cease to vent itself in antagonism to foreigners who like ourselves are well disposed towards China, but will be devoted to establishing a really representative stable and honest Chinese Government." With regard to our own local conditions we fully agree with the chairman's remark that "Canton is no more entirely independent of Hongkong than Hongkong is entirely dependent on Canton," and if the hot heads in Canton think that they can ruin Hongkong they will soon find that they are badly mistaken.

The idea of converting either Canton or Whampoa into a deep sea port and thereby depriving Hongkong of its natural importance is no new one, and in this connection I might remind you of the views of the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang expressed at the annual meeting in 1923 when he said "no development of trade facilities at Canton can in the long run be detrimental to this Colony, and our Chinese friends can be assured that British policy in this matter is bounded by no such narrow outlook as that attributed to it."

It goes without saying that considerable loss has been inflicted on the Colony by the boycott, which has flagrantly violated all treaty rights, but the greatest injury has been done to Chinese themselves. I am confident that the good sense of the bulk of the Chinese people will in due time prevail and that normal friendly relations between Hongkong and Canton will be restored.

The get back at present suffered will then speedily be made good and prosperity will return to this Colony which has unquestionably a great future before it. “Eminently Satisfactory.” In view of the fact that the Corporation's most important field of operations in China, and bearing in mind the abnormally treubious year through which we have passed, I think you will agree with me that the balance sheet placed before us is eminently satisfactory, and that our heartiest congratulations on the splendid year's working are due to the directors, the chief manager and his staff. The stability of the Bank should give pauses to those who think that they can rule British commerce and

the fortunes of this Colony, and give heart to all of us, who what ever troubles may be in front of us are prepared and determined to face them. We are so close to the events happening around us that we are somewhat apt to be obsessed by them.

It is therefore very pleasing to learn from our chairman of the substantial prosperity now being enjoyed in the Straits Settlements after a period of great depression; that our Japanese friends are recovering from the disastrous effects of the earthquake; and that the Philippine Islands are enjoying increased prosperity. I think it is not too much to hope that there long Hongkong will again be enjoying its fair share of good fortune.

Ladies and gentlemen, we are all very proud of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. Incorporated here some sixty years ago by the foresight of our predecessors, built up under the wise guidance of its directors, by the genius of successive chief managers, the Bank has grown to its present commanding position. But the wisdom and foresight of those who have guided its fortunes could not have led it to the position that it holds to day had it not been for the whole named service of an able, loyal and devoted staff. We owe a great deal to the present staff and I all sure you will fully concur in all that the chairman has said of them and will heartily note them the suggested bonus which they so well deserve. Mr. Chairman, I now bag to second the adoption of the reports and accounts, which have been placed before us.

headline: BOLSHIE PLANS.
text:
The Bolsheviks are apparently in no way discouraged by the failure of their attempts to provoke revolutions in Germany, Bulgaria, and Estonia, according to Mr. Zinovieff.

In addressing the sixth Congress of the Communist International at Moscow, he said that although the situation in the Balkans was apparently stabilized, he still hopefully regarded them as a source of pregnant and sudden happenings, which might be fatal to capitalism. Europe held first place in the International's plans for a world revolution, the East second, and America third.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text:
In England Cabinet Ministers cannot afford to keep motor cars. In America, thanks in the main to the enterprise of Mr. Henry Ford, a car is regarded as an essential perquisite to the normal working household. Professors and students, typlits and bricklayers, the humblest operative as well as the wealthiest millionaire owns, or appears to own, a car. Little children drive about in toy automobiles. In Los Angeles there is a car to every four persons, children included. When winter comes the roads of Florida are black not only with the automobiles of the wealthy in search of change and sunshine, but also with the Ford cars of the working men. American civilisation is on wheels.—The Rt. Hon. H. A. L. Fisher in "Scribner's Magazine."

That old Joko about Scotsmen preferring church services by radio because there is no collection plate attached there, will have to be discarded according to officials of the Canadian National Railways (reports the "Canadian National Railways Magazine.") William Stapleton, district passenger agent at Saskatoon, has wired headquarters, that when the Continental Limited, a radio-equipped train on the Canadian National system, was approaching one Sunday morning recently, the operator received the service from Westminster Presbyterian Church, in that city. The sermon of the Rev. George A. Dixon, of Knox Church, Calgary, so delighted the passengers in the radio observation car that a collection was taken up which was handed to the minister of Westminster Church when the train reached Saskatoon shortly after noon.

headline: “BELL BOY 13.” / QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text:
Once in a while a strikes upon the happy combination of having comedy situations worked out by real comedians. In "Bell Boy 13" the story does not rely upon beautiful scenery or gripping drama to carry it; there is comedy, romance, thrills and more comedy.

The plot spins about an uncle who disinherits his nephew because he does not wish him to marry the girl he loves. Then there is the elopement which is in- tercepted by the same uncle just in time to have the girl go on the honeymoon alone; the boy's following of his love, his finding her only to learn that she will not marry him without his uncle's consent and his disinheritance. When he does a bell hop's uniform, however, he turns the tables in such a manner that the boy soon has his poor uncle begging for mercy. The players seem to thoroughly enjoy convulsing the audience. Douglas MacLean's portrayal is one of the funniest of his career. He has a great many splendid comedy characterifications to his credit, but the part of the boy in "Bell Boy is" gives him an opportunity for the sort of fun making at which he skines.

text:

The monocle habit is growing among the suingled sex. The other night at a crowded London night-club no fewer than four ladies were thus adorned, each looking very uncomfortable and obviously afraid that the thing might fall out at any moment. The female eye would appear to be ill adapted to this form of vanity, to which even horn-rimmed spectacles are preferable.

A protest is being raised in the Paris Press against smoking by women in the streets. "After the theatre," expostulates one writer, "it has become an ordinary sight to see a woman produce her cigarette and puff away as she strolls homeward, just like the men. It is mostly foreign women, however, who set this far from graceful example, and we hope they will not find many followers among their French sisters."

The Prince of Wales did not suffer from lack of exercise during his voyage to South Africa. The squash racquet court with its glass roof which he had on the Renown had been moved to the Repulse, and put up at the side of the main deck. It is fitted with electric light, so the Prince can play after dark if his energy so move him. By the Prince's particular desire a billiard table had been installed on board. But the waves and the wind surely had a good deal to say as to its use.

In recent photographs of Princess Mary appearing at public functions, she is shown umbrellaless. Formerly the umbrella was a prominent feature in every photograph of the kind. It was a matter for much chaff amongst her brothers. The Prince of Wales once said, "When Mary is opening a bazaar or a hospital she clings to her umbrella like a drowning can to a straw. First you see the umbrella; then you see Mary." But now the umbrella seems to have disappeared. But why? Has Lord Lascelles said something?

That there is little new under the sun, even with regard to women's fashions, was pointed out by Ethert Brand, curator of the museum at Rotherham in the course of a recent lecture. Referring to an illustration of women dancers on the walls of a Spanish cave, he said these: palaeolithic belles were very near to the present day women with their high hats, chignous, tight waists and bell-shaped skirts. These cave pictures were probably the earliest fashion plates in the world, and were drawn about 20,000 years ago, declared Mr. Brand. Another illustration from Spain showed a costume very much akin to that of the modern flapper.

The greatest interest is taken in Dublin in the manner in which Joseph Devlin's victory in the elections has just been celebrated in Belfast. The proceedings took the form of a huge torchlight procession through west Belfast, the Nationalist stronghold. Electrically illuminated signs, arches and scrolls festooned the streets, great bonfires were lit at the street corners, the flames of which rose upward 20 feet in many cases. The flags, festoons and general decorations took the form of combined green and orange colours. If anyone before the war had said that such a thing would ever be possible, he would have been derided, for in those days the two colours were always a mark or symbol of rivalry and too often of violent hostility. The long procession having wound its way through the chief thoroughfares finished in Smithfield Square where a public meeting was held at which Mr. Devlin said he thanked the people from the depth of his heart for having placed him, not merely at the head of the poll, but so far ahead of the others. His grateful thanks were due, he said, to the many Protestant professional and commercial men who were among the 5,000 Protestant voters whose suffrage he had received. He desired to emphasize this indebtedness. All his energy and labour would be given to fostering good relations between the two communities and to helping toward an improvement in the condition of the workers.

headline: NOTICE / THE HONGKONG & WHAMPOA DOCK CO.,LTD.
text:
NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that an Extraordinary General Meeting of the above Company will be held at the Registered Office of the Company, Queen's Building, Victoria, Hongkong, on MONDAY, the 18th day of May, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon when the subjoined Resolutions will be proposed as Extraordinary Resolutions, viz.:—

(1) That the Articles of Association of the Company be altered in manner following that is to say by the deletion of Article 17 and by the substitution therefor of the following Article, name-ly:—

“17. So long as the issued capital of the Company shall not exceed $6,000,000,” no member shall be entitled “to be registered as the “holder of more than 8,000 “shares” cf the Company.” Should the issued capital of “the Company be increased,” beyond $6,000,000 the “number of shares in respect of which a member “shall be entitled to be “registered shall be increased,” “ed proportionately, but no “member shall be entitled “to be registered in respect of a fraction of a share.”

(2) That the authorised Capital of the Company (which is now $3,000,000 consisting of 60,000 shares of the nominal value of $50 each the whole of which have been issued) be increased to $10,000,000 by the creation of 140,000 additional shares of the nominal value of $50 each ranking (subject as hereinafter mentioned). for dividend and in all other respects pari passu with the shares constituting the Company's present issued Capital.

(3) That 60,000 of the said 140,000 new shares be offered in the first instance (in the proportion of one new share for every old share held by them respectively) to the members of the Company who on the 10th day of June, 1925, are registered in the Company's Share Register as the holders of the said 60,000 old shares at a premium of $10 per share.

(4) That the aforesaid offer be made to members by notice specifying the number of new shares to which a member is entitled. That a member whose registered address is situate in the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $30 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of July, 1925, and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of October, 1925, and such member or his nominee who has not accepted and lodged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due before the 15th day of July, 1925, will be deemed to have declined. That a member whose registered address is situate outside the Far East or his nominee shall pay for such new shares accepted by two instalments, i.e., one instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or

before the 15th day or September, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of July, 1925, until the date of receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and a further instalment of $80 per new share to be paid on or before the 15th day of December, 1925, together with interest calculated at the rate of 6 per cent. per annum on the total amount then payable for the period from the 15th day of October, 1925, until the date of actual receipt of payment by the Company's Bankers and such member outside the Far East or his nominee who has not accepted and ledged with the Company's Bankers the first instalment due on such new shares on or before the 15th day of September, 1925, together with interest as aforesaid will be deemed to have declined. The Directors shall have the right to reject any nominee.

(5) That such of the said: 60,000 new shares as shall be accepted by members both in and outside the Far East shall visit the said; 60,000 old shares rank for dividend as from the 15th day of July, 1925; to the extent of one half of the nominal value of such new shares and as from the: 15th day of October, 1925, equally with the said 60,000 old shares.

(6) That any of the said 60,000 new shares which shall not be taken up by the Company's shareholders in manner aforesaid and the remaining 80,000 unissued new shares may be issued and disposed of in such manner at such time or times and upon such terms as to ranking for dividend and otherwise as the Company's Directors shall in their absolute discretion think fit.

AND NOTICE IS HEREBY ALSO GIVEN that a further Extraordinary General Meeting of the Company will be held at its Registered Office aforesaid on TUESDAY, the 2nd day of June, 1925, at 11 o'clock in the forenoon for the purpose of receiving a Report of the proceedings at the above mentioned meeting and confirming, if thought fit; as Special Resolutions the above mentioned Resolutions.

The Transfer Books of the Company will be closed from WEDNESDAY, the 10th day of 1926, to WEDNESDAY, the 17th day of June, 1925 (both days inclusive) during which period no transfer of shares can be registered.

Dated the 4th day of May, 1925. By Order of the Board of Directors, R. M. DYER, Chief Manager.
